To looſe all here at home, poorely to looſe it,
Poorely and pettiſhly, ridiculouſly
To fling away your fortune? where's your wiſdome?
Where's that you govern'd others by, diſcretion?
Do's your Rule laſtly hold upon your ſelfe? fie brother,
How are ye falne? get up into your honour
The top branch of your bravery, and from thence
Looke and lament how little Memnon ſeemes now.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Hum! tis well ſpoken; but do'ſt thou think, young ſcholler
The tongues of Angels from my happineſſe
Could turne the end I aime at? no: they cannot;
This is no booke caſe brother: will ye doe it?
Uſe no more art, I am reſolv'd.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Ye may, ſir
Command me to doe any thing that's honeſt,
And for your noble end: but this it carries.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ye ſhall not be ſo honour'd; live an Aſſe ſtill,
And learne to ſpell for profit: goe, goe ſtudie.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Ye muſt not hold him up ſo, he is loſt then.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Get thee to ſchoole agen, and talke of turnips,
And find the naturall cauſe out, why a dog
Turnes thrice about e're he ly downe: there's learning.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Come, I will doe it now; 'tis brave, I find it,
And now allow the reaſon.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: O doe ye ſo ſir,
Doe ye find it currant?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Yes, yes, excellent.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I told ye.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I was fooliſh: I have here too
The rareſt way to find the truth out; hark ye,
Ye ſhall be rul'd by me.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I will be: but—

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: I reach it,
If the worſt fall, have at the worſt: wee'le both goe
But two dayes, and 'tis thus; ha?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: 'Twill doe well ſo

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Then if not excellent, doe ye conceive it

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.p: 'Twill worke for certaine A bowle ready.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: O 'twill tickle her
And you ſhall know then by a line

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I like it
But let me not be fool'd againe

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Doubt nothing
You doe me wrong then, get ye in there privat
As I have taught ye; Baſta

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.p: Worke (Exit Memnon.)

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I will doe

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Have ye found the cauſe

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Yes, and the ſtraingeſt, Gentlemen,
That ere I heard of, anon ile tell ye; Stremon
Be you ſtill neere him to affect his fancie
And keepe his thoughts off: Let the Foole and Boy
Stay him, they may doe ſome pleaſure too; Eumenes
VVhat if he had a wench, an handſome whore brought
Rarely dreſt up, and taught to ſtate it?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: VVell Sir

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: His cauſe is meerly heat: and made beleeve
It were the Princeſſe mad for him,

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: I thinke
'Twere not amiſſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Cap.
sp.l: And let him kiſſe her

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: VVhat els?

sp.speaker: 2 Cap.
sp.l: Ile be his bawde ant pleaſe you, young and holeſome
I can aſſure ye he ſhall have

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Faith let him

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: A ſhall, I hope 'twill helpe him, walke a little
Ile tell you how his caſe ſtands, and my project
In which you muſt be mourners, but by all meanes
Stir not you from him: Stremon.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.p: On our Lives Sir Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: O y'ar a pretious Man; two daies in towne
And neuer ſee your old friend?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Prithe pardon me

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: And in my conſcience if I had not ſent

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: No more I would a come; I muſt

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: I find ye
God a mercy want ye never care for me
But when your ſlops are emptie

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Nere feare that wench
Shall find good currant coyne ſtill; is this the old houſe?

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Have ye forgot it?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: And the dore ſtill ſtanding
That goes into the Temple?

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Still.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: The Robes to,
That I was wount to ſhift in here?

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: All here ſtill.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: O ye tuff rogue what troubles have I trotted through?
VVhat feares and frights, every poore mouſe a monſter
That I heard ſtir, and every ſtick I trod on
A ſharp ſting to my conſcience

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Las poore conſcience,

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: And all to liquor thy old bootes wench

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Out beaſt!

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: To new carine thy carkas, that's the truth on't
How does thy keele? does it need nayling? a tother
VVhen all thy linnen's up: and a more yare?

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Fye Fye Sir

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Nere ſtem'd the ſtraights?

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: How you talke?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I am old wench,
And talking to an old Man is like a ſtomacher
It keepes his blood warme

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: But; pray tell me

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Any thing

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Where did the boy meet with ye, at a wench ſure,
At one end of a wench, a Cup of wine ſure

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Thou know'ſt I am too honeſt

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: That's your fault
And that the Surgeon knowes

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Then farewell
I will not faile ye ſoone

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Ye ſhall ſtaye Supper
I have ſworne ye ſhall, by this ye ſhall

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I will wench,
But after Supper for an houre, my buſines

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: And but an houre

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: No by this kiſſe, that ended
I will returne and all night in thine Armes wench

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: No more, ile take your meaning; come 'tis Supper time

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Thou art not well

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Your grace ſees more a great deale
Then I feele (yet I lye) o brother •

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Marke her,
Is not the quicknes of her ey conſumed, wench?
The livelye red and white?

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Nay ſhe is much alter'd
That on my underſtanding, all her ſleep's Ladie
Which were as ſound and ſweet

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Pray doe not force me
Good Madam where I am not, to be ill,
Conceit's a double ſicknes; on my faith your highnes
Is meere miſtaken in me A Dead March within of Drum and Sagbutts

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I am glad on't
Yet this I have ever noted when thou waſt thus
It ſtill forerun ſome ſtrange event: my Siſter
Died when thou waſt thus laſt: harke harke ho,
What mournefull noyſe is this comes creeping forward,
Still it growes neerer, neerer, do ye heare it?

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: It ſeemes ſome Souldiers funerall: ſee it enters

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: What may it meane?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: The Gods keep ye faire Calis

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: This man can ſpeake, and well; a ſtands and views us
Woo'd I were nere worſe look't upon: how humbly
His eyes are caſt now to the earth: pray marke him
And marke how rarely he has ranckt his troubles:
See now a weepes, they all weep; a ſweeter ſorrow
I never look't upon nor one that braver
Became his griefe; your will with us.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Great Ladie Plucks out the Cup.
Excellent beauty

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: He ſpeakes handſomelie
What a rare rhetorician his greif plaies,
That ſtop was admirable

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: See ſee thou Princeſſe
Thou great commander of all hearts

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I have found it,
Oh how my ſoule ſhakes:

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: See, ſee the noble hart
Of him that was the nobleſt: ſee and glory
Like the proud God himſelfe in what thou haſt purchas'd
Behold the heart of Memnon: does it ſtart ye?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Good gods, what has his wildenes done?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Looke boldlie
You boldlie ſed you durſt looke wretched woman,
Nay flie not back faire follie, 'tis too late now
Vertue and blooming honour bleed to death here,
Take it the Legacie of Love bequeath'd ye,
Of cruell Love, a cruell Legacie;
What was the will that wrought it? then can ye weepe?
Imbalme it in your trueſt teares?
If Women can weepe a truth, or ever ſorrow ſunck yet
Into the ſoule of your ſex, for 'tis a Jewell
The VVorlds worth cannot weigh downe,
Take it Ladie; And with it all (I dare not curſe) my ſorrowes
And may they turne to Serpents.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: How ſhe lookes
Still upon him: ſee now a teare ſteales from her

sp.speaker: 2. Cap.
sp.l: But ſtill ſhe keepes her ey firme

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Next read this,
But ſince I ſee your ſpirit ſomewhat troubled
Ile doe it for ye

sp.speaker: 2. Cap.
sp.p:
Still ſhe eyes him mainlie
Goe happy heart for thou ſhalt ly
Intomb'd in her for whom I dy
Example of her cruelty.
Tell her if ſhe chance to chide
Me for ſlownes in her pride
That it was for her I died.
If a teare eſcape her eye
'Tis not for my memory.
But thy rights of obſequy
The Altar was my loving breſt
My heart the ſacrificed beaſt
And I was my ſelfe the Preiſt
Your body was the ſacred ſhrine
Your cruell mind the power divine
Pleas'd with hearts of men not kine

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Now it poures downe

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I like it rarelie Ladie

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: How greedily ſhe ſwallowes up his language?

sp.speaker: 2. Cap.
sp.l: Her eye inhabits on him

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Cruell Ladie,
Great as your beautie ſcornefull; had your power
But equall poiſe on all hearts; all hearts periſh't;
But Cupid has more ſhafts then one more flames too
And now he muſt be open ey'd, 'tis Juſtice:
Live to injoye your longing; live and laugh at
The loſſes and the miſeries we ſuffer;
Live to be ſpoken when your crueltie
Has cut of all the vertue from this Kingdome
Turned honour into earth, and faithfull ſervice

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I ſweare his angers excellent

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Truth and moſt tried love
Into diſdaine and downefall,

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Still more pleaſing,

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Live then I ſay famous for civill ſlaughters,
Live and lay out your triumphs, guild your glories
Live and be ſpoken this is ſhe this Ladie,
This goodly Ladie, yet moſt killing beautie;
This with the two edg'd eyes, the heart for hardnes
Out doing rockes; and coldnes, rockes of Chriſtall
This with the ſwelling ſoule, more coye of Courtſhip
Then the proud ſea is when the ſhores embrace him
Live till the mothers find ye; read your ſtory
And ſowe their barren curſes on your beauty,
Till thoſe that have enjoy'd their loves deſpiſe ye,
Till Virgins pray againſt ye, old age find ye
And even as waſted coales glow in their dying
So may the Gods reward ye in your aſhes:
But y'ar the Siſter of my King; more propheſies
Els I ſhould utter of ye true loves and loyall
Bleſſe themſelves ever from ye: ſo I leave ye

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Prithee be angry ſtill young man: good faire Sir
Chide me againe, what woo • d this man doe pleas'd,
That in his paſſions can bewitch ſoules ſtay,

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Upon my life ſhe loves him

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Pray ſtay

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: No

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I doe command ye

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: No, ye cannot Ladie
I have a ſpell againſt yee, Faith and Reaſon,
Yee are to weak to reach me: I have a heart too,
But not for hawkes meat Ladie

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Even for Charity
Leave me not thus aflicted: you can teach me

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: How can you Preach that Charitie to others
That in your owne ſoule are an Athieſt
Beleeving neither power nor feare: I trouble ye,
The Gods be good unto ye.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Amen.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Ladie, She Swounes

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: O royall Madam, Gentlemen for heav'n ſake, They come back.

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: Give her freſh air ſhe comes again: away ſirs
And here ſtand cloſe till we perceive the working

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Ye have undone all

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: So I feare

sp.speaker: 2. Cap.
sp.l: She loves ye

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: And then all hopes loſt this way

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Peace ſhe riſes

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Now for my purpoſe Fortune

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Wher's the Gentleman

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Gone Madam

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Why gone?

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Has diſpatch't his buſines

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: A came to ſpeake with me
A did,

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: A did not

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: For I had many queſtions

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: On my Faith Madam, he
Talk't a great while to ye

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Thou conceiv'ſt not.
He talk't not as he ſhould doo; o my heart
Away with that ſad ſight; didſt thou ere love me?

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Why doe you make that queſtion?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: If thou didſt
Run run wench, run: nay ſee how thou ſtir'ſt

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Whither?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: If 'twer for any thing to pleaſe thy ſelfe
Thou wood'ſt run to'th devill: but I am growne

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Fie Ladie

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I aſke none of your fortunes, nor your loves
None of your bent deſires I ſlack, ye are not
In love with all men, are ye? one for ſhame
You will leave your honour'd miſtris? why doe ye ſtare ſo
What is that ye ſee about mee, tell me;
Lord what am I become? I am not wilde ſure,
Heaven keepe that from me: o Cleanthe help me
Or I am ſuncke to death

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Ye have offended and mightily, love is incenſt againſt yee
And therefore take my Councell, to the Temple
For that's the ſpeedieſt phyſick: before the Goddeſſe
Give your repentant prayers: aske her will
And from the Oracle attend your ſentence
She is milde and mercifull

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: I will: o Venus
Even as thou lov'ſt thy ſelfe!

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.p: Now for my fortune Exeunt Calis and Women.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: What ſhall I doe?

sp.speaker: 1. Cap.
sp.l: VVhy make your ſelfe

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: I dare not,
No Gentlemen, I dare not be a villaine
Though her bright beauty would entice an Angell
I will to'th King my laſt hope: get him a Woman
As we before concluded: and as ye paſſe
Give out the Spartans are in armes; and terrible
And let ſome letters to that end be fain'd too
And ſent to you, ſome Poets too, to the Generall
And let me worke: be nere him ſtill,

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: We will Sir

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Farwell: and pray for all: what 'ere I will ye
Doe it, and hope a faire end

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: The Gods ſpeed ye. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Stremon Foole, Boy, and Servants.

sp.speaker: Servant.
sp.l: He lies quiet

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Let him lye and as I told ye
Make ready for this ſhew: h'as divers times
Been calling upon Orpheus to appeare
And ſhew the joyes: now I wilbe that Orpheus,
And as I play and ſing like beaſts and trees
I woo'd have you ſhapt and enter: thou a Dog, foole,
I have ſent about your ſutes: the Boy a buſh,
An Aſſe you, you a Lion

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: I a dog?
Ile fit you for a Dog. Bow wow

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: 'Tis excellent
Steale in and make no noiſe

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: Bow wow

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Away rogue. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Good ſweet friend be not long

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Thou think'ſt each houre ten
Till I be ferreting

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: You know I love ye

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I will not be above an houre; let thy robe be readie
And the doore be kept Knock.

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Who knocks there? Cleanthe knocks within.
Yet more buſines?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Have ye more penſioners, the Princeſſe woman?
Nay then ile ſtay a little, what games a foote now?

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Now is the time

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: A rancke bawde by this hand, too
She grinds a both ſides: hey boyes

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: How your brother Siphax?
Loves he the Princeſſe?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Deadlie, and you know
He is a Gentleman deſcended noblie.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: But a ranck knave as ever piſt

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: • old Mother
Heres more gold and ſome jewells

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Heres no villany
I am glad I came to'th hearing

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Alas Daughter,
What would ye have me doe?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Hold off ye old whore;
Ther's more gold comming; alls mine, all

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Doe ye ſhrink now,
Did ye not promiſe faithfully and told me
Through any danger?

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Any I can wade through

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Ye ſhall, and eaſilie the ſin not ſeene neither
Heres for a better ſtole and a new vaile mother
Come ye ſhall be my friend: if all hit

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Hang me
Ile make ye richer then the Goddeſſe.

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Say then
I am yours, what muſt I doe?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: I'th morning
But very early, will the Princeſſe viſit
The Temple of the Goddeſſe, being troubled
With ſtrange things that diſtract her: from the Oracle
(Being ſtrongly too in love) ſhe will demand
The Goddeſſe pleaſure, and a Man to cure her,
That Oracle you give: deſcribe my Brother
You know him perfectly.

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: I have ſeene him often

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: And charge her take the next man ſhe ſhall meet with
When ſhe comes out; you underſtand me

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: VVell.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Which ſhalbe he attending; this is all
And eaſily without ſuſpition ended,
Nor none dare diſobey, 'tis Heaven that does it,
And who dares croſſe it then, or once ſuſpect it?
The venture is moſt eaſie.

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: I will doe it.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: As ye ſhall proſper;

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: As I ſhall proſper.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Take this too, and farewell; but firſt harke hither.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: What a young whores this to betray her miſtris?
A thouſand Cuckolds ſhall that husband be,
That marries thee, thou art ſo miſchievous.
Ile put a ſpoke among your wheeles

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Be conſtant

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: 'Tis done

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.p: Ile doe no more at drop ſhot then Exit Chilax.

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Farewell wench. Exeunt Prieſt and Cleanthe

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter a Servant and R. Bax, and Stremon at the doore.

sp.speaker: Servant.
sp.l: A ſtirs a ſtirs

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Let him, I am ready for him,
He ſhall not this day periſh, if his paſſions
May bee fed with Muſick; are they ready

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: All, all: ſee where he comes

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Ile be ſtraight for him. Exit Stremon.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: How ſad he lookes and ſullen. Stand cloſe.
Here are the Captaines: my feares paſt now.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Put caſe i'th other world
She doe not love me neither: I am old 'tis certaine

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: His ſpirit is a little quieter.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: My blood loſt and my limbes ſtif; my embraces
Like the cold ſtubborne ba • kes • hoa • ie and hear • es
My words worſe: my fame only and atcheivements
Which are my ſtrength, my blood, my youth my faſhion,
Muſt woe her, win her, wed her; that's but wind
And Women are not brought to bed with ſhadowes:
I doe her wrong, much wrong; ſhe is young and bleſſed,
Sweet as the ſpring, and as his bloſſomes tender,
And I a nipping north wind, my head • ung
With hailes, and froſtie Iſicles: are the ſoules ſo too
When they depart hence, lame and old, and love les?
No ſure, 'tis ever youth there; Time and Death
Follow our fleſh no more: and that forc'd opinion
That Spirits have no ſexes, I beleive not
There muſt be love, there is love? what art thou.

lg.l: Orpheus, I am come from the deep's below,
To thee fond man the plagues of love to ſhow:
To the faire fields where loves eternall dwell
Ther's none that came, but firſt they paſſe through hell:
Harke and beware unleſſe thou haſt loved ever,
Beloved againe, thou ſhalt ſee thoſe joyes never.
Hark how they graone that dyed deſpairing,
O take heed thou:
Hark how they houle for over daring
All thoſe were men.
They that be fooles, and dye for fame
They looſe their name,
And they that bleed
Harke how they ſpeed.
Now in cold froſts now ſcorching fires,
They ſit and curſe their loſt deſires:
Nor ſhall theſe ſoules be free from paines and feares,
Till Women waſt them over in their teares.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: How ſhould I know my paſſage is deni'de me
Or which of all the Devills dare

sp.speaker: Eumon.
sp.l: This Song
Was rarely formed to fit him.

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: Charon o Charon
Thou wafter of the ſoules to bliſſe or bant

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Who calls the Fery man of Hell?

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Come near
And ſay who lives in joye, and whom in feare.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Thoſe that dye well; Eternall joy ſhall follow,
Thoſe that dye ill; their owne ſoule ſaie ſhall ſwallow.

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: Shall thy black Bark thoſe guilty ſpirits ſtow
That kill themſelves for love?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: O no no.
My cordage crackes when ſuch great ſins are neare
No winde blowes faire, nor I my ſelfe can ſteare

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: What lovers paſſe and in Elizium raigne?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Thoſe gentle loves that are belov'd againe.

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: This Souldier Loves, and faine wood dye to win,
Shall he goe on?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: No 'tis too foule a ſin
He muſt not come a boord: I dare not rowe,
Stormes of deſpaire and guilty blood will blowe.

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: Shall time releaſe him ſaye?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: No, no, no no.
Nor time nor death can alter us, nor prayer;
My boate is de … and who then d • re
But thoſe appointed come aboord Live ſtill,
And love by reaſon mor • all not by will,

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: And when thy Miſtris ſhall cloſe up thine eyes

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Then come a boord and paſſe,

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Till when be wiſe

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Till when be wiſe.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: How ſtill he ſitts: I hope this Song has ſetled him

sp.speaker: 1. Cap.
sp.l: He • ites his lipp, and rowl •• his fierce eyes yet
I feare for all this

sp.speaker: 2. Cap.
sp.l: Stremon ſtill apply to him;

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Give me more roome then, ſweetlie ſtrike divinely
Such ſtraines and old earth moves at

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: The power I have over both Beaſt and plant
Thou man alone feelſt miſerable want Muſic.
Strike your rare Spirits that attend my will,
And looſe your ſavage wildneſſe by my skill.
This Lion was a man of Warre that died,
As thou wouldſt doe to guild her Ladies pride
This Dog a foole that hung himſelfe for love:
This Ape with daily hugging of a glove,
Forgot to eat and died. This goodly tree,
An uſher that ſtill grew before his Ladie,
Wither'd at roote. This, for he could not wooe,
A grumbling Lawyer: This pyed Bird a page,
That melted out becauſe he wanted age.
Still theſe lye houling on the ſtigian ſhore,
O love no more, o love no more.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: He ſteales off ſilently, as though he would ſleep,
No more but all be nere him, feed his fancie
Good Stremon ſtill; this may lock up his follie.
Yet Heaven knowes I muſt feare him; away ſoftly.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: Did I not doe moſt doggedly?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Moſt rarelie?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: Hee's a brave man when ſhall we dog agen;

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Unty me firſt for Gods ſake,

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: Helpe the Boye; hee's in a wood poore child: good honny Stremon
Lets have a beare baiting; ye ſhall ſee me play.
The rareſt for a ſingle Dog: at head all;
And if I doe not win immortall glorie,
Play, Dog play Devill.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Peace for this time,

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: Prithee.
Lets ſing him a blacke Santis, then lets all howle,
In our owne beaſtly voices; tree keepe your time,
Untye there; bow, wow, wow.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: A way ye Aſſe, away,

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: VVhy let us doe ſomething,
To ſatisfie the Gentleman, hee's mad;
A Gentleman like humour and in faſhion,
And muſt have men as mad about him.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Peace
And come in quicklie, 'tis ten to one els
Heel find a ſtaffe to beat a dog; no more words,
Ile get ye all imployment; ſoft ſoft in all, Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: VVhen cameſt thou over wench?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: But now this evening.
And have bin ever ſince looking out Siphax,
Ith' warres he would have lookt me: ſure has gotten
Some other Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: A thouſand wench, a thouſand
They are as common here as Caterpillers
Among the corne, they eat up all the Souldiers,

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Are they ſo hungry? yet by their leave Chilax,
Ile have a ſnatch too.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Doſt thou love him ſtill wench?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Why ſhould I not? he had my Maiden head
And all my youth.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Thou art come the happieſt
In the moſt bleſſed time, ſweet wench the fitteſt,
If thou darſt make thy fortune: by this light Cloe
And ſo ile kiſs thee: and if thou wilt but let me,
For 'tis well worth a kindnes.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: What ſhood I let ye?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Enjoye thy miniken

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Thou art ſtill old Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Still ſtill and ever ſhalbe: if, I ſay,
Thou wo't ſtrike the ſtroke: I cannot doe much harme wench

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Nor much good

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Siphax ſhall be thy Husband,
Thy very Husband woman, thy foole thy Cuckold,
Or what thou wilt make him: I am over joy'd,
Raviſht cleane raviſht with this fortune; kiſs me,
Or I ſhall looſe my ſelf,

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: My Husband ſed ye?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Sed I? and will ſay Cloe; nay and doe it
And doe it home to; Peg thee as cloſe to him
As birdes are with a pinne to one another;
I have it I can doe it: thou wants clothes too,
And heel be hanged unles he marry thee
Ere he maintaine thee: now he has Ladies Courtiers
More then his back can bend at? multitudes
We are taken up for threſhers, will ye bite?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Yes

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: And let me -

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Yes and let ye -

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: What!

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: VVhy that ye wo't of.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: The turne the good turne?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Any turne the Roche turne;

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: That's the right turne for that turnes up the bellie.
I cannot ſtay take your inſtructions
And ſomething toward howſhold, come, what ever
I ſhall adviſe ye follow it exactlie
And keep your times I point ye; for ile tell ye
A ſtrange way you muſt wade through.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Feare not me Sir.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Come then and lets diſpatch this modicum
For I have but an howre to ſtay, a ſhort one
Beſides more water for another mill
An old weake over ſhot I muſt provide for,
Ther's an old Nunnerie at hand.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: VVhat's that

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: A bawdie Houſe.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: A pox conſume it

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: If the ſtones ('tis bui • t on)
Were but as brickle as the fleſh lives in it,
Your curſe came handſomlie: feare not, ther's Ladies,
And other good ſad people: your pinkt Citizens
That thinke no ſhame to ſhake a ſheet there: Come wench

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: A Souldier and ſo fearefull?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Can ye blame me;
VVhen ſuch a waite lies on me?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Fye upon ye
I tell ye, ye ſhall have her: have her ſafelie,
And for your wife with her owne will,

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Good Siſter-

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: What a diſtruſtfull man are you? to morrow,
To morrow morning -

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Is it poſſible?
Can there be ſuch a happines?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Why hang me
If then ye be not married: if to morrow night,
Ye doe not -

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: O deare Siſter -

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: What ye woo'd doe
What ye deſire to doe; lie with her: Devill,
What a dull man are you?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Nay I believe now,
And ſhall ſhe love me?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: As her life and ſtroke ye,

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: O I will be her ſervant,

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: 'Tis your dutie,

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: And ſhe ſhall have her whole will,

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Yes 'tis reaſon,
She is a Princes, and by that rule boundles

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: What wood' you be, for I woo'd have ye Siſter
Chuſe ſome great place about us: as her woman
Is not ſo fit.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: No, no, I ſhall find places:

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: And yet to be a Ladie of her bedchamber,
I hold not ſo fit neither,
Some great title, beleeve it ſhall be look't out.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Ye may a Dutcheſſe
Or ſuch a toye, a ſmall thing pleaſes me Sir

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: What you will Siſter: if a neighbour Prince,
When we ſhall come to raigne -

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: We ſhall thinke on't,
Be ready at the time and in that place too,
And let me worke the reſt, within this half houre;
The Princeſs will be going, 'tis almoſt morning
Away and mind your buſines,

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Fortune bleſſe us. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I doe beſeech your grace to baniſh me.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Why Gentleman is ſhe not worthy marriage?

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: Moſt worthy, Sir, where worth againe ſhall meet her,
But I like thicke clouds ſailing ſlow and heavy,
Although by her drawne higher, yet ſhall hide her
I dare not be a traitor; and 'tis treaſon,
But to imagin: as you love your honour —

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: 'Tis her firſt maiden doting and if croſt,
I know it kills her.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: How knowes your grace ſhe loves him?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Her woman told me all; beſide his ſtory
Her maid Lucippe on what reaſon to,
And tis beyond all but enjoying.

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: Sir.
Even by your wiſedome; by that great diſcretion
Ye owe to rule and order —

sp.speaker: 2 Lord.
sp.l: This man's mad ſure,
To plead againſt his fortune -

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: And the King too,
Willing to have it ſo?

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: By thoſe dead Princes
From whoſe deſcents ye ſtand a ſtarre admired at,
Lay not ſo baſe a lay upon your vertues
Take heed for honours ſake take heed: the bramble
No wiſe man ever planted by the roſe,
It canckers all her beauty; nor the vine
When her full bluſhes courts the ſun dares any
Choke up with wanton Ivy? good my Lords,
Who builds a monument, the Baſis Jaſper,
And the maine body Brick?

sp.speaker: 2 Lord.
sp.l: Ye wrong your worth,
Ye are a Gentleman deſcended nobly.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: In both bloods truly noble.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Say ye were not,
My will can make ye ſo.

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: No, never, never;
'Tis not deſcent, nor will of Princes does it,
'Tis Vertue which I want, 'tis Temperance,
Man, honeſt man is't fit your Majeſty
Should call my drunkenneſſe, my raſhneſſe brother?
Or ſuch a bleſſed Maid my breach of faith,
For I am moſt lacivious; and fell angers
In which I am alſo miſchievous, her husband?
O Gods preſerve her! I am wild as Winter,
Ambitious as the Devill: out upon me,
I hate my ſelfe, ſir, if ye dare beſtow her
Upon a Subject ye have one deſerves her.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: But him ſhe does not love: I know your meaning.
This young mans love unto his noble brother,
Appeares a mirrour; what muſt now be done Lords?
For I am gravel'd, if ſhe have not him
She dies for certaine, if his brother miſſe her,
Farewell to him, and all our honours.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: He is dead ſir,
Your Grace has heard of that, and ſtrangely.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: No,
I can aſſure ye no there was a trick in't,
Read that, and then know all; what ailes the gentleman?
Hold him; how doe ye ſir? Polidor is ſick ath' ſudden.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Sick ath' the ſudden,
Extreamly ill, wondrous ill.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Where did it take ye?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Here in my head ſir, and my heart, for heaven ſake.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Conduct him to his chamber preſently,
And bid my Doctors—

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: No I ſhall be well ſir,
I doe beſeech your Grace even for the Gods ſake
Remember my poore brother, I ſhall pray then.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Away he growes more weaker ſtill: I will do it,
Or heaven forget me ever. Now your Counſells, Exit. Polidor.
For I am at my wits end; what with you ſir?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: Letters from warlike Pelius.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Yet more troubles?
The Spartans are in Armes, and like to win all:
Supplies are ſent for and the Generall;
This is more croſſe then tother; come let's to him,
For he muſt have her, 'tis neceſſitie,
Or we muſt loſe our honours, let's plead all,
For more then all is needfull, ſhew all reaſon
If love can heare a that ſide, if ſhe yeild
We have fought beſt and won the nobleſt field. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: 1 Cap.
sp.l: I have brought the wench, a luſty wench,
And ſomewhat like the Princeſſe.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: 'Tis the better, let's ſee her,
And goe you in and tell him, that her Grace
Is come to viſit him? how ſleeps he Stremon?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: He cannot, only thinkes, and calls on Polidor,
Swears a will not be fool'd; ſometimes he rages,
And ſometimes ſits and muſes. Exit. Stre.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: He's paſt all helpe ſure?
How doe ye like her?

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: Byth' maſſe a good round Virgin,
And at firſt ſight reſembling, ſhe is well cloth'd too.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: But is ſhe ſound?

sp.speaker: 2 Cap.
sp.l: Of wind and limbe, I warrant her.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: You are inſtructed Lady?

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: Yes, and know ſir
How to behave my ſelfe, ne're feare.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: Where did he get this Vermin?

sp.speaker: 1 Cap.
sp.l: Hang him Badger,
There's not a hole free from him, whores and whores mates,
Doe all pay him obedience.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: Indeed i'th' war,
His quarter was all whore, whore upon whore,
And linde with a whore, beſhrew me 'tis a faire whore.

sp.speaker: 1 Cap.
sp.l: She has ſmockt away her blood; but fair or foule,
Or blind or lame, that can but lift her leg up
Comes not amiſſe to him, he rides like a night mare,
All ages, all Religions.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: Can ye ſtate it?

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: I'le make a ſhift.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: He muſt lie with ye, Lady.

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: Let him, he's not the firſt man I have lain with,
Nor ſhall not be the laſt.

sp.speaker: 2 Cap.
sp.l: A comes, no more words,
She has her leſſon throughly; how he views her?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Goe forward now, ſo, bravely, ſtand!

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Great Lady,
How humbly I am bound—

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: You ſhall not kneele ſir,
Come, I have done you wrong; ſtand up my Souldier,
And thus I make amends — Kiſſes him.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: A plague confound ye,
Is this your ſtate?

sp.speaker: 2 Cap.
sp.l: 'Tis well enough.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: O Lady,
Your royall hand, your hand my deareſt beauty
Is more then I muſt purchaſe: here divine one,
I dare revenge my wrongs: ha?

sp.speaker: 1 Cap.
sp.l: A dam'd foule one.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: The Lees of baudie prewnes: mourning gloves?
All ſpoyl'd by heaven.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ha! who art thou?

sp.speaker: 2 Cap.
sp.l: A ſhame on ye,
Ye clawing ſcabby whore.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I ſay, who art thou?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Why 'tis the Princeſſe ſir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: The divell ſir,
'Tis ſome rogue thing.

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: If this abuſe be love ſir,
Or I that laid aſide my modeſty—

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: So far thou't never find it.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Doe not weepe,
For if ye be the Princeſſe, I will love ye,
Indeed I will, and honour ye, fight for ye,
Come wipe your eyes; by heaven ſhe ſtinkes; who art ta?
Stinkes like a poyſon'd Ratt behind a hanging?
Woman who art ta? like a rotten Cabbage.

sp.speaker: 2 Cap.
sp.l: Y'ar much to blame ſir, 'tis the Princeſſe.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: How?
Shee the Princeſſe?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: And the loving Princeſſe.

sp.speaker: 1. Capt.
sp.l: Indeed the doting Princeſſe.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Come hither once more,
The Princeſſe ſmells like mornings breath, pure Amber,
Beyond the courted Indies in her ſpices
Still a dead rat by heaven; thou art a Princeſſe.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: What a dull whore is this?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I'le tell ye preſently,
For if ſhe be a Princeſſe, as ſhe may be
And yet ſtink too, and ſtrongly, I ſhall find her;
Fetch the Numidian Lyon I brought over,
If ſhe be ſprung from royall blood, the Lyon
He'l doe ye reverence, els

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: I beſeech your Lordſhip?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: He'l teare her all to pieces.

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: I am no Princeſſe, ſir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Who brought thee hither?

sp.speaker: 2. Capt.
sp.l: If ye confeſſe, wee'll hang ye.

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: Good my Lord;

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Who art thou then?

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: A poore retaining whore, ſir,
To one of your Lordſhips Captaines.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Alas poore whore,
Go, be a whore ſtill, and ſtinke worſe: Ha, ha ha Ex. Cloe
What fooles are theſe, and coxcombes? Exit. Memnon.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: I am right glad yet,
He takes it with ſuch lightneſſe.

sp.speaker: 1. Cap.
sp.l: Me thinkes his face too,
Is not ſo clouded as it was; how he lookes?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Where's your dead Rat?

sp.speaker: 2. Cap.
sp.l: The divell dine upon her
Lyons, why what a medicine had he gotten
To try a whore?

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.p: Here's one from Polidor ſtaies to ſpeak with ye.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: With whom?

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: With all; where has the Generall bin?
Hee's laughing to himſelfe extreamly.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Come,
I'le tell thee how: I am glad yet he's ſo merry. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Chilax and Prieſt, Calis, Lady and Nun.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: What lights are thoſe that enter there, ſtill neerer?
Plague a your rotten itch, do you draw me hither
Into the Temple to betray me? was there no place
To ſatisfie your ſin in? Gods forgive me,
Still they come forward;

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Peace ye foole, I have found it,
'Tis the young Princeſſe Calis.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: 'Tis the divell
To claw us for our catterwawling.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Retire ſoftly,
I did not looke for you theſe two houres, Lady,
Beſhrew your haſt: that way,

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: That goes to th'Altar?
Ye old blind Beaſt.

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: I know not any way;
Still they come nearer,
I'le in to th'Oracle;

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: That's well remembred Ile in with ye;

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Doe. Exeunt Prieſt & Chilax.

div.stage: Enter Calis and her Traine with lights ſinging; Lucippe, Cleanthe.

sp.l: O faire ſweet Goddeſſe Queene of Loves,
Soft and gentle, as thy Doves,
Humble ey'd, and ever ruing
Thoſe poore hearts, their Loves purſuing:
O thou mother of delights,
Crowner of all happy nights,
Star of deare content, and pleaſure
Of mutuall loves the endleſſe treaſure,
Accept this ſacrifice we bring
Thou continuall youth and Spring,
Grant this Lady her deſires,
And every houre, wee'll crown thy fires.

sp.speaker: Nun.
sp.l: You about her all retyre,
Whilſt the Princeſſe feedes the fire,
When your Devotions ended be
To the Oracle I will attend ye. Exit. Nun & draws the Curten cloſe to Calis.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Hee will abroad.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: How does his humour hold him?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: He is now growne wondrous ſad, weeps often too,
Talkes of his brother to himſelfe, ſtarts ſtrangely.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Does he not curſe?

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Nor breake out in furie,
Offering ſome new attempt?

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: Neither, toth' Temple
Is all we heare of now: what there he will doe;

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: I hope repent his folly, let's be neare him.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Where are the reſt?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: About a buſineſſe
Concernes him mainly, if heav'n cure this madneſſe,
He's man for ever Stremon.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Does the King know it?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Yes, and much troubled with it, is now gone
To ſeeke his ſiſter out.
Come let's away then. Exeunt Eumen. Stremon, Caliſ.

div.stage: Enter Nun, ſhe opens the Curtain to Calis. Calis at the Oracle, Arras.

sp.speaker: Nun.
sp.l: Peace to your praiers Lady, will it pleaſe ye
To paſſe on to the Oracle.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.p: Moſt humblie. Chilax & Prieſt in the Oracle.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Doe ye heare that?

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Yes, lie cloſe.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: A wildfire take ye,
What ſhall become of me? I ſhall be hang'd now.
Is this a time to ſhake? a halter ſhake ye,
Come up and juggle, come.

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: I am monſtrous fearfull.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Up ye old gaping Oyſter, up and anſwer,
A mouldie mange upon your chops, ye told me
I was ſafe here till the Bell rung.

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: I was prevented,
And did not looke theſe three houres for the Princeſſe.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Shall we be taken?

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Speake for loves ſake Chilax?
I can not, nor I dare not.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.p: I'le ſpeake treaſon, for I had as lieve be hang'd for that

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Good Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Muſt it be ſung or ſed? what ſhall I tell 'em?
They are here? here now preparing.

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: O, my conſcience!

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Plague a your ſpurgall'd conſcience, does it tyre now?
Now when it ſhould be tuffeſt? I could make thee—

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Save us, wee are both undone elſe.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Downe ye dog then,
Be quiet, and be ſtanch to no inundations.

sp.speaker: Nun.
sp.l: Here kneele againe, and Venus grant your wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: O Divine ſtarre of Heaven,
Thou in power above the ſeven:
Thou ſweet kindler of deſires,
Till they grow to mutuall fires:
Thou, O gentle Queen that art,
Curer of each wounded heart.
Thou the fuell, and the flame;
Thou in heaven, and here the ſame:
Thou the wooer, and the wood:
Thou the hunger, and the food:
Thou the prayer, and the prayed;
Thou what is, or ſhall be ſaid:
Thou ſtill young, and golden treſſed,
Make me by thy Anſwer bleſſed.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: When?

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Now ſpeake handſomly, and ſmall by all meanes,
I have told ye what. Thunder.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: But I'le tell you a new tale
Now for my necke verſe; I have heard thy prayers,
And marke me well.

sp.speaker: Nun.
sp.l: The Goddeſſe is diſpleaſed much,
The Temple ſhakes and totters: ſhe appeares,
Bow, Lady, bow.

sp.speaker: Venus.
sp.l: Purge me the Temple round,
And live by this example henceforth ſound
Virgin, I have ſeene thy teares,
Heard thy wiſhes and thy feares,
Thy holy Incence flew above,
Harke therefore, thy doome in love,
Had thy heart bin ſoft at firſt,
Now thou had'ſt alayd thy thirſt:
Had thy ſtubborne will but bended,
All thy ſorrows here had ended;
Therefore be juſt in love,
And ſtrange fortune thou muſt prove,
And, for thou haſt bin ſterne and coy,
A dead love thou ſhalt enjoy.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: O gentle goddeſſe!

sp.speaker: Venus.
sp.l: Riſe, thy doome is ſed,
And feare not; I ſhall pleaſe thee with the dead, Ʋenus aſcends.

sp.speaker: Nun.
sp.l: Goe up into the Temple and there end
Your holy rites, the Goddeſſe ſmiles upon ye.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I'le no more Oracles, nor Miracles,
Nor no more Church worke, Ile be drawn & hang'd firſt:
Am not I torne a pieces with the thunder?
Death, I can ſcarce believe I live yet,
It ga • e me on the buttocks, a cruell, a huge bang,
I had as lieue a had 'em ſcratcht with dog-whips;
Be quiet henceforth, now ye feele the end on't,
I would adviſe ye my old friends the good gentlewoman
Is ſtrucken dumbe and there her grace ſits mumping
Like an old Ape eating a Brawn; ſure the good Goddeſſe
Knew my intent was honeſt, to ſave the Princeſſe.
And how we young men are entic'd to wickedneſſe
By theſe lewd women, I had paid for't els too:
I am monſtrous holy now, and cruel fearefull,
O! 'twas a plaguy thump, charg'd with a vengeance.
sp.stage: Enter Siphax walkes ſoftly over the Stage, and goes in.
sp.l: Woo'd I were well at home; the beſt is 'tis not day:
Who's that? ha? Siphax? I'le be with you anon, ſir,
Ye ſhall be Oracled I warrant ye,
And thunderd too as well as I: your Lordſhip
sp.stage: Enter Memnon, Eumenes, Stremon, and two carrying Torches.
sp.l: Muſt needs enjoy the Princeſſe, yes, ha! torches?
And Memnon comming this way, he's dog mad,
And ten to one appearing thus unto him,
Hee worries me, I muſt goe by him.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Aske me no further queſtions; what art thou?
How doſt thou ſtare? ſtand off; nay looke upon me,
I doe not ſhake, nor feare thee. — Drawes his ſword.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: A will kill me,
This is for Church worke.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Why doſt thou appeare now?
Thou wert fairly ſlain: I know thee Diocles,
And know thine envie to mine honour: but—

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Stay Memnon,
I am a Spirit, and thou canſt not hurt me.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: This is the voyce of Chilax.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: What makes he thus?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: 'Tis true that I was ſlaine in field, but fowly
By multitudes not manhood: therefore marke me,
I doe appeare againe to quit mine honour,
And on thee ſingle.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I accept the challenge.
Where?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: On the Stigian banks

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: When?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Four dayes hence.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Goe noble Ghoſt, I will attend.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I thanke ye.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Ye have ſav'd your throat and handſomly:
Farwell ſir. Exi. Chi.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Sing me the Battell of Peluſium,
In which this Worthie died.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: This will ſpoile all, and make him worſe
Then ere he was, ſitt downe ſir,
And give your ſelfe to reſt.
ARme, arme, arme, arm, the Scouts are all come in
Keepe your rankes cloſe and now your honours win.
Behold from yonder hill, the foe appeares,
Bowes, bills glaves arrowes ſhields, and Speares,
Like a darke wood he comes, or tempest powring,
O view the wings of horſe, the meadows ſcowring,
The vant-guard marches bravely, hark the Drums—dub, dub,
They meet they meet, now the Battell comes,
See how the Arrows fly
That darken all the skie,
Harke how the Trumpets ſound,
Hark how the hills rebound, — Tara-tara-tara.
Hark how the horſes charge: in boyes in boyes in,-tara, tara,
The Battell totters; now the wounds begin,
O how they cry,
O how they dy.
Roome for the valiant Memnon, arm'd with thunder,
See how he breakes the rankes aſunder:
They fly they flie Eumenes has the Chace,
And brave Polibius, makes good his place.
To the plaines to the Woode,
To the Rocks to the floods,
They fly for ſuccour: Follow, follow, follow, Hey, hey.
Harke how the Souldiers hollow
Brave Diocles is dead,
And all his Souldiers fled,
The battell's won, and loſt,
That many a life hath coſt.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Now forward to the Temple. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Are ye gone?
How have I ſcapt this morning? by what miracle?
Sure I am ordain'd for ſome brave end.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: How is it?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Come, 'tis as well as can be.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: But is it poſſible
This ſhould be true you tell me?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt certaine.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: Such a groſſe Aſſe to love the Princeſſe?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Peace,
Pull your robe cloſe about ye: you are perfect
In all I taught ye.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: Sure.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Gods give thee good luck,
'Tis ſtrange my braines ſhould ſtill be beating knaverie
For all theſe dangers: but they are needfull miſchiefes,
And ſuch are Nuts to me, and I muſt doe 'em,
You will remember me—

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: By this kiſſe Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chilax.
sp.l: No more of that, I feare another Thunder.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: We are not i'th' Temple man.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Peace, here he comes,
Now to our buſineſſe handſomely: away now. Exi. Chilax and Cloe.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: 'Twas ſure the Princeſſe, for he kneel'd unto her,
And ſhe lookt every way: I hope the Oracle
Has made me happy: me I hope ſhe lookt for.
sp.stage: Enter Chilax and Cloe at the other doore.
sp.l: Fortune, I will ſo honour thee, Love ſo adore thee,
She is here againe lookes round about againe too,
'Tis done, I know 'tis done; 'tis Chilax with her,
And I ſhall know of him; whoſe that?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Speake ſoftly,
The Princeſſe from the Oracle.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: She views me,
By heav'n ſhe beckens me.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Come neare, ſhe woo'd have ye.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: O royall Lady. Kiſſes her hand.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: She wills ye read that, for belike ſhe's bound to ſilence
For ſuch a time; ſhe is wondrous gracious to ye.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Heav'n make me thankfull.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: She woo'd have ye read it, He Reads.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Siphax, the will of Heaven hath caſt me on thee
To be thy wife, whoſe will muſt be obay'd:
Uſe me with honour, I ſhall love thee dearly,
And make thee underſtand thy worths hereafter;
Convey me to a ſecret Ceremony,
That both our hearts and loves may be united,
And uſe no language, till before my brother
We both appeare, where I will ſhew the Oracle,
For till that time I am bound, I muſt not anſwer.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: O happy I!

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Ye are a made man.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: But Chilax
Where are her women?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: None but your Graces Siſter,
Becauſe ſhe would have it privat to the world yet,
Knowes of this buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: I ſhall thanke the Chilax,
Thou art a carefull man.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Your Graces ſervant.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: I'le find a ſit place for thee.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: If you will not,
There's a good Lady will, ſhe points yee forward,
Away and take your fortune, not a word ſir,
So, you are greas'd I hope. Exit Siph. & Cloe. manet Chi.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Where have you left your Lord?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: I'th' Temple, Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Why are ye from him?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Why the King is with him,
And all the Lords.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Is not the Princeſſe there too.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Yes,
And the ſtrangeſt coile amongſt 'em: She weeps bitterly;
The King entreats, and frownes, my Lord like Autumne
Drops off his hopes by handfulls, all the Temple
Sweats with this Agonie.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Where's young Polidor?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Dead as they ſaid o'th' ſudden.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Dead?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: For certaine,
But not yet knowne abroad,

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: There's a new trouble;
A brave young man he was; but we muſt all die.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Did not the Generall meet you this morning
Like a tall ſtallion Nun?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: No more a that Boy.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: You had been ferreting.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: That's all one, Foole;
My Maſter foole that taught my wits to traffique,
What has your wiſdome done? how have you profited?
Out with your Audit, come: you are not emptie,
Put out mine eye with twelve pence? do you ſhaker?
What thinke you of this ſhaking? here's with coxcombe
Ha boyes? ha my fine raſcalls, here's a Ring, Pulls out a Purſe.
How right they goe?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: O let me ring the fore-bell.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: And here are thumpers, Chickens, golden rogues,
• it wit ye raſcalls.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: I have a Sty here Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I have no gold to cure it, not a penny,
Not one croſſe Cavalier; we are dull Sou'diers,
Groſſe, heavy-headed fellowes; fight for victualls?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: Why; ye are the ſpirits of the time.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: By no meanes.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: The valiant firie.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Fy, fie no.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: Be-lee-me ſir.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I woo'd I could ſir.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: I will ſatisfie ye.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: But I will not content you; alas poore boy,
Thou ſhewſt an honeſt nature weepes for thy Maſter,
There's a red rogue to buy thee handkerchers.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: A was an honeſt Gentleman, I have loſt too.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Ye have indeed your labour Foole; but Stremon,
Doeſt thou want money too? no virtue living?
No firking out at fingers ends?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: It ſeemes ſo.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Will ye all ſerve me?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Yes, when ye are Lord Generall,
For leſſe I will not goe.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: There's gold for thee then,
Thou haſt a ſouldiers minde, Foole.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Here, your firſt man.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I will give thee for thy wit, for 'tis a fine wit,
A daintie diving wit, hold up; juſt nothing,
Goe graze i'th' commons, yet I am mercifull
There's ſix pence; buy a Saucer, ſteale an old gowne,
And beg i'th' Temple for a Prophet, come away boyes,
Let's ſee how things are carried, Foole, up ſirra,
You may chance get a dinner: Boy your preferment
I'le undertake, for your brave Maſters ſake,
You ſhall not periſh.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Pleaſe me well Foole,
And you ſhall light my pipes: Away to th' Temple.
But ſtay, the Kings here, ſport upon ſport Boyes.

div.stage: Enter King, Lords Siphax kneeling, Cloe with a Vaile.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What would you have Captaine,
Speake ſuddenly, for I am wondrous buſie.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: A Pardon, Royall ſir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: For what?

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: For that,
Which was heav'ns will, ſhould not be mine alone ſir;
My marrying with this Lady.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: It needs no Pardon,
For marriage is no ſin.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Not in it ſelfe, ſir,
But in preſuming too much: Yet heav'n knowes
So does the Oracle that caſt it on me,
And — the Princeſſe, royall ſir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What Princeſſe?

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: O be not angrie, my dread King, your Siſter.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: My ſiſter? ſhe's i'th' Temple man.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: She is here ſir.

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: The Captain's mad, ſhe is kneeling at the Altar.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I know ſhe is, with all my heart good Captain,
I do forgive ye both: be unvail'd Lady; Puts off her vaile
Will ye have more forgivenes? the mans frantick,
Come let's goe bring her out: God give yee joy ſir.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.p: How? Cloe? my old Cloe? Exit. King, Lords.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: Even the ſame ſir.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Gods give your manhood much c • ntent.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: The Princeſſe
Lookes ſomething muſtie ſince her comming over.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: 'Twere good, youl'd bruſh her over.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: Fooles and Fidlers
Make ſport at my abuſe too.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: O 'tis the nature
Of us Fooles to make bold with one another,
But you are wiſe, brave ſirs.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Cheere up your Princeſſe,
Believe it ſir, the King will not be angry,
Or ſay he were; why 'twas the Oracle,
The Oracle, and like your Grace, the Oracle.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: And who, moſt mighty Siphax?

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: With mine owne whore.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: With whom els ſhould ye marry ſpeak your conſcience,
Will ye tranſgreſſe the law of Armes, that ever
Rewards the Souldier with his owne ſins?

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: Devills.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: Ye had my maiden-head my youth, my ſweetnes,
Is it not juſtice then? —

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: I ſee it muſt be,
But by this hand. I'le hang a lock upon thee.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: You ſhall not need, my honeſty ſhall doe it.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: If there be wars in all the world—

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: I'le with ye,
For you know, I have bin a ſouldier,
Come, curſe on: when I need another Oracle.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Send for me Siphax, I'le fit ye with a Princeſſe,
And ſo to both your honours.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: And your graces.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: The Devill grace ye all.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: God a mercy Chilax,

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Shall we laugh halfe an houre now?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: No the King comes,
And all the traine.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Away then, our Act's ended. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter King, Caliſ. Memnon and Cleanthe, Curtiſan, Lords.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: You know he do's deſerve ye, loves ye dearly,
You know what bloody violence had us'd The Hearſe ready Polidor, Eumenes & Captains
Upon himſelfe, but that his brother croſt it,
You know the ſame thoughts ſtill inhabit in him
And covet to take birth: Look on him Lady,
The wars have not ſo far conſum'd him yet,
Cold age diſabled him, or ſickneſſe ſunk him
To be abhorr'd: looke on his Honour ſiſter,
That beares no ſtamp of time, no wrinkles on it,
No ſad demoliſhment, nor death can reach it:
Looke with the eyes of heaven that nightlie waken,
To view the wonders of my glorious Maker,
And not the weakneſſe: looke with your vertuous eyes,
And then clad royaltie in all his conqueſts;
His matchleſſe love hung with a thouſand merits
Eternall youth attending, Fame and Fortune,
Time and Oblivion vexing at his vertues,
He ſhall appeare a miracle: looke on our dangers,
Looke on the publique ruine.

sp.speaker: Caliſ.
sp.l: O, deare brother.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Fie, let us not like proud and greedy waters
Gaine, to give off againe: this is our Sea,
And you his Cynthia, govern him, take heed,
His ſtouds have bin as hie, and full as any,
And gloriouſly now is got up to the girdle,
The Kingdomes he hath purchas'd; noble Siſter,
Take not your vertue from him, O take heed
We ebbe not now to nothing, take heed Calis.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: The wil of heaven not mine, which muſt not alter,
And my eternall doome for ought I know
Is fixt upon me; alas, I muſt love nothing.
Nothing that loves againe muſt I be bleſt with:
The gentle Vine climbs up the Oke and clips him.
And when the ſtroke comes, yet they fall together;
Death death muſt I enjoy, and live to love him,
O noble Sir!

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Thoſe teares are ſome reward yet,
Pray let me wed your ſorrowes.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Take 'em Souldier,
They are fruitfull ones, lay but a fight upon 'em,
And ſtrait they will conceive to infinites;
I told ye what, ye could find 'em,
Roome before there. Knock.

div.stage: Enter Funerall, Captaines following, and Eumenes.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: How now, what's this? more drops to th'Ocean?
Whoſe body's this?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.l: The noble Polidor,
This ſpeakes his death.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: My Brother dead?

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: O Goddeſſe!
O cruell, cruell Venus, here's my fortune.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Read Captaine.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.p: Read aloude: farewell my follies. Eumen reades

sp.speaker: 1. Cap.
sp.l: Be wiſe, as you are beauteous, love with judgement,
And look with clear eyes on my noble Brother,
Value deſert and vertue, they are Jewells,
Fit for your worth and wearing: take heed Lady,
The Gods reward ingratitude moſt grievous;
Remember me no more, or if you muſt,
Seeke me in noble Memnons love, I dwell there:
I durſt not live, becauſe I durſt not wrong him,
I can no more, make mee eternall happy
With looking downe upon your loves.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: And did'ſt thou die for me?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Excellent vertue!
What will ye now doe?

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Dwell for euer here ſir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: For me deare Polidor? ô worthy young man!
O love, love, love, love above recompence!
Infinite love, infinite honeſty!
Good Lady leave, you muſt have no ſhare here,
Take home your ſorrowes: here's enough to ſtore me,
Brave glorious griefes! was ever ſuch a brother?
Turne all the ſtories over in the world yet,
And ſearch through all the memories of mankind,
And find me ſuch a friend; h'as out-done all.
Outſtript 'em ſheerely, all, all, thou haſt Polidor,
To die for me; why, as I hope for happineſſe,
'Twas one of the rareſt thought on things
The braveſt, and carried beyond compaſſe of our actions,
I wonder how he hit it, a young man too,
In all the bloſſomes of his youth and beautie,
In all the fulneſſe of his veines and wiſhes
Woed by that Paradice, that would catch heaven;
It ſtarts me extreamly, thou bleſt Aſhes,
Thou faithfull monument, where loue and friendſhip
Shall while the world is, worke new miracles.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: O! let me ſpeake too.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: No not yet, thou man,
For we are but mans ſhadowes, only man,
I have not words to utter him; ſpeake Lady,
I'le thinke a while.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: The Goddeſſe grants me this yet,
I ſhall enjoy the dead: no tombe ſhall hold thee
But theſe two armes, no Trickments but my teares
Over thy Hearſe, my ſorrowes like ſad armes
Shall hang for ever: on the tuffeſt Marble
Mine eyes ſhall weepe thee out an Epitaph,
Love at thy feet ſhall kneele, his ſmart bow broken;
Faith at thy head, youth and the Graces mourners;
O ſweet young man!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Now I begin to melt too.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Have ye enough yet Lady? roome for a gamſter
To my fond Love, and all thoſe idle fancies
A long farwell, thou diedſt for me deare Polidor,
To give me peace, thou haſt eternall glory,
I ſtay and talke here; I will kiſſe thee firſt,
And now I'le follow thee. Polidor riſes.

sp.speaker: Pollidor.
sp.l: Hold, for heavens ſake!

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ha!
Does he live?
Doſt thou deceive me?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Thus farre,
Yet for your good, and honour.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Now deare ſiſter;

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: The Oracle is ended, noble ſir,
Diſpoſe, me now as you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: You are mine then?

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: With all the joyes that may be.

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: Your conſent ſir;

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Ye have it freely.

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: Walke along with me then,
And as you love me, love my will.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: I will ſo.

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: Here worthy Brother, take this vertuous Princeſſe,
Ye have deſerv'd her nobly, ſhe will love ye,
And when my life ſhall bring ye peace, as ſhe does,
Command it, ye ſhall have it.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Sir, I thanke ye.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I never found ſuch goodneſſe in ſuch yeares.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not over-doe me, though I die for't,
O how I love thy goodneſſe, my beſt brother,
You have given me here a treaſure to enrich me,
Would make the worthieſt King alive a begger,
What may I give you back againe?

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: Your love ſir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: And you ſhall have it, even my deareſt love,
My firſt, my nobleſt love, take her againe, ſir,
She is yours, your honeſty has over-run me,
She loves ye, lov'ſt her not? excellent Princeſſe,
Injoy thy wiſh, and now get Generalls.

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: As ye love heaven, love him, ſhe is only yours, ſir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: As ye love heaven, love him, ſhe is only yours, ſir;
My Lord, the King.

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: He will undoe himſelfe ſir,
And muſt without her periſh; who ſhall fight then?
Who ſhall protect your Kingdome?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Give me hearing,
And after that beliefe, were ſhe my ſoule
(As I doe love her equall) all my victories,
And all the living names I have gain'd by warre,
And loving him that good, that vertuous good man,
That only worthy of the name of brother,
I would reſigne all freely, 'tis all love
To me, all marriage rites, the joy of iſſues
To know him fruitfull, that has been ſo faithfull.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: This is the nobleſt difference-take your choiſe ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: I ſee they are ſo brave, and noble both,
I know not which to looke on.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Chuſe diſcreetly,
And vertue guide ye, there all the world in one man
Stands at the marke.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: There all mans honeſtie,
The ſweetneſſe of all youth —

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: O God's!

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: My Armour,
By all the God's ſhe's yours; my armes, I ſay,
And I beſeech your Grace, give me imployment,
That ſhall be now my Miſtreſſe: here my Courtſhip.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Ye ſhall have any thing.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Vertuous Lady,
Remember me, your ſervant now; Young man,
You cannot over-reach me in your goodneſſe;
O love! how ſweet thou look'ſt now? and how gentle,
I ſhould have ſlubber'd thee, and ſtain'd thy beauty;
Your hand, your hand ſir;

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Take her, and Heaven bleſſe her.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: So.

sp.speaker: Po.
sp.l: 'Tis your will ſir, nothing of my merit;
And as your royall gift, I take this bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: And I from heaven this gentleman: thanks Goddeſs.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: So ye are pleas'd now Lady;

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Now or never.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: My cold ſtiffe carkaſſe, would have frozen ye,
Warres, warres.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Ye ſhall have warres.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: My next brave battell
I dedicate to your bright honour (ſiſter,)
Give me a favour, that the world may know
I am your ſouldier.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: This, and all faire Fortunes.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: And he that beares this from me, muſt ſtrike boldly.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I do forgive thee: be honeſt, no more wench.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Come now to Revells, this bleſt day ſhall prove
The happy crown of noble Faith and Love. Exeunt.

div.head: Prologue.
div.l: TO pleaſe all's impoſſible, and to deſpaire
Ruins our ſelves, and dampes the Writers care:
Would we knew what to doe, or ſay, or when
To find the mindes here equall with the men:
But we muſt venture; now to Sea we goe,
Faire fortune with us, give us roome, and blow;
Remember ye'ar all venturers; and in this Play
How many twelve-pences ye have 'ſtow'd this day:
Remember for returne of your delight,
We launch, and plough through ſtormes of feare, and ſpight:
Give us your fore-windes fairely, fill our wings,
And ſteere us right, and as the Saylors ſing,
Loden with Wealth, on wanton ſeas, ſo we
Shall make our home-bound-voyage chearfully;
And you our noble Merchants, for your treaſure
Share equally the fraught, we run for pleaſure.

div.head: Epilogue.
div.l: HEre lyes the doubt now, let our Playes be good,
Our owne care ſayling equall in this Flood;
Our preparations new, new our Attire,
Yet here we are becalm'd ſtill, ſtill i'th' mire,
Here we ſtick faſt; Is there no way to cleare
This paſſage of your judgement, and our feare,
No mittigation of that law? Brave friends,
Conſider we are yours, made for your ends,
And every thing preſerves it ſelfe, each will
If not perverſe, and crooked, utters ſtill
The beſt of that it ventures in: have care
Ev'n for your pleaſures ſake, of what we are,
And doe not ruine all: You may frowne ſtill.
But 'tis the nobler way, to check the will.

sp.speaker: Arſenio.
sp.l: LEandro paid all.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: 'Tis his uſuall cuſtome,
And requiſite he ſhould: he has now put off
The Funerall black, (your rich heirs weares with joy,
When he pretends to weep for his dead Father,)
Your gathering Sires, ſo long heape muck together,
That their kind Sonnes, to rid them of their care
Wiſh them in heaven; Or if they take a taſte
Of Purgatory by the way, it matters not:
Provided they remove hence; What is befalne
To his Father, in the other world, I ask not,
I am ſure his prayre is heard: would I could uſe one
For mine, in the ſame method.

sp.speaker: Arſen.
sp.l: Fy upon thee.
This is prophane,

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Good Doctor, doe not ſchoole me,
For a fault you are not free from: On my life
Were all Heires in Corduba, put too their oathes
They would confeſſe with me, 'tis a ſound Tenet:
I am ſure Leandro do't.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: He is th'owner
Of a faire Eſtate.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: And fairly he deſerves it,
He's a royall Fellow: yet obſerves a meane
In all his courſes, carefull to on whom
He ſhowres his bounties: he that's liberall
To all alike, may doe a Good by chance,
But never out of Judgement! This invites
The prime men of the Citie to frequent
All places he reſorts to, and are happy
In his ſweet Converſe.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Don Jamie the Brother
To the Grandee Don Henrique, appeares much taken
With his behaviour.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: There is ſomething more in't:
Hee needs his Purſe, and knowes how to make uſe on't,
'Tis now in faſhion for your Don, that's poore,
To vow all Leagues of friendſhip with a Merchant
That can ſupply his wants, and howſoe're
Don Jamie's noble borne, his elder Brother
Don Henrique rich and his Revenues long ſince
Encreaſing by marrying with a wealthy Heire
Call'd Madam Violante, he yet holds
A hard hand o're Jamie, allowing him
A bare annuity onely.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Yet 'tis ſaid
He hath no child, and by the Lawes of Spaine
If he die without iſſue, Don Iamie
Inherits his Eſtate.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Why that's the reaſon
Of their ſo many jarres: Though the young Lord
Be ſick of the elder Brother, and in reaſon
Should flatter, and obſerve him, he's of a nature
Too bold and fierce, to ſtoop ſo, but beares up,
Preſuming on his hopes.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: What's the young Lad
That all of em make ſo much of?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſweet-One,
And the beſt condition'd youth, I ever ſaw yet,
So humble and ſo affable, that he wins
The love of all that know him, and ſo modeſt,
That (in deſpight of povertie) he would ſtarve
Rather then aske a courteſie; He's the Sonne
Of a poore caſt-Captaine, one Octavio
And She, that once was calld th' faire Iacinta,
Is happy in being his Mother: for his ſake.
(Though in their Fortunes falne) they are eſteem'd of,
And cheriſh'd by the beſt. O here they come,
I now may ſpare his Character, but obſerve him,
Hee'l juſtifie my report.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: My good Aſcanio
Repaire more often to me: above Women
Thou ever ſhalt be welcome.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: My Lord your favours
May quickly teach a raw untutour'd Youth
To be both rude and ſawcie.

sp.speaker: Leandro.
sp.l: You cannot be
Too frequent where you are ſo much deſir'd:
And give me leave (deare friend) to be your Rivall
In part of his Affection; I will buy it
At any rate.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: Stood I but now poſſeſs'd
Of what my future hope preſages to me,
I then would make it cleare thou hadſt a Patron
That would not ſay but do: yet as I am,
Be mine, I'le not receive thee as a ſervant,
But as my Son (and though I want my ſelf)
No Page attending in the Court of Spain
Shall find a kinder maſter.

sp.speaker: Ars.
sp.l: I beſeech you
That my refuſall of ſo great an offer
May make no ill conſtruction, 'tis not pride
(That common vice is farre from my condition)
That makes you a denyall to receive
A favour I ſhould ſue for: nor the faſhion
Which the country followes, in which to be a ſervant
In thoſe that groan beneath the heavy weight
Of povertie is held an argument
Of a baſe and abject mind, I wiſh my yeares
Were fit to do you ſervice in a nature
That might become a Gentleman (give me leave
To think my ſelf one) My father ſerv'd the King
As a Captain in the field; and though his fortune
Return'd him home a poore man, he was rich
In reputation, and wounds fairly taken.
Nor am I by his ill ſucceſſe deterr'd,
I rather feel a ſtrong deſire that ſwayes me
To follow his Profeſſion, and if heaven
Hath marked me out to be a man, how proud,
In the ſervice of my Country, ſhould I be,
To traile a pike under your brave command.
There, I would follow you as a guid to honour,
Though all the horrours of the Warre made up
To ſtop my paſſage.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: Thou art a hopefull Boye,
And it was bravely ſpoken: For this anſwer,
I love thee more then ever.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Pitty ſuch ſeeds
Of promiſing courage ſhould not grow and proſper

sp.speaker: Aug.
sp.l: What ever his reputed Parents bee,
He ha •• a mind that ſpeakes him right and noble.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: You make him bluſh: it needs not ſweet Aſcanio,
We may heare praiſes when they are deſerv'd,
Or modeſtie unwounded. By my life
I would adde ſomething to the building up
So fair a mind, and if till you are fit
To beare Armes in the field, you'l ſpend ſome yeares
In Salamanca, I'le ſupply your ſtudies
With all conveniences.

sp.speaker: Ars.
sp.l: Your goodneſſe (Signiors)
And charitable favours overwhelm me.
If I were of your blood, you could not be
More tender of me: what then can I pay
(A poore boy and a ſtranger) but a heart
Bound to your ſervice? with what willingnes
I would receive (good Sir) your noble offer,
Heaven can beare witnes for me: but alas
Should I embrace the meanes to raiſe my fortunes,
I muſt deſtroy the lives of my poore Parents
(To whom I ow my being) they in me
Place all their comforts, and (as if I were
The light of their dim eyes) are ſo indulgent
They cannot brook one ſhort dayes abſence from me;
And (what will hardly win belief) though young,
I am their ſteward and their nurſe: the bounties
VVhich others beſtow on me ſerves to ſuſtain 'em,
And to forſake them in their age, in me
VVere more then murther.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: This is a kind of begging
VVould make a Broker charitable.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Here (ſweet heart)
I wiſh that it were more.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: VVhen this is ſpent,
Seek for ſupply from me

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Thy pietie
For ever be remembred: nay take all,
Though 't were my exhibition to a Royall
For one whole yeare.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: High heavens reward your goodnes.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: So Sir, is this a ſlip of your own grafting,
You are ſo prodigall?

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: A ſlip Sir?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Yes,
A ſlip; or call it by the proper name
Your Baſtard.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: You are foul-mouth'd; do not provoke me,
I ſhall forget your Birth, if you proceed,
And uſe you, (as your manners do deſerve) uncivilly.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: So brave? pray you give me hearing,
Who am I Sir?

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: My elder Brother: One
That might have been born a fool and ſo reputed,
But that you had the luck to creep into
The world a yeare before me.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Be more temperate.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: I neither can nor will, unleſſe I learn it
By this example: let him uſe his harſh
Unſavoury reprehenſions upon thoſe
That are his hinds, and not on me. The Land
Our father left to him alone rewards him,
For being twelve moneths elder, let that be
Forgotten, and let his Paraſites remember
One quality of worth or vertue in him
That may authoriſe him, to be a cenſurer
Of me, or of my manners, and I will
Acknowledge him for a tutor, til then, never

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: From whom have you your meanes Sir?

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: From the will
Of my dead father; I am ſure I ſpend not
Nor give't upon your purſe.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: But will it hold out
Without my help?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I am ſure it ſhall I'le ſink elſe
For ſooner I will ſeek aid from a whore,
Then a courteſie from you.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: 'Tis well; you are proud of
Your new Exchequer when you have cheated him
And worn him to the quick, I may be found
In the Liſt of your acquaintance'

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Pray you hold
And give me leave (my Lord) to ſay thus much
(And in mine own defence) I am no Gull
To be wrought on by perſwaſion: nor no Coward
To be beaten out of my meanes, but know to whom
And why I give or lend, and will do nothing
But what my reaſon warrants; you may be
As ſparing as you pleaſe, I muſt be bold
To make uſe of mine own, without your licence.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: 'Pray thee let him alone, he is not worth thy anger
All that he do's (Leandro) is for my good,
I think there's not a Gentleman of Spain,
That ha's a better ſteward, then I have of him.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Your ſteward Sir?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Yes, and a provident one:
Why, he knowes I am given to large Expence,
And therefore layes up for me: could you believe els
That he, that ſixteen years hath worne the yoke
Of barren wedlock, without hope of iſſue.
(His Coffer's full, his Lands, and Vineyards fruitfull)
Could be ſo ſold to baſe, and ſordid thrift,
As almoſt to deny himſelfe, the meanes
And neceſſaries of life? Alas, he knowes
The Lawes of Spaine appoint me for his heire,
That all muſt come to me, if I out-live him,
(Which ſure I muſt doe, by the courſe of Nature,)
And the aſſiſtance of good Mirth, and Seck,
How ever you prove Melancholy.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: If I live,
Thou dearly ſhalt repent this,

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: When thou art dead,
I am ſure I ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Now they begin to burn
Like oppos'd Meteors.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Give them line, and way,
My life for Don Jamie.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Continue ſtill
The excellent Husband, and joyne Farme to Farme,
Suffer no Lordſhip, that in a cleare day
Falls in the proſpect of your coveteous eye
To be an others; Forget you are a Grandee
Take uſe upon uſe, and cut the throats of heires
With cozening Mort-gages: rack your poore Tenants,
Till they looke like ſo many Skeletons
For want of Food; And when that Widowes curſes,
The ruines of ancient Families, teares of Orphans
Have hurried you to the divell, ever remember
All was rak'd up, for me, (your thankfull Brother)
That will dance merrily upon your Grave,
And perhaps give a double Piſtolet
To ſome poore needy Frier, to ſay a Maſſe
To keep your Ghoſt from walking.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: That the Law
Should force me to endure this!

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: Verely,
When this ſhall come to paſſe (as ſure it will)
If you can find a loope-hole, though in hell'
To looke on my behaviour, you ſhall ſee me
Ranſack your Iron Cheſts, and once againe
Pluto's flame-colour'd Daughter ſhall be free
To dominier in Taverns, Maskes, and Revells
As ſhe was us'd, before ſhe was your Captive.
Me thinkes the meere conceipt of it, ſhould make you
Goe home ſick and diſtemper'd if it do's.
I'le ſend you a Doctor of mine owne, and after
Take order for your Funerall.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: You have ſaid, ſir,
I will not fight with words, but deeds to tame you,
Reſt confident I will and thou ſhalt wiſh
This day thou hadſt been dumb. — Exit.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: You have given him a heat.
But with your owne diſtemper.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: Not a whit
Now he is from mine eye, I can be merry,
Forget the cauſe, and him: all plagues goe with him,
Let's talke of ſomething els: what newes is ſtirring?
Nothing to paſſe the time?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: 'Faith it is ſaid
That the next Summer will determine much
Of that we long have talk'd of, touching the Wars.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: What have we to doe with them? Let us diſcourſe
Of what concernes our ſelves. 'Tis now in faſhion
To have you Gallants ſet downe, in a Taverne,
What the Arch-Dukes purpoſe is the next ſpring & what
Defence my Lords (the States) prepare: what courſe
The Emperour takes againſt the encroching Turke,
And whither his Moony-Standards are deſign'd
For Perſia or Polonia: and all this
The wiſer ſort of State-Wormes ſeeme to know
Better then their owne Affaires: this is diſcourſe
Fit for the Counſell it concernes; we are young,
And if that I might give the Theame, 'twere better
To talke of handſome women.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: And that's one,
Almoſt as generall.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Yet none agree
Who are the faireſt.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Some prefer the French,
For their conceited Dreſſings: ſome the plump
Italian Bona-Robas ſome the State
That ours obſerve; and I have heard one ſweare,
(A merry friend of mine) that once in London,
He did enjoy the company of a Gameſter,
(A common Gameſter too) that in one night
Met him th'Italian, French, and Spaniſh waies,
And ended in the Dutch; for, to coole her ſelfe,
She kiſs'd him drunke in the morning.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: Wee may ſpare
The travell of our tongues in forraigne Nations,
When in Corduba, if you dare give credit
To my report (for I have ſeene her, Gallants)
There lives a woman) of a meane birth too,
And meanly match'd) whoſe all-excelling Forme
Diſdaines compariſon with any She
That puts in for a faire one, and though you borrow
From every Country of the Earth the beſt
Of thoſe perfections, which the Clymat yeilds
To help to make her up, if put in Ballance,
This will weigh-downe the Scale.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: You talke of wonders.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: She is indeed a wonder, and ſo kept,
And, as the world deſerv'd not to behold
What curious Nature made without a patterne,
Whoſe Copy ſhe hath loſt too, ſhe's ſhut up,
Sequeſtred from the world.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Who is the owner
