Of ſuch a Jem? I am fir'd.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: One Bartolus,
A wrangling Advocate.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: A knave on Record.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: I am ſure he cheated me of the beſt part
Of my Eſtate.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: Some Buſineſſe calls me hence,
(And of importance) which denies me leiſure
To give you his full character: In few words
(Though rich) he's covetous beyond expreſſion,
And to encreaſe his heape, will dare the Divell,
And all the plagues of darkneſſe: and to theſe
So jealous, as if you would paralell
Old Argus to him, you muſt multiply
His Eies an hundred times: of theſe, none ſleepe.
He that would charme the heavieſt lid, muſt hire
A better Mercurie, then Iove made uſe of:
Bleſſe your ſelves from the thought of him and her
For 'twill be labour loſt: So farewell Signiors.— Exit.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Leandro? in a dreame? wake man for ſhame.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Trayned into a fooles paradiſe with a tale
Of an imagin'd Forme,

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Iamie is noble,
And with a forg'd Tale would not wrong his Friend,
Nor am I ſo much fired with luſt as Envie,
That ſuch a churl as Bartolus ſhould reap
So ſweet a harveſt, half my State to any
To help me to a ſhare.

sp.speaker: Ars.
sp.l: Tuſh do not hope for
Impoſſibilities,

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I muſt enjoy her,
And my prophetique love tells me I ſhall,
Lend me but your aſſiſtance;

sp.speaker: Ars.
sp.l: Give it 'ore,

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: I would not have thee fool'd

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I have ſtrange Engines,
Faſhioning here: and Bartolus on the Anville
Diſwade me not, but help me,

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Take your fortune,
If you come off well; praiſe your wit, if not,
Expect to be the ſubject of our Laughter. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: You met Don Henrique.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: Yes:

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: What comfort bring you?
Speake cheerefully: how did my Letter worke?
On his hard temper? I am ſure I wrot it,
So feelingly, and with the pen of ſorrow,
That it muſt force Co • punction,

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: You are cozen'd;
Can you with one hand prop a falling Tower?
Or with the other ſtop theraging maine,
When it breakes in on the uſurped Shore?
Or any thing that is impoſſible?
And then conclude that there is ſome way left,
To move him to compaſſion.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Is there a Juſtice
Or thunder (my Octavio) and he
Not ſunk unto the center?

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: Good Iacinta.
With your long practiſed patience beare afflictions,
And by provoking it call not on Heavens anger,
He did not onely ſcorne to read your Letter,
But (moſt inhumane as he is) he curſed you,
Curſed you moſt bitterly,

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: The bad mans charity,
Oh that I could forget there were a Tye,
In me, upon him! or the releife I ſeeke,
(If given) were bounty in him, and not debt,
Debt of a deere accompt!

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: Touch not that ſtring,
Twill but encreaſe our Sorrow, and tame ſilence,
(The Balme of the oppreſſed) which hitherto
Hath eas'd your grieved ſoule, and preſerv'd your fame,
Muſt be your Surgeon ſtill.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: If the contagion
Of my misfortunes had not ſpread it ſelf,
Upon my Son Aſcanio, though my wants
Were centupli'd upon • y ſelf, I could be patient:
But he is ſo good, I ſo miſerable,
His pious care his dutie, and obedience,
And all that can be wiſh'd for from a Son,
Diſcharg'd to me, and I, bard of all meanes,
To returne any ſcruple of the debt
I owe him as a Mother, is a Torment,
Too painefull to be borne.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: I ſuffer with you,
In that; yet find in this aſſurance comfort,
High heaven ordaines (whoſe purpoſes cannot alter)
Children that pay obedience to their Parents,
Shall never beg their Bread.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Here comes our joy,
Where has my deareſt been?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I have made (Mother)
A fortunate voyage and brought home rich prize,
In a few houres: the owners too contented,
From whom I tooke it. See heres Gold, good ſtore too
Nay pray you take it,

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Mens Charities are ſo cold,
That if I knew not, thou wert made of Goodnes,
'Twould breed a jealouſie in me by what meanes,
Thou cam'ſt by ſuch a ſum

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Were it ill got,
I am ſure it could not be employed ſo well,
As to relieve your wants. Some noble Friends,
(Rais'd by heavens mercy to me, not my merits)
Beſtow'd it on me.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: It were a ſacriledge
To rob thee of their bounty, ſince they gave it,
To thy uſe onely;

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Buy thee brave Cloathes with it
And fit thee for a fortune, and leave us,
To our neceſſities; why do'ſt thou weep?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Out of my feare, I have offended you;
For had I not, I am ſure you are too kind,
Not to accept the offer of my ſervice,
In which I am a gainer; I have heard
My tutor ſay of all a iereall foule
The Storke's the Embleme of true pietie,
Becauſe when age hath ſeiz'd upon her dam,
And made unfit for flight, the gratefull young one
Takes her upon his back, provides her foode,
Repaying ſo, her tender care of him,
'Ere he was fit to fly, by bearing her:
Shall I then that have reaſon, and diſcourſe
That tell me all I can doe is too litle,
Be more unnaturall then a ſilly Bird?
Or feed or cloth my ſelfe ſuperfluouſly,
And know, nay ſee you want? holy Saints keepe me.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Can I be wretched,
And know my ſelfe the Mother to ſuch Goodnes?

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: Come, let us drie our eyes, wee'll have a Feaſt,
Thanks to our little Steward;

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: And in him,
Beleeve that we are rich.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I am ſure I am,
While I have power to comfort you, and ſerve you.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Is it my fault (Don Henrique) or my fate,
Wha'ts my offence? I came young to your Bed
I had a fruitfull Mother and you met me,
With equall ardour in your May of blood;
And why then am I barren?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: 'Tis not in Man
To yield a reaſon for the will of Heaven,
Which is inſcrutable.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: To what uſe ſerve
Full fortunes, and the meaner ſort of Bleſſings,
When that, which is the Crowne of all our wiſhes,
The period of humane happines,
One only Child that may poſſeſſe what's ours,
Is cruelly denide us?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: 'Tis the curſe,
Of great Eſtates to want thoſe Pledges which,
The poore are happy in: They in a Cottage,
With joy, behold the Modells of their youth,
And as their Roote decaies thoſe budding Branches,
Sprout forth and flouriſh, to renew their age;
But this is the beginning, not the end
To me, of, that miſery againſt my will,
(Since Heaven denies us Iſſue of our owne)
Muſt leave the fruit of all my care and travell
To an unthankfull Brother that inſults,
On my Calamity.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I will rather chooſe,
A Baſtard from the Hoſpitall and adopt him,
And nouriſh him, as mine owne.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Such an evaſion
(My Violante) is forbid to us;
Happy the Romane State, where it was lawfull,
(If our owne Sonnes were vicious) to chooſe one
Out of a vertuous Stock, though of poore Parents,
And make him noble. But the Lawes of Spaine,
(Intending to preſerve all ancient Houſes)
Prevent ſuch free elections; with this my Brothers
Too well acquainted, and this makes him bold to
Reigne 'ore me, as a Maſter,

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I will fire
The Portion I brought with me, 'ere he ſpend,
A Royall of it: No Quirck left? no Quiddit
That may defeate him?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Were I but confirmed,
That you would take the meanes I uſe, with patience,
As I muſt practiſe it with my diſhonour,
I could lay levell with the earth his hopes
That ſoare above the clouds with expectation
To ſee me to my grave.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Effect but this
And our revenge ſhall be to us a Son
That ſhall inherit for us.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Do not repent
When 'tis too late.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I feare not what may fall
He diſpoſeſſ'd that doe's uſurpe on all Exeunt.

div.head: Scena prima
div.stage: Enter Leandro (with a letter writ out) Milanes & Aſermo

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Can any thing, but wonder?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Wonder on,
I am as ye ſee, and what will follow Gentlemen

sp.speaker: Ars.
sp.l: Why doſt thou put on this form? what can this do?
Thou lookeſt moſt ſillily,

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Like a young Clerk
A half pin'd-puppy that would write for a Royall.
Is this a commanding ſhape to win a Beautie?
To what uſe, what occaſion?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Peace ye are fooles,
More ſilly then my out-ſide ſeems ye are ignorant
They that pretend to wonders muſt weave cunningly.

sp.speaker: Ars.
sp.l: What manner of acceſſe can this get? or if gotten
What credit in her eyes?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Will ye but leave me?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Me thinks a yong man and a handſom Gentleman
(But ſure thou art lunatick) me thinks a brave man
That would catch cunningly the beames of Beautie,
And ſo diſtribute 'em, unto his comfort,
Should like himſelf appeare young, high, and buxom.
And in the brighteſt form.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Ye are cozen'd (Gentlemen)
Neither doe I believe this, nor will follow it,
Thus I am, I will begin my voyage,
When you love, lanch it out in ſilks and velvets,
I le love in Serge, and will outgo our Sattins
To get upon my great horſe and appeare.
The ſigne of ſuch a man, and trot my meaſures,
Or fiddle out whole froſty nights (my friends)
Vnder the window, while my teeth keep tune,
I hold no handſomneſſe. Let me get in
There trot and fiddle where I may have faire play,

sp.speaker: Ars.
sp.l: But how get in?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Leave that to me, your patience,
I have ſome toyes here that I dare well truſt to:
I have ſmelt a Vicar out, the call him Lopez.
You are ne're the nearer now,

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: We do confeſſe it.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Weak ſimple men, this Vicar to this Lawyer
Is the moſt inward, Damon.

sp.speaker: Ars.
sp.l: What can this do?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: We know the fellow, and he dwells there.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: So.

sp.speaker: Ars.
sp.l: A poore, thin theef: he help? he; hang the Vicar
Can reading of an—preferre thee?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Thou art dead-ſick in love, and hee'l pray for thee
Have patience (Gentlemen) I ſay this Vicar,
This thing I ſay is all one with the Cloſe Bartolus
(For ſo they call the Lawyer) or his nature
Which I have ſtudied by relation;
And make no doubt I ſhall hit hanſomly,
Will I work cunningly and home: underſtand me.
Next I pray leave me, Leave me to my fortune
Difficilia pulchra, thats my Motto (Gentlemen)
I 'le win this Diamond from the rock and weare her
Or—

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Peace, the Vicar: ſend ye a full ſail, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ars.
sp.l: There's your Confeſſor, but what ſhal be your pennance? exit lea.
A fools head if I fail and ſo forſake me.
You ſhall heare from me daily.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: We will be ready,

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Thin world indeed:

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I'le let him breathe and mark him:
No man would think a ſtranger as I am
Should reap any great commodity from his pigbelly,

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Poore ſtirring for poore Vicars,
Diego And poore Sextons.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: We pray and pray, but to no purpoſe
Thoſe that enjoy our Lands, choak our Devotions.
Our poore thin ſtipends make us arrant dunces,

sp.speaker: Diego
sp.l: If you live miſerably, how ſhall we do (Maſter?)
That are fed only with the ſound of prayers?
We riſe and ring the Bells to get good ſtomacks.
And muſt be fain to eat the ropes with reverence,

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: When was there a Chriſtning (Diego?)

sp.speaker: Dieg.
sp.l: Not this ten weekes:
Alas, they have forgot to get children (Maſter)
The Warres, the Seas, and uſurie undoe us,
Takes off our minds, our edges, blunts our plough-ſhares,
They eat nothing here, but herbs, & get nothing but green ſauce:
There are ſome poore Labourers, that perhaps
Once in ſeven yeare, with helping one another,
Produce ſome few pind—Butter—prints, that ſcarce hold
The chriſtning neither.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Your Gallants, they get Honour,
A ſtrange fantaſticall Birth, to defraud the Vicar,
And the Camp Chriſtens their Iſſues, or the Curtizans,
'Tis a lewd time.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: They are ſo hard-hearted here too,
They will not dye, there's nothing got by Burialls.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Diego, the Ayre's too pure, they cannot periſh:
To have a thin Stipend, and an everlaſting Pariſh,
Lord what a torment 'tis!

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Good ſenſible Maſter,
You are allow'd to pray againſt all weathers,
(Both foule, and faire, as you ſhall find occaſion)
Why not againſt all ayres?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: That's not i'th' Canons,
I would it had, 'tis out of our way forty pence.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange, they are ſtarv'd too yet they wil not die here,
They will not Earth: a good ſtout plague amongſt 'um,
Or halfe a dozen new fantaſticall Fevers
That would turne up their heeles by whole-ſale (Maſter)
And take the Doctors too, in their grave Counſells,
That there might be no naturall help for money;
How merrily would my Bells goe then?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Peace Diego
The Doctors are our friends, let's pleaſe them well,
For though they kill but ſlow, they are certaine (Diego)
We muſt remove into a muddy Ayre,
A moſt contagious Clymat.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: We muſt certaine,
An ayre that is the nurſery of Agues,
Such Agues (Maſter) that will ſhake mens ſoules out,
Ne're ſtay for Poſſets, nor good old wives plaiſters.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Gowts and dead Palſies.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: The dead doe's well at all times,
Yet Gowts will hang an arſſe a long time (Maſter)
The Pox, or Engliſh Surfets if we had 'em;
Thoſe are nich Marle, they make a Church-yard fat,
And make the Sexton ſing, they never miſſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Then Wills and Funerall Sermons come in ſeaſon,
And Feaſts that makes us frolicke.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Would I could ſee' em.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And though I weepe i'th' Pulpit for my Brother,
Yet (Diego) here I laugh.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: The cauſe requires it.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Since people left to die I am dunce (Diego.)

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſtrange thing, I have forgot to dig too.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: A pretious pair of youths; I muſt make toward 'em

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Who's that? look out it ſeemes he would ſpeak to us.
I hope a Marriage, or ſome Wil to make (Diego.)

sp.speaker: Dieg.
sp.l: My friend your buſineſſe?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: 'Tis to that grave Gentleman;
Bleſſe your good learning (Sir)

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And bleſſe you alſo,
He beares a promiſing face, there's ſome hope toward.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I have a Letter to your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Well Sir,
From whence I pray you?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: From Nova Hiſpania, Sir,
And from an ancient friend of yours.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Tis well (Sir)
'Tis very well: the divell a-one I know there.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Take heed of a Snap (Sir) has a cozening countenance,
I doe not like his way.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Let him goe forward.
Cantabit Ʋacuus, They that have nothing, feare nothing,
All I have to looſe (Diego) is my learning,
And when he has gotten that, he may put it in a Nut ſhell,

body.p: SIgnior Lopez, Since my arrivall from Cordova to theſe parts I have written divers Letters unto you but as yet received no Anſwer of any (Good, and very good) And although ſo great a forgetfulneſſe might cauſe a want in my due correſpondence yet the deſire I have ſtill to ſerve you muſt more prevaile with me (Better and better: the divell a man know I yet) and therefore with the preſent occaſion offered I am willing to crave a continuance of the favours, which I have heretofore received from you and doe recommend my Son Leandro the Bearer to you with requeſt that he may be admitted in that Univerſitie till ſuch time as I ſhall arive at home; his ſtudies he will make you acquainted withall: This kindneſſe ſhall ſupply the want of your ſlackneſſe: And ſo heaven keep you.

sp.l: Alonzo Tiveria very well,
A very ancient friend of mine, I take it,
For till this houre I never heard his Name, yet.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: You looke (Sir) as if ye had forgot my Father.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: No, no, I look as I would remember him,
For that I never remembred, I cannot forget (Sir)

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: The ſame (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And now i'th' Indies?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: He may be any where,
For ought that I conſider.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Thinke againe (Sir)
You were Students both at one time in Salamanca,
And, as I take it, Chamber-fellowes.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Nay, ſure you muſt remember.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Would I could.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I have heard him ſay, you were Goſſips too.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Very likely,
You did not heare him ſay, to whom? for we Students
May often-times over-reach our memories,
Do'ſt thou remember (Diego) this ſame Signiour?
Thou haſt been mine theſe twenty yeares.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Remember?
Why this Fellow would make ye mad: Nova Hiſpania?
And Signiour Tiveria? what are theſe?
He may as well name ye Friends out of Cataya
Take heed I beſeech our worſhip: doe you heare, (my friend?)
You have no Letters for me?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Not any Letter,
But I was charged to doe my Fathers love
To the old honeſt Sexton Diego; are you he (Sir?)

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Ha? have I friends, and know'em not? my name is Diego,
But if either I remember you, or your Father,
Or Nova Hiſpania (I was never there Sir)
Or any kindred that you have — for heaven-ſake, Maſter,
Let's caſt about a little, and conſider,
We may dreame out our time.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: It ſeemes I am deceiv'd (Sir)
Yet, that you are Don Lopez all men tell me,
The Curat here, and have bin ſome time (ſir)
And you the Sexton Diego, ſuch I am ſent too,
The Letter tells as much: may be they are dead,
And you of the like names ſucceed: I thank ye gentlemen,
Ye have done honeſtly, in telling truth,
I might have bin forward els. For that Lopez
That was my Fathers friend, I had a charge,
(A charge of Money) to deliver (Gentlemen)
Five hundred Duckets, a poore ſmall gratuity,
But ſince you are not he, good ſir, let me thinke,
I pray ye be patient.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Pray ye ſtay a little,
Nay, let me remember, I beſeech ye ſtay, Sir.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: An honeſt noble friend, that ſends ſo lovingly;
An old friend too; I ſhall remember ſure, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Thou ſayſt true Diego.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: 'Pray ye conſider quickly,
Doe, doe, by any meanes, me thinkes already
A grave ſtaid gentleman comes to my memory.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: He's old indeed, ſir.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: With a goodly white Beard,
(For now he muſt be ſo: I know he muſt be)
Signior Alonzo, (Maſter.)

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I begin to have him.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: 'Has bin from hence, about ſome twenty years (ſir.)

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Som five and twenty (ſir.)

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: You ſay moſt true (ſir)
Juſt to an houre; 'tis now juſt five and twenty,
A ſine ſtraite timber'd man, and a brave ſouldier,
He married: let me ſee, —

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: De Caſtro's Daughter.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: The very ſame.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Thou art a very Raſcall,
De Caſtro is the Turke to thee, or any thing:
The Money rubbs 'em into ſtrange remembrances,
For as many Duckets more they wou d remember Adam.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Give me your hand, you are welcome to your countrey,
Now I remember plainly, manifeſtly,
As freſhly, as if yeſterday I had ſeene him,
Moſt heartily welcome, ſinfull that I am,
Moſt ſinfull man, why ſhould I looſe this Gentleman?
This loving old Companion? we had all one ſoule, ſir,
He dwelt here hard by, at a handſome—

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Farme ſir,
You ſay moſt true.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Lord, Lord, that time ſhould play the treacherous knave thus?
Why, he was the onely friend, I had in Spaine (ſir)
I knew your Mother too, a handſome Gentlewoman,
She was married very young: I married 'em:
I doe remember now the Maskes and Sports then,
The Fire-workes, and the fine delights; good faith, ſir,
Now I looke in your face, whoſe eies are thoſe Diego?
Nay, if he be not juſt Alonzo's picture—

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Lord how I bluſh for theſe two impudents?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Well Gentleman, I thinke your name's Leandro;

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: It is indeed (ſir)
Gra'-mercy Letter, thou hadſt never knowne els.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I have dandled ye, and kiſt ye and plaid with ye
A hundred, and a hundred times, and danc'd ye,
And ſwong ye in my Bell-ropes, ye lov'd ſwinging.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A ſweet Boy.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Sweet lying knaves.
What would theſe doe for thouſands?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A wondrous ſweet Boy then it was, ſee now
Time that conſumes us, ſhoots him up ſtill ſweeter.
How do's the noble Gentleman? how fares he?
When ſhall we ſee him? when will he bleſſe his Country?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: O, very ſhortly, ſir, till his returne,
He has ſent me over to your charge.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And welcome,
Nay, you ſhall know you are welcome to your friend, ſir,

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: And to my Study (ſir) which muſt be the Law,
To further which, he would entreat your care
To plant me in the favour of ſome man
That's expert in that knowledge: for his paines
I have three hundred Duckets more: For my Diet,
Enough (ſir) to defray me: which I am charged
To take ſtill, as I uſe it, from your cuſtodie,
I have the money ready, and I am weary.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Sit down, ſit down, and once more ye are moſt welcome,
The Law you have hit upon moſt happily,
Here is a Maſter in that Art, Bartolus,
A neighbour by, to him I will preferre ye,
A learned man, and my moſt loving Neighbour,
I'll doe ye faithfull ſervice (ſir.)

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: He's an Aſſe,
And ſo wee'll uſe him; he ſhall be a Lawyer.

sp.speaker: Lo.
sp.l: But if ever he recover this mony again: before Diego.
And get ſome pretty pittance: my Pupill's hungry.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Pray ye Sir, unlade me.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I'le refreſh ye Sir;
When ye want, you know your Exchequer.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: If all this get me but acceſſe, I am happy.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Come, I am tender of ye,

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I'll goe with ye,
To have this Fort betray'd theſe fooles muſt fliece me.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: My Amaranta, a retir'd ſweet life,
Private and cloſe, and ſtill, and houſwifely.
Becomes a Wife, ſets off the grace of woman
At home to be beleev'd both young, and handſome,
As Lil • ies that are caſde in chriſtall Glaſſes,
Makes up the wonder: ſhew it abroad, 'tis ſtale,
And ſtill and the more eyes cheapen it, 'tis more ſlubberd,
And what need windowes open to inviting?
Or evening Tarraſſes, to take opinions?
When the moſt wholſome Ayre (my wife) blowes inward,
When good thoughts are the nobleſt Campanions,
And old chaſt ſtories (wife) the beſt diſcourſes;
But why doe I talke thus, that know thy nature?

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: You know your own diſeaſe: diſtruſt, & jealouſies,
And thoſe two, give theſe Leſſons, not good meaning,
What triall is there of my honeſtie,
When I am mew'd at home? to what end, Husband,
Serves all the vertvous thoughts, and chaſt behaviours
Without their uſes? Then they are known moſt excellent
When, by their contraries the are ſet off, and burniſh'd,
If ye both hold me faire, and chaſt, and vertuous,
Let me goe feareleſſe out, and win that greatneſſe;
Theſe Seeds grow not to Shades, and conceal'd places
Set 'em i'th' heat of all, then they riſe glorious.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Peace, ye are too ſoude.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: You are too covetous,
If that be rank'd a vertue, you have a rich one,
Set me (like other Lawyers wives) off handſomely,
Attended as I ought, and as they have it,
My Coach, my people, and my handſome women,
My will, in honeſt things.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Peace Amaranta:

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: They have content, rich clothes, and that ſecures 'em,
Bindes, to their carefull Husbands, their obſervance,
They are merry, ride abroad, meet, laugh,

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt too:

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: And freely may converſe with proper Gentlemen,
Suffer temptations daily to their honour.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You are now too far again: thou ſhalt have any thing,
Let me but lay up for a handſome Office,
And then my Amaranta —

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: Here's a thing now,
Ye place as pleaſure to me: all my retinue,
My Chamber-maid, my Kitchin-maid, my friend,
And what ſhe failes in, I muſt doe my ſelfe.
A ſoyle to ſet my Beauty off, I thanke ye,
You will place the Devill next for a Companion,

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: No more ſuch words (good wife)
What would you have (Maid?)

sp.speaker: Moor.
sp.l: Maſter Curate, and the Sexton, & a ſtranger (ſir)
Attend to ſpeake with your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: A ſtranger?

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: You had beſt to be jealous of the man you know not.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Pree thee no more of that.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: 'Pray ye goe out to 'em,
That will be ſafeſt for ye, I am well here,
I onely love your peace, and ſerve like a ſlave for it.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: No, no, thou ſhalt not; 'tis ſome honeſt Client,
Rich, and litigious, the Curate has brought to me,
Pre'thee goe in (my Duck) I'll but ſpeake to 'em,
And returne inſtantly.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: I am commanded,
One day you will know my ſufferance.— Exit.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And reward it.
So, ſo, faſt bind, faſt find; Come in my Neighbours,
My loving Neighbours pray ye come in, ye are welcome,

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Bleſſe your good reverence.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Good-day, good Maſter Curate,
And neighbour Diego, welcome: what's your buſineſſe?
And 'pray ye be ſhort (good friends) the time is pretious,
Welcome, good ſir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: To be ſhort then with your Maſterſhip.
(For I know your ſeverall houres, are full of buſineſſe)
We have brought ye this young-man, of honeſt parents,
And of an honeſt face.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: It ſeemes ſo (Neighbours)
But to what end?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: To be your Pupill (Sir)
Your Servant, if you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I have travell'd far, ſir.
To ſeeke a worthy man,

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Alas, good Gentleman,
I am a poore man, and a private too,
Unfit to keep a Servant of your Reckoning;
My houſe a little Cottage, and ſcarce able
To hold my ſelfe, and thoſe poore few live under it;
Beſides, you muſt not blame me Gentleman,
If I were able to receive a Servant,
To be a little ſcrupulous of his dealing
For in theſe times—

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Pray let me anſwer that (ſir)
Here is fiue hundred Duckets, to ſecure him,
He cannot want (ſir) to make good his credit,
Good gold, and coyne.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And thats an honeſt pledge;
Yet ſure, that needs not, for his face, and carriage,
Seeme to declare an in-bred honeſty,

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: And for I have a ripe mind to the Law (ſir)
(In which I underſtand you live a Maſter)
The leaſt poore corner in your houſe, poore Bed (ſir)
(Let me not ſeeme intruding to your Worſhip)
With ſome Books to inſtruct me, and your Counſell,
Shall I reſt moſt content with: other Acquaintance
Then your grave preſence, and the grounds of Law
I dare not covet, nor I will not ſeeke (ſir)
For ſurely mine owne nature deſires privacie.
Next, for your monthly paines (to ſhew my thanks,)
I doe proportion out ſome twenty Duckets;
As I grow riper, more: three hundred now (ſir)
To ſhew my love to learning, and my Maſter,
My diet, I'll defray too, without trouble.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Note but his mind to learning.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: I do ſtrangely, yes, and I like it too, thankes to his money.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Would he would live with me, and learn to dig too.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A wondrous modeſt man (ſir.)

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: So it ſeemes,
His deare love to his Studie muſt be nouriſh'd
Neighbour, he's like to prove.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: With your good counſell,
And with your diligence, as you will ply him;
His Parents, when they know your care—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Come hither;

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: An honeſter young man, your worſhip ne're kept,
But he is ſo baſhfull—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: O I like him better,
Say I ſhould undertake ee, which indeed (ſir)
Will be no little ſtraightneſſe to my living,
Conſidering my Affaires, and my ſmall houſe (ſir)
For I ſee ſome promiſes that pull me to ye;
Could you content your ſelfe, at firſt thus meanly,
To lye hard, in an out —part of my houſe (ſir?)
For I have not many Lodgings to allow ye;
And ſtudie ſhould be ſtill remote from company;
A little fire ſometimes too, to refreſh ye;
A Student muſt be frugall: ſometimes Lights too,
According to your labour.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Any thing (ſir)
That's dry, and wholſome: I am no bred-wanton.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Then I receive you: but I muſt deſire ye
To keep within your confines.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Ever ſir,
There's the Gold, and ever be your ſervant,
Take it and give me Bookes: may I but prove (ſir)
According to my wiſh, and theſe ſhall multiply.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Do, ſtudy hard, pray ye take him in, and ſettle him,
He's onely fit for you; Shew him his Cell (ſir.)

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Take a good heart; and when ye are a cunning Lawyer,
I'le ſell my Bells and you ſhall prove it lawfull,

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: Come, ſir, with me: neighbors I thank your diligence.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I'l come ſometimes, and crack a caſe with ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Welcome — Exit.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Here's mony got with eaſe: here, ſpend that jovially,
And pray for the Foole, the Founder.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Many more Fooles
I heartily pray may follow his example,
Lawyers, or Lubbers, or of what condition,
And many ſuch ſweet friends in Nova Hiſpania.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: It will do well; Let 'em but ſend their moneys,
Come from what quarter of the world, I care not,
I'll know 'em inſtantly; nay I'll be a kin to 'em;
I cannot miſſe a man, that ſends me money:
Let him Law there, long as his Duckets laſt, Boy,
I'll grace him, and prefer him.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I'l turn Trade (Maſter) and now live by the living
Let the dead ſtinke, 'tis a poore ſtinking Trade.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: If the young Foole now
Should chance to chop upon his faire Wife (Diego.)

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: And handle her Caſe (Maſter) that's a law point,
A point would make him ſtart, and put on his Spectacles
A hidden point, were worth the canvaſſing.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Now ſurely, ſurely, I ſhould love him (Diego)
And love him heartily: nay, I ſhould love my ſelfe,
Or any thing that had but that good fortune,
For to ſay truth the Lawyer is a dog-bolt,
An arrant worme: and though I call him worſhipfull,
I wiſh him a canoniz'd Cuckold (Diego)
Now, if my youth doe dub him—

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: He is too demure (ſir.)

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: If he do ſting her home.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: There's no ſuch matter,
The woman was not borne to ſo much bleſſedneſſe,
He has no heate: ſtudy conſumes his oyle (Maſter,)

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Let's leave it to the will of Fate, and preſently
Over a cup of luſtie Sack, let's prophecie.
I am like a man that dreampt he was an Emperour,
Come Diego, hope, & whilſt he laſts, we'll lay it on. Exit.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Angelo, Millanes, did you ſee this wonder?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: And you Arſenio?

sp.speaker: Ar •
sp.l: Yes he's gon (Sir)
Strangely disguis'd, he's ſet upon his voyage.
Love guide his thoughts: he's a brave honeſt fellow,
Sit cloſe Don Lawyer, ô that arrant knave now,
How he will ſtinke, will ſmoake againe, will burſt:
He's the moſt arrant Beaſt.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: He may be more beaſt.

sp.speaker: Ja,
sp.l: Let him beare ſix, and ſix, that all may blaze him,
The villany he has ſowed into my Brother,
And from his State the Revenue he has reach'd at:
Pay him, my good Leandro, take my praiers.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: And all our wiſhes plough with his fine white heifer.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Marke him (my deare Friend) for a famous Cuckold,
Let it out-live his Bookes, his paines, and heare me,
The more he ſeeks to ſmother it with Juſtice, Enter a Servant.
Let it blaze out the more: what news Andrea?

sp.speaker: Andr.
sp.l: Newes I am loth to tell ye: but I am charg'd (Sir)
Your Brother layes a ſtrict command upon ye,
No more to know his houſe, upon our danger,
I am ſorry (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: 'Faith never be: I am glad on't,
He keepes the houſe of pride, and foolery:
I meane to ſhun it: ſo returne my Anſwer,
'Twill ſhortly ſpew him out; Come, let's be merry,
And lay our heads together, carefully
How we may helpe our friend; and let's lodge neare him,
Be ſtill at hand: I would not for my patrimony,
But he ſhould crown his Lawyer, a learned Monſter,
Come, let's away I am ſtark mad till I ſee him. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: Why, will ye bring men in, and yet be jealous?
Why will ye lodge a young man, a man able,
And yet repine?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He ſhall not trouble thee (Sweet)
A modeſt poore ſlight thing, did I not tell thee
He was onely given to the Booke, and for that
How royally he paies? finds his owne meat too.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I will not have him here: I know your courſes,
And what fits you will fall into of madneſſe.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Y'faith, I will not Wife,

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I will not try ye,

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He comes not neare thee: ſhall not dare to tread
Within thy Lodgings, in an old out-Roome
Where Logs, and Coles were layd.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Now ye lay fire; Fire to conſume your quiet.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Didſt thou know him,
Thou wouldſt thinke as I doe: he diſquiet thee?
Thou mayſt weare him next thy heart, & yet not warme him,
His mind (poore man) 's o'th' Law, how to live after,
And not on lewdneſſe: on my conſcience
He knowes not how to looke upon a woman
More then by reading what Sex ſhe is.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I doe not like it (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Do'ſt thou not ſee (Foole)
What preſents he ſends hourely in his gratefulneſſe?
What delicate meates?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You had beſt truſt him at your Table,
Doe and repent it doe.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: If thou be'ſt willing,
By my troth, I thinke he might come, he's ſo modeſt,
He never ſpeakes: there's part of that he gave me,
He'll eat but halfe a dozen bits, and riſe immediatly,
Even as he eats, he ſtudies: he'll not diſquiet thee,
Doe as thou pleaſeſt (Wife.)

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: What means this Wood-cocke? Knock within.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: Retire (Sweet) there's one knocks: come in, your buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: My Lord Don Henrique, would entreat ye, Sir,
To come immediatly, and ſpeake with him,
He has buſineſſe of ſome moment.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'll attend him,
I muſt be gon: I pre'thee thinke the beſt (wife)
At my returne I'll tell thee more, good morrow;
Sir, keep ye cloſe, and ſtudy hard: an houre hence
I'll read a new Caſe to ye:— Exit. Leandro within.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I'll be ready. Enter Amaranta.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: So many hundred Duckets, to ly ſcurvily?
And learne the pelting law? this ſounds but ſlenderly,
But very poorely: I would ſee this fellow
Very faine ſee him, how he lookes: I will find
To what end, and what ſtudy: there's the place:
I'll goe o'th' other ſide, and take my Fortune;
I think there is a window. Exit. Enter Leandro.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: He's gone out
Now, if I could but ſee her: ſhe is not this way:
How naſtily he keepes his houſe? my Chamber,
If I continue long, will choak me up,
It is ſo damp: I ſhall be mortifide
For any woman, if I ſtay a moneth here:
I'll in, and ſtrike my Lute, that ſound may call her. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: He keeps very cloſe: Lord, how I long to ſee him:
A Lute ſtrooke handſomely, a voice too; I'll heare that:
Theſe Verſes are no Law, they ſound too ſweetly,
Now I am more deſirous. (Leandro peeping.)

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe certain.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: What's that that peeps?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: O, admirable face!

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Sure 'tis the man.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I will goe out a little.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Hee lookes not like a foole, his face is noble:
How ſtill he ſtands?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I am ſtrucken dumb, with wonder,
Sure all the Excellence of Earth dwells here.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: How pale he looks? yet how his eies like torches,
Fling their beames round: how manly his face ſhewes?
He comes on: ſurely he will ſpeak: he is made moſt handſomly:
This is no Clerk behaviour; Now I have ſeen ye,
I'l take my time: husbād ye have brought home tinder. Ex

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Sure ſhe has transform'd me,
I had forgot my tongue cleane,
I never ſaw a face yet, but this rare one,
But I was able boldly to encounter it,
And ſpeak my mind, my lips were lock upon me,
This is divine, and onely ſerv'd with reverence;
O moſt faire cover, of a hand far fairer,
Thou bleſſed Innocence, that gaurds that whiteneſs,
Live next my heart. I am glad I have got a relick, A noiſe within.
A relick when I pray to it, may work wonders.
Harke, there s ſome noyſe: I muſt retire againe.
This bleſſed Apparition, makes me happy;
I'll ſuffer, and I'll ſacrifice my ſubſtance.
But I'll enjoy: now ſoftly to my Kennell. Exit.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: You know my cauſe ſufficiently?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I doe (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: And though it will impaire my honeſty,
And ſtrike deep at my Credit, yet (my Bartolus)
There being no other evaſion left to free me
From the vexation of my ſpightfull Brother,
That moſt inſultingly raignes over me,
I muſt and will goe forward.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Doe (my Lord)
And looke not after credit, we ſhall cure that,
Your bended honeſtie, we ſhall ſet right (Sir)
We Surgeons of the Law, doe deſperate cures (Sir)
And you ſhall ſee how heartily I'll handle it:
Marke how I'll knock it home: be of good cheare (Sir)
You give good Fees, and thoſe beget good Cauſes,
The prerogative of your crownes will carry the matter,
(Carry it ſheere) The Aſſiſtant fits to morrow,
And he's your friend, your monied men love naturally,
And as your loves are cleare, ſo are your Cauſes.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: He ſhall not want for that.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: No, no, he muſt not,
Line your Cauſe warmly (Sir) the times are Aguiſh,
That holds a Plea in heart; hang the penurious,
Their Cauſes (like their purſes) have poore Iſſues.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: That way, I was ever bountifull.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Tis true (Sir)
That makes ye fear'd forces the Snakes to kneele to ye,
Live full of money, and ſupply the Lawyer,
And take your choice of what mans lands you pleaſe (Sir)
What pleaſures, or what profits; what revenges,
They are all your owne: I muſt have witneſſes
Enough, and ready.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: You ſhall not want (my Bartolus.)

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Subſtantiall fearleſs ſoules, that wil ſwear ſuddenly,
That will ſweare any thing.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: They ſhall ſweare truth too.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: That's no great matter: for varietie
They may ſweare truth, els 'tis not much look'd after:
I will ſerve Proceſſe, preſently, and ſtrongly
Upon your Brother, and Octavio,
Jacintha and the Boy; provide your proofes (Sir)
And ſet 'em fairely off, be ſure of Witneſſes,
Though they coſt money, want no ſtore of witneſſes,
I have ſeen a handſome Cauſe, ſo fowly loſt (Sir,)
So beaſtly caſt away for want of Witneſſes.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: There ſhall want nothing.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Then be gone, be provident,
Send to the Judge, a ſecret way: you have me,
And let him underſtand the heart.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I ſhall (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And feele the pulſes ſtrongly beat, I'll ſtudy,
And at my houre, but mark me, goe, be happy,
Goe and beleeve i'th' Law.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I hope 'twill helpe me. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Lopez, Diego and foure Pariſhioners and Singers.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Nea'r talke to me, I will not ſtay amongſt ye,
Debauſh'd and ignorant lazie knaves I found ye,
And fooles I leave ye, I have taught theſe twenty yeares,
Preacht ſpoon-meat to ye, that a child might ſwallow,
Yet ye are Block-heads ſtill: what ſhould I ſay to ye?
Ye have neither faith, nor money left to ſave ye,
Am I a fit companion for ſuch Beggers?

sp.p: If the Shepheard will ſuffer the ſheep to be ſcab'd (ſir)

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: No, no, ye are rotten.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Would they were, for my ſake.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I have nointed ye, and tar'd ye with my doctrine,
And yet the murren ſticks to ye, yet ye are mangy,
I will avoid ye. Two chaires ſet out.
Pray ye (Sir) be not angry,
In the pride of your new Caſſock, doe not part with us,
We doe acknowledge ye a carefull Curat,
And one that ſeldome troubles us with Sermons,
A ſhort ſlice of a Reading ſerves us (Sir)
We doe acknowledge ye a quiet Teacher,
Before You'll vex your Audience, you'll ſleep with 'em,
And that's a loving thing.
We grant ye (Sir)
The onely benefactor to our Rowling,
To all our merry Sports, the firſt provoker,
And at our Feaſts we know there is no reaſon,
But you that edifie us moſt, ſhould eat moſt.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I will not ſtay for all this, ye ſhall know me
A man borne to a more beſeeming fortune
Then ringing all-in, to a rout of Dunces.
We will increaſe your Tithes, you ſhall have Egs too,
Though they may prove moſt dangerous to our Iſſues.
I am a Smith; yet thus far out of my love
You ſhall have the tenth horſe I prick, to pray for,
I am ſure I prick five hundred in a yeare (Sir.
I am a Cooke a man of a dride conſcience,
Yet thus far I relent: you ſhall have tith porrage.

sp.p: Your ſtipend ſhal be rais'd too (good neighbour Diego.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Would ye have me ſpeak for ye? I am more angry
Ten times more vex'd not to be pacified:
No there be other places for poore Sextons
Places of profit (Friends) fine ſtirring places,
And people that know how to uſe our Offices,
Know what they were made for: I ſpeak for ſuch Capons?
Ye ſhall find the Key o'th' Church,
Under the doore (Neighbours,)
You may goe in, and drive away the dawes.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: My Surpleſſe, with one ſleeve, you ſhall find there,
For to that dearth of Linnen, you have driven me;
And the old Cutworke Cope, that hangs by gymitrie:
Pray ye turne em carefully, they are very tender:
The remnant of the Books, lie where they did (Neighbours)
Half puft away with the Church-wardens pipings.
Such ſmoaky zeales they have againſt hard places,
The poore-mans Box is there too: if ye find any thing
Beſide the poſie, and that halfe rub'd out too,
For feare it ſhould awake too much charitie
Give it to pious uſes, that is, ſpend it:

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: The Bell-ropes, they are ſtrong enough to hang ye,
So we bequeath ye to your deſtiny.
'Pray ye be not ſo haſtie.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I'll ſpeake a proud word to ye,
Would ye have us ſtay?
We doe moſt hearilty pray ye.
I'll draw as mighty drinke (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A ſtrong motive,
The ſtronger ſtill the more ye come unto me.
And I'll ſend for my Daughter:

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: This may ſtir too:
The Maiden is of age, and muſt be edified.
You ſhall have any thing: looſe our learned Vicar?
And our moſt conſtant friend; honeſt deare Diego?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Yet all this will not do: I'll tell ye (Neighbours)
And tell ye true: if ye will have us ſtay,
If you will have the comforts of our companies,
You ſhall be bound to doe us right in theſe points,
You ſhall be bound, and this the obligation,
Dy when 'tis fit, that we may have fit duties,
And doe not ſeeke to draw—out our undoings,
Marry tryde women, that are free, and fruitfull,
Get children in abundance, for your Chriſtnings,
Or ſuffer to be got, 'tis equall juſtice,

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Let Weddings, Chriſtnings, Churchings, Funerals,
And merry Goſſippings goe round, go round ſtill,
Round as a Pig, that we may find the profit.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: And let your old men fall ſick handſomely:
And dy immediatly, their Sonnes may ſhoot up:
Let women dy oth' ſullens too, 'tis naturall,
But be ſure their Daughters be of age firſt,
That they may ſtock us ſtill: your queazie young wives
That periſh undeliver'd, I am vext with,
And vext abundantly, it much concernes me,
There's a childes buriall loſt, looke that be mended.

sp.speaker: Lo.
sp.l: Let 'em be brought to bed, then dy when they pleaſe,
Theſe things conſidered (Country-men) and ſworne to
All theſe, and all our ſports againe, and gambolls.
We muſt dy, and we muſt live, and we'll be merry,
Every man ſhall be rich by one another.
We are here to morrow, and gone to day: for my part
If getting children can be-friend my Neighbours,
I'll labour hard but I will fill your Font (Sir.)
I have a Mother now, and an old Father,
They are as ſure your own, within theſe two moneths—
My Siſter muſt be prayd for too, ſhe is deſperate,
Deſperate in love.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Keepe, deſperate men farre from her,
Then 'twill goe hard: doe you ſee how melancholy?
Doe you marke the man? do you profeſſe ye love him?
And would doe any thing to ſtay his fury?
And are ye unprovided to refreſh him,
To make him know your loves? fie Neighbours,
We'll doe any thing,
We have brought Muſick to appeaſe his ſpirit,
And the beſt Song we'll give him.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Pray ye ſit down (Sir)
They know their duties now, and they ſtand ready
To tender their beſt mirth.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Tis well, proceed Neighbours,
I am glad I have brought ye to underſtand good manners,
Ye had Puritan hearts a-while, ſpurn'd at all paſtimes,
But I ſee ſome hope now.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: We are ſet proceed Neighbours.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: What ayles this Prieſt? how highly the thing takes it?

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Lord how it looks? has he not bought ſome Prebend?
Leandro's money, makes the Raſcall merry,
Merry at heart; he ſpies us.

sp.speaker: Lo.
sp.l: Be gon Neighbours, The Bar & Book ready on a Table.
Here are ſome Gentlemen: be gone good Neighbours,
Be gon, and labour to redeeme my favour,
No more words but be gon: theſe two are Gentlemen,
No company for cruſty-handed fellowes.

sp.speaker: Dieg.
sp.l: We will ſtay for a yeare or two, and trie ye:

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Fill all your hearts with joy, we will ſtay with ye,
Be gone no more; I take your paſtimes graciouſly:
Would ye with me (My friends?)

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: We would looke upon ye,
For me-thinks ye looke lovely.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Ye have no Letters?
Nor any kind Remembrances?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Remembrances?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: From Nova Hiſpania, or ſome part remote (Sir)
You looke like travell'd men: may be ſome old friends
That happily I have forgot; ſome Signeours
In China, or Cataya; ſome Companions—

sp.speaker: Dieg.
sp.l: In the Mogulls Court, or elſe-where.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: They are mad ſure.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Ye came not from Peru? doe they look (Diego)
As if they had ſome miſtery about 'em?
Another Don Alonzo now?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I marry,
And ſo much money, Sir, from one you know not,
Let it be who it will.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: They have gracious favours.
Would ye be private?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: There's no need on't (Sir)
We come to bring ye a Remembrance from a Merchant.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Tis very well, 'tis like I know him.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: No. ſir,
I doe not thinke ye doe.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A new miſtake (Diego)
Let's carry it decently.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: We come to tell ye,
You have received great ſummes from a young Factor
They call Leandro, that has rob'd his Maſter,
Rob'd him, and run away.

sp.speaker: Dieg.
sp.l: Let's keep cloſe (Maſter)
This newes comes from a cold Country.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: By my faith it freezes,

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Is not this true? doe you ſhrink now (good man Curate)
Doe I not touch ye?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: We have a hundred Duckets
Yet left, we doe beſeech ye ſir—

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: You'll hang both.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: One may ſuffice.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I will not hang alone (Maſter)
I had the leaſt part, you ſhall hang the higheſt.
Plague o' this Tiveria, and the Letter,
The divell ſent it poſt, to pepper us,
From Nova Hiſpania we ſhall hang at home now.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: I ſee ye are penitent, and I have compaſſion:
Ye are ſecure both; doe but what we charge ye,
Ye ſhall have more gold too, and he ſhall give it,
Yet ne're indanger ye.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Command us (Maſter)
Command us preſently, and ſee how nimbly —

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: And if we doe not handſomely endeavour —

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Goe home and till ye heare more keep private,
Till we appeare againe, no words, (Vicar)
There's ſomething added.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: For you too.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: We are ready.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Goe, and expect us hourely, if ye falter,
Though ye had twenty lives—

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: We are fit to looſe 'em.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt expedient that we ſhould hang both.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: If we be hang'd, we cannot blame our fortune.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Farewell, and be your owne friends.

sp.speaker: Lop,
sp.l: We expect ye. — Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.p: We cited to the Court! A Bar. Table-booke, 2 chairs, & paper ſtandiſh ſet out.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: It is my wonder,

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: But not our fear, (Iacintha) wealthy men
That have Eſtates to looſe, whoſe conſcious thoughts
Are full of inward guilt, may ſhake with horrour,
To have their Actions ſifted or appeare
Before the Judge. But we that know our ſelves
As innocent, as poore, that have no Fleece
On which the Talons of the griping Law
Can take ſure hold, may ſmile with ſcorne on all
That can be urg'd againſt us.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: I am confident
There is no man ſo covetous, that deſires
To raviſh our wants from us, and leſſe hope
There can be ſo much Juſtice left on earth,
(Though ſude and call'd upon) to eaſe us of
The burthen of our wrongs.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: What thinkes Aſcanio?
Should we be call'd in queſtion or accus'd
Unjuſtly, what would you doe to redeeme us,
From tirannous oppreſſion?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I could pray
To him that ever has an open eare
To heare the innocent, and right their wrongs;
Nay, by my troth, I thinke I could out plead
An Advocate, and ſweat as much as he
Do's for a double Fee, ere you ſhould ſuffer
In an honeſt cauſe.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: Happy ſimplicitie!

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: My deareſt, and my beſt one: Don Iamie,

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: And the Advocate, that caus'd us to be ſummond.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: My Lord is mov'd, I ſee it in his lookes,
And that man, in the Gowne, in my opinion
Lookes like a proaguing knave.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Peace, give them leave.

sp.speaker: Iam.
sp.l: Serve me with Proceſſe?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: My Lord, you are not lawleſſe.

sp.speaker: Iam.
sp.l: Nor thou honeſt;
One, that not long ſince was the buckram Scribe,
That would run on mens errands for an Aſpe • ,
And from ſuch baſeneſſe, having rais'd a Stock
To bribe the covetous Judge, call'd to the Bar,
So poore in practiſe too, that you would plead
A needy Clyents Cauſe, for a ſtarv'd hen,
Or halfe a little loyn of Veale, though fly blowne,
And theſe, the greateſt Fees you could arrive at
For juſt proceedings; but ſince you turn'd Raſcall —

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Good words, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Iam.
sp.l: And grew my Brothers Bawd
In all his vitious courſes, ſoothing him
In his diſhoneſt practiſes, you are growne
The rich, and eminent knave, in the divels name,
What am I cited for?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You ſhall know anon,
And then too late repent this bitter language,
Or I'll miſſe of my ends.

sp.speaker: Iam.
sp.l: Wer't not in Court,
I would beat that fat of thine, rais'd by the food
Snatch'd from poore Clyents mouthes, into a jelly:
I would (my man of Law) but I am patient,
And would obey the Judge.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Tis your beſt courſe:
Would every enemy I have would beat me,
I would wiſh no better Action.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: 'Save your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: My numble ſervice.

sp.speaker: Iam.
sp.l: My good Boy, how doſt thou?
Why art thou call'd into the Court?

div.stage: Enter Aſſiſtant, Henrique, Officer, and Witneſſes.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I know not,
But 'tis my Lord the Aſſiſtants pleaſure
I ſhould attend here.

sp.speaker: Iam.
sp.l: He will ſoone reſolve us.

sp.speaker: Offi.
sp.l: Make way there for the Judge.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: How? my kind Brother?
Nay then 'tis ranck: there is ſome villany towards.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: 'Tis Seſſions purchas'd at our ſuit, Don Henrique,
Hath brought us hither, to heare and determine
Of what you can prefer.

sp.speaker: Henrique.
sp.l: I doe beſeech
The honourable Court, I may be heard
In my Advocate.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: 'Tis granted.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: humh, humh.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: That preface
If left out in a Lawyer, ſpoyles the Cauſe,
Though ne're ſo good, and honeſt.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: If I ſtood here,
To plead in the defence of an ill man,
(Moſt equall Judge) or to accuſe the innocent
(To both which, I profeſſe my ſelfe a ſtranger)
It would be requiſite I ſhould deck my Language
With Tropes and Figures, and all flouriſhes
That grace a Rethorician, 'tis confeſs'd
Adulterate Mettals, need the Gold-ſmiths Art,
To ſet 'em off; what, in it ſelfe is perfect
Contemnes a borrowed gloſſe: This Lord (my Client)
Whoſe honeſt cauſe, when 'tis related truly,
Will challenge Juſtice, finding in his conſcience
A tender ſcruple of a fault long ſince
By him committed, thinkes it not ſufficient
To be abſolv'd of't, by his Confeſſor,
If that in open Court, he publiſh nor
What was ſo long conceal'd.

sp.speaker: Iam.
sp.l: To what tends this?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: In his young yeares (it is no miracle
That youth, and heat of Blood, ſhould mix together)
He look'd upon this woman, on whoſe face
The ruines yet remaine of excellent forme,
He look'd on her, and lov'd her.

sp.speaker: Iac:
sp.l: You good Angels,
What an impudence is this?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And us'd all meanes
Of Service, Courtſhip, Preſents, that might win her
To be at his devotion: but in vaine
Her maiden Fort impregnable held out
Untill he promis'd Marriage; and before
Theſe Witneſſes a ſolemne Contract paſs'd
To take her as his wife.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Give them their oath.

sp.speaker: Iam.
sp.l: They are incompetent Witneſſes, his own Creatures,
And will ſweare any thing for halfe a royall.

sp.speaker: Off.
sp.l: Silence.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Proceed.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Upon this ſtrong aſſurance
He did enjoy his wiſhes to the full,
Which ſatisfied and then with eyes of Judgement
(Had winck'd with luſt before) conſidering duly
The inequality of the Match, he being
Nobly deſcended, and allyed, but ſhe
Without a name, or Family, ſecretly
He purchas'd a Divorce, to diſanull
His former Contract, marrying openly
The Lady Violante.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: As you ſit here
The Deputy of the great King, who is
The Subſtitute of that impartiall Judge
With whom, or Wealth, or titles prevaile nothing,
Grant to a much wrong'd Widow, or a Wife
Your patience, with liberty to ſpeake
In her owne Cauſe, and let me face to face
To this bad man, deliver what he is:
And if my wrongs, with his ingratitude ballanc'd,
Move not compaſſion, let me die unpittied;
His teares, his oathes, his perjuries, I paſſe o're
To thinke of them is a diſeaſe; but death
Should I repeat them. I dare not deny,
(For Innocence cannot juſtifie what's falſe)
But all the Advocate hath alleadged concerning
His falſhood and my ſhame in my conſent,
To be moſt true: But now I turne to thee,
To thee Don Henrique, and if impious Acts
Have left thee blood enough to make a bluſh,
I'll paint it on thy cheekes. Was not the wrong
Sufficient to defeat me of mine honour,
To leave me full of ſorrow, as of want,
The witneſſe of thy luſt, left in my womb,
To teſtifie thy falſhood, and my ſhame?
But now ſo many yeares I had conceal'd
Thy moſt inhumane wickedneſſe, and won
This Gentleman, to hide it from the world
To Father what was thine (for yet by heaven,
Though in the City, he pas'd for my husband,
He never knew me as his wife)

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange:
Give him an Oath.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: I gladly ſweare, and truly.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: After all this (I ſay) when I had borne
Theſe wrongs, with Saint-like patience ſaw another
Freely enjoy, what was (in Juſtice) mine,
Yet ſtill ſo tender of thy reſt, and quiet,
I never would divulge it, to diſturb
Thy peace at home, yet thou moſt barbarous,
To be ſo careleſſe of me, and my Fame,
(For all reſpect of thine in the firſt ſtep
To thy baſe luſt, was loſt) in open Court Cheſſ-boord and men ſet ready.
To publiſh my diſgrace? and on record,
To write me up an eaſie-yeilding wanton?
I thinke can find no preſident: In my extreames,
One comfort yet is left, that though the Law
Divorce me from thy bed, and made free way
To the unjuſt embraces of an other,
It cannot yet deny that this thy Son
(Looke up Aſcanio ſince it is come out)
Is thy legitimate heire.

sp.speaker: Iam.
sp.l: Confederacie:
A trick (my Lord) to cheat me; e're you give
Your Sentence grant me hearing.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: New Chymera's?

sp.speaker: Iam.
sp.l: I am (my Lord) ſince he is without Iſſue,
Or hope of any his undoubted Heire,
And this forg'd by the Advocate, to defeat me
Of what the Lawes of Spaine, confer upon me,
A meere Impoſture, and conſpiracie
Againſt my future fortunes,

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: You are too bold.
Speak to the Cauſe Don Henrique.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I confeſſe,
(Though the acknowledgement muſt wound mine honour,
That all the Court hath heard touching this Cauſe,
Or with me, or againſt me) is moſt true:
The later part my Brother urg'd, excepted:
For what I now doe, is not out of Spleene
(As he pretends) but from remorſe of conſcience)
And to repaire the wrong that I have done
To this poore woman: And I beſeech your Lordſhip
To thinke I have not ſo far loſt my reaſon,
To bring into my Familie, to ſucceed me,
The ſtranger—Iſſue of anothers Bed,
By proofe, this is my Son, I challenge him,
Accept him, and acknowledge him, and deſire
By a definitive Sentence of the Court,
He may be ſo recorded, and full powre
To me, to take him home.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: A ſecond rape
To the poore remnant of Content, that's left me,
If this be granted: and all my former wrongs
Were but beginnings to my miſeries,
But this the height of all: rather then part
With my Aſcanio, I'll deny my oath,
Profeſſe my ſelfe a Strumpet, and endure
What puniſhment ſoe're the Court decrees
Againſt a wretch that hath forſworne her ſelfe,
Or plai'd the impudent whore.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: This taſtes of paſſion,
And that muſt not divert the courſe of Juſtice;
Don Henrique, take your Son, with this Condition
You give him maintenance, as becomes his birth,
And 'twill ſtand with your honour to doe ſomething
For this wronged woman: I will compell nothing,
But leave it to your will. Break up the Court:
It is in vaine to move me; my doom's paſs'd,
And cannot be revok'd. — Exit.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: There's your reward.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: More Cauſes: and ſuch Fees. Now to my Wife,
I have too long bin abſent: Health to your Lordſhip,

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: You all look ſtrangely, and I feare beleeve
This unexpected fortune makes me proud,
Indeed it do's not: I ſhall ever pay you
The duty of a ſon, and honour you
Next to my Father: good my Lord, for yet
I dare not call you uncle, be not ſad,
I never ſhall forget thoſe noble favours
You did me being a ſtranger, and if ever
I live to be the maſter of a fortune,
You ſhall command it.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Since it was determi'nd
I ſhould be cozen'd, I am glad the profit
Shall fall on thee, I am too tough to melt,
But ſomething I will do.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Pray you take leaue
Of your ſteward (gentle Brother) the good husband
That takes up all for you.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Very well, mock on,
It is your turn: I may have mine— Exit.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: But do not
Forget us deare Aſcanio

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Do not feare it.
I Every day will ſee you: every houre
Remember you in my prayers.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: My grief's too great
To be expreſſed in words— Exit.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Take that and leave us,
Leave us without reply, nay come back ſirrah
And ſtudy to forget ſuch things as theſe
As are not worth the knowledge.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: O good Sir.
Theſe are bad principles—

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Such as you muſt learn
Now you are mine for wealth and poverty
Can hold no friendſhip: and what is my will
You muſt obſerve and do, though good or ill. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Where is my wife? 'fore heaven, I have done wonders
Done mighty things to day, my Amaranta,
My heart rejoyces at my wealthy Gleanings,
A rich litigious Lord I love to follow,
A Lord that builds his happineſſe on brawlings,
O 'tis a bleſſed thing to have rich Clyents,
Why, wife I ſay, how fares my ſtudious Pupill?
Hard at it ſtill? ye are too violent
All things muſt have their reſts they will not laſt els
Come out and breathe. Leandro within

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I do beſeech you pardon me
I am deeply in a ſweet point Sir,

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'le inſtruct ye:
I ſay take breath, ſeek health firſt, then your ſtudy,
O my ſweet ſoul I have brought thee golden birds home,
Birds in abundance: I have done ſtrange wonders:
There's more a hatching too.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Have ye done good husband?
Then 'tis a good day ſpent

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Good enough chicken,
I have ſpred the nets o'th' law, to catch rich booties,
And they come flttering in: how do's my Pupil?
My modeſt thing, haſt thou yet ſpoken to him?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: As I paſt by his chamber I might ſee him,
But he is ſo bookiſh,

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And ſo baſhfull too,
I faith he is, before he will ſpeak, he will ſtarve there

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I pitie him a little.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: So do I too.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: And if he pleaſe to take the aire o'th gardens
Or walk i'th' inward roomes, ſo he moleſt not—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He ſhall not trouble thee, he dare not ſpeak to thee
Bring out the Cheſſe-board —come let's have a game wife,
I'le try your maſterie, you ſay you are cunning

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: As learned as ye are (Sir) I ſhall beat ye

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: Here he ſteales out, put him not out of countenance
'Prethee look another way, he will be gone elſe
Walk and refreſh your ſelf I'l be with you preſently,

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I'le take the aire a little.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Twill be healthfull.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Will ye be there? then here? Ile ſpare ye that man,

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: 'Would I were ſo neare too, and a mate fitting.

sp.speaker: A.
sp.l: What think ye (Sir) to this? have at your Knight now

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Twas ſubtilly playd: your Queen lies at my ſervice
Pre thee look off, he is ready to pop in again,
Look off I ſay, do'ſt thou not ſee how he bluſhes?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I do not blaſt him:

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: But ye do, and burn too.
What killing looks ſhe ſteals?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I have you now cloſe,
Now for a Mate.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: You are a bleſſed man that may ſo have her.
Oh that I might play with her— knock within

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Who's there? I come you cannot ſcape me now wife
I come, I come, knock

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Moſt bleſſed hand that calls him.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Play quickly wife.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: 'Pray ye give leave to think, Sir,

sp.speaker: Moore
sp.l: An honeſt neighbour that dwells hard by (Sir)
Would fain ſpeak with your worſhip about buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: The devil blow him off.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Play.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I will ſtudy:
For if you beat me thus, you will ſtill laugh at me— knock

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He knocks again; I cannot ſtay. Leandro
'Pray thee come near.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I am well (Sir) here,

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Come hither:
Be not afraid but come.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Here's none will bite (Sir)

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: God forbid Lady.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: 'Pray come nearer.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Yes forſooth.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Pre thee obſerve theſe men: juſt as they ſtand here
And ſee this Lady, do not alter 'em,
And be not partiall, Pupill.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: No indeed Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Let her not move a pawn, I'le come back preſently
Nay you ſhall know I am a Conquerour.
Have an eye Pupill— Exit.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Can ye play at Cheſſe Sir?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: A little Lady.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: But you cannot tell me
How to avoid this Mate, & win the Game too
Ha's noble eyes: ye dare not friend me ſo farre.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I dare do any thing that's in mans power, Lady,
To be a friend to ſuch a noble beauty.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: This is no Lawyers language: I pray ye tell me,
Whether may I remove, Ye ſee I am ſet round?
To avoid my husband.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I ſhall tell ye happily.
But happily you will not be inſtructed.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Yes, and I thank ye too, ſhall I move this man?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Thoſe are unſeemly: move one can ſerve ye
Can honour ye, can love ye.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: 'Pray ye tell quickly
He will return and then

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I'le tell ye inſtantly
Move me, and I wil move any way to ſerve ye
Move your heart this way (Lady)

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: 'Pray ye heare me.
Behold the ſport of Love, when he is imperious
Behold the ſlave of Love

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Move my Queen this way?
Sure, he's ſome worthy man: then if he hedge me
Or here to open him.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Do but behold me
If there be pity in you, do but view me,
But view the miſery I have undertaken
For you the povertie.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: He will come preſently.
Now play your beſt Sir, though I looſe this Rook here
Yet I get Libertie.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I'le ſeize your fair hand
And warm it with a hundred, hundred kiſſes
The God of love warm your deſires but equal
That ſhall play my game now.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: What do you mean Sir?
Why do you ſtop me?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: That ye may intend me.
The time ha's bleſt us both: Love bids us uſe it.
I am a Gentleman nobly deſcended:
Young to invite your Love, rich to maintain it.
I bring a whole heart to ye, thus I give it,
And to thoſe burning altars thus I offer,
And thus divine lips, where perpetuall Sping grows.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Take that, ye are too ſaucy.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: How proud Lady?
Strike my deſerts?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I was too blame.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: What wiſe, there?
Heaven keep my houſe from thieves.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I am wretched:
Opened, diſcovered, loſt to my wiſhes.
I ſhall be whooted at.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: What noiſe was this (wife?)
Why doſt thou ſmile?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: This proud thing will betray me.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Why theſe lie here? what anger (deare?)

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Why none, Sir,
Onely a chance, your pupill ſaid he plaid well,
And ſo indeed he do's: he undertook for ye
Becauſe I would not ſit ſo long time idle
I made my Liberty avoided your mate,
And he again as cunningly endangered me,
Indeed he put me ſtrangely to it. When preſently
Hearing you come, and having broke his ambuſh too
Having the ſecond time brought off my Queen fair,
I roſe o'th' ſudden ſmilingly to ſhew ye,
My apron caught the Cheſſe-board, and the men,
And there the noiſe was.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Thou art grown a Maſter,
For all this, I ſhall beat ye.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Or I, Lawyer,
For now I love her more, 'twas a neat anſwer,
And by it hangs a mighty hope, I thank her
She gave my pate a ſound knock that it rings yet,
But you ſhall have a ſounder if I live Lawyer,
My heart akes yet I would not be in that fear—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I am glad ye are a gameſter, Sir, ſometimes
For recreation we two ſhall fight hard at it.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: He will prove too hard for me,

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I hope he ſhall do,
But your Ches-board is too hard for my head, line that good Lady,

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I have been attoning two moſt wrangling neighbours,
They had no money, therefore I made even
Come, let's go in, and eat, truly I am hungry.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.p: I have eaten already, I muſt intreat your pardon

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Do as ye pleaſe, we ſhall expect ye at ſupper.
He ha's got a little heart, now it ſeems handſomly,

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You'l get no little head, if I do not look to ye.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: If ever I do catch thee again thou vanity—

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.p: I was too blame to be ſo raſh, I am ſorie— Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Heare but my reaſons,

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: O my patience heare 'em.
Can cunning falſhood colour an excuſe?
With any ſeeming ſhape of borrowed truth?
Extenuate this wofull wrong, not error.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: You gave conſent that to defeat my brother
I ſhould take any courſe,

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: But not to make
The cure more loathſome then the fowle diſeaſe:
Was't not enough you took me to your bed,
Tir'd with looſe dalliance, and with emptie veines,
All thoſe abilities ſpent before and waſted,
That could conferre the name of mother on me?
But that (to perfect my account of ſorrow)
For my long barrenneſſe you muſt highten it
By ſhewing to my face, that you were fruitfull
Hug'd in the baſe embraces of another?
If Solitude that dwelt beneath my roofe,
And want of children was a torment to me
What end of my vexation to behold
A baſtard to upbraid me with my wants?
And heare the name of father paid to ye
Yet know my ſelf no mother,
What can I ſay?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: ſhall I confeſſe my fault and ask your pardon?
Will that content ye?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: If it could make void,
What is confirm'd in Court No, no, Don Henrique
You ſhall know that I find my ſelf abus'd,
And adde to that I have a womans anger,
And while I look upon this Baſilisk
Whoſe envious eyes hath blaſted all my comforts
Reſt confident I'le ſtudy my dark ends,
And not your pleaſures,

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Noble Lady, heare me,
Not as my Fathers ſon, but as your ſervant,
Vouchſafe to heare me, for ſuch in my duty,
I ever will appeare: And far be it from
My poore ambition, ever to looke on you,
But with that reverence; which a ſlave ſtands bound
To pay a worthy Miſtris: I have heard
That Dames of higheſt place, nay Queenes themſelves,
Diſdaine not to be ſerv'd by ſuch as are
Of meaneſt Birth: and I ſhall be moſt happie,
To be emploi'd when you pleaſe to command me
Even in the courſeſt Office, as your Page,
I can wayte on your trencher:: fill your wine
Carry your pontafles, and be ſometimes bleſs'd
In all humilitie to touch your feete
Or if that you eſteeme that too much grace
I can run by your Coach: obſerve your lookes
And hope to gaine a fortune by my ſervice,
With your good favour, which now, as a Son,
I dare not challenge

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: As a Son,

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Forgive me
I will forget the name, let it be death
For me to call you Mother.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Still upbraided?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: No way left to appeaſe you?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: None: now heare me,
Heare what I vow before the face of heaven,
And if I breake it all plagues in this life,
And thoſe that after death are fear'd, fall on me,
While that this Baſtard ſtaies under my rooffe,
Looke for no peace at home, for I renounce
All Offices of a wife,

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: What am I falne to?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I will not eate, nor ſleepe with you and thoſe howres
Which I ſhould ſpend in prayers for your health
Shall be emploi'd in Curſes,

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Terrible.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: All the day long, i'le be as tedious to you
As lingring fevers, and i'le watch the nights,
To ring alon'd your ſhame and breake your ſleepes
Or if you doe but ſlumber, i'le appeare
In the ſhape of all my wrongs, and like a fury
Fright you to madnes, and if all this faile
To worke out my revenge, I have friends and kinſmen,
That will not ſit downe tame with the diſgrace
That's offer'd to our noble familie
In what I ſuffer,

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: How am I devided
Betweene the duties I owe as a Husband,
And pietie of a Parent?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I am taught Sir
By the inſtinct of nature that obedience
Which bids me to prefer your peace of mind,
Before thoſe pleaſures that are deareſt to me
Be wholy hers (my Lord) I quit all parts,
That I may challenge: may you grow old together
And no diſtaſt e're find you and before
The Characters of age are printed on you
May you ſee many Images of your ſelves,
Though I, like ſome falſe Glaſſe, that's never look'd in
Am caſt a ſide, and broken from this hower
(Unles invited, which I dare not hope for)
I never will ſet my forbidden feete,
Over your threſhold: onely give me leave
Though caſt off to the world, to mention you,
In my devotions 'tis all I ſue for
And ſo I take my laſt leave

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Though I am
Devoted to a wife nay allmoſt ſol'd
A ſlave to ſerve her pleaſures, yet I cannot
So part with all humanity, but I muſt
Shew ſomething of a Father: thou ſhalt not goe
Unfurniſh'd and unfriended too: take that
To guard thee from neceſſities; may thy goodnes
Meet many favours, and thine innocence
Deſerve to be the heire of greater fortunes,
Then thou wer't borne to. Scorne me not Violante
This baniſhment is a kind of civill death,
And now, as it were at his Funerall
To ſhed a teare or two, is not unmanly
And ſo farewell for ever: one word more,
Though I muſt never ſee thee (my Aſcanio)
When this is ſpent (for ſo the Judge decreed)
Send to me for ſupply: are you pleas'd now?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Yes: I have cauſe: to ſee you howle and blubber
At the parting of my torment, & your ſhame Bed ready, wine, table Standiſh & Paper.
'Tis well: proceed: ſupply his wants: doe doe:
Let the great dowre I brought ſerve to maintain
Your Baſtards riots: ſend my Clothes and Jewells,
To your old acquaintance, your deare dame his Mother
Now you begin to melt, I know 'twill follow,

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Is all I doe miſconſtrude?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I will take
A courſe to right my ſelfe a ſpeeding one:
By the bleſſ'd Saints, I will; if I prove cruell
The ſhame to ſee thy fooliſh pitty taught me
To looſe my naturall ſoftnes, keepe off from me
Thy flateries are infectious, and i'le fle thee
As I would doe a Leaper.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Let not fury
Tranſport you ſo: you know I am your Creature,
All love, but to your ſelf, with him, hath left me
I'le ioyne with you in any thing

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: In vaine
I'le take mine owne waies, and will have no partners,

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I will not croſſe you,

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Doe not, they ſhall find
That to a Woman of her hopes beguil'd
A viper troad on, or an Aſpick's, mild. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Sits the game there? I have you by mine order,
I love Leandro for't

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: But you muſt ſhew it
In lending him your helpe, to gain him meanes
And opportunitie.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: He ſhall want nothing,
I know my Advocate to a hayre, and what
Will fetch him from his prayers, if he uſe any,
I am honyed with the project: I would have him horn'd
For a moſt pretious Beaſt.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: But you looſe time;

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I am gon, inſtruct you Diego, you will find him
A ſharpe and ſubtle knave, give him but hints
And he will amplifie: Se all things ready
I'll fetch him with a vengeance.— Exit.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: If he faile now,
Wee'll give him over too,

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Tuſh he is fleſh'd,
And knowes what vaine to ſtrike for his owne credit.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: All things are ready.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Then we ſhall have a merry Scene, no're feare it.

div.head: Scena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Amaranta (with a note) and Moore.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: Is thy Maſter gone out?

sp.speaker: Moore.
sp.l: Even now, the Curat fetch'd him,
About a ſerious buſineſſe as it ſeem'd,
For he ſnatch'd up his Cloak, and bruſh'd his hat ſtrait,
Set his Band handſomely, and out he gallop'd.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: 'Tis well, 'tis very well, he went out (Egla.)
As luckily, as one would ſay, goe Husband,
He was call'd by providence: fling this ſhort paper
Into Leandro's Cell, and waken him,
He is monſtrous vexed, and muſty, at my Cheſſe-play;
But this ſhall ſupple him, when he has read it:
Take your owne recreation for two houres,
And hinder nothing.

sp.speaker: Moore.
sp.l: If I doe, I'll hang for't. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: If that you lov'd Aſcanio for himſelfe,
And not your private ends, you rather ſhould
Bleſſe the faire opportunitie, that reſtores him
To his Birth-right, and the Honours he was borne to,
Then grieve at his good Fortune.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Grieve Octavio?
I would reſigne my Eſſence, that he were
As happy as my love could faſhion him,
Though every bleſſing that ſhould fall on him,
Might prove a curſe to me, my ſorrow ſprings
Out of my feare, and doubt he is not ſafe.
I am acquainted with Don Henrique's nature,
And I have heard too much the fiery temper
Of Madam Violante: can you thinke
That ſhe, that almoſt is at war with heaven
For being barren, will with equall eyes
Behold a Son of mine?

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: His Fathers care,
That for the want of Iſſue tooke him home,
(Though with the forfeiture of his owne fame)
Will looke unto his ſafetie.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Step-mothers
Have many eyes, to find a way to miſchiefe,
Though blind to goodneſſe.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: Here comes Don Jamy,
And with him our Aſcanio.

sp.speaker: Jamy.
sp.l: Good youth leave me,
I know thou art forbid my company,
And onely to be ſeene with me, will call on
Thy Fathers anger.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Sir if that to ſerve you
Could looſe me any thing (as indeed it cannot)
I ſtill would follow you. Alas I was borne
To doe you hurt but not to help my ſelfe,
I was, for ſome particular end, tooke home,
But am caſt off againe.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Is't poſſible?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: The Lady, whom my Father calls his wife
Abhors my ſight, is ſick of me, and forc'd him
To turne me out of dores.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: By my beſt hopes
I thanke her crueltie, for it comes neere
A ſaving charitie.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I am onely happy
That yet I can relieve you, 'pray you ſhare:
My Father's wondrous kind, and promiſes
That I ſhould be ſupplide: but ſure the Lady
Is a malitious woman, and I feare
Meanes me no good.

sp.speaker: Iamy.
sp.l: I am turn'd a ſtone with wonder,
And know not what to thinke.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: From my Lady,
Your private eare and this—

sp.speaker: Iamy.
sp.l: New Miracles?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: She ſayes, if you dare make your ſelfe a Fortune,
She will propoſe the meanes; My Lord Don Henrique
Is now from home and ſhe alone expects you,
If you dare truſt her ſo, if not deſpaire of
A ſecond offer, Exit.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Though there were an Ambuſh
Layd for my life, I,ll on and ſound this ſecret,
Retire thee (my Aſcanio) with thy Mother:
But ſtir not forth, ſome great deſigne's on foot,
Fall what can fall, if e're the Sun be ſet,
I ſee you not, give me dead.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: We will expect you,
