And ſo I ſhare my bowels amongſt you all.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: A noble Duke, a very noble Duke.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Afore there Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: You'r faithfully met good Monſieur Mount Marine.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Be advis'd, the time is alter'd.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Is he not the ſame man he was afore?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Still the ſame man to you Sir.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: You have received mighty grace, be thankfull.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Let me not dye in ignorance;

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: You ſhall not.
Then know the King out of his loue hath pleaſed
To ſtile him Duke of Burgundy.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: O great Duke,
Thus low, I plead for pardon, and deſire
To be enrol'd amongſt your pooreſt ſlaves.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Sir you have mercy, and withall my hand,
From henceforth let me call you one of mine.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Make room afore there, and diſmiſſe the people.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Every man to his houſe in peace and quiet.

sp.speaker: Peop.
sp.l: Now heaven preſerve the Duke, heaven bleſſe the Duke.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: This letter came this morn from my Cozen
To the great Lady, high and mighty Ducheſſe
Of Burgundy, be theſe delivered O,
For a ſtronger lace to keep my breath
That I may laugh the nine dayes till the wonder
Fall to an ebb: the high and mighty Ducheſſe?
The high and mighty God? what a ſtile is this?
Methinks it goes like a Duchy lope-man,
A ladder of 100. rounds will faile
To reach the top on't, well my Gentle Cozen
I know by theſe contents your itch of honour;
You muſt to the Court, you ſay, and very ſhortly:
You ſhall be welcome; and if your wife have wit
I'le put her in a thriving courſe, if not
Her own ſin on her owne head, not a blot
Shall ſtaine my reputation, only this
I muſt for healths ſake ſometimes
Make an aſſe of the tame moyle my husband;
'Twill do him good, and give him freſher brains,
Me freſher blood.
Now for the noble Duke, I heare him comming.
Your Grace is well return'd.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: As well as may be:
Never in younger health, never more able:
I meane to be your bed-fellow this night,
Let me have good encounter.

sp.speaker: Bow.
sp.l: Bleſſe me heaven
What a hot meat this greatneſſe is?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: It may be ſo,
For I'le be ſworn he hath not got a ſnap
This two months on my knowledge, or her woman
Is damd for ſwearing it.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I thank you Gentlemen for your attendance
And alſo your great paines, pray know my lodgings
Better and oftner, do ſo Gentlemen.
Now by my honour, as I am a Prince,
I ſpeake ſincerely, know my lodgings better,
And be not ſtrangers, I ſhall ſee your ſervice
And your deſervings, when you leaſt expect.

sp.speaker: Om.
sp.l: We humbly thank your Grace for this great favor.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Jaques?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Your Grace.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Be ready for the Countrey,
And let my Tenants know the Kings great love:
Say I would ſee them, but the waight at Court
Lyes heavy on my ſhoulders: let them know
I do expect their duties in attendance
Againſt the next feaſt, wait for my comming
To take up poſt horſe, and be full of ſpeed. Exit Jaques.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I would deſire your Grace—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: You ſhall deſire, and have your
Full deſire, ſweet Ducheſſe ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: To have ſome conference with a Gentleman
That ſeems not altogether void of reaſon?
He talks of titles, and things neare the Crown,
And knowing none ſo fit as your good Grace,
To give the difference in ſuch points of State—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What is he? If he be noble, or have any part
That's worthy our converſe, We do accept him.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I can aſſure your Grace his ſtraine is noble,
But he's very ſubtle.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Let him be ſo.
Let him have all the braines, I ſhall demonſtrate
How this moſt Chriſtian Crown of France can beare
No other ſhew of title then the Kings.
I will goe in and meditate for halfe an houre,
And then be ready for him preſently,
I will convert him quickly or confound him.

sp.speaker: Ser
sp.l: Is mad Shattillion here?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Is here, and's Lady,
I prethee ſervant fetch him hither.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Why, what do you meane to put him to?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: To chat with the mad lad my husband;
'Twill be brave to heare them ſpeake, babl,
Stare, and prate.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: But what ſhall be the end of all this, Lady?

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.l: Leave that to me, now for the grand diſpute,
For ſee here comes Shattillion: as I live me thinks
All France ſhould beare part of his griefes.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I le fetch my Lord the Duke.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Where am I now, or whether will you lead me?
To my death? I crave my priviledge,
I muſt not dye but by juſt courſe of law.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: His Majeſty hath ſent by me your pardon,
He meant not you ſhould dye; but would intreate you
To lay the full ſtate of your Title open,
Unto a grave and noble Gentleman.
The Duke of Burgundy who here doth come,
Who either by his wiſedome will confute you,
Or elſe informe and ſatisfie the King.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: May 't pleaſe your grace, this is the Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Is this he that chops • ogicke with my liege?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Dee mocke me? you are great, the time will come
When you ſhall be as much contemned as I,
Where are the ancient complements of France,
That upſtarts brave the Princes of the bloud?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Your title Sir, in ſhort.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: He muſt Sir,
Be a better ſtates man then your ſelfe, that can
Trip me in any thing, I will not ſpeake
Before theſe witneſſes.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Depart the roome, for none ſhall ſtay,
No not my deareſt Dutches.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Wee'le ſtand behind the Arras & heare all. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: In that chaire take your place, I in this,
Diſcourſe your title now.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Sir you ſhall know,
My loves true title, mine by marriage,
Setting aſide the firſt race of French Kings
Which will not here concerne us, as Pharamond,
With Clodian, Meron, and Chilperik,
And to come downe unto the ſecond race,
Which we will likewiſe ſlip—

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: But take me with you.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I pray you give me leave, of Martell Charles,
The Father of King Pippin, who was, Sir,
To Charles the great and famous Charlemaine.
And to come to the third race of French Kings,
Which will not be great ly pertinent in this cauſe,
Betwixt the King and me, of which you know
HVGH CAPET was the firſt,
Next his Sonne Robert, Henry then, and Phillip
With Lewis, and his Sonne a Lewis too,
And of that name the ſeventy, but all this
Springs from a female as it ſhall appeare.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Now give me leave, I grant you this your title
At the firſt ſight carryes ſome ſhew of truth;
But if ye weigh it well ye ſhall finde light.
Is not his Majeſtie poſſeſt in peace,
And juſtice executed in his name,
And can you thinke the moſt Chriſtian King
Would do this if he ſaw not reaſon for it?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: But had not the tenth Lewis a ſole daughter?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I cannot tell.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: But anſwer me directly.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: It is a moſt ſeditious queſtion.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Is this your juſtice?

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: I ſtand for my King.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Was ever heire apparant thus abus'd?
I'le have your head for this.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why, do your worſt.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Will no one ſtir to apprehend this traytor?
A guard about my perſon will? none come?
Muſt my owne royall hands performe the deede?
Then thus I do arreſt you.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Treaſon, help.

div.stage: Enter Wife, Long, and Bew. and Servant.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Help, help, my Lord and husband.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Help thy Duke.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Forbeare his graces perſon.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Forbeare you to touch him that,
Your heire apparant weds,
But by this hand I will have all your heads. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: How doth your grace?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why? well.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: How do you finde his title?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: 'Tis a dangerous one,
As can come by a female.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I 't is true,
But the law Salicke, cuts him off from all.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I do beſeech your grace how ſtands his title?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Pew, nothing, the law Shallicke cuts him off from all

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: My gracious husband you muſt now prepare,
In all your graces pomp to entertaine
Your cozen, who is now a convertite,
And followes here, this night he will be here.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Be ready all in haſt, I do intend,
To ſhew before my cozens wondring face Exeunt omnes.
The greatneſſe of my pomp, and of my place.

div.head: Actus quartus.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: Sirra is all things carried to the Taylor,
The meaſure and the faſhion of the gowne
With the beſt trim?

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Yes Sir & 'twill be ready within this two dayes.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: For my ſelfe I care not,
I have a ſuite or two of ancient velvet;
Which with ſome ſmall correcting and addition
May ſteale into the preſence.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Would my Gowne were ready husband, I'le lay my life,
To make you ſomething ere to morrow night.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: It muſt not bee
Before we ſee the Duke, and have advice,
How to behave ourſelves: lets in the while,
And keep our ſelves from knowledge till time ſhall call us

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I much admire the fierce maſculine ſpirit,
Of this dread Amazon.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: This following night I'le have a wench in ſolace.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Sir, I heare you,
And will be with you if I live, no more.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: My Lady would intreate your preſence Gentlman.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: We will obey your Lady, ſhe is worthy.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: You light alone, a word, or two.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Your will Sir.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Harke in your eare, wilt thou be maried? ſpeake, wilt thou marry?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Maried? to whom Sir?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: To a proper fellow, landed, and able bodied,

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Why do you flout me Sir?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: I ſweare I do not, I love thee for thy Ladies ſake, be free,

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: If I could meet ſuch matches as you ſpeake of,
I were a very child to looſe my time, Sir.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: What ſaieſt thou to Mounſier Bewford.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir I ſay hee's a proper Gentleman, and far
Above my meanes to looke at.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Doſt thou like him?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Yes Sir, and ever did.

sp.speaker: Long
sp.l: He is thine owne.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You are too greate in promiſes.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Be rul'd and follow my advice, he ſhall be thine

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Would you would make it good Sir.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Do but thus,
Get thee a cuſhion underneath thy cloathes,
And leave the reſt to me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I'le be your ſcholler,
I cannot looſe much by the venture ſure.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Thou wilt looſe a prettie maiden head, my rogue,
Or I am much o'th bow hand, you'le remember
If all this take effect, who did it for you,
And what I may deſerve for ſuch a kindneſſe.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Yours Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Save ye Sir.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Save the King.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I pray you Sir, which is the neareſt way?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Save the King, this is the neareſt way.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Which is the neareſt way to the poſt houſe?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: God ſave the King and his poſt horſe.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I pray Sir direct me to the houſe;

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Heaven ſave the King, you cannot catch me Sir.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I do not underſtand you Sir.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: You do not, I ſay you cannot catch me Sir.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Not catch you Sir?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: No Sir, nor can the King,
With all his ſtratagems, and his forced tricks,
Although he put his nobles in diſguiſe;
Never ſo oft to ſift into my words,
By courſe of law, lay hold upon my life.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: It is buſineſſe that my Lord the Duke
Is by the King imployed in, and he thinks
I am acquainted with it.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: I ſhall not need to ripp the cauſe up,
From the firſt to you,
But if his Majeſty had ſuffered me
To marry her, though ſhe be after him,
The right heire generall to the Crowne of France.
I would not have convayed her into Spaine,
As it was thought, nor would I ere have joyn'd,
With the reformed Churches to make them,
Stand for my cauſe.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I do not thinke you would.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I thanke you Sir,
And ſince I ſee you are a favorer
Of vertues, kept in bondage;
Tell directly to my ſoveraigne King,
For ſo I will acknowledge him for ever,
How you have found my ſtaid affections
Setled for peace, and for the preſent ſtate.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Why Sir?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: And good Sir tell him further this,
That notwithſtanding all ſuggeſtions
Brought to him againſt me and all his ſuſpitions,
Which are innumerall to my treaſons,
If he will warrant me but publique tryall,
I'le freely yeild my ſelfe into his hands;
Can he have more then this?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: No by my troth.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: I would his Majeſty would heare but reaſon,
As well as you.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: But Sir you do miſtake me,
For I never ſaw the King
In all my life but once, therefore good Sir,
May it pleaſe you to ſhew me which is the poſt houſe.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: I cry you mercie Sir, then you'r my freind.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: And ſuch men are very rare with me,
The poſt houſe is hard by, farewell;

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I thanke you Sir, I muſt ride hard to night,
And it is darke already.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I am cruell to ſend this man directly to his death
That is my freind, and I might eaſily ſave him,
He ſhall not dye, come backe my freind, come backe.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: What is your will?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: do you not know?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Not I.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: And do you gather nothing by my face?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Vertue is ever innocent,
La not the fault on me, I greive for you,
And wiſh that all my teares might win your ſafety.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Why Sir?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Alas good freind you are undone,
The more ill fortune, mine to be the meanes
Of your ſad overthrow: you know not me.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: No truely Sir.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Would you had never ſeene me,
I am a man purſu'd by the whole ſtate
And ſure ſome one hath ſeene me talke with you.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Yes divers Sir.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Why then your head is gon.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I'le out of towne.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Would it were ſoone enough,
Stay if you love your life, or elſe you are taken.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: What ſhall I do?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: I'le venture deeply for him,
Rather then to caſt away an innocent,
Take courage friend, I will preſerve thy life,
With hazard of mine owne.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I thanke you Sir.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: This night thou ſhalt be lodg'd within my doores,
Which ſhall be all lookt faſt, and in the morne
I'le ſo provide, you ſhall have free acceſſe,
To the Sea ſide and ſo be ſhipt away,
Ere any know it.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Good Sir ſuddainly I am afraide to dye.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Then follow me. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: This way he went, and there's the houſe I hope,
His better Angell hath directed him,
To leave the wandring ſtreetes, poore Gentleman.
Would I were able with as free a hart,
To ſet his ſoule right, as I am to grieue,
The ruine of his fame, which God forgive me;
Sir if you be within, I pray Sir ſpeake to me.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I am within and will be, what are you?

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: A friend.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: No Sir you muſt pardon me,
I am acquainted with none ſuch: be ſpeedy,
Friend there is no other remedy.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: A word Sir I ſay I am your friend.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: You cannot ſcape by any other meanes,
Be not feareful, God ſave the King,
What's your buſineſſe Sir?

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: To ſpeake with you.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Speake out then?

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: Shall I not come up?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not: flye if thou beeſt thin own friend,
There lyes the ſute and all the furniture
Belonging to the head, on with it friend.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: Sir do you heare?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I do, God bleſſe the King,
It was a habit I had laid aſide,
For my owne perſon if the ſtate had forced me.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: Good Sir unlocke your dore.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Be full of ſpeede, I ſee ſome 20 Musketeeres in ambuſh,
What ere thou art, know I am here and will be,
Seeſt thou this bloody ſword that cryes revenge?
Shake not my friend, through millions of theſe foes
I'le be thy guard and ſet thee ſafe aboard.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: Dare you not truſt me Sir?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: My good before me,
And my alleagance to the King I tell thee
Captaine (for ſo I gueſſe thee by thy armes)
And the looſe flancks of halberdeeres about thee,
Thou art too weake and fooliſh to attempt me.
If you be ready follow me, and harke you
Upon your life ſpeake to no living wight,
Except my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not call agen; thus with my ſword,
And the ſtrong faith I beare unto the King;
Whom God preſerve, I will deſcend my chamber,
And cut thy throate, I ſweare I'le cut thy throate,
Steale after me and live.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: I will not ſtay.
The furie of a man ſo farr diſtracted. Exit Love.
Where's the Officer that dares not enter,
To intrap the life of my diſtreſſed friend?
I, have you hid your ſelfe? you muſt be found,
What do you feare? is not authority on your ſide
Nay, I know the Kings command
Will be your warrant, why then feare you? ſpeake
What ſtrange deſignes are theſe? Shattillion,
Be reſolute and beare thy ſelfe upright,
Though the whole world deſpiſe thee: ſoft, me thinks.
I heard a ruſhing which was like the ſhake
Of a diſcovered Officer, I'le ſearch
The whole ſtreete over, but I'le finde thee out. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Jaques. in womens a parrell.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: How my joyntes do ſhake, where had I been
But for this worthy Gentleman, that
Hath ſome touch of my infortunes: would I were
Safe under hatches once for Callicut,
Farewell the pomp of Court, I never more
Can hope to be a Duke or any thing,
I never more ſhall ſee thy glorious face;
Of my faire ſpreading Lord that loved me well.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Flye you ſo faſt? I had a ſight of you,
But would not follow you; I was too wiſe,
You ſhall not lead me with a cunning tricke,
Where you may catch me; poore Shatillion;
Hath the Kings anger left thee never a friend?
No, all mens loves move by the breath of Kings.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: It is the Gent. that ſav'd my life, Sir.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Bleſſe Shatillion, another plot.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: No Sir, 'tis I.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Why, who are you?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Your friend whom you preſerved.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Whom I preſerved?
My friend? I have no woman friend but one,
Who is to cloſe in priſon to be here;
Come neere let me looke on you.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: 'Tis I.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: You ſhould not be a woman by your ſtature.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I am none Sir.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I know it, then keepe off,
Strange men and times! how I am ſtill preſerv'd?
Here they have ſent a yeoman of the guard
Diſguis'd in womans cloathes to worke on me,
To make love to me; and to trap my words,
And ſo inſnare my life, I know you Sir,
Stand back upon your perill, can this bee
In chriſtian common weales? from this time forth
I'le cut off all the meanes to worke on me.
I'le nere ſtirr from my houſe: and keep my doores
Lockt day and night, and cheapen meat and drink
At the next ſhops by ſignes, out of my window,
And having bought it draw it up in my garters.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Sir, will you help me?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Do not follow me,
I'le take a courſe to live deſpight of men. Exit Shat.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: He dares not venture for me, wretched Jaques
Thou art undone for ever and for ever,
Never to riſe againe: what ſhall I do?
Where ſhall I hide me? heres one to take me,
I muſt ſtand cloſe, and not ſpeake for my life.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: This is the time of night, and this the haunte,
In which I uſe to catch my wasccoatieres,
It is not very darke, no I ſhall ſpie 'em,
I have walkt out in ſuch a pitchy night.
I could not ſee my fingers this farr off,
And yet have brought whom venſon by the ſmell,
I hope they have not left their old walke, ah?
Have I ſpied you ſitting by this light?
To me theres no ſuch fine ſight in the world,
As a white-apron twixt twelve and one;
See how it gliſters? do you thinke to ſcape?
So now I have you faſt; come and do not ſtrive,
It takes away the edge of appetite;
Come I'le be liberall every way, Exeunt
Take heed you make no noyſe for waking of the watch.

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: Now the bleſſing of ſome happy guide,
To bring us to the Duke and we are ready.
Come forward ſee the doore is opend,
And two of his Gent. I'le ſpeake to them,
And marke how I behave my ſelfe, God ſaue yee;
For leſſe I cannot wiſh to men of ſort, & of your ſeeming
Are you of the Dukes?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: We are Sir, and your ſervants, your ſalutes,
We give you backe againe with many thankes.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: When did you heare ſuch words before wife? peace,
Do you not dare to anſwer yet; s't fit
So meane a Gentleman as my ſelfe ſhould crave,
The preſence of the great Duke your Maſter?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Sir you may.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Shall we deſire your name and buſineſſe Sir,
And wee will preſently informe him of you.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: My name is Cleremont

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You are his graces kinsman,
Or I am much miſtaken;

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: You are right,
Some of his noble blood runs through theſe veines,
Though far unworthy of his graces knowledge.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Sir we muſt all be yours; his graces kinſman,
And we ſo much forgetfull? 'twas a rudeneſſe,
And muſt attend your pardon, thus I crave it:
Firſt to this beauteous Lady, whom I take
To be your wife Sir, next your mercie.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: You have it Sir, I do not like this kiſſing,
It lyes ſo open to a world of wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: This is the merry fellow, this is he
That muſt be noble too.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: And ſo he ſhall.
If all the art I have can make him noble,
I'le dub him with a Knight-hood; if his wife
VVill be but forward, and joyne iſſue,
I like her above excellent.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: VVilt pleaſe you
To walke a turne or two, whilſt to the Duke
VVe make your comming known? Exit Ser. & Long.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: I ſhal attend, Sir.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Theſe Gentlemen are very proper men,
And kiſſe the beſt that ere I taſted.
For goodneſſe-ſake husband let us never more
Come neare the Countrey, what ſo ere betide us;
I am in malice with the memory
Of that ſame ſtinking dung-hill.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: VVhy now you are my chicken and my dear,
Love where I love, hate where I hate, now
You ſhall have twenty gownes, and twenty chaines,
See, the doore is opening.

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.l: Roome afore there, the Duke is entring.

div.stage: Enter Duke, Wife, Long. Servant, Maria.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: 'Tis the Duke, even he himſelfe, be merry,
This is the golden age the Poet ſpeaks on.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I pray it be not brazen'd, by their faces,
And yet me thinks they are the neateſt pieces
For ſhape and cutting that ere I beheld.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: Moſt gracious Duke, my poor Spouſe & my ſelfe
Do kiſſe your mighty foote, and next to that
The great hand of your Ducheſſe, ever wiſhing
Your honours ever-ſpringing, and your yeares.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Cozen?

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: Your Graces vaſſall, far unworthy
The nearneſſe of your blood.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Correct me not, I know the word I ſpeake,
And know the perſon.
Though I be ſomething higher then the place
VVhere common men have motion, and diſcending
Down with my eye, their formes are leſſened to me,
Yet from this pitch can I behold my owne,
From millions of thoſe men that have no marke,
And in my fearfull ſtoop, can make them ſtand.
VVhen others feele my ſoule and periſh, Cozen
Be comforted, you are very welcome, ſo
Is your faire wife: the charge of whom I give
To my own deareſt and beſt beloved.
Tell me, have you reſolv'd your ſelfe for Court,
And utterly renounce the ſlaviſh Countrey,
VVith all the cares thereof?

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: I have ſir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Have you diſmiſt your eating houſhold,
Sold your hangings of Nebuchadnezar, for ſuch they were,
As I remember, with the furnitures
Belonging to your beds and chambers?

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: I Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Have you moſt carefully tane off the lead,
From your roofe weake with age, and ſo prevented
The ruine of your houſe, and clapt him
In a ſummer ſuite of thatch to keepe him coole?

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: All this I have perform'd.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Then lend me all your hands, I will embrace my Cozen
VVho is an underſtanding Gentleman,
And with a zeale mighty as is my name,
Once more I bid you welcome to the Court;
My ſtate againe.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: As I was telling you your husband
Muſt be no more Commander, looke to that,
Be ſeverall at meate, and lodging, let him have
Boord-wages and dyet 'mongſt his men it'h towne
For pleaſure if he be given too't let him have it,
Elſe as your own fancie ſhall direct you.
Cozen, you ſee this mighty man here: he was an aſſe
When he came firſt to towne: indeed he was
Juſt ſuch another coxcomb as your husband,
God bleſſe the mark and every good mans childe!
This muſt not ſtir you Cozen.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Heaven forbid?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Sweet Maria, provide the cuſhion ready for it.

sp.speaker: Mat.
sp.l: It ſhall be done.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Receive all your advices from our ſelfe,
Be once a day with us, and ſo farewell
For this time, my faire Cozen; Gentlemen
Conduct him to his lodging.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Farewell, and think upon my words.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I ſhall obſerve them. Exit Duke and Ducheſſe.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: Health, and the Kings continuall love attend you.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: O for a private place to eaſe my lungs!
Heaven give me patience, ſuch a paire of Jades
Were never better ridden to this houre,
Pray heaven they hold out to the journeys end.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Twitch him aſide good Monſieur, whilſt I breake
Upon the body of his ſtrength, his wife,
I have a conſtant promiſe: ſhe is my own.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Ply her to wind-ward Monſieur, you have taken
The moſt compendious way to raiſe your ſelfe,
That could have been delivered by a councell.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: I have ſome certaine aimes Sir: but my wife—

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Your wife? you muſt not let that trouble you.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: It will Sir, to ſee her in a ſtrangers armes.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: What mean you? let her alone, be wiſe, ſtir not a foot
For if you do, all your hopes are buryed:
I ſweare you are a loſt man if you ſtir.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: I thanke you Sir, I will be more advis'd.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: But what great Office do you levell at?

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: Sir, they are kiſſing.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Let them kiſſe,
And much may do their good hearts; they muſt kiſſe
And kiſſe, and double kiſſe, and kiſſe againe,
Or you may kiſſe the poſt for any riſing:
Had your noble Kinſman ever mounted
To theſe high Spheres of honour, now he moves in,
But for the kiſſes of his wife?

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: I Know not.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Then I doe; credite me, he had been loſt,
A fellow of no mark, and no repute,
Had not his wife kiſt ſoone, and very ſweetly
She was an excellent woman, and diſpatcht him
To his full, being in a moment Sir— Exit Long. & Wife.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: But yet me thinks he ſhould not take her Sir
Into a private roome.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Now ſtand and flouriſh,
You are a made man for ever.
I doe envy you if you ſtand your fortunes up,
You are the happieſt man: but your great Cozen
This day in Court: well I will marry ſurely,
And not let every man out-run me thus.
'Tis time to be mine owne friend, I live
In towne here, and direct the readieſt way,
To other men, and be a ſlave my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: Nay good Sir be not mov'd, I am your ſervant,
And will not be ungratefull for this knowledge.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Will you be walking home?

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: I would de • ire to have my wife a long.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You are too raw,
Be gon and take no notice where you left her,
Let her returne at leiſure, if ſhe ſtay
A moneth 'twill be the better, underſtand me
This Gentleman can doe't. Exit Cozen.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: I will Sir, & wife remember me a Duke, a Duke wife.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Aboard her Longaveile ſhee's thine owne,
To me the fooling of this foole, is venerie. Exit Servant.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Come, preethe come, have I not crownes? behold
And follow me, here; not a word, go in
Grope by the walls, and you ſhall finde a bed,
Lye downe there, ſee, ſee, a turne or two to give
My blood ſome heate; and I am preſently
For action, darkneſſe by thy leave I come. Exit Bew.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I am perfect in my leſſon, be my ſpeed,
Thou God of marriage, this is the doore, I'le knock.

sp.speaker: Bew. within.
sp.l: Whoſe there? I cannot come yet.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Mounſier Bewford?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Stay 'till I light a candle, who are ye?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir? a poore Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: O come in, I'le finde a time for you too, be not loude.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir you have found that time already, ſhame
On my ſoule therefore.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Why? what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Do you not ſee Sir, is your light ſo dim?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Do you not waite on the Lady Mount Marine?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I do Sir, but my love on you.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Poore ſoule! how cam'ſt thou by this big belly?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: By your ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: By heaven I ne're toucht your body.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, unſweare that oath agen, I'le tell you all;
Theſe two yeares I have lov'd you, but the meanes
How to enjoy you, I did never know
Till twelfe night laſt, when hearing of your game
To take up wenches private in the night,
I apprehended ſtraight this courſe to make
My ſelfe as one of them, and waite your coming;
I did ſo, and enjoyed you, and now this child
That now is quicke within me: hide my ſhame,
And marry me: or elſe I muſt be forc't—

sp.speaker: Long within.
sp.l: Monſieur Bewford, Monſieur Bewford.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Whoſe that calls?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Are you a bed?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: No Sir, the hangings.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Nay Mounſieur, I'le forbid that, we'le have faire play
Lend me your candle, are you taken Bewford?
A lecher of your practice, and cloſe carriage
To be diſcovered thus? I am a ſham'd
So great a Maſter in his art ſhould faile,
And ſtagger in his grounds.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Your wide,
This woman and my ſelfe are man and wife,
And have been ſo this halfe yeare,
Where are you now? have I been diſcovered?
You cannot breake ſo eaſily on me Sir,
I am to wary to be opend by you.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: But theſe are but illuſions to give couler
To your moſt miſticke leacherie, but Sir
The belly hath betray'd you all, it muſt out.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Good Longavile believe me on my faith,
I am her husband.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: On my faith I cannot unleſſe I ſaw
Your hands faſt and your heartes.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Why Longavile when did I give that to your eares
That was not truth? by all the world ſhe's mine,
She is my wife and to confirme you better
I give my ſelfe againe, here take my hand
And I yours, we are once more married,
Will this content you?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Yes, I am believing, and God give you joy.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: My loving wife I will not wrong thee,
Since I am thine and only loved of thee
From this houre I, vow my ſelfe a new man,
Be not jealous: for though I had a purpoſe,
To have ſpent an hower or two in ſolace otherwiſe,
And was provided for it, yet my love
Shall put a better temper to my blood,
Come out thou woman of unholſome life,
Be ſorry for thy ſinnes, and learne to mend,
Nay never hide your face, you ſhall be ſeene.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Jaques, why Jaques, art thou that Jaques,
The very ſtaffe, and right hand of our Duke?
Speake, thou bearded Venus.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I am he, by miracle preſerv'd to be that Jaques,
Within this two houres Gentlemen, poore Jaques
Was but as coarſe in grave: a man of wiſedome,
That of my conſcience if he had his right
Should have a pretty ſtate, but that's all one
That noble Gentleman did ſave this life,
I keepe it for him, 'tis his owne.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Oh Bachus! is all the world drunke? come wee'le to the Duke
And give thankes for this delivery.

div.head: Actus quintus.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Not gon unto my Tenants to relate
My grace and honour; and the mightyneſſe
Of my new name which would have ſtruck a terrour
Through their courſe doublets, to their very hearts?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Alas great Lord and Maſter, I could ſcarce
With ſafety of my life returne againe
Unto your graces houſe, and but for one
That had ſome mercie, I had ſure been hang'd.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: My houſe?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Yes Sir, this houſe, your houſe 'ith towne.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Jaques we are diſpleas'd, hath it no name?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: What name?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Dull rogue; what hath the King beſtowed
So many honours, open'd all his ſpringes,
And ſhowerd his graces downe upon my head,
And has my houſe no name? no title yet?
Burgundy houſe you Aſſe.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Your graces mercy,
And when I was come off, and had recover'd
Burgundy houſe, I durſt not yet be ſeene,
But lay all night for feare of purſuiuants
In Burgundy privie houſe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: O Sir, 'tis well,
Can you remember now? but Jaques know
Since thy intended journey is ſo croſte,
I will go downe my ſelfe this morning.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Have I not ſaid this morning?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: But conſider,
That nothing is prepared yet for your journey,
Your graces teames not here to draw your cloathes;
And not a carrier yet in town to ſend by.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I ſay once more go about it,
You'r a wiſe man, you'de have m • linger time,
Till I have worne theſe cloathes out: will ye go?
Make ye ready wife. Exit. Jaques.

sp.speaker: Dutches.
sp.l: I am ſo, mighty Duke.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Nay for the Countrey.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: How? for the Countrey?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes I am reſolv'd to ſee my Tenants in this bravery
Make them a ſumptuous feaſt, with a ſlight ſhew,
Of Dives, and Lazarus, and a ſquib or two,
And ſo returne.

sp.speaker: Dutches.
sp.l: VVhy Sir? you are not mad?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How many Dukes have ye known mad? I pray ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: You are the firſt Sir, and I hope the laſt,
But you are ſtark horne mad.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Forbeare good wife.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: As I have faith you'r mad: your hornes
Have been to heavy for you, and have broke
Your skull in pieces: If you be in earneſt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: VVell you ſhall know my skull and wits are whole
Ere I have done, and yet I am in earneſt.

sp.speaker: Dutches.
sp.l: VVhy, do you think I'le go?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I know you ſhall.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: I ſhall? by what authority ſhall I?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I am your husband.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: True I confeſſe it,
And by that name the world hath given you
A power to ſway me; but Sir you ſhall know
There is a greater bond that tyes me here,
Alleagance to the King; has he not heapt
Thoſe honours on you to no other end,
But to ſtay you here, and ſhall I have a hand
In the offending ſuch a gracious Prince?
Beſides, our owne undoings lyes uppon't,
Were there no other cauſe, I do not ſee,
Why you ſhould go: If I ſhould ſay you ſhould not.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Do you thinke ſo?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Yes faith.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Now good wife make me underſtand that point.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Why that you ſhall, did I not bring you hither?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.p: And were not all thoſe honours wrought out of the fire by me?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: By you?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: By me; how ſtrang you make it?
When you came firſt did you not walke the Town,
In a long cloake halfe compaſſe? an old hat,
Linde with vellure, and on it for a band,
A skeine of crimſon cruell?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I confeſſe it.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: And tooke baſe courſes?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Baſe?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.p: Baſe by this light, extreame baſe, and ſcurvie, monſtrous baſe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What were theſe courſes, wife?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Why you ſhall know,
Did you not thus attired trot up and down,
Plotting for vild and lowſie offices,
And agreed with the Sergiant of the beares,
To buy his place? deny this if you can.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why it is true.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: And was not that monſtrous baſe?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Be advis'd wife, a beares a princly beaſt.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: A beare?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes wife, and one ſide venſon.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: You'r more then one ſide foole, I'm ſure of that

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: But ſince you have vext me wife, know you ſhall go
Nor you ſhall never have penny from me.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Nay I have done, and though I know 'twill be
Your overthrow, I'le not forſake you now.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Be ready then. Exit Duke.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: What are you married Bewford?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.p: I as faſt as words, and hearts, and hands & Prieſt can make us.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: O Gentlemen, we are undone.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: For what?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: This Gentleman the Lord of lorne my husband,
Will be gon downe to ſhew his play fellowes,
Where he is gay.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: What, downe into the Countrey?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Yes faith, was ever foole but he ſo croſſe?
I would as faine be gracious to him,
As he could wiſh me, but he will not let me;
Speake faithfully, will he deſerve my mercy?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: According to his merits he ſhould weare,
A guarded coate, and a great wooden dagger.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: If there be any woman that doth knowe,
The duties 'twixt a husband and his wife,
Will ſpeake but one word for him he ſhall ſcape;
Is not that reaſonable? but ther's none,
Be ready therefore, to purſue the plot
We had againſt a pinch, for he muſt ſtay.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: VVaite you here for him whilſt I go
And make the King acquainted with your ſport,
For feare he be incens'd for our attempting;
Places of ſo great honour. Exit Long.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Go, be ſpeedy.

div.stage: Enter Duke, Cozen, Wife, Jaques, Man.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come let me ſee how all things are diſpoſed of.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: One Cart will ſerve for all your furniture,
With roome enough behinde to eaſe the footman
A capcaſe for your linnen, and your plate,
VVith a ſtrange locke that opens with Amen;
For my young Lord becauſe of eaſie portage,
A quiver of your graces linde with Cunney,
Made to be hang'd about the Nurſes neck,
Thus with a ſcarfe or towell.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Very good.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Nay, 'tis well, but had you ſtaid another weeke,
I would have had you, furniſht in ſuch pomp,
As never Duke of Burgundy was furniſht,
You ſhould have had a ſumpter though't had coſt me
The laying on my ſelfe: where now you are faine,
To hire a rippers mare, and buy new doſſers,
But I have got them painted with your armes,
VVith a faire darnex Carpet of my owne
Laid croſſe for the more ſtate.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Jaques I thanke you: your Carpet ſhall be bruſht
And ſent you home; what, are you ready wife?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: An houre agoe

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I cannot chuſe but kiſſe thy royall lips,
Deare Dutches mine, thou art ſo good a woman.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Yould ſay ſo if you knew all, goodman Duckling.

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: This was the happieſt fortune could befall me
Now in his abſence will I follow cloſe
Mine owne preferment, and I hope e ere long,
To make my meane and humble name ſo ſtrong,
As my great Couzens, when the world ſhall know,
I beare too hot a ſpirit to live low
The next Spring wil I down my wife and houſhold,
I'le have My Uſhers, and my foure Lacquies,
Six ſpare croches too: but mum, no more,
What I intend to do, I'le keep in ſtore.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Mountye, mountye, Iaques, be our querry.

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.l: To horſe there Gentlemen, and fall in couples.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come honoured Ducheſſe. Enter Longavile.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Stand thou proud man.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Thieves, Iaques, raiſe the people.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: No, raiſe no people, 'tis the Kings command,
Which bids thee once more ſtand thou haughty man,
Thou art a monſter, for thou art ungratefull,
And like a fellow of a rebell nature,
Haſt flung from his embraces: and for
His honours given thee, haſt not returnd
So much as thanks, and to oppoſe his will,
Reſolv'd to leave the Court, and ſet the Realm
A fire, in diſcontent, and open action:
Therefore he bids thee ſtand thou proud man,
Whilſt with the whisking of my ſword about
I take thy honours off: this firſt ſad whiske
Takes off thy Duke-dome, thou art but an Earl.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: You are miſtaken, Longavile.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: O would I were, this ſecond whiske divides
Thy Earldome from thee, thou art yet a Baron.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No more whisks if you love me Longavile.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Two whisks are paſt, and two are yet behind,
Yet all muſt come, but not to linger time.
With theſe two whisks I end, now Mount Marine,
For thou art now no more, ſo ſays the King,
And I have done his Highneſſe will with griefe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Diſgraced from my honours?

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: 'Tis too certaine.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I am no Traitor ſure that I know of;
Speak Iaques? haſt thou ever heard me utter word
Tending to treaſon, or to bring in the enemy?

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: Alas ſir I know nothing,
Why ſhould your Worſhip bring me in to hang me?
God's my judge Gentlemen I never medled
But with the bruſhing of his cloaths, or fetching
In water in a morning for his hands.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: Are theſe the honours of this place? Antony
Help me to take her gowne off quickly
Or I'le ſo ſwinge ye for't—

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Why husband? Sir?

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: I'le not looſe a penny by this towne.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Why what do you meane ſir, have her to her lodging,
And there undreſſe her, I will waite upon her.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: Indeed you ſhall not, your moneth is out I take it,
Get you out before me wife:
Couzen farewell, I told you long agoe,
That pride begins with pleaſure, ends with woe.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Goe thy way ſentences, 'twill be thy fortune,
To live and dye a Cuckold and Church-warden.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: O my poor husband! what a heavy fortune
Is fallen upon him?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Me thinks 'tis ſtrange,
That heaven fore-warning great men of their falls,
With ſuch plaine tokens, they ſhould not avoid them?
For the laſt night betwixt eleven and twelve,
Two great and hideous blazing ſtars were ſeen
To fight a long houre by the clocke, the one
Dreſt like a Duke, the other like a King,
Till at the laſt the crowned ſtar ore-came.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Why do ye ſtand ſo dead, Monſieur Marine?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: So Caeſar fell when in the Capitoll
They gave his body two and thirty wounds.
Be warned all ye Peers, and by my fall,
Hereafter learn to let your wives rule all.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Monſieur Marine, pray let me speak with you;
Sir I muſt wave you to conceale this party,
It ſtands upon my utter overthrow;
Seem not diſcontented, nor do not ſtir a foote,
For if you do, you and your hope—
I ſweare you are a loſt man if you ſtir.
And have an eye to Bewford, he'l tempt you.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Come, come, for ſhame goe downe;
Were I Marine, by heaven I would goe down:
And being there, I would rattle him ſuch an anſwer
Should make him ſmoake.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Good Monſieur Bewford peace
Leave theſe rebellious words,
Or by the honours which I once enjoyed,
And yet may ſweare by,
I'le tell the King of your proceedings;
I am ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: You talkt of going down when 'twas not fit,
But now let's ſee your ſpirit,
A thouſand and a thouſand will expect it.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why wife, are you mad?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: No nor drunk, but I'de have you know your own ſtrength

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: You talk like a moſt fooliſh woman wife;
I tell you I will ſtay, yet I have a
Cratchet troubles me.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: More cratchets yet?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Follow me Jaq. I muſt have thy counſell,
I will returne againe, ſtay you there Wife.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I fear this loſſe of honour will give him ſome few ſtooles.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: No, no, he is reſolv'd, he will not
Stir a foote I'le lay my life.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: I but hee's diſcontented, how ſhall we reſolve that
And make him ſtay with comfort?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Faith Bewford we muſt even let nature work,
For hee's the ſweeteſt temper'd man for that
As one can wiſh, for let men but goe about to foole him,
And hee'l have his finger as deep in 't as the beſt;
But ſee where he comes frowning, bleſſe us all!

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Off with your hats, for here doth come
The high and mighty Duke of Burgundy.
What ever you may think, I have thought
And thought, and thought upon't, and I finde it plaine,
The King cannot take backe what he has given,
Unleſſe I forfeit it by courſe of Law.
Not all the water in the river Sene,
Can waſh the blood out of theſe Princely veines.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: God a mercy husband, thou art the beſt
To worke out a thing at a pinch, in France.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I will aſcend my ſtate againe,
Ducheſſe take your place,
And let our Champion enter.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Has he his Champion? that's excellent.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: And let loud muſick ſound before his entrance.
Sound Trumpet.

div.stage: Enter Iaques in armour, one carrying a Scuchion before him, and a two-handed ſword.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: How well our Champion doth demean himſelfe,
As if he had been made for ſuch an action?
Me thinks his ſturdy trunchion he doth wield,
Like Mars approaching to a bloody field.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I think ther's no man ſo deſperate
To dare encounter with our Champion,
But truſt me, Iaques, thou haſt pleas'd us well;
Once more our warlike muſick, then proceed. En: Shat.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: What wondrous age is this? what cloſe proceedings?
I heare the clang of Trumpets in this houſe,
To what intent do not our States-men ſearch?
O no, they look not into ſimple truth;
For I am true, and they regard not me,
A man in armour too: God ſave the King
The world will end, theres nought but treachery.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.p: I Ja. ſervant to the high & mighty Godfrey Duke of Burgundy, do come hither to prove by natural ſtrength and activity of my body, without the help of ſorcery, inchantment, or negromancy, that the ſaid Godfrey late of Mount Marine, & now of Burgundy, hath perfect right therto, notwithſtanding the Kings command to the contrary, & no other perſon whatſoever: & in token that I wilbe ready to make good the ſame: I throw down my gage, wch is my honour, pronounced the 37. of Feb. ſtilo novo, God ſave the D.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Of all the plots the King hath laid for me
This was the ſhrewdeſt, 'tis my life they ſeeke,
And they ſhall have it: if I ſhould refuſe
To accept the challenge in the Kings behalfe,
They have ſome cauſe to take away my life,
And if I do accept it, who can tell,
But I may fall by doubtfull chance of war?
'Twas ſhrewd, but I muſt take the leaſt of evills,
I take thy gauntlet up thou treacherous man,
That ſtands in armed coate againſt the King,
Whom God preſerve, and with my ſingle ſword
Will juſtifie whatever he commands;
I'le watch him for catching of my words.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Jaques goe on, defend our Princely title.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Why ſhrinkſt thou backe? thou haſt an evill cauſe;
Come forward man, I have a rocke about me,
I fight for my true Liege.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Goe forward Jaques.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I do beeſeech your Grace to pardon me,
I will not fight with him, with any elſe
I'le ſhew my reſolution ſpeedily.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Come do thy worſt, for the King ſhall ſee
All is not true that is reported of me.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I may not fight with him by law of armes.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What? ſhall my title fall? wilt thou not fight?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Never with him that once hath ſav'd my life.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Dar'ſt thou not fight? behold then I doe goe
Strong with the zeale I beare my Soveraign,
And ſeize upon that haughty man himſelfe.
Deſcend the ſteps that (thou haſt thus uſurpt
Againſt the King and State) downe to the ground,
And if thou doe utter but a ſyllable
To croſſe the Kings intent, thou art but dead;
There, lye upon the earth and pine and dye.
Did ever any man wade through ſuch ſtormes,
To ſave his life, as poore Shattillion?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I feare this challenge hath ſpoil'd all.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Ne're feare it, hee'l work it out againe ſervant.
See where Shattillions Love, poor Lady, comes. En: Love.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Jaques.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.p: Lye ſtill ſir if you love your life, I'le whiſtle when he's gone,

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: O Gentlemen, I charge you by the love
Which you beare to women, take ſome pitty
On this diſtreſſed man, help to reſtore
That pretious jewell to him he hath loſt.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Lady what ever power doth lye in us
By art or prayer, or danger, we are yours,

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: A ſtrange conceite hath wrought this malady,
Conceites againe muſt bring him to himſelfe,
My ſtrict denyall to his will wrought this?
And if you could but draw his wilder thoughts
To know me, he would ſure recover ſenſe.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: That charge I'le undertake.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Looke Jaques, look, for Gods ſake let me riſe,
This greatneſſe is a Jade, I cannot ſit it.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: His ſword is up, and yet he watcheth you.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I'le down again, pray for thy Maſter, Jaques.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Now the King may ſee all the ſuggeſtions are not true,
He hath receiv'd againſt my loyalty;
When all men elſe refuſe, I fight his battails,
And thruſt my body into dangers mouth;
I am become his Champion, and this ſword
Has taught his enemies to know themſelves;
O that he would no more be jealous of me!

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Monſieur Shattillion, the King aſſigns you,
That for this valiant loyall act of yours,
He hath forgot all jealouſies and feares,
And never more will tempt you into danger.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: But how ſhall I believe this? what new token
Of reconcilement will he ſhew me?
Let him releaſe my poor love from her torment,
From her hard fare and ſtrict impriſonment.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: He hath done this to win your after-love,
And ſee your Lady ſent you from the King
By theſe two Gentlemen: be thankfull for her.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: She lives, ſhe lives, I know her by the power
Shoots from her eyes.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: Riſe deare Sbattillion.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I Know my duty,
Next unto my King, I am to kneele to you.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.p: I'le have you riſe, fetch me a chair, ſit down Shat.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I am commanded, and faith tell me Miſtris,
What uſage have you had? pray be plaine?

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: O my moſt lov'd Shattillion, paine enough,
But now I am free, thanks to my God and King.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: His eyes grow very heavy, not a word,
That his weak ſenſes may come ſweetly home.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: The King is honourable.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: When do you whiſtle Jaques?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: By and by.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Come hither Monſieur, canſt thou laugh a little?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: So thou ſhalt then. Bewford how doſt thou?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Why well.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I'me glad on't, and how does thy wife?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Why you may ſee her Sir, ſhe ſtands behind you.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: By the maſs ſhe's there indeed, but wher's her belly?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Belly?

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: Her great belly man: what haſt thou ſent thee?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: A boy I'le lay my life, it tumbled ſo.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Catcht by this light.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I'le be a goſſip Bewford.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: And I.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I have an odd Apoſtle ſpoone.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: S' foote catcht.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Why what's the matter Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: He's married to your woman.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: And I not know it?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Twas a veniall ſin.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Gall, gall, gall.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Forgive her Monſieur Bewford, 'twas her love.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: You may riſe if you pleaſe, I muſt endure it.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: See how my great Lord lyes upon the ground
And dare not ſtir yet?
Jaques, whiſtles?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Jaques, Jaq. is the Kings Champion gone yet,

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: No, but hee's aſleep.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Is he aſleep art ſure?

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: I am ſure he is, I heare him ſnore.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Then by your favours Gentlemen I riſe,
And know I am a Duke ſtill.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: And I am his Champion.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Hold thee there, and all France cannot mend thee.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I am a Prince as great within my thoughts
As when the whole ſtate did adorn my perſon;
What tryall can be made to try a Prince?
I will oppoſe this noble corps of mine
To any danger that may end the doubt.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Great Duke and husband there is but one way
To ſatisfie the world of our true right,
And it is dangerous.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What may it be?
Were it to bring the great Turke bound in chaines
Through France in triumph: or to couple up
The Sophie, and great Preſter Iohn together,
I would attempt it Ducheſſe, tell the courſe.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: There is a ſtrong opinion through the world,
And no doubt grounded on experience
That Lyons will not touch a lawfull Prince,
If you be confident then of your right,
Amongſt the Lions beare your naked body,
And if you come off cleare and never winch,
The world will ſay you are a perfect Prince.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I thank you Ducheſſe for your kinde advice,
But now we do not affect thoſe ravenous beaſts.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: A Lyon is a beaſt to try a King;
But for the triall of ſuch a ſtate like this
Pliny reports a maſtive dog will ſerve.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: We will not deale with dogs at all: but men.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You ſhall not need to deale with them at all,
Hark you Sir, the King doth know you are a Duke:

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No, does he?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Yes, and is content you ſhall be, but with this caution,
That none know it but your ſelfe:
For if ye do, he'l take it away by act of Parliament.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Here's my hand, and whilſt I live or breath,
No living wight ſhall know I am a Duke.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Marke me directly Sir, your wife may know it.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: May not Jaques?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Yes, he may.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: May not my countrey Couzen?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: By no meanes ſir, if you love your life and ſtate.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Well then, know all I am no Duke.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: No I'le ſweare it.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: See he wakes.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Where am I, or where have I been all this while?
Sleep hath not ſate ſo ſound upon mine eyes
But I remember well that face;
O thou too cruell, leave at length to ſcorne
Him that but looking on thy beauty dyes,
Either receive me, or put out my eyes.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: Deareſt Shattillion ſee upon my knees,
I offer up my love, forget my wrongs.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Art thou mine own?

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: By heaven I am.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Then all the world is mine.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: I have ſtranger things to tel thee, my deareſt love.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Tell nothing but that thou art mine own:
I do not care to know where I have been,
Or how I have liv'd, or any thing,
But that thou art my own.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Well wife, though 'twere a trick that made us wed,
Wee'l make our ſelves merry ſoone in bed.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Know all I am no Duke.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: What ſaye?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Jaques?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I am a Duke.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.l: Are yee?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes faith, yes faith.
But it muſt only run amongſt our ſelves,
And Jaques thou ſhalt be my Secretary ſtill.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Kinde Gentlemen, leade in Shattillion,
For he muſt needs be weak and ſickly yet.
Now all my labours have a perfect end as I could wiſh,
Let all young ſprightly wives that have
Dull fooliſh Coxcombs to their husbands,
Learn by me their duties, what to doe,
VVhich is to make 'em fooles, and pleaſe 'em too.

div.head: The Prologue.
div.l: WIt is become an anticke: and puts on
As many ſhapes of variation,
To court the times applauſe, as the times dare,
Change ſeverall faſhions, nothing is thought rare
Which is not new and follow'd, yet we know,
That what was worne ſome twenty yeare agoe,
Comes into grace againe, and we purſue
That cuſtome, by preſenting to your view
A play in faſhion then, not doubting now
But 'twill appeare the ſame, if you allow
Worth to their noble memory, whoſe name,
Beyond all power of death live in their fame.

div.head: The Epilogue.
div.l: THe Monuments of vertue and deſert,
Appeare more goodly when the gloſſe of art
Is eaten off by time, then when at firſt
They were ſet up, not cenſur'd at the worſt.
We have done our beſt for your contents to fit
With new paines this old monument of wit.

sp.speaker: Lodovico.
sp.l: THe truth is Piſo, ſo ſhe be a woman
And rich and holſome, let her be of what
Condition & Complection it pleaſe,
She ſhall pleaſe me I am ſure; Thoſe men are fooles
That make their eyes their chooſers, not their needes.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Me thinks I would have her honeſt too, & handſom.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Yes if I could have both, but ſince they are
Wiſhes ſo neare impoſſibilities,
Let me have that that may be.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: If it were ſo,
I hope your conſcience would not be ſo nice
To ſtart at ſuch a bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: No beleeve me,
I doe not thinke I ſhould.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: But thou would'ſt be
I doe not doubt upon the leaſt ſuſpition
Unmercifully jealous

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: No I ſhould not,
For I believe thoſe mad that ſeeke vexations,
A wife, though ſhe be honeſt, is a trouble,
Had I a wife as faire as Hellen was
That drew ſo many Cuckolds to her cauſe,
Theſe eyes ſhould ſee another in my Saddle
Ere I beleeve my beaſt would carry double.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: So ſhould not I by'r Lady, and I thinke
My patience (by your leave) as good as yours,
Report would ſtirre me mainely, I am ſure on't.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Report? you are unwiſe; report is nothing;
For if there were a truth in what men talke,
I meane of this kind, this part of the world
I am ſure would be no more cal'd Chriſtendom.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: What then?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Why Cuckoldome, for we ſhould looſe
Our old faiths cleane, and hold their new opinions:
If talke could make me ſweat, before I would marry,
I'de tie a ſurer knot, and hang my ſelfe;
I tell thee there was never woman yet,
Nor never hope there ſhall be, though a Saint,
But ſhe has been a ſubject to mens tongues,
And in the worſe ſenſe: and that deſperate husband,
That dares give up his peace, and follow humours
(Which he ſhall find too buſie, if he ſeek'em)
Beſide the forcing of himſelfe an Aſſe
He dyes in chaines, eating himſelfe with anger.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Having theſe Antidotes againſt opinion
I would marry any one; an arrant whore.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Thou doſt not feele the nature of this phiſick
Which I preſcribe not to beget diſeaſes,
But where they are, to ſtop them.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: I conceive ye.
What thinkeſt thou? thy way of the widow Lelia?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Faith thou haſt found out one I muſt confeſſe
Would ſtagger my beſt patience: From that woman
As I would bleſſe my ſelfe from plagues and ſurfets
From men a war at Sea, from ſtormes, and quickſands,
From hearing Treaſon and concealing it,
From daring of a Madman, or a Drunkard,
From Hereſie, ill wine, and ſtumbling poſt horſe;
So would I pray each morning, and each night
(And if I ſaid each houre, I ſhould not lye)
To be delivered of all theſe in one,
The woman thou haſt named.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Thou haſt ſet her in a pretty Letany.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Pray take my councell.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: When I am my ſelfe
Ile heare you any way; love me though thus
As thou art honeſt, which I dare not be
Leſt I deſpiſe my ſelfe. Farewell. Exit. Iulio.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Doe you heare my friend: Sir are you not a ſetter,
For the faire widdow here of famous memory?

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Ha? am I taken for a Bawd? oh God
To mine owne child too? miſery, I thanke thee
That keepes me from their knowledge: Sir beleeve me
I underſtand ye not.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: You love plaine dealing.
Are you not percell Bawd? confeſſe your Function,
It may be we would uſe it.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Were ſhe worſe,
As I feare ſtrangely ſhe is ill enough,
I would not heare this tamely.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Heer's a ſhilling
To ſtrike good luck withall.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Heer's a Sword Sir
To ſtrike a Knave withall, thou lyeſt, and baſely,
Be what thou woult.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Why how now Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: You are many: I ſhall meete you, Sir, againe,
And make you underſtand, y'ave wrongd a woman
Compard with whom thy Mother was a ſinner. Farewell. Exit Fa.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: He has amazd me.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: With a blow?
By'r Lady twas a ſound on; are ye good
At taking knocks? I ſhall know you hereafter:
You weare too blame to tempt a man ſo far
Before you knew him ce ••• ine: h'as not hurt ye?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: No I think.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: We were too blame indeed to goe ſo far,
For men may be miſtaken: if he had ſwinged us
H'ad ſerv'd us right: Beſhrew my heart I think,
VVe have done the Gentlewoman as much wrong too,
For hang me, if I know her
In my particular.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Nor I; this tis to credit
Mens idle tongues; I warrant they have ſed
As much by our two mothers.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Like enough.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I ſee a beating now and then does more
Move and ſtir up a mans contrition
Then a ſharpe Sermon, here probatum eſt.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: What ſhall I tell your Siſter?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Tell her this,
Till ſhe be better converſation'd
And leave her walking by her ſelfe, and whyning
To her old melancholly Lute, I'le keepe
As far from her as the Gallowes. Exit Servant.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Who's that Fredrick?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Yes marry is't. O Angelo how do'ſt thou?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Save you Sir, how does my Miſtris?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: She is in love I thinke, but not with you.
I can aſſure you, ſaw ye Fabritio?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Is he come over?

sp.speaker: Fred
sp.l: Yes a weeke agoe: Shall we dyne?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I cannot:

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Pre'thee doe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Beleeve me I have buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Have you too, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: No ſir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Why then let's dyne together:

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Goe then: Farewell good Angelo,
Commend me to your friend.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I will. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Doe not diſſemble Franc, mine eyes are quicker
Then ſuch obſervers, that do ground their faith
Upon one ſmile or teare; y'ar much alterd,
And are as empty of thoſe Excellencies
That were companions to you; I meane mirth
And free diſpoſure of your blood and Spirit,
As you were borne a mourner.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: How I pre'thee?
For I perceive no ſuch change in my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: Come, come, this is not wiſe, nor provident
To halt before a Cripple: If you love
Be liberall to your friend, and let her know it,
I ſee the way you run, and know how tedious
'Twill prove without a true companion.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Sure thou wouldſt have me love.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Yes marry would I
I ſhould not pleaſe ye elſe.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: And who for gods ſake?
For I aſſure my ſelfe, I know not yet:
And pre'thee Clora, ſince thou'lt have it ſo
That I muſt love, and doe I know not what:
Let him behold a pretty handſome fellow,
And young, and if he be a little valiant
Twill be the better; and a little wiſe
And faith a little honeſt.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Well I will ſound ye yet for all your craft.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Heigh ho! I'le love no more.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Then one; and him
You ſhall love Franck.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Which him? thou art ſo wiſe
People will take thee ſhortly for a witch:
But prethee tell me Clora, if I were
So mad as thou wouldſt make me, what kind of man
Wouldſt thou imagine him?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Faith ſome pretty fellow?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: With a cleane ſtrength, that cracks a cudgell well
And dances at a wake, and plaies at nine holes.
O God what pretty commendations thou haſt given him'
Faith if were in love, as I thanke God
I doe not thinke I am; this ſhort Epiſtle
Before my love would make me burne the legend.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: You are too wilde, I meane ſome gentleman.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: So doe not I, till I can know'em wiſer:
Some Gentleman, no Clora, till ſome Gentleman
Keepe ſome land, and fewer whores beleeve me
Ile keepe no love for him, I doe not long
To goe a foot yet, and ſolicite cauſes.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: What thinke you then of an adventurer?
I meane ſome wealthy Merchant.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Let him venture
In ſome decaid Crare of his owne: he ſhall not
Rig me out, that's the ſhort on't; out upon't:
What young thing of my yeares would endure
To have her husband in another Country
Within a moneth after ſhe is married
Chopping for rotten Rayſons, and lye pining
At home under the mercy of his fore-man? no,
Though they be wealthy, and indifferent wiſe
I doe not ſee that I am bound to love'em.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: I ſee ya're hard to pleaſe; yet I will pleaſe ye.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Faith not ſo hard neither, if conſidered;
What woman may deſerve as? ſhe is worthy:
But why do we beſtow our ttme ſo idely?
Preethee let us entertaine ſome other talke,
This is as ſickly to me as faint weather.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Now I believe I ſhall content you Francke,
What thinke you of a Courtier?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Faith ſo ill,
That if I ſhould be full, and ſpeake but truth,
'Twold ſhew as if I wanted charity,
Prethee good wench let me not raile upon 'em,
Yet I have an excellent ſtomach, and muſt do it;
I have no mercie of theſe infidels;
Since I am put in minde on't, good beare with me,
Can no man fit you? I will finde him out.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: This ſomer fruite, that you call Courtier,
While you continue cold and froſty to him
Hangs faſt, and may be found: but when youfling
Too full a heate of your affections —
Upon his roote and make him ripe too ſoone,
Youl' finde him rotten 'ith the handling;
His oathes and affections are all one
With his apparrell, things to ſet him off,
He has as many Miſtriſſes, as Faithes,
And all appocripha; his true beliefe
Is onely in a private Surgeon,
And for my ſingle ſelfe, I'de ſooner venture—
A new converſion of the Jndies,
Then to make Courtiers, able men or honeſt.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: I do believe you love no Courtier,
And by my troth to gheſſe you into love
With any I can thinke of; is beyond
Either your will, or my imagination.
And yet I am ſure y'ar caught: and I will know him,
Ther's none left now worthy the thinking of;
Unles it be a Souldier, and I am ſure,
I would ever bleſſe my ſelfe from ſuch a fellow.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Why preethee?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Out upon 'em firelockes,
They are nothing 'ith world, but Buff and Scarlet,
Tough unhewne peeces, to hack ſwords upon;
I had as liev be courted by a Cannon,
As one of thoſe.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Thou art too malitious,
Upon my faith me thinks they're worthy men.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Say ye ſo? I'le pull ye on a little further.
VVhat worth can be in thoſe men, whoſe profeſſion
Is nothing ith' world but drinke and damn me,
Out of whoſe violence they are poſſeſt
VVith legions of unwholſome whores and quarrels;
I am of that opinion, and will dye in't,
There is no underſtanding, nor can be
In a ſouſt Souldier.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Now 'tis ignorance
I eaſily perceive that thus provokes thee,
And not the love of truth; I'le lay my life
If God had made thee man, thou hadſt been a coward.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: If to be valiant, be to be a Souldier; I'le tel ye true,
I had rather be a Coward, I am ſure with leſſe ſin.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: This hereſie muſt be look'd too in time: for if it ſpread
'Twill grow too peſtilent; were I a Scholler
I would ſo hamper thee for thy opinion,
That ere I left, I would write thee out of credit
VVith all the world, and make thee not beleev'd
Even in indifferent things; that I would leave thee
A reprobate out of the ſtate of honour.
By all good things, thou haſt flung aſperſions
So like a foole (for I am angry with thee)
Upon a ſort of men; (that let me tell thee
Thy mothers mother would have been a Saint
Had ſhe conceiv'd a Souldier) they are people
(I may commend 'em, while I ſpeake but truth)
Of all the old world, only left to keepe
Man as he was, valiant and vertuous:
They are the modell of thoſe men, whoſe honours
VVe heave our hands at when we heare recited.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: They are, and I have all I ſought for, 'tis a ſouldier
You love, hide it no longer; you have betray'd your ſelfe;
Come, I have found your way of commendations,
And what I ſaid, was but to pull it from ye.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: 'Twas pretty, are you grown ſo cunning, Clora?
I grant I love a ſouldier; But what ſouldier
VVill be a new taske to ye? But all this
I doe imagine was but laid to draw me
Out of my melancholy.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: I will have the man
Ere I forſake ye.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I muſt to my chamber.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: May not I goe along?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Yes, but good wench
Move me no more with theſe fond queſtions,
They worke like Rubarb with me.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.l: VVell, I will not. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Laelia and her waiting woman.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: How now? who was that you ſtaid to ſpeak withal.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: The old man forſooth.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: VVhat old man?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.p: The poor old man that uſes to come hither he that you call Father.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Have you diſpatched him?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: No; he would faine ſpeake with you.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Wilt thou never learn more manners, then to draw in ſuch
Needy raſcalls to diſquiet me? goe, anſwer him I wil
Not be at leiſure.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: He will needs ſpeak with you; and good old man he weeps ſo,
That by my troth I have not the heart to deny him, pray let you are not in love
Him ſpeake with you.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Lord how tender ſtomach'd you are grown of late?
With him, are ye; if ye be, ſtrike up the match; you ſhal have
Three, l. & a paire of blankets; will ye goe anſwer him?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Pray let him ſpeak with you, he wil not away elſe.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Well, let him in then if there be no remedy; I thank God I am
Able to abuſe him, i ſhal nere come cleer elſe of him.
Now Sr. what is your buſineſs? pray be ſhort; for I have other
Matters of more moment to call me from ye.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: If you but looke upon me like a daughter
And keepe that love about ye that makes good
A Fathers hope, you'l quickly finde my buſineſſe,
And what I would ſay to you, and before
I aske, will be a giver: ſay that ſleepe,
I meane that love, or be but num'd within ye,
The nature of my want is ſuch a ſearcher,
And of ſo mighty power, that where he findes
This dead forgetfulneſſe, it works ſo ſtrongly,
That if the leaſt heate of a childes affection
Remaine unperiſh'd, like another nature,
It makes all new againe; pray do not ſcorne me,
Nor ſeeme to make your ſelfe a greater buſineſſe
Then my relieving.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: If you were not old
I ſhould laugh at ye; what a vengeance ailes ye
To be ſo childiſh to imagine me
A founder of old fellows? make him drinke wench,
And if there be any cold meate in the Buttery,
Give him ſome broken bread and that, and rid him.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Is this a childs love? or a recompence
Fit for a fathers care? O Lelia,
Had I been thus unkind, thou hadſt not been;
Or like me miſerable: But 'tis impoſſible
Nature ſhould dye ſo utterly within thee,
And looſe her promiſes; thou art one of thoſe
She ſet her ſtamp more excellently on,
Then common people, as fore-telling thee
A generall example of her goodneſſe;
Or ſay ſhe could lye, yet religion
(For love to parents is religious)
Would leade thee right againe: Looke well upon me
I am the roote that gave thee nouriſhment,
And made thee ſpring faire, do not let me periſh
Now I am old and ſapleſſe.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: As I live
I like ye far worſe now ye grow thus holy,
I grant you are my father; am I therefore
Bound to conſume my ſelfe and be a begger
Still in relieving you? I doe not feele
Any ſuch mad compaſſion yet within me.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I gave up all my ſtate to make yours thus.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: 'Twas as ye ought to do, and now ye cry for't
As children do for babies backe againe.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: How wouldſt thou have me live?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I would not have ye,
Nor know no reaſon Fathers ſhould deſire
To live, and be a trouble, when children
Are able to inherit, let them dye,
'Tis ſit, and lookt for, that they ſhould do ſo.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Is this your comfort?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: All that I feele yet.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I will not curſe thee.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: If you do I care not.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Pray you give me leave to weep

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Why pray take leave,
If it be for your eaſe.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Thy mother dyed,
Sweet peace be with her, in a happy time.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: She did Sir, as ſhe ought to do, would you
Would take the paines to follow; what ſhould you
Or any old man do wearing away
In this world with diſeaſes, and deſire
Only to live to make their children ſcourge-ſticks,
And hoord up mill-money? me thinks a marble
Lyes quieter upon an old mans head
Then a cold fit a'th palſey.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: O good God!
To what an impudence thou wretched woman,
Ha •• thou begot thy ſelfe againe! well, juſtice
Will puniſh diſobedience.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: You miſtake Sir;
Twill puniſh beggers, fye for ſhame go worke
Or ſerve, you are grave enough to be a Porter
In ſome good man of worſhips houſe, and give
Sententious anſwers to the commers in,
A pretty place; or be of ſome good Conſort,
You had a pleaſant touch 'ath Cithron once,
If idelneſſe have not bereft you of it:
Be any thing but old, and beggarly,
Two ſinnes that ever do out grow compaſſion;
If I might ſee you offer at a courſe
That were a likely one, and ſhew'd ſome proffit,
I would not ſtick for ten groates, or a noble.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Did I beget this woman?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Nay, I know not:
And 'till I know, I will not thanke you for't;
How ever, he that got me had the pleaſure,
And that me thinkes, is a reward ſufficient.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: I am ſo ſtrangly ſtroken with amazement,
I know not where I am, nor what I am.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: You had beſt take freſh aire ſome where elſe, 'twill bring ye
Out of your trance the ſooner.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Is all this
As you meane Lelia?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Yes believe me is it,
For yet I cannot thinke you are ſo fooliſh,
As to imagine you are young enough
To be my heire, or I ſo old to make
A Nurſe at theſe yeares for you, and attend
While you ſup up my State in penny pots
Of Malmſey: when I am excellent at Cawdles,
And Cullices. and have enough ſpare gold
To boyle away, you ſhall be welcome to me;
'Till when I'de have you be as merry Sir
As you can make your ſelfe with that you have,
And leave to trouble me with theſe relations;
Of what you have beene to me, or you are,
For as I heare them, ſo I looſe them; this
For ought I know yet, is me reſolution.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Well God be with thee, for I feare thy end
Will be a ſtrange example. Exit Father.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Fare ye well Sir;
Now would ſome poore tender harted foole have wept,
Relented, and have been undone: ſuch children
I thanke my underſtanding I hate truely,
For by my troth I had rather ſee their teares;
Then feele their pitties: my deſires and ends
Are all the kindred that I have, and friends. Enter Woman.
Is he departed?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Yes, but heer's another.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Not of his tribe I hope; bring me no more
I would wiſh you ſuch as he is, If thou ſeeſt
They looke like men of worth, and ſtate, and carry
Ballaſt of both ſides like tall Gentlemen
Admit 'em, but no ſnakes to poyſon us
With poverty; wench you muſt learne a wiſe rule,
Looke not upon the youthes of men, and making,
How they diſcend in blood, nor let their tongues
Though they ſtrike ſodainly, and ſweet as muſique
Corrupt thy fancy: ſee, and ſay them faire too,
But ever keep thy ſelfe without their diſtance:
Unleſſe the love thou ſwallows be a pill,
Gilded to hide the bitterneſſe it brings,
Then fall on without feare wench, yet ſo wiſely
That one encounter cloy him not; nor promiſe
His love hath made thee more his, then his moneyes;
Learne this and thrive,
Then let thine honour ever,
(For that's the laſt rule) be ſo ſtood upon,
That men may fairely ſee
'Tis want of meanes, not vertue makes thee fall;
And if you weepe 'twill be a great deale better,
And draw on more compaſſion, which includes
A greater tenderneſſe of love and bounty;
