This is enough at once, digeſt it well:
Go let him in wench, if he promiſe proffit,
Not elſe.
O you are welcome my faire ſervant,
Upon my troth I have been longing for ye.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: This, by her rule ſhould be a liberall man,
I ſee the beſt on's may learne every day.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Ther's none come with you.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: You do the wiſer,
For ſome that have been here (I name no man)
Out of their malice, more then truth, have done me
Some few ill offices.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: How, ſweete?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Nay nothing,
Onely have talk't a little wildely of me;
As their unruly youth directed 'em:
Which though they bite me not, I would have wiſh'd
Had light upon ſome other that deſerv'd 'em.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Though ſhe deſerve this of the looſeſt tongue,
(Which makes my ſinne the more) I muſt not ſee it;
Such is my miſery: I would I knew him.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: No, no, let him go,
He is not worth your anger: I muſt chide you
For being ſuch a ſtranger to your Miſtris,
Why would you be ſo, Servant?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: I ſhould chide,
If chiding would worke any thing upon you:
For being ſuch a ſtranger to your Servant,
I meane to his deſires: when my deare Miſtris,
Shall I be made a happy man?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Fy Servant
What do you meane, unhand me, or by heav'n,
I ſhall be very angry, this is rudeneſſe.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: 'Twas but a kiſſe or two, that thus offends you

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: 'Twas more I thinke then you have warrant for.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: I am ſorry I deſerv'd no more.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: You may,
But not this rough way Servant: we are tender,
And ought in all to be reſpected ſo;
If I had been your horſe, or whore, you might
Back me with this intemperance; I thought
You had lov'd as worthy men, whoſe faire affections
Seeke pleaſures warranted, not puld by violence,
Do ſo no more.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: I hope you are not angry?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I ſhould be with another man, I am ſure,
That durſt appeare but halfe thus violent.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: I did not meane to raviſh ye

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: You couldot.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: You are ſo willing—

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Me thinkes this ſhadow,
If you had ſo much ſhame as fits a woman:
At leaſt of your way, Miſtris, long ere this
Had been lay'd of to me that underſtand ye.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: That underſtand me? Sir ye underſtand,
Nor ſhall no more of me then modeſty,
Will without feare deliver to a ſtranger;
You underſtand I am honeſt; elſe I tell yee
(Though you were better far then Iulio)
You, and your underſtanding are two fooles,
But were we Saints, thus we are ſtill rewarded.
I ſee that woman had a pretty catch on't,
That had made you the Maſter of a kindneſſes,
She durſt not anſwer openly; o me!
How eaſily we women may be cozen'd?
I tooke this Iulio as I have a faith,
(This young diſſembler with the ſober vizard)
For the moſt modeſt temper'd Gentleman,
The cooleſt, quieteſt, and beſt companion;
For ſuch an one I could have wiſh'd a woman.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: You have wiſh'd me ill enough a conſcience,
Make me no worſe for ſhame: I ſee the more
I worke by way of ſervice to obtaine ye
You worke the more upon me. Tell me truely
(While I am able to believe a woman,
For if you uſe me thus, that faith will periſh)
What is your end, and whether will you pull me?
Tell me, but tell me that I may not ſtart at,
And have a cauſe to curſe ye.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Bleſſe me goodneſſe!
To curſe me did you ſay Sir? let it be
For too much loving you then, ſuch a curſe
Kill me withall and I ſhall be a Martyr;
You have found a new way to reward my doting,
And I confeſſe a fit one for my folly,
For you your ſelfe if you have good within ye,
And dare be Maſter of it, know how deadly
This hart has held you ever; oh good God!
That I had never ſeene that falſe mans eyes,
That dare reward me thus with feares and curſes,
Nor never heard the ſweetneſſe of that tongue,
That will when this is knowne, yet cozen women:
Curſe me good Iulio, curſe me bitterly,
I do deſerve it for my confidence,
And I beſeech thee, if thou haſt a goodneſſe
Of power yet in thee to confirme thy wiſhes,
Curſe me to earth; for what ſhould I do here
Like a decaying flower, ſtill withering
Under his bitter wordes, whoſe kindly heate
Should give my poore hart life? No, curſe me Iulio,
Thou canſt not do me ſuch a benefit
As that, and well done, that the heav'ns may heare it.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Oh faire teares were you but as chaſt, as ſubtill,
Like Bones of Saints, ye would worke miracles;
What were theſe women to a man that knew not
The thouſand, thouſand wayes of their deceiving?
What riches had he found? Oh he would thinke
Himſelfe ſtill dreaming of a bleſſedneſſe,
That like continuall ſpring ſhould flouriſh ever.
For if ſhe were as good as ſhe is ſeeming,
Or like an Eagle could renew her vertues,
Nature had made another world of ſweetneſſe;
Be not ſo greiv'd ſweet Miſtris, what I ſed
You do, or ſhould know, was but paſſion;
Pray wipe your eyes and kiſſe me; take theſe trifles,
And weare them for me, which are onely rich
When you will put them on; Indeed I love ye,
Beſhrew my ſicke hart, if I grieve not for ye.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Will you diſſemble ſtill? I am a foole,
And you may eaſily rule me, if you flatter,
The ſin will be your owne.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: You know I doe not.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: And ſhall I be ſo childiſh once againe,
After my late experience of your ſpight
To credit you? you doe not know how deepe
(Or if you did, you would be kinder to me,)
This bitterneſſe of yours have ſtrooke my heart.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I pray no more.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Thus you would doe I warrant,
If I were married to you.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Married to me?
Is that your end?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Yes, Is not that the beſt end,
And as all hold, the nobleſt way of love?
Why doe you looke ſo ſtrange Sir? doe not you
Deſire it ſhould be ſo?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Stay.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Anſwer me.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Farwell. Exit Julio.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I, are you there? are all theſe teares loſt then?
Am I ſo overtaken by a foole
In my beſt daies and tricks? my wiſe fellow
Ile make you ſmart for't as I am a woman,
And if thou beeſt not timber, yet Ile warme thee:
And is he gon?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: He's not ſo lightly ſtrooke
To be recovered with a baſe repentance,
I ſhould be ſorry then: Fortune I pre'thee
Give me this man but once more in my armes,
And if I looſe him, women have no charmes. Exeunt omnes

sp.speaker: Iaco.
sp.l: SEigneur, What thinke you of this ſound of warrs?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: As onely of a ſound; they that intend
To doe are like deepe waters that run quietly
Leaving no face of what they were behind 'em,
This rumour is too common and too loude
To carry truth.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Shall we never live to ſee
Men looke like men againe,
Upon a march?
This cold dull ruſty peace makes us appeare
Like empty Pictures, onely the faint ſhadowes
Of what we ſhould be:
Would to God my Mother
Had given but halfe her will to my begetting
And made me woman, to ſit ſtill and ſing,
Or be ſicke when I liſt, or any thing
That is too idle for a man to thinke of:
Would I had been a whore 'thad been a courſe
Certaine, and of my conſcience of more gaine
Then two commands, as I would handle it:
Faith I could wiſh I had been any thing
Rather then what I am, a Soldier
A Carriere, or a Cobler, when I knew
What 'twas to weare a Sword firſt; for their trades
Are and ſhall be a conſtant way of life,
While men ſend cheeſes up, or weare out buskins.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Thou art a little too impatient,
And mak'ſt thy anger a far more vexation
Then the not having warrs: I am a Soldier
Which is my whole Inheritance, yet I
Though I could wiſh a breach with all the world
If not diſhonourable, I am not ſo malitious,
To curſe the faire peace of my Mother Countrey;
But thou want'ſt money; and the firſt ſupply
Will bury theſe thoughts in thee.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Pox a peace.
It fills the Kingdome full of holydayes,
And onely feedes the wants of whores and pipers;
And make the idle drunken Rogues, get Spinſters.
'Tis true I may want money, and no litle,
And almoſt cloathes too: of which if I had both
In full abundance: yet againſt all peace,
That brings up miſchiefe thicker then a ſhowre,
I would ſpeake louder then a Lawyer;
By heaven it is the ſurfet of all youth,
That makes the toughneſſe, and the ſtrength of nations
Melt into women. 'Tis an eaſe that broodes
Theeves, and baſterds onely.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: This is more,
(Though it be true) then we ought to lay open,
And ſeaſons onely of an indiſcretion,
Believe me Captaine ſuch diſtemper'd ſpirits
Once out of motion, though they be proofe valiant,
If they appeare thus violent and fierie,
Breed but their owne diſgraces; and are nearer
Doubt, and ſuſpect in Princes, then rewardes.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: 'Tis well they can be neere 'em any way,
But call you thoſe true ſpirits, ill affected
That whil'ſt the warres were, ſerv'd like walls and ribs,
To girdle in the Kingdome?
And now falne
Through a faint peace into affliction,
Speake but their miſeryes? come, come, Fabritio
You may pretend what patience ye pleaſe,
And ſeeme to yoake your wants like paſſions;
But while I know thou art a Souldier,
And a deſerver, and no other harveſt
But what thy Sword reapes for thee to come in,
You ſhall be pleas'd to give me leave to tell ye,
You wiſh a Devill of this muſty peace:
To which prayer,
As one that's bound in conſcience, and all
That love our trade, I cry, Amen.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Prethee no more, we ſhall live well enough,
There's wayes enough beſides the warrs to men
That are not loggs, and lye ſtill for the handes
Of others to remove 'em.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: You may thrive Sir,
Thou art young and handſome yet, and well enough
To pleaſe a widdow: thou canſt ſing, and tell
Theſe fooliſh love-tales; and indite a little,
And if need be, compile, a pretty matter
And dedicate it to the honourable,
Which may a waken his compaſſion,
To make ye Clarke a'th kitchen, and at length
Come to be married to my Ladyes woman,
After ſhe's crack't 'ith ring.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: 'Tis very well Sir.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: But what doſt thou thinke ſhall become of me,
With all my imperfections? let me dye
If I thinke I ſhall ever reach above
A forlorne Tapſter, or ſome frothy fellow,
That ſtincks of ſtale beere.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Captaine Jacamo,
Why ſhould you thinke ſo hardly of your vertues?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: What vertues? by this light I have no vertue,
But downe right buffeting: what can my face
That is no better then a ragged Map now
Of where I have marcht and traveled profit me?
Unleſſe it be for Ladyes to abuſe, and ſay
'Twas ſpoil'd for want of a Bongrace when I was young,
And now 'twill make a true prognoſtication
Of what man muſt be? Tell me of a fellow
That can mend noſes, and complaine,
So tall a ſouldier ſhould want teeth to his ſtomach?
And how it was great pitty, that it was,
That he that made my body, was ſo buſied
He could not ſtay to make my leggs too? but was driven
To clap a paire of cat-skins to my knees, for which
I am indebted to two Schoole-boyes? this
Muſt follow neceſſary.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Ther's no ſuch matter.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Then for my morals, and thoſe hidden pieces,
That art beſtowes upon me, they are ſuch
That when they come to light: I am ſure will ſhame me.
For I can neither write, nor read, nor ſpeake
That any man ſhall hope to proffet by me,
And for my Languages, they are ſo many
That put them altogether, they will ſcarce
Serve to beg ſingle beere in: the plaine truth is,
I love a Souldier, and can lead him on,
And if he fight well I dare make him drunk:
This is my vertue, and if this will do
I'le ſcramble yet amongſt 'em.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: 'Tis your way
To be thus pleaſant ſtill, but feare not man
For though the warrs fail, we ſhall ſcrew our ſelves
Into ſome courſe of life yet.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Good Fabritio,
Have a quick eye upon me, for I feare
This peace will make me ſomething that I love not;
For by my troth though I am plaine and dudgion,
I would not be an Aſſe: and to ſell parcels,
I can as ſoone be hang'd; preethee beſtowe me
And ſpeake ſome little good, though I deſerve not.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Come wee'l conſider more: ſtay, this
Should be another winde-fall of the warrs.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: He lookes indeed like an old tater'd Colours,
That every winde would borrow from the Staffe;
Theſe are the hopes we have for all our hurts:
They have not caſt his tongue too.

sp.speaker: Father.
sp.l: They that ſay
Hope never leaves a wretched man that ſeekes her,
I thinke are either patient fooles, or lyers,
I am ſure I finde it ſo, for I am maſter'd,
With ſuch a miſery and griefe together
That that ſtay'd Anchor men lay hold upon
In all their needs, is to me lead that bowes,
Or breakes, with every ſtrong ſea of my ſorrowes.
I could now queſtion heaven, (were it well
To looke into their juſtice) why thoſe faultes,
Thoſe heavy ſinnes, other provoke 'em with
Should be rewarded on the heads of us,
That hold the leaſt alliance to their vices?
But this would be too curious; for I ſee
Our ſuffering, not diſputing, is the end,
Reveal'd to us of all theſe miſeryes.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Twenty ſuch holy Hermits in a Campe,
Would make 'em all Carthuſians, I'le be hang'd
If hee know what a whore is: or a health,
Or have a nature liable to learne,
Or ſo much honeſt nurture to be drunke.
I do not thinke he has the ſpleene to ſweare
A greater oath then Sempſters utter Sockes with,
S'pur him a queſtion.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: They are ſtrangers both
To me, as I to them I hope: I would not have
Me and my ſhame together known by any,
I'le rather lye my ſelfe unto another.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I need not aske you Sir your Countrey,
I heare you ſpeake this tongue: pray what more are ye?
Or have you been? if it be not offenſive
To urge ye ſo far, miſery in your yeares,
Gives every thing a tongue to queſtion it.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Sir, though I could be pleas'd to make my ills
Only mine owne, for grieving other men,
Yet to ſo faire and courteous a demander
That promiſes compaſſion, at worſt, pity,
I will relate a little of my ſtory.
I am a Gentleman, however thus
Poore and unhappy; which beleeve me ſir
Was not borne with me: for I well have tri'd
Both the extreams of fortune; and have found
Both dangerous: my younger yeares provok'd me,
Feeling in what an caſe I ſlept at home,
Which to all ſtirring ſpirits is a ſickneſſe,
To ſee far Countreyes, and obſerve their Cuſtomes.
I did ſo; and I travelld till that courſe
Stor'd me with language, and ſome few ſlight manners,
Scarce worth my money; when an ich poſſeſt me
Of making armes my active end of travell.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: But did you ſo?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I did; and twenty winters
I wore the Chriſtian Cauſe upon my ſword
Againſt his enemies, at Buda ſiege
Full many a cold night have I lodg'd in armour
When all was frozen in me but mine honour:
And many a day, when both the Sun and Canon
Strove, who ſhould moſt deſtroy us: have I ſtood
Malld up in ſteele, when my rough ſinews ſhrunke,
And this parch'd body ready to conſume
As ſoone to aſhes, as the pike I bore:
Want has been to me as another nature,
Which makes me with this patience ſtill profeſſe it;
And if a Souldier may without vaine-glory
Tell what h'as done, beleeve me Gentlemen
I could turne over annals of my dangers:
With this poor weakneſſe have I mann'd a breach,
And made it firme with ſo much blood, that all
I had to bring me off alive was anger.
Thrice was I made a ſlave, and thrice redeem'd
At price of all I had; The miſeries
Of which times, if I had a heart to tell,
Would make ye weep like children; But I'le ſpare ye

sp.speaker: Ja
sp.l: Fabricio, we two have been ſouldiers
Above theſe fourteen yeares, yet a my conſcience
All we have ſeen, compar'd to his experience
Has been but cudgel-play, or Cock-fighting.
By all the faith I have in armes, I reverence
The very poverty of this brave fellow:
Which were enough it ſelfe, and his to ſtrengthen
The weakeſt towne againſt halfe Chriſtendome.
I was never ſo aſham'd of ſervice
In all my life before, now I conſider
What I have done; and yet the rogues would ſweare
I was a valiant fellow; I do finde
The greateſt danger I have brought my life through,
Now I have heard this worthy, was no more
Then ſtealing of a May-pole, or at worſt,
Fighting at ſingle billet with a Barge-man.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I do believe him Jacamo.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Beleeve him?
I have no faith within me, if I doe not.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I ſee they are ſouldiers?
And if we may judge by affections
Brave and deſerving men: how they are ſtir'd
But with a meer relation of what may be?
Since I have wonne beliefe, and am not known,
Forgive me honour, i'le make uſe of thee.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Sir would I were a man, or great, or able
To looke with liberall eyes upon your vertue.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Let's give him all we have, and leave off prating:
Here Souldier, there's even five months pay: be merry,
And get thee handſome cloths.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: What meane you Jacamo?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Ye are a foole.
The very ſtory's worth a hundred pound.
Give him more money.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Gentlemen, I know not
How I am able to deſerve this bleſſing.
But if I live to ſee faire dayes againe,
Something i'le doe in honour of your goodneſſe,
That ſhall ſhew thankfulneſſe, if not deſert.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: If you pleaſe Sir, till we procure ye place,
To eate with us, or weare ſuch honeſt garments
As our poor meanes can reach to, you ſhall be
A welcome man; to ſay more, were to feede ye
Only with words; we honour what y'ave been,
For we are ſouldiers, though not neere the worth
You ſpake of lately.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I do gheſſe ye ſo,
And knew, unleſſe he were a ſouldier,
He could not find the way to know my wants.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: But me thinks all this while y'are too temperate;
Do you not tell men ſometimes of their dulneſſe
When you are grip't, as now you are with need?
I do, and let them know thoſe ſilkes they weare
The Warre weaves for 'em: and the bread they eate
We ſow, and reape again to feed their hunger:
I tell them boldly, they are maſters of
Nothing but what we fight for: their faire women
Lye playing in their armes, whilſt we like Lares
Defend their pleaſures: I am angry too,
And often raile at theſe forgetfull great men
That ſuffer us to ſue for what we ought
To have flung on us, ere we aske.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I have
Too often told my griefes that way, when all
I reapt, was rudeneſſe of behaviour;
In their opinions men of Warre that thrive,
Muſt thank 'em when they raile: and wait to live.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Come Sir, I ſee your wants need more relieving,
Then looking what they are: pray goe with us.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I thanke you Gentlemen: ſince you are pleas'd
To do a benefit, I dare not croſſe it,
And what my ſervice or endeavours may
Stand you in need, you ſhall command, not pray.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.p: So you ſhall us; i'le to the Taylors with you bodily Exeunt

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Well, if this be true; I'le believe a woman
When I have nothing elſe to do.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: 'Tis certaine; if there be a way of truth,
In bluſhes, ſmiles, and commendatious;
For by this light, have heard her praiſe you fellow
In ſuch a pitch, as if ſh'ad ſtudied
To croude the worths of all men into him,
And I imagine theſe are ſeldome us'd
Without their ſpeciall ends, and by a maide
Of her deſires and youth.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: It may be ſo.
She's free as you or I am, and may have
By that prerogative, a liberall choiſe
In the beſtowing of her love.

sp.speaker: Lod
sp.l: Beſtowing?
If it be ſo, ſhe has beſtowed her ſelfe
Upon a trim youth: Piſo, what do you call him?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Why, Captain Jacamo.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: O Captaine Jack-boy,
That is the Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I thinke he be
A Gentleman at worſt.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: So think I too,
Would he would mend Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: And a tall one too.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Yes of his teeth; for of my faith I thinke
They are ſharper then his ſword, and dare do more
If the Beuffe meet him fairely.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Very well.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Now do I wonder what ſhe meanes to doe
When ſhe has married him.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Why well enough,
Traile his pike under him, and be a Gentlewoman
Of the brave Captaines company.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Doe you heare me?
This woman is my ſiſter, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: I am glad ſhe is none of mine: but Fredericke,
Thou art not ſuch a foole ſure to be angry
Unleſſe it be with her; We are thy friends man.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I thinke ye are.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Yes faith, and do but tell thee
How ſhee will utterly orethrow her credit,
If ſhe continue gracing of this pot-gun.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: I thinke ſhe was bewitcht, or mad, or blinde,
She would never have taken ſuch a ſcar-crow elſe
Into protection: of my life he lookes
Of a more ruſty ſwarth complexion
Then an old arming doublet.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: I would ſend
His face to the Cutlers then, and have it ſanguin'd,
'Twill looke a great deale ſweeter; then his noſe
I would have ſhorter, and my reaſon is,
His face will be ill mounted elſe.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: For his body,
I will not be my own Judge, leaſt I ſeeme
A railer, but let others look upon't,
And if they finde it any other thing
Then a trunke-ſeller, to ſend wines downe in,
Or a long walking-bottle, I'le be hang'd for't:
His hide, (for ſure he is a beaſt) is ranker
Then the Muſcovy leather: and grain'd like it.
And by all likeli-hoods he was begotten
Between a ſtubborn paire of winter boots.
His body goes with ſtraps, he is ſo churliſh.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Hee's poor and beggerly beſides all this:
And of a nature farre uncapable
Of any benefit: for his manners cannot
Shew him a way to thanke a man that does one,
He's ſo uncivill: you may do a part
Worthy a brother, to perſwade your ſiſter
From her undoing: if ſhe prove ſo fooliſh
To marry this caſt Captaine, looke to finde her
Within a month, where you, or any good man
Would bluſh to know her: ſelling cheeſe and prunes,
And retayl'd bottle ale: I grieve to think
Becauſe I lov'd her, what a march this Captaine
Will ſet her into.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You are both, beleeve me,
Two arrant Knaves; and were it not for taking
So juſt an execution from his hands
You have beli'd thus, I would ſwaddle ye,
Till I could draw off both your skins like ſcaberds.
That man that you wrong'd thus, though to me
He be a ſtranger, yet I know, ſo worthy,
However low in fortune, that his worſt parts,
The very wearing of his cloths, would make
Two better Gentlemen then you dare be,
For there is vertue in his outward things.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Belike you love him then.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Yes marry do I.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: And will be angry for him.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: If you talke
Or pull your face into a ſtich againe,
As I love truth I ſhall be very angry.
Do not I know thee, though thou haſt ſome land
To ſet thee out thus among Gentlemen,
To be a prating and vain-glorious aſſe?
I do not wrong thee now, for I ſpeake truth.
Doe not I know thou haſt been a cudgel'd coward,
That has no cure for ſhame but cloath of ſilver?
And thinkſt the wearing of a gawdy ſuite
Hides all diſgraces?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: I underſtand you not, you hurt not me
Your anger flies ſo wide.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Signeur Frederick,
You much miſtake this Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: If you would pleaſe to be leſſe angry,
I would tell you how.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You had better ſtudy Sir
How to excuſe your ſelfe if ye be able,
Or I ſhall tell you once againe.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Not me Sir;
For I proteſt what I have ſaid, was only
To make you underſtand your ſiſters danger.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: He might if it pleas'd him conceive it ſo.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I might if it pleas'd me ſtand ſtill and heare
My ſiſter made a may-game, might I not?
And give allowance to your liberall jeſts
Upon his perſon, whoſe leaſt anger would
Conſume a legion of ſuch wretched people,
That have no more to juſtifie their actions
But their tongues ends? that dare lye every way
As a mill grindes? From this houre I renounce
All part of fellowſhip that may hereafter
Make me take knowledge of ye, but for Knaves;
And take heed, as ye love whole skins, and coxcombs,
How, and to whom ye prate thus; for this time
I care not if I ſpare ye: do not ſhake,
I will not beat ye, though ye doe deſerve it
Richly.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: This is a ſtrange courſe Fredericke;
But ſure you do not, or you would not know us,
Beate us?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: 'Tis ſomewhat low Sir, to a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I'le ſpeak but few words, but I'le make 'em truths;
Get you gone both, and quickly, without murmuring,
Or looking big: and yet before you goe
I will have this confeſt, and ſeriouſly,
That you two are two raſcalls.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Two Raſcals.
Come ſpeake it from your hearts, or by this light
My ſword ſhall flye among ye; anſwer me,
And to the point directly.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: You ſhall have
Your will for this time: ſince we ſee y'are grown
So far untemperate; Let it be ſo Sir
In your opinion.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Do not mince the matter,
But ſpeake the words plaine; and you Lodovick
That ſtand ſo tally on your reputation,
You ſhall be he ſhall ſpeake it.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: This is pretty,

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Let me not ſtay upon't.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Well we are raſcalls,
Yes Piſo, we are raſcals. Exit Lod. and Piſo.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Get ye gone now, not a word more, y'are raſcals.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: That ſhould be Fredericke.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: 'Tis he: Fredericke?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: A friend Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: It is ſo, by the voyce
I have ſought you Gentlemen, and ſince I have found you,
So neare our houſe, I'le force ye ſtay a while,
I pray let it be ſo.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: It is too late,
Wee'l come and dine to morrow with your ſiſter,
And do our ſervices.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Who were thoſe with you?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: We met two came from hence:
Two idle fellows,
That you ſhall beate hereafter, and I'le tell ye
Some fitter time a cauſe ſufficient for it.

sp.speaker: Fabr.
sp.l: But Fredericke, tell me truly; do you thinke
Shee can affect my friend?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No certainer
Then when I ſpeake of him, or any other,
She entertaines it with as much deſire
As others do their recreations.

sp.speaker: Fabr.
sp.l: Let not him have this light by any meanes;
He will but thinke he's mockt, and ſo grow angry,
Even to a quarrell: he's ſo much diſtruſtfull
Of all that take occaſion to commend him—
Women eſpecially: for which he ſhuns
All converſation with 'em, and beleeves
He can be but a mirth to all their Sex.
Whence is this muſique?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: From my ſiſters chamber.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: The touch is excellent' let's be attentive.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Harke, are the waights abroad?

sp.speaker: Fabr.
sp.l: Be ſofter prethee,
'Tis private muſicke.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: What a dyn it makes?
I had rather hear a Jews-trump then theſe Lutes,
They crye like Schoole-boyes.

sp.speaker: Fabr.
sp.l: Prethee Jacamo.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Well I heare, or ſleepe, I care not whether.

body.head: The SONG.
body.stage: Enter at the window Francke and Clora.

sp.l: TEll me deareſt what is Love?
'Tis a lightning from above,
'Tis an arrow, 'tis a fire,
'Tis a boy they call Deſire.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.l: 'Tis a grave,
Gapes to have
Thoſe poore fooles that long to prove.
Tell me more, are women true?
Yes, ſome are, and ſome as you.
Some are willing, ſome are ſtrange,
Since you men firſt taught to change.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.l: And till troth
Be in both,
All ſhall love, to love anew.
Tell me more yet, can they grieve?
Yes, and ſicken ſore, but live:
And be wiſe, and delay,
When you men are as wiſe as they.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.l: Then I ſee
Faith will be,
Never till they both beleeve.

sp.speaker: Franc.
sp.l: Clora, come hither; who are theſe below there?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Where?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Ha? I ſhould know their ſhapes
Though it be darkiſh; there are both our brothers,
What ſhould they make thus late here?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: What's the tother?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: What tother?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: He that lyes along there.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: O, I ſee him
As if he had a branch of ſome great Petigree
Grew out on's belly.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: That ſhould be,
If I have any knowledge in proportion.—

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: They ſee us.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis no matter.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: VVhat a log
Is this, to ſleep ſuch muſique out?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No more let's heare 'em.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: If I have any knowledge in proportion,
The Captaine Jacamo, thoſe are his legs
Upon my conſcience.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: By my faith, and neate ones.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: You mean the boots, I thinke they are neate by nature,

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: As thou art knaviſh, would I ſaw his face!

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: 'Twould ſcare you in the dark.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: A worſe then that
Has never ſcar'd you Clora to my knowledge.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: 'Tis true, for I never have ſeen a worſe;
Nor while I ſay my prayers heartily,
I hope I ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: VVell, I am no tell tale:
But is it not great pitty, tell me Clora,
That ſuch a brave deſerving Gentleman
As every one delivers this to be,
Should have no more reſpect, and worth flung on him
By able men? VVere I one of theſe great ones,
Such vertues ſhould not ſleep thus.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: VVere he greater
He would ſleep more I thinke: I'le waken him.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.l: Away ye foole.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Is he not dead already, and they two taking order
About his Blacks? me thinks they are very buſie,
A fine cleane coarſe he is: I would have him buried
Even as he lyes, croſſe legg'd, like one o'th Templers
(If his weſt-phaly gammons will hold croſſing)
And on his breſt, a buckler with a pike in't,
In which I would have ſome, learned Cutler
Compile an Epitaph, and at his feete
A muſquet, with this word upon a Labell
VVhich from the cocks mouth thus ſhould be delivered,

l.hi: I have diſcharg'd the office of a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.l: VVell, if thy Father were a Souldier
Thus thou wouldſt uſe him.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: Such a Souldier,
I would indeed.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: If he heare this, not all
The power of man could keep him from the windowes
• ill they were downe and all the dores brok open:
For Gods ſake make her cooler: I dare not venture
To bring him elſe: I know he will goe to buffetts
Within five words with her, if ſhe holds this ſpirit;
Let's waken him, and away, we ſhall heare worſe elſe.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Well if I be not even with thee Clora
L • t m • be hang'd for this: I know thou doſt it
Onely to anger me, and purge your witt
Which would breake out elſe.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: I have found ye,
Ile be no more croſſe, bid'em good night

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: No, no, they ſhall not know, we have ſeen'em;
Shut the window. Exit Fran. and Clora.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Will you get up Sir?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Have you paid the Fidlers?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: You are not left to doe it: Fie upon thee,
Haſt thou forſworne manners?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Yes unleſſe
They would let me eate my meate without long graces
Or drinke without a preface to the pledger;
Oft will it pleaſe you, ſhall I be ſo bold ſir
Let me remember your good bedfellow,
And lye and kiſſe my hand unto my Miſtris
As often as an Ape does for an Aple;
Theſe are meere Schiſmes in Soldiers; wher's my friend?
Theſe are to us as bitter as purgations,
We love that generall freedome we are bred to;
Hang theſe faint fooleries, they ſmell of peace,
Doe they not friend?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Faith Sir to me they are
As things indifferent, yet I uſe'em not,
Or if I did, they would not prick my conſcience.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Come, ſhall we goe? 'tis late.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Yes any whether,
But no more Muſick, it has made me dull.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Faith any thing but drinking diſturbs thee Jacomo
Wee'l ev'n to bed.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Content.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Thou wilt dreame of wenches.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I never thinke of any I thanke God
But when I am drunke, and then tis but to caſt
A cheape way how they may be all deſtroyd
Like vermine; let's away I am very ſleepy.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: I, thou art ever ſo, or angry, come. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I Will but ſee her once more Angilo
That I may hate her more, and then I am
My ſelfe againe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I would not have thee tempt luſt,
Tis away dangerous, and will deceive thee
Hadſt thou the conſtancy of all men in thee.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Having her ſins before me, I dare ſee her
Were ſhe as catching as the plague, and deadly,
And tell her ſhe is fouler then all thoſe
And far more peſtilent, if not repentant,
And like a ſtronge man, chide her well, and leave her.

sp.speaker: Arg.
sp.l: 'Tis eaſily ſaid, of what complexion is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Make but a curious frame unto thy ſelfe
As thou wouldſt ſhape an Angell in thy thought
Such as the Poets, when their fancies ſweat
Imagine Iuno is, or faire eyde Pallas
And one more excellent, then all thoſe figures
Shalt thou finde her; ſhees browne, but of a ſweetnes,
(If ſuch a poore word may expreſſe her beauty)
Beleeve me Angilo would doe more miſchiefe
With a forc't ſmile, then twenty thouſand Cupids
With their love quivers, full of Ladies eyes,
And twice as many flames, could fling upon us.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Of what age is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: As a Roſe at faireſt,
Neither a bud, nor blown, but ſuch a one,
Were there a Hercules to get againe
With all his glory, or one more then he
The god would chooſe out mongſt a race of women
To make a mother of; ſhe is outwardly
All that bewitches ſenſe; all that entiſes,
Nor is it in our vertue to uncharme it.
And when ſhe ſpeakes, oh Angilo, then muſick
(Such as old Orpheus made, that gave a ſoule
To aged mountaines, and made rugged beaſts
Lay by their rages; and tall trees that knew
No ſound but tempeſts, to bow downe their branches
And heare, and wonder; and the Sea, whoſe ſurges
Shooke their white heads in heaven, to be as midnight
Still, and attentive; ſteales into our ſoules
So ſuddenly, and ſtrangely, that we are
From that time no more ours but what ſhe pleaſes.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Why looke, how far you have thruſt your ſelfe againe
Into your old diſeaſe? are you that man
With ſuch a reſolution, that would venture
To take your leave of folly, and now melt
Even in repeating her?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: I had forgot me.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: As you will ſtill doe.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: No, the ſtrongeſt man
May have the grudging of an ague on him,
This is no more; let's go, I would faine be fit
To be thy friend againe, for now I am no mans.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Goe you, I dare not goe, I tell you truely
Nor were it wiſe I ſhould.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I am well.
And if I can, will keepe my ſelfe ſo.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Ha? thou mak'ſt me ſmile, though I have little cauſe,
To ſee how prettily thy feare becomes thee;
Art thou not ſtrong enough to ſee a woman?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Yes, twenty thouſand: but not ſuch a one
As you have made her; Ile not lye for'th matter:
I know I am fraile, and may be coſen'd too
By ſuch a Syren.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Faith thou ſhalt goe, Angilo

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Faith but I will not; no I know how far Sir
I am able to hold out, and will not venture
Above my depth: I doe not long to have
My ſleepe ta'ne from me, and goe pulingly
Like a poore wench had loſt her market money;
And when I ſee good meat, ſit ſtill and ſigh,
And call for ſmall beere; and conſume my wit
In making Anagrams, and faithfull poſes;
I doe not like that Itch, I am ſure I had rather
Have the maine pox, and ſafer.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt goe,
I muſt needs have thee as a witneſſe with mee
Of my repentance; as thou lov'ſt me goe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Well I will goe, ſince you will have it ſo,
But if I prove a foole too, looke to have me
Curſe you continually, and fearefully.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: And if thou ſeeſt me fall againe, good Angilo
Give me thy councell quickly leaſt I periſh.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Pray God I have enough to ſave my ſelfe,
For as I have a ſoule, I had rather venture
Upon a ſavage Iſland, then this woman. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: From whom Sir, comes this bounty? for I thinke
You are miſtaken.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: No Sir, 'tis to you,
I am ſure my Miſtris ſent it.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Whoes your Miſtris,
That I may give her thanks?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The vertuous Widow,

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: The vertuous widow Sir? I know none ſuch:
Pray what's her name?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Laelia.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I knew you err'd
'Tis not to me I warrant ye; there Sir,
Carry it to thoſe ſhe feedes fat with ſuch favours,
I am a ſtranger to her.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Good Sir take it,
And if you will, I'le ſweare ſhe ſent it to you,
For I am ſure mine eye never went off ye
Since you forſook the Gentlemen you talk'd with
Juſt at her doore.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Indeed I talkt with two
Within this halfe houre in the ſtreet.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Tis you Sir,
And none but you I am ſent to: wiſer men
Would have been thankfull ſooner, and receiv'd it,
'Tis not a fortune every man can brag of,
And from a woman of her excellence.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Well Sir, I am Chatechiz'd; what more belongs to 't?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: This only Sir; ſhe would intreat you come
This evening to her without faile.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You gheſſe where.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Sir I have a tongue elſe. Exit Ser.
She is down-right Devill; or elſe my wants
And her diſobedience have provok't her
To looke into her foule ſelfe, and be ſorry.
I wonder how ſhe knew me? I had thought
I had been the ſame to all, I am to them
That chang'd me thus: God pardon me for lying,
For I have paid it home: many a good man
That had but found the profit of my way
Would forſweare telling true againe in haſt.
Here are my praters; now if I did well
I ſhould be labour 'em, but I have found
A way to quiet 'em, worth a thouſand on't.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: If we could get a fellow that would do it.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: What villany is now in hand?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: 'Twill be hard to be done in my opinion
Unleſſe we light upon an Engliſh-man
With ſeven-ſcore ſurfets in him.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Are the Engliſh-men ſuch ſtubborn drinkers?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Not a leake at Sea
Can ſucke more liquor; you ſhall have their children
Chriſtned in mull'd ſacke, and at five yeares old, able
To knocke a Dane downe: Take an Engliſh-man
And cry St. George, and give him but a raſher,
And you ſhall have him upon even terms
Defy a hogſhead; ſuch a one would do it
Home boy, and like a work-man: at what weapon?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Sherry ſack: I would have him drinke ſtark dead,
If it were poſſible: at worſt paſt pottage.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: What is the end then?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Doſt thou not perceive it?
If he be drunke dead, ther's a faire end of him.
If not, this is my end, or by enticing,
Or by deceiving, to conduct him where
The foole is, that admires him; and if ſober,
His nature be ſo rugged, what wilt be
When he is hot with wine? come lets about it,
If this be done but handſomely, I'le pawne
My head ſhe hath done with ſouldiers.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: This may do well.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Here's a new way to murther men alive,
I'le choake this traine: God ſave ye Gentlemen.
It is to you, ſtay: yes it is to you.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: What's to me?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: You are fortunate,
I cannot ſtand to tell you more now, meete me
Here ſoone, and you'l be made a man. Exit Father.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: What Viſion's this?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: I know not.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Well, I'le meet it,
Think you ot'h other, and let me a while
Dreame of this fellow.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: For the Drunkard, Lodowicke,
Let me alone.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Come, let's about it then. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, pray let me laugh extreamly.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Why? prethee why? haſt thou ſuch cauſe?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Yes faith, my brother wil be here ſtraightway, &—

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: The other party: ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: VVhat party?
VVench thou art not drunke.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: No faith.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Faith thou haſt been among the bottles Clora;

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Faith but I have not Franke: Prethee be handſom,
The Captaine comes along too, wench.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: O is that it?
That tickles ye.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Yes, and ſhall tickle you too,
You underſtand me?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: By my troth thou art grown
A ſtrange lewd wench: I muſt e'ne leave thy company,
Thou wilt ſpoile me elſe.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Nay, thou art ſpoil'd to my hand;
Hadſt thou been free, as a good wench ought to be,
VVhen I went firſt a birding for thy Love,
And roundly ſaid, that is the man muſt doe it,
I had done laughing many an houre agoe.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: And what doſt thou ſee in him, now thou knowſt him,
To be thus laught at?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Prethee be not angry
And I'le ſpeake freely to thee.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Doe, I will not.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Then as I hope to have a handſome husband,
This fellow in mine eye, and Franke I am held
To have a ſhrewd gheſſe at a pretty fellow,
Appeares a ſtrange thing.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Why how ſtrange for Gods ſake?
He is a man, and one that may content
(For any thing I ſee) a right good woman:
And ſure I am not blinde.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: There lyes the queſtion?
For, but you ſay he is a man, and I
Will credit you, I ſhould as ſoone have thought him
Another of Gods creatures; out upon him,
His body, that can promiſe nothing
But lazineſſe and long ſtrides.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Theſe are your eyes;
Where were they Clora, when you fell in love
With the old foot-man, for ſinging of Queen Dido?
And ſwore he look'd in his old velvet trucks
And his ſlyc't Spaniſh Jerkin, like Don Iohn?
You had a parlous judgment then, my Clora.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Who told you that?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I heard it.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Come, be friends,
The Souldier is a Mars, no more, we are all
Subject to ſlide away.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Nay, laugh on ſtill.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: No faith, thou art a good wench, and 'tis pity
Thou ſhouldſt not be well quarred at thy entring,
Thou art ſo high flown for him: Look, whoſe there?

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Prethee goe ſingle, what ſhould I do there,
Thou knowſt I hate theſe viſitations,
As I hate peace or perry.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Wilt thou never
Make a right man?

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: You make a right foole of me
To lead me up and down to viſit women,
And be abus'd and laugh'd at; let me ſterve
If I know what to ſay, unleſſe I aske 'em
What their ſhooes coſt?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Fye upon thee, coward,
Canſt thou not ſing?

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Thou knoweſt I can ſing nothing
But Plump • on parke.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Thou't be bold enough,
When thou art enterd once.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I had rather enter
A breach: If I miſcarry, by this hand
I will have you by'th eares for't.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Save ye Ladies.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: Sweet brother I dare ſweare, you'r welcome hither,
So is your Friend;

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Come, bluſh not, but ſalute 'em.

sp.speaker: Franck.
sp.l: Good Sir beleeve your Siſter; you are moſt welcome,
So is this worthy Gentleman whoſe vertues
I ſhall be proud to be acquainted with.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: She has found me out already, and has paid me;
Shall we be going?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Peace;
Your goodneſſe Lady
Will ever be afore us, for my ſelfe
I will not thanke you ſingle, leſt I leave
My friend, this Gentleman, out of acquaintance.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: More of me yet?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Would I were able Sir,
From either of your worths to merit thankes.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: But brother, is your friend thus ſad ſtill? me thinks
'Tis an unſeemly nature in a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: What hath ſhe to do with me, or my behaviour?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: He do's but ſhew ſo, prethee to him Siſter.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: If I do not breake thy head, I am no Chriſtian,
If I get off once.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Sir, we muſt intreat you
To thinke your ſelfe more welcome, and be merry,
'Tis pitty a faire man of your proportion
Should have a ſoule of ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Very well;
Pray Gentlewoman what would you have me ſay?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Do not you know Sir?

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: Not ſo well as you
That talke continually.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: You have hither, Sir.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: I thank him, ſo he has,
Faire fall his ſweet face for't.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Let my face
Alone, I would wiſh you, leaſt I take occaſion
To bring a worſe in queſtion.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Meaning mine?
Brother, where was your friend brought up? h'as ſure
Been a great lover in his youth of pottage,
They lye ſo dull upon his underſtanding.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: No more of that, thou'lt anger him at heart.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Then let him be more manly, for he lookes
Like a great School-boy that had been blown up
Laſt night at duſt-point.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: You will never leave
Till you be told how rude you are, fye Clora.
Sir will it pleaſe you ſit?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: And I'le ſit by you.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Woman be quiet, and be rul'd I would wiſh you.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: I have done, Sir Captaine.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Art thou not aſham'd?

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: You are an aſſe, I'le tell you more anon.
You had better ha been hang'd then brought me hither.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: You are grown a ſullen foole; either be handſom,
Or by this light I'le have wenches baite thee;
Goe to the Gentlewoman, and give her thanks,
And hold your head up; what?

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: By this light I'le brain thee.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Now ô my faith this Gentleman do's nothing
But it becomes him rarely; Clora, look
How well this little anger, if it be one,
Shews in his face.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Yes, it ſhewes very ſweetly.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Nay do not bluſh Sir, ô my troth it does,
I would be ever angry to be thus.
Fabritio, ô my conſcience if I ever
Do fall in love, as I will not forſwear it
Till I am ſomething wiſer, it muſt be,
I will not ſay directly with that face,
But certainly, ſuch another as that is,
And thus diſpoſe my chance to hamper me.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Doſt thou heare this, and ſtand ſtill?

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: You will prate ſtill;
I would you were not women, I would take
A new courſe with ye.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Why couragious?

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: For making me a ſtone to whet your tongues on.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Prethee ſweet Captaine.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Goe, goe ſpin, goe hang.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Now could I kiſſe him.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: If you long for kicking,
You'r beſt come kiſſe me, do not though, I'de wiſh ye,
I'le ſend my Foot-man to thee, he ſhall leap thee,
And thou wantſt horſing: I'le leave ye Ladies.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Beſhrew my heart you are unmannerly
To offer this unto a Gentleman
Of his deſerts, that comes ſo worthily
To viſite me, I cannot take it well.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: I come to viſite you, you fooliſh woman?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I, though you did Sir, and for that I thanke you,
I would be loth to looſe thoſe thankes; I knowe
This is but ſome odd way you have, and faith
It do's become you well to make us merry;
I have heard often of your pleaſant veine.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: What wouldſt thou ask more?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Pray thou ſcurvy fellowe
Thou haſt not long to live; adieu deare Damſels,
You ſilthy women farewell, and be ſober,
And keepe your chambers.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Farewell old Don Diego.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Away, away, you muſt not be ſo angry,
To part thus roughly from us; yet to me
This do's not ſhew, as if 'twere yours, the wars
May breed men ſomething plain I know,
But not thus rude; give me your hand good Sir
I know 'tis white, and—

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: If I were not patient,
What would become of you two prating houſwives?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: For any thing I know, we would in to ſupper,
And there begin a health of luſty Claret
To keep care from our hearts, and it ſhould be—

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Faith to whom? Mark but this Jacamo.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Even to the handſomeſt fellow now alive.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Do you know ſuch a one?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: He may be gheſt at,
Without much travel.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: There's another item.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: And he ſhould be a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: 'Twould be better.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: And yet not you ſweet Captaine

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Why not he?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Well; I ſhall live to ſee your husbands beate you,
And hiſſe 'em on like ban-dogs.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Green ſickneſſes and ſerving-men light on ye
With greaſy Codpieces, and woollen ſtockings,
The Devill (if he dare deal with two women)
Be of your counſels: Farewell Plaiſterers— Exit Jacamo.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: This fellow will be mad at Mid-ſumer
Without all doubt.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I thinke ſo too.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I am ſorry
Hee's gone in ſuch a rage; but ſure this holds him
Not every day.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Faith every other day
If he come neare a woman.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: I wonder how his mother could endure
To have him in her belly he's ſo boyſterous.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: He's to be made more tractable I doubt not.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Yes, if they taw him as they do whit-leather
Upon an iron, or beate him ſoft like Stock-fiſh.

div.head: Scaena quarta.
div.stage: Enter Laelia and her waiting woman with a vaile.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Art ſure 'tis he?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Yes, and another with him.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: The more the merryer; did you give that money
And charg'd it to be delivered where I ſhewed you?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Yes, and what elſe you bad me.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: That brave fellow,
Though he be old, what e're he be, ſhews toughneſſe,
And ſuch a one I long for, and muſt have
At any price; theſe young ſoft melting griſtles
Are only for my ſafer ends.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: They are here.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Give me my vaile, and bid the boy goe ſing
That ſong above, I gave him: the ſad Song:
Now if I miſſe him, I am curſt, goe wench
And tell 'em I have utterly forſworn
All company of men; yet make a venture
At laſt to let 'em in; thou knowſt theſe things,
Doe 'em to'th life.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: I warrant you I am perfect.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Some ill woman for her uſe would give
A million for this wench, ſhe is ſo ſubtle.

div.stage: Enter to the doore Julio and Angilo.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Good Sir deſire it not, I dare not do it,
For ſince your laſt being here, Sir, beleeve me
She has griev'd her ſelfe out of all company,
And (ſweet ſoule) almoſt out of life too.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Prethee,
Let me but ſpeake one word.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: You will offend Sir
And yet your name is more familiar with her
Then any thing but ſorrow, good Sir goe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: This little varlet hath her leſſon perfect,
Theſe are the baites they bob with.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Faith I will not.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: I ſhal be chidden cruelly for this;
But you are ſuch a Gentleman—

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: No more.

sp.speaker: Aug.
sp.l: There's a new Tyre-wench; peace, thou art well enough.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: What, has ſhe muſique?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Yes; for Gods ſake ſtay,
'Tis all ſhe feedes upon.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Alas poore ſoule.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Now will I pray devoutly, for there's need ont.

lg.l: AWay delights, goe ſeeke ſome other dwelling,
For I muſt dye.
Farewell falſe Love, thy tongue is ever telling
Lye after lye.
For ever let me reſt now from thy ſmarts,
Alas, for pitty goe,
And fire their hearts
That have been hard to thee, mine was not ſo.
Never againe deluding love ſhall know me,
For I will dye:
And all thoſe griefes that thinke to over-grow me
Shall be as I.
For ever will I ſleepe, while poore maids cry,
Alas for pity ſtay
And let us dye
With thee, men cannot mocke us in the day.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Miſtris? not one word, Miſtris if I grieve ye
I can depart againe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Let's goe then quickly,
For if ſhe get from under this darke cloud,
We ſhall both ſweate I feare for't.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Do but ſpeake
Though you turne from me, and ſpeake bitterly,
And I am gone, for that I think will pleaſe you.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Oh that all women were thus ſilent ever,
What fine things they were.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: You have look'd on me,
When (if there be beliefe in womens words
Spoken in teares) you ſwore you lov'd to do ſo.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: O me my heart!

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Now Julio play the man,
Or ſuch another will undoe thee:
Would I had any thing to keepe me buſie
I might not heare her; thinke but what ſhe is,
Or I doubt mainly, I ſhall be i'th maſh too.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.l: Pray ſpeake againe;

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Where is my woman?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Here.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Mercy upon me! what a face ſhe has?
Would it were vail'd againe.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Why did you let
This flattering man in to me? did not I
Charge thee to keep me from his eyes againe,
As carefully as thou wouldſt keep thine owne?
Thou haſt brought me poyſon in a ſhape of heaven
Whoſe violence will breake the hearts of all,
Of all weake women, as it has done mine,
That are ſuch fooles to love, and looke upon him.
Good Sir be gone, you know not what an eaſe
Your abſence is.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: By heaven ſhe is a wonder,
I cannot tell what 'tis, but I am ſqueamiſh.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Though I deſire to be here more then heaven
As I am now, yet if my ſight offend you,
So much I love to be commanded by you
That I will goe: Farewell—

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I ſhould ſay ſomething
E're you depart, and I would have you heare me:
But why ſhould I ſpeak to a man that hates me?
And will but laugh at any thing I ſuffer?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: If this be hate—

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Away, away deceiver.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Now help me Angilo!

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I am worſe then thou art.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Such teares as thoſe might make another woman
Believe thee honeſt Julio: almoſt me
That know their ends, for I confeſſe they ſtir me.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: What will become of me? I cannot goe now
If you would hang me, from her: o brave eye!
Steale me away for Gods ſake Julio.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Alas poor man! I am loſt againe too ſtrangely.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: No, I will ſooner truſt a Crocadile
When he ſheds teares, for he kills ſodainly,
And ends our cares at once; or any thing
That's evill to our natures, then a man;
I finde there is no end of his deceivings,
Nor no avoyding 'em, if we give way:
I was requeſting you to come no more,
And mocke me with your ſervice, 'tis not well,
Nor honeſt to abuſe us ſo far: you may love too;
For though, I muſt confeſſe I am unworthy
Of your love every way: yet I would have you
Thinke I am ſomewhat too good to make ſport of.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Will you believe me?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: for your vows and oaths,
And ſuch deceiving teares as you ſhed now,
I will as you doe, ſtudy to forget 'em.

sp.speaker: Jul
sp.l: Let me be moſt despis'd of men—

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: No more;
There is no new way left, by which your cunning
Shall once more hope to catch me; no, thou falſe man
I will avoid thee, and for thy ſake all
That beare thy ſtamp; as counterfeit in love.
For I am open ey'd againe, and know thee.
Goe, make ſome other weepe, as I have done,
That dare believe thee: goe, and ſweare to her
That is a ſtranger to thy cruelty,
And knowes not yet what man is, and his lyings,
How thou di'ſt daily for her: poure it out
In thy beſt lamentations; put on ſorrow,
As thou canſt, to deceive an Angell, Julio,
And vow thy ſelfe into her heart, that when
I ſhall leave off, to curſe thee for thy falſhood,
Still a forſaken woman may be found,
To call to heaven for vengeance.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: From this houre,
I heartily deſpiſe all honeſt women;
I care not if the world tooke knowledge on't,
I ſee there's nothing in them, but that folly
Of loving one man only: give me henceforth
(Before tne greateſt bleſſing can be thought of)
If this be one, a whore; that's all I aime at.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Miſtris, the moſt offending man is heard
Before his ſentence, why will you condemn me
E're I produce the truth to witneſſe with me
How innocent I am of all your angers?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: There is no truſting of that tongue, I know't,
And how far if it be believed it kills; no more Sir.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: It never lyed to you yet; if it did
'Twas only when it cal'd you mild and gentle.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Good Sir no more; make not my underſtanding
After I have ſuffered thus much evill by you,
So poor to thinke I have not reach'd the end
Of all your forc'd affections; yet becauſe
I once lov'd ſuch a ſorrow too too dearly,
As that would ſtrive to be; I do forgive ye
Even heartily, as I would be forgiven,
For all your wrongs to me; my charity
Yet loves you ſo far, (though againe I may not)
And wiſh when that time comes, you will love truly
(If you can ever doe ſo) you may finde
The worthy fruit of your affections,
True love againe, not my unhappy harveſt,
Which like a foole I ſow'd in ſuch a heart
So drye and ſtonie, that a thouſand ſhowres
From theſe two eyes, continually rayning,
Could never ripen.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Y'ave conquer'd me:
I did not thinke to yield, but make me now,
Even what you will my Lelia, ſo I may
Be but ſo truly happy to enjoy you.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: No, no, thoſe fond imaginations,
Are dead and buried in me, let 'em reſt.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: I'le marry you.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: The Devill thou wilt Iulio
How that word waken'd me? come hither friend,
Thou art a foole, looke ſtedfaſtly upon her
Though ſhe be all that I know excellent
As ſhe appeares, though I could fight for her,
And run through fire; though I am ſtarke mad too
Never to be recover'd, though I would
Give all I had l'th world to lye with her
Even to my naked ſoule, I am ſo far gone,
Yet me thinks ſtill we ſhould not doate away
That that is ſomething more then ours, our honours
I would not have thee marry her by no meanes,
Yet I ſhould do ſo; is ſhe not a whore?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: She is; But ſuch a one—

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: 'Tis true, ſhe's excellent,
And when I well conſider, Iulio
I ſee no reaſon we ſhould be confin'd
In our affections; when all creatures elſe
Enjoy ſtil where they like.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: And ſo will I then,

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: He's faſt enough I hope now, if I hold him.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: You muſt not do ſo though, now I conſider
Better what 'tis.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Do not conſider Angilo,
For I muſt do it.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: No I'le kill thee firſt.
I love thee ſo well that the wormes ſhall have thee
Before this woman, friend.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: I was your counſell.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: As I was a knave,
Not as I lov'd thee.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: All this is loſt upon me Angilo,
For I muſt have her: I will marry yee
When you pleaſe; pray looke better on me.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Nay then no more friend; farewell Iulio,
I have ſo much diſcretion left me yet
To know, and tell thee thou art miſerable.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Stay thou art more then ſhe, and now I finde it.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Is he ſo?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.p: No, I'le ſee thee ſterv'd firſt. Exit Lel.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Friend.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Fly her as I do, Iulio, ſhe's a witch.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Beate me away then, I ſhall grow heere ſtill elſe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: That were the way to have me grow there with thee
Farewell for ever. Exit Ang.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Stay, I am uncharm'd,
Farewell thou curſed houſe, from this houre be
More hated of me then a Leproſie. Exit Iulio.

sp.speaker: Lelia.
sp.l: Both gon? a plague upon 'em both,
Am I deceiv'd againe? Oh I would raile
And follow 'em; but I feare the ſpight of people,
'Till I have emptied all my gall; the next
I ſeize upon, ſhall pay their follies
To the laſt penny; This will worke me worſe
He that comes next, by heav'n ſhall feele their curſe. Exit.

div.head: Scaena quinta.
div.stage: Enter Iacamo at one doore Fabritio at another.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: O yee are a ſweet youth, ſo uncivilly
To rayle and run away?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: O are you there Sir?
I am glad I have found ye, you have not now your Ladies
To ſhew your wit before.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Thou woult not, woult 'a?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: What a ſweet youth I am, as you have made me,
You ſhall know preſently.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Put up your ſword
I have ſeene it often, 'tis a Fox.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: It is ſo,
And you ſhall feele it too; will you diſpatch Sir?
And leave your mirth out? or I ſhall take occaſion
To beate ye, and diſgrace you too.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Well ſince, there is no other way to deale with you
Let's ſee your ſword, I am ſure you ſcorne all odds,
I will fight with you —

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.p: How now? they meaſure, and Fab: get his Sword.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Nay ſtand out,
Or by this light I'le make yee.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: This is ſcurvy
And out of feare done.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: No Sir out of judgement,
For he that deales with thee, thou'rt growne ſo boyſtrous
Muſt have more wits, or more lives then another,
Or alwayes be in Armor, or inchanted;
Or he is miſerable.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Your end of this Sir?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: My end is only mirth to laugh at thee,
Which now I'le do in ſafety; ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Shart? then I am growne ridiculous.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Thou art,
And wilt be ſhortly ſport for little children,
If thou continueſt this rude ſtubborneneſſe.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: O God, for any thing that had an edge?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Fye, what a ſhame it is,
To have a lubber ſhew his teeth?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Why doſt thou laugh at me thou wretched fellow?
Speake with a pox; and looke ye render me
Iuſt ſuch a reaſon —

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I ſhall dye with laughing.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: As no man can finde fault with: I ſhall have
Another Sword; I ſhall ye fleering puppy.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Does not this teſtineſs ſhew finely in thee?
Once more take heed of children, if they finde thee
They'le breake up ſchoole, to beare thee company,
Thou wilt be ſuch a paſtime, and whoo'te at thee:
And call thee bloody bones, and Spade, and Spitfire,
And Gaffer Madman; and go by Ieronimo,
And will with wiſpe and come aloft, and crack rope,
And old Saint Dennis with the dudgeon Codpeeece:
And twenty ſuch names.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: No I thinke they will not.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Yes but they will: and Nurſes ſtill their children
Onely with thee, and • ere take him Iacanio.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Gods pretious, That I were but over thee
One Steeple height: I would fall and breake thy neck.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: This is the reaſon I laugh at thee,
And while thou art thus, will do: tell me one thing.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I wonder how thou durſt thus queſtion me,
Pre'thee reſtore my Sword.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Tell me but one thing,
And it may be I will: Nay Sir; keep out

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Well I will be your foole now, ſpeake your minde Sir.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Art thou not breeding Teeth?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: How? Teeth?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Yes Teeth, thou would'ſt not be ſo froward elſe.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Teeth?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Come, 'twill make thee
A little reumatique, but that's all one,
Weel'e have a Bib, for ſpoyling of thy doublet;
And a fring'd Muckender, hang at thy girdle,
I'le be thy Nurſe, and get a Corall for thee:
And a fine Ring of Bells.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Faith this is ſomewhat
Too much Fabritio, to your friend that loves you;
Me thinkes your goodneſſe, rather ſhould invent,
A way to make my follies leſſe, then breed 'em;
I ſhould have been more moderate to you,
But I ſee ye deſpiſe me.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Now I love yee,
There, take your Sword, continue ſo: I dare not
Stay now to try your patience, Soone I'le meet yee,
And as you love your honours, and your ſtate,
Redeeme your ſelfe well to the Gentlewoman,
Farewell 'till ſoone. Exit Fab.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Well I ſhall thinke of this. Exit Jac.

div.head: Scaena Sexta.
div.stage: Enter Hoſt, Piſo, and Boy with a glaſſe of wine.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Nothing 'ith world but a dri'd Tongue or two—

sp.speaker: Hoſt
sp.l: Taſt him and tell me.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Is a valiant wine,
This muſt be he mine Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: This ſhall be Ipſe,
Oh he 's a develiſh bitten wine, a Tyrant;
Where he layes hold Sir, This is he that ſcornes
Small Beere ſhould quench him, or a fooliſh Caudell
Bring him to bed; no if he flinch I'le ſhame him,
And draw him out to mull amongſt old Midwives.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: There is a Souldier, I would have thee better
Above the reſt, becauſe he thinkes there's no man
Can give him drinke enough.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: What kinde of man?

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: That thou mayſt know him perfectly, hee's one
Of a left-handed making, a lanck thing,
As if his belly were tane up with ſtraw,
To hunt a match.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Has he no beard to ſhew him?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Faith but a little; yet enough to note him,
Which growes in parcells here, and there a remnant:
And that thou maiſt not miſſe him, he is one
That weares his fore-head in a vellet ſcabberd.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: That note's enough, he's mine, I'le fuddle him
Or lye 'ith ſudds; you will be here too?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Yes, till ſoone, farewell and beare up.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: If I do not,
Say I am recreant; I'le get things ready.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: 'TIs ſtrange thou ſhould'ſt be thus, with thy diſcretion

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I am ſure I am ſo.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: I am well you ſee.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Keep your ſelfe warme then, & go home, & ſleepe,
And pray to God thou maiſt continue ſo;
Would I had gon to'th Devill of an arrant,
When I was made a foole to ſee her: Leave me
I am not fit for converſation.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Why, thou art worſe then I was.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Therefore leave me,
The nature of my ſickneſſe is not eas'd
By company, or councell, I am mad,
And if you follow me with queſtions
Shall ſhew my ſelfe ſo.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: This is more then errour.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Pray be content, that you have made me thus,
And do not wonder at me.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Let me know, but what you meane to do and I am gon
I would be lo'ath to leave you thus elſe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Nothing
That needs your feare, that is ſufficient;
Farewell, and pray for me.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: I would not leave you.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: You muſt and ſhall.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: I will then: would yon woman
Had been ten fathom under ground, when firſt
I ſaw her eyes.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Yet ſhe had been dangerous,
For to ſome wealthy Rocke of pretious ſtone,
Or mine of gold as tempting, her faire body
Might have been turn'd; which once found out by labour
And brought to uſe, having her ſpells within it,
Might have corrupted States, and ruin'd Kingdomes
Which had been fearefull (Friend) Go, when I ſee thee
Next, I will be as thou art, or no more.
Pray do not follow me, you'l make me angry.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Heav'n grant you may be right againe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Amen. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Score a gallon of Sack, and a pinte of Olives to the Vnicorne.

sp.speaker: Above within.
sp.l: Why drawer?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: A non, a non.

sp.speaker: Another boy.
sp.l: Looke into the Nags head there.

sp.speaker: 2. Boy.
sp.l: Score a quart of Claret to the Bar,
And a pound of Sauſages into the flower-pott.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.l: The Divell's in their throates, anon, anon.

sp.speaker: 2. Ser.
sp.p: Mull a pinte of Sack there for the women in the Flower-deluce, & put in ginger enough, they belch like potguns,
sp.l: And Robbin fetch Tobacco for the Peacock, they will not
Drunke till midnight elſe: how now how does my Maſter.

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: Faith he lyes drawing on a pace.

sp.speaker: 1. Boy.
sp.l: That's an ill ſigne.

sp.speaker: 2. Boy.
sp.l: And fumbles with the pots too.

sp.speaker: 1. Boy.
sp.l: Then ther's no way but one with him.

sp.speaker: 2. Boy.
sp.l: All the reſt.
Except the Captaine are in Limbo patrum,
Where they lye ſod in ſack.

sp.speaker: 1. Boy.
sp.l: Does he beare up ſtill.

sp.speaker: 2. Boy.
sp.l: Afore the winde ſtill, with his lightes up bravely
All he takes in I think he turnes to Iuleps,
Or has a world of Stoage in his belly,
The reſt looke all like fire-drakes, and lye ſcatter'd
Like ruſhes round about the roome. My Maſter
Is now the louing'ſt man, I thinke above ground,

sp.speaker: 1. Boy.
sp.l: Would he were always drunke then.
Within. Drawer.

sp.speaker: 2. B.
sp.l: Anon, anon Sir,

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: And ſwears I ſhall be free to morrovv, and ſo vveeps
And calls upon my Miſtris.

sp.speaker: 2 B.
sp.l: Then he's right.

sp.speaker: 1. B.
sp.l: And ſvvears the Captain muſt lye this night with her
And bad me breake it to her vvith diſcretion,
That he may leave an iſſue after him:
Able to entertaine a dutch Ambaſſador,
And tells him feelingly how ſweete ſhe is,
And hovv he ſtoole her from her friendes i'th Countrey;
And brought her up diſguiz'd vvith the Carriers,
And vvas nine nights bereaving her her maiden head,
And the tenth got a dravver, here they come.
Within cry drawer. Anon, anon, ſpeake to the Tyger, Peter.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Ther's my Bells boyes, my ſilver Bell.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Would he vvere hang'd
As high as I could ring him.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Captaine.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Hoe Boy.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Robin, ſufficient ſingle Beere, as cold as chriſtall,
Quench Robin, quench.

sp.speaker: 1. Boy.
sp.l: I am gon Sir.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Shall vve beare up ſtill? Captaine hovv I love thee?
Sweete Captaine let me kiſſe thee, by this hand
I love thee next to Malmeſey in a morning,
Of things tranſitory.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I love thee too, as far as I can love a fatt man.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Do'ſt thou Captaine?
Sweetly? and hartily?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: With all my heart Boy.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Then welcome death, come cloſe mine eyes ſweet Captaine
Thou ſhalt have all.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: What ſhall your wife have then?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Why ſhe ſhall have beſides my bleſſing, and a ſilver ſpoone
Enough to keepe her ſtirring in the world,
Three little Children, one of them was mine
Upon my conſcience, th'other two are Pagans.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: 'Twere good ſhe had a little fooliſh money,
To rub the time a way with.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Not a rag,
Not a Deniere, no let her ſpin a Gods name:
And raiſe her houſe againe,

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not dye though,
Boy ſee your Maſter ſafe delivered,
He's ready to lye in.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: God night.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: God morrow,
Drinke tell the Cow come home, 'tis all pay'd boyes.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: A pox of Sack.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Marry God bleſſe my Buts, Sack is a jewell,
'Tis comfortable Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: More Beere boy.
Uery ſufficient ſingle Beere.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Here Sir.
How is it Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: But ev'n ſo, ſo.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Go before finely Robin, and prepare
My wife, bid her be right and ſtreight, I come boy
And Sirha, if they quarrell let 'em uſe,
Their owne diſcretions, by all meanes, and ſtir not,
And he that's kill'd ſhall be as ſweetly buried;
Captaine, adieu, adieu ſweet bully Captai ne,
One kiſſe before I dye, one kiſſe.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Farewell Boy.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: All my ſweet boyes farewell. Exit Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Go ſleep, you are drunke.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Come Gentlemen, I'le ſee you at your Lodging,
You looke not luſtily, a quart more.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: No Boy.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Get us a Torch.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: 'Tis day Sir.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: That's all one.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Are not thoſe the ſtars, thou ſcurvy Boy?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Is not Charle-waine there, tell me that, there?

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Yes;
I have paid 'em truely: do not vex him Sirha.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Confeſſe it Boy, or as I live I'le beate
Midnight into thy braines.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I do confeſſe it.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Then live, and draw more ſmall Beere preſently.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Come Boyes, let's hug together, and be loving,
And ſing, and do brave things cheerely my hearts,
A pox a being ſad; now, could I fly
And turne the world about upon my finger,
Come ye ſhall love me, I am an honeſt fellow:
Hang care and fortune, we are friendes.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: No Captaine.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Do not you love me? I love you too dearely.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: No by no meanes; you are a fighting Captaine,
And kill up ſuch poore people as we are, by'th dozens.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: As they kill flyes with Fox-tailes, Captaine.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Well Sir.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Me thinkes now as I ſtand, the Captaine ſhewes,
To be a very mercifull young man.
(And pre'thee Piſo, let me have thy opinion)

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Then he ſhall have mercy, that mercifull is,
Or all the Painters are Apocrypha.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: I am glad you have your witts yet, will ye go?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: You had beſt ſay we are drunke.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Ye are.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Yee lye.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Y'are Rascalls, drunken rascalls.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: 'Tis ſufficient.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: And now I'le tell you why, before I beate yee,
You have been tampring any time theſe three dayes,
Thus to diſgrace me.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: That's a lye too.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Well Sir,
Yet I thanke God I have turn'd your points on you,
For which I'le ſpare yee ſomewhat, halfe a beating.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: I'le make you fart fire Captaine, by this hand,
And ye provoke, do not provoke I'de wiſh you.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: How do you like this?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Sure I am inchanted.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Stay till I draw.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Deſpatch then, I am angry.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: And thou ſhalt ſee how ſodainly I'e kil thee.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Thou darſt not draw, ye cold, tame, mangy Cowards
Ye drunken Rogues, can nothing make you valiant?
Not wine, nor beating?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: If this way be ſufferd
'Tis very well.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Go ther's your way, go and ſleep:
I have pitty on you, you ſhall have the reſt
To morrow when wee meete.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Come Lodowick,
Hee's monſtrous drunke now, ther's no talking with him.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: I am ſo, when I am ſober, I'le do more. Exit Lod. & Piſo.
Boy wher's mine Hoſt?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Hee's on his bed a ſleepe Sir. Exit Boy.

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Let him alone then: Now am I high proofe
For my action, now could I fight bravely,
And charge into a wilde fire; or I could love
Any man living now, or any woman,
Or indeed any creature that loves Sack
Extreamly, monſtrouſly; I am ſo loving,
Iuſt at this inſtant, that I might be brought
I feele it, with a little labour, now to talke
With a juſtice of peace, that to my nature
I hate next an ill Sword: I will do
Some ſtrange brave thing now, and I have it here:
Pray God the ayre keepe out; I feele it buzing. Exit.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Shee loves him too much, that's the plaine truth Fredrick
For which if I might be beleev'd, I thinke her
A ſtrange forgetter of her ſelfe; ther's Iulio,
Or twenty more—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: In your eye I believe you,
But credit me the Captaine is a man:
Lay but his rough affections by, as worthy.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: So is a reſty Iade, a horſe of ſervice,
If he would leave his nature, give me one
By your leave Sir to make a husband of
Not to be wean'd, when I ſhould marry him;
Me thinkes a man is miſery enough,

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You are too bitter,
I would not have him worſe.
Yet I ſhall ſee you hamper'd one day Lady,
I do not doubt it, for this hereſie

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: I'le burne before; come pre'thee leave this ſadneſſe;
This walking by thy ſelfe to ſee the Divell,
This mumps, this Lachrimae, this love in ſippets;
It fitts thee like a French-hood.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Does it ſo?
I am ſure it fits thee to be ever talking,
And nothing to the purpoſe, take up quickly;
Thy witt will founder of all foure elſe wench,
I thou hold'ſt this pace; take up when I bid thee.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Before your Brother fly?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I can endure it.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Heer's Raw-head come againe; Lord how he lookes?
Pray God we ſcape with broken pates.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Were I hee,
Thou ſhould'ſt not want thy wiſh, he has been drinking
Has he not Fredrick?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Yes but do not finde it.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Peace and let's heare his wiſedome.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You will mad him.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I am ſomewhat bold, but that's all one.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: A ſhort and pithy ſaying of a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: As I live
Thou art a ſtrange mad wench.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: To make a parſon.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Ladyes I meane to kiſſe yee

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: How he wipes his mouth like a young Preacher;
We ſhall have it.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: In order as you ly before me; firſt
I'le begin with you.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: With me Sir?

sp.speaker: Iac.
sp.l: Yes
If you will promiſe me to kiſſe in eaſe.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I care not if I venture.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I will kiſſ according to mine owne inventions
As I ſhall ſee cauſe; ſweetly I would wiſh you,
I love ye.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Do you Sir?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Yes indeed do I,
