That a hard hearted man, and an old Souldier
Should have ſo much kind moyſture: when his mother dyde
He laughed aloud, and made the wickedſt Ballads—

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.l: 'Tis like enough: he never lov'd his Parents;
Nor can I blame him, for they neere lov'd him.
His mother dream'd before ſhe was deliverd
That ſhe was brought abed with a Buzzard, and ever after
She whiſtled him up to th'world, his brave clothes too
He has flung away: and goes like one of us now:
Walks with his hands in's pockets, poore and ſorrowfull,
And gives the beſt inſtructions. —

sp.speaker: 2 Sol.
sp.l: And tells ſtories
Of honeſt and good people that were honourd,
And how they were remembred: and runs mad
If he but hear of any ungratefull perſon,
A bloudy, or betraying man—

sp.speaker: 3. Sol.
sp.l: If it be poſſible
That an Arch-Villain may ever be recovered,
This penitent Raſcall will put hard: 'twere worth our labour
To ſee him once againe.

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.l: He ſpares us that labour
For here he comes.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: — Bleſſe ye my honeſt friends,
Bleſſe ye from baſe unworthy men; come not neare me:
For I am yet too taking for your company.

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.l: Did I not tell ye?

sp.speaker: 2. Sol.
sp.l: What booke's that?

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.l: No doubt
Some excellent Salve for a ſore heart, are you
Septinius, that baſe knave, that betrayd Pompey?

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: I was, and am; unleſſe your honeſt thoughts
Will look upon my penitence, and ſave me
I muſt be ever Villaine: O good Souldiers
You that have Roman hearts, take heede of falſehood:
Take heede of blood; take heede of foule ingratitude,
The Gods have ſcarce a mercy for thoſe miſchiefes,
Take heede of pride, 'twas that that brought me to it.

sp.speaker: 2. Sol.
sp.l: This fellow would make a rare ſpeech at the gallowes

sp.speaker: 3. Sol.
sp.l: 'Tis very fit he were hangd to edifie us:

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Let all your thoughts be humble, and obedient,
Love your Commanders, honour them that feede ye:
Pray, that ye may be ſtrong in honeſty
As in the uſe of armes; Labour, and diligently
To keepe your hearts from eaſe, and her baſe iſſues;
Pride, and ambitious wantonneſſe, thoſe ſpoyld me:
Rather looſe all your limbs, then the leaſt honeſty,
You are never lame indeed, till loſſe of credit
Benum ye through: Scarrs, and thoſe maimes of honour
Are memorable crutches, that ſhall beare
When you are dead, your noble names to Eternity.

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.l: I cry.

sp.speaker: 2. Sol.
sp.l: And ſo doe I.

sp.speaker: 3. Sol.
sp.l: An excellent villaine.

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.l: A more ſweet pious knave, I never heard yet.

sp.speaker: 2. Sol.
sp.l: He was happie he was Raſcall, to come to this
Who's this? a Prieſt?

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: O ſtay, moſt holy Sir!
And by the Gods of Egypt, I conjure ye,
(Iſis, and great Oſiris) pitty me,
Pitty a loaden man, and tell me truly
With what moſt humble Sacrifice I may
Waſh off my ſin, and appeaſe the powers that hate me?
Take from my heart thoſe thouſand thouſand furies,
That reſtleſſe gnaw upon my life, and ſave me?
Oreſtes bloody hands fell on his Mother,
Yet, at the holy altar he was pardon'd.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: Oreſtes out of madneſſe did his murther,
And therefore he found grace: thou (worſt of all men)
Out of cold blood, and hope of gaine, baſe lucre,
Slewſt thine own Feeder: come not neare the altar,
Nor with thy reeking hands pollute the Sacrifice,
Thou art markt for ſhame eternall. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Looke all on me,
And let me be a ſtory left to time
Of blood and Infamy, how baſe and ougly
Ingratitude appears, with all her profits,
How monſtrous, my hoped grace, at Court? good ſouldiers
Let neither flattery, nor the witching ſound
Of high and ſoft preferment, touch your goodneſſe:
To be valiant, old, and honeſt, O what bleſſedneſſe—

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.l: Doſt thou want any thing?

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Nothing but your prayers:

sp.speaker: 2 S.
sp.l: Be thus, and let the blind Prieſt do his worſt,
We have gods as well as they, and they will heare us.

sp.p: Come, cry no more: thou haſt wep't out twenty Pompeyes.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: So penitent?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: It ſeemes ſo.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Yet for all this
We muſt employ him.

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.l: Theſe are the armed Souldier-leaders:
Away: and let's tot'h Fort, we ſhall be ſnapt elſe. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: How now? why thus? what cauſe of this dejection?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Why doſt thou weepe?

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Pray leave me, you have ruin'd me,
You have made me a famous Villain.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Does that touch thee?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: He will be hard to win: he feels his lewdneſſe,

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: He muſt be won, or we ſhall want our right hand.
This fellow dares, and knows, and muſt be heartned,
Art thou ſo poore to blench at what thou haſt done?
Is Conſcience a comrade for an old ſouldier?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: It is not that: it may be ſome diſgrace
That be takes heavily; and would be cheriſh'd,
Septinius ever ſcorn'd to ſhew ſuch weakneſſe.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Let me alone; I am not for your purpoſe,
I am no wa new man.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: We have new affairs for thee
Thoſe that would raiſe thy head.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: I would 'twere off,
And in your bellies for the love you beare me.
I'le be no more Knave: I have ſtings enough
Already in my breaſt.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt be noble:
And who dares thinke then that thou art not honeſt?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt command in Chief, all our ſtrong Forces
And if thou ſerv'ſt an uſe, muſt not all juſtifie it?

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: I am Rogue enough.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Thou wilt be more, and baſer:
A poor Rogue is all rogues: open to all ſhames:
Nothing to ſhadow him: doſt thou think crying
Can keep thee from the cenſure of the Multitude?
Or to be kneeling at the altar ſave thee?
'Tis poore and ſervile:
Wert thou thine own Sacrifice
'Twould ſeeme ſo low, people would ſpit the fire out.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Keep thy ſelf glorious ſtil, though ne're ſo ſtaind,
And that will leſſen it, if not work it out
To goe complaining thus: and thus repenting
Like a poore Girle that had betraid her maiden-head—

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: I'le ſtop mine eares.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Will ſhew ſo in a ſouldier,
So ſimply, and ſo ridicolouſly, ſo tamely—

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: If people would believe thee, 'twer ſome honeſty,
And for thy penitence would not laugh at thee
(As ſure they will) and beat thee, for thy poverty:
If they would allow thy foolery, there were ſome hope.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: My foolery?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Nay, more then that, thy miſery,
Thy monſtrous miſery.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: He begins to hearken:
Thy miſery ſo great, men will not bury thee.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: That this were true!

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Why does this conquering Caeſar
Labour through the worlds deep Seas of toyls & troubles,
Dangers, and deſperate hopes? to repent afterwards?
Why does he ſlaughter thouſands in a Battell,
And whip his Countrey with the Sword? to cry ſor't?
Thou killdſt great Pompey: hee'l kil all his kinred,
And juſtifie it: nay raiſe up Trophies to it,
When thou heareſt him repent: (he's held moſt holy too)
And cry for doing daily bloody murthers,
Take thou example, and goe aske forgiveneſſe,
Call up the thing thou nam'ſt thy conſcience,
And let it work: then 'twill ſeeme well Septinius.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: He does all this.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Yes: and is honoured for it;
Nay call'd the honoured Caeſar, ſo maiſt thou be:
Thou wert born as neere a Crowne as he.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: He was poore.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: And deſperate bloody tricks got him this credit.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: I am afraid you will once more—

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Help to raiſe thee:
Off with thy pining blacke, it dulls a Souldier,
And put on reſolution like a man,
A noble Fate waits on thee.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: I now feele
My ſelfe returning Raſcall ſpeedily.
O that I had the power—

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt have all:
And doe all through thy power, men ſhall admire thee,
And the vices of Septinius, ſhall turn vertues.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Off: off: thou muſt off: off my cowardize,
Puling repentance off.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Now thou ſpeakſt nobly.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Off my dejected looks: and welcome impudence:
My daring ſhall be Deity, to ſave me:
Give me inſtructions, and put action on me:
A glorious cauſe upon my ſwords point (Gentlemen)
And let my wit, and valour work: you will raiſe me,
And make me out-dare all my miſeries?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: All this, and all thy wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Uſe me then,
Womaniſh feare farewell: I'le never melt more,
Lead on, to ſome great thing, to weale my ſpirit:
I cut the Cedar Pompey, and I'le fell
This huge Oake Caeſar too.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Now thou ſingſt ſweetly:
And Ptolomy ſhall crowne thee for thy ſervice: (Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: He's well wrought: put him on apace for cooling.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: THe tumult ſtill encreaſes.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: O my fortune!
My lu •• full folly rather! but 'tis well,
And worthily I am made a bondmans prey,
That after all my glorious victoryes,
In which I paſſ'd ſo many ſeas of dangers:
When all the Elements conſpir'd againſt me,
Would yeild up the dominion of this head
To any mortall power; ſo blinde and ſtupid:
To truſt theſe baſe Egyptians, that proclaim'd
Their per • uries, in noble Pompeys death,
And yet that could not warn me.

sp.speaker: Dol.
sp.l: Be ſtill, Caeſar,
Who ever lov'd to exerciſe his fate,
Where danger look't moſt dreadfull.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: If you fall,
Fall not alone: let the King and his Siſter
Be buried in your ruines: on my life
They both are guilty: reaſon may aſſure you
Photinus nor Achillas durſt attempt you,
Or ſhake one Dart, or Sword, aim'd at your ſafety,
Without their warrant.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: For the young King I know not
How he may be miſſed; but for his Siſter
(Unequall'd Cleopatra) 'twere a kinde
Of blaſphemy to doubt her: ougly treaſon
Durſt never dwell in ſuch a glorious building,
Nor can ſo cleare and great a ſpirit, as hers is,
Admit of falſehood.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let us ſeize on him then:
And leave her to her fortune.

sp.speaker: Dol.
sp.l: If he have power
Uſe it to your ſecurity, and let
His honeſty acquit him; if he be faſe,
It is too great an honour he ſhould dye
By your victorious hand.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: He comes: and I
Shall do as I finde cauſe.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: Let not great Caeſar
Impute the breach of hoſpitality,
To you (my gueſt) to me; I am contemn'd,
And my rebellious ſubjects lift their hands
Againſt my head: and would they aim'd no farther,
Provided that I fell a ſacrifice
To gaine you ſafety: that this is not faign'd,
The boldneſſe of my innocence may confirme you:
Had I bin privy to their bloody plot,
I now had led them on, and given faire gloſſe
To their bad cauſe, by being preſent with them:
But I that yet taſte of the puniſhment,
In being falſe to Pompey, will not make
A ſecond fault to Caeſar uncompell'd
With ſuch as have not yet ſhooke off obedience,
I yeild my ſelfe to you, and will take part
In all your dangers.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: This pleades your excuſe,
And I receive it.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: If they have any touch,
Of juſtice, or religion, I will uſe
The athority of our Gods, to call them back,
From their bad purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Ap.
sp.l: This part of the pallace,
Is yet defenſible: we may make it good,
Till your powers reſcue us.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Caeſar beſeig'd?
Oſtaine to my great actions: 'twas my cuſtome
An Army routed, as my feete had wings
To be firſt in the chaſe: nor walls, nor Bulworkes
Could guard thoſe that eſcap'd the Battailes fury
From this ſtrong Arme, and I to be encloſ'd
My heart! my hart! but 'tis necesſity,
To which the Gods muſt yeild, and I obey,
'Till I redeeme it, by ſome glorious way. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Secunda.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Ther's no retiring now, we are broke in:
The deed paſt hope of pardon: if we proſper
A will be ſtilde lawfull, and we ſhall give lawes
To thoſe that now command us: ſtop not at
Or loyalty, or duty, bold Ambition,
To dare and power to do, gave the firſt difference
Betweene the King, and ſubject, Caeſars Motto,
Aut Caeſar aut Nihil, each of us muſt claime,
And uſe it as our owne.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: The deed is bloody
If we conclude in Ptolomies death.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: The better
The globe of Empire muſt be ſo manur.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Rome, that from Romulus firſt tooke her name
Had her walls watered with a Crymſon ſhowr
Draind from a Brothers heart: nor was ſhe rais'd
To this prodigious height, that overlooks
Three full parts of the Earth, that pay her tribute,
But by enlarging of her narrow bounds
By the Sack of Neighbour Cities, were made hers
Till they were Cemented with the Blood of thoſe
That did poſſeſſe 'em: Ceſar, Ptolomy,
(Now I am ſteeld) to me are empty names
Eſteem'd as Pompeys was.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Well ſaid Septinius,
Thou now art right againe.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: But what courſe take we
For the Princeſſe Cleopatra?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Let her live
A while to make us ſport: ſhe ſhall authorize
Our undertakings to the ignorant people,
As if what we do were by her command:
But our triumvirat Government once confirm'd,
Shee beares her Brother company, that's my Province:
Leave me to work her.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: I will undertake
For Ptolomy.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Ceſar ſhall be my taske,
And as in Pompey I began a names
I'le perfect it in Caeſar.

div.stage: Enter (above) Caeſar, Ptolomy, Achoreus, Appollodorus, Anthony, Dollabella.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: 'Tis reſolv'd then
Wee'l force our paſſage.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: See: they do appeare
As they deſir'd a parley.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: I am proud yet
I have brought them to capitulate.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: Now Photinus?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Now Ptolomy?

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: No addition?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: We are equall,
Though Caeſars name were put into the ſcale,
In which our worth is weighd.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Preſumptuous Villaine,
Upon what grounds haſt thou preſum'd to raiſe
Thy ſervile hand againſt the King, or me,
That have a greater name?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: On thoſe, by which
Thou didſt preſume to paſſe the Rubicon
Againſt the Laws of Rome; and at the name
Of traytor ſmile, as thou didſt when Marcellus
The Conſull, with the Senats full conſent
Pronounc'd thee for an enemy to thy Country,
Yet thou wentſt on, and thy rebellious Cauſe
Was crown'd with fair ſucceſs: why ſhould we fear then?
Thinke on that Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: O the gods! be brav'd thus?
And be compelld to beare this from a ſlave
That would not brooke great Pompey his Superiour?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Thy glories now have touch'd the higheſt point,
And muſt deſcend.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Deſpaire, and thinke we ſtand
The Champions of Rome, to wreak her wrongs
Upon whoſe liberty thou haſt ſet thy foote.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: And that the ghoſts of all thoſe noble Romans
That by thy ſword fell in this Civill warre,
Expect revenge.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Dar'ſt thou ſpeak, and remember
There was a Pompey?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: There is no hope to ſcape us:
If that againſt the odds we have upon you
You dare come forth and fight, receive the honour
To dye, like Romans, if ye faint, reſolve
To ſtarve, like wretches: I diſdain to change Exit.
Another ſyllable with you.

sp.speaker: An • .
sp.l: Let us dye nobly:
And rather fall upon each others ſword
Then come into theſe villains hands.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: That Fortune
Which to this howre hath been a friend to Caeſar,
Though for a while ſhe cloath her brow with frowns
Will ſmile again upon me; who will pay her,
Or ſacrifice or vowes, if ſhe forſake
Her beſt of works in me? or ſuffer him
Whom, with a ſtrong hand ſhe hath led triumphant
Through the whole Weſtern world, & Rome acknowledgd
Her Soveraign Lord, to end in gloriouſly,
A life admir'd by all? the threatned danger
Muſt by a way more horrid, be avoided,
And I will run the hazard: Fire the Pallace,
And the rich Magazines that neighbour it,
In which the wealth of Aegypt is contain'd:
Start not, it ſhall be ſo; that while the people
Labour in quenching the enſuing flames,
Like Caeſar, with this handfull of my friends
Through fire, and ſwords, I force a paſſage to
My conquering Legions. King, if thou darſt follow
Where Caeſar leads, or live, or dye a Free-man;
If not, ſtay here a bond-man to thy ſlave,
And dead, be thought unworthy of a grave. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Tertia.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: I feele my reſolution melts againe,
And that I am not knave alone, but foole
In all my purpoſes. This Devill Photinus
Employs me, as a property, and grown uſeleſſe
Will ſhake me off againe: he told me ſo
When I kill'd Pompey: nor can I hope better
When Caeſar is diſpatch'd: Services done
For ſuch as only ſtudy their owne ends,
Too great to be rewarded, or return'd
With deadly hate: I learnd this principle
In his own Schoole: yet ſtill he fooles me: well:
And yet he truſts me; Since I in my nature
Was faſhion'd to be falſe, wherefore ſhould I
That kill'd my Generall, and a Roman, one
To whom I owe all nouriſhments of life
Be true to an Aegyptian? to ſave Caeſar,
And turn Photinus plots on his own head,
As it is in my power, redeem my credit,
And live, to lye, and ſwear again in faſhion,
Oh, 'twere a Maſter-piece? ha? — me Ceaſar,
How's he got off?

div.stage: Enter Caeſar, Ptolomy, Antony, Dollabella. Achoreus, Appollodorus, Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: The fire has tooke,
And ſhews the City, like a ſecond Troy,
The Navy too is ſcorch'd, the people greedy
To ſave their wealth, and houſes, while their ſouldiers
Make ſpoile of all: only Achillas troops
Make good their guard: break through them, we are ſafe:
I'le lead you like a Thunder-bolt.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Stay Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Who's this? the dog Septinius?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Cut his throat.

sp.speaker: Dol.
sp.l: You barkt but now, fawne you ſo ſoone?

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: O heare me,
What I'le deliver is for Caeſars ſafety,
For all your good.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Good from a moneth like thine,
That never belch'd but blaſphemy & treaſon, on Feſtivall dayes

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: I am an altered man: altered indeed,
And I will give you cauſe to ſay I am a Roman.

sp.speaker: Dol.
sp.l: Rogue, I grant thee.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Truſt me, I'le make the paſſage ſmooth and eaſy,
For your eſcape.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I'le truſt the Devill ſooner,
And make a ſafer bargaine.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: I am truſted,
With all Photinus ſecrets.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: There's no doubt then,
Thou wilt be falſe.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Still to be true to you.

sp.speaker: Dol.
sp.l: And very likely.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Be breife, the meanes?

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Thus Caeſar:
To me alone, but bound by terrible oathes
Not to diſcover it, he hath reveal'd
A diſmall vault, whoſe dreadfull mouth do's open
A mile beyond the Citty: in this cave
Lye but two houres conceal'd.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: If you believe him,
Hee'le bury us alive.

sp.speaker: Dol.
sp.l: I'le fly in the ayre firſt.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Then in the dead of night, I'le bring you backe
Into a private roome, where you ſhall finde
Photinus, and Achillas, and the reſt
Of their Commanders, cloſe at Counſell.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Good: what followes?

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Fall me fairly on their throates,
Their heads cut off and ſhorn, the multitude
Will eaſily diſperſe.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: O Devill! away with him:
Nor true to friend nor enemy? Caeſar ſcornes
To find his ſafety, or revenge his wrongs
So baſe a way: or owe the meanes of life
To ſuch a leaprous Traytor. I have towr'd
For victory like a Faulcon in the clouds,
Not dig'd for't like a Moale: our Swords, and Cauſe
Make way for us; and that it may appeare
We tooke a noble courſe, and hate baſe Treaſon,
Some ſouldiers, that would merit Caeſars favour,
Hang him on yonder turret, and then follow
The lane, this ſword makes for you. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.l: Here's a Belt,
Though I dye for it I'le uſe it.

sp.speaker: 2 Sold.
sp.l: Tis too good
To truſſe a Cur in.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Save me, here's gold.

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.l: If Rome
Were offered for thy ranſome, it could not help thee.

sp.speaker: 2 Sold.
sp.l: Hang not an arſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.l: Goad him on with thy ſword:
Thou doſt deſerve a worſer end; and may
All ſuch conclude ſo, that their friends betray.

div.head: Scena Quarta.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: We are loſt.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: Undon.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Confuſion, Fire, and Swords,
And fury in the ſouldiers face, more horrid
Circle us round.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: The Kings command they laugh at,
And jeere at Caeſars threats.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: My brother ſeizd on
By the Roman, as thought guilty of the tumult,
And forc'd to beare him company, as mark'd out
For his protection, or revenge.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: They have broke
Into my Cabinet: my Trunks are ranſak'd.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I have loſt my Jewels too; but thats the leaſt:
The barbarous Raſcalls, againſt all humanity,
Or ſenſe of pity, have kill'd my little dog,
And broke my monkeys chaine.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: They rufled me:
But that I could endure, and tire 'em too,
Would they proceed no further.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: O my ſiſter!

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: My Queen, my Miſtreſſe!

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Can you ſtand unmov'd
When an Earth-quake of rebellion ſhakes the City?
And the Court trembles?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Yes Arſino,
And with a maſculine conſtancy deride
Fortunes worſt malice, as a ſervant to
My Vertues, not a Miſtreſs: then we forſake
The ſtrong fort of our ſelves, when we once yield,
Or ſhrink at her aſſaults; I am ſtill my ſelfe,
And though diſ-roab'd of Sovereignty, and raviſht
Of ceremonious duty, that attends it,
Nay, grant they had ſlav'd my body, my free mind
Like to the Palm-tree, walling fruitfull Nyle,
Shall grow up ſtraighter, and enlarge it ſelfe
Spight of the envious weight that loads it with:
Think of thy birth (Arſino) common burthens
Fit common ſhoulders; teach the multitude
By ſuffering nobly what they feare to touch at:
The greatneſſe of thy mind does ſoare a pitch,
Their dim eyes (darkned by their narrow ſoules)
Cannot arrive at.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I am new created,
And owe this ſecond being to you (beſt ſiſter)
For now I feele you have infus'd into me
Part of your fortitude.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: I ſtill am fearfull:
I dare not tell a lye: you that were born
Daughters, and Siſters unto Kings, may nouriſh
Great thoughts, which I, that am your humble handmaid
Muſt not preſume to ryvall.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Yet (my Eros)
Though thou haſt profited nothing, by obſerving
The whole courſe of my life, learn in my death,
Though not to equall, yet to imitate
Thy fearleſſe Miſtreſſe.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: O, a man in armes?
His weapon drawn too?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Though upon the point
Death ſate, I'le meete it, and out-dare the danger.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Keep the watch ſtrong, and guard the paſſage ſure
That leads unto the Sea.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: What ſea of rudeneſſe
Breaks in upon us? or what Subjects breath
Dare raiſe a ſtorme, when we command a calm?
Are duty, and obedience fled to heaven,
And in their roome, ambition and pride
Sent into Aegyt? that face ſpeaks thee Photinus,
A thing thy Mother brought into the world:
My Brothers, and my Slave: but thy behaviour,
Oppos'd to that an inſolent Intruder
Upon that Soveraignty thou ſhouldſt bow to,
If in the gulph of baſe ingratitude,
All loyalty to Ptolomy the King
Be ſwallowed up, remember who I am,
Whoſe Daughter, and whoſe Siſter: or ſuppoſe
That is forgot too; let the name of Caeſar
Which Nations quake at, ſtop the deſperate madneſſe
From running headong on to thy confuſion.
Throw from thee quickly thoſe rebellious armes,
Tnd let me read ſubmiſſion in thine eyes,
Ahy wrongs to us, we will not only pardon,
But be a ready advocate, to plead for thee
To Caeſar, and my Brother.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Plead my pardon?
To you I bow, but ſcorn as much to ſtoop thus
To Ptolomy, to Caeſar? Nay the gods,
As to put off the figure of a man,
And change my Eſſence, with a ſenſuall beaſt:
All my deſignes, my counſels, and dark ends
Were aym'd to purchaſe you.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: How durſt thou, being
The ſcorne of baſeneſſe, nouriſh ſuch a thought?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: They that have power are royall: and thoſe baſe
That live at the devotion of an other,
What birth gave Ptolomy, or fortune Caeſar,
By Engines faſhiond in this Protean Anvill
I have made mine: and onely ſtoop at you,
Whom I would ſtill preſerve free to command me;
For Caeſars frownes, they are below my thoughts,
And but in theſe faire eyes, I ſtill have read
The ſtory of a ſupreame Monarchy,
To which all hearts with mine, gladly pay tribute,
Photinus name, had long ſince bin as great
As Ptolomies ere was, or Caeſars is,
This made me as a weaker tye to unlooſe
The knot of loyalty, that chain'd my freedom;
And ſlight the feare that Caeſars threats might cauſe,
That I and they might ſee no Sun appeare
But Cleopatra, in th' Egyptian Spheare.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: O giantlike Ambition! married to
Cymerian darkneſſe! in conſiderate foole,
(Though flatter'd with ſelve love) could'ſt thou beleeve,
Were all Crownes on the earth, made into one,
And that (by Kings) ſet on thy head: all Scepters,
Within thy graſpe, and laid downe at my feete,
I would vouchſafe a kiſſe to a no-man?
A guelded Evenuch?

sp.speaker: Phot.
sp.l: Faireſt, that makes for me:
And ſhewes it is no ſenſuall appetite,
But true love to the greatneſſe of thy ſpirit,
That when that you are mine ſhall yeild me pleaſures:
Hymen, though bleſſing a new married paire
Shall bluſh to thinke on, and our certaine Iſſue,
The glorious ſplendour of dread Majeſty:
Whoſe beames ſhall dazell Rome, and awe the world:
My wants in that kinde, others ſhall ſupply,
And I give way to it.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Baſer then thy birth:
Can there be Gods, and heare this, and no thunder,
Ram thee into the earth?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: They are a ſleepe,
And cannot heare thee:
Or with open eyes,
Did Jove looke on us, I would laugh and ſweare
That his artillary is cloid by me:
Or if that they have power to hurt, his Bolts
Are in my hand.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Moſt impious!

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: They are dreames,
Religious fooles ſhake at: yet to aſſure thee,
If Nemeſis, that ſcourges pride, and ſcorne,
Be any thing but a name ſhe lives in me:
For by my ſelfe (an oath to me more dreadfull
Then Stix is to your Gods) weake Ptolomy dead,
And Caeſar (both being in my toile) remov'd
The pooreſt Raſcalls, that are in my Camp
Shall, in my preſence, quench their Iuſtfull heate
In thee, and young Arſinoe; while I laugh
To heare you howle in vaine:
I deride thoſe Gods,
That you thinke can protect you,

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: To prevent thee,
In that I am the Miſtreſs of my fate:
So hope I of my Siſter, to confirme it,
I ſpit at thee, and ſcorne thee.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: I will tame,
That haughty courage, and make it ſtoop too.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Never:
I was borne to command and I will dye ſo.

div.stage: Enter Achillas and Souldiers, with the body of Ptolomy.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: The King dead? this is a faire entrance to,
Our future happineſſe.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: O my Deare Brother?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Weepe not Arſinoe, common women do ſoe,
Nor looſe a teare for him, it cannot helpe him:
But ſtudy to dye nobly.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Caeſar fled?
'Tis deadly aconite to my cold heart:
It choakes my vitall ſpirits: where was your care?
Did the guardes ſleepe?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: He rowz'd them with his ſword:
We talke of Mars, but I am ſure his courage
Admits of no compariſon but it ſelfe,
And (as inſpir'd by him) his following friends
With ſuch a confidence, as you Eagletss prey
Under the large wing of their feircer dam,
Brake through our troopes, and ſcatterd 'em, he went on:
But ſtill purſude by us: when on the ſudaine,
He turn'd his head, and from his eyes flew terrour;
Which ſtrooke in us no leſſe feare, and amazement,
Then if we had encounter'd with the lightning,
Hurld from Joves clowdy brow.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: 'Twas like my Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: We falne back, he made on, and as our feare
Had parted from us, with his dreadfull lookes,
Againe we follow'd: but got neare the ſea:
On which his navy anchord; in one hand
Holding a ſcroll he had, above the waves,
And in the other graſping faſt his ſword
As it had bin a trident, forg'd by Ʋulcan,
To calme the raging Ocean, he made away
As if he had bin Neptune: his friends like
So many Tritons follow'd their bold ſhowts,
Yeilding a chearefull muſique; we ſhowr'd darts,
Upon them but in vaine, they reach'd their ſhips,
And in their ſafety we are ſunck; for Caeſar
Prepares for war.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: How fell the King?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Unable,
To follow Caeſar, he was trod to death
By the purſuers, and with him the Prieſt,
Of Iſis good Achoreus.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: May the Earth,
Lye gently on their aſhes.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: I feele now,
That there are powers above us: and that 'tis not
Within the ſearching policies of man,
To alter their decrees.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: I laugh at thee:
Where are thy threates now, (foole) thy ſcoffs, and ſcornes
Againſt the Gods? I ſee calamity
Is the beſt Miſtris of Religion,
And can convert an Atheiſt.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: O they come,
Mountaines fall on me! O, for him to dye
That plac'd his heaven on earth, is an aſſurance
Of his deſcent to hell; where ſhall I hide me?
The greateſt daring to a man diſhoneſt,
Is but a baſtard courage, ever fainting. Exit.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.p: Looke on your Caeſar; baniſh feare (my faireſt) You now are ſafe.

sp.speaker: Sce.
sp.l: By Ʋenus, not a kiſſe
Till our worke be done: the Traitors once diſpatch'd
To it, and wee'le cry aime.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: I will be ſpeedy. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Farewell againe Arſinoe; how now Eros,
Ever faint-harted?

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: But that I am aſſur'd,
Your excellency can command the Generall,
I feare the Souldiers, for they looke as if
They would be nibling too.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: He is all honour,
Nor do I now repent me of my favours;
Nor can I thinke nature e're made a woman,
That in her prime deſerv'd him.

div.stage: Enter Caeſar, Sceva, Antony, Dollabella, Souldiers, With the heads.

sp.speaker: Ars.
sp.l: He's come backe,
Purſue no farther; curb the Souldiers fury.
See (beauteous Miſtris) their accurſed heads,
That did conſpire againſt us.

sp.speaker: Sceva.
sp.l: Furies plague 'em,
They had too faire an end, to dye like Souldiers,
Pompey fell by the ſword; the croſſe, or halter
Should have diſpatch'd them.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: All is but death (good Sceva)
Be therefore ſatisfied, and now (my deareſt)
Looke up on Caeſar, as he ſtill appear'd
A Conquerour, and this unfortunate King
Entomb'd with honour, wee'le for Rome, where Caeſar
Will ſhew he can give Kingdome: for the Senate,
(Thy brother dead) ſhall willingly decree
The Crowne of Egypt, (that was his) to thee.

div.head: The Prologue.
div.l: NEw Titles, warrant not a Play for new,
The ſubject being old: and 'tis as true,
Freſh, and neate matter may with eaſe be fram'd
Out of their Stories, that have oft been nam'd
With glory on the Stage: what borrows he
From him that wrote olde Priams Tragedy.
That writes bis love to Hecuba? Sure, to tell
Of Caeſars amorous heates, and how he fell
In the Capitoll, can never be the ſame
To the Judicious: Nor will ſuch blame
Thoſe that penn'd this, for Barrenneſſe when they finde
Young Cleopatra here, and her great mind
Expreſs'd to the height, with us a Maid, and free,
And how he rated her Virginity.
We treat not of what boldneſſe ſhe did dye,
Nor of her fatall Love to Anthony.
What wee preſent and offer to your view,
(Ʋpon their Faiths) the Stage yet never knew.
Let Reaſon then, firſt to your wills give Lawes,
And after judge of them, and of their Cauſe.

div.head: The Epilogue.
div.l: I Now ſhould wiſh another had my place,
But that I hope to come off, and with grace.
And but expreſſe ſome ſigne that you are pleas'd,
We of our doubts, they of their feares are eas'd.
I would beg further (Gentlemen) and much ſay
In the favour of our ſelves, them, and the Play;
Did I not reſt aſſur'd; the moſt I ſee
Hate Impudence, and cheriſh modeſty.

div.head: Scaena prima.
div.stage: Enter two Serving-men, Peter and Anthony.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: I Would we were remov'd from this Town, Anthony
That we might taſte ſome quiet: for mine owne part,
I'me almoſt melted with continuall trotting
After enquities, dreames, and revelations,
Of who knowes, whom or where? ſerve wenching ſoldiers,
That know no other Paradice but Plackets:
Ile ſerve a Prieſt in Lent, firſt and eate Bell-ropes.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.l: Thou art the froward'ſt foole —

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Why good tame Anthony?
Tell me but this: to what end came we hither?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: To wait upon our Maſters.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: But how Anthony?
Anſwer me that; reſolve me there good Anthony?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: To ſerve their uſes.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Shew your uſes Anthony.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: To be imploy'd in any thing.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: No Anthony,
Not any thing I take it; nor that thing
We travell to diſcover, like new Iſlands;
A ſalt itch ſerve ſuch uſes; in things of moment,
Concerning things I grant yee, not things errant,
Sweet Ladies things, and things to thank the Surgeon:
In no ſuch things, ſweet Anthony, put caſe —

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: Come, come, all will be mended: this inviſible woman
Of infinite report for ſhape and vertue,
That bred us all this trouble to no purpoſe,
They are determin'd now no more to thinke on,
But fall cloſe to their ſtudies.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Was there ever
Men knowne to run mad with report before?
Or wonder after that they know not where
To finde? or if found, how to enjoy? are mens braines
Made now a dayes of Malt, that their affections
Are never ſober? but like drunken people
Founder at every new fame? I do believe too
That men in love are ever drunke, as drunken men
Are ever loving.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: Prethee be thou ſober,
And know, that they are none of thoſe, not guilty
Of the leaſt vanity of love, onely a doubt
Fame might too farre report, or rather flatter
The graces of this woman, made them curious
To finde the truth, which ſince they finde ſo blotted
And lock'd up from their ſearches, they are now ſetled
To give the wonder ever.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Would they were ſetled
To give me ſome new ſhooes too: for I'le be ſworne
Theſe are e'ne worne out to the reaſonable ſoules
In their good worſhips buſineſſe: and ſome ſleep
Would not doe much amiſſe, unleſſe they meane
To make a Bell-man on me: and what now
Meane they to ſtudy, Anthony, Morall Philoſophy
After their mar-all women?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: Mar a fooles head.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: 'Twill mar two fools heads, & they take not heed,
Beſides the Giblets to 'em.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: Will you walke Sir,
And talke more out of hearing? your fooles head
May chance to finde a wooden night-cap elſe.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: I never lay in any. Enter Don John and Fredrick.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: Then leave your lying,
And your blinde Propheſying: here they come,
You had beſt tell them as much.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I am no tell-tale. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I would we could have ſeen her though: for ſure
She muſt be ſome rare creature, or report lyes,
All mens reports too,

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I could well wiſh I had ſeen her;
But ſince ſhe is ſo conceal'd, ſo beyond venture
Kept and preſerv'd from view, ſo like a Paradice,
Plac't where no knowledg can come near her; ſo guarded
As 'twere impoſſible, though knowne to reach her,
I have made up my beliefe.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: Hang me from this houre
If I more thinke upon her, or believe her,
But as ſhe came a ſtrong report unto me,
So the next Fame ſhall looſe her.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis the next way:
But whither are you walking?

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: My old round
After my meat, and then to bed.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis healthfulll.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: Will not you ſtir?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I have a little buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Upon my life this Lady ſtill—

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Then you will looſe it.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Pray let's walke together.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Now I cannot.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: I have ſomething to impart.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: An houre hence
I will not miſſe to meet you.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Where?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Ith' high ſtreet;
For not to lye, I have a few Devotions
To doe firſt, then I am yours.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Remember. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaen. 2.
div.stage: Enter Petruchio, Antonio, and two Gent.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Cut his winde-pipe, I ſay.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Fie Antonio.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Or knock his brains out firſt, then forgive him
If you doe thruſt, be ſure it be to th' hilts,
A Surgeon may ſee through him.
You are too violent,
Too open, undiſcreet.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Am I not ruin'd?
The honour of my houſe crack'd? my bloud poyſon'd?
My credit, and my name?
Be ſure it be ſo,
Before ye uſe this violence. Let not doubt,
And a ſuſpecting anger ſo much ſway ye,
Your wiſedome may be queſtion'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I ſay kill him,
And then diſpute the cauſe; cut off what may be,
And what is, ſhall be ſafe.
Hang up a true man,
Becauſe 'tis poſſible he may be theeviſh:
Alas, is this good Juſtice?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: I know as certaine,
As day muſt come againe; as cleare as truth.
And open as beliefe can lay it to me,
That I am baſely wrong'd, wrong'd above recompence;
Malitiouſly abus'd, blaſted for ever
In name and honour, loſt to all remembrance,
But what is ſmear'd, and ſhamefull; I muſt kill him,
Neceſſitie compells me.
But think better

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: There is no other cure left: yet witneſſe with me
All that is faire in man, all that is noble,
I am not greedy of this life I ſeek for,
Nor thirſt to ſhed mans bloud; and would 'twere poſſible
I wiſh it with my ſoule, ſo much I tremble
To offend the ſacred Image of my Maker,
My ſword could onely kill his crimes: no 'tis honour,
Honour, my noble friends, that idoll honour,
That all the world now worſhips, not Petruchio
Muſt doe this juſtice.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let it once be done,
And 'tis no matter, whether you, or honour,
Or both be acceſſarie.
Doe you weigh Petruchio
The value of the perſon, power, and greatneſſe,
And what this ſparke may kindle?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: To performe it,
So much I am ty'd to reputation,
And credit of my houſe, let it raiſe wild-ſires,
That all this Dukedome ſmoak, and ſtormes that toſſe me
Into the ſtormes of everlaſting ruine,
Yet I muſt through; if yee dare ſide me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Dare?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Ye're friends indeed, if not.
Here's none flies from you,
Doe it in what deſigne ye pleaſe, wee'll back ye.
But then be ſure yee kill him.
Is the cauſe
So mortall, nothing but his life?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Beleeve me,
A leſſe offence has been the deſolation
Of a whole name.
No other way to purge it?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: There is, but never to be hoped for,
Thinke an houre more,
And if then ye finde no ſafer road to guide yee,
Wee'll ſet up our reſts too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Mine's up already,
And hang him for my part,
Goes leſſe than life.
If we ſee noble cauſe, 'tis like our ſwords
May be as free and forward as your words. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: The civill order of this Towne Bellonia
Makes it belov'd, and honour'd of all travellers,
As a moſt ſafe retirement in all troubles;
Beſide the wholſome ſeat, and noble temper
Of thoſe mindes that inhabit it, ſafely wiſe,
And to all ſtrangers vertuous: But I ſee
My admiration has drawne night upon me,
And longer to expect my friend may pull me
Into ſuſpition of too late a ſtirrer,
Which all good Governments are jealous of.
Ile home, and thinke at liberty: yet certaine,
'Tis not ſo farre night as I thought; for ſee,
A faire houſe yet ſtands open, yet all about it
Are cloſe, and no lights ſtirring: there may be foule play:
Ile venture to look in: if there be knaves,
I may doe a good office. Woman within.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: Signieur?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: What? how is this?

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: Signieur Fabritio?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Ile goe nearer.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: This is a womans tongue, here may be good done.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: Who's there?

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: I.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: Where are ye?

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: Here.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: O come, for heavens ſake!

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: I muſt ſee what this meanes,

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: I have ſtay'd this long houre for you, make no noiſe,
For things are in ſtrange trouble: here, be ſecret,
'Tis worth your care; begone now; more eyes watch us,
Then may be for our ſafeties.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: Harke ye?

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: Peace: good night.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: She is gone, and I am loaden; fortune for me;
It weighes well, and it feeles well; it may chance
To be ſome pack of worth: by th' maſſe 'tis heavie;
If it be Coyne or Jewels, 'tis worth welcome:
Ile ne're refuſe a fortune: I am confident
'Tis of no common price: now to my lodging:
If it hit right, Ile bleſſe this night. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange,
I cannot meet him; ſure he has encountred
Some light o' love or other, and there meanes
To play at In and In for this night. Well Don John,
If you doe ſpring a leak, or get an itch,
Til ye claw off your curl'd pate, thank your night-walks:
You muſt be ſtill a bootehalling: one round more,
Though it be late, Ile venture to diſcover ye,
I doe not like your out-leaps.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Welcome to Towne, are ye all fit?
To point Sir,

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Where are the horſes?
Where they were appointed.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Be private, and whatſoever fortune
Offer it ſelfe, let's ſtand ſure.
Feare not us,
'Ere ye ſhall be endangered, or deluded,
Wee'll make a black night on't.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: No more, I know it;
You know your Quarters?
Will you goe alone ſir?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Ye ſhall not be farre from me, the leaſt noiſe
Shall bring ye to my reſcue.
We are counſell'd. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.l: Was ever man ſo paid for being curious?
Ever ſo bob'd for ſearching out adventures,
As I am? did the devill lead me? muſt I needs be peeping
Into mens houſes where I had no buſineſſe,
And make my ſelfe a miſchiefe? 'Tis well carried;
I muſt take other mens occaſions on me,
And be I know not whom: moſt finely handled:
What have I got by this now? what's the purchaſe?
A piece of evening Arras worke, a childe,
Indeed an Infidell: this comes of peeping:
A lumpe got out of lazineſſe; good white bread
Let's have no bawling with yee: 'ſdeath, have I
Knowne Wenches thus long, all the wayes of wenches,
Their ſnares and ſubtilties? have I read over
All their Schoole learnings, div'd into their quiddits,
And am I now bum-fidled with a Baſtard?
Fetch'd over with a Carde of five, and in mine old dayes,
After the dire maſſacre of a million
Of Maiden-heads? caught the common way, ith'night too
Under anothers name, to make the matter
Carry more weight about it? well Don Iohn,
You will be wiſer one day, when ye have purchas'd
A beavy of theſe Butter prints together,
With ſearching out conceal'd iniquities,
Without commiſſion: why, it would never grieve me,
If I had got this Ginger-bread: never ſtirr'd me,
So I had had a ſtroak for't: 't had been Juſtice
Then to have kept it; but to raiſe a dayrie
For other mens adulteries, conſume my ſelfe in candles,
And ſcowring works, in Nurſes Bells and Babies,
Onely for charity, for meere I thank you,
A little troubles me: the leaſt touch for it,
Had but my breeches got it, had contented me.
Whoſe e're it is, ſure t' had a wealthy mother,
For 'tis well cloathed, and if I be not cozen'd,
Well lin'd within: to leave it here were barbarous,
And ten to one would kill it: a more ſin
Then his that got it: well, I will diſpoſe on't,
And keep it, as they keep deaths heads in rings,
To cry, memento to me; no more peeping.
Now all the danger is to qualifie
The good old gentlewoman, at whoſe houſe we live,
For ſhe will fall upon me with a Catechiſme
Of foure houres long: I muſt endure all;
For I will know this mother: Come good wonder,
Let you and I be jogging: your ſtarv'd trebble
Will waken the rude watch elſe: All that bee
Curious night-walkers, may they finde my fee. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Sure hee's gone home:
I have beaten all the purlewes,
But cannot bolt him: if he be a bobbing
'Tis not my care can cure him: To morrow morning
I ſhall have further knowledge from a Surgeons—
Where he lyes moord, to mend his leaks.

sp.speaker: Con,
sp.l: I'me ready,
And through a world of dangers am ſlown to yee.
Be full of haſte and care, we are undone elſe:
Where are your people? which way muſt we travell?
For heaven ſake ſtay not here ſir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What may this prove?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Alas I am miſtaken, loſt, undone.
For ever periſh'd. Sir, for heaven ſake tell me,
Are ye a Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I am.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Of this place?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No, borne in Spain.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: As ever you lov'd honour,
As ever your deſires may gaine their ends,
Doe a poore wretched woman but this benefit,
For I am forc'd to truſt yee.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Y'ave charm'd me,
Humanity and honour bids me helpe ye;
And if I faile your truſt.—

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: The time's too dangerous
To ſtay your proteſtations: I beleeve ye,
Alas, I muſt believe ye: From this place,
Good noble Sir, remove me inſtantly,
And for a time, where nothing but your ſelfe,
And honeſt converſation my come neare me,
In ſome ſecure place ſettle me. What I am,
And why thus boldly I commit my credit
Into a ſtrangers hand, the feares and dangers,
That force me to this wilde courſe, at more leiſure
I ſhall reveale unto you.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Come, be hearty,
He muſt ſtrike through my life that takes ye from me.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: He will ſure come. Are yee well arm'd?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Never feare us.
Here's that will make 'em dance without a Fiddle.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: We are to look for no weak foes, my friends,
Nor unadviſed ones.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Beſt gamſters make the beſt game,
We ſhall fight cloſe and handſome then.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: You are a thought too bloudy.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Why? all Phyſitians
And penny Almanacks allow the opening
Of veines this moneth: why doe ye talke of bloudy?
What come we for, to fall to cuffes for apples?
What, would ye make the Cauſe a Cudgell quarell?
On what termes ſtands this man? is not his honour
Open'd to his hand, and pickt out like an Oyſter?
His credit like a quart pot knockt together,
Able to hold no liquor? cleare but this point.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Speak ſoftly, gentle Couzen.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Ile ſpeak truely;
What ſhould men doe ally'd to theſe diſgraces,
Lick o're his enemie, ſit downe, and dance him?
You are as farre o'th' bow hand now.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And crie;
That's my fine boy, thou wilt doe ſo no more child.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Here are no ſuch cold pitties.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: By Saint Jaques
They ſhall not finde me one: here's old tough Andrew,
A ſpeciall friend of mine, and he but hold,
He ſtrike 'em ſuch a horne-pipe: knocks I come for,
And the beſt bloud I light on; I profes it,
Not to ſcarre Coſter-mongers; If I looſe mine owne,
Mine audits loſt, and fare-well five and fifty.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Let's talke no longer, place your ſelves with ſilence,
As I directed yee; and when time calls us,
As ye are friends, ſo ſhew your ſelves.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: So be it. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena. 9.
div.stage: Enter Don John and his Land-lady.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Nay Son, if this be your regard.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Good mother.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Good me no goods; your Cozen, and your ſelf
Are welcome to me, whilſt you beare your ſelves
Like honeſt and true Gentlemen: Bring hither
To my houſe, that have ever been reputed
A gentlewoman of a decent, and faire carriage,
And ſo behav'd my ſelf?

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: I know ye have.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Bring hither, as I ſay, to make my name
Stinke in my neighbours noſtrills? your Deviſes,
Your Brats, got out of Alligant, and broken oathes?
Your Linſey Woolſey worke, your haſty puddings?
I foſler up your filch'd iniquities?
Y'are deceiv'd in me, Sir, I am none
Of thoſe receivers.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Have I not ſworne unto you,
'Tis none of mine, and ſhew'd you how I found it?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Ye found an eaſie foole that let you get it,
She had better have worne paſtornes.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Will yee heare me?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Oathes? what doe you care for oathes to gaine your ends,
When ye are high and pamper'd? What Saint know ye?
Or what Religion, but your purpos'd lewdneſſe,
Is to be look'd for of ye? nay, I will tell ye,
You will then ſweare like accus'd Cut-purſes,
As far of truth too; and lye beyond all Faulconers:
I'me ſick to ſee this dealing.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Heaven forbid Mother.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Nay, I am very ſick.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Who waits there?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sir. within.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Bring down the bottle of Canary wine.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Exceeding ſick, heav'n helpe me.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Haſte ye ſirrah,
I muſt ev'n make her drunk; nay gentle mother;

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Now ſie upon ye, was it for this purpoſe
You fetch'd your evening walks for your digeſtions,
For this pretended holineſſe? no weather,
Not before day could hold ye from the Matins.
Were theſe your bo-peep prayers? ye have praid well,
And with a learned zeale: watcht well too; your Saint
It ſeems was pleas'd as well: ſtill ſicker, ſicker.
sp.stage: Enter Anthony with a bottle of wine.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: There is no talking to her till I have drencht her.
Give me: here mother take a good round draught,
'Twill purge ſpleen from your ſpirits: deeper mother.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: I, I, ſonne; you imagine this will mend all.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: All y'faith Mother.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: I confeſſe the Wine
Will doe his part.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Ile pledge ye.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: But ſonne John.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: I know your meaning mother; touch it once more,
Alas you look not well; take a round draught,
It warmes the bloud well, and reſtores the colour,
And then wee'll talke at large.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: A civill gentleman?
A ſtranger? one the Town holds a good regard of?

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Nay I will ſilence there.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: One that ſhould weigh his faire name? oh, a ſtichl

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: There's nothing better for a ſtitch, good mother,
Make no ſpare of it, as you love your health,
Mince not the nutter.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: As I ſaid, a gentleman,
Lodge in my houſe? now heav'ns my comfort, Signior!

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: I look'd for this.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: I did not thinke you would havo us'd me thus;
A woman of my credit: one, heaven knowes,
That lov'd you but too tenderly.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Deare mother,
I ever found your kindneſſe, and acknowledge it.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: No, no, I am a fool to counſell yee. Where's the infant?
Come, lets ſee your Workmanſhip.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: None of mine, Mother.
But there 'tis, and a luſty one.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Heaven bleſſe thee,
Thou hadſt a haſty making; but the beſt is,
'Tis many a good mans fortune: as I live
Your owne eyes Signior, and the nether lip
As like yee, as ye had ſpit it.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: I am glad on't.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Bleſſe me, what things are theſe?

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: I thought my labour
Was not all loſt, 'tis gold, & theſe are jewels,
Both rich, and right I hope.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Well, well ſonne Iohn,
I ſee ye are a wood-man, and can chuſe
Your Deere, though it be i'th darke, all your diſcretion
Is not yet loſt; this was well clapt aboard:
Here I am with you now; when as they ſay
Your pleaſure comes with profit; when ye muſt needs do,
Doe where ye may be done to, 'tis a wiſedome
Becomes a young man well: be ſure of one thing,
Looſe not your labour and your time together,
It ſeaſons of a foole, ſonne, time is pretious,
Worke wary whilſt ye have it; ſince ye muſt traffick
Sometimes this ſlippery way, take ſure hold Signior,
Trade with no broken Merchants, make your lading,
As you would make your reſt, adventurouſly,
But with advantage ever.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: All this time mother,
The childe wants looking too, wants meat and Nurſes.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Now bleſſing o' thy care; it ſhall have all,
And inſtantly; Ile ſeek a Nurſe my ſelfe, ſonne;
'Tis a ſweet childe: ah my young Spaniard;
Take you no further care ſir.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: Yes of theſe Jewels,
I muſt by your leave Mother: theſe are yours,
To make your care the ſtronger: for the reſt
Ile finde a Maſter; the gold for bringing up on't,
I freely render to your charge.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: No more words,
Nor no more children, (good ſonne) as you love me,
This may doe well.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: I ſhall obſerve your Morals.
But where's Don Ferdinand (Mother)

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Ten to one
About the like adventure: he told me.
He was to finde you out. Exit.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: Why ſhould he ſtay thus?
There may be ſome ill chance in't: ſleep I will not,
Before I have found him: now this woman's pleas'd,
Ile ſeek my friend out, and my care is eas'd. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: Beleeve ſir, 'tis as poſſible to doe it,
As to remove the City; the maine faction,
Swarm throgh the ſtreets like hornets, arm'd with angers
Able to ruine States: no ſafety left us,
Nor meanes to dye like men, if inſtantly
You draw not back againe,

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: May he be drawne
And quarter'd too, that turnes now; were I ſurer
Of death then thou art of thy fears, and with death
More then thoſe feares are too.
Sir, I feare not.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I would not crack my vow, ſtart from my honour,
Becauſe I may finde danger; wound my ſoule,
To keep my body ſafe.
I ſpeak not ſir,
Out of a baſeneſſe to you.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: No, nor doe not
Out of a baſeneſſe leave mo: what is danger,
More then the weakneſſe of our apprehenſions?
A poor cold part o'th bloud? who takes it hold of?
Cowards, and wicked livers: valiant mindes
Were made the Maſters of it, and as hearty Seamen
In deſperate ſtormes, ſtem with a little Rudder
The tumbling ruines of the Ocean:
So with their cauſe & ſwords do they do dangers.
Say we yere ſure to dye all in this venture,
As I am confident againſt it: is there any
Amongſt us of ſo fat a ſenſe, ſo pamper'd,
Would chule luxuriouſly to lye a bed,
And purge away his ſpirit, ſend his ſoule out
In Sugar-lops, and Syrups? give me dying,
As dying out to be, upon mine enemy,
Parting with man-kinde, by a man that's manly:
Let 'em be all the world, and bring along
Cain's envy with 'em, I will on.
You may ſir,
But with what ſafety?
Since 'tis come to dying,
You ſhall perceive ſir, here be thoſe amongſt us
Can dye as decently as other men,
And with as little ceremony: on brave ſir.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: That's ſpoken heartily.
And he that flinches
May he dye lowzie in a ditch.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: No more dying,
There's no ſuch danger in it:
What's a clock?
Somewhat above your houre.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Away then quickly,
Make no noiſe, and no trouble will attend us. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena. 11.
div.stage: Enter Fredericke, and Peter, (with a candle.)

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Give me the candle: ſo goe you out that way.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: What have we now to doe?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: And o' your life ſirrah,
Let none come neare the doore without my knowledge,
No not my Land lady, nor my friend.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: 'Tis done ſir.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Nor any ſerious buſineſſe that concerns me.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Is the winde there agen?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Be gone.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I am ſir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Now enter without feare.—And noble Lady
That ſafety and civility yee wiſh'd for
Shall truely here attend you: no rude tongue
Nor rough behaviour knows this place, no wiſhes
Beyond the moderation of a man,
Dare enter here: your owne deſires and Innocence,
Joyn'd to my vow'd obedience, ſhall protect you,
Were dangers more then doubts.

sp.speaker: Coaſt.
sp.l: Ye are truely noble,
And worth a womans truſt: let it become me,
(I doe beſeech you ſir) for all your kindneſſe,
To render with my thanks, this worthleſſe trifle;
I may be longer troubleſome.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Faire offices
Are ſtill their owne rewards: Heav'n bleſſe me Lady
From ſelling civill courteſies: may it pleaſe ye,
If ye will force a favour to oblige me,
Draw but that cloud aſide, to ſatisfie me
For what good Angel I am engag'd,

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: It ſhall be.
For I am truely confident yee are honeſt:
The Piece is ſcarce worth looking on.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Truſt me
The abſtract of all beauty, ſoule of ſweetneſſe,
Defend me honeſt thoughts, I ſhall grow wilde elſe:
What eyes are there, rather what little heavens,
To ſtirre mens contemplations? what a Paradice
Runs through each part ſhe has? good bloud be temperate:
I muſt look off: too excellent an object
Confounds the ſenſe that ſees it Noble Lady,
If there be any further ſervice to caſt on me,
Let it be worth my life, ſo much I honour ye,
Or the engagement of whole Families.

sp.speaker: Const.
sp.l: Your ſervice is too liberall, worthy ſir,
Thus farre I ſhall entreat.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Command me Lady.
You make your power too poore.

sp.speaker: Const.
sp.l: That preſently
With all convenient haſte, you would retire
Unto the ſtreet you found me in.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis done.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: There, if you finde a gentleman oppreſt
With force and violence, doe a mans office,
And draw your ſword to reſcue him.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Hee's ſafe,
Be what he will, and let his foes be devills,
Arm'd with your pitty, I ſhall conjure 'em.
Retire, this key will guide ye: all things neceſſary
Are there before ye.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: All my prayers goe with ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ye clap on proof upon me: men ſay gold
Do's all, engages all, works through all dangers:
Now I ſay beauty can do more: The Kings Exchequer,
Nor all his wealthy Indies, could not draw me
Through halfe thoſe miſeries this peece of pleaſure
Might make me leap into: we are all like ſea-Cards,
All our endeavours and our motions,
(As they doe to the North) ſtill point at beauty,
Still at the faireſt: for a handſome woman,
(Setting my ſoule a ſide) it ſhould goe hard,
But I would ſtraine my body: yet to her,
Unleſſe it be her owne free gratitude,
Hopes ye ſhall dye, and thou tongue rot within me,
E're I infringe my faith: now to my reſcue. Exit.

div.head: Scaena prima.
div.stage: Enter Duke, purſued by Petruchio, Antonio, and that Faction.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: YOu will not all oppreſſe me?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Kill him ith' wanton eye: let me come to him.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Then yee ſhall buy me dearely.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Say you ſo ſir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I ſay cut his Wezand ſpoile his peeping.
Have at your love-ſick heart ſir. Enter Don John.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Sure 'tis fighting.
My friend may be engag'd: fie gentlemen,
This is unmanly oddes.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Ile ſtop your mouth ſir. Du. fals down, Don Ioh. beſtrides him.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Nay, then have at thee freely:
Ther's a plumb ſir to ſatisfie your longing.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Away: I hope I have ſped him: here comes reſcue.
We ſhall be endangered: where's Antonio?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I muſt have one thruſt more ſir.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Come up to me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: A miſchiefe confound your fingers.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: How is't?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Well:
Ha's giv'n me my quiet us eſt, I felt him
In my ſmall guts, I'me ſure, has feez'd me:
This comes of ſiding with ye.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Can you goe ſir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I ſhould goe man, and my head were of,
Never talke of going.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Come, all ſhall be well then. Enter the Dukes Faction.
I heare more reſcue comming.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let's turne back then;
My skull's uncloven yet, let me but kill.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Away for heaven ſake with him.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: How is't?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Well ſir,
Onely a little ſtagger'd.

sp.speaker: Faction Du.
sp.l: Lets purſue 'em.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: No not a man, I charge ye: thanks good coat,
Thou haſt ſav'd me a ſhrewd welcome: 't was put home too,
With a good minde I'me ſure on't.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Are ye ſafe then?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: My thanks to you brave ſir, whoſe timely valour,
And manly courteſie came to my reſcue,

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: Ye' had foule play offer'd ye, and ſhame befall him
That can paſſe by oppreſſion.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: May I crave ſir,
But thus much honour more, to know your name?
And him I am ſo bound to?

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: For the Bond ſir,
'Tis every good mans tye: to know me further
Will little profit ye; I am a ſtranger,
My Countrey Spaine; my name Don Iohn, a gentleman
That lyes here for my ſtudy.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I have heard ſir,
Much worthy mention of ye, yet I finde
Fame ſhort of what ye are.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: You are pleas'd ſir,
To expreſſe your courteſie: may I demand
As freely what you are, and what miſchance
Caſt you into this danger?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: For this preſent
I muſt deſire your pardon: you ſhall know me
Ere it be long ſir, and a nobler thanks,
Then now my will can render.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Your will's your owne ſir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What is't you look for ſir, have yee loſt any thing?

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: Onely my hat i'th ſcuffle; ſure theſe fellowes
Were night-ſnaps.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: No, believe ſir: pray ye uſe mine,
For 'twil be hard to finde your owne now.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: No ſir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Indeed ye ſhall, I can command another:
I doe beſeech ye honour me.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: I will ſir,
And ſo Ile take my leave.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Within theſe few dayes
I hope I ſhall be happy in your knowledge.
Till when I love your memory. Exit Duke, &c. Enter Fredrick.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: I yours.
This is ſome noble fellow.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis his tongue ſure.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ye' are fairely met ſir:
I thought ye had been a Bat-fowling: prethee tell me,
What Revelations haſt thou had to night,
That home was never thought of?

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: Revelations?
Ile tell thee Fredrick. but before I tell thee,
Settle thy underſtanding.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis prepar'd, ſir.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: Why then mark what ſhall follow. This night Fredr.
This bawdy night.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I thought no leſſe.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: This blinde night,
What doſt think I have got?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: The Pox it may be.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: Would 'twere no worſe: ye talke of Revelations,
I have got a Revelation will reveale me,
An arrant Coxcombe while I live.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What is't?
Thou haſt loſt nothing?

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: No, I have got I tell thee.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: What haſt thou got?

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: One of the Infantry, a childe.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: A chopping child, man.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Give ye joy, ſir.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: A lump of lewdneſſe Fredrick, that's the truth on't:
This Town's abominable.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: I ſtill told ye Iohn
Your whoring muſt come home; I counſell'd ye:
But where no grace is—

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: 'Tis none o'mine, man.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Anſwer the Pariſh ſo.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: Cheated introth.
Peeping into a houſe, by whom I know not,
Nor where to find the place agen: no Fredricke,
Had I but kiſt the ring fort; 'tis no poor one,
That's my beſt comfort, for't has brought about it
Enough to make it man.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Where is't?

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: At home.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: A ſaving voyage: But what will you ſay Signior,
To him that ſearching out your ſerious Worſhip,
Has met a ſtranger fortune?

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: How, good Frederick?
A militant girle now to this boy would hit it?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No, mine's a nobler venture: What do you think Sir
Of a diſtreſſed Lady, one whoſe beauty
Would overſell all Italy?

sp.speaker: Joh,
sp.l: Where is ſhe—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: A woman of that rare behaviour,
So qualified, as admiration
Dwels round about her: of that perfect ſpirit—

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: I marry Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: That admirable carriage,
That ſweetnes in diſcourſe; young as the morning,
Her bluſhes ſtaining his.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: But where's this Creature?
Shew me but that.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: That's all one, ſhee's forth comming,
I have her ſure Boy.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: Harke ye Fredrick.
What truck betwixt my Infant?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis too light Sir,
Stick to your charges good Don John, I am well.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: But is there ſuch a wench?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Firſt tell me this,
Did ye not lately as ye walk'd along,
Diſcover people that were arm'd, and likely
To doe offence?

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Yes mary, and they urg'd it
As far as they had ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Pray goe forward.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: A Gentleman I found ingag'd amongſt e'm,
It ſeemes of noble breeding, I'm ſure brave mettall,
As I return'd to looke you, I ſet in to him,
And without hurt (I thanke heaven) reſcued him,
And came my ſelfe off ſafe too.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: My work's done then:
And now to ſatisfie you, there is a woman,
Oh Iohn, there is a woman—

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Oh, where is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: And one of no leſſe worth then I aſſure ye;
And which is more, falne under my protection.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.p: I am glad of that: forward ſweet Fredrick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: And which is more then that, by this nights wandring,
And which is moſt of all, ſhe is at home too Sir.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: Come, lets be gone then.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Yes, but 'tis moſt certaine,
You cannot ſee her, Iohn.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: She has ſworne me
That none elſe ſhall come neare her: not my Mother
Till ſome few doubts are clear'd.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Not look upon her? What chamber is ſhe in?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: In ours.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Let's goe I ſay:
A womans oathes are wafers, breake with making,
They muſt for modeſtie a litle: we all know it.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No, I'le aſſure you Sir.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Not ſee her?
I ſmell an old dog trick of yours, well Fredrick,
Ye talkt to me of whoring, let's have faire play,
Square dealing I would wiſh ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: When 'tis come.
Which I know never will be, to that iſſue,
Your ſpoone ſhall be as deep as mine Sir.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Tell me,
And tell me true, is the cauſe honourable,
Or for your eaſe?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: By all our friendſhip, Iohn,
'Tis honeſt, and of great end.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: I am anſwer'd:
But let me ſee her though: leave the doore open
As yee goe in.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: I dare not.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: Not wide open,
But juſt ſo, as a jealous husband
Would levell at his wanton wife through.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: That courteſie,
If ye deſire no more, and keep it ſtrictly,
I dare afford yee: come, 'tis now neare morning. Ex.

div.head: Scaene 2.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Nay the old woman's gone too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Shee's a Catterwauling
Among the gutters: But conceive me, Peter,
Where our good Maſters ſhould be?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Where they ſhould be,
I doe conceive, but where they are, good Anthony—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I, there it goes: my Maſters bo-peep with me,
With his ſlye popping in and out agen,
Argued a cauſe, a frippery cauſe.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Beleeve me,
They bear up with ſome carvell.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I doe believe thee,
For thou haſt ſuch a Maſter for that chaſe,
That till he ſpend his maine Maſt—

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Pray remember
Your courteſie good Anthony; and withall,
How long 'tis ſince your Maſter ſprung a leak,
He had a ſound one ſince he came. Lute ſounds within.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Harke.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Doeſt not hear a Lute?
Agen?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Where is't?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Above in my Maſters chamber.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: There's no creature: he hath the key himſelf man.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: This is his Lute: let him have it. Sing within a little.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I grant you; but who ſtrikes it?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: An admirable voice too, harke ye.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Art ſure we are at home?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Without all doubt, Peter.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Then this muſt be the Devill.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let it be. Sing agen.
Good Devill ſing againe: O dainty devill,
Peter beleve it, a moſt delicate devill,
The ſweeteſt Devill— Enter Fredrick & Don Iohn.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: If ye could leave peeping.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: I cannot by no meanes.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Then come in ſoftly,
And as ye love your faith, preſume no further
Then yee have promiſed.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: What make you up ſo early ſir?

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: You ſir in your contemplations.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: O pray ye peace ſir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Why peace ſir?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Doe you heare?

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: 'Tis your Lute.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Pray yee ſpeak ſoftly.
She's playing on't.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The houſe is haunted ſir,
For this we have heard this halfe yeare.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ye ſaw nothing;

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Not I.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Nor I Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Get us our breakfaſt then,
And make no words on't; wee'll undertake this ſpirit,
If it be one.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This is no devill Peter. Sing. Exeunt Servants.
Mum, there be Bats abroad.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Stay, now ſhe ſings.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: An Angels voice Ile ſweare.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Why did'ſt thou ſhrug ſo?
Either allay this heat; or as I live
I will not truſt ye.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Paſſe: I warrant ye. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: To curſe thoſe ſtarres, that men ſay governe us,
To raile at fortune, fall out with my Fate,
And taske the generall world, will helpe me nothing:
Alas, I am the ſame ſtill, neither are they
Subject to helpes, or hurts: Our owne deſires
Are our owne fates, our owne ſtars, all our fortunes,
Which as we ſway 'em, ſo abuſe, or bleſſe us.

div.stage: Enter Fredrick, and Don John peeping.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Peace to your meditations.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: Pox upon ye,
Stand out oth' light.

sp.speaker: Const.
sp.l: I crave your mercy ſir,
My minde o're-charg'd with care made me unmannerly.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Pray yee ſet that minde at reſt, all ſhall be perfect.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: I like the body rare; a handſome body,
A wondrous handſome body: would ſhe would turne:
See, and that ſpightfull puppy be not got
Between me and my light againe,

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Tis done,
As all that you command ſhall bee: the gentleman
Is ſafely off all danger.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: How ſhall I thank ye ſir? how ſatisfie?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Speak ſoftly, gentle Lady, all's rewarded,
Now does he melt like Marmalad.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: Nay, 'tis certaine,
Thou art the ſweeteſt woman I e're look'd on:
I hope thou art not honeſt.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: None diſturb'd yee?

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: Not any ſir, nor any ſound came neare me,
I thank your care.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis well.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: I would faine pray now,
But the Devill and that fleſh there, o' the world,
What are we made to ſuffer?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Hee'll enter;
Pull in your head and be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Harke ye Fredricke,
I have brought ye home your Pack-ſaddle.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Pox upon yee.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Nay let him enter: fie my Lord the Duke,
Stand peeping at your friends.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Ye are cozen'd Lady,
Here is no Duke.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: I know him full well Signior.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Hold thee there wench.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: This mad-brain'd foole will ſpoile all.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I doe beſeech your grace come in.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: My Grace,
There was a word of comfort.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Shall he enter,
Who e're he be?

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Well follow'd Fredrick.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Come in then. Enter Don John.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: 'Bleſſe yee Lady:

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Nay ſtart not, though he be a ſtranger to ye,
Hee's of a Noble ſtraine, my kinſman, Lady,
My Countrey-man, and fellow Traveller,
One bed containes us ever, one purſe feeds us,
And one faith free between us; do not fear him,
Hee's truely honeſt.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: That's a lye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: And truſty:
Beyond your wiſhes: valiant to defend,
And modeſt to converſe with, as your bluſhes.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Now may I hang my ſelf; this commendation
Has broke the neck of all my hopes: for now
Muſt I cry, no forſooth, and I forſooth, and ſurely,
And truely as I live,, and as I am honeſt.
Has done theſe things for 'nonce too; for hee knowes,
Like a moſt envious Raſcall as he is,
I am not honeſt, nor deſire to be,
Eſpecially this way: h'as watch'd his time,
But I ſhall quit him.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: Sir, I credit ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Goe kiſſe her John.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: Plague o' your commendations.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Sir, I ſhall now deſire to be a trouble.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Never to me, ſweet Lady: Thus I ſeale
My faith, and all my ſervice.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: One word Signeur.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Now 'tis impoſſible I ſhould be honeſt,
She kiſſes with a conjuration
Would make the devill dance: what points ſhe at?
My leg I warrant, or my well knit body:
Sit faſt Don Fredrick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Twas given him by that gentleman
You took ſuch care of; his owne being loſt ith' ſcuffle.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: With much joy may he weare it: 'tis a right one,
I can aſſure ye Gentleman, and right happy
May you be in all fights for that faire ſervice.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Why doe ye bluſh?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: 'T had almoſt cozen'd me,
For not to lye, when I ſaw that, I look'd for
Another Maſter of it: but 'tis well. Knock within.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Who's there? Ent. Anthony.
Stand ye a little cloſe: Come in Sir,
Now what's the newes with you?

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.l: There is a gentlemen without,
Would ſpeak with Don John,

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Who ſir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I do not know Sir, but he ſhews a man
Of no meane reckoning.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Let him ſhew his name,
And then returne a little wiſer.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Well Sir. Exit Anthony.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: How doe you like her Iohn?

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: As well as you Fredrick,
For all I am honeſt: you ſhall finde it ſo too.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Art thou not honeſt?

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Art thou an Aſſe?
And modeſt as her bluſhes? What a block-head
Would e're have popt out ſuch a dry Apologie,
For his deare friend? and to a Gentlewoman,
A woman of her youth, and delicacy.
They are arguments to draw them to abhorre us.
An honeſt morall man; 'tis for a Conſtable:
A handſome man, a wholſome man, a tough man,
A liberall man, a likely man, a man
Made up like Hercules, unſlak'd with ſervice:
The ſame to night, to morrow night, the next night,
And ſo to perpetuitie of pleaſures,
Theſe had been things to hearken too, things catching:
But you have ſuch a ſpiced conſideration,
Such qualmes upon your worſhips conſcience,
Such-chil-blaines in your bloud, that all things pinch ye,
Which nature, and the liberall world makes cuſtome,
And nothing but faire honour, O ſweet honour,
Hang up your Eunuch honour: That I was truſty,
And valiant, were things well put in; but modeſt!
A modeſt gentleman I ô wit where waſt thou?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I am ſorrie John,

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: My Ladies gentlewoman
Would laugh me to a Schoole-boy, make me bluſh
With playing with my Codpeece point: fie on thee,
A man of thy diſcretion?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: It ſhall be mended:
And henceforth yee ſhall have your due. Enter Anthony.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: I look fort: How now, who is't?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: A gentleman of this towne
And calls himſelfe Petruchio. Enter Conſtantia.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Ile attend him.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: How did he call himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Doe's it concerne you ought?

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: O gentlemen,
The houre of my deſtruction is come on me,
I am diſcover'd, loſt, left to my ruine:
As ever ye had pitty—

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Doe not feare,
Let the great devill come, he ſhall come through me:
Loſt here, and we about ye?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Fall before us?

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: O my unfortunate eſtate, all angers
Compar'd to his, to his—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Let his, and all mens,
Whilſt we have power and life: ſtand up for heaven ſake.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I have offended heaven too; yet heaven knows—

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: We are all evill:
Yet heaven forbid we ſhould have our deſerts.
What is a?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Too too neare to my offence ſir;
O he will cut me peece-meale.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Tis no Treaſon?

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Let it be what it will: if a cut here,
Ile finde him cut-worke.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: He muſt buy you deare,
With more than common lives.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: Feare not, nor weep not:
By heaven Ile fire the Towne before yee periſh,
And then, the more the merrier, wee'll jog with yee.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Come in, and dry your eyes.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Pray no more weeping:
Spoile a ſweet face for nothing? my returne
Shall end all this I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Heaven grant it. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: This man ſhould be of ſpeciall rank:
For theſe commends carry no common way,
No ſlight worth with 'em:
A ſhall be he. Ent. Don Iohn.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: 'Save yee ſir: I am ſorrie
My buſineſſe was ſo unmannerly, to make ye
Wait thus long here.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Occaſions muſt be ſerv'd ſir:
But is your name Don John?

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: It is Sir.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Then,
Firſt, for your owne brave ſake I muſt embrace yee:
Next, from the credit of your noble friend
Hernando de Aluara, make yee mine:
Who layes his charge upon me in this Letter
To look yee out, and for the goodneſſe in yee,
Whilſt your occaſions make yee reſident
