In this place, to ſupply yee, love and honour yee;
Which had I knowne ſooner—

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Noble ſir,
You'll make my thanks too poore: I weare a ſword, ſir,
And have a ſervice to be ſtill diſpos'd of,
As you ſhall pleaſe command it.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Gentle ſir,
That manly courteſie is half my buſineſſe:
And to be ſhort, to make ye know I honour ye,
And in all points believe your worth like Oracle,
And how above my friends, which are not few,
And thoſe not ſlack, I eſtimate your vertues,
Make your ſelfe underſtand, This day Petruchio,
A man that may command the ſtrength of this place,
Hazzard the boldeſt ſpirits; hath made choice
Onely of you, and in a noble office.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Forward, I am free to entertaine it.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Thus then:
I doe beſeech ye mark me.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: I ſhall doe it.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Ferrara's Duke, would I might call him wort hie,
But that he has raz'd out from his family,
As he has mine with Infamie, This man,
Rather this powerfull Monſter, we being left
But two of all our houſe, to ſtock out memories,
My Siſter, and my ſelfe; with arts, and witch-crafts,
Vowes, and ſuch oathes heaven has no mercy for,
Drew to diſhonour this weak maid, by ſtealthes,
And ſecret paſſages I knew not of,
Oft he obtain'd his wiſhes, oft abus'd her:
I am aſham'd to ſay the reſt: This purchas'd,
And his hot bloud allay'd, as friends forſake us
At a miles end upon our way, he left her,
And all our name to ruine.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: This was foule Play,
And ought to be rewarded ſo.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: I hope ſo;
He ſcap'd me yeſter-night: which if he dare
Againe adventure for, heaven pardon him,
I ſhall with all my heart.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: For me, brave Signior,
What doe yee intend?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Onely, faire ſir, this truſt,
Which from the commendations of this Letter,
I dare preſume well placed, nobly to beare him
By word of mouth a ſingle challenge from me,
That man to man, if he have honour in him,
We may decide all difference.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Faire, and noble,
And I will doe it home: When ſhall I viſite ye?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Pleaſe you this after-noon, I will ride with yee:
For at a Caſtle ſix mile hence, we are ſure
To finde him.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.l: Ile be ready.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: To attend ye,
My man ſhall wait: with all my Ex. Petr. Enter Fredr.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: My ſervice ſhall not faile yee.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: How now?

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: All's well: who doſt thou think this wench is?
Gheſſe, and thou canſt?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I cannot.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Be it knowne then,
To all men by theſe preſents, this is ſhe,
She, ſhe, and only ſhe, our curious coxcombs
Were errant two moneths after.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Who, Constantia?
Thou talk'ſt of Cocks and Bulls.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: I talke of wenches,
Of Cocks and Hens Don Frerdick; this is the Pullet
We two went proud after.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: It cannot be.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: It ſhall be;
Siſter to Don Petruchio: I know all man.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Now I beleeve.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Goe to, there has been ſtirring,
Fumbling with Linnen Fredrick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis impoſſible,
You know her faine was pure as fire.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: That pure fire
Has melted out her maiden-head: ſhe is crickt:
We have all that hope of our ſide, boy.

sp.speaker: Fred,
sp.l: Thou tell'ſt me,
To my imagination, things incredible:
I ſee no looſe thought in her.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: That's all one,
She is looſe ith' hilts by heaven: but the world muſt know
A faire way, upon vow of marriage.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: There may be ſuch a ſlip.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: And will be Fredrick,
Whil'ſt the old game's a foot: I feare the boy too
Will prove hers too I took up.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Good circumſtance
May cure all this yet.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: There thou hitſt it, Fredrick:
Come, let's walke in and comfort her: her being here
Is nothing yet ſuſpected: anon Ile tell thee
Wherefore her brother came, who by this light
Is a brave noble fellow, and what honour
H'as done to me a ſtranger: there be Irons
Heating for ſome, will hiſte into their heart blouds,
'Ere all be ended; ſo much for this time.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Well ſir Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: CCome ye doe know.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I do not by this hand Miſtris.
But I ſuſpect.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: That if egges continue
At this price, women wil ne're be ſav'd
By their good works.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: I will know.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Yee ſhall, any thing
Lyes in my power: The Duke of Loraine now
Is ſeven thouſand ſtrong: I heard it of a fiſh-wife,
A woman of fine knowledge.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Sirrah, ſirrah.

sp.speaker: Pe.
sp.l: The Popes Buls are broke looſe too and 'tis ſuſpected
They ſhall be baited in England.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Very well ſir.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: No, 'tis not ſo well neither.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: But I ſay to yee,
Who is it keeps your Maſter company?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I ſay to you, Don Iohn.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: I ſay what woman?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I ſay ſo too.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: I ſay againe, I will know.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I ſay 'tis fit yee ſhould.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: And I tell thee
He has a woman here.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: And I tell thee
'Tis then the better for him.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: You are no Bawd now?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Would I were able to be call'd unto it:
A worſhipfull vocation for my elders;
For as I underſtand it is a place
Fitting my betters farr.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Was ever Gentlewoman
So frumpt off with a foole? well ſawcy ſirrah,
I will know who it is, and for what purpoſe;
I pay the rent, and I will know how my houſe
Comes by theſe Inflamations: if this geere hold,
Beſt hang a ſigne-poſt up, to tell the Signiors,
Here ye may have lewdneſſe at Liverie. Ent. Fredrick.

sp.speaker: Pet,
sp.l: 'Twould be a great eaſe to your age.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: How now?
Why what's the mater Land-lady?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: What's the matter?
Ye uſe me decently among ye gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Who has abus'd her, you ſir?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: 'Ods my witneſſe
I will not be thus treated, that I will not.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I gave her no ill language.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Thou lyeſt lewdly,
Thou tookſt me up at every word I ſpoke,
As I had been a Mawkin, a flurt Gillian;
And thou thinkſt, becauſe thou canſt write & read,
Our noſes muſt be under thee.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Dare you ſirrah?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Let but the truth be known Sir, I beſeech ye,
She raves of wenches, and I know not what ſir:

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Go to, thou know'ſt too well, thou wicked varlet,
Thou inſtrument of evill.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: As I live Sir,
She is ever thus till dinner.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Get ye in,
Ile anſwer you anon ſir.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: By this hand
Ile break your Poſſit pan. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Then by this hood
Ile lock the meat up.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Now your grief, what is't?
For I can gheſſe—

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Ye may with ſhame enough,
If theer were ſhame amongſt yee; nothing thought on,
But how yee may abuſe my houſe: not ſatisfi'd
With bringing home your Baſtards to undoe me,
But you muſt drill your whores here too; my patience
Becauſe I beare, and beare, and carry, all,
And as they ſay am willing to groan under)
Muſt be your make-ſport now.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No more of theſe words.
Nor no more murmurings Lady: for you know
That I know ſomething. I did ſuſpect your anger,
But turne it preſently and handſomely,
And beare your ſelfe diſcreetly to this woman,
For ſuch a one there is indeed.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: 'Tis well ſonne.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Leaving your devils Matins, and your melanchollies,
Or we ſhall leave our lodgings.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: You have much need
To uſe theſe vagrant wayes, and to much profit:
Ye had that might content
(At home within your ſelves too) right good gentlemen,
Wholſome, and yee ſaid handſome: But you gallants,
Boaſt that I was to beleeve ye—

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Leave your ſuſpicion:
For as I live there's no ſuch thing.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Mine honour;
And 'twere not for mine honour.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Come, your honour,
Your houſe, and you too, if you dare beleeve me
Are well enough: ſleek up your ſelf, leave crying, Bowle of wipe ready.
For I muſt have yee entertain this Lady
With all civility, ſhe well deſerves it,
Together with all ſecreſie: I dare truſt yee,
For I have found ye faithfull: when you know her
You will find your owne fault; no more words, but doe it.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: You know you may command me. Ent. Don. Ioh.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: Worſhipfull Lady,
How does thy Velvet ſcabbard? by this hand
Thou look'ſt moſt amiably: now could I willingly
And 'twere not for abuſing thy Geneva print there,
Venture my body with thee.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: You'll leave this roperie,
When you come to my yeares.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: By this light
Thou art not above fifteen yet, a meere girle,
Thou haſt not half thy teeth: come—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Prethee Iohn
Let her alone, ſhe has been vex'd already:
Shee'll grow ſtarke mad man.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: I would ſee her mad,
An old mad woman

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Prethee be patient.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Is like a Millers Mare, troubled with tooth-ache.
Shee'll make the rareſt faces.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Goe, and doe it,
And doe not mind this fellow.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Well Don John.
There will be times agen; when O good Mother,
What's good for a carnoſity in the Bladder?
O the green water, mother.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: Doting take yee,
Doe ye remember that?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: She has payd ye now ſir.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Clarry, ſweet mother, Clarry.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Are ye ſatisfied?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Ile never whore againe; never give Petticoats
And Waſtcoats at five pound a peece; good Mother,
Quickly Mother: now mock on Son.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: A devill grinde your old chaps. Exit Land.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: By this hand wench
Ile give thee a new hood for this.
Has ſhe met with your Lordſhip?
Touch-wood rake her. Enter Anthony.
Shee's a rare ghoſtly mother.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Below attends yee
The Gentlemans man ſir that was with yee.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: Well Sir;
My time is come then: yet if my project hold,
You ſhall not ſtay behinde: Ile rather truſt. Enter Conſtan.
A Cat with ſweet milk Fredrick; by her face
I feele her feares are working.

sp.speaker: Const.
sp.l: Is there no way,
I doe beſeech yee think yet, to divert
This certaine danger?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: 'Tis impoſſible:
Their honours are engag'd.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Then there muſt be murther,
Which, Gentlemen, I ſhall no ſooner heare of,
Then make one int: you may, if you pleaſe ſir,
Make all goe leſſe yet.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Lady wer't mine owne cauſe,
I could diſpence: but loaden with my friends truſt,
I muſt go on; though generall maſſacres
As much I feare—

sp.speaker: Conſt,
sp.l: Doe ye heare ſir; for heavens pittie
Let me requeſt one love of you.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Yes any thing.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: This gentleman I find too reſolute,
Too hot, and fiery for the cauſe, as ever
You did a vertuous deed, for honours ſake
Go with him, and allay him: your fair temper
And noble diſpoſition, like wiſh'd ſhowres,
May quench thoſe eating fires, that would ſpoile all elſe.
I ſee in him deſtruction.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I will doe it;
And 'tis a wiſe conſideration,
To me, a bounteous favour: harke ye John,
I will goe with yee.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Indeed I will,
Ye goe upon a hazard: no denyall;
For as I live, Ile goe.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Then make ye ready,
For I am ſtraight a horſe-back.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: My ſword on,
I am as ready as you: what my beſt labour,
With all the Art I have can work upon 'em,
Be ſure of, and expect faire end: the old gentlewoman
Shall wait upon you; ſhe is both grave and private,
And yee may truſt her in all points.

sp.speaker: Const.
sp.l: Ye are noble:
And ſo I kiſſe your hand.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: That ſeale for me too,
And I hope happy iſſue Lady.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: All heavens care upon yee, and my prayers.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: So,
Now my mind's at reſt.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Away, 'tis late John. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaene 2.
div.stage: Enter Antonio, a Surgeon, and 2. Gent.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Come ſir▪ be hearty: all the worſt is paſt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Give me ſome Wine.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: 'Tis death Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis a horſe ſir.
'Sbloud, to be dreſt to the tune of Ale onely,
Nothing but ſawces to my ſores.

sp.speaker: 2 Gen.
sp.l: Fie Antonio,
You muſt be govern'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Has given me a dam'd Gliſter,
Only of ſand and ſnow water, gentlemen,
Has almoſt ſcour'd my guts out.

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: I have giv'n you that ſir
Is fitteſt for your ſtate.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And here he feeds me
With rotten ends of rooks, and drown'd chickens,
Stewd Pericraniums, and Pia-maters;
And when I goe to bed, by heaven 'tis true gentlemen,
He rolls me up in Lints, with Labels at 'em,
That I am juſt the man ith' Almanack,
In head and face, is Aries place.

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: Wilt pleaſe ye
To let your friends ſee ye open'd?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Will it pleaſe you ſir
To let me have a wench: I feele my body
Open enough for that yet?

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: How, a wench?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Why look yee gentlemen; thus I am us'd ſtill,
I can get nothing that I want.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: Leave theſe things,
And let him open ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: De'ye heare Surgeon?
Send for the Muſick, let me have ſome pleaſure
To entertaine my friends, beſide your Sallads,
Your green ſalves, and your ſearches, and ſome wine too,
That I may onely ſmell to it: or by this light
Ile dye upon thy hand, and ſpoyle thy cuſtome.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: Let him have Muſick. Ent. Rowl. with wine.

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: 'Tis ith' houſe, and ready,
If he will aske no more: but wine— Muſick.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: He ſhall not drink it.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Will theſe things pleaſe yee?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Yes, and let 'em ſing

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis too long.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Ile have John Dorrie,
For to that warlike tune I will be open'd.
Give me ſome drinke, have yee ſtopt the leakes well Surgeon,
All will runne out elſe?

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: Feare not.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sit downe Gentlemen:
And now advance your plaiſters. Song of Joh. Dorry.
Give 'em ten ſhillings friends: how doe ye finde me?
What Symptomes doe you ſee now?

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: None Sir, dangerous:
But if you will be rul'd—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What time?

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: I can cure ye
In forty dayes, ſo you will not tranſgreſſe me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I have a dog ſhall lick me whole in twenty:
In how long canſt thou kill me?

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: Preſently.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Doe it; there's more delight in't.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: You muſt have patience.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Man, I muſt have buſines; this fooliſh fellow
Hinders himſelfe: I have a dozen Raſcalls
To hurt within theſe five dayes: good man mender,
Stop me up with Parſley, like ſtuft Beefe,
And let me walke abroad.

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: Ye ſhall walke ſhortly.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: For I muſt finde Petruchio.

sp.speaker: 2. Gent.
sp.l: Time enough.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Come lead him in, and let him ſleep: within theſe three dayes
Wee'll beg yee leave to play.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: And then how things fall,
Wee'll certainly informe yee.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: But Surgion promiſe me
I ſhall drinke Wine then too.

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: A little temper'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Nay, Ile no tempering Surgion,

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: Well, as't pleaſe ye,
So ye exceed not.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Farewell: and if ye finde
The Mad ſlave, that thus ſlaſht me, commend me to him,
And bid him keep his skin cloſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Take your reſt ſir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I have told yee all I can, and more then yet
Thoſe Gentlemen know of me; ever truſting
Your Councell and concealement: for to me
You ſeem a worthy woman; one of thoſe
Are ſeldome found in our ſex, wiſe and vertuous,
Direct me I beſeech ye.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Ye ſay well Lady,
And hold yee to that poynt; for in theſe buſineſſes
A womans councell that conceives the matter,
(Doe ye marke me, that conceives the matter Lady)
Is worth ten mens engagements: She knows ſomething'
And out of that can worke like wax: when men
Are giddy-headed, either out of wine,
Or a more drunkenneſſe, vaine oſtentation,
Diſcovering all: there is no more keep in 'em,
Then hold upon an Eeles taile: nay 'tis held faſhion
To defame now all they can.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I, but theſe gentlemen—

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Doe not you truſt to that: theſe gentlemen
Are as all Gentlemen of the ſame Barrell:
I, and the ſelfe ſame pickle too. Be it granted,
They have us'd yee with reſpect and faire behaviour,
Yet ſince ye came: doe you know what muſt follow?
They are Spaniards, Lady, Gennets of high mettle,
Things that will thraſh the devill, or his dam,
Let 'em appeare but cloven.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Now heaven bleſſe me.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Mad Colts will court the wind: I know 'em Lady
To the leaſt haire they have; and I tell you,
Old is I am, let but the pinte pot bleſſe 'em,
They'll offer to my yeares—

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Such rude gambolls—

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: To you?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: I, and ſo handle me, that oft I am forc'd
To fight of all foure for my ſafety: there's the yonger,
Don John, the arrantſt Jack in all this City:
The other, time has blaſted, yet he will ſtoop,
If not ore-flowne, and freely on the quarry;
Has been a Dragon in his dayes. Bur Tarmont,
Don Jenkin is the Devill himſelfe, the Dog-dayes,
The moſt incomprehenſible whore-maſter,
Twenty a night is nothing: Beggers, Broom-women,
And thoſe ſo miſerable, they look like famine,
Are all ſweet Ladies in his drink.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: He's a handſome Gentleman.
Pitty he ſhould be maſter of ſuch follies.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Hee's ne're without a noiſe of Sirrenges
In's pocket, thoſe proclame him; birding pills,
Waters to coole his conſcience, in ſmall Viols;
With thouſand ſuch ſufficient emblemes: the truth is,
Whoſe chaſtily he chops upon, he cares not.
He flies at all; Baſtards upon my conſcience,
He has now in making multitudes; The laſt night
He brought home one; I pitty her that bore it,
But we are all weake veſſels, ſome rich woman
(For wiſe I dare not call her) was the mother,
For it was hung with Jewels: the bearing cloath
No leſſe then Crimſon Velvet.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: 'Tis true Lady.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Was it a Boy too?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: A brave Boy; deliberation
And judgement ſhewd in's getting, as I'le ſay for him,
He's as well paced for that ſport—

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: May I ſee it?
For there is a neighbour of mine, a Gentlewoman,
Has had a late miſchance, which willingly
I would know further of; now if you pleaſe
To be ſo curteous to me.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Ye ſhall ſee it:
But what do ye thinke of theſe men now ye know 'em,
And of the cauſe I told ye of? Be wiſe,
Ye may repent too late elſe; I but tell ye
For your owne good, and as you will find it Lady.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I am advis'd.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: No more words then; do that,
And inſtantly, I told ye of be ready:
Don Iohn, I'le fit ye for your frumps,

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I ſhall be:
But ſhall I ſee this Child?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Within this halfe houre,
Let's in, and there thinke better; ſhe that's wiſe,
Leapes at occaſion firſt; the reſt pay for it. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaene 4.
div.stage: Enter Petruchio, Don Iohn. and Fredrick.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Sir, he is worth your knowledg; and a Gentleman
If I that ſo much love him, may commend him,
Of free and vertuous parts; and one, if ſoule play
Should fall upon us, for which feare I brought him,
Will not flie backe for phillips.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Ye much honour me,
And once more I pronounce ye both mine.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Stay, what Troope
Is that below i'th valley there?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Hawking I take ir.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: They are ſo; 'tis the Duke, 'tis even he Gentlemen,
Sirrah, draw backe the Horſes till we call ye,
I know him by his company.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I thinke too
He bends up this way.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: So he does.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Stand you ſtill
Within that Covert till I call: you Fredrick,
By no meanes be not ſeen, unleſſe they offer
To bring on odds upon us; he comes forward,
Here will I waite him fairely: to your Cabins.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I need no more inſtruct ye?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Feare me not,
I'le give it him, and boldly. Ex: Pet. and Fred.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Feed the Hawkes up,
Wee'l flie no more to day: O my bleſt fortune,
Have I ſo fairely met the man!

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Ye have Sir,
And him you know by this,

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Sir all the honour,
And love—

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: I do beſeech your Grace ſtay there,
(For I know you too now) that love and honour
I come not to receive; nor can you give it,
Till ye appeare faire to the world; I muſt beſeech ye
Diſmiſſe your traine a little.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Walke aſide,
And out of hearing I command ye: Now Sir,

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Laſt time we met, I was a friend.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: And Nobly
You did a friends office: let your buſineſſe
Be what it may, you muſt be ſtill—

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Your pardon,
Never a friend to him, cannot be friend
To his own honour.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: In what have I tranſgreſs'd it?
Ye make a bold breach at the firſt Sir.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Bolder,
You made that breach that let in infamy
And ruine, to ſurprize a noble ſtocke.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Be plaine Sir.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: I will, and ſhort;
Ye have wrong'd a Gentleman
Little behind your ſelfe, beyond all juſtice,
Beyond mediation of all friends.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: The man, and manner of wrong?
The wrong, ye have whord his Siſter.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: What's his will in't?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: His will is to oppoſe you like a Gentleman,
And ſingle, to decide all.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Now ſtay you Sir,
And heare me with the like beliefe: this Gentleman
His Siſter that you named, 'tis true I have long loved,
Nor was that love laſcivious, as he makes it;
As true, I have enjoy'd her: no leſſe truth
I have a child by her: But that ſhe, or he,
Or any of that family are tainted
Suffer diſgrace, or ruine, by my pleaſures,
I weare a Sword to ſatisfie the world no,
And him in this cauſe when he pleaſe; for know Sir,
She is my wife, contracted before Heaven,
(Witneſſe I owe more tye to, then her Brother)
Nor will I flye from that name, vvhich long ſince
Had had the Churches approbation,
But for his jealous danger.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Sir, your pardon,
And all that was my anger, now my ſervice.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Faire ſir, I knew I ſhould convert ye; had we
But that rough man herd now too—

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: And ye ſhall Sir
Whoa, hoa, hoo.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: I hope ye have laid no Ambuſh? Enter Petru.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Only friends.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: My noble Brother welcome:
Come put your Anger off, we'l have no fighting,
Unleſſe you will maintaine I am unworthy
To beare that name.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Do you ſpeake this hartely?

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: upon my ſoule, and truly; the firſt Prieſt
Shall put you out of theſe doubts.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Now I love ye;
And I beſeech you pardon my ſuſpitions,
You are now more then a Brother, a brave friend too.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: The good man's over-joyd Enter Fred.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: How now, how goes it?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Why, the man 'has his mare agen, and all's well Fredrick,
The Duke profeſſes freely hee's her husband.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis a good hearing.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Yes, for modeſt Gentlemen.
I muſt preſent ye: may it pleaſe your Grace
To number this brave Gentleman, my friend
And noble kinſman, amongſt thoſe your ſervants.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: O my brave friend! you ſhowre your bounties on me
Amongſt my beſt thoughts Signior, in which number
You being worthily diſpos'd already,
May place your friend to honour me.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: My love ſir,
And where your Grace dares truſt me, all my ſervice.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Why? this is wondrcus happy: But now Brother,
Now comes the bitter to our ſweet: Conſtantia.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Why, what of her?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Nor what, nor where, do I know?
Wing'd with her feares laſt night, beyond my knowledge,
She quit my houſe, but whether—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Let not that—

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: No more good Sir, I have heard too much.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Nay ſinke not,
She cannot be ſo loſt.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Nor ſhall not Gentlemen;
Be free agen, the Ladie's found; that ſmile Sir,
Shewes ye diſtruct your Servant.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: I do beſeech ye.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Ye ſhall beleeve me: by my ſoule ſhe is ſafe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Heaven knows, I would beleeve Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ye may ſafely.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: And under noble uſage: this faire Gentleman
Met her in all her doubts laſt night, and to his guard
(Her feares being ſtrong upon her) ſhe gave her perſon,
who waited on her, to our lodging; where all reſpect,
Civill and honeſt ſervice now attend her.

sp.speaker: Pet
sp.l: Ye may beleeve now.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Yes, I do, and ſtrongly:
Well my good friends, or rather my good Angels,
For ye have both preſerved me; when theſe vertues
Dye in your friends remembrance—

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Good your grace
Loſe no more time in complement, 'tis too pretious,
I know it by my ſelfe, there can be no hell
To his that hangs upon his hopes; eſpecially
In way of luſtly pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: He has hit it.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: To horſe againe then, for this night I'le crowne
With all the joyes ye wiſh for.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Happy Gentlemen. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: This is the maddeſt miſchiefe: never foole
Was ſo fubd off, as I am; made ridiculous,
And to my ſelfe, mine owne Aſſe: truſt a woman,
I'le truſt the Devill firſt; for he dare be
Better then's word ſometime: what faith have I broke?
In what obſervance failed? Let me conſider, Enter Don Iohn. and Fred.
For this is monſtrous uſage.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Let them talke,
Wee'll ride on faire and ſoftly.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Well Conſtantia,

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Conſtantia, what's this fellow? ſtay by all means.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Ye have ſpun your ſelfe a faire thred now.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Stand ſtill Iohn.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: What cauſe had you to fly? what feare poſſeſt ye?
Were you not ſafely lodg'd from all ſuſpition?
Us'd with all gentle meanes? did any know
How ye came thether, or what your ſin was.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: ſmell ſome juggling John.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Yes, Fredricks, I feare it will be found ſo.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: So ſtrangely,
Without the counſell of your friends; ſo deſperatly
To put all dangers on ye?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: So deceitfully
After a ſtrangers lure?

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Did ye marke that Fredrick?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: To make ye appeare more monſter; and the Law
More cruell to reward ye? to leave all,
All that ſhould be your ſafegard, to ſeeke evils?
Was this your wiſedome? this your promiſe? well
He that incited ye—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Marke that too.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: 'Had better have plough'd farther off; now Lady,
What will your laſt friend, he that ſhould preſerve ye,
And hold your credit up, the brave Antonio,
Thinke of this ſlip? he'll to Petruchio,
And call for open juſtice.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe Fredrick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: But what that he is John.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: I do not doubt yet
To bolt ye out, for I know certainly
Ye are about the Towne ſtill: ha, no more words. Ex.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Well.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Very well.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Diſcreetly.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Finely carried.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You have no more of theſe tricks?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Ten to one Sir,
I ſhall meet with 'em if ye have.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Is this honeſt?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Was it in you a friends part to deale double?
I am no aſſe Don Fredrick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: And Don Iohn,
It ſhall appeare I am no foole;
Diſgrace me to make yourſelfe a lecher?
'Tis boyiſh, 'tis baſe.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: 'Tis falſe, and moſt unmanly to upbraid me,
Nor will I be your boiſter Sir,

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Thou wanton boy, thou hadſt better have been Eunuch,
Thou common womans curteſie, then thus
Laſcivious, baſely to have bent mine honour.
A friend? I'le make a horſe my friend firſt!

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Holla, holla,
Ye kicke to faſt ſir: what ſtrange braines have you got,
That dare crow out thus bravely? I better been a Eunuch?
I privy to this dog tricke? cleare your ſelfe,
For I know where the wind ſits, and moſt nobly,
Or as I have a life—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No more: they'r horſes. A noyſe within like horſes.
Nor ſhew no diſcontent: to morrow comes;
Let's quietly away: if ſhe be at home,
Our jealouſies are put off.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: The fellow Enter Duke, Petruchio.
We have loſt him in our ſpleenes, like fooles.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Come Gentlemen,
Now ſet on roundly; ſuppoſe ye have all miſtreſſes,
And mend your pace according,

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Then have at ye. Exeunt

div.head: Scaena prima.
div.stage: Enter Duke, Petruchio, Fredrick, and Iohn.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: NOw to Bollonia, my moſt honoured brother,
I dare pronounce yea hearty, and ſafe welcome,
Our loves ſhall now way-lay ye; welcome Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: The ſame to you brave Sir; Don Fredrick
Will ye ſtep in, and give the Lady notice
Who comes to honour her?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Bid her be ſuddain,
We come to ſee no curious wench: a night-gowne
Will ſerve the turne: here's one that knowes her neerer.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I'le tell her what ye ſay Sir. Ex. Fred.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: My deare brother,
Ye are a merry Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Now will the ſport be
To obſerve her alterations; how like wildfire
She'll leap into your boſome; then ſeeing me,
Her conſcience, and her feares creeping upon her
Dead as a fowle at ſouſe, ſhe'll ſinke.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Faire brother,
I muſt entreat you—

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I conceive your mind Sir,
I will not chide her: yet ten duckets Duke,
She falls upon he knees, ten more ſhe dare not—

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: I muſt not have her frighted.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Well you ſhall not: Enter Fred. and Peter.
But like a ſummers evening againſt heate,
Marke how I'le guild he cheekes?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: How now.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ye may Sir:
Not to abuſe your patience, noble friends,
Nor hold ye off with tedious circumſtance,
For you muſt know,—

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Where is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Gone Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: What did you ſay Sir?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Gone, by heaven removed,
The woman of the houſe too.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Well Don Fredrick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Don Iohn, it is not well, but—

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Gone?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: This fellow
Can teſtifie I lye not.

sp.speaker: Peter
sp.l: Some foure houres after
My Maſter was departed with this Gentleman,
My fellow and my ſelfe, being ſent of buſineſſe,
(As we muſt thinke) of purpoſe—

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Hang theſe circumſtances,
They appeare like owles, to ill ends.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Now could I eate
The devil in his own broath, I am ſo tortur'd.
Gone?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Gone?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Directly gone, fled, ſhifted: what would you have me ſay?

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Well Gentlemen,
Wrong not my good opinion.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: For your Dukedome
I will not be a knave Sir.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: He that is
A rot run in his bloud.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: But harke ye Gentlemen,
Are ye ſure ye had her here, did ye not dreame this.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Have you your noſe Sir?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Then we had her.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Since you are ſo ſhort, beleeve your having her
Shall ſuffer more conſtruction.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Let it ſuffer,
But if I be not cleere of all diſhonour,
Or practice that may taint my reputation,
And ignorant of where this woman is,
Make me your Cities monſter.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: I beleeve ye.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: I could lye with a witch now, to be reveng'd
Upon that Raſcall did this.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Only thus much
I would deſire your Grace, for my minde gives me
Before night yet ſhe is yours: ſtop all opinion,
And let no anger out, till full cauſe call it,
Then every mans owne work's to juſtifie him,
And this day let us give to ſearch: my man here
Tels me, by chance he ſaw out of a window
(Which place he has taken note of) ſuch a face
As our old Landladies, he beleeves the ſame too,
And by her hood aſſures it: Let's firſt thether,
For ſhe being found, all's ended.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Come, for heavens ſake,
And Fortune, and thou beeſt not ever turning,
If there be one firme ſtep in all thy reelings,
Now ſettle it, and ſave my hopes: away friends. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: With all my jewels?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: All Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And that money
I left i'th' trunke?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The Trunke broke, and that gone too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Franſciſco of the plot?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Gone with the wench too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The mighty poxe go with 'em: belike they thought
I was no man of this world, and thoſe trifles
Would but diſturbe my conſcience.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Sure they thought Sir,
You would not live to perſecute 'em.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Whore and Fidler,
Why, what a conſort have they made? Hen and bacon?
Well my ſweet Miſtris, well good Madam martaile?
You that have hung about my neck, and lick't me,
I'le try how handſomely your Ladyſhip
Can hang upon a Gallowes, there's your Maſter-piece;
But harke ye Sirrah, no imagition Bawd ready above.
Of where they ſhould be?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: None Sir, yet we have ſearch'd
All places we ſuſpected; I beleeve Sir,
They have taken towards the Ports.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Get me a conjurer,
One that can raiſe a water devill, I'le port 'em;
Play at duck and drake with my money? take heed Fidler;
I'le dance ye by this hand, your Fidle-ſticke
I'le greaſe of a new faſhion, for preſuming
To medle with my degamboys: get me a Conjurer,
Enquire me out a man that lets out devils:
None but my C. Cliffe ſerve your turne?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I know not—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: In every ſtreet, Tom foole, any bleare-eyd people
With red heads, and flat noſes can performe it;
Thou ſhalt know 'em by their half gowns & no breeches:
Mount my mare Fidler? ha boy? up at firſt daſh?
Sit ſure, I'le clap a nettle, and a ſmart one,
Shall make your filly firck: I will find Fidier,
I'le put you to your plundge boy: Sirrah meet me
Some two houres hence at home; In the meane time
Find out a conjurer and know his price,
How he will let his devils by the day out,
I'le have 'em, and they be above ground. Exit Ant.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Now bleſſe me,
What a mad man is this? I muſt do ſomething
To pleaſe his humour: ſuch a man I'le aske for,
And tell him where he is: but to come neare him,
Or have any thing to do with his don devills,
I thanke my feare, I dare not, nor I will not. Exit.

div.head: Scaene 3.
div.stage: Enter Duke, Petruchio, Fredrick, John, Peter, Servant with bottles.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Whether wilt thou lead us?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: 'Tis hard by ſir.
And ten to one this wine goes thether.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Forward.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Are they growne ſo merry.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: 'Tis moſt likely
She has heard of this good fortune, and determines
To waſh her ſorrowes off.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo; that houſe ſir
Is it: out of that window certainly
I ſaw my old Miſtriſſes face.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: They are merry indeed, Muſicke.
Harke I here Muſicke too.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Excellent Muſick.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Would I were ev'n among 'em and alone how,
A pallat for the purpoſe in a corner,
And good rich wine within me; what gay ſport
Could I make in an houre now? Song.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Harke a voice too;
Let's not ſtir yet by any meanes.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Was this her owne voyce?

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Yes ſure.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis a rare one. Enter Bawd (above)

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: The Song confirmes her here too: for if ye marke it,
It ſpake of liberty, and free enjoying
The happy end of pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Looke ye there ſir,
Do ye know that head?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis my good Landlady,
I find feare has done all this.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Shee I ſweare,
And now do I know by the hanging of her hood,
She is parcell drunke: ſhall we go in?

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Not yet Sir.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: No, let 'em take their pleaſure,

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: When it is higheſt, Muſicke.
Wee'll ſtep in, and amaze 'em: peace more Muſicke.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: This Muſick murders me; what bloud have I now?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I ſhould know that face. Enter Fran. and Exit.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: By this light 'tis he Fredricks,
That bred our firſt ſuſpitions, the ſame fellow.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: He that we overtooke, and overheard too
Diſcourſing of Conſtantia.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Still the ſame;
Now he ſlips in.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: She muſt be here Sir:
This is the very fellow, I told your Grace Enter Fran.
We found upon the way; and what his talke was.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Why, ſure I know this fellow; yes, 'tis he,
Franciſco, Antonio's Boy, a rare Muſitian,
He taught my Siſter on the Lute, and is ever
(She loves his voice ſo well) about her: certaine,
Without all doubt ſhe is here: it muſt be ſo.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Here? that's no queſtion: what ſhould our hen o'th game elſe
Do here without her? if ſhe be not here
(I am ſo confident) let your Grace beleeve,
We two are arrant Raſcalls, and have abus'd ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I ſay ſo too.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Why there's the hood againe now,
The guard that guides us; I know the fabricke of it.
And know the old tree of that ſaddle yet, 'twas made of
A hunting hood, obſerve it.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Who ſhall enter?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: I'le make one.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: I, another.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: But ſo carry it,
That all her joyes flow not together.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: If we told her,
Your Grace would none of her?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: By no meanes Signior,
'Twould turne her wild, ſtarke frantick.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Or aſſur'd her—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Nothing of that? ſtarve nature? this ye may ſir.
That the conditions of our feare yet ſtand
On nyce and dangerous knittings: or that a little
I ſeeme to doubt the child.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Would I could draw her
To hate your Grace with theſe things.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Come let's enter, Exit. Pet. and Ioh. Muſick.
And now he ſees me not, I'le ſearch her ſoundly.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Now lucke of all ſides.

sp.speaker: Fred
sp.l: Doubt it not: more Muſicke:
Sure ſhe has heard ſome comfort.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Yes, ſtand ſtill ſir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: This is the maddeſt ſong.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Applyed for certaine Claping of a doore.
To ſome ſtrange mellancholly ſhe is loden with.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Now all the ſport begins—harke?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: They are amongſt'em,
The feares now, and the ſhakings? Trampling above.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Our old Lady
(Harke how they run) is euen now at this inſtant Ceaſe Muſick Petr. and Iohn within.
Ready to looſe her head peice by Don Iohn,
Or creeping through a Cat hole.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Bring 'em downe,
And you ſir, follow me.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Hee's angry with 'em,
I muſt not ſuffer this.
Bowle downe the Bawd there Iohn within.
Old Erra mater: you Lady leachery
For the good will I beare to'th game, moſt tenderly
Shall be lead out, and laſh'd.

div.stage: Enter Petruchio, Iohn, Whore, and Bawd, with Franciſco.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Is this Conſtantia?
Why Gentlemen? what do you meane? is this ſhe?

sp.speaker: Whore
sp.l: I am Conſtantia ſir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: A Whore ye are ſir.

sp.speaker: Whore
sp.l: 'Tis very true: I am a Whore indeed ſir.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: She will not lye yet, though ſhe ſteale.

sp.speaker: Whore
sp.l: A plaine whore,
If you pleaſe to imploy me.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: And an impudent—

sp.speaker: Whore
sp.l: Plaine dealing now is impudence.
One if you will ſir, can ſhew ye as much ſport
In one halfe houre, and with as much variety,
As a far wiſer woman can in halfe a yeare:
For there my way lies.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Is ſhe not drunk too?

sp.speaker: Whore
sp.l: A little guilded o're ſir,
Old ſack, old ſacke boyes.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: This is ſaliant.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: A brave bold queane.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Is this your certainty?
Do ye know the man ye wrong thus, Gentlemen?
Is this the woman meant?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: That your Landlady?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: I know not what to ſay.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Am I a perſon
To be your ſport Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: I do beleeve now certaine
I am a knave; but how, or when—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What are you?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Bawd to this peece of pye meat.

sp.speaker: Bawd
sp.l: A poore Gentlewoman
That lyes in Towne, about Law buſineſſe,
And't like your worſhips.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: You ſhall have Law, beleeve it.

sp.speaker: Bawd
sp.l: I'le ſhew your maſterſhip my caſe.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: By no meanes,
I had rather ſee a Cuſtard.

sp.speaker: Bawd
sp.l: My dead husband
Left it even thus ſir.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Bleſſe mine eyes from blaſting,
I was never ſo frighted with a caſe.

sp.speaker: Bawd
sp.l: And ſo ſir—

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Enough, put up good velvet head.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What are you two now,
By your owne free confeſſions?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What you ſhall thinke us,
Though to my ſelfe I am certaine, and my life
Shall make that good and perfect, or fall with it.

sp.speaker: Io.
sp.l: We are ſure of nothing (Fred) that's the truth on't:
I do not think my nam's Don John, nor dare not
Beleeve any thing that concernes me, but my debts,
Nor thoſe in way of payment: things are ſo carried,
What to entreat your Grace, or how to tell ye
We are, or we are not, is paſt my cunning,
But I would faine imagine we are honoſt,
And o' my conſcience, I ſhould fight in't—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Thus then,
For we may be all abus'd.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: 'Tis poſſible,
For how ſhould this concerne them?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Here let's part—
Untill to morrow this time: we to our way,
To make this doubt out, and you to your way;
Pawning our honours then to meet againe,
When if ſhe be not found.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: We ſtand engaged
To anſwer any worthy way we are cald to.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: We aske no more.

sp.speaker: Whore
sp.l: Ye have done with us then?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: No Dame.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: But is her name Conſtantia?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Yes a moveable
Belonging to a friend of mine: come out Fidler,
What ſay you to this Lady; be not fearfull?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Saving the reverence of my Maſters pleaſure,
I ſay ſhe is a whore, and that ſhe has robb'd him,
Hoping his hurts would kill him.

sp.speaker: Whore.
sp.l: Who provok't me?
Nay ſirrah ſqueak, Ile ſee your treble ſtrings
Ty'd up too; if I hang, Ile ſpoyle your piping,
Your ſweet face ſhall not ſave yee.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Thou dam'd impudence,
And thou dry'd devill; where's the Officer?

sp.speaker: Peter
sp.l: Hee's here ſir. Enter Officer.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Lodge theſe ſafe till I ſend for 'em;
Let none come to 'em, nor no noiſe be heard
Of where they are, or why: away.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: By this hand
A handſome whore: Now will I be arreſted,
And brought home to this officers: a ſtout whore,
I love ſuch ſtirring ware: pox o' this buſineſſe,
A man muſt haunt out morſells for another,
And ſtarve himſelf: a quick-ey'd whore, that's wild-fire,
And makes the bloud dance through the veines like billowes.
I will reprive this whore.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Well, good luck with ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: As much attend your Grace.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: To morrow certaine—

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: If we out-live this night ſir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Come Don John,
We have ſomething now to doe.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.l: I am ſure I would have.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: If ſhe be not found, we muſt fight.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: I am glad on't,
I have not fought a great while.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: If we dye—

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.p: Ther's ſo much money ſav'd in lecherie. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena prima.
div.stage: Enter Duke, Petruchio below, and Vechio above.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: IT ſhould be here abouts.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Your grace is right,
This is the houſe I know it.

sp.speaker: Voch.
sp.l: Grace?

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: 'Tis further
By the deſcription we received.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Good my Lord the Duke,
Believe me, for I know it certainly,
This is the very houſe.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: My Lord the Duke?

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Pray heaven this man Prove right now.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Beleeve it, hee's a moſt ſufficient Scholler,
And can doe rare tricks this way; for a figure,
Or raiſing an appearance, whole Chriſtendome
Has not a better; I have heard ſtrange wonders of him.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: But can he ſhew us where ſhe is?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Moſt certaine,
And for what cauſe too ſhe departed.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Knock then,
For I am great with expectation,
Till this man ſatisfie me: I feare the Spaniards,
Yet they appeare brave fellowes: can he tell us?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: With a wet finger, whether they be falſe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Away then.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Who's within here? Enter Vechio.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Your Grace may enter.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: How can he know me?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: He knowes all.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: And you ſir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: What do you call his name?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Why, Peter Vechio.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: They ſay he can raiſe devills,
Can he make 'em
Tell truth too, when he has raiſ'd 'em? for beleeve it,
Theſe devils are the lyingſt Raſcalls.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: He can compell 'em.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: With what? can he
Tye ſquibs in their tailes, and fire the truth out?
Or make 'em eate a bawling Puritan,
Whoſe ſanctified zeale ſhall rumble like an Earthquake?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: With Spels man?

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: I with ſpoones as ſoone, doſt thou thinke
The devill ſuch an Aſſe as people make him?
Such a poore coxcomb? ſuch a penny foot poſt?
Compel'd with croſſe and pile to run of errands?
With Aſteroth, and Behemoth, and Belfagor?
Why ſhould he ſhake at ſounds, that lives in a ſmiths forg?
Or if he do—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Without all doubt he do's Iohn.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Why ſhould not Bilbo raiſe him, or a paire of bullyons,
They go as big as any? or an unſhod Car,
When he goes tumble, tumble o're the ſtones,
Like Anacreons drunken verſes, make us tremble?
Theſe make as fell a noyſe; me thinkes the collick
Well handled, and fed with ſmall beere—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis the vertue—

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: The vertue? nay, and goodneſſe fetch him up once,
Has loſt a friend of me; the wiſe old Gentleman
Knowes when, and how; I'le lay this hand to two pence,
Let all tho Conjurers in Chriſtendome,
With all their ſpells, and vertues call upon him,
And I but thinke upon a wench, and follow it,
He ſhall be ſooner mine then theirs; where's vertue?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Thou art the moſt ſufficient, (I'le ſay for thee)
Not to beleeve a thing —

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: O ſir, ſlow credit
Is the beſt child of knowledge; I'le go with ye,
And if he can do any thing, I'le thinke
As you would have me.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Let's enquire a long,
For certaine we are not far off.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Nor much nearer. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaene 3.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: You loſt her yeſternight.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: How thinke you ſir?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Is your name Vechio?

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Yes ſir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: And you can ſhew me
Theſe; things you promiſe.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Your graces word bound to me,
No hand of Law ſhall ſeize me.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: As I live ſir—

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: And as I live, that can do ſomething too ſir.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: I take your promiſes: ſtay here a little,
Till I prepare ſome Ceremonies, and I'le ſatisfie ye.
The Ladies name's Conſtantia?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Yes

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: I come ſtraight. Exit Vech.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Sure hee's a learned man.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: The moſt now living;
Did your grace marke when we told all theſe circumſtances,
How ever and anon he bolted from us
To uſe his ſtudies helpe?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Now I thinke rather
To talke with ſome familiar.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Not unlikely,
For ſure he has 'em ſubject.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: How could he elſe
Tell when ſhe went, and who went with her?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: True.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Or hit upon mine honour: or aſſure me
The Lady lov'd me dearely?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: 'Twas ſo.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Now,
I do beſeech your Grace ſit downe, and you ſir;
Nay pray ſit cloſe like brothers.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: A rare fellow.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: And what ye ſee, ſtir not at, nor uſe a word,
Untill I aske ye; for what ſhall appeare
Is but weake apparition and thin ayre
Not to be held, nor ſpoken too. Knocking within.

div.stage: John, Frederick, and a Servant within.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: We are counſelled—

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: What noiſe is that without there?

sp.speaker: Fred. Within.
sp.l: We muſt ſpeake with him.

sp.speaker: Ser. Within.
sp.l: Hee's buſie Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Iohn. Within.
sp.l: That's all one friend,
We muſt, and will ſpeake with him.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Let 'em in ſir,
We know their tongues and buſineſſe, 'tis our owne,
And in this very cauſe that we now come for,
They alſo come to be inſtructed.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Let 'em in then:
Sit down, I know your meaning.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: The Duke before us,
Now we ſhall ſure know ſomething.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Not a queſtion,
But make your eyes, your tongues—

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: This is a ſtrange jugler,
Neither indent before hand for his payment,
Nor know the breadth of the buſineſſe; ſure his devell
Comes out of Lapland were they ſell men winds,
For dead drinke, and old doublets.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Peace, he conjures.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Let him, he cannot raiſe my devill.

sp.speaker: Fred,
sp.l: Prethee peace.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Appeare, appeare,
And you ſoft winds ſo cleare,
That dance upon the leaves, and make them ſing
Gentle love-layes to the Spring,
Gilding all the vales below
With your verdure as ye blow,
Raiſe theſe formes from under ground
With a ſoft and happy ſound. Soft Muſick.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.l: This is an honeſt Conjurer, and a pretty Poet;
I like his words well, there's no bumbaſt in 'em,
But do you thinke now, he can cudgell up the devill,
With this ſhort ſtaffe of Verſes?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Peace the ſpirits— 2. Shapes of women paſſe by.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Nay, and they be no worſe—

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Do ye know theſe faces?

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Sit ſtill upon your lives then: and marke what follows:
Away, away.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Theſe devils do not paint ſure?
Have they no ſweeter ſhapes in hell? Conſtantia paſſes by.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Harke now Iohn.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: I marry, this moves ſomething like, this devill
Carries ſome metall in her gate.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: I find ye,
You would ſee her face unvail'd?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Be uncovered.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: O heaven!

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Peace.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: See how ſhe bluſhes.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: This devill for my money; this is ſhe Boy,
Why thou ſhake? I burne.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Sit ſtill, and ſilent.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: She lookes back at me; now ſhe ſmiles ſir.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Silence.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I muſt riſe, or burſt. Exit. Conſt.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Ye ſee what followes—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: O gentle ſir this ſhape agen.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: I cannot,
'Tis all diſolv'd againe: this was the figure.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: The very ſame ſir.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: No hope once more to ſee it?

sp.speaker: Ve.
sp.l: You might have kept it longer, had ye ſpar'd it,
Now 'tis impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: No meanes to find it?

sp.speaker: Ve.
sp.l: Yes that there is: ſit ſtill a while, there's wine
To thaw the wonder from your hearts: drinke well ſir.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: This Conjurer is a right good fellow too,
A lad of mettle; two ſuch devils more
Would make me a Conjurer: what wine is it?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Hollock.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.l: The devil's in it then, looke how it dances?
Well, if I be—

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: We are all before ye,
That's your beſt comfort ſir.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Byth' mas brave wine;
Nay, and the Devils live in this hell, I dare venture
Within theſe two months yet to be delivered
Of a large legion of 'em. Enter Vechio.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Here 'a comes,
Silence of all ſides Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Good your grace,
Obſerve a ſtricter temper, and you too gallants,
You'l be deluded all elſe. This merry devill
That next appeares, for ſuch a one you'l find it,
Muſt be cal'd up by a ſtrange incantation,
A Song, and I muſt ſing it: pray beare with me,
And pardon my rude pipe; for yet ere parting
Twenty to one I pleaſe ye.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: We are arm'd Sir.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Nor ſhall you ſee us more tranſgreſſe.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What think'ſt thou
Now Iohn?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Why, now do I thinke Fredrick,
(And it I thinke amiſſe heaven pardon me,)
This honeſt Conjurer, with ſome foure or five
Of his good fellow devils, and my ſelfe,
Shall be yet drunke ere midnight. Song.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Peace, he conjures.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Why, this is the Song Fredrick: twenty pound now
To ſee but our Don Gillian.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Peace it appeares.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: I cannot peace: devils in French hoods Fredrick?
Sathans old Siringes?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What's this?

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Peace.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: She, Boy.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What doſt thou meane?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: She, Boy, I ſay.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: She, boy.
The very child too Fredrick;

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: She laughes on us
Aloud Iohn, has the devill theſe affections?
I do beleeve 'tis ſhe indeed.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Stand ſtill.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.l: I will not;
Who calls Jeronimo from his naked bed?
Sweet Lady, was it you? If thou beeſt the devill,
Firſt, having croſt my ſelfe, to keep out wildfire,
Then ſaid ſome ſpeciall prayers to defend me
Againſt thy moſt unhallowed hood: have at thee.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Hold ſir, I am no devill.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: That's all one.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: I am your very Landlady.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: I defie thee:
Thus as St. Dunſtan blew the devils noſe
With a paire of tongs, even ſo right worſhipfull—

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Sweet ſon, I am old Gillion.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: This is no ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Art thou old Gillian, fleſh and bone?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: I am Son.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.p: Sit ſtill ſir, now I'le ſhew you all. Ex. Vech.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Where's thy bottle?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Here, I beſeech ye ſon—

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: For I know the devill
Cannot aſſume that ſhape.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Tis ſhe Iohn, certaine—

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: A hogs poxe o'your mouldy chaps, what make you
Tumbling and juggling here?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: I am quit now Signior,
For all the prankes you plaid, and railings at me,
For to tell true, out of a trick I put
Upon your high behaviours, which was a lye,
But then it ſerv'd my turne, I drew the Lady
Unto my kinſmans here, only to torture
Your Don-ſhips for a day or two; and ſecure her
Out of all thoughts of danger: here ſhe comes now.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: May I yet ſpeake?

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Yes, and embrace her too,
For one that loves you deerer—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: O my ſweeteſt.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Bluſh not, I will not chide ye.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: To add more
Unto the joy I know, I bring ye, ſee ſir,
The happy fruit of all our vowes.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Heavens bleſſing
Be round about thee ever.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Pray bleſſe me to,
For if your grace be well inſtructed this way,
You'l find the keeping halfe the getting.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: How ſir?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: I'le tell ye that anon.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: 'Tis true this Gentleman
'Has done a charity worthy your favour,
And let him have it deare ſir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: My beſt Lady
She has, and ever ſhall have: ſo muſt you ſir,
To whom I am equall bound, as to my being.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Your Graces humble ſervants—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Why kneele you ſir?

sp.speaker: Ve.
sp.l: For pardon for my boldneſſe: yet 'twas harmleſſe
And all the art I have ſir; thoſe your grace ſaw
Which you thought ſpirits, were my neighbours children
Whom I inſtruct in Grammer, here, and Muſick;
Their ſhapes, the peoples fond opinions,
Beleeving I can conjure, and oft repairing
To know of things ſtolne from 'em, I keepe about me,
And alwaies have in readineſſe; by conjecture
Out of their owne confeſſions, I oft tell 'em
Things, that by chance have fallen out ſo: which way
(Having the perſons here, I knew you ſought for)
I wrought upon your grace: my end is mirth,
And pleaſing, if I can, all parties.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I beleeve it,
For you have pleas'd me truly: ſo well pleas'd me,
That when I ſhall forget it—

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Here's old Antonio,
I ſpide him at a window, comming mainely
I know about his whore, the man you light on,
As yon diſcovered unto me: good your Grace,
Let's ſtand by all, 'twill be a mirth above all,
To obſerve his pelting fury.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: About a wench ſir?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: A young whore that has rob'd him,

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: But do you know ſir,
Where ſhe is?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Yes, and will make that perfect—

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: I am inſtructed well then.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: If he come
To have a devill ſhew'd him, by all meanes
Let me be he, I can rore rarely.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Be ſo,
But take heed to his anger.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Slip in quickly,
There you ſhall find ſuites of all ſorts: when I call,
Be ready and come forward. Ex. all but Vech.
Who's there come in?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Are you the Conjurer?

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Sir I can do a little
That way, if you pleaſe to imploy me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Preſently ſhew me a devill that can tell—

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Where your wench is.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You are i'th'right; as alſo where the Fidler
That was conſenting to her.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Sit ye there ſir,
Ye ſhall know preſently: can ye pray heartily?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Why, is your devill ſo furious?

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: I muſt ſhew ye
A forme, may chance affright ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: He muſt fart fire then:
Take you no care for me.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Aſcend Aſterth, Enter Don John like a Spirit.
Why, when, appeare I ſay—Now queſtion him.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Where is my whore Don devill?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Gone to China,
To be the great Chams Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: That's a lye devill:
Where are my jewels?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Pawn'd for Peticoates.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: That may be; where's the Fidler?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: Condemn'd to th' Gallowes,
For robbing of a Mill.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The lyingſt devill
That e're I dealt withall, and the unlikelieſt:
What was that Raſcall hurt me?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: I.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: I.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Who was he?

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: I.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Do ye here conjurer,
Dare you venture your devill?

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Then I'le venture my dagger;
Have at your devils pate; do ye mew? Enter all.

sp.speaker: Vech.
sp.l: Hold.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Hold there,
I do command ye hold.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Is this the devill?
Why Conjurer—

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: 'Has been a devill to you ſir.
But now you ſhall forget all: your whores ſafe,
And all your Jewels: your Boy too.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Now the devill indeed
Lay his ten claws upon thee, for my pate
Finds what it is to be a fend.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: All ſafe?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Pray ye know this perſon: all's right now.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Your grace
May now command me then: but where's my whore?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Ready to goe to whiping.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: My whore whipt?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Yes, your whore without doubt Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Whipt? pray Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Why, would you have her once more rob ye? the young boy
You may forgive, he was intic'd.

sp.speaker: Iohn
sp.l: The Whore ſir,
Would rather carry pitty: a hanſome Whore.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: A Gentleman I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Let's in all.
And if we ſee contrition in your whore ſir,
Much may be done.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Now my deare faire, to you,
And the full conſummation of my Vow.

div.head: Prologue.
div.l: APtneſſe for mirth to all, this inſtant night
Thalia hath prepar'd for your delight,
Her choice and curious Viands, in each part,
Seaſon'd with rarities of wit, as Art;
Nor feare I to be tax'd for a vaine boaſt,
My promiſe will finde credit with the moſt,
When they know Ingenuous Fletcher made it, hee
Being in himſelfe a perfect Comedie.
And ſome ſit here, I doubt not dare a verre,
Living he made that houſe a Theater
Which he pleas'd to frequent; and thus much we
Could not but pay to his loud memorie.
For our ſelves we doe entreat that you would not
Expect ſtrange turnes, and windings in the Plot,
Objects of State, and now and then a Rhime,
To gall particular perſons, with the time;
Or that his to wring Muſe hath made her flight
Nearer your apprehenſion then your ſight:
But if that ſweet expreſsions, quick conceit,
Familiar language, faſhion'd to the weight
Of ſuch as ſpeake it, have the power to raiſe
Your grace to us, with Trophies to his praiſe:
We may profeſſe, preſuming on his skill,
If his Chances pleaſe not you, our fortune's ill.

div.head: Epilogue.
div.l: VVE have not held you long, nor doe I ſee
One brow in this ſelected company
Aſſuring a diſlike, our paines were eas'd.
Could we be confident that all riſe pleas'd:
But ſuch ambition ſoares too high: If wee
Have ſatisfi'd the beſt, and they agree
In a faire cenſure, We have our reward;
And in them arm'd, deſire no ſurer guard.

sp.speaker: Theodor.
sp.l: CAptaine, your friend's prefer'd, the Princeſſe has her,
Who, I aſſure my ſelfe, will uſe her nobly;
A prettie ſweet one 'tis indeed.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Well bred Sir,
I doe deliver that upon my credit,
And of an honeſt ſtock.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: It ſeemes ſo Captaine,
And no doubt will doe well.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Thanks to your care ſir;
But tell me Noble Colonell, why this habit
Of diſcontent is put on through the Army?
And why your valiant father, our great Generall,
The hand that taught to ſtrike, the Love that lead all;
Why he, that was the father of the warte,
He that begot, and bred the Souldier,
Why he ſits ſhaking of his Armes, like Autumne,
His Collours folded, and his Drums cas'd up,
The tongue of war for ever ty'd within us?

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: It muſt be ſo: Captaine you are a ſtranger,
But of a ſmall time here a ſouldier,
Yet that time ſhewes ye a right good, and great one,
Elſe I could tell yee houres are ſtrangely alterd:
The young Duke has too many eyes upon him,
Too many feares 'tis thought too, and to nouriſh thoſe,
Maintains too many Inſtruments.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Turne their hearts,
Or turn their heeles up, heaven: 'Tis ſtrange it ſhould be.
The old Duke lov'd him dearely.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: He deſerv'd it;
And were he not my Father, I durſt tell yee,
The memorable hazzards he has run through
Deſerv'd of this man too; highly deſerv'd too;
Had they been leſſe, they had been ſafe Putskie,
And ſooner reach'd regard.

sp.speaker: Put
sp.l: There you ſtrook ſure ſir.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Did I never tell thee of a vow he made
Some yeares before the old Duke dyed?

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: I have heard yee
Speake often of that vow; but how it was,
Or to what end, I never underſtood yet?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Ile tell thee then: and then thou wilt finde the reaſon:
The laſt great Muſter, ('twas before ye ſerv'd here,
Before the laſt Dukes death, whoſe honour'd bones
Now reſt in peace) this yong Prince had the ordering,
(To Crowne his fathers hopes) of all the Army:
Who (to be ſhort) put all his power to practiſe;
Faſhion'd, and drew 'em up: but alas, ſo poorely
So raggedly and looſely, ſo unſouldier'd,
The good Duke bluſh'd, and call'd unto my father,
Who then was Generall: Goe Archus ſpeedily,
And chide the Boy, before the ſouldier finde him,
Stand thou between his ignorance and them,
Faſhion their bodies new to thy direction;
Then draw thou up, and ſhew the Prince his errours.
My Sire obey'd, and did ſo; with all duty
Inform'd the Prince, and read him all directions:
This bred diſtaſte, diſtaſte grew up to anger,
And anger into wilde words broke out thus:
Well Archus, if I live but to command here,
To be but Duke once, I ſhall then remember,
I ſhall remember truely, truſt me, I ſhall,
And by my Fathers hand; the reſt his eyes ſpoke.
To which my Father anſwer'd (ſomewhat mov'd too)
And with a vow he ſeal'd it: Royall ſir,
Since for my faith and fights, your Icorne and anger
Onely purſue me; if I live to that day,
That day ſo long expected to reward me,
By his ſo ever noble hand you ſwore by,
And by the hand of Juſtice, never Armes more
Shall rib this body in, nor ſword hang here, ſir:
The Conflicts I will doe you ſervice then in,
Shall be repentant prayers. So they parted.
The time is come; and now you know the wonder.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: I finde a feare too, which begins to tell me,
The Duke will have but poore and ſlight defences
If his hot humour raigne, and not his honour:
How ſtand you with him, Sir?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: A perdue Captaine,
Full of my fathers danger.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: He has rais'd a young man,
They ſay a ſlight young man, I know him not,
For what deſert?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Beleeve it, a brave Gentleman,
Worth the Dukes reſpect, a cleere ſweet Gentleman,
And of a noble ſoule: Come, let's retire us,
And wait upon my father, who within this houre
You will finde an alter'd man.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: I am ſorry for't ſir. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaene 2.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: Is't not a handſome wench?

sp.speaker: 2. Wom.
sp.l: She is well enough, Madam:
I have ſeen a better face, and a ſtraiter body,
And yet ſhe is a pretty Gentle-woman.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: What thinkſt thou Peteſca?

sp.speaker: Petes.
sp.l: Alas, Madam, I have no skill, ſhe has a black eye,
Which is of the leaſt too, and the dulleſt water;
And when her mouth was made, for certaine Madam,
Nature intended her a right good ſtomach.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: She has a good hand.

sp.speaker: 2 Wom.
sp.l: 'Tis good enough to hold faſt.
And ſtrong enough to ſtrangle the neck of a Lute.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: What thinke ye of her colour?

sp.speaker: Peteſ.
sp.l: If it be her owne
'Tis good black bloud: right weather-proofe
I warrant it.

sp.speaker: 2 Wom.
sp.l: What a ſtrange pace ſhe has got?

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: That's but her breeding.

sp.speaker: Peteſ.
sp.l: And what a manly body? me thinks ſhe looks
As though ſhe would pitch the Barre, or goe to Buffets.

sp.speaker: 2 Wom.
sp.l: Yet her behaviour's utterly againſt it,
For me thinks ſhe is too baſhfull.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: Is that hurtfull?

sp.speaker: 2 Wo.
sp.l: Even equall to too bold: either of 'em Madam
May doe her injurie when time ſhall ſerve her.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: You diſcourſe learnedly, cal in the wench. Ex. Gent.
What envious fooles are you? Is the rule generall,
That women can ſpeak handſomely of none,
But thoſe they are bred withall?

sp.speaker: Peteſ.
sp.l: Scarce well of thoſe Madam,
If they believe they may out-ſhine 'em any way:
Our natures are like oyle, compound us with any thing,
Yet ſtil we ſtrive to ſwim o'th' top:
Suppoſe there were here now,
Now in this court of Moſco, a ſtranger Princeſſe,
Of bloud and beauty equall to your excellence,
As many eyes and ſervices ſtuck on her;
What would you think?

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: I would thinke ſhe might deſerve it.

sp.speaker: Peteſ.
sp.l: Your grace ſhall give me leave not to believe ye;
I know you are a woman, and ſo humourd:
Ile tell yee Madam, I could then get more gownes on ye,
More caps & feathers, more ſcarfs, & more ſilk ſtockings,
With rocking you a ſleep with nightly railings
Upon that woman, then if I had nine lives
I could weare out: by this hand ye'would ſcratch her eyes out.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: Thou art deceiv'd foole; Enter Gentlewom. and Alinda.
Now let your own eyes mock ye.
Come hither girle: hang me & ſhe be not a handſom one.

sp.speaker: Peteſ.
sp.l: I feare it will prove indeed ſo.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: Did you ever ſerve yet
In any place of worth?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: No Royall Lady.

sp.speaker: Peteſ.
sp.l: Hold up your head; ſie.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: Let her alone, ſtand from her.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: It ſhall be now,
Of all the bleſſings my poore youth has pray'd for,
The greateſt and the happieſt to ſerve you;
And might my promiſe carrie but that credit
To be believ'd, becauſe I am yet a ſtranger,
Excellent Lady, when I fall form dutie,
From all the ſervice that my life can lend me,
May ever-laſting miſerie then finde me.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: What think ye now? I doe believe, and thank ye;
And ſure I ſhall not be ſo farre forgetfull,
To ſee that honeſt faith die unrewarded:
What muſt I call your name?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Alinda Madam.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: Can yee ſing?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: A little, when my griefe will give me leave, Lady.

sp.speaker: Olm.
sp.l: VVhat griefe canſt thou have wench?
Thou art not in love?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: If I be Madam, 'tis onely with your goodneſſe;
For yet I never ſaw that man I ſighed for.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: Of what yeares are you?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: My mother oft has told me,
That very day and houre this land was bleſt
With your moſt happy birth, I firſt ſaluted
This worlds faire light: Nature was then ſo buſie,
And all the Graces to adorne your goodneſſe,
I ſtole into the world poore and neglected.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: Something there was, when I firſt look'd upon thee,
Made me both like and love thee: now I know it;
And you ſhall find that knowledge ſhall not hurt you:
I hope ye are a Maid?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: I hope ſo too, Madam;
I am ſure for any man: and were I otherwiſe,
Of all the ſervices my hopes could point at,
I durſt not touch at yours.

div.stage: Flouriſh. Enter Duke, Burris, and Gent.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: The great Duke, Madam.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Good morow, ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: A good day to your highneſſe.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: I am come to pray you uſe no more perſwaſions
For this old ſtubborne man: nay to command ye:
His ſaile is ſwell'd too full: he is grown too inſolent,
Too ſelf-affected, proud: thoſe poore ſlight ſervices
He has done my father, and my ſelf, has blowne him
To ſuch a pitch, he flyes to ſtoop our favours.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: I am ſorry ſir: I ever thonght thoſe ſervices
Both great and noble.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: However, may it pleaſe yee
But to conſider 'em a true hearts ſervants,
Done out of faith to you, and not ſelfe-fame:
But to conſider royall ſir, the dangers;
When you have ſlept ſecure, the mid-night tempeſts,
That as he marcht ſung through his aged locks;
When you have ſed at full, the wants and famines;
The fires of heaven, when you have found all temperate,
Death with his thouſand doores—

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: I have conſider'd;
No more: and that I will have, ſhall be.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: For the beſt,
I hope all ſtill.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: What handſome wench is that there?

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: My ſervant, ſir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Prethee obſerve her Burris.
Is ſhe not wondrous handſome? ſpeak thy freedome.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Shee appeares no leſſe to me ſir.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Of whence is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Her father I am told is a good gentleman,
But farre off dwelling: her deſire to ſerve me
Brought her to th' Court, & here her friends have left her.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: She may find better friends:
Ye are welcome faire one,
I have not ſeen a ſweeter: By your Ladies leave:
Nay ſtand up ſweet, we'll have no ſuperſtition:
You have got a ſervant; you may uſe him kindly,
And he may honour ye: Exit Duke and Burris.
Good morrow ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Good morrow to your Grace. How the wench bluſhes?
How like an Angel now ſhe looks?

sp.speaker: 1 VVom.
sp.l: At firſt jumpe
Jumpe into the Dukes armes? we muſt look to you,
Indeed we muſt, the next jump we are journeymen.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I ſee the ruine of our hopes already,
Would ſhe were at home again, milking her fathers cows

sp.speaker: 1 Wo.
sp.l: I feare ſhee'll milke all the great Courtiers firſt.

sp.speaker: Olim.
sp.l: This has not made yee proud?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: No certaine, Madam.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: It was the Duke that kiſt yee.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: 'Twas your brother,
And therefore nothing can be meant but honour.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: But ſay he love ye?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: That he may with ſafety:
A Princes love extends to all his ſubjects.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: But ſay in more particular?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Pray feare not:
For vertues ſake deliver me from doubts, Lady:
'Tis the name of King, nor all his promiſes,
His glories, and his greatnſſe ſtuck about me,
Can make me prove a Traitor to your ſervice:
You are my Miſtris, and my noble Maſter,
Your vertues my ambition, and your favour
The end of all my love, and all my fortune:
And when I faile in that faith—

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: I beleeve thee,
Come wipe your eyes; I doe: take you example—

sp.speaker: Petſ.
sp.l: I would her eyes were out.

sp.speaker: 1 Wom.
sp.l: If the winde ſtand in this doore,
We ſhall have but cold cuſtome: ſome trick or other,
And ſpeedily.

sp.speaker: Peteſ.
sp.l: Let me alone to think on't,

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Come, be you neare me ſtill.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: With all my duty. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaene 3.
div.stage: Enter Archas, Theodor, Putskie, Ancient, and Souldiers, carrying his armour peece-meale, his Colours wound up, and his Drums in Caſes.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: This is the heavieſt march we e're trod Captain,

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: This was not wont to be: theſe honour'd pieces
The fierie god of warre himſelfe would ſmile at,
Buckl'd upon that body, were not wont thus,
Like Reliques to be offer'd to long ruſt,
And heavy-ey'd oblivion brood upon 'em

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: There ſet 'em downe: and glorious war fare well;
Thou childe of honour and ambitious thoughts,
Begot in bloud, and nurſ'd with Kingdomes ruines;
Thou golden danger, courted by thy followers
Through fires and famines, for one title from thee,
Prodigall man-kinde ſpending all his fortunes;
A long farewell I give thee: Noble Armes,
You ribs for mighty mindes, you Iron houſes,
Made to defie the thunder-claps of Fortune,
Ruſt and conſuming time muſt now dwell with yee:
And thou good Sword that knewſt the way to conqueſt,
Upon whoſe fatall edge deſpaire and death dwelt,
That when I ſhooke thee thus, fore-ſhew'd deſtruction,
Sleep now from bloud, and grace my Monument:
Farewell my Eagle; when thou flew'ſt, whole Armies
Have ſtoopt below thee: At Paſſage I have ſeen thee,
Ruffle the Tartars, as they fled thy furie;
And bang 'em up together, as a Taſſell,
Upon the ſtreach, a ſtock of fearefull Pigeons.
I yet remember when the Volga curl'd,
The aged Volga, when he heav'd his head up,
And rais'd his waters high, to ſee the ruines,
The ruines out Swords made, the bloudy ruines;
Then flew this Bird of honour bravely, Gentlemen;
But theſe muſt be forgotten: ſo muſt theſe too,
And all that tend to Armes, by me for ever.
Take 'em you holy men; my Vow take with 'em,
Never to weare 'em more: Trophies I give 'em,
And ſacred Rites of warre to adorne the Temple:
There let 'em hang, to tell the world their maſter
Is now Devotions ſouldier, fit for prayer,
Why doe ye hang your heads? why look you ſad friends?
I am not dying yet.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: Ye are indeed to us ſir.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Dead to our fortunes, Generall.

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: Youll finde a better,
A greater, and a ſtronger man to lead yee,
And to a ſtronger fortune: I am old friends,
Time, and the wars together make me ſtoop, gentlemen,
Stoop to my grave: my minde unfurniſh'd too,
Emptie and weak as I am: my poore body,
Able for nothing now but contemplation,
And that will be a taske too to a Souldier:
Yet had they but encourag'd me, or thought well
Of what I have done, I thinke I ſhould have ventur'd
For one knock more, I ſhould have made a ſhift yet
To have broke one ſtaffe more handſomly, and have dyed
Like a good fellow, and an honeſt ſouldier,
In the head of ye all, with my ſword in my hand,
And ſo have made an end of all with credit.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: Well, there will come an houre, when all theſe injuries
Theſe ſecure ſlights—

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Ha! no more of that ſirrah,
Not one word more of that I charge ye.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: I muſt ſpeak ſir.
And may that tongue forget to found your ſervice,
That's dumbe to your abuſes.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Underſtand foole,
That voluntary I ſit downe.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: You are forced ſir,
