VVith, or againſt our ſiſter, ſpeed in fight.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Rocca, the firſt news of Miranda ſervice
Let me have notice of.

sp.speaker: Roc
sp.l: You ſhall: The Moore
VVaytes you without.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Admit her, ha, ha, ha.
Oh, how my fancies run at tilt! Gomera
Loves Oriana; ſhe, as I ſhould gheſſe,
Affects Miranda; theſe are two deer friends,
As firme, and full of fire, as ſteele and flint.
To make 'em ſo now, one againſt the other: En. Zanthia
Stay, let me like it better, Zanthia;
Firſt tell me this, did Don Gomera uſe
To give his viſits to your Miſtris?

sp.speaker: Zan.
sp.l: Yes, and Miranda too: but ſeverally.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: VVhich did ſhe moſt apply to?

sp.speaker: Zan.
sp.l: Faith to neither:
Yet infinitely I have heard her praiſe 'em both,
And in that manner, that were both one man
I thinke ſhe was in love with't.
Another Letter you muſt frame for me
Inſtantly, in your Ladies Character,
To ſuch a purpoſe as I'le tell thee ſtrait,
Go in, and ſtay me: go my Tinder-box,
Croſſe lines i'le croſſe; ſo, ſo: my after-game
I muſt play better: woman, I will ſpread
My vengeance over Malta, for thy ſake:
Spaniard, Italian, like my ſteele and ſtone,
I'le knock you thus together, were ye out
To light my dark deeds, whilſt I ſeeme preciſe,
And winck to ſave the ſparcles from mind eyes.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Norandine, Miranda, and Souldiers and Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How is it Sir?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Pray ſet me down; I coole,
And my, wounds ſmart.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I hope yet
Though there be many, ther's none dangerous.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I know not, nor I care not much, I got 'em,
Like a too forward foole; but I hope the Surgeons
Will take an order I ſhall not leave 'em ſo
I make the rogues more work then all the Iſland,
And yet they give me the hardeſt words for my money.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I am glad ye are ſo ſprightly: ye fought bravely
Go call the Surgeons Souldiers: wondrous nobly
Upon my life, I have not ſeen ſuch valour,
Maintained ſo long, and to ſo large a ruin,
The oddes ſo ſtrong againſt ye.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I thank ye,
And thank ye for your help, your timely ſuccour.
By th' mas, it came ith' nick ſir, and well handled;
Stoutly, and ſtrongly handled: we had duckt elſe,
My Turke had Turk'd me elſe: but he has wel paid for't.
Why what a Signe for an Almanack h'as made me?

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: I am glad to finde ye here ſir, of neceſſity
I muſt have come aboard elſe; and brave Captain
We all joy much in your faire victory,
And all the Iſland ſpeaks your valour nobly.
Have ye brought the Turke in that ye took?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: He rides there.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: If he were out again, the devill ſhould bring him.
H'as truely circumcis'd me.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: I have a buſineſſe
Which much concernes ye, preſently concernes ye;
But not this place nor people: pray ye draw off ſir,
For tis of that weight to ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ile walt on ye,
I muſt crave leave a while: my care dwels with ye,
And I muſt wait my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Your ſervant ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Believe I ſhall, and what my love can miniſter;
Keep your ſtout heart ſtill.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: That's my beſt Phyſitian.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And I ſhall keepe your fame faire. Exit.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Ye are too Noble.
A brave young fellow, of a matchleſſe ſpirit;
He brought me off like thunder, charg'd, and boorded,
As if he had been ſhot to ſave mine honour:
And when my fainting men tyr'd with their labour,
And lacke of blood gave to the Turke aſſurance
The day was his; when I was cut in ſhreds thus,
And not a corn of Powder left to bleſſe us,
Then flew his Sword in, then his Cannon roard,
And let flie blood and death in ſtorms amongſt em.
Then might I heare their ſleepy Prophet howl'd too,
And all their ſilver Creſcents then I ſaw
Like falling Meteors ſpent, and ſet for ever
Under the Croſſe of Malta; death ſo wanton
I never lookt upon, ſo full of revell. Enter Surgeon
I will not be dreſt yet: Me thought that fellow
Was fit for no converſation, nor no Chriſtian
That had not halfe his brains knockt out, no Souldier.
Oh valiant young man, how I love thy vertue.

sp.speaker: 1 Soul.
sp.l: Pray ye ſir be dreſt, alaſſe ye bleed apace yet.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Tis but the ſweat of honour (alas) thou milkſop,
Thou man of March-paine, canſt thou feare to ſee
A few light hurts, that bluſh they are no bigger,
A few ſmall ſcratches? get ye a Cawdle ſirha,
Your finger akes: and let the old wives watch thee:
Bring in the booty, and the priſoners;
By Heaven Ile ſee 'em, and diſpoſe 'em firſt,
Before I have a drop of blood wipt from me; goe. Exeunt Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: You'l faint ſir.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: No, ye lie ſir, like an Aſſe, ſir;
I have no ſuch pigs hurt in my belly.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: By my life Captaine
Theſe hurts are not to be jeſted with.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: If thou hadſt 'em:
They are my companions foole, my family;
I cannot eate nor ſleepe without their company.
Doſt take me for St Davy, that fell dead
With ſeeing of his noſe bleed? Enter Souldiers with booty.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Here they come ſir:
But would you would be dreſt.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Pox: dreſſe thy ſelfe firſt,
Thou faintſt a great deale faſter whats all this?

sp.speaker: 1 Sould.
sp.l: The money and the merchandize ye took ſir.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: A goodly purchaſe: Is it for this we venture
Our liberties and lives? what can all this doe?
Get me ſome dozen ſurfeits, ſome ſeven freſh whores,
And twenty pot-alleys and to: and then I am vertuous.
Lay the Knights part by, and that to pay the Souldier:
This is mine own, I think I have deſerv'd it:
Come, now looke to me, and grope me like a chambermaid,
Ile neither ſtart, nor ſpeake; what's that i'th truſſe there?

sp.speaker: 2 Soul.
sp.l: Tis cloth of Tiſſew ſir, and this is Scarlet.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I ſhall looke redder ſhortly then, I feare me,
And as a Captaine ought, a great deale prowder.
Can ye cure me of that crack, Surgeon?

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Yes, when your Suit's at pawn, ſir.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: There's for your playſter.
A very learned Surgeon: what's in that pack there?

sp.speaker: 1 Soul.
sp.l: Tis Engliſh Cloth.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: That's a good weare indeed,
Both ſtrong, and rich: but it has a vertue
A twang of the own Country, that ſpoiles all:
A man ſhall nere be ſober in't: Where are the Gentlemen
That ventur'd with me, both their lives and fortunes?
Come forward my faire ſpirits; Norandine
Forgets his worth, when he forgets your valours.
You have loſt an eye, I ſaw ye face all hazards:
You have one left yet, to chooſe your Miſtris.
You have your leg broke with a ſhot; yet ſitting,
I ſaw you make the place good with your Pike ſtill.
And your hand's gone; a good heart wants no inſtruments;
Share that amongſt ye: there's an eye, an arme,
And that wil beare you up, when your legs cannot.
Oh where's the honeſt Saylor? that poore fellow,
Indeed that bold brave fellow, that with his Musket
Taught them new waies how to put their caps off;
That ſtood the fire of all the fight, twice blowne,
And twice I gave him drownd: welcome aſhore knave;
Give me thy hand, if they be not both loſt: faith thou art welcome,
My tough knave welcom: thou wilt not ſhrink ith'waſhing.
Hold, there's a piece of Scarlet, get thee hanſome.
And this to buy thee Buttons.

sp.speaker: Sayl.
sp.l: Thank ye Captaine,
Command my life at all houres.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Thou durſt give it.
You have deſerv'd too.

sp.speaker: 3 Soul.
sp.l: We have ſeen the fight ſir.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Yes: coyld up in a Cable, like ſalt Eeles;
Or buried low ith'ballaſſe: do you call that fighting?
Where be your wounds? your knocks? your want of limbs rogues?
Art not thou he that ask'd the Maſter-gunner
Where thou mightſt lie ſafeſt? and he ſtrait anſwered,
Put thy head in that hole new bor'd with a Cannon,
For twas a hundred to one, another ſhot would not hit there:
Your wages you ſhall have, but for rewards
Take your owne waies: and get ye to the Tavernes;
There, when ye are hot with Wine 'mongſt your admirers,
Take Ships, and Towns, and Caſtles at your pleaſures,
And make the great Turk ſhake at your valours.
Bring in the priſoners now my brave Muſulmans,
You that are Lords oth' Sea, and ſcorn us Chriſtians,
Which of your mangy lives is worth this hurt here?
Away to priſon with 'em, ſee 'em ſafe;
You ſhall finde we have Gallies too, and ſlaves too.

sp.speaker: 1 Soul.
sp.l: What ſhall be done with this woman ſir?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Pox take her,
Twas ſhe that ſet me on to fight with theſe rogues,
That Ring worme rot it: what can you doe now
With all your paintings, and your pouncings Lady,
To reſtore my blood again? you, and your Cupid
That have made a Carbinado of me; plague take ye,
Ye are too deep ye rogue, this is thy worke woman,
Thou louſie woman; death, you go too deep ſtill.
The ſeeing of your ſimpring ſweetneſſe: — ye Filly,
Ye Tit, ye-Tomboy, what can one nights gingling,
Or two, or ten, ſweet heart, and oh▪ my deare chicken,
Scratching my head, or fumbling with my fore-maſt,
Doe me good now? ye have powder'd me for one yeere,
I am in ſowce I thank ye; thanke your beauty,
Your moſt ſweet beauty: pox upon thoſe goggles.
We cannot fight like honeſt men, for honour,
And quietly kill one another as we ought,
But in ſteps one of you; the devils holineſſe
And you muſt have a daunce: away with her,
She ſtinks to me now.

sp.speaker: 1 Soul.
sp.l: Shall I have her Captaine?

sp.speaker: 2 Soul.
sp.l: Or I?

sp.speaker: 3 Soul.
sp.l: Ile marry her.

sp.speaker: 4 Soul.
sp.l: Good Captaine, I.

sp.speaker: 3 Soul.
sp.l: And make her a good Chriſtian; lay hands on her;
I know ſhe's mine.

sp.speaker: 2 Soul.
sp.l: Ile give my full ſhare for her: have ye no manners
To thruſt the woman ſo?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Share her among ye;
And may ſhe give ye as many hurts as I have,
And twice as many aches.

sp.speaker: Luſc.
sp.l: Noble Captaine,
Be pleas'd to free me from theſe Souldiers wildneſſe,
Till I but ſpeake two words.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Now for your maidenhead,
You have your booke, proceed.

sp.speaker: Luſc.
sp.l: Victorious ſir,
Tis ſeldome ſeen in men ſo valiant,
Minds ſo devoyd of vertue: he that can conquer,
Should ever know how to preſerve his conqueſt,
Tis but a baſe theft elſe. Valour's a vertue,
Crown of mens actions here; yours as you make it.
And can you put ſo rough a foyle as violence,
As wronging of weake woman to your triumph?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Let her alone.

sp.speaker: Luſc.
sp.l: I have loſt my husband, ſir;
You feel not that: him that I love; you care not:
When fortune fals on you thus, you may grieve too;
My liberty, I kneele not for; mine honour,
(if ever vertuous honour toucht your heart yet)
Make deere, and precious, ſir: you had a mother.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: The rougy thing ſpeaks finely, neat: who took ye?
For he muſt be your guard.

sp.speaker: Luſc.
sp.l: I wiſh no better,
A Noble Gentleman, and Nobly us'd me,
They cal'd his name Miranda.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: You are his then:
Ye have light upon a young man worth your ſervice,
I free ye from all the reſt: and from all violence;
He that doth offer't, by my head he hangs for't:
Go ſee her ſafe kept, till the Noble Gentleman
Be ready to diſpoſe her: thank your tongue,
You have a good one, and preſerve it good ſtill:
Souldiers, come wait on me, Ile ſee ye paid all. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: I knew ye lov'd her, vertuouſly ye lov'd her,
Which made me make that haſt: I knew ye priz'd her
As all fair minds do goodneſſe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Good Aſtorius,
I muſt confeſſe I do much honour her,
And worthily I hope ſtill.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: Tis no doubt ſir,
For on my life ſhe is much wrong'd.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Very likely:
And I as much tormented I was abſcent.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: You need not feare, Peter Gomera's Noble,
Of a tryd faith and valour.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This I know too:
But whilſt was not there, and whilſt ſhe ſuffer'd;
Whilſt vertue ſuffer'd, friend, oh how it loads me!
Whilſt innocence and ſweetneſſe ſunke together,
How cold it ſits here? if my arme had fought her,
My truth, though naked, ſtood againſt all treaſons,
My Sword here graſped, love on the edge, and honour,
And but a ſignall from her eye to ſeale it,
If then ſhe had been loſt; I brag too late,
And too much I decline the Noble Peter.
Yet ſome poor ſervice I would do her ſweetneſſe,
Alas ſhe needs it, my Aſtorius,
The gentle Lady needs it.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: Noble ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And what I can: prethee bear with this weaknes.
Often I do not uſe theſe womens weapons
But where true pitty is. I am much troubled,
And ſomething have to do, I cannot forme yet.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: Ile take my leave, ſir, I ſhall but diſturb ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And pleaſe you for a while: and pray to fortune
To ſmile upon this Lady.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: All my help ſir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Gomera's old and ſtiffe: and he may loſe her,
The winter of his yeeres and wounds upon him:
And yet he has done bravely hithero;
Mountferrats fury, in his heat of ſummer,
The whiſtling of his Sword like angry ſtormes,
Renting up life by th' roots, I have ſeen him ſcale
As if a Falcon had run up a traine,
Claſhing his warlike pynions, his ſteel'd curaſſe,
And at his pitch inmew the Town below him.
I muſt do ſomething. Enter Collonna.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Noble ſir, for Heaven ſake
Take pity of a poore afflicted Chriſtian
Redeem'd from one affliction to another.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Boldly you aske that, we are bound to give it.
From what affliction ſir?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: From cold, and hunger:
From nakedneſſe, and ſtripes.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A priſoner?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: A ſlave, ſir, in the Turkiſh prize, new taken;
That in the heat of fight, when your brave hand
Brought the Dane ſuccour, got my yrons off,
And put my ſelfe to mercy of the Ocean.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: And ſwom to Land?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: I did ſir, Heaven was gracious;
But now a ſtranger, and my wants upon me,
Though willingly I would preſerve this life ſir,
With honeſty and truth; I am not look'd on;
The hand of pity, that ſhould give for Heaven ſake,
And charitable hearts are grown ſo cold, ſir,
Never remembring what their fortunes may be.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou ſayſt too true: of what profeſſion art thou?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: I have been better traind; and can ſerve truly,
Where truſt is laid upon me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A hanſome fellow;
Haſt thou ere bore Armes?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: I have trod full many a march, ſir,
And ſome hurts have to ſhew: before me too, ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Pity this thing ſhould ſtarve, or forced for want
Come to a worſe end. I know not what thou mayſt be.
But if thou thinkſt it fit to be a ſervant,
Ile be a Maſter, and a good one to thee,
If ye deſerve, ſir.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Elſe I aske no favour.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Then ſir, to try your truſt, becauſe I like you,
Go to the Dane, of him receive a woman,
A Turkiſh priſoner; for me receive her,
I heare ſhe is my prize: looke fairly to her,
For I would have her know, though now my priſoner,
The Chriſtians need no Schoolmaſters for honour.
Take this to buy thee clothes: this Ring, to help thee
Into the fellowſhip of my houſe: ye are a ſtranger,
And my ſervants will not know ye elſe; there keep her,
And with all modeſty preſerve your ſervice.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: A foule example finde me elſe: Heaven thank ye.
Of Captaine Norandine?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: The ſame.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Tis done ſir:
And may Heavens goodneſſe ever dwell about ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Wait there till I come home.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: I ſhall not faile, ſir. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena tertia.
div.stage: Enter Mountferrat with a Letter, and Abdella.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Tis ſtrange it ſhould be ſo, that your high mettle
ſhould check thus poorly: dully; moſt un-manly.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Let me alone.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Thus leadenly?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: — take ye.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: At every childiſh feare? at every ſhadow?
Are you Mountferrat, that have done ſuch deeds?
Wrought through ſuch bloody fields, men ſhake to ſpeak of?
Can ye go back? is there a ſafety left yet
But fore-right? is not ruine round about ye?
Have ye not ſtil theſe armes, that Sword, that heart whol?
Is't not a man ye fight with, and an old man,
A man halfe kil'd already? Am not I here
As lovely in my blacke to entertaine thee,
As high, and full of heat, to meet thy pleaſures?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I wil be alone.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Ye ſhall: farewell ſir;
And doe it bravely, never think of conſcience:
There is none to a man reſolved be happy. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: No, moſt unhappy wretch, as thou haſt made me
More devil then thy ſelfe, I am.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Alone,
And troubled too, I take it: how he ſtarts?
All is not hanſome in thy heart Mountferrat.
God ſpeed ye ſir, I have been ſeeking of ye:
They ſay you are to fight to day.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: What then?

sp.speaker: Mir
sp.l: Nay nothing but good fortune to your Sword, ſir.
Ye have a cauſe requires it, the Iſlands ſafety,
The orders, and your honours.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: And do you make a queſtion
I wil not fight it Nobly?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ye dare fight,
Ye have, and with as great a confidence as juſtice,
I have ſeen ye ſtrike as home, and hit as deadly.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Why are theſe queſtion then?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ile tell ye quickly.
Ye have a Lady in your cauſe, a faire one,
A gentler never trod on ground, a Nobler.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Do ye come on ſo faſt? I have it for ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: The Sunne nere ſaw a ſweeter.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Theſe I grant ye:
Nor dare I againſt beauty heave my hand up,
It were unmanly, ſir; too much unmanly:
But when theſe excellencies turn to ruine,
To ruine of themſelves, and thoſe protect 'em;
When vertue's loſt luſt, and diſhonour enter'd,
Loſſe of our ſelves, and ſouls baſely projected—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Do you think tis ſo?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Too ſure.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And can it be?
Can it be thought Mountferrat, ſo much ſweetnes,
So great a magazine of all things precious,
A mind ſo heavenly made, prethee obſerve me.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I thought ſo to: now by my holy Order,
He that had told me, (till experience found it
Too bold a proof) this Lady had been vitious—
I weare no dull Sword ſir, nor hate I vertue,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Againſt her brother? to the man has bred her?
Her blood and honour?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Where ambitious luſt
Deſires to be above the rule preſcribed her,
Takes hold, and wins, poore chaſtity, cold duty,
Like faſhions old forgot, ſhe flings behind her,
And puts on blood and miſchiefe, death, and ruine,
To raiſe her new built hopes, new faith to faſten her:
Ma' foy, ſhe is as foule, as heaven is beauteous.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou lieſt; thou lieſt Mountferrat: thou lieſt baſely.
Stare not, nor ſwell not with thy pride: thou lieſt;
And this ſhall make it good.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Out with your heat firſt,
Ye ſhall be fought withall.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: By — that Lady,
The vertue of that woman, were all the good deeds
Of all thy families bound in one fagot,
From Adam to this houre, but with one ſparkle
Would fire that wiſpe, and turn it to light aſhes.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Oh pitifull young man, ſtroke blind with beauty!
Shot with a womans ſmile: poore, poore Miranda;
Thou hopeful young man once; but now thou loſt man:
Thou naked man of all that we call Noble,
How art thou cozend? didſt thou know what I do,
And how far thy deare honour (mark me foole)
Which like a father I have kept from blaſting,
Thy tender honour is abus'd▪ but fight firſt,
And then too late, thou ſhalt know all.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou lieſt, ſtil.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Stay, now Ile ſhew thee all, and then Ile kil thee.
I love thee ſo deere, time ſhall not diſgrace thee.
Read that.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: It is her hand: it is moſt certaine;
Good Angels keep me: that I ſhould be her agent
To betray Malta, and bring her to the Baſha,
That on my tender love lay all her project!
Eyes, never ſee again, melt out for ſorrow,
Did the divell do this?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: No, but his Dam did it,
The vertuous Lady that you love ſo deerly;
Come, wil ye fight again?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, prethee kill me:
For Heaven ſake, and for goodneſſe ſake diſpatch me,
For the diſgrace ſake that I gave thee, kill me.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Why, are ye guilty?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I have liv'd Mountferrat,
To ſee diſhonour ſwallow up all vertue,
And now would dye: by heavens eternall brightneſſe,
I am as cleere as Innocence.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I knew it,
And therefore kept this Letter from all knowledge,
And this ſword from anger, ye had died elſe.
And yet I lye, and baſely lye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: O vertue!
Unſpotted vertue, whether art thou vaniſh'd?
What haſt thou left to abuſe our fraileties
In ſhape of goodneſſe?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Come, take courage, man,
I have forgiven and forgot your raſhneſſe,
And hold you faire as light in all your actions,
And by my troth I griev'd your love; take comfort,
There be more women.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And more miſchiefe in 'em.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: The juſtice I ſhall doe, to right theſe villaines
Shall make ye man againe: i'le ſtrike it ſure Sir.
Come, looke up bravely: put this puling paſſion
Out of your minde; one knock for thee Miranda,
And for the Boy, the grave Gomera gave thee,
When ſhe accepted thee her Champion;
And in thy abſence, like a valiant Gentleman,
I yet remember it: he is too young,
Too Boyiſh, and to tender, to adventure :
I'le give him one ſound rap for that: I love thee,
Thou art a brave young ſparke.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Boy did he call me?
Gomera call me Boy?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: It pleas'd his gravity,
To think ſo of ye then: they that doe ſervice,
And honeſt ſervice, ſuch as thou, and I doe,
Are either knaves, or Boyes.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Boy, by Gomera?
How look'd he when he ſaid it? for Gomera
Was ever wont to be a vertuous Gentleman,
Humane, and ſweet.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Yes, when he will, he can be;
But let it goe, I would not breed diſſention;
'Tis an unfriendly office, and had it been
To any of a higher ſtraine then you Sir,
The well known, well approved, and lov'd Miranda,
I had not thought on't: 'twas happly, his haſte too,
And zeale to her.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A Traytor and a Boy too?
Shame take me if I ſuffer't: puff: farewell love.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Ye know my buſineſſe, I muſt leave ye Sir,
My houre grows on a pace.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I muſt not leave you
I dare not, nor I will not, till your goodneſſe
Have granted me one curteſie: ye ſay ye love me?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I doe, and deerely: ask, and let that curteſie
Nothing concerne mine honour,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You muſt doe it.
Or you will never ſee me more:

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: What is it?
It ſhall be great that puts ye of; pray ſpeake it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Pray let me fight to day: good, deere Mountferrat,
Let me, and bold Gomera—

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Fie Miranda,
Doe ye weigh my worth ſo little?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: On my knees,
As ever thou had'ſt true touch of a ſorrow
Thy friend conceiv'd, as ever honour lov'd thee.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Shall I turne recreant now?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis not thy cauſe,
Thou haſt no reputation wounded in't,
Thines but a generall zeale: 'death: I am tainted,
The deereſt twyn to life, my credit's murder'd,
Baffell'd, and boy'd,

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I am glad ye have ſwallow'd it,
I muſt confeſſe I pitty ye; and 'tis a juſtice,
A great one too, you ſhould revenge theſe injuries:
I know it, and I know ye fit and bold to doe it,
And man, as much as man may: but Miranda,
Why doe ye kneel?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: By — I'le grow to the ground here,
And with my ſword digge up my grave, and fall in't
Unleſſe thou grant me: deere Mountferrat, friend,
Is any thing in my power, to my life, Sir?
The honour ſhall be yours.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I love ye deerely,
Yet ſo much I ſhould tender.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I'le preſerve all:
By — I will: or all the ſinne fall with me,
Pray let me.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Ye have won: i'le once be coward
To pleaſure you.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I kiſſe your hands, and thanke ye.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Be tender of my credit, and fight bravely.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Blow not the fire that flames.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I'le ſend mine Armor,
My man ſhall preſently attend ye with it,
For you muſt arme immediately, the houre cals,
I know 'twill fit ye right; be ſure, and ſecret,
And laſt be fortunate; farewell; ye are fitted:
I am glad the load's off me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: My beſt Mountferrat. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Doctor, I will ſee the Combat, that's the truth on't
If I had never a Legge, I would crawle to ſee it.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: You are moſt unfit, if I might councell ye,
Your wounds ſo many, and the ayre —

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: The Halter;
The ayres as good an ayre, as fine an ayre;
Would'ſt thou have me live in an oven?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Beſide the noyſe, Sir:
Which to a tender body.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: That's it, Doctor,
My body muſt be cur'd with all: if you'll heale me quickly,
Boyle a Drum-head in my broth: I never proſper,
With knuckles o'veale, and birds in ſorrell ſops,
Cawdles, and Cullyſſes; they waſh me away
Like a horſe had eaten grains: if thou wilt cure me
A pickled herring, and a pottle of Sack, Doctor,
And halfe a dozen trumpets.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Ye are a ſtrange Gentleman,

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: As ere thou knew'ſt: wilt thou give mean other gliſter
That I may ſit cleanly there, like a french Lady,
When ſhe goes to a Mask at Court? where's thy hoboy?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: I am glad ye are growne ſo merry. Enter Aſtor: & Caſtr.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Welcome Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: We come to ſee you ſir; and glad we are
To ſee you thus, thus forward to your health, ſir.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I thank my Doctor here.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Nay, thanke your ſelfe ſir,
For by my troth, I know not how he's cur'd,
He nev'r obſerves any of our preſcriptions.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Give me my money again then, good ſweet Doctor,
Wilt thou have twenty ſhillings a day for vexing me.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.p: That ſhall not ſerve ye ſir; Drums a far off, A low March.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Then forty ſhall ſir,
And that will make ye ſpeake well: harke the Drums

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: They begin to beat to th' field: O noble Dane,
Never was ſuch a ſtake, I hope of innocence
Plaid for in Malta and in blood before.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: It makes us hang our heads all.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: A bold villaine:
If there be treaſon in it: accuſe poore Ladies?
And yet they may do miſchief to: i'le be with ye:
If ſhe be innocent, I ſhall finde it quickly,
And ſomething then i'le ſay.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: Come, leane on us, ſir,

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I thank ye Gentlemen: and domine Doctor,
Pray bring a little ſneezing powder in your Pocket,
For feare I ſound when I ſee blood.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: You are pleaſant. Exeunt.

sp.p: Are the Combatants come in? The Seaffold ſet out and the ſtaires.

sp.l: Yes.
Make the field cleere there.
That's done too.
Then to the priſoner: the grand Maſter's coming,
Let's ſee that all be ready there.
Too ready.
How ceremonious our very ends are?
Alas, ſweet Lady,
If ſhe be innocent, Floriſh.
No dodbt but juſtice will direct her Champion Enter Valetta: Norandine Aſhor. Caſtriot: c.
Away: I heare 'em come:
Pray heavwn ſhe proſper.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Give Captain Norandine a chaire.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I thank your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Sit ſir, and take your eaſe: your hurts require it.
You come to ſee a womans cauſe deſcrided:
That's all the knowledge now, or name I have for her:
They ſay a falſe, a baſe, and treacherous woman,
And partly prov'd too.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Pitty it ſhould be ſo:
And if your Lordſhip durſt aske my opinion,
Sure, I ſhould anſwer no: ſo much I honour her:
And anſwer't with my life too: But Gomera
Is a brave Gentleman; the other valiant,
And if he be not good, doggs gnaw his fleſh off,
And one above 'em both will finde the truth out.
He never failes, ſir,

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: That's the hope reſts with me.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: How nature, and his honour ſtruggle in him!
A ſweet, cleere, noble Gentleman. Within, make roome there Enter Oriana; Ladies, Executioner, Abdel; la: 1 Guard.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Make roome there.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Go up: and what you have to ſay, ſay there,

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Thus I aſcend: neerer I hope to heaven,
Nor do I fear to tread this dark black Manſion:
The I mage of my grave each foot we move,
Goes to it ſtill: each houre we leave behinde us,
Knols ſadly toward it: My noble Brother,
For yet mine innocence dares cals ye ſo,
And you the friends to vertue, that come hither,
The Chorus to this Tragick Scaene behold me,
Behold me with your juſtice, not with pitty,
(My cauſe was ne're ſo poore to aske compaſſion,)
Behold me in this ſpotleſſe white I weare,
The Embleme of my life, of all my actions,
So ye ſhall finde my ſtory, though I periſh:
Behold me in my Sex, I am no Souldier,
Tender, and full of fears our bluſhing Sex is,
Unhardned with relentleſſe thoughts; unhatcht
With blood, and bloody practiſe: alas we tremble;
But when an angry dreame afflicts our fancies,
Dye with a tale well told: had I been practis'd,
And known the way of miſchiefe, travell'd in it,
And given my blood, and honour up to reach it,
Forgot religion, and the line I ſprung on,
Oh heaven, I had been ſit then for thy juſtice,
And then in black as dark as hell, I had howl'd here.
Laſt, in your own opinions weigh mine innocence;
Amongſt ye I was planted from an Infant
(would then if heaven had ſo been pleas'd, I had periſh'd)
Grew up, and goodly, ready to bear fruit,
The honourable fruit of marriage:
And am I blaſted in my bud with treaſon?
Boldly, and baſely of my faire name raviſh'd,
And hither brought to finde my reſt in ruine?
But he that knowes all he that rights all wrongs,
And in his time reſtores, knows me: I have ſpoken.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: If ye be innocent, heaven will protect ye,
And ſo I leave ye to his Sword ſtrikes for ye,
Farewell.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: O that went deepe: farewell deere brother,
And howſoe'r my cauſe goes, ſee my body
(upon my knees I ask it) buried chaſtely;
For yet, by holy truth, it never treſpaſſ'd.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: Iuſtice ſit on your cauſe; & heaven fight for ye.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Two of ye Gentlemen, doe me but the honour
To lead me to her: good my Lord, your leave too:

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: You have it ſir.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Give me your faire hands feareleſſe,
As white as this I ſee your Innocence,
As ſpotleſſe, and as pure: be not afraid Lady,
You are but here brought to your nobler fortune,
To adde unto your life immortall ſtory:
Vertue, through hardeſt things arrives at happineſſe,
Shame follow that blunt ſword that looſes you:
And he that ſtrikes againſt you: I ſhall ſtudy
A curſe or two for him: once more your faire hands,
I never brought ill luck yet; be feareleſſe happy.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I thank ye, noble Captain.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: So I leave ye.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Call in the Knights ſeverally. Enter ſeverally Gomera, and Miranda.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: But two words to my Champion,
And then to heaven and him, I give my cauſe up:

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: Speake quickly: and ſpeake ſhort.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I have not much ſir.
Noble Gomera, from your own free vertue,
You have undertaken here a poore Maids honour,
And with the hazard of your life: and happily
You may ſuſpect the cauſe, though in your true worth
You will not ſhew it, therefore take this teſtimony
(And as I hope for happineſſe, a true one)
And may it ſteel your heart, and edge your good ſword,
Ye fight for her as ſpotleſſe of theſe miſchiefes,
As heaven is of our ſinnes, or truth of errors,
And ſo defie that treacherous man, and proſper.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Bleſſing o'thy heart Lady.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Give the ſignall to 'em. Low Alarmes.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: 'Tis bravely fought Gomera; follow that blows,
Well ſtrooke againe boy: looke upon the Lady,
And gather ſpirit: brave againe: lye cloſe.
Lye cloſe I ſay: he fights aloft, and ſtrongly:
Cloſe for thy life: a — o' that fell buffet:
Retire, and gather breath: ye have day enough knights;
Looke lovely on him Lady: to't againe now,
Stand, ſtand Gomera, ſtand: one blow for all now.
Gather thy ſtrength together; God bleſſe the woman:
Why, wher's thy noble heart? heaven bleſſe the Lady.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Oh, Oh!

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: She is gone, ſhe is gone:

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Now ſtrike it.
Hold, hold: he yeelds: hold thy brave ſword, he's conquer'd:
He's thine Gomera, now be joyfull Lady:
What could this theefe have done, had his cauſe beene equall?
He made mv heart ſtrings tremble.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: Off with his Cask there;
And Executioner, take you his head next.

sp.speaker: Abdel.
sp.l: Oh curſed fortune!

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Stay, I beſeech ye ſir, and this one honour
Grant me, I have deſerv'd it, that this villaine
May live one day, to envy at my juſtice,
That he may pine, and dye before the ſword fall.
Viewing the glory, I have wone her goodneſſe.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: He ſhall, and you the harveſt of your valour
Shall reape brave ſir, abundantly.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: I have ſaved her.
Preſerv'd her ſpotleſſe worth from black deſtruction,
Her white name to eternity delivered,
Her youth, and ſweetneſſe, from a timeleſſe rain.
Now Lord Valetta, if this bloody labour
May but deſerve her favour.

sp.speaker: Mir,
sp.l: Stay and heare me firſt.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Of with his Cask, this is Miranda's voice.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: 'Tis he indeed, or elſe mine eyes abuſe me,
What makes he here thus?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: The young Miranda?
Is he mine enemy too?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: None has deſer'd her
If worth muſt carry it, and ſervice ſeeke her,
But he that ſaved her honour.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: That's I Miranda.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, no, that's I Gomera, be not ſo forward,
In bargaine for my love, ye cannot cozen me.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: I fought it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And I gave it: which is nobler?
Why every Gentleman would have done as much
As you did: fought it: that's a poore deſert, ſir,
They are bound to that; but then to make that fight ſure,
To doe as I did, take all danger from it
Suffer that coldneſſe, that muſt call me now
Into diſgrace for ever, into pitty.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: I undertook firſt, to preſerve from hazzard.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And I made ſure no hazzard ſhould come neere hir.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: 'Twas T defide Mountferrat.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Twas I wrought him,
You had had a darke day elſe; twas I defide
His conſcience firſt, 'twas I that ſhook him there,
Which is the brave defiance.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: My life and honour
At ſtake I lay'd,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: My care; and truth layby it
Leaſt that ſtake might be loſt: I have deſerv'd her,
And none but I; the Lady might have periſh'd,
Had Fell Mountferrat ſtrooke it, from whoſe malice
With cunning, and bold confidence I catch'd it,
And 'twas high time, and ſuch a ſervice Lady
For you, and for your innocence, for who knows not
The all devouring ſword of fierce Mountferrat?
I ſhew'd ye what I could doe, had I beene ſpightfull
Or Maſter but of halfe the poyſon he beares,
(Hell take his heart for't) and beſhrow theſe hands Maddam,
With all my heart, I wiſh a miſchiefe on 'em,
They made ye once looke ſad: ſuch another fright
I would not put ye in, to owne the Iſland,
Yet pardon me, 'twas but to ſhew a Souldier,
Which, when I had done, I ended your poore coward.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Let ſome looke out, for the baſe Knight Mountferrat.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I hope he's far enough if his man be truſty:
This was a ſtrange misfortune; I muſt not know it.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: That moſt deboſh'd knight! come down ſweet ſiſter.
My ſpotleſſe Siſter; now, pray thanke theſe Gentlemen,
They have deſerv'd both truly, nobly of ye.
Both excellently deerely, both all the honour
All the reſpect and favour.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Both ſhall have it;
And as my life, their memories i'le nouriſh.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Ye are both true Knights, and both moſt worthy Lovers,
Here ſtands a Lady ripen'd with your fervice,
Yong, faire, and (now I dare ſay) truly honourable:
'Tis my will ſhe ſhall marry: marry now,
And one of you (ſhe cannot take more nobly) your deerts
Begot this will, and bred it; both her beauty
Cannot enjoy: dare ye marke me your umpler?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Mir. With all our Soules.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: He muſt not then be angry
That looſes her.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: O, that were Sir, unworthy,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A little ſorrow he may finde.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: 'Tis manly.
Gomera, you are a brave accompliſh'd Gentleman
A braver no where lives then is Miranda,
In the white way of vertue, and true valour.
Ye have been a pilgrime long: yet no man farther
Has trod thoſe thorny ſteps then young Miranda,
You are gentle: he is gentleneſſe ſelfe: Experience
Cals you her brother; 'tis his hopefull heire.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: The young man now, and 't be thy will.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Your hand iir;
You uhdertooke firſt: nobly undertook,
This Ladies cauſe: you made it good, and fought it
You muſt be ferv'd firſt: take her, and enjoy her,
I give her to you: kiſſe her; are you pleas'd now?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: My joy's ſo much I cannot ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Nay, faireſt ſir;
You muſt not be diſpleaſed: you breake your promiſe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I never griev'd at good, nor dare I now ſir,
Though ſomething ſeeme ſtrange to me.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: I have provided
A better match for you: more full of beauty,
I'le wed ye to our Order: there's a Miſtreſſe,
Whoſe beauty ne're decayes: time ſtands below her:
Whoſe honour Ermin-like, can never ſuffer,
Spot, or black ſoyle; whoſe eternall iſſue
Fame brings up at her breaſts, and leaves 'em ſaintied.
Her you ſhall marry.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I muſt humbly thanke ye.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: Saint Thomas Fort, a charge of no ſmall valew
I give ye too, in preſent, to keepe waking
Your noble ſpirits; and to breed ye pious,
Ile ſend ye a probation Roabe; weare that
Till ye ſhall pleaſe to be our brother: how now?

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.p: Mountferrat's fled ſir. Enter Actorius.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Let him goe a while
Till we have done theſe rites, and ſeen theſe coupled:
His miſchiefe now lyes open: come all friends now.
And ſo let's march to th' Temple, ſound thoſe Inſtruments,
That were the ſignall to a day of blood;
Evill beginning houres may end in good. Floriſh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Come, we'll have wenches man, and all brave things.
—Let her goe: we'll want no Miſtreſſes,
Good ſwords, and good ſtrong Armours.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thoſe are beſt Captain.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: And fight 'till Queenes be in love with us, and run
Ile ſee ye at the Fort within theſe two dayes,
And let's be merry prethee.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: By that time I ſhall.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Why that's well ſaid: I like a good heart truly.

div.head: Scaena prima.
div.stage: Enter Norandine, and Servant, Corporall and Souldiers above.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The daye's not yet broak Sir.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: 'Tis the cooler riding,
I muſt goe ſee Miranda: bring my horſe
Round to the South Port: i'le out here at the beach
And meet ye at the end oth' Sycamores,
'Tis a ſweet walke, and if the wind be ſtirring
Serves like a fan to coole. Corporall and Watch above ſinging.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Which walke?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Why that ſir,
Where the fine City dames meet to make matches.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I know it.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Speed ye then: what mirth is this?
The watches are not yet diſcharged, I take it:
Theſe are brave careleſſe Rogues; i'le hear the Song out
And then i'le fit ye for't, merry Companions:
Here's notable order, now for a trick to tame ye—
Owgh, owgh.

sp.speaker: 1. Wat.
sp.l: Hark, hark, what's that below us? who goes there?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Owgh, owgh, owgh.

sp.speaker: 2. W.
sp.l: 'Tis a Beare broke looſe: pray call the Corporall.

sp.speaker: 1 W.
sp.l: The Dutchmans huge fat ſow.
I ſee her now, and five fine piggs.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Owgh, owgh.

sp.speaker: Corp.
sp.l: Now, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: 1 W.
sp.l: Here's the great fat Sow, Corporall.
The Dutch-mans Sow, and all the Piggs, brave fat piggs,
You have been wiſhing long ſhe would breake looſe.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Owgh, owgh.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe indeed, there's a white pigg now ſucking,
Looke, looke, doe you ſee it firs.

sp.speaker: 1 Wat.
sp.l: Yes, very well ſir.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: A notable fat whorſon; come two of ye.
Goe downe with me, we'll have a tickling breakfaſt.

sp.speaker: 2 W.
sp.l: Let's eat 'em at the Croſſe.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: There's the beſt liquor.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I'le liquor ſome of ye, ye lazy rogues,
Your mindes are of nothing but eating and ſwilling:
What a ſweet beaſt they have made of me? a Sow?
Hogge upon hogge? I heare 'em come. Enter Cor. below and watch.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Go ſoftly, and fall upon 'em finely, nimbly.

sp.speaker: 1 W.
sp.l: Bleſſe me.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Why, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: 1 W.
sp.l: Oh the devill!
The devill, as high as a Steeple.

sp.speaker: 2 W.
sp.l: There he goes Corporall,
His feet are cloven too.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Stand, ſtand I ſay: death' how I ſhake?
Where be your Muskets?

sp.speaker: 1 W.
sp.l: There's no good of them:
Where be our Prayers, man?

sp.speaker: 2 W.
sp.l: Lord, how he ſtalks: ſpeak to him Corporall.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Why, what a devill art thou.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Owgh owgh.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: A dumb devill.
The worſt devill that could come, a dumb devil,
Give me a Musket; he gathers in to me,
I'th name of—ſpeak what art thou?—ſpeake devill,
Or Ile put a plumb in your belly.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Owgh, owgh, owgh.

sp.speaker: Corp.
sp.l: Fie, fie, in what a ſweat I am! Lord bleſſe me,
My Muskets gone too, I am notable to ſtirre it.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Who goes there? ſtand ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Corp.
sp.l: Sure I am inchaunted.
Yet here's my harbert ſtill: nay, who goes there ſir,
What have I loſt my ſelfe? what are ye?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: The Guard.

sp.speaker: Corp.
sp.l: Why what are we then: he's not half ſo long now.
Nor he has no taile at all, I ſhake ſtill damnably.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: The word.

sp.speaker: Corp.
sp.l: 'Have mercy on me, what word do's he meane,
Prethee devill if thou be'ſt the devill,
Doe not make an Aſſe of me; for I remember yet
As well as I am here, I am the Corporall,
Ile lay my life on't devill.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Thou art damn'd:

sp.speaker: Corp.
sp.l: That's all one: but am not I the Corpo all?
I would give a thouſand pound to be reſolv'd now,
Had not I Souldiers here?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: No, not a man,
Thou art deboſh'd, and cozen'd.

sp.speaker: Corp.
sp.l: That may be,
It may be I am drunk; Lord, where have I been?
Is not this my Halbert in my hand?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: No, 'tis a May-pole.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Why then I know not who I am, nor what,
Nor whence I come.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Ye are an arrand raſcall;
You Corporall of a watch.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: 'Tis the Dane's voyce: you are no devill then.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: No, nor no Sow, ſir.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Of that I am right glad ſir,
I was ne're ſo frighted in my life, as I am a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Tall watchmen,
A guard for a Gooſe, you ſing away your Centuries.
A carefull company: let me out oth' port here,
I was a little merry with your worſhips:
And keepe your guards ſtrong, though the devill walk.
Hold, there's to bring ye into your wits againe.
Goe off no more to hunt Piggs: ſuch another trick
And you will hunt the gallowes.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Pray Sir pardon us:
And let the devill come next, i'le make him ſtand
Or make him ſtinck.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Doe doe your duty truly.
Come let me cut, and come away: no more rage. Exe.

div.head: Scaena ſecunda.
div.stage: Enter Abdella with a Letter, and Rocca.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Write thus to me? he hath fearfully, and baſely
Betray'd his own cauſe; yet to free himſelfe
He now aſcribes the fault to me.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: I know not.
What he hath done: but what he now deſires,
His Letters have imform'd you.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Yes, he is
Too well acquainted with the power he holds,
Over my mad affections: I want time
To write: but pray you tell him, if I were
No better ſteeld in my ſtrong reſolutions
Then he hath ſhown himſelfe in his; or thought
There was a hell hereafter, or a Heaven,
But in enjoying him, I ſhould ſtick here,
And move no further: bid him yet take comfort;
For ſomething I wil doe, the devill would quake at,
But Ile unty this nuptiall knot of love,
And make way for nis wiſhes: in the mean time
Let him lie cloſe, for he is ſtrictly ſought for,
And practiſe to love her, that for his ends
Scornes feare and danger. Enter Oriana, and Velleda.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: All this I will tell him. Exit Rocca.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Do ſo: farewell. My Lady, with my fellow,
So earneſt in diſcourſe! what ere it be
Ile ſecond it.

sp.speaker: Vel.
sp.l: He is ſuch a Noble husband,
In every circumſtance, ſo truely loving,
That I might ſay, and without flattery, Maddam
The Sun ſees not a Lady but your ſelfe
That can deſerve him.

sp.speaker: Abd
sp.l: Of all men I ſay
That dare (for tis a deſperate adventure)
Weare on their free necks the ſweet yoak of woman,
(For they that do repine, are no true husbands)
Give me a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Why, are they more loving
Then other men?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: And love too with more judgement;
For, but obſerve, you Courtier is more curious
To ſet himſelfe forth richly then his Lady;
His baths, perfumes, nay paintings too, more coſtly
Then his frugality wil allow to her,
His clothes as chargeable; and grant him but
A thing without a beard, and he may paſſe
At all times for a woman, and with ſome
Have better welcome: Now, your man of Lands
For the moſt part is carefull to manure them,
But leaves his Lady fallow; your great Merchant
Breakes oftner for the debt he ows his wife,
Then with his creditos; and that's the reaſon
She looks elſewhere for payment: Now your Souldier—

sp.speaker: Vel.
sp.l: I mary, do him right.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Firſt, who has one,
Has a perpetuall guard upon her honour;
For while he weares a Sword, Iſander her ſelfe
Dares not barke at it: next, ſhe ſits at home,
Like a great Queen, and tends him forth to fetch in
Her Tribute from all parts; which being brought home,
He layes it at her feet, and ſeeks no further
For his reward, thcn what ſhe may give freely,
And with delight too, from her own Exchequer
Which he finds ever open.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Be more modeſt.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Why, we may ſpeak of that we are glad to taſte of,
Among our ſelves I mean.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Thou talkſt of nothing.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Of nothing Madam? You have found it ſomething;
Or with the raiſing up this pretty mount here,
My Lord hath dealt with ſpirits. Enter Gomera.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Two long houres abſent?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Thy pardon, Sweet: I have been looking on
The prize that was brought in by the brave Dane,
The valiant Norandine, and have brought ſomething,
That may be thou wilt like of; but one kiſſe,
And then poſſeſſe my purchaſe: there's a piece
Of cloth of Tiſſew) this of purpler Velvet,
And as they ſweare of the right Tyrian dye,
Which others here but weawy counterfeit:
If they are worth thy uſe, weare them; if not,
Beſtow them on thy women.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Here's the husband.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: While there is any trading oh the Sea
Thou ſhalt want nothing; tis a Souldiers glory,
How ever he neglect himſelfe, to keep
His Miſtris in full luſtre.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: You exceed ſir.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Yet there was one part of the prize di ſpos'd of.
Before I came, which I grieve that I miſs'd of,
Being almoſt aſſured, it would have been
A welcome preſent.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Pray you ſay, what was it?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: A Turkiſh Captive of incomparable beauty,
And without queſtion, in her Countrey Noble;
Which as companion to thy faithfull Noble;
I would have given thee for thy ſlave.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: But was ſhe
Of ſuch an exquiſite forme?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Moſt equiſite.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: And well deſcended?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: So the habit promis'd,
In which ſhe was taken.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Of what yeeres?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Tis ſaid
A Virgin of fourteen.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I pity her,
And wiſh ſhe were mine, that I might have the means
T' entertain her gently.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: She's now Miranda's,
And as I have heard, made it her ſuit to be ſo.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Miranda;s? then her fate deſerves not pity,
But envy rather.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Envy Oriana?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Yes, and their envy that live free.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: How's this?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Why, ſhe is faln into the hands of one,
So full of that, which in men we ſtile goodnes,
That in her being his ſlave, ſhe is happier far
Then if ſhe were confirm'd the Sultans Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Miranda is indeed a Gentleman
Of faire deſert, and better hopes, but yet
He hath his equals.

sp.speaker: 0ri.
sp.l: Where? I would go far,
As I am now, though much unfit for travailes,
But to ſee one that without injury
Might be put in the ſcale, or paralleld,
In any thing that's Noble, with Mirands;
His knowledge in all ſervices of war,
And ready courage, to put into act
That knowing judgement, as you, are a Souldier
You beſt may ſpeak of. Nor can you deliver,
Nor I heare with delight, a better ſubject.
And heaven did well, in ſuch a lovely feature
To place ſo chaſte a mind; for he is of
So ſweet a carriage, ſuch a winning nature,
And ſuch a bold, yet well diſpos'd behaviour;
And to all theſe, h'as ſuch a charming tongue,
That if he would ſerve under Loves freſh colours,
What monumentall Trophies might he raiſe,
Of his free conqueſts, made in Ladies favours?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Yet you did'ſts, reſiſ him, when he was
An earneſt ſuitor to you.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Yes I did;
And if I were again ſought to, I ſhould;
But muſt aſcribe it rather to the fate
That did appoint me yours, then any power
Which I can call mine own.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Ev'n ſo?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Thanks fortune,
The plot I had to raiſe in him, doubts of her,
Thou haſt effected.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I could tell you too,
What cauſe I have to love him, with what reaſon.
In thankfulneſſe, he may expect from me,
All due obſervance; but I paſſe that, as
A benefit, for which in my behalfe
You are his debtor.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: I perceive it takes,
By his chang'd lookes.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: He is not in the City?
Is he my Lord?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Who Lady?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Why Miranda,
Having you here, can there be any elſe
Worth my enquiry?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: This is ſomewhat more.
Then love to vertue,

sp.speaker: Ori:
sp.l: Faith when he comes hither
(as ſometimes, without queſtion you ſhall meet him)
Invite him home.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: To what end?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: To dine with us,
Or ſup.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: And then to take a hard bed with you:
Mean you not ſo?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: If you could win him to it,
▪Twould be the better; for his entertainment,
Leave that to me, he ſhall finde Noble uſage,
And from me a free welcome.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Have you never
Heard of a Roman Lady (Oriana)
Remembred as a preſident for Matrons,
(Chaſte ones, I pray you underſtand) whoſe husband
Tax'd for his ſowre breath by his Enemy,
Condemn'd his wife, for not acquainting him
With his infirmity?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Tis a common one;
Her anſwer was, having kis'd none but him,
She thought it was a generall diſeaſe
All men were ſubject to; but what infer you
From that my Lord?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Why, that this vertuous Lady
Had all her thoughts ſo fix'd upon her Lord,
That ſhe could finde no ſpare time to ſing praiſes
Of any other; nor would ſhe imploy
Her husband (though perhaps in debt to yeeres
As far as I am) for an inſtrument
To bring home younger men that might delight her
With their diſcourſe, or —

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: What my Lord?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Their perſons,
Or if I ſhoutd ſpeak plainer—

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: No it needs not,
You have ſaid enough to make my innocence know
It is ſuſpected.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: You betray your ſelfe
To more then a ſuſpition; could you elſe
To me that live in nothing but love to you
Make ſuch a groſſe diſcovery, that your luſt
Had ſold that heart I thought mine, to Miranda?
Or riſe to ſuch a height in impudence,
As to preſume to worke my yeelding weakneſſe
To play for your bad ends, to my diſgrace
The Wittall, or the Pander?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Doe not ſtudy
To print more wounds, (for that were tyranny)
Upon a heart that is pierced through already.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Thy heart? thou haſt pierc'd through mine honor falſe one,
The honour of my houſe, foole that I was,
To give it up to the deceiving truſt
Of wicked woman: for thy ſake, vild creature,
For all I have done well in, in my life,
I have dig'd a grave, all buried in a wife;
For thee I have defi'd my conſtant Miſtris,
That never fail'd her ſervant, glorious war;
For thee, refus'd the fellowſhip of an Order
Which Princes through all dangers have been proud
To fetch as far as from Jeruſalem:
And am I thus rewarded?

sp.speaker: Vel.
sp.l: By all goodneſſe,
You wrong my Lady, and deſerve her not,
When you are at your beſt: repent your raſhneſſe,
Twil ſhow well in you.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Do, and aske her pardon.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: No, I have liv'd too long, to have my faith
(My tri'd faith) call'd in queſtion, and by him
That ſhould know true affection is too tender
To ſuffer an unkind touch, without ruine;
Study ingratitude, all, from my example;
For to be thankfull now, is to be falſe.
But be it ſo, let me die, I ſee you wiſh it;
Yet dead for truth, and pities ſake, report
What weapon you made choice of, when you kild me.

sp.speaker: Vel.
sp.l: She faints,

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: What have ye done?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: My laſt breath cannot
Be better ſpent, then to ſay I forgive you;
Nor is my death untimely, ſince with me
I take along, what might have been hereafter
In ſcorn delivered for the doubtfull iſſue
Of a ſuſpected mother.

sp.speaker: Vel.
sp.l: Oh, ſhe's gone.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: For ever gone. Are you a man?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: I grow here.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Open her mouth, and powre tills Cordiall in it;
If any ſpark of life be unquench'd in her,
This will recover her.

sp.speaker: Vel.
sp.l: Tis all in vain,
She's ſtiffe already: live I, and ſhe dead?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: How like a murtherer I ſtand? look up,
And heare me curſe my ſelfe, or but behold
The vengance I wilt take for't Oriana,
And then in peace forſake me: Jealouſie,
Thou loathſome vomit of the fiends below,
What deſperate hunger made me to receive thee
Into my heart, and ſoule? I let thee forth,
And ſo in death finde eaſe; and do's ray fault then
Deſerve no greater puniſhment? no, Ile live
To keep thee for a fury▪ to torment me,
And make me know what hell is on the earth:
All joyes and hopes forſake me; all mens malice,
And all the plagues they can inflict, I wiſh it
Fall thick upon me: Let my teares be laught at,
And may my enemies ſmile to heare me groane,
And dead, may I be pitied of none. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Pray you ſir why was the Ordnance of the Fort Diſcharg'd ſo ſodainly?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Twas the Governours pleaſure,
In honour of the Dane, a cuſtome us'd,
To ſpeake a Souldiers welcome.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Tis a fit one:
But is my Maſter here too?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Three daies ſince.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Might I demand without offence, ſo much,
Is't pride in him (however now a ſlave)
That I am not admitted to his preſence?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: His curteſie to you, and to mankind
May eaſily reſolve you, he is free
From that poore vice which onely empty men
Eſteem a vertue.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What's the reaſon then,
As you imagine, ſir?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Why I will tell you;
You are a woman of a tempting beauty,
And he, however vertuous, as a man
Subject to humane frailties; and how far
They may prevaile upon him, ſhould he ſee you,
He is not ignorant: and therefore chooſes,
With care t'avoyd the cauſe that may produce
Some ſtrange effect, which wil not well keep ranck
With the rare temperance, which is admired
In his life hitherto.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: This much increaſes
My ſtrong deſire to ſee him.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: It ſhould rather
Teach you to thank the Prophet that you worſhip,
That you are ſuch a mans, who though he may
Do any thing which youth and heat of blood
Invites him to, yet dares not give way to them:
Your entertainment's Noble, and not like
Your preſent fortune; and it all thoſe teares
Which made grief lovely in you, in the relation
Of the ſad ſtory, that forc'd me to weep too,
Your husbands hard fate were not counterfeit;
You ſhould rejoyce that you have means to pay
A chaſt life to his memory, and bring to him
Thoſe ſweets, which while he liv'd he could not taſte of:
But if you wantonly beſtow them on
Another man, you offer violence
To him, though dead; and his griev'd ſpirit will ſuffer
For your immodeſt looſneſſe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why, I hope ſir,
My willingneſſe to looke on him, to whom
I owe my life and ſervice, is no proofe
Of any unchaſt purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: So I wiſh too,
And in the confidence it is not, Lady,
I dare the better tell you he will ſee you
This night, in which by him I am commanded,
To bring you to his chamber; to what end
I eaſily ſhould gueſſe, were I Miranda;
And therefore, though I can yeild liitle reaſon,
(But in a generall love to womens goodneſſe)
Why I ſhould be ſo tender of your honour,
I willingly would beſtow ſome counſaile of you,
And would you follow it?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Let me firſt heare it,
And then I can reſolve you.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: My advice then
Is, that you would not, (as moſt Ladies uſe
When they prepare themſelves for ſuc encounters)
Study to adde, by artificiall dreſſings
To native excellence; yours (without help)
But ſeen as it is now, would make a Hermit
Leave his deaths head, & change his after hopes
Of endleſſe comforts for a few ſhort minutes
Of preſent pleaſures; to prevent which, Lady,
Practice to take away from your perfections,
And to preſerve your chaſtity unſtain'd,
The moſt deform'd ſhape that you can put on
To cloud your bodies faire gifts, or your minds,
(It being laboured to ſo chaſte an end)
Will prove the faireſt ornament.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: To take from
The workmanſhip of Heaven, is an offence
As great, as to endeavour to adde to it;
Of which Ile not be guilty: Chaſtity
That lodges in deformity, appeares rather
A mulct impos'd by nature, then a bleſſing;
And tis commendable onely when it conquers,
Though nere ſo oft aſſaulted, in reſiſtance:
For me, Ile therefore ſo diſpoſe my ſelfe,
That if I hold out, it ſhall be with honour;
Or if I yeeld, Miranda ſhall finde ſomething
To make him love his victory. Exit.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: With what cunning
This woman argues for her own damnation?
Nor ſhould I hold it for a miracle,
Since they are all born Sophiſters, to maintaine
That luſt is lawfull, and the end and uſe
Of their creation: would I never had
Hop'd better of her; or could not believe,
Though ſeen the mine, I muſt ever grieve. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Miranda, Norandine, Servants with lights.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Ile ſee you in your chamber. A Table out tow ſtools.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Pray ye no farther:
It is a ceremony I expect not,
I am no ſtranger here, I know my lodging,
And have ſlept ſoundly there, when the Turks Cannon
Playd thick upon't: O 'twas Royall Muſicke,
And to procure a ſound ſleep for a Souldier,
Worth forty of your Fiddles. As you love me
Preſſe it no further.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You will overcome.
Waite on him carefully.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I have tooke ſince ſupper
A rouſe or two too much, and by—
It warms my blood.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You'l ſleep the better for't.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: — on't, I ſhould, had but I a kind wench
To pull my Boot-hoſe off, and warm my night-cap,
There's no charme like it: I love old Adams way;
Give me a diligent Eve, to wait towards bed-time,
Hang up your ſmooth chin page: and now I think on't,
Where is your Turkiſh priſoner?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: In the Caſtle,
But yet I never ſaw her.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Fie upon you:
See her for ſhame? or, hark ye, if you would
Performe the friends part to me, the friends part,
It being a faſhion of the laſt edition,
Far from panderiſme, now ſend her to me;
You look ſtrange on't, no entertainments perfect
Without it on my word; no livery like it;
Ile tell her, he lookes for it as duly
As for his ſee; there's no ſuit got without it,
Gold is an aſſe to't.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Go to bed, to bed.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Well, if ſhe come, I doubt not to convert her,
If not, the ſin lie on your head.
Good night Exit Nor. and Servants.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: There you ſhall findc hint Lady: you know what I have ſaid,
And if you pleaſe you may make uſe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: No doubt ſir.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: From hence I ſhall heare all.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Come hither young one.
Beſhrew my heart, a handſome wench: come neerer,
A very handſome one: doo not you grieve, Sweet,
You are a priſoner?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: The loſſe of liberty
No doubt ſir, is a heavy and ſharpe burden
To them that feele it truly: But your ſervant,
Your humble handmayd, never felt that rigor,
Thanks to that Noble wil: no want, no hunger,
(Companions ſtill to ſlaves) no violence,
Nor any unbeſeeming act, we ſtart at,
Have I yet met with; all content and goodneſſe,
Civility, and ſweetneſſe of behaviour
Dwell round about me; therefore, worthy Maſter,
I cannot ſay I grieve my liberty.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Do not you fancieme too cold a Souldier,
Too obſtinate an enemy to youth,
That had ſo faire a Jewell in my Cabinet,
And in ſo long a time, would nere look on it?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: What can ſhe ſay now?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Sure I deſir'd to ſee ye,
And with a longing wiſh.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: There's all her vertue.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Purſu'd that full deſire to give ye thanks ſir,
The onely Sacrifice I have left, and ſervice
For all the vertuous care you have kept me ſafe with.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: She holds well yet.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: The pretty foole, ſpeaks finely:
Come ſit down here.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: O ſir, tis moſt unſeemly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ile have it ſo: fit cloſe; now tell me truly,
Did you ere love yet?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My yeeres will anſwer that ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And did you then love truly?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: So I thought ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Can ye love me ſo?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Now!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: With all my duty;
I were unworthy of thoſe favours elſe,
You daily ſhowre upon me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What thinkſt thou of me?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I think ye are a truely worthy Gentleman,
A pattern, and a pride to the age ye live in,
Sweet as the commendations all men give ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A pretty flattering rogue; dare ye kiſſe that ſweet man
Ye ſpeak to ſweetly of? Come,

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Farewell vertue.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What haſt thou goe between thy lips? kiſſe once more.
Sure thou haſt a ſpell there.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: More then ere I knew ſir.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: All hopes goe now.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I muſt tell you a thing in your eare, and you muſt heare me,
And heare me willingly, and grant me ſo too,
Twill not be worth my asking elſe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: It muſt be
A very hard thing fir, and from my power,
I ſhall deny your goodneſſe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Tis a good wench; I muſt lie with ye Lady.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Tis ſomething ſtrange:
For yet in all my life I knew no bedfellow.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You will quiekly finde that knowledge.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: To what end ſir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Art thou ſo innocent, thou canſt not gueſſe at it?
Did thy dreams never direct thee?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: 'Faith none yet ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ile tell thee then: I would meet thy youth and pleaſure;
Give thee my youth for that, by Heaven ſhe fires me,
And teach thy faire white armes, like wanton Ives,
A thouſand new embraces,

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Is that all ſir?
And ſay I ſhould try, may not we lie quietly?
Upon my conſcience I could.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That's as we make it.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Grant that, that likes ye beſt, what would ye doe then?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What would I do? certainly, I am no baby,
Nor brought up for a Nun; hark in thine eare.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Fie, fie, ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I wold get a brave boy on thee,
A warlike boy.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Sure we ſhall get ill Chriſtians.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: We'l mend 'em in the breeding then.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Sweet Maſter.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Never beliefe in woman come neere me more.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My beſt and nobleſt ſir, if a poor Virgin,
(For yet by —I am ſo) ſhould change ſo far
(Seeing your excellence, and able ſweetneſſe)
To forget her ſelfe, and ſlip into your boſome,
Or to your bed, out of a doting on ye,
Take it the beſt way; have you that cruell heart,
That murdring mind too?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes by my troth (Sweet) have I,
To lie with her.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: And do you think it wel done?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That's as ſhe'l think when tis done; come to bed wench,
For thou art ſo pretty, and ſo witty a companion,
We muſt not part to night.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Faith let me go ſir,
And think better on't.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Y faith thou ſhalt not;
I warrant thee Ile think on't.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I have heard 'em ſay here,
You are a mayd too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I am ſure I am, wench,
If that will pleaſe thee.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I have ſeen a wonder,
And would you loſe that for a little wantonneſſe,
(Conſider my ſweet Maſter, like a man, now,)
For a few honied kiſſes, ſleight embraces,
That glory of your youth, that crown of ſweetneſſe?
Can ye deliver that unvalued treaſure?
Would ye forſake, to ſeeke your own diſhonour,
What gone, no age recovers, nor repentance?
To a poore ſtranger?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Hold there again, thou art perfect.

sp.speaker: Luc
sp.l: I know you do but try me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And I know
Ile try you a great deale further: prethee to bed;
I love thee, and ſo well: come kiſſe me once more;
Is a maidenhead ill beſtow'd o' me?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What's this ſir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why, tis the badge (my Sweet) of that holy Order
I ſhortly muſt receive, the Croſſe of Malta.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What vertue has it?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: All that we call vertuous.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Who gave it firſt?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: He that gave all, to ſave us.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why then tis holy too?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: True ſign of holineſſe,
The badge of all his Souldiers that profeſſe him.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: The badge of all his ſouldiers that profeſſe him,
Can ſave in dangers?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: In troubles comfort?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You ſay true, ſweet.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: In ſickneſſe, reſtore health?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: All this it can do.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Preſerve from evils, that afflict our frailties.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I hope ſhe will be Chriſtian: all theſe truly.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why are you ſick then, ſick to death with luſt?
In danger to be loſt? no holy thought,
ln all that heart, nothing but wandring frailties
Wild as the wind, and blind as death or ignorance,
Inhabit there.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Forgive me heaven, ſhe ſayes true.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Dare ye profeſſe that badg, prophan that goodnes?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Thou haſt redeemd thy ſelf again, moſt rarely.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: That holines and truth ye make me wonder at?
Blaſt all the bounty heaven gives, that remembrance.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: O excellent woman.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Fling it from ye quickly,
If ye be thus reſolu'd; I ſee a vertue
Appear in't like a ſword, both edges flaming
That wil conſum ye, and your thoughts, to aſhes,
Let them profeſſe it that are pure, and noble,
Gentle, and juſt of thought, that build the croſſe,
Not thoſe that break it, by—if ye touch me,
Even in the act, ile make that croſſe, and curſe ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You ſhall not (fair) I did diſſemble with ye,
And but to try your faith, I faſhioned all this:
Yet ſomething you provoakt me: this fair croſſe,
By me (if he but pleaſe to help, firſt gave it)
Shall ne'r be worne upon a heart corrupted;
Go to your reſt, my modeſt, honeſt ſervant,
My fair, and vertuous maid, and ſleep ſecure there,
For when you ſuffer, I forget this ſigne here.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: A man of men too: O moſt perfect Gentleman!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: All ſweet reſt to your ſir; I am halfe a Chriſtian,
The other half, i'le pray for; then for you, ſir;

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This is the fowleſt play i'le ſhew, good night, ſweet.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: The Sun's not ſet yet?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Would it were,
Never to riſe againe to light the world.
And yet, to what vaine purpoſe do I wiſh it,
Since though I were inviron'd with thick miſts,
Black as Cymerian darkneſſe, or my crimes,
There is that here, upon which, as an anvile
Ten thouſand hammers ſtrike, and every ſpark
They force from it, to me's an other Sun
To light me to my ſhame?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Take hope, and comfort.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: They are aides indeed, but yet as far from me,
As I from being innocent: this cave faſhioned
By provident nature, in this ſolid Rock
To be a den for beaſts, alone, receives me,
And having prov'd an enemy to mankinde,
All humane helpes forſak me.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: I'le ne'r leave you,
And wiſh you would call back that noble courage
That old invicible fortitude of yours
That us'd to ſhrink at nothing.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Then it did not.
But 'twas when I was honeſt; then in the height
Of all my hapineſſe, of all my glories,
Of all delights, that made life pretious to me,
I durſt die Rocca; death it ſelf then to me
Was nothing terrible, becauſe I knew,
The fame of a good Knight woulde ever live
Freſh on my memory; but ſince I fell
From my integrity, and diſmis'd thoſe guards,
Thoſe ſtrong aſſurances of innocence,
That conſtancy fled fron me, and what's worſe,
Now I am loathſome to my ſelf; and life
A burthen to me, rackd with ſad remembrance
Of what I have done, and my preſent horrors
Unſufferable to me, torturd with deſpair
That I ſhall ne'r find mercy; hell about me,
Behind me, and before me, yet I dare not
Still fearing worſe, put off my wretched being. Enter Abdella

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: To ſee this would deterre a doubtfull man
From miſcheivous intents, much more the practiſe
Of what is wicked: here's the Moore, look up ſir,
Some eaſe may come from her.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: New trouble rather,
And I expect it.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Who is this? Mountferrat?
Riſe up for ſhame, and like a river dride up
With a long drought, from me, your bounteous Sea
Receive thoſe tides of comfort, that flow to you;
If ever I lookt lovely, if deſert
Could ever challenge welcom; if revenge,
And unexpected wreak, were ever pleaſing
Or could endear the giver of ſuch bleſſings,
All theſe I come adorn'd with, and as due
Make challenge of thoſe ſo long wiſhd embraces
Which you (unkind) have hitherto denyde me.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Why, what have you done for me?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Made Gomera
As truly miſerable, as you thought him happy,
Could you wiſh more?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: As if his ſickneſſe could
Recover me; the injuries I received
Were Orianas.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: She has paid deer for them,
She's dead.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Dead: my hate could reach no further:
Taking advantage of her in a ſwoon,
Under pretence to give a Cordiall to her
I poyſond her: what ſtupid dulneſſe is this?
What you ſhould entertain with ſacrifice,
Can you receive ſo coldly?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Bloody deeds
Are gratefull offrings, pleaſing to the devill,
And thou, in thy black ſhape, and blacker actions
Being hels perfect character, art delighted
To do what I though infinitly wicked,
Tremble to hear: thou haſt in this tane from me
All meanes to make amends with penitence,
To her wrongd vertues, and diſpoild me of
The poor remainder of that hope was left me,
For all I have already, or muſt ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: I did it for the beſt.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: For thy worſt ends,
And be aſſurd, but that, I think to kill thee
Would but prevent, what thy deſpair muſt force thee
To do unto thy ſelf, and ſo to adde to
Thy moſt aſſur'd damnation, thou went dead now,
But get thee from my ſight: and if luſt of me
Did ever fire thee (love, I cannot call it)
Leap down from thoſe ſteep Rocks, or take advantage
Of the next Tree, to hang thy ſelf, and then
I may laugh at it.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: In the mean time
I muſt be bold, to do ſo much for you, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Mount,
sp.l: Why grinſt thou, devill?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: That 'tis in my power,
To puniſh thy ingratiude; I made triall
But how you ſtood affected, and ſince I know
I am us'd only for a property,
I can, and will revenge it to the full.
For, underſtand, in thy contempt of me
Thoſe hopes of Oriana, which I could
Have changd to certainties, are loſt for ever.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Why, lives ſhe?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Yes, but never to Mountf • rrat,
Although it is in me, with as much eaſe
To give her freely up to thy poſſeſſion,
As to remove this ruſh, which yet deſpaire of,
For by my much wrongd love, flattery, nor threats,
Teares, prayers, nor vowes, ſhall ever win me to it:
So with my curſe, I leave thee.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Prethee ſtay,
Thou knowſt'I doat on thee, and yet thou art
So peeviſh, and perverſe, ſo apt to take
Triffles unkindly from me.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: To perſwade me
To break my neck, to hang, then damn my ſelf,
With you are trifles.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: 'T was my melancholy
That made me ſpeak I know not what: forgive,
I will redem my fault.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Believe him Lady.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: A thouſand times I will demand thy pardon,
And keep the reckoning on thy lips, with kiſſes.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Ther's ſomething els, that would prevaile more with me.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt have all thy wiſhes do but bleſſe me
With meanes to ſatisfie my madde deſires
For once in Oriana, and for ever
I am thine, only thine my beſt Abdella.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Were I aſſur'd of this, and that you would
Having enioyd her.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Any thing: make choice of
Thine own conditions.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Swear then, that performed.
(To free me from all doubts and fears hereafter)
To give me leave to kill her.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: That our ſafety
Muſt of neceſſity urge us to.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Then know
It was not poyſon, but a ſleeping potion
Which ſhe received, yet of ſufficient ſtrength
So to bind up her ſences, that no ſigne
Of life appeard in her, and thus thought dead
In her beſt habit, as the cuſtome is
You know in Malta, with all ceremonies
She's buried in her families monument,
In the Temple of St. Iohn; i'le bring you thither,
Thus, as you are diſguiſd; ſome ſix howers hence
The potion will leave working.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Let us haſte then. Diſcover Tombe

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Be my good angel, guid me.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: But remember
You keep your Oath.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: As I deſire to proſper
In what I undertak.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: I ask no more. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Here ſir, I have got the Key, I borrowd it
Of him that keeps the Church, the door is open.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Look to the horſes then, and pleaſe the fellow.
After a few devotions, i'le retire.
Be not far off, there may be ſome uſe of ye,
Give me the light: come friend, a few good prayers
Were not beſtowd in vaine now, even from you ſir.
Men that are bred in blood, have no way left 'em,
No bath, no purge, no time to weare it out
Or waſh it off, but penitence, and prayer:
I am to take the order, and my youth
Loaden I muſt confeſſe with many follies,
Circled and bound about with ſins as many
As in the houſe of memory live figures.
My heart i'le open now, my faults confeſſe.
And riſe a new man, heaven I hope, to a new life.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I have no great devotion, at this inſtant,
But for a prayer or two, I will not out ſir,
Hold up your finger, when you have praid enough.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Go you to that end.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I ſhall ne'r pray alone ſure,
sp.p: I have bin ſo us'd to anſwer the Clerk: would I had a cuſhion, for I ſhall ne'r make a good Hermit, and knee till my knees are horn, theſe ſtones are plaguy hard where ſhal I begin now? for if I do not obſerve a method, I ſhall be out preſently.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Whats that ſir? did ye heare?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ha; to your prayers.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: 'Twas here abouts, t'has put me clean awry now,
I ſhall ne'r get in again, ha, by Land,
And water, all children, and all women,
I there it was I left.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Never tell me ſir,
Here's ſomething got amongſt us.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I heard a groane:
A diſmall one,—Ori. Oh, Oh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Here, tis here ſir, 'tis here ſir;
A devill in the wall.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Tis ſome illuſion
To fright us from devotion—Ori. Oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Why tis here,
The ſpirit of a hunteſman choakd with butter,
Her's a new tomb, new trickments too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: For certaine,
This has not bin three dayes here.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: And a Tablet
With rimes upon't.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I prethee read 'em Norandine.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: An Epi—and Epi—taff. I think 'tis, I 'tis taff, an Epitaff.
Upon the moſt excell, excell—lent—and.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou canſt not read.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I have ſpoild imine eyes with gunpowder,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: An Epitaph upon the moſt vertuous, and excellent Lady
