The honor of Chaſtity, Oriana.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: The grand maſters ſiſter: how a devil came ſhe here?
When ſlipt ſhe out oth'way, the ſtone's but half upon her.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Tis is a ſodain chang: certain the miſchiefe
Mountferrat offerd to her broak her heart-ſtrings.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Would he were here, I would be the clerk my ſelf,
And by this little light. I would bury him alive here,
Her's no lamenting now.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: There tis.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Sure from the monument, the very ſtone groanes for her.
Oh, deer Lady: bleſſing of women, vertue of thy ſex;
How art thou ſet for ever, how ſtolne from us.
Babling, and prating now converſe with women.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Sir it riſes, it looks up. She riſes up.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Heaven bleſſe us.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: It is in womans cloathes, it riſes higher.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: It looks about, and wonders, ſure ſhe lives ſir.
Tis ſhe, tis Oriana, tis that Lady.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Shall I go to her?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Where am I!

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Stand ſtill.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: What place is this?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: She is as live as I am.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: What ſinell of earth, and rotten bones, what dark place.
Lord, whether am I carried?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: How ſhe ſtares,
And ſets her eyes upon him.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How is't deer Lady?
Do you know me, how ſhe ſhakes?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: You are a man.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A man that honours you.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: A cruell man,
Ye are all cruell: are you in your grave too?
For ther's no truſting cruell man, above ground.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Byr' Lady, that goes hard.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: To do your ſervice
And to reſtore ye to the joyes you were in.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I was in joyes indeed, and hope—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: She ſincks againe
Again ſhe is gon; ſhe is gon: gon as a ſhadow,
She ſinks for ever, friend.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: She is cold now,
She is certainly departed, I muſt cry too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: The bleſſed angels guide thee: put the ſtone too,
Beauty thou art gon to duſt, goodneſſe to aſhes.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Pray take it well: we muſt all have our houres ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I, thus we are; and all our painted glory,
A buble that a boy blowes in toth' ayre,
And there it breaks.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I am glad ye ſav'd her honour yet.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Would I had ſav'd her life now too: oh heaven
For ſuch a bleſſing, ſuch a timely bleſſing
O friend, what deer content 't would be, what ſtory
To keep my name from wormes?

sp.speaker: Oria
sp.l: Oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: She lives again,
'Twas but a trance.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Pray ye call my man in preſently
Help with the ſtone firſt, oh ſhe ſtirs againe.
Oh call my man away.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I fly, I fly ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Upon my knees O heaven, O heaven I thank thee. The living heat ſteales into every member; En. Colonn. & Come help the Coffin out, ſoftly, and ſodainly Norand. VVhere is the Clerk?.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Drunk above, he is ſure ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Sirah, you muſt be ſecret.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: As your ſoule ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Softly good friend, take her into your armes.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Put in the cruſt againe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And bring her out there when I am a horſeback
My man, and I will tenderly conduct her
Unto the Fort; ſlay you, and watch what iſſue,
And what inquirie's for the body.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Well ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And when ye have done, come back to me.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Softly, oh ſoftly.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: She growes warmer ſtill ſir.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: What ſhall I do with' Key?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou canſt not ſtir now,
Leave it ith' door: go get the horſes ready. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: The door's already open, the Key in it. En. Rocca Mountferrat Abdella. With a dark lanthorn.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: What were thoſe paſt by?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Some ſcout of Souldiers, I think.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: It may be well ſo, for I ſaw their horſes,
They ſaw not us I hope.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: No, no, we were cloſe,
Beſide they were far off.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: What time of night is't?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Much about twelve I think.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Let me go in firſt
For by the leaving open of the door here
There may be ſome body in the Church: give me the Lanthorne.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: You'l love me now I hope.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Make that good to me
Your promiſe is engaged for.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Why ſhe is there
Ready prepar'd, and much about this time
Life will look up again.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Come in all's ſure,
Not a foot ſtirring, nor a tongue.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Heaven bleſſe me,
I never enter'd with ſuch unholy thoughts
This place before.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Ye are a fearfull foole,
If men have appetites allow'd 'em,
And warm deſires, are there not ends too for 'em?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Whether ſhall we carry her?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Why, to the bark, ſir,
I have provided one already waites us
The wind ſtands wondtrous fair too for our paſſge.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: And there, when ye'have enjoyd her, for ye have that liberty
Let me alone to ſend her to feed fiſhes,
I'le no more ſighes for her.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Where is the monument?
Thou art ſure ſhe will awake about this time?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Moſt ſure, If ſhe be not knockt oth'head: give me the Lanthorn,
Here 'tis, how is this, the ſtone off?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: I, and nothing
Within the monument, that's worſe, no body
I am ſure of that, nor ſigne of any here,
But an empty Coffin.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: No Lady.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: No, nor Lord ſir,
This Pye has bin cut up before.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Either the Devill
Muſt doe theſe tricks—

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Or thou, damn'd one, worſe;
Thou black ſwoln pitchie cloud, of all my afflictions:
Thou night hag, gotten when the bright Moone ſufferd
Thou hell it ſelf confin'd in fleſh: what trick now?
Tell me, and tell me quickly what thy miſchief
Has done with her, and to what end, and whether
Thou haſt remov'd her body, or by this holy place
This ſword ſhall cut thee into thouſand peeces.
A thouſand thouſand, ſtrow thee ore the Temple
A ſacrifice to thy black ſire, the Devill.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Tell him, you ſee he's angry.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Let him burſt,
Neither his ſword, nor anger do I ſhake at,
Nor will yeild to feed his poor ſuſpitions,
His idle jealouzies, and madde dogs heares
One thought againſt my ſelf: ye have done a brave deed
A manly, and a valiant peece of Service
When ye have kill'd me; reckon't amongſt your Battels:
I am ſorry ye are ſo poore, ſo weake a gentleman
Able to ſtand no fortune: I diſpoſe of her?
My miſchiefe make her away? a likely project,
I muſt play booty againſt my ſelfe, if any thing croſſe ye
I am the devill, and the devils heire,
All plagues, all miſchiefes.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Will I ye leave and doe yet?

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I have done too much,
For, far too much for ſuch a thankleſſe fellow,
If I be devill, you created me,
I never knew thoſe arts, nor bloody practiſes
(— o' your cunning heart, that mine of miſchiefe)
Before your flatteries won 'em into me,
Here did I leave her, leave her with that certainty
About this houre to wake again.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Where is ſhe?
This is the laſt demand.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Did I now know it,
And were I ſure, this were my lateſt minute
I would not tell thee: ſtrike, and then i'le curſe thee:

sp.speaker: Rocca
sp.l: I ſee a light, ſtand cloſe, and leave your angers.
We all miſcarry elſe. Enter Gomera, Page with Torch.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I am now careleſſe,

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Peace, prethee peace, ſweet, peace, all friends,

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Stand cloſe then.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Waite there Boy, with the light, till I call to thee,
In darkneſſe was my ſoule and ſences clouded
When my faire Jewell fell, the night of jealouſie,
In all her blackneſſe drawn about my judgement:
No light was let into me: to diſtinguiſh
Betwixt my ſuddain anger and her honour,
A blinde ſad Pilgrimage ſhall be my pennance,
No comfort of the day will I looke up at:
Far darker then my jealous Ignorance
Each place of my aboad ſhall do my: prayers
No ceremonious lights ſhall ſet off more;
Bright Armes, and all that carry luſtre, life,
Society, and ſollace, I forſake ye.
And were it not once more to ſee her beauties
(For in her bed of death, ſhe muſt be ſweet ſtill,)
And on her cold ſad lips ſeal my repentance;
Thou child of heaven, faire light I could not miſſe thee.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.p: I know the tongue, would I were out againe I have done him too much wrong to looke upon him.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: There is no ſhifting now, boldneſſe, and confidence
Muſt carry it now away: he is but one neither,
Naked as you are, of a ſtrength far under

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: But he has a cauſe above me,

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: That's as you handle it.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Peace: he may goe againe, and never ſee us.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: I feele I weepe apace, but where's the flood,
The torrent of my teares, to drown my fault in,
I would I could now like a loaden cloud
Begotten in the moyſt ſouth, drop to nothing
Give me the Torch, Boy.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Now he muſt diſcover us.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: He has already, never hide your head
Be bold, and brave, if we muſt dye together.

sp.speaker: Gom:
sp.l: Who's there? what friend to ſorrow? The Tombe wide open
The Stone off too? the body gone, by —
Looke to the doore Boy: keep it faſt, who are ye?
What ſacrilegious villaines? falſe Mountferrat,
The wolfe to honour, has thy helliſh hunger,
Brought thee to tear the body out oth'tomb too?
Has thy foule mind ſo far wrought on thee? ha,
Are you there too? nay, then I ſpie a villany
I never dream't of yet, thou ſinfull uſher
Bred from that rottenneſſe, thou bawd to miſchiefe,
Doe you bluſh through all your blackneſſe? will not that hide it?

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I cannot ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: You are well met, with your dam, ſir,
Art thou a Knight? did ever on that ſword,
The Chriſtian cauſe ſit nobly? could that hand fight,
Guided by fame, and fortune? that heart inflame thee,
With vertuous fires of valour, to fall off,
Fall off ſo ſuddainly, and with ſuch fouleneſſe,
As the falſe Angels did, from all their glory?
Thou art no Knight, honour thou never heard'ſt of,
Nor brave deſires could ever build in that breaſt,
Treaſon, and tainted thoughts, are all the Gods
Thou worſhip'ſt, all the ſtrength thou hadſt: and fortune;
Thou didſt things out of feare, and falſe heart, villaine
Out of cloſe traps and treacheries, they have rais'd thee.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Thon rav'ſt old man.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Before thou get'ſt off from me,
Had'ſt thou the glory of thy firſt fights on thee
Which thou haſt baſely loſt, thy nobleſt fortunes,
And in their greateſt luſtres, I would make thee
Before we part, confeſſe, nay, kneele, and doe it,
Nay, crying kneele, coldly for mercy, crying:
Thou art the recreant'ſt Rogue, time ever nouriſh'd,
Thou art a dogge, I will make thee ſweare, a dog ſtav'd,
A mangy Cur-dogge; doe you creep behind the Altar?
Looke how it ſweats, to ſhelter ſuch a raſcall;
Firſt, with thy venemous tooth infect her chaſte life,
And then not dare to doe; next, rob her reſt,
Steale her dead body out oth' grave.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I have not.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.p: Prethee come out, this is no place to quarrell in, Valiant Mountferrat come,

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I will not ſtir.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Thou haſt thy ſword about thee,
That good ſword, that never fail'd thee: prethee come,
We'l have but five ſtroakes for it, on, on Boy,
Here's one would faine be acquainted with thee,
Would wondrous fain cleave that Calves-head of yours ſir,
Come, prethee let's diſpatch, the Moone ſhines finely:
Prethee be kill'd by me, thou wilt be hang'd elſe,
But it may be, thou long'ſt to be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Out with him, Sir,
You ſhall have my ſword too: when he's diſpatch'd once
We have the world before us.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Wilt thou walke fellow,
I never knew a Rogue, hang arſe-ward ſo,
And ſuch a deſperate knave too.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Pray goe with him,
Something I'le promiſe too,

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: You would be kill'd then?
No remedy; I ſee,

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: If thou dar'ſt doe it?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.p: Yes, now I dare; lead out, i'le follow preſently Vnder the Mount i'le meet ye.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Goe before me,
He have ye in a ſtring too.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: As I am a Gentleman,
And by this holy place, I will not faile thee,
Feare not, thou ſhalt be kill'd, take my word for it
I will not faile.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: If thou ſeap'ſt thou haſt Cats luck,
The Mount?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: The ſame: make haſte, I am there before elſe.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Goe get ye home; now if he ſcape I am Cowar'd.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Well, now I am reſolv'd, and he ſhall finde it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How is it with the Lady?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Sir, as well
As it can be with one, who feeling knowes now
What is the curſe the divine juſtice lay'd
On the firſt ſinfull woman.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Is ſhe in travell?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Yes ſir; and yet the troubles of her mind
Afflict her more, then what her body ſuffers,
For in the extremity of her paine, ſhe cries out,
Why am I here? Where is my Lord Gomera,
Then ſometimes names Miranda, and then ſighes,
As if to ſpeake, what queſtionleſſe ſhe loves well,
If heard, might doe her injury.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Heavens ſweet mercy
Looke gently on her,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Prethee tell her, my Prayers
Are preſent with her, and good wench provide
That ſhe want nothing: what's thy name?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Lucinda? there's a proſperous omen in it,
Bea Lucina to her, and bring word
That ſhe is ſafe delivered of her burthen,
And thy rewards thy liberty: come Collonna,
We will goe ſee how th' Engineer has mounted
The Canon the great Maſter ſent, be carefull.
To view the workes, and learn the diſcipline
That is us'd here: I am to leave the world
And for your ſervice, which I have found faithfull.
The charge that's mine, if I have any power
Hereafter may concerne you.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: I ſtill finde
A noble Maſter in you,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis but juſtice,
sp.p: Thou do'ſt deſerve it in thy care, and duty. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena quarta.
div.stage: Enter Gomera, Mountferrat, Rocca, Abdella, with a Piſtoll.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.p: Here's even ground, i'le ſtir no foot beyond it, Before I have thy head.

sp.speaker: Maunt.
sp.l: Draw Rocca.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Coward,
Hath inward guilt, rob'd thee as well of courage
As honeſty? that without oddes thou dar'ſt not
Anſwer a ſingle Enemy?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: All advantage
That I can take, expect.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: We know you are valiant,
Nor doe we purpoſe to make further triall
Of what you can doe now: but to diſpatch you.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: And therefore fight, and pray together.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Villaines,
Whoſe baſeneſſe, all diſgracefull words made one,
Cannot expreſſe; ſo ſtrong is the good cauſe
That ſeconds me, that you ſhall feele, with horrour
To your proud hopes, what ſtrength is in that arme,
Though old, that holds a ſwor made ſharp by juſtice.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: You come then here, to prate? fight.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Helpe Rocca, now,
Or I am loſt forever; how comes this?
Are villany, and weakneſſe twynes?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: I am gone too.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: You ſhall not ſcape me, wretches,

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I muſt doe it,
All will goe wrong elſe. ſhoots him

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Treacherous bloody woman,
What haſt thou done?

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Done a poor womans part,
And in an inſtant, what theſe men ſo long
Stood fooling for.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: This aide was unexpected,
I kiſſe thee for't,

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: His right armes onely ſhot,
And that compell'd him to forſake his ſword,
He's elſe unwounded.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Cut his throat.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Forbeare.
Yet doe not hope 'tis with intent to ſave thee.
But that thou maiſt live to thy farther torment
To ſee who triumphes over thee: come Mountferrat,
Here joyne thy foot to mine, and let our hearts
Meet with our hands, the contract that is made
And cemented with blood, as this of ours is,
Is a more holy ſanction, and much ſurer,
Then all the ſuperſtitious ceremonies Enter Norandine.
You Chriſtians uſe.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Who's this?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Betray'd againe?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: By the report it made, and by the wind
The Piſtoll was diſcharged here.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: As ever thou lov'ſt valour, or wear'ſt Armes
To puniſh baſeneſſe, ſhew it.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: O the devill,
Gomera wounded, and my Brache black beauty
An actor in it?

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: If thou ſtrik'ſt, i'le ſhoot thee.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: How? fright me with your Pot-gun? what art thou?
Good heaven, the Rogue, the traytor rogue Mountferrat
To ſwinge the neaſt of you, is a ſport unlook'd for,
Hels— conſume you.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: As thou art a man;
I am wounded, give me time to anſwer thee.

sp.speaker: Go.
sp.l: Durſt thou urge this? this hand can hold a ſword yet.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Well done: to ſee this villaine, makes my hurts
Bleed freſh againe, but had I not a bone whole,
In ſuch a cauſe I ſhould doe thus, thus Raſcals. Enter Corporall and watch.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Diſarme them, and ſhoot any that reſiſts.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Hold Corporall; I am Gomera,

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Tis well yet, that once in an age you can
Remember what you watch for; I had thought
You had again been making out your parties
For ſucking piggs.
'Tis well:

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: As you will anſwer
The contrary with your lives, ſee theſe forth coming.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: That we ſhall doe.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: You bleed a pace: good Souldiers
Goe helpe him to a Surgeon,

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Dare the worſt,
And ſusser like your ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: From me learne courage.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Now for Miranda, this newes will be to him
As welcome, as 'tis unexpected: Corporall,
There's ſomething for thy care to night: my horſe there.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: How do's my Boy?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Oh, wondrous luſty, Madam,
A little Knight already: you ſhall live
To ſee him toſſe a Turke.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Gentle Lucinda,
Much muſt I thank thee for thy care, and ſervice.
And may I grow but ſtrong to ſee Ʋaletta, Enter Miranda, Norandine, Collonna.
My husband, and my brother, thou ſhalt finde
I will not barely thank thee.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Looke Captaine, we muſt ride away this mornning
The Auberge ſits to day, and the great Maſter
Writes plainly, I muſt or deliver in
(The yeere expir'd) my probation weed,
Or take the Cloake: you likewiſe Norandine
For your full ſervice, and your laſt aſſiſtance
In falſe Mountferrats apprehenſion
Are here commanded to aſſociate me; my twin in this high honour.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.p: Ile none on't: doe they think to bind me to live chaſte, ſober, and temperately, all dayes of my life? they may as ſoone tye an Engliſhman to live ſo: I ſhall be a ſweet Dane, a ſweet Captaine, goe up and downe drinking ſmall beere, and ſwearing odds neagues; no Ile live a Squire at Armes ſtill, and doe thou ſo too; and thou beeſt wiſe: I have found the myſtery now, why the Gentlemen weare but three barres of the croſſe, and the knights the whole one.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why Captaine?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.p: Mary ſir, to put us in remembrance, we are but three quarters croſs'd in our licence, and pleaſures: but the poore Knights croſs'd altogther; the brothers at Armes, may yet meet with their Siſters at Armes, now and then, in brotherly love; but the poore Knights cannot get a Lady for love, nor money: 'tis not ſo in other Countries I wis, pray haſte you, for i'le along, and ſee what will come on't. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Collonna, provide ſtrait, all neceſſaries
For this remove, the Lytter for the Lady,
And let Lucinda beare her company,
You ſhall attend on me.

sp.speaker: Coll.
sp.l: With all my duties Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How fare you, gracious Miſtreſſe?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: O Miranda.
You pleas'd to honour me with that faire title
When I was free, and could diſpoſe my ſelfe;
But now, no ſmile, no word, no looke, no touch
Can I impart to any, but as theft
From my Gomera; and who dares accept,
Is an unſurper.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Leave us; I have touch'd thee,
(Thou fairer vertue, then thou'rt beautifull)
Hold but this teſt, ſo rich an one was never Altar ready, Tapers & booke
Try'd by the hand of man, on the vaſt earth:
Sit brighteſt Oriana, is it ſinne
Still to profeſſe I love you, ſtill to vow
I ſhall doe ever? heaven my witneſſe be,
'Tis not your eye, your cheeke, your tongue, no part
That ſuperficially doth ſnare young men,
Which has caught me; read over in your thoughts
The ſtory that this man hath made of you,
And thinke upon his merit.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Onely thought
Can comprehend it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And can you be ſo
Cruell, thankeleſſe, to deſtroy his youth
That ſav'd your honour, gave you double life?
Your own, and your faire Infants? that when fortune
(The blind foe to all beauty, that is good,)
Bandied you from one hazard to another,
Was even heavens Meſſenger, by providence
Call'd to the Temple, to receive you there,
Into theſe Armes, to give eaſe to your throwes,
As if't had thunder'd; take thy due Miranda,
For ſhe was thine; Gomera's jealouſie
Strooke death unto thy heart; to him be dead,
And live to me, that gave thee ſecond life:
Let me but now enjoy thee: Oh regard
The torturing fires of my affections.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh maſter them, Miranda, as I mine;
Who follows his deſires, ſuch tyrants ſerves
As will oppreſſe him, inſupportably.
My flames, Miranda, riſe as high as thine,
For I did love thee 'fore my marriage,
Yet would I now conſent, or could I think
Thou wert in earneſt, (which by all the ſoules
That have (for chaſtity) been ſanctified
I cannot) in a moment I doe know
Thou'ldſt call faire temperance up to rule thy blood,
Thy eye was ever chaſte, thy countenance too honeſt,
And all thy woings was like maidens talk;
Who yeeldeth unto pleaſures, and to luſt
Is a poore captive, that in Golden Fetters
(And pretious (as he thinkes) but holding gyves)
Frets out his life.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Find ſuch another woman,
And take her for his labour, any man:

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I was not worthy of thee, at my beſt,
Heaven knew I was not, I had had thee elſe;
Much leſſe now gentle ſir; Mirandas deeds
Have been as white, as Orianas fame,
From the beginning, to this point of time,
And ſhall we now begin to ſtaine both thus?
Think on the legend which we two ſhall breed
Continuing as we are, for chaſteſt dames
And boldeſt Souldiers to peruſe and read,
I and read thorough, free from any act
To cauſe the modeſt caſt the booke away,
And the moſt honour'd Captaine fold it up.

sp.speaker: Mir;
sp.l: Faireſt; let goe my hand: my pulſe beats thick,
And my mov'd blood rides high in every vaine,
Lord of thy ſelfe now, Souldier, and ever:
I would not for Aleppo, this fraile Bark,
This barke of fleſh, no better fleeres-man had
Then has Mountferrat's: may you kiſſe me, Lady?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: No; though't be no eſſentiall injury,
It is a circumſtance due to my Lord,
To none elſe: and my deereſt friend, if hands
Playing together, kindle heate in you,
What may the game at lips provoke unto?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Oh what a tongue is here? whil'ſt ſhe doth teach
My heart to hate my fond unlawfull love,
She talkes me more in love, with love to her,
My fires ſhe quencheth with her arguments,
But as ſhe breathes 'em, they blow freſher fires.
Sir further: now my flame cooles; husband, wife,
There is ſome holy myſtery in thoſe names
That ſure the unmarried cannot underſtand.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Now thou art ſtrait, and do'ſt enamour me,
So far beyhnd a carnall earthly love;
My very ſoule doats on thee, and my ſpirits
Doe embrace thine, my minde doth thy mind kiſſe,
And in this pure conjunction we enjoy
A heavenlyer pleaſure then if bodies met:
This, this is perfect love, the other ſhort,
Yet languiſhing fruition, every Swaine
And ſweating Groome may claſp, but our's refinde
Two in ten ages cannot reach unto;
Nor is our ſpirituall love, a barren joy,
For mark what bleſſed iſſue we'll beget,
Deerer then children to poſterity,
A great example to mens continence,
And womens chaſtity, that is a childe
More faire, and comfortable, then any heire.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: If all wives were but ſuch, luſt would not finde
One corner to inhabit, ſinne would be
So ſtrange, remiſſion ſuperfluous:
But one petition, I have done.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: What (Sweet?).

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: To call me Lord, if the hard hand of death ſeize on Gomera firſt.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh, much too worthy;
How much you undervalue your own price,
To give your unbought ſelfe, for a poore woman,
That has been once ſold, us'd, and loſt her ſhow?
I am a garment worne, a veſſell crack'd,
A zoane untide, a Lilly trod upon,
A fragrant flowre cropt by anothers hand,
My colour ſullyde, and my odour chang'd,
If when I was new bloſſom'd, I did feare
My ſelfe unworthy of Mirandas ſpring:
Thus over-blown, and ſeeded, I am rather
Fit to adorn his Chimney, then his bed.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Riſe miracle: ſave Malta, with thy vertue,
If words could make me proud, how has ſhe ſpoke,
Yet I will try her to the very block:
Hard-hearted, and uncivill Oriana,
Ingratefull payer of my induſtries,
That with a ſoft painted hypocriſie
Cozen'ſt, and geer'ſt my perturbation,
Expect a witty, and a fell revenge:
My comfort is, all men will thinke thee falſe,
Beſide thy husband having been thus long Enter Nor. Collonna & Lucinda with a Childe.
(on this occaſion) in my Fort, and power.
Ile heare no more words: Captaine, let's away
With all care ſee to her: and you Lucinda
Attend her diligently: ſhe is a wonder.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Have you found ſhe was well delivered:
What, had ſhe a good Mid-wife, is all well?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You are merry Norandine.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why weepe you, Lady?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Take the poor Babe along.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Madam 'tis here.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Diſſembling death, why didſt thou let me live
To ſee this change, my greateſt cauſe to grieve? Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena ſecunda.
div.stage: Enter Aſtorius, Caſtriot, Valetta, Gomera, Synnet: Knights, 2 Biſhops, Mountferrat, guarded by Corporall and Souldiers, Abdella, a Gentleman with a cloake, ſword, and Spurres: Gomara.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: A tender husband haſt thou ſhew'd thy ſelfe
My deereſt brother, and thy memory
After my life, in brazen Characters,
Shall monumentally be regiſter'd
To ages conſequent, till times running hand,
Beats back the world to undiſtinguiſh'd Chaos,
And on the top of that thy name ſhall ſtand
Freſh, and without decay.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Oh honour'd ſir!
If hope of this, or any bliſſe to come
Could lift my load of griefe off from my ſoule,
Or expiate the treſpaſſe' gainſt my wife,
That in one houres ſuſpition I begat,
I might be won to be a man againe,
And fare like other husbands, ſleepe and eate,
Laugh, and forget my pleaſing penitence;
But till old nature can make ſuch a wife
Againe, I vow ne're to reſume the order
And habits, that to men are neceſſary,
All breath i'le ſpend in ſighes, all ſound in groanes,
And know no company but my waſting moans.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: This will be wilfull murder on your ſelf,
Nor like a Chriſtian doe you beare the chance
Which th'inſcrutable will of heaven admits.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: What would you have my weakneſſe doe, that
Suffer'd it ſelfe thus to be practis'd on,
By a damn'd hell-hound, and his agent dam,
The impious mid-wife to obortive birthes,
And cruell inſtrument to his decrees?
By forgery they firſt aſſail'd her life,
Heaven playing with us yet, in that, he wrought
My deereſt friend, the ſervant to her vertue
To combat me, againſt his Miſtreſſe truth.
That yet effectleſſe, this enchanting witch,
Bred banefull jealouſie againſt my Lady,
My moſt immaculate Lady, which ſeiz'd on her
Almoſt to death: Oh yet! not yet content,
She in my hand put (to reſtore her life
As I imagin'd) what did execute
Their devilliſh malice, farther, great with childe,
Was this poore innocent, that too was loſt,
They doubled death upon her, not ſtaying there,
They have done violence unto her Tomb,
Not granting reſt unto her in the grave:
I wiſh Miranda had injoy'd my prize;
For ſure I'm puniſh'd for uſurping her,
Oh what a Tyger is reſiſted Luſt?
How it doth forrage all?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Part of this tale
I grant you true; but 'twas not poyſon given her.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I would it had, we had been farre enough,
If we had been ſo wiſe, and had not now
Stood curtſing for your mercies here.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Beſide,
What is become oth' body? we know not.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Peace impudents,
And deere Gomera practiſe patience
As I my ſelf muſt, by ſome meanes at laſt
We ſhall diſſolve this riddle.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Wherefore comes
This villaine in the feſtivall array,
As if he triumph'd for his treacherie?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: That is by our appointment: give us leave,
You ſhall know why a non. Enter Miranda, Norandine, Collona.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: One of the Eſguard.

sp.speaker: Eſg.
sp.l: The Gentlemen are come,

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Truyce then a while
With our ſad thoughts; what are you both reſolv'd?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Not I my Lord: your downe right Captain ſtill
Ile live, and ſerve you, not that altogether
I want compunction of conſcience,
I have enough to ſave me, and that's all,
Bar me from drink, and drabs, ev'n hang me too,
You muſt ev'n make your Captaines capons firſt,
I have too much fleſh for this ſpirituall Knighthood,
And therefore do deſire forbearance, ſir,
Till I am older, or more mortifide,
I am too ſound yet.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: What ſay you Miranda?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: With all pure zeale to Heaven, duty to you,
I come to undergo it.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: Proceed toth' ceremony.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Before you match with this bright honor'd title,
Admir'd Miranda, pardon what in thought
I ever did tranſgreſſe againſt your vertue,
And may you find more joy with your new bride
Then poor Gomera ere in joyd with his.
But 'twas mine own crime, and I ſuffer for't:
Long wear your dignity, and worthily,
Whilſt I obſcurely in ſome corner vaniſh,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Have ſtronger thoughts, and better, firſt I crave
According to the order of the Court
I may diſpoſe my captives, and the fort,
That with a clean and purified heart
The fittiler I may endue my roabe.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Tis granted. Enter Oriana vaild, Ladies, Lucinda, child.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Bring the captives. To your charge
And ſtaid tuition my moſt noble friend;
I then commend this Lady; ſtart not off
A fairer, and a chaſter never liv'd;
By her own choyce you are her Guardian,
For telling her I was to leave my fort,
And to abandon quite all worldly cares.
Her own requeſt was, to Gomeras hands
She might be given in cuſtody, for ſh'ad heard
He was a Gentleman wiſe, and temperate,
Full of humanity to womenkind,
And cauſe he had bin married knew the better
How to entrat a Lady.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: What Country woman is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Borne a Greek.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Gomera, 'twill be barbarous to deny
A Lady, that unto your refuge flyes,
And ſeekes to ſhrowd her under vertues wing.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Excuſe me noble ſir; oh think me not
So dull a devill, to forget the loſſe
Of ſuch a matchleſſe wife as I poſſes'd,
And ever to endure the ſight of woman:
Were ſhe the abſtract of her ſex for forme,
The only warehouſe of perfection,
Where there no Roſe, nor Lilly but her Cheek,
No Muſick but her tongue; vertue but hers;
She muſt not reſt near me, my vow is graven,
Here in my heart, irrevocably breath'd
And when I break it,

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: This is rudeneſſe Spaniard,
Unſeaſonably you play the Timoniſt,
Put on a diſpoſition is not yours,
Which neither fits you, nor becomes you.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: We cannot force you but we would perſwade.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Beſeech you Sir, no more I am reſolv'd
To forſake Malta, tread a Pilgrimage
To faire Jeruſalem, for my Ladies ſoule,
And will not be diverted.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You muſt beare
This Child along 'we then.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: VVhat Child?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: How's this?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Nay then Gomera, thou art injurious,
This child is thine, and this rejected Lady
Thou haſt as often known, as thine own wife,
And this I'le make good on thee, with my ſword.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Thou durſt as well blaſpheme: if ſuch a ſcandall
(I crave the rights due to a Gentleman)
Women unvaile.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Will you refuſe me yet?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: My wife!

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: My ſiſter!

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Some body, thank Heaven
I cannot ſpeak.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: All praiſe be ever given:

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: This ſaves our lives, yet would ſhe had bin dead;
The very ſight of her afflicts me more
Then fear of puniſhment, or my diſgrace.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: How came you to the Temple?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Sir, to do
My poor devotions, and to offer thanks
For ſcaping a temptation ne'r perform'd
VVith this faire virgin. I reſtore a wife
Earth cannot paralell: and buſie nature
If thou wilt ſtill make women, but remember
To work 'em by this ſampler; take heed ſir,
Henceforth you never doubt ſir.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: VVhen I do
Death take me ſodainly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: To encreaſe your happineſſe
To your beſt wife, take this addition.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Alack, my poor knave.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: The confeſſion
The Moor made 't ſeemes was truth.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.p: Mary was it ſir; the only truth that ever iſſud out of hell, which her black jawes reſemble; a plague o' your bacon-face, you muſt be giving drinks with a vengance; ah thou branded bitch: do'ye ſtare, gogles, I hope to make winter bootes o' thy hide yet, ſhe feares not damning: hell fire cannot parch her blacker then ſhe is: do'ye grin, chimney ſweeper.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: VVhat is't Mranda?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That you would pleaſe Lucinda might attend you.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: That ſuit ſir, I conſent not to.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My husband?
My deereſt Angelo?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: More liggam bobs; is not this the fellow that ſwom
Like a duck to th'ſhoare in our ſea-ſervice?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: The very ſame, do not you know me now ſir,
My name is Angelo, though Colonna vaild it,
Your Countryman, and kinſman born in Florence,
VVho from the neighbour Iſland here of Goza
VVhas captive lead, in that unfortunate day
VVhen the Turk bore with him three thouſand ſoules;
Since in Conſtantinople have I liv'd
VVhere I beheld this Turkiſh Damoſell firſt.
A tedious ſuitor was I for her love,
And pittying ſuch a beauteous caſe ſhould hide
A ſoule prophan'd with infidelity,
I labourd her converſion with my love,
And doubly won her, to faire faith her ſoule
She firſt betroth'd, and then her faith to me,
But fearfull there to conſummate this contract
VVe fled, and in that flight were tane againe
By thoſe ſame Gallies, fore Valletta fought.
Since in your ſervice I attended her,
VVhere, what I ſaw, and heard, hath joy'd me more
Then all my paſt afflictions greiv'd before.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: Wonders crown wonders: take thy wife Miranda.
Be henceforth called our Malta's better angell,
And thou her evill Mountferrat.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.p: Wee'l call him Cacodemon, with his block gib there, his Succuba, his devils ſeed, his ſpawn of Phlegeton, that o' my conſcience was bred o' the ſpume of Cocitus; do ye ſnarle you black jill? ſhe looks lie the Picture of America.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Why ſtay we now.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This laſt petition to the Court,
I may bequeath the keeping of my Fort
To this my kinſman, toward the maintenance
Of him, and his faire vertuous wife; diſcreet,
Loyall, and valiant I dare give him you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: You muſt not ask in vaine, ſir.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: My beſt thanks
To you my noble Cozen, and my ſervice
To the whole Court; may I deſerve this bounty.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: Proceed to th'ceremony, one of our Eſguard
Degrade Mountferrat firſt

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I will not ſue
For mercy, 'twere in vaine; fortune thy worſt. Muſick

div.stage: An altar diſcovered, with Tapers, and a book on it. The two Biſhops ſtand on each ſide of it Mountferrat as the Song is ſinging aſcends up the altar.

sp.l: See ſee, the ſtaine of honor, vertues foe,
Of Virgins fair fames, the foule overthrow,
That broken hath his oath of chaſtity
Diſhonor'd much this holy dignity,
Off with his Roab, expell him forth this place,
Whilſt we rejoyce, and ſing at his diſgrace.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Since by thy actions thou haſt made thy ſelf
Unworthy of that worthy ſigne thou wear • ſt,
And of our ſacred order, into which
For former vertues, we receiv'd thee firſt,
According to our Statutes, Ordinances,
For praiſe unto the good, a terror to
The bad, and an example to all men;
We here deprive thee of our habit, and
Declare thee unworthy our ſociety,
From which we do expell thee, as a rotten
Corrupted, and contagious member.

sp.speaker: Eſq.
sp.l: Uſing th'authority th'Superiour
Hath given unto me, I unty this knot,
And take from thee the pleaſing yoak of heaven:
We take from off thy breaſt this holy croſſe,
Which thou haſt made thy burthen, not thy prop;
Thy ſpurs we ſpoile thee off, eleaving thy heeles
Bare of thy honour, that have kick'd againſt
Our orders precepts: next we reave thy ſword,
And give thee armeleſſe to thy enemies,
For being foe to goodneſſe, and to God,
Laſt, 'bout thy ſtiff neck, we this halter hang,
And leave thee to the mercy of the Court.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Inveſt Miranda.
Faire child of vertue, honors bloome
That here with burning zeale doſt come
With joy to ask the white croſſe cloak,
And yeild unto this pleaſing yoake
That being yong, vowes chaſtity,
And chooſeſt wilfull poverty;
As this flame mounts, ſo mount thy zeale, thy glory
Riſe paſt the Stars, and fix in Heaven thy ſtory.

sp.speaker: 1. Biſh.
sp.l: What crave you gentle ſir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Humble admittance
To be a brother of the holy Hoſpitall
Of great Jeruſalem.

sp.speaker: 2. Biſh.
sp.l: Breath out your vow.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: To heaven and all the bench of Saints above
Whoſe ſuccour I implore t'enhable me,
I vow henceforth a chaſte life, not to enjoy
Any thing proper to my ſelf; obedience
To my ſuperiours, whom Religion,
And Heaven ſhall give me: ever to defend
The vertuous fame of Ladies, and to oppugne
Even unto death the Chriſtian enemy,
This do I vow to accompliſh.

sp.speaker: Eſq.
sp.l: Who can tell,
H'as he made other vow, or promis'd marriage
To any one, or is in ſervitude?

sp.speaker: All
sp.l: He's free from all theſe.

sp.speaker: 1. Biſh.
sp.l: Put on his ſpurs, and girt him with the ſword,
The ſcourge of infidels, and tipes of ſpeed.
Buildſt thy faith on this

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: On him that di'd
On ſuch a ſacred figure, for our ſins.

sp.speaker: 2. Biſh.
sp.l: Here, then we fix it on thy left ſide, for
Thy encreaſe of faith, Chriſtian defence, and ſervice
To th'poor, and thus near to thy heart we plant it
That thou maiſt love it even with all thy heart,
With thy right hand protect, preſerve it whole,
For if thou fighting 'gainſt heavens enemies
Shall fly away, abandoning the croſſe
The Enſigne of thy holy Generall,
With ſhame thou juſtly ſhalt be rob'd of it
Chas'd from our company, and cut away
As an infectious putrified limb.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I aske no favour.

sp.speaker: 1 Biſh.
sp.l: Then receive the yoak
Of him that makes it ſweet, and light, in which
Thy ſoule find her eternall reſt.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Moſt welcome.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Welcome, our noble brother.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Break up the Court; Mountferrat, though your deeds
Conſpiring 'gainſt the lives of innocents
Hath forfeited your own, we will not ſtaine
Our white Croſſe with your blood: your doom is then
To marry this coagent of your miſchiefes
Which done, we baniſh you the continent,
If either, after three dayes here be found
The hand of Law, layes hold upon your lives.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.p: Away French ſtallion, now you have a Barbary mare of your own, go leap her, and engender young devillings.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: VVe will find ſomething, noble Norandine
To quit your merit: ſo to civill feaſts,
According to our cuſtomes; and all pray
The dew of grace, bleſſe our new Knight to day. Exeunt.

div.head: THE WOMANS PRIZE: OR, The Tamer Tamed.
Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Moroſo, Sophocles, and Tranio, with Roſemary, as from a wedding.

sp.speaker: Moroſo.
sp.l: GOd give 'em joy.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Amen.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Amen, ſay I to:
The Puddings now i'th proof; alas poor wench,
Through what a mine of patience muſt thou worke,
Ere thou know'ſt good houre more?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Tis too true: Certaine,
Me thinks her father has dealt harſhly with her,
Exceeding harſhly, and not like a Father,
To match her to this Dragon; I proteſt
I pity the poore Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Me thinks now,
He's not ſo terrible as people think him.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: This old thiefe flatters, out of meere devotion,
To pleaſe the father for his ſecond daughter.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: But ſhall he have her?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Yes, when I have Rome.
And yet the father's for him.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Ile aſſure ye,
I hold him a good man.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Yes ſure a wealthy,
But whether a good womans man, is doubtfull.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Would 'twere no worſe.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: What though his other wife,
Out of her moſt abundant ſoberneſſe,
Out of her daily huy and cries upon him,
(For ſure ſhe was a Rebell) turn'd his temper,
And forc'd him blow as high as ſhe? do'ſt follow
He muſt retain that long ſince buried Tempeſt,
To this ſoft maid?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I feare it.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: So do I too:
And ſo far, that if God had made me woman,
And his wife that muſt be—

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: What would you doe ſir?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I would learn to eate Coales with an angry Cat,
And ſpit fire at him: I would (to prevent him)
Do all the ramping, roaring tricks, a whore
Being drunke, and tumbling ripe, would tremble at:
There is no ſafety elſe, nor morall wiſdome,
To be a wife, and his.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: So I ſhould think too.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: For yet the bare remembrance of his firſt wife
(I tell ye on my knowledge, and a truth too)
Will make him ſtart in's ſleep, and very often
Cry out for Cudgels, Colſtaves, any thing;
Hiding his Breeches, out of feare her Ghoſt
Should walk, and weare 'em yet. Since his firſt marriage,
He is no more the ſtill Petruchio,
Then I am Babylon.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: He's a good felloW,
And on my word I love him: but to think
A fit match for this tender ſoule—

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: His very frowne, if ſhe but ſay her prayers
Louder then men talk treaſon, makes him tindar;
The motion of a Diall, when he's teſty,
Is the ſame trouble to him as a water-worke;
She muſt do nothing of her ſelfe; not eate,
Drink, ſay ſir how do ye, make her ready, unready,
Unleſſe he bid her.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: He will bury her
Ten pound to twenty ſhillings, within theſe three weeks.

sp.speaker: Tra:
sp.l: Ile be your halfe.

div.stage: Enter Jaques with a pot of Wine.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: He loves her moſt extreamly,
And ſo long 'twil be honey-moon. Now Jaques
You are a buſie man I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Yes certaine,
This old ſport muſt have egges,

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Not yet this ten daies.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Sweet Gentlemen with Muskadell.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: That's right ſir.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: This fellow broods his Maſter: ſpeed ye Jaques.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: We ſhall be for you preſently.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Your worſhips
Shal have it rich and neat: and o' my conſcience
As welcom as our Lady day: O my old ſir,
When ſhall we ſee your worſhip run at Ring?
That houre a ſtanding were worth money

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: So ſir.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Upon my little honeſty, your Miſtris,
If I have any ſpeculation, muſt thinke
This ſingle thrumming of a Fiddle,
Without a Bow, but ev'n poore ſport.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Y'are merry.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Would I were wiſe too: ſo God bleſs your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: The fellow tels you true. Exit Jaq.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: When is the day man?
Come, come, you'l ſteale a marriage.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Nay believe me:
But when her father pleaſes I am ready,
And all my friends ſhall know it.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Why not now?
One charge had ſerv'd for both.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: There's reaſon in't.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Call'd Rowland.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Will ye walke?
They'l think we are loſt: Come Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You have wip't him now.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: So will he never the wench I hope.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I wiſh it. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Now Livia, if you'l goe away to night,
If your affections be not made of words.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I love you, and you know how dearly Rowland,
Is there none neere us? my affections ever
Have been your ſervants; with what ſuperſtition
I have ever Sainted you—

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Why then take this way.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Twill be a childiſh and a leſſe proſperous courſe,
Then his that knows not care: why ſhould we do
Our honeſt and our hearty love ſuch wrong,
To over-run our fortunes?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Then you flatter.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Alas you know I cannot.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What hopes left elſe
But flying to enjoy ye?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: None ſo far,
For let it be admitted we have time,
And all things now in other expectation,
My father's bent againſt us; what but ruine,
Can ſuch a by-way bring us? if your feares
Would let you look with my eyes, I would ſhew you,
And certain, how our ſtaying here would win us
A courſe, though ſomewhat longer, yet far ſurer.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: And then Moroſo h'as ye.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: No ſuch matter:
For hold this certaine, begging, ſtealing, whoring,
Selling, (which is a ſin unpardonable)
Of counterfeit Cods, or muſty Engliſh Crac • s,
Switches, or ſtones for th'toothache ſooner finds me,
Then that drawn Fox and Moroſo.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: But his money,
If wealth may win you—

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: If a Hog may be
High Prieſt among the Jewes: his money Rowland?
Oh Love forgive me, what faith haſt thou?
Why, can his money kiſſe me?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Behind,
Laſd out upon a Petticote: or graſpe me
While I cry, O good thank you? o' my troth
Thou makſt me merry with thy feare: or lie with me,
As you may do? alas, what fooles you men are?
His mouldy money? half a dozen Riders,
That cannot ſit but ſtampt faſt to their Saddles?
No Rowland, no man ſhall make uſe of me;
My beauty was born free, and free Ile give it
To him that loves, not buys me. You yet doubt me.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I cannot ſay I doubt ye.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Goe thy waies,
Thou art the prettieſt puling piece of paſſion:
Y faith I will not faile thee.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I had rather—

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Prethee believe me, if I do not carry it,
For both our goods—

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: But—

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: What but?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I would tell you.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I know all you can tell me; all's but this,
You would have me, and lie with me; is't not ſo?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Why you ſhall; will that content you? Goe.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.p: I am very loth to goe. Enter Byancha, and Maria.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Now o' my conſcience
Thou art an honeſt fellow: here's my ſiſter;
Go, prethee goe; this kiſſe, and credit me,
Ere I am three nights older, I am for thee:
You ſhall heare what I do.
Farewell.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Farewell. Exit Rowland.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Alas poore foole, how it looks?
It would ev'n hang it ſelfe, ſhould I but croſſe it.
For pure love to the matter I muſt hatch it.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Nay never look for merry houre Maria,
If now you make it not; let not your bluſhes,
Your modeſty, and tenderneſſe of ſpirit,
Make you continuall Anvile to his anger:
Believe me, ſince his firſt wife ſet him going,
Nothing can bind his rage: Take your own Councell,
You ſhall not ſay that I perſwaded you.
But if you ſuffer him—

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay, ſhall I do it?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Have you a ſtomack to't?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I never ſhew'd it.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Twill ſhew the rarer, and the ſtronger in you.
But do not ſay I urg'd you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am perfect,
Like Curtius to redeeme my Countrey, have I
Leap'd into this gulph of marriage, and Ile do it.
Farewell all poorer thoughts, but ſpight & anger,
Till I have wrought a miracle. Now coſen,
I am no more the gentle tame Maria;
Miſtake me not; I have a new ſoule in me
Made of a North-wind, nothing but tempeſt;
And like a tempeſt ſhall it make all ruins,
Till I have run my will out.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: This is brave now,
If you continue it; but your own will lead you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Adieu all tenderneſſe, I dare continue;
Maides that are made of feares and modeſt bluſhes,
View me, and love example.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Here is your ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Here is the brave old mans love.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: That loves the young man.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I and hold thee there wench: what a grief of heart is't,
When Papbos Rebels ſhould up rowſe old night,
To ſweat againſt a Cork; to lie and tell
The clock o'th longs, to riſe ſport-ſtarv'd?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Deere ſiſter,
Where have you been you talke thus?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why at Church, wench;
Where I am tide to talke thus: I am a wife now.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo, and a modeſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You are an aſſe;
When thou art married once, thy modeſty
Will never buy thee Pins.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: 'Bleſſe me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: From what?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: From ſuch a tame foole as our cozen Livia?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: You are not mad.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes wench, and ſo muſt you be,
Or none of our acquantance, marke me Livia.
Or indeed ſit for our ſex: Tis bed time.
Pardon me yellow Hymen, that I meane
Thine offrings to protract, or to keepe faſting
My valiant Bridegroome.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Whether will this woman?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: You may perceive her end.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Or rather feare it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Dare you be partner in't?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Leave it Maria,
I feare I have mark'd too much, for goodneſſe leave it;
Deveſt you with obedient hands to bed.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: To bed? No Livia, there are Comets hang
Prodigious over that yet; there's a fellow
Muſt yet before I know that heat (nere ſtart wench)
Be male a man, for yet he is a monſter;
Here muſt his head be Livia.

sp.speaker: Liv
sp.l: Never hope it.
Tis as eaſie with a Sive to ſcoope the Ocean, as
To tame Petruchio.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay: Lucina heare me,
Never unlock the treaſure of my womb
For humane fruit, to make it capable;
Nor never with thy ſecret hand make briefe
A mothers labour to me; if I doe
Give way unto my married husbands will,
Or be a wife, in any thing but hopes,
Till I have made him eaſie as a child,
And tame as feare, he ſhall not win a ſmile,
Or a pleas'd look, from this auſterity,
Though it would pull another Joynture from him,
And make him ev'ry day another man;
And when I kiſſe him, till I have my will,
May I be barren of delights, and know
Onely what pleaſures are in dreams, and gueſſes.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: A ſtrange Exordium.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: All the ſeverall wrongs
Done by Emperious husbands to their wives
Theſe thouſand yeeres and upwards, ſtrengthen thee:
Thou haſt a brave cauſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And Ile doe it bravely
Or may I knit my life out ever after.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: In what part of the world got ſhe this ſpirit?
Yet pray Maria, looke before you truly,
Beſides the obedience of a wife,
Which you will finde a heavy imputation,
Which yet I cannot thinke your own, it ſhews
So diſtant from your ſweetneſſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Tis I ſweare.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Weigh but the perſon, and the hopes you have,
To worke this diſperate cure.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A weaker ſubject
Would ſhame the end I aime at, diſobedience.
You talk too tamely: By the faith I have
In mine own Noble will, that childiſh woman
That lives a priſoner to her husbands pleaſure,
Has loſt her making, and becomes a beaſt,
Created for his uſe, not fellowſhip.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: His firſt wife ſaid as much.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: She was a foole,
And took a ſcurvy courſe; let her be nam'd
'Mongſt thoſe that wiſh for things, but dare not do 'em:
I have a new daunce for him.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Are you of this faith?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Yes truly, and wil die in't.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Why then let's all weare breeches.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Now thou comſt neere the nature of a woman;
Hang theſe tame hearted Eyaſſes, that no ſooner
See the Lure out, and heare their husbands halla,
But cry like Kites upon 'em: The free Haggard
(Which is that woman, that hath wing, and knowes it,
Spirit, and plume) wil make an hundred checks,
To ſhew her freedome, ſaile in ev'ry ayre,
And look out ev'ry pleaſure; not regarding
I ure, nor quarry, till her pitch command
What ſhe deſires, making her foundred keeper
Be glad to fling out traines, and golden ones,
To take her down again.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: You are learned ſiſter;
Yet I ſay ſtill take heed.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A witty ſaying;
Ile tell thee Livia, had this fellow tired
As many wives as horſes under him,
With ſpurring of their patience; had he got
A Patent, with an Office to reclaime us
Confirm'd by Parliament; had he all the malice
And ſubtilty of Devils, or of us,
Or any thing that's worſe then both.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Hey, hey boyes, this is excellent.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Or could he
Caſt his wives new again, like Bels to make 'em
Sound to his will; or had the fearfull name
Of the firſt breaker of wilde women: yet,
Yet would I undertake this man, thus ſingle,
And ſpight of all the freedom he has reach'd to,
Turn him and bend him as I liſt, and mold him
Into a babe again; that aged women,
Wanting both teeth & ſpleen, may Maſter him.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Thou wilt be chronicl'd.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That's all I aime at.

sp.speaker: Liv
sp.l: I muſt confeſſe, I do with all my heart
Hate an Emperious husband, and in time
Might be ſo wrought upon.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: To make him cuckold?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: If he deſerve it.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Then Ile leave ye Ladies.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Thou haſt not ſo much Noble anger in thee.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Goe ſleep, goe ſleep, what we intend to do,
Lies not for ſuch ſtarv'd ſoules as thou haſt Livia.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Good night: the Bridegroom will be with you preſently.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That's more then you know.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: If ye worke upon him,
As you have promiſed, ye may give example,
Which no doubt will be followed.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: So.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Good night: we'l trouble you no further.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: If you intend no good, pray doe no harm.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: None, but pray for you. Exit Livia.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: 'Cheere wench?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Now Byancha,
Thoſe wits we have let's wind 'em to the height,
My reſt is up wench, and I pull for that
Will make me ever famous. They that lay
Foundations, are halfe builders all men ſay.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: My Maſter forſooth.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Oh how do's thy Maſter? prethee commend me to him.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: How's this? my Maſter ſtaies forſooth.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why let him ſtay, who hinders him forſooth?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: The Revel's ended now,
To viſit you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am not ſick.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I mean to ſee his chamber, forſooth.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Am I his Groom? where lay he laſt night, forſooth?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: In the low matted Parlour.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: There lies his way by the long Gallery.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I mean your chamber: y'ar very merry Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Tis a good ſigne I am ſound hearted Jaques:
But if you'l know where I lie, follow me;
And what thou ſeeſt, deliver to thy Maſter.

sp.speaker: Bja.
sp.l: Do gentle Jaques. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Ha, is the wind in that dore?
By'r Lady we ſhall have foule weather then:
I doe not like the ſhuffling of theſe women,
They are mad beaſts when they knock their heads together:
I have obſerv'd them all this day; their whiſpers,
One in anothers eare, their ſignes, and pinches,
And breaking often into violent laughters:
As if the end they purpos'd were their own.
Call you this weddings? Sure this is a knavery,
A very trick, and dainty knavery,
Marvellous finely carried, that's the comfort:
What would theſe women doe in waies of honour,
That are ſuch Maſters this way. Well, my Sir
Has been as good at finding out theſe toyes,
As any living; if he loſe it now,
At his own perill be it. I muſt follow. Exit.

div.head: Scena tertia.
div.stage: Enter Servants with lights, Petruchio, Petronius, Moroſo, Tranio, and Sophocles.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You that are married, Gentlemen, home at ye
For a round wager now.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Of this nights Stage?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.p: I am your firſt man: a paire of Gloves of twenty ſhillings.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Done: who takes me up next? I am for all bets.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Well luſty Laurence, were but my night now,
Old as I am, I would make you clap on Spurs,
But I would reach you, and bring you to your trot too:
I would Gallants.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Well ſaid good Will; but where's the ſtaffe boy, ha?
Old father time, your houre-glaſſe is empty.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: A good tough traine would break thee all to pieces;
Thou haſt not breath enough to ſay thy prayers.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Set how theſe boyes deſpiſe us. Will you to bed ſonne?
This pride will have a fall.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Upon your daughter;
But I ſhall riſe again, if there be truth
In Egges, and butter'd Paſnips.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Wil you to bed ſon, & leave talking;
To morrow morning we ſhall have you looke,
For all your great words, like St. George at Kingſton,
Running a foot-back from the furious Dragon,
That with her angry tayle belabours him
For being lazie.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: His courage quench'd, and ſo far quench'd—

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Tis well ſir.
What then?

sp.speaker: Saph.
sp.l: Fly, fly, quoth then the fearfull dwarfe;
Here is no place for living man.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: Well my maſters, if I doe ſinke under my buſineſſe, as I finde tis very poſſible, I am not the firſt that has miſcarried; So that's my comfort, what may be done without impeach or waſte, I can and will doe.
sp.l: How now is my faire Bride a bed?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: No truly ſir.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.p: Not a bed yet? body o' me: we'l up and rifle her: here's a coyle with a mayden-head, tis not intayl'd, is it?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: If it be, ile try all the Law i'th Land, but Ile cut it off: let's up, let's up, come.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: That you cannot neither.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Unleſſe you'll drop through the Chimney like a Daw, or force a breach i'th windows: you may untile the houſe, tis poſſible.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What doſt thou meane?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: A morall ſir, the Ballat will expreſſe it:

l.hi: The wind and the rain has turnd you back again,

sp.l: And you cannot be lodged there. The truth is all the doores
Are baracadoed; not a Cathole, but holds a murd'rer in't.
She's victual'd for this moneth.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Art not thou drunk?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: He's drunk, he's drunk; come, come, let's up.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Yes, yes, I am drunke: ye may goe up, ye may Gentlemen, but take heed to your heads: I ſay no more.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Ile try that. Exit Soph.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: How doſt thou ſay? the door faſt lock'd fellow?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Yes truly ſir, tis lock'd, and guarded too; and two as deſperate tongues planted behind it, as ere yet batterd: they ſtand upon their honours, and will not give up without ſtrange compoſition, Ile aſſure you; marching away with their Pieces cockt, and Bullets in their mouthes will not ſatisfie them.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: How's this? how's this they are?
Is there another with her?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Yes marry is there, and an Engineir.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Who's that for Heavens ſake?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Colonell Byancha, ſhe commands the workes: Spinala's but a ditcher to her, there's a halfe-moon; I am but a poore man, but if you'l give me leave, Ile venture a yeeres wages, draw all your force before it, and mount your ableſt piece of battery, you ſhall not enter it theſe three nights yet.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I ſhould laugh at that good Jaques.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Beat back again, ſhe's fortified for ever.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Am I drunk now ſir?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: He that dares moſt, goe up now, and be cool'd.
I have ſcap'd a pretty ſcowring.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: What are they mad? have we another Bedlam? They doe not talke I hope?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.p: Oh terribly, extreamly fearfull, the noiſe at London-bridge is nothing neere her.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: How got ſhe tongue?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: As you got taile, ſhe was born to't.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Lock'd out a doors, and on my wedding-night?
Nay, and I ſuffer this, I may goe graze:
Come Gentlemen, Ile batter; are theſe vertues?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.p: Do, and be beaten off with ſhame, as I was: I went up, came to th' doore, knockd, no body anſwered; knock'd lowder, yet heard nothing: would have broke in by force; when ſuddenly a water-worke flew from the window with ſuch violence, that had I not duck'd quickly like a Fryer, caetera quis neſcit? The chamber's nothing but a meere Oſtend, in every window Pewter cannons mounted, you'l quickly finde with what they are charg'd, ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Why then tantara for us.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.p: And all the lower works lin'd ſure with ſmall ſhot, long tongues with Fire-locks, that at twelve ſcore blanke hit to the heart: now and ye dare go up

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: The window opens, beat a parley firſt;
I am ſo much amaz'd my very haire ſtands.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Why how now daughter: what intrenc'd?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A little guarded for my ſafety ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: For your ſafety Sweet-heart why who offends you?
I come not to uſe violence.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I thinke you cannot ſir, I am better fortified.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I know your end,
You would faine reprieve your Maiden-head
A night, or two.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, or ten, or twenty, or ſay an hundred;
Or indeed, till I liſt lie with you.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: That's a ſhrewd ſaying; from this preſent houre,
I never will believe a ſilent woman.
When they break out they are bonfires.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Till you liſt lie with him? why who are you Madam?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: That trim Gentlemans wife, ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Cry you mercy, do you command too?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes marry do's ſhe, and in chiefe.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: I doe command, and you ſhall go without:
(I mean your wife, for this night)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And for the next too wench, and ſo as't follows.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Thou wilt not, wilt 'a?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes indeed deere father,
And till he ſeale to what I ſhall ſet down,
For any thing I know, for ever.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Indeed theſe are Bugs-words.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You heare ſir, ſhe can talke, God be thanked.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I would I heard it not ſir.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I finde that all the pity beſtowd upon this woman,
Makes but an Anagram of an ill wife,
For ſhe was never vertuous.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Youl let me in I hope, for all this jeſting.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Hope ſtill Sir.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: You will come down I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am ſure I will not.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Ile fetch you then.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: The power of the whole County cannot ſir,
Unleſſe we pleaſe to yeild, which yet I thinke
We ſhal not; charge when you pleaſe, you ſhall
Heare quickly from us.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Bleſſe me from a Chicken of thy hatching,
Is this wiving?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Prethee Maria tell me what's the reaſon,
And do it freely, you deale thus ſtrangely with me?
You were not forc'd to marry, your conſent
Went equally with mine, if not before it:
I hope you do not doubt I want that mettle
A man ſhould have to keepe a woman waking;
I would be ſorry to be ſuch a Saint yet:
My perſon, as it is not excellent,
So tis not old, nor lame, nor weak with Phyſick,
But wel enough to pleaſe an honeſt woman,
That keeps her houſe, and loves her husband.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Tis ſo.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: My means and my conditions are no ſhamers
Of him that owes 'em, all the world knows that,
And my friends no reliers on my fortunes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: All this I believe, and none of all theſe parcels
I dare except againſt; nay more, ſo far
I am from making theſe the ends I aime at,
Theſe idle outward things, theſe womens feares,
That were I yet unmarried, free to chooſe
Through all the Tribes of man, i'ld take Petruchio
In's ſhirt, with one ten Groats to pay the Prieſt,
Before the beſt man living, or the ableſt
That ev'r leap'd out of Lancaſhire, and they are right ones.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Why do you play the foole then, and ſtand prating
Out of the window like a broken Miller!

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: If you wil have me credit you Maria,
Come down, and let your love confirme it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay there ſir, that bargain's yet to make.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Play ſure wench, the pucks in thine own hand.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Let me die lowſie, it theſe two wenches
Be not brewing knavery to ſtock a Kingdome.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Why this is a Riddle:
I love you, and I love you not.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: It is ſo:
And till your own experience do untie it,
This diſtance I muſt keep.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: If you talk more,
I am angry, very angry.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am glad on't, and I wil talke.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Prethee peace,
Let me not think thou art mad. I tell thee woman,
If thou goeſt forward, I am ſtill Petruchio.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And I am worſe, a woman that can feare
Neither Petruchio Furius, nor his fame,
Nor any thing that tends to our allegeance;
There's a ſhort method for you, now you know me.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: If you can carry't ſo, tis very wel.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: No you ſhall carry it, ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Peace gentle Low-bel.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Uſe no more words, but come down inſtantly,
I charge thee by the duty of a child.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Prethee come Maria, I forgive all.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay there; That duty, that you charge me by
(If you conſider truly what you ſay)
Is now another mans, you gave't away
I'th Church, if you remember, to my husband:
So all you can exact now, is no more
But onely a due reverence to your perſon,
Which thus I pay: Your bleſſing, and I am gone
To bed for this night.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: This is monſtrous:
That bleſſing that St. Dunſtan gave the Devil,
If I were neere thee, I would give thee—
Pull thee down by th' noſe.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Saints ſhould not rave, ſir;
A little Rubarb now were excellent.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Then by that duty you owe to me Maria,
Open the doore, and be obedient: I am quiet yet.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I do confeſſe that duty; make your beſt on't.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Why give me leave, I will.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Sir, there's no learning
An old ſtiffe Jade to trot: you know the morall.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yet as I take it ſir, I owe no more
Then you owe back again.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You wil not Article?
All I owe, preſently, let me but up, ile pay.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Y'are too hot, and ſuch prove Jades at length;
You do confeſſe a duty or reſpect to me from you again:
That's very neere, or full the ſame with mine?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Then by that duty, of reſpect, or what
You pleaſe to have it, goe to bed and leave me,
And trouble me no longer with your fooling;
For know, I am not for you.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Well, what remedy?

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: A fine ſmart Cudgell. Oh that I were neer thee.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: If you had teeth now, what a caſe were we in?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Theſe are the moſt authentique Rebels, next Tyrone, I ever read of.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A weeke hence, or a fortnight, as you beare you,
And as I finde my will obſerv'd, I may
With interceſſion of ſome friends be brought
May be to kiſſe you; and ſo quarterly
To pay a little rent by compoſition,
You underſtand me?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Thou Boy, thou.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: Well there are more Maides then Maudlin, that's my comfort.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, and more men then Michael.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I muſt not to bed with this ſtomach, and no meat Lady.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Feed where you will, ſo it be ſound, and wholſome,
Elſe live at livery, for i'le none with you.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: You had beſt back one of the dairy maids, they'l carry.
But take heed to your girthes, you'l get a bruiſe elſe.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Now if thou would'ſt come down, and tender me:
All the delights due to a marriage bed,
Studdy ſuch kiſſes as would melt a man,
And turne thy ſelfe into a thouſand figures,
To adde new flames unto me, I would ſtand
Thus heavy, thus regardleſſe, thus deſpiſing
Thee, and thy beſt allurings: all thy beauty
That's laid upon your bodies, mark me well,
For without doubt your mind's are miſerable,
You have no maskes for them: all this rare beauty,
Lay but the Painter, and the ſilke worme by,
The Doctor with his dyets, and the Taylor,
And you appeare like flead Cats, not ſo handſome.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And we appeare like her that ſent us hither,
That onely excellent and beauteous nature;
Truly our ſelves, for men to wonder at,
But too divine to handle; we are Gold,
In our own natures pure; but, when we ſuffer
The husbands ſtamp upon us then alayes,
And baſ ones of you, men are mingled with us,
And make us bluſh like Copper.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Then, and never
Till then are women to be ſpoken of,
For till that time you have no ſoules I take it:
Good night: come Gentlemen; i'le faſt for this night,
But by this hand—well: I ſhall come up yet?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Noe.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: There will I watch thee like a wither'd Jewry,
Thou ſhalt neither have meat, fire, nor Candle,
Nor any thing that's eaſie: doe you rebell ſo ſoone?
Yet take mercy.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Put up your Pipes; to bed ſir; i'le aſſure you
A moneths ſeige will not ſhake us.

sp.speaker: Moro.
sp.l: Well ſaid Colonell.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: To bed to bed Petruchio: good night Gentlemen,
You'l make my Father ſicke with ſitting up:
Here you ſhall finde us any time theſe ten dayes,
Unleſſe we may march off with our contentment.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Ile hang firſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And i'le quarter if I doe not,
Ile make you know, and feare a wife Petruchio,
There my cauſe lies.
You have been famous for a woman tamer,
And beare the fear'd-name of a brave wife-breaker:
A woman now ſhall take thoſe honours off,
And tame you; nay, never look ſo bigge, ſhe ſhall beleeve me,
And I am ſhe: what thinke ye; good night to all,
Ye ſhall finde Centines.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: If ye dare ſally. Exeunt above.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.p: The devill's in 'em, ev'n the very devill, the downe right devill.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: Ile devill 'em: by theſe ten bones I will: i'le bring it to the old Proverb no ſport no pie: — taken down i'th top of all my ſpeed; this is fine dancing: Gentlemen, ſtick to me. You ſee our Freehold's touch'd, and by this light, we will beleaguer'em, and either ſtarve 'em out, or make 'em recreant.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Ile ſee all paſſages ſtopt, but thoſe about 'em:
If the good women of the Towne dare ſuccour 'em,
We ſhall have warres indeed.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Ile ſtand perdue uppn 'em.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: My regiment ſhall lye before.

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: I think ſo, 'tis grown too old to ſtand.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Let's in, and each provide his tackle,
We'l fire'em out, or make'em take their pardons,
Heare what I ſay, on their bare knees —
Am I Petruchio, fear'd, and ſpoken of,
And on my wedding night am I thus jaded? Exe. Omnes.

div.head: Scaena quarta.
div.stage: Enter Rowland, and Pedro, at ſeverall doores.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Now Pedro?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Very buſie Maſter Rowland.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What haſte man?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I beſeech you pardon me,
I am not mine own man.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Thou art not mad?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: No; but beleeve me, as haſty—

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: The cauſe good Pedro?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: There be a thouſand ſir; you are not married?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Not yet.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Keepe your ſelfe quiet then.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: You'l finde a Fiddle
That never will be tun'd elſe: from all women— Exit. Enter Iaques,

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What ailes the fellow tro? Iaques?

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: Your friend ſir.
But very full of buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Nothing but buſineſſe?
Prethee the reaſon, is there any dying?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I would there were ſir.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: But thy buſineſſe?

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: Ile tell you in a word,
I am ſent to lay
An impoſition upon Sowſe and Puddings,
Paſties, and Penny Cuſtards, that the women
May not releeve you Rebels: Fare ye well ſir.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: How does my Miſtreſſe?

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: Like a reſty jade.
She's ſpoil'd for riding. Exit Iaques.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What a devill ayle they? Enter Sophocles.
Cuſtards, and penney Paſties, Fooles and Fiddles,
What's this to'th purpoſe? O well met.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Now Rowland.
I cannot ſtay to talk long.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What's the matter?
Here's ſtirring, but to what end? whether goe you?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: To view the works.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What workes?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: The womens Trenches.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Trenches? are ſuch to ſee?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I doe not jeſt ſir.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I cannot underſtand you.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Doe not you heare
In what a ſtate of quarrell the new Bride
Stands with her husband?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Let him ſtand with her, and there's an end.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: It ſhould be, but by'r Lady
She holds him out at Pikes end, and defies him,
And now is fortifide; ſuch a Regiment of Rutters
Never defied men braver: I am ſent
To view their preparation.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: This is newes
Stranger then Armes in the ayre, you ſaw not
My gentle Miſtreſſe?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Yes, and meditating
Upon ſome ſecret buſineſſe, when ſhe had found it
She leapt for joy, and laugh'd, and ſtraight retir'd
To ſhun Moroſo.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: This maybe for me.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Will you along?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Farewell. Exit Sophocles.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Farewell ſir.
What ſhould her muſing meane, and what her joy in't,
If not for my advantage? ſtay ye; may not Enter Livia at one doore, and Moroſo at another harkning.
That Bob-taile Jade Moroſo, with his Gold,
His gew-gaudes, and the hope ſhe has to ſend him
Quickly to duſt, excite this? here ſhe comes,
And yonder walkes the Stallion to diſcover:
Yet i'le ſalute her: ſave you beauteous miſtreſſe.

sp.speaker: Livi.
sp.l: The Fox is kennell'd for me: ſave you ſir.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Why doe you looke ſo ſtrange?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I uſe to looke ſir
Without examination.

sp.speaker: Moro.
sp.l: Twenty Spur-Royals for that word.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Belike then
The object diſcontents you?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Yes it does.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Is't come to this? you know me, doe you not?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Yes as I may know many by repentance.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Why doe you breake your faith?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Ile tell you that too,
You are under age, and no band holds upon you.

sp.speaker: Moro.
sp.l: Excellent wench.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Sue out your underſtanding,
And get more haire, to cover your bare knuckle
(For Boyes were made for nothing, but dry kiſſes,)
And if you can, more manners.

sp.speaker: Moro.
sp.l: Better ſtill.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: And then if I want Spaniſh gloves, or ſtockings,
A ten-pound waſte-coate, or a Nag to hunt on,
It may be I ſhall grace you to accept 'em.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Farewell, and when I credit women more,
May I to Smith-field, and there buy a Jade,
(And know him to be ſo) that breakes my neck.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Becauſe I have knowne you, Ile be thus kinde to you;
Farewell, and be a man, and i'le provide you,
Becauſe I ſee y'are deſperate, ſome ſtai'd Chamber-maid
That may relieve your youth, with wholeſome doctrin.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: She's mine from all the world: ha wench?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.p: Ha Chicken? — gives him a box o'th eare and Ex.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: How's this? I do not love theſe favours: ſave you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.p: The devill take thee— wrings him byth' noſe.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: There's a love token for you: thank me now.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Ile thinke on ſome of ye, and if I live,
My noſe alone ſhall not be plaid withall. Exit.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: A Box o'th eare doe you ſay?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Yes ſure a ſound one,
Beſide my noſe blown to my hand; if Cupid
Shoot Arrows of that waight, i'le ſweare devoutly,
Has ſude his liverie, and no more a Boy.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: You gave her ſome ill language?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Not a word,

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Or might be you weare fumbling?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Would I had ſir.
I had been a forehand then; but to be baffel'd,
