And have no feeling of the cauſe—

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Be patient,
I have a medicine clapt to her back will cure her.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: No ſure it muſt be afore ſir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: O' my Conſcience,
When I got theſe two wenches (who till now
Ne'r ſhew'd their riding) I was drunck with Baſtard,
Whoſe nature is to forme things like it ſelfe
Heady, and monſtrous: did ſhe ſlight him too?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: That's all my comfort: a meere Hobby-horſe
She made childe Rowland: ſ'foot ſhe would not know him,
Not give him a free look, not reckon him
Among her thoughts, which I held more then wonder,
I having ſeene her within's three dayes kiſſe him
With ſuch an appetite as though ſhe would eat him.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: There is ſome trick in this: how did he take it?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Ready to cry; he ran away.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I feare her.
And yet I tell you, ever to my anger,
She is as tame as Innocency; it may be
This blow was but a favour.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Ile be ſworne
'Twas well tye'd on then.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Goe too, pray forget it,
I have beſpoke a Prieſt: and within's two houres
Ile have ye married; will that pleaſe you?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Ile ſee it done my ſelfe, and give the Lady
Such a ſound exhortation for this knavery
Ile warrant you, ſhall make her ſmell this Moneth on't,

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Nay good ſir, be not violent.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Neither—

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: It may be
Out of her earneſt love, there grew a longing
(As you know women have ſuch toyes) in kindneſſe,
To give me a box o'th eare or ſo.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: It may be.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I reckon for the beſt ſtill: this night then
I ſhall enjoy her.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: You ſhall hanſell her.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Old as I am, i'le give her one blow for't
Shall make her groane this twelve-moneth.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Where's your joynture?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I have a joynture for her.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Have your Councell
Peruſ'd it yet?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: No Councell, but the night, and your ſweet daughter
Shall ere peruſe that Joynture.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Very well ſir.

sp.speaker: Moro.
sp.l: Ile no demurrers on't nor no rejoynders.
The other's ready ſeal'd.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Come then lets' comfort
My Son Petruchio, he's like little Children
That looſe their Bables, crying ripe.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Pray tell me,
Is this ſtern woman ſtill upon the flaunt
Of bold defiance?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Still, and ſtill ſhe ſhall be
Till ſhe be ſtarv'd out: you ſhall ſee ſuch juſtice,
That women ſhall be glad after this tempeſt
To tye their husbands ſhooes, and walke their horſes;
That were a merry world: doe you heare the rumour,
They ſay the women are in Inſurrection,
And meane to make a —

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: They'l ſooner
Draw upon walls as we doe: Let 'em, let 'em,
We'l ſhip 'em out in Cuck-ſtooles, there they'l ſaile
As brave Columbus did, till they diſcover
The happy Iſlands of obedience.
We ſtay too long, Come.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Now Saint George be with us. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Now if I can but get in hanſomely,
Father I ſhall deceive you, and this night
For all your private plotting, i'le no wedlock;
I have ſhifted ſaile, and finde my Siſters ſafety
A ſure retirement; pray to heaven that Rowland
Do not beleeve too farre, what I ſaid to him,
For y'on old Foxcaſe forc'd me, that's my feare.
Stay, let me ſee, this quarter fierce Petruchio
Keepes with his Myrmidons: I muſt be ſuddaine,
If he ſeize on me, I can looke for nothing
But Marſhall Law; to this place have I ſcap'd him;
Above there. Enter Maria, and Byancha above.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: A Friend.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Who are you?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Looke out and know.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Alas poore wench who ſent thee,
What weake foole made thy tongue his Orator?
I know you come to parly.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Y'are deceiv'd,
Urg'd by the goodnes of your cauſe I come
To doe as you doe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Y'ar too weake, too fooliſh,
To cheat us with your ſmoothneſſe: doe not we know
Thou haſt been kept up tame?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Beleeve me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No, prethee good Livia
Utter thy Eloquence ſomewhere elſe.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Good Coſen
Put up your Pipes; we are not for your palat,
Alas we know who ſent you.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: O' my word —

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Stay there; you muſt not thinke your word,
Or by your Maydenhead, or ſuch Sonday oathes
Sworne after Even-Song, can inveigle us
To looſe our hand-faſt: did their wiſdomes thinke
That ſent you hither, we would be ſo fooliſh,
To entertaine our gentle Siſter Sinon,
And give her credit, while the woodden Jade
Petruchio ſtole upon us: no good Siſter,
Goe home, and tell the merry Greekes that ſent you,
I • ium ſhall burn, and I, as did Aeneas,
will on my back, ſpite of the Myrmidons,
Carry this warlike Lady, and through Seas
Unknown, and unbeleev'd, ſeek out a Land,
Where like a race of noble Amazons,
We'le root our ſelves and to our endleſſe glory
Live, and deſpiſe baſe men.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Ile ſecond ye.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: How long have you been thus?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: That's all one Coſen.
I ſtand for freedome now.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Take heed of lying;
For by this light, if we doe credit you,
And finde you tripping, his infliction
That kill'd the Prince of Orenge, will be ſport
To what we purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Let me feele the heavieſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Swear by thy Sweet-heart Rowland (for by your mayden-head,
I feare 'twill be too late to ſwear) you meane
Nothing but faire and ſafe, and honourable
To us, and to your ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I ſweare.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Stay yet,
Sweare as you hate Moroſo, that's the ſureſt,
And as you have a certaine feare to finde him
Worſe then a poore dride Jack, full of more Aches
Then Autumne has; more knavery, and uſury,
And foolery, and brokery, then doggs-ditch:
As you doe conſtantly beleeve he's nothing
But an old empty bagge with a grey beard,
And that beard ſuch a Bob-taile, that it lookes
Worſe then a Mares taile eaten off with Fillyes:
As you acknowledge, that young hanſome wench
That lyes by ſuch a Bilbo blade, that bends
With ev'ry paſſe he makes to'th hilts, moſt miſ • rable,
A dry nurſe to his Coughes, a fewterer
To ſuch a naſty fellow, a rob'd thing
Of all delights youth lookes for: and to end,
One caſt away on courſe beef, born to bruſh
That everlaſting Caſſock that has worne
As many Servants out, as the Northeaſt paſſage
Has conſum'd Saylors: if you ſweare this, and truly
Without the reſervation of a gowne
Or any meritorious Petticoate,
'Tis like we ſhall beleeve you.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I doe ſweare it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay yet a little; came this wholeſome motion
(Deale truly Siſter) from your own opinion,
Or ſome ſuggeſtion of the Foe?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Nev'r feare me,
For by that little faith I have in husbands,
And the great zeale I beare your cauſe, I come
Full of that liberty, you ſtand for, Siſter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: If we beleeve, and you prove recreant Livia,
Think what a maym you give the noble Cauſe
We now ſtand up for: Thinke what women ſhall
An hundred yeare hence ſpeak thee, when examples
Are look'd for, and ſo great ones, whoſe relations
Spoke as we doe th'em wench, ſhall make new cuſtoms.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: If you be falſe, repent, goe home, and pray,
And to the ſerious women of the City
Confeſſe your ſelfe; bring not a ſinne ſo heynous
To load thy ſoule, to this place: mark me Livia,
If thou bee it double, and betray'ſt our honours,
And we fail in our purpoſe: get thee where
There is no women living, nor no hope
There ever ſhall be.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: If a Mothers daughter,
That ever heard the name of ſtubborn husband
Found thee, and know thy ſinne.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Nay, if old age,
One that has worne away the name of woman,
And no more left to know her by, but railing,
No teeth, nor eyes nor legges, but woodden ones
Come but i'th wind-ward of thee, forſure ſhe'l ſmell thee
Thou'lt be ſo ranck, ſhe'l ride thee like a night-mare,
And ſay her Prayers back-ward to undoe thee,
She'l curſe thy meat and drink, and when thou marrieſt,
Clap a ſound ſpell for ever on thy pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Children of five yeare old, like little Fayries
Will pinch thee into motley, all that ever
Shall live, and heare of thee, I meane all women;
Will (like ſo many furies) ſhake their Keyes,
And toſſe their flaming diſtaffes o're their heads,
Crying Revenge: take heed, 'tis hideous:
Oh 'tis a fearefull office, if thou had'ſt
(Though thou bee'ſt perfect now) when thou cam'ſt, hither,
A falſe Imagination, get thee gone,
And as my learned Cozen ſaid repent,
This place is ſought by ſoundneſſe.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: So I ſeeke it,
Or let me be a moſt deſpis'd example.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I doe beleeve thee, be thou worthy of it.
You come not empty?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: No, Here's Cakes, and cold meat,
And tripe of proofe: behold here's wine, and beere,
Be ſuddaine, I ſhall be ſurpriz'd elſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Meet at the low Parlor doore, there lyes a cloſe way:
What fond obedience you have living in you,
Or duty to a man, before you enter,
Fling it away, 'twill but defile our Offrings.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Be wary as you come,

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I warrant ye. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: 1 Mai.
sp.l: How goes your buſineſſe Girles?
A foot, and faire.
If fortune favour us: away to your ſtrength
The Country Forces are ariv'd, be gone.
We are diſcover'd elſe.
Arme? and be valiant.
Think of our cauſe.
Our Juſtice.
'Tis ſufficient. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena quarta.
div.stage: Enter Rowland and Tranio at ſeverall doores.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Now Rowland?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: How yoe you?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: How do'ſt thou man,
Thou look'ſt ill:

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes, pray can you tell me Tranio,
Who knew the devill firſt?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: A woman.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Thou haſt heard I am ſure of Eſculapius.
So were they not well acquainted?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: May be ſo,
For they had certaine Dialogues together.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: He ſold her fruit, I take it?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Yes, and Cheeſe
That choak'd all mankinde after.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Canſt thou tell me
Whether that woman ever had a faith
After ſhe had eaten?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: That's a Schoole queſtion

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: No
'Tis no queſtion, for beleeve me Tranio,
That cold fruit after eating bread naught in her
But windy promiſes, and chollick vowes
That broke out both wayes.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Thou ha'ſt heard I am ſure
Of Eſculapius, a farre famed Surgeon,
One that could ſet together quarter'd Traytors,
And make 'em honeſt men.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: How do'ſt thou Rowland?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Let him but take, (if he dare doe a cure
Shall get him fame indeed) a faithleſſe woman,
There will be credit for him, that will ſpeake him,
A broken woman Tranio, a baſe woman,
And if he can cure ſuch a rack of honour
Let him come here, and practiſe.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Now for honours ſake
Why what ayl'ſt thou Rowland?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I am ridden Tranio.
And Spur-gald to the life of patience
(Heaven keepe my wits together) by a thing
Our worſt thoughts are too noble for, a woman.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Your Miſtreſſe has a little frown'd it may be?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: She was my Miſtreſſe.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Is ſhe not?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: No Tranio.
She has done me ſuch diſgrace, ſo ſpitefully,
So like a woman bent to my undoing,
That henceforth a good horſe ſhall be my Miſtreſſe,
A good Sword, or a Booke: and if you ſee her,
Tell her I doe beſeech you, even for love ſake.—

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I will Rowland.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: She may ſooner
Count the good I have thought her,
Our old love and our friend-ſhip,
Shed one true teare, meane one houre conſtantly,
Be old, and honeſt, married, and a maide,
Then make me ſee her more, or more beleeve her:
And now I have met a Meſſenger, farewell ſir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Alas poore Rowland, I will doe it for thee:
This is that dogge Moroſo, but I hope
To ſee him cold i'th mouth firſt 'er he enjoy her:
Ile watch this young man, deſperate thoughts may ſeize him,
And if my purſe, or councell can, i'le eaſe him. Exit

div.head: Scaena quinta.
div.stage: Enter Petruchio, Petronius, Moroſo, and Sophocles.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: For looke you Gentlemen, ſay that I grant her
Out of my free and liberall love, a pardon,
Which you and all men elſe know ſhe deſerves not,
(Teneatis amici) can all the world leave laughing?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I thinke not.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: No by — they cannot;
For pray conſider, have you ever read,
Or heard of, or can any man imagine.
So ſtiffe a Tomb boy, of ſo ſet a ma ice,
And ſuch a brazen reſolution,
As this young Crab-tree? and then anſwer me,
And marke but this too friends, without a cauſe,
Not a foule word comes croſſe her, not a feare,
She juſtly can take hold on, and doe you thinke
I muſt ſleepe out my anger, and endure it,
Sow pillows to her eaſe, and lull her miſchiefe?
Give me a Spindle firſt: no, no my Maſters,
Were ſhe as faire as Nell a Greece, and houſe-wife,
As good as the wife Saylors wife, and young ſtill,
Never above fifteene; and theſe tricks to it,
She ſhould ride the wild Mare once a week, ſhe ſhould.
(Believe me friends ſhe ſhould) I would tabor her,
Till all the Legions that are crept into her,
Flew out with fire i'th tailes.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Me thinks you erre now,
For to me ſeems, a little ſufferance
Were a far ſurer cure.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes, I can ſuffer,
Where I ſee promiſes of peace and amendment.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Give her a few conditions.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Ile be hangd firſt.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Give her a crab-tree-cudgell.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: So I will;
And after it a flock-bed for her bones.
And hard egges, till they brace her like a Drum,
She ſhall be pamperd with —
She ſhall not know a ſtoole in ten moneths Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: This muſt not be. Enter Jaques.

sp.speaker: Jaq
sp.l: Arme, arme, out with your weapons,
For all the women in the Kingdom's on ye; Enter Pedro.
They ſwarm like waſpes, and nothing can deſtroy 'em,
But ſtopping of their hive, and ſmothering of 'em.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Stand to your guard ſir, all the devils extant
Are broke upon us, like a cloud of thunder;
There are more women, marching hitherward,
In reſcue of my Miſtris, th • n ere turn'd taile
At Sturbridge Faire; and I believe, as fiery.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: The forlorn-hope's led by a Tanners wife,
I know her by her hide; a deſperate woman:
She flead her husband in her youth, and made
Raynes of his hide to ride the Pariſh. Take 'em all together,
They are a genealogy of Jennets, gotten
And born thus, by the boyſterous breath of husbands;
They ſerve ſure, and are ſwift to catch occaſion,
(I meane their foes, or husbands) by the fore-locks,
And there they hang like favours; cry they can,
But more for Noble ſpight, then feare: and crying
Like the old Gyants that were foes to Heaven,
They heave ye ſtoole on ſtoole, and fling main Potlids
Like maſſie rocks, dart ladles, toſſing Irons,
And tongs like Thunderbolts, till overlayd,
They fall beneath the waight; yet ſtill aſpiring
At thoſe Emperious Godſheads, that would tame 'em.
There's nere a one of theſe, the worſt and weakeſt,
(Chooſe where you will) but dare attempt the rayſing
Againſt the ſoveraigne peace of Puritans,
A May-pole, and a Morris, maugre mainly
Their zeale, and Dudgeon-daggers: and yet more,
Dares plant a ſtand of battring Ale againſt 'em,
And drinke 'em out o'th Pariſh

sp.speaker: Saph.
sp.p: Lo you fierce Petruchio, this comes of your impatience.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: There's one brought in the Beares againſt the Canons
Of the Town, made it good, and fought 'em.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Another, to her everlaſting fame, erected
Two Ale-houſes of eaſe: the quarter-ſeſſions
Running againſt her roundly; in which buſineſſe
Two of the diſannullers loſt their night-caps:
A third ſtood excommunicate by the cudgell.
The Cunſtable, to her eternall glory,
Drunke hard, and was converted, and ſhe victor.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Then are they victualed with pies and puddings,
(The trappings of good ſtomacks) noble Ale
the true defendor, Sawſages, and ſmoak'd ones,
If need be, ſuch as ſerve for Pikes; and Porke,
(Better the Jewes never hated:) here and there
A bottle of Metheglin, a ſtout Bricaine
That wil ſtand to 'em, what elſe they want, they war for.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Come to councell,

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Now you muſt grant conditions or the Kingdom
Will have no other talke but this.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Away then, and let's adviſe the beſt.

sp.speaker: Soph:
sp.l: Why doe you tremble?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Have I liv'd thus long to be knockt o'th head,
With halfe a waſhing beetle? pray be wiſe ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Come, ſomething Ile doe; but what it is I know not.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: To councel then, and let's avoyd their follies.
Guard all the doors, or we ſhal not have a cloke left. Exe

div.stage: Enter three mayds, at ſeverall doors.

sp.l: How goes the buſineſſe, girles?
A foot, and faire.
If fortune favour us: away to your ſtrength,
The Country forces are ariv'd; be gon we are diſcovered elſe.
Arme, and be valiant.
Think of our cauſe.
Our iuſtice.
Tis ſufficient. Exeunt

div.head: Scena tertia.
div.stage: Enter Petronius, Petruchio, Moroſo, Sophocles, and Tranio.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I am indifferent, though I muſt confeſſe,
I had rather ſee her carted.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No more of that ſir.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Are ye reſolv'd to give her fair conditions?
Twill be the ſafeſt way.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I am diſtracted,
Would I had run my head into a halter
When I firſt woo'd her: if I offer peace,
She'l urge her own conditions, that's the devil.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Why ſay ſhe do?

sp.speaker: Petru:
sp.l: Say, I am made an Aſſe, then;
I know her aime: may I with reputation
(Anſwer me this) with ſafety of mine honour,
(After the mighty mannage of my firſt wife,
Which was indeed a fury to this Filly,
After my twelve ſtrong labours to reclaime her,
Which would have made Don Hercules horn mad,
And hid him in his hide) ſuffer this Sicely,
Ere ſhe have warm'd my ſheets, ere grappel'd with me,
This Pinck, this painted Foyſt, this Cockle-boat,
To hang her Fights out, and defie me friends,
A wel known man of war? if this be equal,
And I may ſuffer, ſay, and I have done?

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: I do not think you may.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You'l make it worſe ſir.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Pray heare me good Petruchio: but ev'n now,
You were contented to give all conditions,
To try how far ſhe would carry: Tis a folly,
(And you wil find it ſo) to clap the curb on,
Er you be ſure it proves a naturall wildneſſe,
And not a forc'd. Give her conditions,
For on my life this tricke is put into her.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: I ſhould believe ſo too.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: And not her own.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You'l finde it ſo.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Then if ſhe flownder with you,
Clap ſpurs on, and in this you'l deale with temperance,
Avoyd the hurry of the world.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: And looſe Muſick above.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: No honour on my life, ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I wil do it.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: It ſeems they are very merry. Enter Jaques.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Why God hold it.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Now Jaques?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: They are i'th flaunt, ſir.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Yes we heare 'em.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: They have got a ſtick of Fiddles, and they firke it
In wondrous waies, the two grand Capitanos,
(They brought the Auxiliary Regiments)
Daunce with their coats tuckt up to their bare breeches,
And bid them kiſſe 'em, that's the burden;
They have got Metheglin, and audacious Ale,
And talke like Tyrants.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: How knoweſt thou?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I peep't in Song!
At a looſe Lansket.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Harke.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: A Song, pray ſilence. All the women above.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: They look out.

sp.speaker: Petru
sp.l: Good ev'n Ladies.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Good you good ev'n ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: How have you ſlept to night?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Exceeding well ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Did you not wiſh me with you?

sp.speaker: Mar:
sp.l: No, believe me,
I never thought upon you.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Is that he?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: She has drunk hard, mark her hood.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: You are —

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Learuedly drunk, Ile hang elſe: let her utter.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And I muſt tell you, viva voce friend,
A very fooliſh fellow.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: There's an Ale figure.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I thank you Suſan Brotes.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Forward ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: You have eſpouſed here a hearty woman,
A comely, and couragious.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Wel I have ſo.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And to the comfort of diſtreſſed damſels,
Weomen out-worn in wedlock, and ſuch veſſels,
This woman has defied you.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: It ſhould ſeem ſo.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And why?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes, can you tell?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: For thirteen cauſes.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Pray by your patience Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Forward ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Do you mean to treat of all theſe?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Who ſhall let her?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Doe you heare, Velvet-hood, we come not now
To heare your doctrine.

sp.speaker: Cunt.
sp.l: For the firſt, I take it,
It doth divide it ſelfe into ſeven branches.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Harke you good Maria,
Have you got a Catechiſer here?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Good zeale.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Good three pil'd predication, will you peace,
And heare the cauſe we come for?

sp.speaker: Cunt.
sp.l: Yes Bob-tailes
We know the cauſe you come for, here's the cauſe,
But never hope to carry her, never dream
Or flatter your opinions with a thought
Of baſe repentance in her.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Give me ſack,
By this, and next ſtrong Ale.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Sweare forward ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: By all that's cordiall, in this place we'l bury
Our bones, fames, tongues, our triumphs; and then all
That ever yet was chronicl'd of woman;
But this brave wench, this excellent deſpiſer,
This bane of dull obedience, ſhall inherit
His liberall wil, and march off with conditions
Noble, and worth her ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: She ſhall Tom Tilers,
And brave ones too; My hood ſhal make a hearſe-cloth,
And I lie under it, like Jone o Gaunt,
Ere I goe leſſe, my Diſtaffe ſtucke up by me,
For the eternall Trophce of my conqueſts;
And loud fame at my head, with two main Bottles,
Shall fill to all the world the glorious fall
Of old Don Gillian.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Yet a little further,
We have taken Armes in reſcue of this Lady;
Moſt juſt and Noble: if ye beat us off
Without conditions, and we recant,
Uſe us as we deſerve; and firſt degrade us
Of all our ancient chambring: next that
The Symbols of our ſecrecy, ſilke Stockings,
Hew of our heeles; our petticotes of Armes
Teare of our bodies, and our Bodkins breake
Over our coward heads.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And ever after
To make the tainture moſt notorious,
At all our Creſts, videlicet our Plackets.
Let Laces hang, and we returne againe
Into our former titles, Dayry maids.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: No more wars: puiſſant Ladies, ſhew conditions,
And freely I accept 'em.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Call in Livia;
She's in the treaty too. Enter Livia above.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: How, Livia?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Heare you that ſir?
There's the conditions for ye, pray peruſe 'em.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Yes, there ſhe is: t'had been no right rebellion,
Had ſhe held off; what think you man?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Nay nothing.
I have enough o'th proſpect: o'my conſcience,
The worlds end, and the goodneſſe of a woman
Will come together.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Are you there ſweet Lady?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Cry you mercy ſir, I ſaw you not: your bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.p: Yes when I bleſſe a jade, that ſtumbles with me. How are the Articles?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: This is for you ſir;
And I ſhal think upon't.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: You have us'd me finely.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: There's no other uſe of thee now extant,
But to be hung up; caſſock, cap, and all,
For ſome ſtrange monſter at Apothecaries.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: I heare you whore.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: It muſt be his then ſir,
For need wil then compell me.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Bleſſing on thee.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: He wil undoe me in meere pans of Coles
To make him luſtie.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: There's no talking to 'eni;
How are they ſir?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: As I expected: Liberty and clothes, Reads.
When, and in what way ſhe wil: continuall moneys,
Company, and all the houſe at her diſpoſe;
No tongue to ſay, why is this? or whether wil it;
New Coaches, and ſome buildings, ſhe appoints here,
Hangings, and hunting-horſes: and for Plate
And Jewels for her private uſe, I take it,
Two twouſand pound in preſent: then for Muſick,
And women to read French;

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: This muſt not be.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And at the latter end a clauſe put in,
That Livia ſhal by no man be importun'd.
This whole moneth yet, to marry.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: This is monſtrous.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: This ſhall be done, Ile humor her awhile:
If nothing but repentance, and undoing
Can win her love, Ile make a ſhift for one.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: When ye are once a bed, all theſe conditions
Lie under your own ſeale.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Do yo like 'em?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes.
And by that faith I gave you fore the Prieſt
Ile ratifie 'em.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Stay, what pledges?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No, Ile take that oath;
But have a care you keep it.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Tis not now
As when Andrea liv'd.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: If you do juggle,
Or alter but a Letter or theſe Articles
We have ſet down, the ſelf-ſame perſecution.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Miſtruſt him not.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: By all my honeſty —

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Enough I yield.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: What's this
Inſerted here?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: That the two valiant women that command here
Shall have a Supper made em, and a large one,
And liberall entertainment without grudging,
And pay for all their Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: That ſhall be too;
And if a tun of Wine wil ſerve to pay 'em,
They ſhall have juſtice: I ordaine ye all
Pay-maſters, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Then we ſhall have ſport boyes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: We'l meet you in the Parlour.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Ne'r looke ſad ſir, for I will doe it.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: There's no danger in't.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: For Livia's Article, you ſhall obſerve it,
I have tyde my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: I wil.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Along then: now
Either I break, or this ſtiffe plant muſt bow. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Come, you ſhall take my counſell.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I ſhall hang firſt.
Ile no more love, that's certaine, tis a bane,
(Next that they poyſon Rats with) the moſt mortall:
No, I thank Heaven, I have got my ſleep again,
And now begin to write ſence; I can walk ye
A long howre in my chamber like a man,
And think of ſomething that may better me;
Some ſerious point of Learning, or my ſtate;
No more ay-mees, and miſeries Tranio
Come neer my brain. Ile tell thee, had the devil
But any eſſence in him of a man,
And could be brought to love, and love a woman,
Twould make his head ake worſer then his hornes doe;
And make him with a fire he never felt yet,
Would make him dance. I tell thee there is nothing
(It may be thy caſe Tranio, therefore heare me:)
Under the Sun (reckon the maſſe of follies
Crept into th'world with man) ſo deſperate,
So madde, ſo ſenceleſſe, poor and baſe, ſo wretched,
Roguy, and ſcurvy.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: VVhether wilt thou Rowland?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: As tis to be in love.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: And why for vertues ſake?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: And why for vertues ſake? do'ſt thou not conceive me?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No by my troth.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Pray then, and hartely
For fear thou fall into 't: I'le tell thee why too,
(For I have hope to ſave thee) when thou loveſt,
And firſt beginſt to worſhip the gilt calfe,
Imprimis, thou haſt loſt thy gentry,
And like a prentice flung away thy freedom.
Forthwith thou art a ſlave.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: That's a new Doctrine.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Next thou art no more man.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: VVhat then?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: A Fryppery;
Nothing but brayded haire, and penny riband,
Glove, garter, ring, roſe, or at beſt a ſwabber,
If thou canſt love ſo neer to keep thy making,
Yet thou wilt looſe thy language.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: VVhy.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: O Tranio,
Thoſe things in love, ne'r talke as we do,

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: No without doubt, they ſigh and ſhake the head,
And ſometimes whiſtle dolefully.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No tongue?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes Tranio, but no truth in't, nor no reaſon,
And when they cant (for tis a kind of canting)
Ye ſhall hear, if you reach to underſtand 'em
(Which you muſt be a foole firſt, or you cannot)
Such gibbriſh; ſuch believe me, I proteſt Sweet,
And oh deer Heavens, in which ſuch conſtellations
Raigne at the births of lovers, this is too well,
And daigne me Lady, daigne me I beſeech ye
You poor unworthy lump, and then ſhe licks him

sp.speaker: Tra
sp.l: A — on't, this is nothing.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Thun ha'ſt hit it:
Then talks ſhe ten times worſe, and wryes and wriggles,
As though ſhe had the itch (and ſo it may be.)

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Why thou art grown a ſtrange diſcoverer.

sp.speaker: Row
sp.l: Of mine own follies Tranio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: VVilt thou Rowland,
Certaine ne'r love again?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I think ſo, certain,
And if I be not dead drunk, I ſhall keep it.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Tell me but this; what do'ſt thou think of women?

sp.speaker: Row
sp.l: VVhy as I think of fiddles, they delight me,
Till their ſtrings break.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: VVhat ſtrings?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Their modeſties,
Faithes, vowes and maidenheads, for they are like Kits
They have but foure ſtrings to 'em.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: VVhat wilt thou
Give me for ten pound now, when thou next loveſt,
And the ſame woman ſtill?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Give me the money;
A hundred, and my Bond for't.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: But pray hear me.
I'le work all meanes I can to reconcile ye:

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Do, do, give me the money.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: VVork Tranio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You ſhall go ſometimes where ſhe is.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes ſtraight.
This is the firſt good I ere got by woman.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You would think it ſtrange now, if an other beauty
As good as hers, ſay better.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Well.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Conceive me,
This is no point o'th wager.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: That's all one.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Love you as much, or more, then ſhe now hates you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Tis a good hearing, let 'em love: ten pound more,
I never love that woman.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: There it is;
And ſo an hundred, if you loſe.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Tis done;
Have you an other to put in?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No, no ſir.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I am very ſorry: now will I erect
A new Game and go hate for th' bell, I am ſure
I am in excellent caſe to win.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I muſt have leave.
To tell you, and tell truth too, what ſhe is,
And how ſhee ſuffers for you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Ten pound more,
I never believe you.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No ſir, I am ſtinted.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Well, take your beſt way then.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Let's walk, I am glad
Your ſullen feavor's off.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Shal't ſee me Tranio
A monſtrous merry man now: let's to the Wedding,
And as we go, tell me the generall hurry
Of theſe madde wenches, and their workes.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: And do thy worſt.

sp.speaker: Tra
sp.l: Something i'le do.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Do Tranio. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: A paire of ſtocks beſtride 'em, are they gone?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Yes they are gon; and all the pans i'th Town
Beating before 'em: what ſtrange admonitions
They gave my Maſter, and how fearfully
They threaten'd, if he brok 'em?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: O' my conſcience
Has found his full match now.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: That I believe too.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: How did ſhe entertaine him?

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: She lookt on him.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: But ſcurvely.

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: With no great affection
That I ſaw: and I heard ſome ſay he kiſſ'd her,
But 'twas upon a treaty, and ſome coppies
Say but her cheek.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Iaques, what wouldſt thou give
For ſuch a wife now?

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: Full as many prayers
As the moſt zealous Puritane conceives
Out of the meditation of fat veale,
Or birds of prey, cram'd capons, againſt Players,
And to as good a tune too, but againſt her:
That heaven would bleſſe me from her: mark it Pedro,
If this houſe be not turn'd within this fortnight
With the foundation upward, i'le be carted.
My comfort is yet that thoſe Amorities,
That came to back her cauſe, thoſe heathen whores had
their hoods hallowed with ſack.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: How div'liſh drunk they were?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: And how they tumbled, Pedro, didſt thou marke
The Countrey Cavaliero?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Out upon her,
How ſhe turn'd down the Bagget?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I that ſunke her.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: That drink was wel put to her; what a ſober ſalt
When the chaire fel, ſhe fetchd, with her heels upward?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: And what a piece of Landskip ſhe diſcoverd?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Didſt mark her, when her hood ſel in the Poſſet?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Yes, and there rid, like a Dutch hoy; the Tumbrel,
When ſhe had got her ballaſſe.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: That I ſaw too.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: How faine ſhe would have drawn on Sophocles
To come aboord, and how ſhe ſimperd it—

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I warrant her, ſhe has been a worthy ſtriker.

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: I'th heat of Summer there had been ſome hope on't.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Hang her.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: She offerd him a Harry-groat, and belcht out,
Her ſtomack being blown with Ale, ſuch Courtſhip,
Upon my life has givn him twenty ſtooles ſince:
Believe my calculation, theſe old women
When they are tippled, and a little heated
Are like new wheels, theyl roare you all the Town ore
Till they be greaſd.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: The City Cinque • pace
Dame toſſe and Butter, had he Bob too?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Yes,
But ſhe was ſullen drunk, and given to filching,
I ſee her offer at a Spoon; my maſter
I do not like his looke, I feare has faſted
For all this preparation; lets ſteale by him. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Not let you touch her all this night?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Not touch her.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Where was your courage?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Where was her obedience?
Never poore man was ſham'd ſo; never Raſcall
That keeps a ſtud of whores was us'd ſo baſely.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Pray you tell me one thing truly;
Do you love her?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I would I did not, upon that condition
I paſt thee halfe my Land.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: It may be then,
Her modeſty requir'd a little violence?
Some women love to ſtruggle.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: She had it,
And ſo much that I ſweat for't, ſo I did,
But to no end: I waſht an Ethiope;
She ſwore my force might weary her, but win her
I never could, nor ſhould, till ſhe conſented;
And I might take her body priſoner,
But for her mind or appetite—

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Tis ſtrange;
This woman is the firſt I ever read of,
Refus'd a warranted occaſion,
And ſtanding on ſo faire termes.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I ſhall quit her.

sp.speaker: Soph,
sp.l: Uſ'd you no more art?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes, I ſwore to her,
And by no little ones, if preſently
Without more diſputation on the matter,
She grew not neerer to me, and diſpatcht me
Out of the pain I was, for I was nettl'd,
And willingly, and eagerly, and ſweetly,
I would to her Chamber-maid, and in her hearing
Begin her ſuch a hunteſ-up.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Then ſhe ſtarted?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: No more then I do now; many ſhe anſwered
If I were ſo diſpos'd, ſhe could not help it;
But there was one cal'd Iaques, a poor Butler
One that might well content a ſingle woman.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: And he ſhould tilt her.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: To that ſence, and laſt
She bad me yet theſe ſix nights look for nothing,
Nor ſtrive to purchaſe it, but faire good night,
And ſo good morrow, and a kiſſe or two
To cloſe my ſtomach, for her vow had ſeald it,
And ſhe would keep it conſtant.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Stay ye, ſtay ye,
Was ſhe thus when you woo'd her?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Nothing Sophocles,
More keenely eager, I was oft afraid
She had bin light, and eaſy, ſhe would ſhowre
Her kiſſes ſo upon me.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Then I fear
An other ſpoke's i'th wheele.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Now thou haſt found me,
There gnawes my devill, Sophocles, O patience
Preſerve me; that I make her not example
By ſome unworthy way; as fleaing her,
Boyling, or making verjuce, drying her.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I hear her.

sp.speaker: Petru
sp.l: Mark her then, and ſee the heire
Of ſpight and prodigality, ſhe has ſtudied
A way to begger's both, and by this hand Maria at the dore, and Servant and woman.
She ſhall be if I live a Doxy.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Fy Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I do not like that dreſſing, tis too poor,
Let me have ſix gold laces, broad and maſſy.
And betwixt ev'ry lace a rich embroydry,
Line the gown through with pluſh, perfum'd, and purffle
All the ſleeves down with pearle.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What think you Sophocles.
In what point ſtands my ſtate now?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: For thoſe hangings
Let 'em be carried where I gave appointment,
They are too baſe for my uſe, and beſpeak
New pieces of the civill wars of France,
Let 'em be large and lively, and all ſilke work,
The borders gold.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I marry ſir, this cuts it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That fourteen yardes of ſatten give my woman,
I do not like the colour, tis too civill:
Ther's too much ſilk i'th lace too; tell the Dutchman
That brought the mares, he muſt with all ſpeed ſend me
An other ſuit of horſes, and by all meanes
Ten calf of Hawkes for 'th River, I much care not
What price they beare, ſo they be ſound, and flying,
For the next winter, I am for the Country;
And mean to take my pleaſure; wher's the horſe man?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: She meanes to ride a great horſe.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: With a ſide ſadle?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes, and ſhee'l run a tilt within this twelve-month

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: To morrow Ile begin to learne, but pray ſir
Have a great care he be an eaſy doer,
Twill ſpoyle a Scholler els.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: An eaſy doer,
Did you hear that?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes, I ſhal meet her morals
Er it be long I fear not.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: O good morrow.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Good morrow Lady, how is't now.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Faith ſickly,
This houſe ſtands in an ill ayre.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yet more charges?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Subject to rots, and hewms; out on't, tis nothing
But a tild fog.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What think of the Lodge then?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I like the ſeate, but tis too little, Sophocles
Let me have thy opinion, thou haſt judgement.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Tis very well.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What if I pluck it down,
And built a ſquare upon it, with two courts
Still riſing from the entrance?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And i'th midſt
A Colledge for yong Scolds.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And to the Southward
Take in a garden of ſome twenty acres,
And caſt it off the Italian faſhion, hanging.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And you could caſt your ſelf ſo too; pray Lady
Will not this coſt much money?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Some five thouſand,
Say ſix: Ile have it battel'd too.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And gilt; Maria,
This is a fearfull courſe you take pray think on't,
You are a woman now, a wife, and his
That muſt in honeſty, and juſtice look for
Some due obedience from you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That bare word
Shall coſt you many a pound more, build upon't;
Tell me o • due obedience? what's a husband?
What are we married for, to carry ſumpters?
Are we not one peece with you, and as worthy
Our own intentions, as you yours?

sp.speaker: Petru
sp.l: Pray hear me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Take two ſmall drops of water, equall weigh'd,
Tell me which is the heavieſt, and which ought
Firſt to diſcend in duty?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You miſtake me;
I urge not ſervice from you, nor obedience
In way of duty, but of love, and oredit;
All I expect is but a noble care
Of what I have brought you, and of what I am,
And what our name may be

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That's in my making.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Tis true it is ſo.

sp.speaker: Mar
sp.l: Yes it is Petruchio,
For there was never man without our molding,
Without our ſtampe upon him, and our juſtice,
Left any thing three ages after him
Good, and his own.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Good Lady underſtand him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I do too much, ſweet Sophocles, he's one
Of a moſt ſpightfull ſelf condition,
Never at peace with any thing but age,
That has no teeth left to return his anger:
A Bravery dwels in his blood yet, of abuſing
His firſt good wife; he's ſooner fire then powder,
And ſooner miſchief.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: If I be ſo ſodain
Do not you fear me?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No nor yet care for you,
And if it may be lawfull, I defie you:

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Do's this become you now?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: It ſhall become me.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Thou diſobedient, weak, vain-glorious woman,
Were I but half ſo wilfull, as thou pightfull,
I ſhould now drag thee to thy duty.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Drag me?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: But I am friends again: take all your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Now you perceive him Sophocles.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I love thee
Above thy vanity, thou faithleſſe creature.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Would I had been ſo happy when I married,
But to have met an honeſt man like thee,
For I am ſure thou art good, I know thou art honeſt,
A hanſome hurtleſſe man, a loving man,
Though never a penny with him; and thoſe eyes,
That face, and that true heart; weare this for my ſake,
And when thou thinkſt upon me pity me:
I am caſt away, Exit Mar.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Why how now man?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Pray leave me,
And follow your advices.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: The man's jealous:

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I ſhall find a time ere it be long, to aske you
One or two fooliſh queſtions.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I ſhall anſwer
As wel as I am able, when you call me:
If ſhe mean true, tis but a little killing,
And if I do not venture its—
Farewel ſir. Exit Soph.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Pray farewell. Is there no keeping
A wife to one mans uſe? no wintering
Theſe cattell without ſtraying? tis hard dealing,
Very hard dealing, Gentlemen, ſtrange dealing:
Now in the name of madneſſe, what ſtar raign'd,
What dog-ſtar, bull, or bear-ſtar, when I married
This ſecond wife, this whirlwind, that takes all
Within her compaſſe? was I not wel warnd,
(I thought I had, and I believe I know it,)
And beaten to repentance in the daies
Of my firſt doting? had I not wife enough
To turn my love too? did I want vexation,
Or any ſpeciall care to kill my heart?
Had I not ev'ry morning a rare breakfaſt,
Mixt with a learned Lecture of ill language,
Louder then Tom o' Lincoln; and at dinner,
A dyet of the ſame diſh? was there evening
That ere paſt over us, without thou knave,
Or thou whore, for digeſtion? had I ever
A pull at this ſame poor ſport men run mad for,
But like a cur I was faine to ſhew my teeth firſt,
And almoſt worry her? and did Heaven forgive me,
And take this Serpent from me? and am I
Keeping tame devils now again? my heart akes;
Something I muſt do ſpeedily: Ile die,
If I can hanſomely, for that's the way
To make a Raſcall of her; I am ſick,
And Ile go very neer it, but Ile periſh. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Livia, Byancha, Tranio, and Rowland.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Then I muſt be content ſir, with my fortune.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: And I with mine.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I did not think, a look,
Or a poore word or two, could have diſplanted
Such a fix'd conſtancy, and for your end too.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Come, come, I know your courſes: there's no gewgaws,
Your Rings, and Bracelets, and the Purſe you gave me,
The money's ſpent in entertaining you
At Plays, and Cherry-gardens.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: There's your Chain too.
But if you'l give me leave, Ile weare the haire ſtill;
I would yet remember you.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Give him his love wench;
The yong man has imployment for 't.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Fie Rowland.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: You cannot fie me out a hundred pound
With this poore plot: yet, let me nere ſee day more,
If ſomething do not ſtruggle ſtrangely in me.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Young man, let me talk with you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Wel young woman.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: This was your Miſtris once.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Are ye honeſt?
I ſee you are young, and hanſome.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I am honeſt.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Why that's wel ſaid: and there's no doubt your judgement
Is good enough, and ſtrong enough to tell you
Who are your foes, and friends: why did you leave her?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: She made a puppy of me.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Be that granted:
She muſt doe ſo ſometimes, and oftentimes;
Love were too ſerious elſe.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: A witty woman.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Had you lov'd me—

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I would I had.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: And deerly;
And I had lov'd you ſo: you may love worſe ſir,
But that is not materiall.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I ſhal looſe.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Some time or other for variety
I ſhould have cal'd you foole, or boy, or bid you
Play with the Pages: but have lov'd you ſtil,
Out of all queſtion, and extreamly too;
You are a man made to be loved:

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: This woman
Either abuſes me, or loves me deadly.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Ile tell you one thing, if I were to chooſe
A husband to mine own mind, I ſhould think
One of your mothers making would content me,
For o' my conſcience ſhe makes good ones.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Lady,
Ile leave you to your commendations:
I am in again, The divel take their tongues.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: You ſhall not goe.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I wil: yet thus far Livia,
Your ſorrow may induce me to forgive you,
But never love again; if I ſtay longer,
I have loſt two hundred pound.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Good ſir, but thus much—

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Turn if thou beeſt a man.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: But one kiſſe of you;
One parting kiſſe, and I am gone too.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Come,
I ſhall kiſſe fifty pound away at this clap:
We'l have one more, and then farewel.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Farewel.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Wel, go thy waies, thou bearſt a kind heart with thee.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: H'as made a ſtand.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: A noble, brave young fellow,
Worthy a wench indeed.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I wil: I wil not. Exit Rowland.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: He's gone: but ſhot agen; play you but your part,
And I will keep my promiſe: forty Angels
In fair gold Lady: wipe your eyes: he's yours
If I have any wit.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Ile pay the forfeit.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Come then, lets ſee your ſiſter, how ſhe fares now,
After her skirmiſh: and be ſure, Moroſo
Be kept in good hand; then all's perfect, Livia.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: O Jaques, Jaques, what becomes of us?
Oh my ſweet Maſter.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Run for a Phyſitian,
And a whole peck of Pothecaries, Pedro.
He wil die, didle, didle die: if they come not quickly,
And bring all people that are skilfull
In Lungs and Livers: raiſe the neighbours,
And all the Aquavite-bottles extant;
And, O the Parſon, Pedro; O the Parſon,
A little of his comfort, never ſo little;
Twenty to one you finde him at the Buſh,
There's the beſt Ale.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I fly. Exit Pedro.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Out with the Trunks, ho:
Why are you idle? Sirha, up to th'Chamber,
And take the hangings down, and ſee the Linnen
Packt up, and ſent away within this halfe houre.
What are the Carts come yet? ſome honeſt body
Help down the cheſts of Plate, and ſome the wardrobe,
Alas we are undone elſe.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Pray forſooth,
And I beſeech ye, tell me, is he dead yet?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No, but is drawing on: out with the Armour.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Then Ile goe ſee him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Thou art undone then fellow: no man that has
Been neere him come neere me.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Why how now Lady, what means this?

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Now daughter, how dos my ſonne?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Save all you can for Heaven ſake.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Be of good comfort ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: O my Casket.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: How do's thy husband woman?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Get you gon, if you mean to ſave your lives: the ſickneſſe.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Stand further off, I prethee.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Is i'th houſe ſir,
My husband has it now;
Alas he is infected, and raves extreamly:
Give me ſome counſell friends.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Why lock the doores up,
And ſend him in a woman to attend him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I have beſpoke two women; and the City
Hath ſent a watch by this time: meat nor money
He ſhall not want, nor prayers.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: How long is't
Since it firſt tooke him?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: But within this three houres. Enter Watch.
I am frighted from my wits: —O here's the watch;
Pray doe your Office, lock the doores up friends,
And patience be his Angel.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: This comes unlook'd for:

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Ile to the lodge; ſome that are kind and love me,
I know wil viſit me. Petrucho within.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: Doe you heare my Maſters: ho, you that locke the doores up.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Tis his voyce.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Hold, and let's heare him.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Wil ye ſtarve me here: am I a Traytor, or an Heretick.
Or am I grown infectious?

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Pray ſir, pray.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I am as wel as you are, goodman puppy.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Pray have patience,
You ſhall want nothing ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I want a cudgell,
And thee, thou wickedneſſe.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: He ſpeakes wel enough.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Had ever a ſtrong heart ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Wil ye heare me?
Firſt be pleas'd
To think I know ye all, and can diſtinguiſh
Ev'ry mans ſeverall voyce: you that ſpoke firſt,
I know my father in law; the other Tranio,
And I heard Sophocles; the laſt, pray marke me,
Is my dam;d wife Maria:
If any man miſdoubt me for infected,
There is mine arme, let any man looke on't.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Save ye Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Petron:
sp.l: O welcome Doctor,
Ye come in happy time; pray your opinion,
What think you of his pulſe?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: It beats with buſieſt,
And ſhews a general inflammation,
Which is the ſymptome of a peſtilent feaver,
Take twenty ounces frow him.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Take a foole;
Take an ounce from mine arme, and Doctor Deuz-ace,
Ile make a cloſe-ſtoole of your Velvet coſtard.
—Gentlemen, doe ye make a may-game on me?
I tell ye once againe, I am as ſound,
As wel, as wholſome, and as ſenſible,
As any of ye all: Let me out quickly,
Or as I am a man, Ile beat the wals down,
And the firſt thing I light upon ſhall pay for't.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Nay we'l go with you Doctor.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Tis the ſafeſt;
I ſaw the tokens ſir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Then there is but one way.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Wil it pleaſe you open?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: His fit grows ſtronger ſtill.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Let's ſave our ſelves ſir,
He's paſt all worldly cure.
Friends do your office.
And what he wants, if money, love, or labour,
Or any way may win it, let him have it.
Farewell, and pray my honeſt friends — Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Why Raſcals,
Friends, Gentlemen, thou beaſtly wife, Jaques;
None heare me? who at the doore there?

sp.speaker: 1 Watch.
sp.l: Thinke I pray ſir,
Whether you are going, and prepare your ſelfe.

sp.speaker: 2 Watch.
sp.l: Theſe idle thoughts diſturbe you, the good Gentlewoman
Your wife has taken care you ſhall want nothing.

sp.speaker: Petru
sp.l: Shall I come out in quiet? anſwer me,
Or ſhall I charge a fowling-piece, and make
Mine own way; two of ye I cannot miſſe,
If I miſſe three; ye come here to aſſault me.
I am as excellent wel, I thank Heav'n for't,
And have as good a ſtomacke at this inſtant—

sp.speaker: 2 Watch.
sp.l: That's an ill ſigne.

sp.speaker: 1 Watch.
sp.l: He draws on; he's a dead man,

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And ſleep as ſoundly; wil ye looke upon me?

sp.speaker: 1 Watch.
sp.l: Do you want Pen and Inke? while you have ſence ſir,
Settle your ſtate.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Sirs, I am wel, as you are;
Or any Raſcall living.

sp.speaker: 2 Watch.
sp.l: would you were ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Look to your ſelves, and if you love your lives,
Open the doore, and fly me, for I ſhoot elſe;
— Ile ſhoot, and preſently, chain-bullets;
And under foure I will not kill.

sp.speaker: 1 Watch.
sp.l: Let's quit him,
It may be it is trick: he's dangerous.

sp.speaker: 2 Watch.
sp.p: The devill take the hinmoſt, I cry. Exit watch running.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Have among ye;
The doore ſhall open too, Ile have a faire ſhoot;
Are ye all gone? tricks in my old daies, crackers
Put now upon me? and by Lady Green-ſleeves?
Am I grown ſo tame after all my triumphs?
But that I ſhould be thought mad, if I rail'd
As much as they deſerve againſt theſe women,
I would now rip up from the primitive cuckold,
All their arch-villanies, and all their dobles,
Which are more then a hunted Hare ere thought on:
When a man has the faireſt, and the ſweeteſt
Of all their ſex, and as he thinks the nobleſt,
What has he then? and Ile ſpeake modeſtly,
He has a Quartern-ague, that ſhall ſhake
All his eſtate to nothing; never cur'd,
Nor never dying; H'as a ſip to venture
His fame, and credit in, which if he man not
With more continuall labour then a Gally
To make her tith, either ſhe grows a Tumbrell
Not worth the cloth ſhe weares; or ſprings more leakes
Then all the fame of his poſterity
Can ever ſtop againe: I could raile twenty daies;
Out on 'em hedge-hogs,
He that ſhal touch 'em, has a thouſand thorns
Runs through his fingers: If I were unmarried,
I would do any thing below repentance,
Any baſe dunhill ſlavery; be a hang-man,
Ere I would be a husband: O the thouſand,
Thouſand, ten thouſand waies they have to kil us!
Some fall with too much ſtringing of the Fiddles,
And thoſe are fooles; ſome, that they are not ſuffer'd,
And thoſe are Maudlin-lovers: ſome, like Scorpions,
They poyſon with their tailes, and thoſe are Martyrs;
Some die with doing good, thoſe Benefactors,
And leave 'em land to leap away: ſome few,
For thoſe are rareſt, they are ſaid to kill
With kindneſſe, and faire uſage; but what they are
My Catologue diſcovers not: onely tis thought
They are buried in old wals with their heeles upward.
I could raile twenty daies together now.
Ile ſeek 'em out, and if I have not reaſon,
And very ſenſible, why this was done,
Ile go a birding yet, and ſome ſhall ſmart for't. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: That I do love her, is without all queſtion,
And moſt extreamly, deerly, moſt exactly;
And that I would ev'n now, this preſent Monday,
Before all others, maids, wives, women, widdows,
Of what degree or calling, marry her,
As certaine too; but to be made a whim-wham,
A Jib-crack, and a Gentleman o'th firſt houſe
For all my kindneſſe to her.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: How you take it?
Thou get a wench, thou get dozen night-caps;
Wouldſt have her come, and lick thee like a calfe,
And blow thy noſe, and buſſe thee?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Not ſo neither.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: What wouldſt thou have her do?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Do as ſhe ſhould do;
Put on a clean ſmock, and to Church, and marry,
And then to bed a Gods name, this is faire play,
And keeps the Kings peace; let her leave her bobs,
I have had too many of them, and her quillets,
She is as nimble that way as an Eele;
But in the way ſhe ought to me eſpecially,
A ſow of Lead is ſwifter.

sp.speaker: Petron
sp.l: Quoat your griefes down.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Give faire quarter, I am old and craſie,
And ſubject to much ſumbling, I confeſſe it;
Yet ſomething I would have that's warme, to hatch me:
But underſtand me I would have it ſo,
I buy not more repentance in the bargaine
Then the ware's worth I have; if you allow me
Worthy your Son-in-law, and your allowance,
Do it a way of credit; let me ſhow ſo,
And not be troubled in my viſitations,
With blows, and bitterneſſe, and down right railings,
As if we were to couple like two cats,
With clawing, add loud clamour:

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Thou fond man
Haſt thou forgot the Ballard, crabbed age,
Can May and Ianuary match together,
And nev'r a ſtorm between 'em? ſay ſhe abuſe thee,
Put caſe ſhe doe.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Wel.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Nay, believe ſhe do's.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I doe believe ſhe do's.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: And div'liſhly:
Art thou a whit the worſe?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: That's not the matter,
I know, being old, tis fit I am abus'd;
I know tis hanſome, and I know moreover
I am to love her ſor't.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Now you come to me.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Nay more then this; I find too, and finde certain,
What Gold I have, Pearle, Bracelets, Rings, or Owches,
Or what ſhe can deſire, Gowns, Petticotes,
Waſtcotes, Enbroydered-ſtockings, Scarffs, Cals, Feathers
Hats, five pound Garters, Muffs, Masks, Ruffs, & Ribands,
I am to give her for't.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Tis right, you are ſo.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: But when I have done all this, and think it duty,
Is't requiſit an other bore my noſtrils?
Riddle me that.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Go get you gone, and dreame
She's thine within theſe two daies, for ſhe is ſo;
The boy's beſide the ſaddle: get warm broths,
And feed apace; think not of worldly buſineſſe,
It cools the blood; leave off your tricks, they are hateful,
And meere forerunners of the ancient meaſures;
Contrive your beard o'th top cut like Verdugoes;
It ſhows you would be wiſe, and burn your night-cap,
It looks like halfe a winding-ſheet, and urges
From a young wench nothing but cold repentance:
You may eate Onyons, ſo you'l not be laviſh.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I am glad of that.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: They purge the blood, and quicken,
But after 'em, conceive me, ſweep your mouth,
And where there wants a tooth, ſtick in a clove.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Shall I hope once againe, ſay't,

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: You ſhall ſir:
And you ſhall have your hope. Enter Byancha and Tranio.

sp.speaker: Moro.
sp.l: Why there's a match then.

sp.speaker: Byan.
sp.l: You ſhall not finde me wanting, get you gon.
Here's the old man, he'l think you are plotting elſe
Something againſt his new Sonne. Exit Tranio.

sp.speaker: Moro.
sp.l: Fare ye well ſir. Exit Moroſo.

l.hi: And ev'ry Buck had his Doe,
And ev'ry Cuckold a Bell at his Toe:
Oh what ſport ſhould we have then, then Bayes then,
O what ſport ſhould we have then?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: This is the ſpirit, that inſpires 'em all.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Give you good ev'n.

sp.speaker: Petro
sp.l: A word with you Sweet Lady.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: I am very haſty ſir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: So your were ever.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Well what's your will?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Was not your skilfull hand
In this laſt ſtratagem? were not your miſchiefes
Eeking the matter on?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: In's ſhutting up?
Is that it?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Ile tell you.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Doe,

sp.speaker: By
sp.l: And truly.
Good old man, I doe grieve exceeding much,
I feare too much.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I am ſorry for your heavineſſe.
Belike you can repent then?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: There you are wide too.
Not that the thing was done (conceive me rightly)
Do's any way moleſt me.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: What then Lady?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: But that I was not in't, there's my ſorrow, there
Now you underſtand me, for Ile tell you,
It was ſo ſound a peece, and ſo well carried,
And if you marke the way, ſo hanſomely,
Of ſuch a heigth, and excellence, and art
I have not known a braver, for conceive me,
When the groſſe foole her husband would be ſick —

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Pray ſtay.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Nay, good, your patience: and no ſence for't,
Then ſtept your daughter in.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: By your appointment.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: I would it had, on that condition
I had but one halfe ſmock, I like it ſo well;
And like an excellent cunning woman, cur'd me
One madneſſe with an other, which was rare,
And to our weake beleifes, a wonder.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Hang ye,
For ſurely, if your husband looke not to ye,
I know what will.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: I humbly thank your worſhip.
And ſo I take my leave.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: You have a hand I heare too.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: I have two ſir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: In my youg daughters buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: You will finde there
A fitter hand then mine, to reach her frets,
And play down diddle to her.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I ſhall watch ye.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Doe.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: And I ſhall have juſtice.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Where?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: That's all one;
I ſhall be with you at a turne hence forward.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Get you a poſſet too; and ſo good ev'n ſir.

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: And as I told your worſhip, all the hangings,
Braſſe, Pewter, Plate, ev'n to the very looking-glaſſes.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: And that that hung for our defence, the Armor,
And the march Beere was going too: Oh Iaques
What a ſad ſight was that?

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: Even the two Rundlets,
The two that was our hope, of Muskadell,
(Better nev'r tongue tript over) theſe two Cannons,
To batter brawne withall at Chriſtmas, ſir
Ev'n thoſe two lovely twyns, the enemy
Had almoſt cut off cleane.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Goe trim the houſe up.
And put the things in order as they were. Exit Ped. and Iaq.
I ſhall finde time for all this: could I finde her
But conſtant any way, I had done my buſineſſe;
Were ſhe a whore directly, or a ſcold,
An unthrift, or a woman made to hate me,
I had my wiſh, and knew which way to rayne her:
But while ſhe ſhewes all theſe, and all their loſſes,
A kinde of linſey woolſey, mingled miſchiefe
Not to be gheſt at, and whether true, or borrowed,
Not certaine neither, what a hap had I, Enter Maria.
And what a tydie fortune, when my fate
Flung me upon this Beare-whelp? here ſhe comes
Now if ſhe have a colour, for the fault is
A cleanly one, upon my conſcience
I ſhall forgive her yet, and finde a ſomething
Certaine, I married for: her wit: Ile marke her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Not let his wife come neere him in his ſicknes,
Not come to comfort him? ſhe that all lawes
Of heaven, and Nations have ordain'd his ſecond,
Is ſhe refus'd? and two old Paradoxes,
Peeces of five and fifty, without faith
Clapt in upon him? h'as a little pet,
That all young wives muſt follow neceſſary
Having their Mayden-heads—

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: This is an Axiome
I never heard before.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Or ſay rebellion
If we durſt be ſo foule, which two faire words
Alas win us from, in an houre, an inſtant,
We are ſo eaſie, make him ſo forgetfull
Both of his reaſon, honeſty, and credit,
As to deny his wife a viſitation?
His wife, that (though ſhe was a little fooliſh,)
Lov'd him, Oh heaven forgive her for't! nay doted,
Nay had run mad, had ſhe not married him,

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Though I doe know this falſer then the devill,
I cannot chooſe but love it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What doe I know
But thoſe that came to keepe him, might have kill'd him,
In what a caſe had I been then? I dare not
Beleeve him ſuch a baſe, deboſh'd companion,
That one refuſall of a tender maide
Would make him faigne this ſ • ckneſſe out of need,
And take a Keeper to him of foureſcore
To play at Billiards; one that mew'd content
And all her teeth together; not come neere him?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: This woman would have made a moſt rare Jeſuite
She can prevaricate on any thing:
There was not to be thought a way to ſave her
In all imagination, beſide this.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: His unkinde dealing, which was, worſt of all,
In ſending, who knowes whether, all the plate,
And all the houſhold-ſtuffe, had I not croſt it,
By a great providence, and my friends aſſiſtance
Which he will thanke me one day for: alas,
I could have watch'd as well as they, have ſerv'd him
In any uſe, better, and willinger.
The Law commands me to doe it, love commands me.
And my own duty charges me.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Heav'n bleſſe me.
And now I have ſaid my Prayers, Ile goe to her:
Are you a wife for any man?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: For you Sir.
If I were worſe, I were better; That you are well,
At leaſt, that you appeare ſo, I thanke heaven,
Long may it hold and that you are here, I am glad too,
But that you have abus'd me wretchedly,
And ſuch a way that ſhames the name of husband,
Such a malicious mangy way, ſo mingled,
(Never looke ſtrangely on me, I dare tell you)
With breach of honeſty, care, kindneſſe, manners.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Holla, you kick too faſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Was I a ſtranger?
Or had I vow'd perdition to your perſon?
Am I not married to you, tell me that?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I would I could not tell you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Is my preſence,
The ſtock I come of, which is worſhipfull,
If I ſhould ſay right worſhipfull, I ly'd not,
My Grandſire was a Knight.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: O'the Shire?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A Souldier,
Which none of all thy Family e're heard off,
But one conductor of thy name, a Graſier
That ran away with pay: or am I grown
(Becauſe I have been a little peeviſh to you,
Onely to try your temper) ſuch a dogge-latch
I could not be admitted to your preſence?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: If I endure this, hang me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And two deaths heads,
Two Harry Groats, that had their faces worne,
Almoſt their names away too.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Now heare me.
For I will ſtay no longer.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: This you ſhall:
How ever you ſhall think to flatter me,
For this offence, which no ſubmiſſion.
Can ever mediate for, you'l finde it ſo,
What ever you ſhall doe by interceſſion,
What you can offer, what your Land can purchaſe,
What all your friends, or families can win,
Shall be but this, not to forſweare your knowledge,
But ever to forbeare it: now your will ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Thou art the ſubtleſt woman I think living,
I am ſure the lewdeſt; now be ſtill, and marke me;
Were I but any way addicted to the devill,
I ſhould now think I had met a play-fellow
To profit by, and that way the moſt learned
That ever taught to murmur. Tell me thou,
Thou moſt poor, paltry ſpitefull whore: doe you cry?
Ile make you roare, before I leave.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Was it not ſinne enough, thou Fruiterer
Full of the fall thou eat'ſt: thou devils broker,
Thou Seminary of all ſedition,
Thou ſword of veng'ance, with a thred hung o're us,
Was it not ſinne enough, and wickednes
In full abundance? was it not vexation
At all points, cap a pe? nay, I ſhall pinch you,
Thus like a rotten raſcall to abuſe.
The name of heaven, the tye of marriage,
The honour of thy friends; the expectation
Of all that thought thee vertuous, with rebellion,
Childiſh and baſe rebellion, but continuing.
After forgiveneſſe too, and worſe, your miſchiefe,
And againſt him ſetting the hope of heaven by,
And the deere reſervation of his honour
Nothing above ground could have won to hate thee:
Well goe thy wayes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You ſhall heare me out firſt:
What puniſhment mai'ſt thou deſerve, thou thing,
Thou Idle thing of nothing, thou pull'd Primroſe,
That two houres after, art a weed, and wither'd,
For this laſt flouriſh on me? am I one
Selected out of all the husbands living,
To be ſo ridden by a Tit of ten pence,
Am I ſo blind and Bed-rid? I was mad,
And had the Plague, and no man muſt come neere me,
I muſt be ſhut up, and my ſubſtance bezel'd,
And an old woman watch me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Well ſir, well,
You may well glory in't.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And when it comes to opening, 'tis my plot,
I muſt undoe my ſelfe forſooth: do'ſt heare me?
If I ſhould beat thee now, as much may be,
Do'ſt thou not well deſerve it, o' thy conſcience,
Do'ſt thou not cry, come beat me?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I defie you.
And my laſt loving teares farwell: the firſt ſtroke,
The very firſt you give me if you dare ſtrike,
Try me, and you ſhall finde it ſo, for ever
Never to be recall'd: I know you love me,
Mad till you have enjoy'd me; I doe turne
Utterly from you, and what man I meet firſt,
That has but ſpirit to deſerve a favour,
Let him beare any ſhape, the worſe the better,
Shall kill you, and enjoy me; what I have ſaid
About your fooliſh ſickneſſe, e're you have me
As you would have me, you ſhall ſweare, is certaine,
And challenge any man, that dares deny it;
And in all companies approve my actions,
And ſo farwell for this time. Exit Mar.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Grief goe with thee,
If there be any witchcrafts, herbes, or potions,
Saying my Prayers back-ward, Fiends, or Fayries
That can againe unlove me, I am made. Exit.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Miſtreſſe, you muſt doe it.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Are the writings ready I told you of?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Yes they are ready, but to what uſe I know not.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Y'are an Aſſe, you muſt have all things conſtru'd,

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Yes, and peirc'd too,
Or I finde little pleaſure.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Now you are knaviſh,
Goe too, fetch Rowland hither preſently,
Your twenty pound lies bleeding elſe: ſhe is married
Within theſe twelve houres, if we croſſe it not,
And ſee the Papers of one ſize.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I have ye.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: And for diſpoſing of 'em.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: If I faile you
Now I have found the way, uſe Marſhall Law
And cut my head off with a hand Saw:

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Wel ſir.
Petronius and Moroſo I'le ſee ſent for
About your buſineſſe; goe.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I am gone. Exit Tra.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Ho Livia. Enter Livia.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: A friend of yours, Lord how you looke now,
As if you had loſt a Carrick.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: O Byancha.
I am the moſt undone, unhappy woman.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Be quiet wench, thou ſhalt be done, and done,
And done, and double done, or all ſhall ſplit for't,
No more of theſe minc'd paſſions, they are mangy,
And eaſe thee of nothing, but a little wind,
An apple will doe more: thou fear'ſt Moroſo.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Even as I feare the Gallowes.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Keepe thee there ſtill.
And you love Rowland? ſay.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: If I ſay not
I am ſure I lye.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: What would'ſt thou give that woman,
In ſpight of all his anger, and thy feare,
And all thy Fathers policy, that could
Clap ye within theſe two nights quietly
Into a Bed together?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Why fairely,
At half ſword man and wife: now the red blood comes,
I marry now the matters chang'd.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Me thinks you ſhould not mock me.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Mock a pudding.
I ſpeake good honeſt Engliſh, and good meaning.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I ſhould not be ungratefull to that woman.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: I know thou would'ſt not, follow but my Counpell
And if thou haſt him not, deſpight of fortune
Let me nev'r know a good night more; you muſt
Be very ſick o'th inſtant.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Well, what follows?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: And in that ſickneſſe ſend for all your friends,
Your Father, and your feavor old Moroſo,
And Rowland ſhall be there too.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: What of theſe?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Doe you not twitter yet? of this ſhall follow
That which ſhall make thy heart leape, and thy lips
Venture as many kiſſes, as the Merchants
Doe dollars to the East-Indies: you ſhall know all,
But firſt walke in, and practiſe, pray be ſick.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I doe beleeve you: and I am ſick.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Doe
To bed then, come, Ile ſend away your Servants
Poſt for your Foole, and Father; and good fortune,
As we meane honeſty, now ſtrike an up-ſhot. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Nay, on my conſcience, I have loſt my money,
But that's all one: Ile never more perſwade you,
I ſee you are reſolute, and I commend you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: But did ſhe ſend for me?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You dare beleeve me.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I cannot tell, you have your waies for profit
Allow'd you Tranio, as well as I
Have to avoid 'em feare:

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No, on my word ſir
l deale directly with you. Enter Servant.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: How now fellow,
Whither Poſt you ſo faſt?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: O ſir my Maſter
Pray did you ſee my Maſter?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Why your Maſter?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Sir his Jewell.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: With the gilded Button?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: My pretty Miſtreſſe Livia.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What of her?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Is falne ſick o'th ſuddaine.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: How o'th ſullens?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: O'th ſuddaine ſir, I ſay, very ſick:

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: It ſeemes ſhe hath got the toothach with raw apples.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: It ſeemes you have got the headach, fare you well ſir.
You did not ſee my Maſter?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Who told you ſo?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No, no, he did not ſee him.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Farewell blew bottle. Exit Servant.
What ſhould her ſickneſſe be?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: For you it may be.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes when my braines are out, I may beleeve it,
Never before I am ſure: yet I may ſee her
'Twill be a point of honeſty:

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: It will ſo.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: It may be not too: you would faine be fingring
This old ſinne-offring of two hundred, Tranio,
How daintily, and cunningly you drive me
Up like a Deere to'th toyle, yet I may leape it,
And what's the woodman then?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: A looſer by you.
Speake will you go or not? to me 'tis equall.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Come what goes leſſe?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Nay not a penny Rowland.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Shall I have liberty of conſcience
Which by interpretation, is ten kiſſes?
Hang me if I affect her: yet it may be,
This whorſon manners will require a ſtrugling,
Of two and twenty, or by'r-Lady thirty.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: By'r-lady Ile require my wager then,
For if you kiſſe ſo often, and no kindneſſe,
I have loſt my ſpeculation, i'le allow you —

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Speake like a Gamſter now.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: It may be two.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Under a dozen Tranio 'ther's no ſettings,
You ſhall have forty ſhillings, winck at ſmall faults.
Say I take twenty, come, by all that's honeſt
I doe it but to vex her.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Ile no by-lowes.
If you can love her doe, if you can hate her,
Or any elſe that loves you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Prethee Tranio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Why farewell twenty pound, twill not undoe me;
You have my reſolution.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: And your money,
Which ſince you are ſo ſtubborne, if I forfeit,
Make me a Jack o' Lent, and breake ſhins
For untag'd points and Compters: Ile goe with you,
But if thou gett'ſt a penny by the bargaine;
A parting kiſſe is lawfull?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I allow it.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Knock out my braines with Apples; yet a bargaine:

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I tell you, i'le no bargaines; win, and weare it.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Thou art the ſtrangeſt fellow.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: That's all one.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Along then, twenty pound more if thou dar'ſt,
I give her not a good word.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Not a Penny. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Prethee, entreat her come, I will not trouble her Exit Pedro.
Above a word or two; ere I endure
This life, and with a woman, and a vow'd one
To all the miſchiefes ſhe can lay upon me,
Ile goe to Plough again, and eat leeke Porridge;
Begging's a pleaſure to 't not to be numberd:
No there be other Countries Iaques for me, and other people, yea, and other women.
If I have need, here's money, there's your ware,
Which is faire dealing, and the Sunne, they ſay
Shines as warme there, as here, and till I have loſt
Either my ſelfe, or her, I care not whether
Nor which firſt.

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: Will your worſhip heare me?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And utterly outworne the memory
Of ſuch a curſe as this, none of my Nation
Shall ever know me more.

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: Out alas ſir
What a ſtrange way doe you runne?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Any way,
So I out-runne this raſcall.

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: Me thinkes now,
If your good worſhip could but have the patience.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: The patience, why the patience?

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: Why i'le tell you,
Could you but have the patience.

sp.speaker: Peru.
sp.l: Well the patience.

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: To laugh at all ſhe do's, or when ſhe railes,
To have a drum beaten o'th top o'th houſe,
To give the neighbours warning of her Larme,
As I doe when my wife rebels.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Thy wife?
Thy wife's a Pigeon to her a meere ſlumber,
The dead of night's not ſtiller.

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: Nor an Iron Mill.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: But thy wife is certaine.

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.l: That's falſe Doctrine,
You never read of a certaine woman.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Thou know'st her way.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I ſhould doe, I am ſure.
I have ridden it night, and day, this twenty yeare.

sp.speaker: Petri.
sp.l: But mine is ſuch a drench of Balderdaſh,
Such a ſtrange carded cunningneſſe, the Rayne-bow
When ſhe hangs bent in heaven, ſheds not her colours
Quicker and more then this deceitfull woman Enter Ped.
