Weaves in her dyes of wickedneſſe: what ſayes ſhe?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Nay not a word ſir, but ſhe pointed to me,
As though ſhe meant to follow; pray ſir bear it
Ev'n as you may, I need not teach your worſhip,
The beſt men have their croſſes, we are all mortall.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What ailes the fellow?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: And no doubt ſhe may ſir

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What may ſhe, or what do's ſhe, or what is ſhe?
Speake and be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: She's mad Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Heaven continue it.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Amen if't be his pleaſure

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: How mad is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: As mad as heart can wiſh ſir: ſhe has dreſt her ſelf
(Saving your worſhips reverence) iuſt i'th cut
Of one of thoſe that multiply i'th Suburbs
For ſingle money, and as durtily:
If any ſpeake to her, firſt ſhe whiſtles,
And then begins her compaſſe with her fingers,
And points to what ſhe would have.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What new waye's this?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: There came in Maſter Sophocles,

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And what
Did Maſter Sophocles when he came in?
Get my Truncks ready ſirha, i'le be gone straight.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: He's here to tell you Enter Sophocles.
She's horne mad Iaques.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Call ye this a woman?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes ſir, ſhe is a woman,

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Sir, I doubt it.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I had thought you had make experience,

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Yes I did ſo.
And almoſt with my life.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You rid too faſt ſir.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Pray be not miſtaken: by this hand
Your wife's as chaſte, and honeſt as a virgin,
For any thing I know: 'tis true ſhe gave me
A Ring.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: For rutting.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: You are much deceiv'd ſtill,
Beleeve me, I never kiſt her ſince, and now
Coming in viſitation, like a friend,
I thinke ſhe is mad ſir, ſuddainly ſhe ſtarted,
And ſnatch'd the Ring away, and drew her knife out,
To what intent I know not.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Is this certaine?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: As I am here ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I beleeve ypvi honeſt. Enter Maria.
And pray continue ſo.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: She comes.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Now Damſell,
What will your beauty doe, if I forſake you?
Doe you deale by ſignes, and tokens? as I gheſſe then,
You'l walke abroad, this Sommer, and catch Captaines,
Or hire a peece of holy ground i'th Suburbs,
And keepe a neaſt of Nuns?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: O doe not ſtir her!
You ſee in what a caſe ſhe is?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: She is dogged,
And in a beaſtly caſe I am ſure: Ile make her
If ſhe have any tongue, yet tatle Sophocles
Prethee obſerve this woman ſeriouſly,
And eye her well, and when thou haſt done, but tell me
(For thou haſt underſtanding) in what caſe
My ſence was, when I choſe this thing.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Ile tell you
I have ſeene a ſweeter—

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: An hundred times cry oyſters.
Ther's a poore Begger wench about Black-Fryers
Runs on her breech may be an Empreſſe to her.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Nay, now you are too bitter.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Nev'r a whit ſir:
Ile tell thee woman; for now I have day to ſee thee,
And all my wits about me, and I ſpeake
Not out of paſſion neither (leave your mumping)
I know you're well enough: Now would I give
A million but to vex her: when I choſe thee
To make a Bedfellow, I tooke more trouble,
Then twenty Termes can come too, ſuch a cauſe
Of ſuch a title, and ſo everlaſting
That Adams Genealogie may be ended
Ere any law find thee: I tooke a Leproſie,
Nay worſe, the plague, nay worſe yet, a poſſeſſion
And had the devill with thee, if not more:
And yet worſe, was a beaſt, and like a beaſt
Had my reward, a Jade to fiing my fortunes;
For who that had but reaſon to diſtinguiſh
The light from darkneſſe, wine from water, hunger
from full ſaciety, and Fox from ferne buſh
That would have married thee?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: She is not ſo ill.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: She's worſe then I dare think of: ſhe's ſo lewd,
No Court is ſtrong enough to bear her cauſe.
She hath neither manners, honeſty, behavour,
Wiſe-hood, nor woman-hood, nor any morall
Can force me think ſhe had a mother, no
I do believe her ſtedfaſtly, and know her
To be a woman-Woolfe by tranſmigration,
Her firſt forme was a Ferrets undergrounde,
She kils the memories of men: not yet?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Do you think ſhe's ſenſible of this?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I care not,
Be what ſhe will the pleaſure I take in her,
Thus I blow off, the care I took to love her,
Like this point I unty, and thus I looſe it,
The husband I am to her, thus I ſever:
My vanity farwell: yet, for you have bin
So neer me as to bear the name of wife,
My unquench'd charity ſhall tell you thus much
(Though you deſerve it well) you ſhall not beg,
What I ordan'd your Jointure, honeſtly
You ſhall have ſetled on you: and half my houſe,
The other half ſhall be imploy'd in prayers,
(That meritorious charge Ile beat alſo
Yet to confirm you chriſtian) your apparrell,
And what belongs to build up ſuch a folly,
Keep I beſeech you, it infects our uſes,
And now I am for travell.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Now I love you,
And now I ſee you are a man ile talk to you,
And I forget your bitterneſſe.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: How now man?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: O Pliny, if thou wilt be ever famous
Make but this woman all thy wonders.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sure ſir
You have hit upon a happy courſe, a bleſſed,
And what will make you vertuous?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: She'l ſhip me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A way of underſtanding I long wiſhd for,
And now tis come, take heed you fly not back ſir,
Me thinks you look a new man to me now,
A man of excellence, and now I ſee
Some great deſign ſet in you: you may think now
(And ſo may moſt that know me) 'twere my part
Weakly to weep your loſſe, and to reſiſt you,
Nay hang about your neck and like a dotard
Urge my ſtrong tie upon you: but I love you,
And all the world ſhall know it, beyond woman,
And more prefer the honour of your Country,
Which chiefly you are born for, and may perfect,
The uſes you may make of other Nations,
The ripening of your knowledge, converſation,
The full ability, and ſtrength of judgement,
Then any private love, or wanton kiſſes.
Go worthy man, bring home underſtanding.

sp.speaker: So • h.
sp.l: This were an excellent woman to breed Schoolmen.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: For if the Merchant through unknown Seas plough
To get his wealth, then deer ſir, what muſt you
To gather wiſdome? go, and go alone,
Only your noble mind for your companion,
And if a woman may win credit with you,
Go far: too far you cannot: ſtill the farther
The more experience finds you: and go ſparing,
One meale a week will ſerve you, and one ſute,
Through all your travels: for you'l find it certaine,
The poorer and the baſer you appear,
The more you look through ſtill.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Do'ſt hear her?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What would this woman do if ſhe were ſuffer'd,
Upon a new adventure?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Make us nothing,
I wonder that ſhe writes not.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Then when time,
And fulneſſe of occaſion have new made you,
And ſquard you from a ſot into a Signour,
Or neerer from a lade into a courſer;
Come home an aged man, as did Ʋlyſses,
And I your glad Penelope.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: That muſt have
As many lovers as I languages,
And what ſhe do's with one i'th day, i'th night
Undoe it with an other.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Much that way ſir;
For in your abſence, it muſt be my honour,
That, that muſt make me ſpoken of hereafter,
To have temptations, and not little ones
Daily and hourely offerd me, and ſtrongly,
Almoſt believed againſt me, to ſet off
The faith, and loyalty of her that loves you

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What ſhould I do?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Why by my—I would travell,
Did not you mean ſo?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Alas no, nothing leſſe man:
I did it but to try ſir, ſhee's the devill,
And now I find it, for ſhe drives me, I muſt go:
Are my trunks down there, and my horſes ready?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Sir, for your houſe, and if you pleaſe to truſt me
With that you leave behinde.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Bring down the money.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: As I am able, and to my poor fortunes,
I'le govern as a widow: I ſhall long
To hear of your wel-doing, and your profit:
And when I hear not from you once a quarter,
I'le wiſh you in the Indies, or Cataya,
Thoſe are the climes muſt make you.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: How's the wind?
She'l wiſh me out o'th world anon.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: For France.
Tis very faire; get you aboard to night ſir,
And looſe no time, you know the tide ſtaies no man,
I have cold meats ready for you.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Far thee well.
Thou ha'ſt foold me o'th Kingdom with a vengeance,
And thoue canſt foole me in againe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Not I ſir,
I love you better, take your time, and pleaſure.
Ile ſee you horſd.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I think thou wouldſt ſee me hangd too,
Were I but halfe as willing.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Any thing
That you think well of, I dare look upon.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You'l bear me to the lands end Sophocles,
And other of my friends I hope.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Nev'r doubt ſir,
You cannot want companions for your good:
I am ſure you'l kiſſe me ere I go; I have buſineſſe,
And ſtay long here I muſt not.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Get thee going.
For if thou tarrieſt but an other Dialogue
Ile kick thee to thy Chamber.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Far you well Sir,
And bear your ſelfe, I do beſeech you once more,
Since you have undertaken doing wiſely,
Manly, and worthily, tis tor my credit,
And for thoſe flying fames here of your follies,
Your gambols, and ill breeding of your youth,
For which I underſtand you take this travell,
Nothing ſhould make me leave you els, ile deale
So like a wife, that loves your reputation,
And the moſt large addition of your credit,
That thoſe ſhall die: if you want Limon-waters,
Or any thing to take the edge o'th Sea off,
Pray ſpeak, and be provided.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Now the Devill,
That was your firſt good maſter, ſhoure his bleſſing
Upon ye all: into whoſe cuſtody—

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I do commit your Reformation,
And ſo I leave you to your Stilo novo. Exit Maria

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I will go: yet I will not: once more Sophocles
Ile put her to the teſt.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: You had better go.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I will go then: let's ſeek my father out,
And all my friends to ſee me faire aboard:
Then women, if there be a ſtorme at Sea,
Worſe then your tongues can make, and waves more broken
Then your diſſembling fayths are, let me feele
Nothing but tempeſts, till they cracke my Keele.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Petronius, and Byancha with foure papers.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Now whether I deſerve that blame you gave me,
Let all the world diſcern ſir.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: If this motion,
(I mean this fair repentance of my Daughter)
Spring from your good perſwaſion, as it ſems ſo,
I muſt confeſſe I have ſpoke too boldly of you,
And I repent.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: The firſt touch was her own,
Taken no doubt from diſobeying you,
The ſecond I put to her, when I told her
How good, and gentle yet, with free contrition
Again you might be purchas'd: loving woman,
She heard me, and I thank her, thought me worthy
Obſerving in this point: yet all my councell,
And comfort in this caſe, could not ſo heal her
But that grief got his ſhare too, and ſhe ſickend.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: I am ſorry ſhe's ſo ill, yet glad her ſickneſſe
Ha's got ſo good a ground. Enter Moroſo.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Here comes Moroſo.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: O you are very welcome,
Now you ſhall know your happineſſe.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I am glad on't.
What makes this Lady here?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: A diſh for you ſir
You'l thank me for hereafter.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: True Moroſo,
Go get you in, and ſee your Miſtris.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: She is ſick ſir,
But you may kiſſe her whole.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: How.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Comfort her.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: VVhy am I ſent for ſir?

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Will you in, and ſee?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: May be ſhe needs confeſſion.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: By St. Mary,
She ſhall have abſolution then and pennance,
But not above her carriage.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Get you in foole. Exit. Mor.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.p: Here comes the other too. En. Rowland and Tranio.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Now Tranio.
Good ev'n to you too, and you are welcome.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: I have a certaine Daughter.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Would you had ſir.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: No doubt you know her well.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Nor never ſhall ſir.
She is a woman, and the waies unto her
Are like the finding of a certaine path
After a deep falne Snow.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Well thats by'th by ſtill.
This Daughter that I tell you of is falne
A little crop ſick, with the dangerous ſurfeit
She took of your affection.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Mine ſir?

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Yes ſir.
Or rather, as it ſeemes, repenting.
And there ſhe lies within, debating on't,

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Well ſir.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: I think 'twere well you would ſee her.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: If you pleaſe ſir;
I am not ſqueamiſh of my viſitation.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: But, this ile tell you, ſhe is alter'd much,
You'l finde her now an other Livia.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I have enough o'th old ſir.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: No more foole,
To look gay babies in your eyes yong Rowland,
And hang about your prety neck.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I am glad on't,
And thank my Fates I have ſcapd ſuch execution,

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: And buſſe you till you bluſh againe.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Thats hard ſir,
She muſt kiſſe ſhamefully ere I bluſh at it,
I never was ſo boyiſh; well, what followes?

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: She's mine now, as I pleaſe to ſettle her,
At my command, and where I pleaſe to plant her:
Only ſhe would take a kind of farwell of you,
And give you back a wandring vow or two,
You left in pawn; and two or three ſlight oaths
She lent you too, ſhe looks for.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: She ſhall have 'em
With all my heart ſir, and if you like it better,
A free releaſe in writing.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Thats the matter,
And you from her, you ſhall have an other Rowland,
And then turne taile to taile, and peace by with you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: So be it: your twenty pound ſweats Tranio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: 'Twill not undoe me Rowland, do your worſt.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Come, ſhall we ſee her Sir?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: What ere ſhe ſaies
You muſt beare manly Rowland, for her ſickneſſe
Has made he rſomewhat teatiſh.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Let her talke
Till her tongue ake I care not: by this hand
Thou haſt a handſome face wench, and a body
Daintely mounted; now do I feele an hundred
Runing directly from me, as I piſt it.
sp.stage: Enter Livia diſcovered abed, and Moroſo by her.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: pray draw 'em ſoftly, the leaſt hurry ſir
Puts her to much impatience.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: How is't daughter?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: O very ſick, very ſick, yet ſomewhat
Better I hope; a little lightſommer,
Becauſe this goodman has forgiven me;
Pray ſet me higher; Oh my head:

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Wel done wench.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Father, and all good people that ſhal heare me,
I have abus'd this man perniciouſly; was never old man humbled ſo;
I have ſcornd him, and cal'd him naſty names,
I have ſpit at him,
Flung Candles ends in's beard, and cald him harrow,
That muſt be drawn to all he dos: contemn'd him,
For me thought then he was a beaſtly fellow.
(Oh God my ſide) a very beaſtly fellow.
And gave it out, his caſſock was a Barge-cloth,
Pawnd to his predeceffor by a Sculler,
The man yet living: I gave him purging-comfits
At a great chriſtning once,
That ſpoyl'd his Chamblet breeches; and one night
I ſtrewd the ſtaires with peaſe, as he paſt down;
And the good Gentleman (woe worth me for't)
Ev'n with his reverent head, this head of wiſdome,
Told two and twenty ſtaires, good and true;
Miſt not a ſtep, and as we ſay verbatim
Fell to the bottome, broke his caſting Bottle,
Loſt a fair toad-ſtone of ſome eighteen ſhillings,
Jumbled his joynts together, had two ſtooles,
And was tranſlated. All this villany
Did I: I Livia, I alone, untaught.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: And I unask'd, forgive it.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Where's Byancha?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Here Cozen.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Give me drinke,

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: O'my diſſembler, you and I muſt part.
Come neerer ſir.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I am ſorry for your ſickneſſe.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Be ſorry for your ſelfe ſir, you have wrong'd me,
But I forgive you; are the papers ready?

sp.speaker: Bya
sp.l: I have'em here: wilt pleaſe you view 'em?

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Shew 'em the young man too, I know he's willing
To ſhift his ſailes too: tis for his more advancement;
Alas, we might have beggerd one another;
We are young both, and a world of children
Might have been left behind to curſe our follies:
We had been undone Byancha, had we married,
Undone for ever: I confeſſe I lov'd him,
I care not who ſhall know it, moſt intirely;
And once, upon my conſcience, he lov'd me;
But farewell that, we muſt be wiſer coſen.
Love muſt not leave us to the world: have you done?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes, and am ready to ſubſcribe.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Pray ſtay then:
Give me the papers, and let me paruſe 'em,
And ſo much time, as may afford a teare
At our laſt parting.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Pray retire, and leave her,
Ile call ye preſently.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Come Gentlemen, the ſhowre muſt fall.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Would I had never ſeen her.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Thou haſt done bravely wench.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Pray Heaven it prove ſo.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: There are the other papers: when they come
Begin you firſt, and let the reſt ſubſcribe
Hard by your ſide; give 'em as little light
As Drapers doe their wares.

sp.speaker: Liv
sp.l: Didſt mark Moroſo,
In what an agony he was, and how he cry'd moſt
When I abus'd him moſt?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: That was but reaſon.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Oh what a ſtinking thief is this?
Though I was but to counterfeit, he made me
Directly ſick indeed. Tames-ſtreet to him
Is a meere Pomander.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Let him be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Amen.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: And lie you ſtill.
And once more to your buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Call 'em in.
Now if there be a power that pities lovers,
Helpe now, and heare my prayers.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Is ſhe ready?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: She has done her lamentations: pray go to her.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Rowland, come neer me, and before you ſeale,
Give me your hand: take it again; now kiſſe me,
This is the laſt acquaintance we muſt have;
I wiſh you ever happy: there's the paper.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Pray ſtay a little.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Let me never live more
But I do begin to pity this young fellow;
How heartily he weeps!

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: There's Pen and Inke ſir.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Ev'n here I pray you. Tis a little Emblem
How neere you have been to me.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: There..

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Your hands too,
As witneſſes.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: By any means
To th' booke ſonne.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: You muſt deliver it.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: There Livia, and a better love light on thee,
I can no more.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: To this you muſt be witneſſe too.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: We wil.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Doe you deliver it now.

sp.speaker: Lyv.
sp.l: Pray ſet me up;
There Rowland, all thy old love back: and may
A new to come exceed mine, and be happy.
I muſt no more.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Farewell:

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: A long farewell. Exit Rowl.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Leave herby any means, till this wild paſſion
Be off her head; draw all the Curtaines cloſe,
A day hence you may ſee her, twil be better,
She is now for little company.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Pray tend her.
I muſt to horſe ſtraight: you muſt needs along too,
To ſee my ſonne aboard; were but his wife
As ſit for pity, as this wench, I were happy.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Time muſt do that too: fare ye wel; to morrow
You ſhall receive a wife to quit your ſorrow. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena ſecunda.
div.stage: Enter Jaques, Pedro, and Porters, with Cheſt and Hampers.

sp.speaker: Jag.
sp.l: Bring 'em away ſirs.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Muſt the great Trunks go too

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Yes, and the Hampers; nay be ſpeedy Maſters;
He'l be at Sea before, us elſe.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: O Jaques,
What a moſt bleſſed turn haſt thou?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I hope ſo.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: To have the Sea between thee and this woman,
Nothing can drown her tongue, but a ſtorm.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: By your leave,
We'l get us up to Paris with all ſpeed;
For on my ſoule, as far as Amyens
She'l carry blanke; away to Lyon key
And ſhip 'em preſently, we'l follow ye.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Now could I wiſh her in that Trunk:

sp.speaker: Jaq
sp.l: God ſhield man,
I had rather have a Beare in't.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Yes, Ile tell ye:
For in the paſſage if a Tempeſt take ye,
As many doe, and you lie beating for it,
Then, if it pleaſ'd the fates, I would have the Maſter
Out of a powerfull providence, to cry,
Lighten the ſhip of all hands, or we periſh;
Then this for one, as beſt ſpar'd, ſhould by all means
Over-board preſently.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: O' that condition,
So we were certaine to be rid of her,
I would wiſh her with us: But believe me Pedro,
She would ſpoyle the fiſhing on this coaſt for ever,
For none would keepe her company, but Dog-fiſh,
As curriſh as her ſelfe; or Porpiſces,
Made to all fatall uſes: The two Fiſh-ſtreets
Were ſhe but once ariv'd amongſt the Whitings,
Would ſing a wofull miſereri Pedro,
And mourn in poor John, till her memory
Were caſt o' ſhore agen, with a ſtrong Sea-breach:
She would make god Neptune, and his fire-forke,
And all his demi-gods, and goddeſſes,
As weary of the Flemmiſh channell Pedro,
As ever boy was of the ſchoole: tis certain,
If ſhe but meet him faire, and were wel angred,
She would break his god-head.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Oh her tongue, her tongue.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Rather her many tongues.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Or rather ſtrange tongues.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Her lying tongue.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Her liſping tongue.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Her long tongue.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Her lawleſſe tongue.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Her loud tongue.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: And her lickriſh —

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Many other tongues, and many ſtranger tongues
Then ever Babel had to tell his ruines,
Were women rais'd withall; but never a true one.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Home with your ſtuffe agen; the journeys ended.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: What do's your worſhip meane?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Your Maſter, O Petruobio, O poore fellows.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: O Jaques, Jaques.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: O your, Maſter's dead,
His body comming back; his wife, his devil;
The grieſe of— her

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Has kild him?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Kild him, kild him.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Is there no law to hang her.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Get ye in,
And let her know her miſery, I dare not
For feare impatience ſeize me, ſee her more,
I muſt away agen: Bid her for wife-hood,
For honeſty, if ſhe have any in her,
Even to avoyd the ſhame that follows her.
Cry if ſhe can: your weeping cannot mend it.
The body wil be here within this houre, ſo tell her;
And all his friends to curſe her. Farewell fellowes.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: O Jaques, Jaques.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: O my worthy Maiſter.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: O my moſt beaſtly Miſtris, hang her.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Split her.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Drown her directly.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Starve her.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Stinke upon her.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Stone her to death: may all ſhe eate be Eggs,
Till ſhe run kicking mad for men.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: And he,
That man, that gives her remedy, pray Heav'n
He may ev'n ipſo facto, loſe his longings.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Let's goe diſcharge our ſelves, and he that ſerves her,
Or ſpeaks a good word of her from this houre,
A ſeagly curſe light on him, which is, Pedro;
The feind ride through him booted, and ſpurd, with a Sythe at's back. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena tertia.
div.stage: Enter Rowland, and Tranio ſtealing behind him.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What a dull aſſe was I to let her go thus?
Upon my life ſhe loves me ſtill: wel Paper,
Thou onely monument of what I have had,
Thou all the love now left me, and now loſt,
Let me yet kiſſe her hand, yet take my leave
Of what I muſt leave evere Farewell Livia.
Oh bitter words, Ile read ye once again,
And then for ever ſtudy to forget ye.
How's this? let me look better on 't: A Contract?
— a Contract, ſeal'd, and ratified,
Her fathers hand ſet to it, and Maroſo'st
I do not dream ſure, let me read again,
The ſame ſtill: tis a contract.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Tis ſo Rowlands;
And by the vertue of the ſame, you pay me
An hundred pound to morrow.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Art ſure Tranio,
We are both alive now?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Wonder not, ye have loſt.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: If this be true, I grant it.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Tis moſt certaine,
There's a Ring for you to, you know it.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: When ſhall I have my money?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Stay ye, ſtay ye,
When ſhall I marry her?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: To night.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Take heed now
You do not trifle me; if you doe,
You'l finde more payment, then your money comes to:
Come ſweare; I know I am a man, and finde
I may deceive my ſelfe: Sweare faithfully,
Sweare me directly, am I Rowland?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Am I awake?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Ye are.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Am I in health?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: As far as I conceive.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Was I with Livia?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You were, and had his contract.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: And ſhall I enjoy her?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Yes, if ye dare.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Sweare to all theſe.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: As thou art honeſt, as thou haſt a conſcience,
As that may wring thee if thou lyeſt; all theſe
To be no viſion, but a truth, and ſerious.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Then by my honeſty, and faith, and conſcience;
All this is certaine.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Let's remove our places.
Sweare it again.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: By—tis true.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I have loſt then, and Heaven knows I am glad out.
Let's goe, and tell me all, and tell me how,
For yet I am a Pagan in it.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I have a Prieſt too,
And all ſhall come as even as two Teſters. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Petronius, Sophocles, Moroſo, and Petruchio born in a Coffin.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Set down the body, and one call her out.
sp.stage: Enter Maria in blacke, and Jaques.
sp.l: You are welcome to the laſt caſt of your fortunes;
There lies your husband, there your loving husband,
There he that was Petruchio, too good for ye;
Your ſtubborn, and unworthy way has kild him
Ere he could reach the Sea; if ye can weep,
Now ye have cauſe begin, and after death
Do ſomething yet to th'world, to thinke ye honeſt.
So many teares had ſav'd him, ſhed in time;
And as they are (ſo a good mind goe with 'em)
Yet they may move compaſſion.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Pray ye all heare me,
And judge me as I am, not as you covet,
For that would make me ye more miſerable:
Tis true, I have cauſe to grieve, and mighty cauſe;
And truely and unfainedly I weep it.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I ſee there's ſome good nature yet left in her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: But what's the cauſe? miſtake me not, not this man,
As he is dead, I weep for; Heaven defend it,
I never was ſo childiſh: but his life,
His poore unmanly wretched fooliſh life,
Is that my full eyes pity, there's my mourning.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Doſt thou not ſhame?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I do, and even to water,
To think what this man was, to think how ſimple,
How far below a man, how far from reaſon,
From common underſtanding, and all Gentry,
While he was living here he walkt amongſt us.
He had a happy turn he dyed; ile tell ye,
Theſe are the wants I weep for, not his perſon:
The memory of this man, had he liv'd
But two yeers longer, had begot more follies,
Then wealthy Autumne flyes: But let him reſt,
He was a foole, and farewell he; not pitied,
I meane in way of life, or action
By any underſtanding man that's honeſt;
But onely in's poſterity, which I
Out of the feare his ruines might out live him
In ſome bad iſſue, like a carefull woman,
Like one indeed born onely to preſerve him,
Denyd him meanes to raiſe.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Unbutton me,
—I die indeed elſe? O Maria,
Oh my unhappineſſe, my miſery.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Go to him whore;—if he periſh,
Ile ſee thee hang'd my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Why, why Maria.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I have done my worſt, and have my end, forgive me;
From this houre make me what you pleaſe: I have tam'd ye,
And now am vowd your ſervant: Look not ſtrangly,
Nor feare what I ſay to you. Dare you kiſſe me?
Thus I begin my new love.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Once againe?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Once again Miria!
O Gentlemen, I Know not where I am.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Get ye to bed then: there you'l quickly know ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Never no more your old tricks?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Never ſir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You ſhall not need, for as I have a faith
No cauſe ſhall give occaſion.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: As I am honeſt,
And as I am a maid yet, all my life
From this houre ſince, ſince ye make ſo free profeſſion,
I dedicate in ſervice to your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I marry, this goes roundly off.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Go Jaques,
Get all the beſt meat may be bought for money,
And let the hogſheds blood, I am born again:
Well little England, when I ſee a husband
Of any other Nation ſtern or jealous,
Ile wiſh him but a woman of thy breeding,
And if he have not butter to thy bread,
Till thy teeth bleed, ile never truſt my travell.

div.stage: Enter Rowland, Livia, Byancha, and Tranio.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: What have we here?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Another morris, ſir.
That you muſt pipe too.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: A poore married couple
Deſire an offering ſir.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Never frown at it,
You cannot mend it now: there's your own hand;
And yours Moroſo, to confirme the bargaine.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: My hand?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Or mine?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: You'l finde it ſo.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: A trick.
By — a trick.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Yes ſir, we trickt ye.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Father.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Haſt thou lyen with him? ſpeake?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Yes truly ſir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: And haſt thou done the deed boy?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I have done ſir,
That, that will ſerve the turne, I think.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: A match then,
Ile be the maker up of this: Moroſo,
There's now no remedy you ſee, be willing;
For be, or be not, he muſt have the wench.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Since I am over-reach'd, let's in to dinner,
And if I can Ile drink't away.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: That's wel ſaid.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Well ſirha, you have playd a tricke, look to't,
And let me be a grandſire within's twelvemoneth,
Or by this hand, Ile curtaile halfe your fortunes.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: There ſhall not want my labour ſir: your money;
Here's one has undertaken.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Well, Ile truſt her,
And glad I have ſo good a pawn.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Ile watch ye.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Lets in, and drink of all hands, and be joviall:
I have my colt again, and now ſhe carries;
And Gentlemen, whoever marries next,
Let him be ſure he keep him to his Text. Exeunt.

div.head: PROLOGUE.
div.l: LAdies to you, in whoſe defence and right,
Fletchers brave Muſe prepar'd her ſelf to fight
A battaile without blood, 'twas well fought too,
(The victory's yours, though got with much ado.)
We do preſent this Comedy, in which
A rivulet of pure wit flowes, ſtrong and rich
In Fancy, Language, and all parts that may
Adde grace and ornament to a merry Play.
Which this may prove. Yet not to go too far
In promiſes from this our female war,
We do intreat the angry men would not
Expect the mazes of a ſubtle plot,
Set Speeches, high expreſſions; and what's worſe,
in a true Comedy, politique diſcourſe.
The end we ayme at, is to make you ſport;
Yet neither gall the City, nor the Court.
Heare, and obſerve his Comique ſtraine and when
Y'are ſick of melancholy, ſee't agen.
'Tis no deere Phyſick, ſince 'twill quit the coſt:
Or his intentions, with our pains, are loſt.

div.head: EPILOGUE.
div.l: THe Tamer's tam'd, but ſo, as nor the men
Can finde one juſt cauſe to complaine of, when
They fitly do conſider in their lives,
They ſhould not raign as Tyrants o'r their wives.
Nor can the women from this preſident
Inſult, or triumph: it being aptly meant,
To teach both Sexes due equality;
And as they ſtand bound, to love mutually.
If this effect, ariſing from a cauſe
Well layd, and grounded, may deſerve applauſe,
We ſomething more then hope, our honeſt ends
Will keep the men, and women too, our friends.

div.head: LOVE CURE OR, The Martial Maid.

sp.speaker: Vitelli.
sp.p: ALvarez pardon'd?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.p: And return'd.

sp.speaker: Lamo.
sp.l: I ſaw him land
At St. Lucars, and ſuch a generall welcome
Fame, as harbinger to his brave actions,
Had with the eaſie people, prepard for him,
At if by his command alone, and fortune
Holland with thoſe low Provinces, that hold out
Againſt the Arch-Duke, were again compel'd
With their obedience to give up their lives
To be at his devotion.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: You amaze me,
For though I have heard, that when he fled from Civill
To ſave his life (then forfeited to Law
For murthering Don Pedro my deer Uncle)
His extreame wants inforc'd him to take pay
In th'Army ſat down then before Oſtena,
'Twas never yet reported, by whoſe favour
He durſt preſunt to entertain a thought
Of comming home with pardon.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: 'Tis our nature
Or not to hear, or not to give beliefe
To what we wiſh far from our enemies.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Sir 'tis moſt certaine the Infantas letters
Aſſiſted by the Arch-Dukes, to King Philip
Have not alone ſecur'd him from the rigor
Of our Caſtillian Juſtice, but return'd him
A free man, and in grace.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: By what curſ'd meanes
Could ſuch a fugitive ariſe unto
The knowledge of their highneſſes? much more
(Though known) to ſtand but in the leaſt degree
Of favour with them?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: To give ſatisfaction
To your demand, though to praiſe him I hate,
Can yeild me ſmall contentment, I will tell you,
And truly, ſince ſhould I detract his worth,
'T would argue want of merit in my ſelf.
Briefly, to paſſe his tedious pilgrimage
For ſixteene years, a baniſh'd guilty-man,
And to forget the ſtormes, th'affrights, the horrors
His conſtancy, not fortune overcame,
I bring him, with his little ſon, grown man
(Though 'twas ſaid here he took a daughter with him)
To Oſtends bloody ſeige that ſtage of war
Wherein the flower of many Nations acted,
And the whole Chriſtian world ſpectators were;
There by his ſon, or were he by adoption
Or nature his, a brave Scene was preſented,
Which I make choyce to ſpeak of, ſince from that
The good ſucceſſe of Alvarez, had beginning,

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: So I love vertue in an enemy
That I deſire in the relation of
This young mans glorious deed, you'ld keep your ſelf
A friend to truth, and it.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.l: Such was my purpoſe;
The Town being oft aſſaulted, but in vaine,
To dare the prow'd defendants to a ſally,
Weary of eaſe, Don Inigo Peralta
Son to the Generall of our Caſtile forces
All arm'd, advanc'd within ſhot of their wals,
From whence the muskateers plaid thick upon him,
Yet he (brave youth) as careleſſe of the danger,
As carefull of his honor, drew his ſword,
And waving it about his head, as if
He dar'd one ſpirited like himſelf, to triall
Of ſingle valor, he made his retreat
With ſuch a ſlow, and yet majeſtique pace,
As if he ſtill cald low'd, dare none come on?
When ſodainly from a poſterne of the town
Two gallant horſe-men iſſued, and o're-took him,
The army looking on, yet not a man
That durſt relieve the raſh adventurer,
Which Lucio, ſon to Alvarez then ſeeing,
As in the vant-guard he ſat bravely mounted,
Or were it pity of the youths miſfortune,
Care to preſerve the honour of his Country,
Or bold deſire to get himſelfe a name,
He made his brave horſe, like a whirle wind bear him,
Among the Combatants: and in a moment
Diſchar'd his Petronell, with ſuch ſure aime
That of the adverſe party from his horſe,
One tumbled dead, then wheeling round, and drawing
A faulchion ſwift as lightning, he came on
Upon the other, and with one ſtrong blow
In view of the amazed Town, and Campe
He ſtrake him dead, and brought Peralta off
With double honour to himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: 'Twas brave:
But the ſucceſſe of this?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: The Campe receiv'd him
With acclamations of joy and welcome,
And for addition to the faire reward
Being a maſſy chain of gold given to him
By yong Peralta's Father, he was brought
To the Infantas preſence kiſſ'd her hand,
And from that Lady, (greater in her goodneſſe
Then her high birth) had this encouragement
Go on youngman; yet not to feed thy valour
With hope of recompence to come, from me,
For preſent ſatisfaction of what's paſt,
Aske any thing that's fit for me to give,
And thee to take, and be aſſur'd of it.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Excellent princeſſe.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: And ſtil'd worthily
The heart bloud, nay the ſoule of Souldiers.
But what was his requeſt?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: That the repeale
Of Alvarez, makes plaine: he humbly begd
His Fathers pardon, and ſo movingly
Told the ſad ſtory of your uncles death
That the Infanta wept, and inſtantly
Granting his ſuit, working the Arch-duke to it,
Their Letters were directed to the King,
With whom they ſo prevaild, that Alvarez
Was freely pardon'd.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: 'Tis not in the King
To make that good.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Not in the King? what ſubject
Dares contradict his power?

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: In this I dare,
And wil: and not call his prerogative
In queſtion, nor preſume to limit it.
I know he is the Maſter of his Lawes,
And may forgive the forfeits made to them,
But not the injury done to my honour;
And ſince (forgeting my brave Uncles merits
And many ſervices, under Duke D' Alva)
He ſuffes him to fall, wreſting from Juſtice
The powerfull ſword, that would revenge his death,
I'le fill with this Aſtrea's empty hand,
And in my juſt wreake, make this arme the Kings,
My deadly hate to Alvarz, and his houſe,
Which as I grew in years, hath ſtill encreaſ'd,
As if it cal'd on time to make me man,
Slept while it had no object for her fury
But a weak woman, and her talk'd of Daughter:
But now, ſince there are quarries, worth her ſight
Both in the father, and his hopefull ſon,
I'le boldly caſt her off, and gorge her full
With both their hearts: to further which your friendſhip,
And oathes will your aſſiſtance, let your deedes
Make anſwer to me; uſeleſſe are all words
Till you have writ performance with your Swords.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Go fetch my work: this ruffe was not well ſtarch'd,
So tell the maid, 'thas too much blew in it,
And look you that the Partrich and the Pullen
Have cleane meat, and freſh water, or my Mother
Is like to hear on't.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: O good Sir Iaques helpe me: was there ever ſuch an Hermaphrodite heard of? would any wench living, that ſhould hear and ſee what I do, be wrought to believe, that the beſt of a man lies under this Petticoate, and that a Cod-peece were far fitter here, then a pind-Placket?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: You had beſt talk filthily: do; I have a tongue
To tell my Mother, as well as ears to heare
Your ribaldry.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: May you have ten womens tongues that way I am ſure: why my yong Mr. or Miſtris, Madam, Don or what you wil, what the devill have you to do with Pullen, or Partrich? or to ſit pricking on a clowt all day? you have a better needle, I know, and might make better work, if you had grace to uſe it.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Why, how dare you ſpeak this before me, ſirha?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Nay rather, why dare not you do what I ſpeak? — though my Lady your mother, for fear of Vitelli and his faction, hath brought you up like her daughter, and h'as kept you this 20 year, which is ever ſince you were born, a cloſe priſoner within dores, yet ſince you are a man, and are as wel provided as other men are, me thinks you ſhould have the ſame motions of the fleſh, as other Cavaliers of us are inclin'd unto.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Indeed you have cauſe to love thoſe wanton motions,
They having hope you to an excellent whipping,
For doing ſomething, I but put you in mind of it,
With the Indian mayd, the governour ſent my mother
From Mexico.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Why, I but taught her a Spaniſh trick in charity, and holp the King to a ſubject that may live to take grave Maurice priſoner, and that was more good to the State, then a thouſand ſuch as you are ever like to do: and I wil tell you, (in a fatherly care of the Infant I ſpeak it) if he live (as bleſſe the babe, in paſſion I remember him) to your years, ſhall he ſpend his time in pinning, painting, purling, and perfuming as you do? no, he ſhall to the wars, uſe his Spaniſh Pike, though with the danger of the laſh, as his father has done, and when he is provoked, as I am now, draw his Toledo deſperatly, as —

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: You will not Kill me? oh.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: I knew this would ſilence him: how he hids his eys?
If he were a wench now, as he ſeems, what an advantage
Had I, drawing two Toledos, when one can do this?
But oh me, my Lady: I muſt put up: young Maſter
I did but jeſt. O cuſtom, what ha'ſt thou made of him?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: For bringing this, be ſtill my friend; no more
A ſervant to me.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Here,
Even here where I am happy to receive
Aſſurance of my Alvarez returne,
I wil kneell down: and may thoſe holy thoughts
That now poſſeſſe me wholy, make this place
a Temple to me, where I may give thanks
For this unhop'd for bleſſing Heavens Kind hand
Hath pour'd upon me.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Let my duty Madam
Preſume, if you have cauſe of joy, to entreat
I may ſhare in it.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: 'Tis well, he has forgot how I frighted him yet.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt: but firſt kneel with me Lucio,
No more Poſt bumina now, thou haſt a Father,
A Father living to take off that name,
Which my too credulous fears, that he was dead,
Beſtow'd upon thee: thou ſhalt ſee him Lucio,
And make him young again, by ſeeing thee,
Who only hadſt a being in my Womb
When he went from me, Lucio: O my joyes,
So far tranſport me, that I muſt forget
The ornaments of Matrons, modeſty,
And grave behaviour; but let all forgive me
If in th'expreſſion of my ſoules beſt comfort
Though old, I do a while forget mine age,
And play the wanton in the entertinement
Of thoſe delights I have ſo long deſpair'd of.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Shall I then ſee my Father?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: This houre Lucio;
Which reckon the begining of thy life
I mean that life, in which thou ſhalt appeare
To be ſuch as I brought thee forth: a man,
This womaniſh diſguiſe, in which I have
So long conceal'd thee, thou ſhalt now caſt off,
And change thoſe qualities thou didſt learn from me,
For maſculine virtues, for which ſeek no tutor,
But let thy fathers actions be thy precepts;
And for thee Zancho, now expect reward
For thy true ſervice.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Shall I? you hear fellow Stephano, learne to know me more reſpectively; how do'ſt tnou think I ſhall become the Stewards chaire ha? will not theſe ſlender hanches ſhow well with a chaine, and a gold night-Cap after ſupper when I take the accompts?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Haſte, and take down thoſe blacks, with which my chamber
Hath like the widow, her ſad Miſtris, mourn'd,
And hang up for it, the rich Perſian arras,
Uſ'd on my wedding night: for this to me
Shall be a ſecond marriage: ſend for Muſique,
And will the cooks to uſe their beſt of cunning
To pleaſe the palat.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Will your Ladiſhip have a Potato-pie, tis a good ſtirring diſh for an old Lady, after a long Lent.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.p: Be gon I ſay: why ſir, you can go faſter?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: I could Madam: but I am now to practiſe the Stewards pace, that's the reward I look for: every man muſt faſhion his gate, according to his calling: you fellow Stephano, may walk faſter, to overtake preferment: ſo, uſher me.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Pray Madam, let the waſcoat I laſt wrought
Be made up for my Father: I wil have
A cap and boote-hoſe ſutable to it.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Of that.
Wee'l think hereafter Lucio: our thoughts now
Muſt have no object, but thy Fathers welcome,
To which thy helfe—

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: With humble gladneſſe Madam. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Where loſt we Syaevedra?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: He was met
Entring the City by ſome Gentlemen
Kinſmen, as he ſaid of his own, with whom
For complement ſake (for ſo I think he term'd it)
He was compel'd to ſtay: though I much wonder
A man that knowes to do, and has done well
In the head of his troop, when the bold foe charg'd home,
Can learn ſo ſodainly to abuſe his time
In apiſh entertainment: for my part
(By all the glorious rewards of war)
I had rather meet ten enemies in the field
All ſworn to fetch my head, then be brought on
To change an houres diſcourſe with one of theſe
Smooth City fools, or tiſſen Cavaliers,
Then only Gallans, as they wiſely think,
To get a Jewell, or a wanton Kiſſe
From a Court-lip, though painted.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: My Love Clara
(For Lucio is a name thou muſt forget
With Lucio bold behaviour) though thy breeding
I'the camp may plead ſomething in the excuſe
Of thy rough manners, cuſtome having chang'd,
Though not thy Sex, the ſoftneſſe of thy nature,
And fortune (then a cruell ſtepdame to thee)
Impos'd upon thy tender ſweetneſſe, burthens
Of hunder, cold, wounds, want, ſuch as would crack
The ſinewes of a man, not borne a Souldier:
Yet now ſhe ſmiles, and like a naturall mother
Looks gently on thee, Clara, entertaine
Her proffer'd bounties with a willing boſome;
Thou ſhalt no more have need to uſe thy ſword;
Thy beauty (which even Belgia hath not alter'd)
Shall be a ſtronger guard, to keep my Clara,
Then that has bin, (though never us'd but nobly)
And know thus much.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Sir, I know only that
It ſtands not with my duty to gaine-ſay you,
In any thing: I muſt, and will put on
What faſhion you think beſt: though I could wiſh
I were what I appeare.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Endeavour rather. Muſick.
To be what you are, Clara, entring here
As you were borne, a woman.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Let choice Muſick
In the beſt voyce that ere touch'd humane eare,
For joy hath tide my tongue up, ſpeak your welcome.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: My ſoule, (for thou giv'ſt new life to my ſpirit)
Myriads of joyes, though ſhort in number of
Thy vertues, fall on thee; Oh my Eugenia,
Th'aſſurance, that I do embrace thee, makes
My twenty years of ſorrow but a dreame,
And by the Nectar, which I take from theſe,
I feele my age reſtor'd, and like old AEſon
Grow young againe.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: My Lord, long wiſh'd for welcome,
Tis a ſweet briefneſſe, yet in that ſhort word
All pleaſures which I may call mine, begin,
And may they long increaſe, before they finde
A ſecond period: let mine eyes now ſurfet
On this ſo wiſh'd for object, and my lips
Yet modeſtly pay back the parting kiſſe
You truſted with them, when you fled from Civill
With little Clara my ſweet daughter: lives ſhe?
Yet I coul'd chide my ſelfe, having you here
For being ſo coveteous of all joyes at once,
'Tenquire for her, you being alone, to me
My Clara, Lucio, my Lord, my ſelfe;
Nay more then all the world.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: As you, to me are.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Sit down, and let me feed upon the ſtory
Of your paſt dangers, now you are here in ſafety
It will give relliſh, and freſh appetite
To my delights, if ſuch delights can cloy me.
Yet do not Alvarez, let me firſt yeild you
Accompt of my life in your abſence, and
Make you acquainted how I have preſerv'd
The Jewell left lock'd up in my womb,
When you, in being forc'd to leave your country,
Suffer'd a civill death. within Claſhing ſwords.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Doe my Eugenia,
Tis that I moſt deſire to he are,

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Then know Sayavedra within.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: What voyce is that?
If you are noble Enemies, Vitelli within.
Oppreſſe me not with odds, but kill me fairely,
Stand off, I am too many of my ſelfe. Enter Bobadilla.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Murther, murther murther, your friend my Lord,
Don Syavedra is ſet upon in the Streets, by your enemies
Vitelli, and his Faction: I am almoſt kill'd with looking on them.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Ile free him, or fall with him: draw thy ſword
And follow me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Fortune I give thee thankes
For this occaſion once more to uſe it. Exit.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Nay, hold not me Madam; if I doe any hurt, hang me.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Oh I am dead with feare! let's flye into
Your Cloſet, Mother.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: No houre of my life
Secure of danger? heav'n be mercifull,
Or now at once diſpatch me. Enter Vitelli, purſued by Alvarez, & Sayavedra, Clara beating of Anaſtro.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Follow him
Leave me to keepe theſe off.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Aſſault my friend
So neere by houſe?

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: Nor in it will ſpare thee,
Though 'twere a Temple: & Ile mak it one,
I being the Prieſt, and thou the ſacrifice,
Ile offer to my uncle.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Haſte thou to him,
And ſay I ſent thee:

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Twas put bravely by,
And that: and yet comes on, and boldly rare,
In the warres, where emulation and example
Joyn to encreaſe the courage, and make leſſe
The danger; valour, and true reſolution
Never appear'd ſo lovely: brave againe:
Sure he is more then man, and if he fall;
The beſt of vertue, fortitude would dye with him:
And can I ſuffer it? forgive me duty,
So I love valour, as I will protect it
Againſt my Father, and redeeme it, though
'Tis forfeited by one I hate.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Come on,
All is not loſt yet: You ſhall buy me deerer
Before you have me: keep off.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Feare me not,
Thy worth has tooke me Priſoner, and my ſword
For this time knowes thee onely for a friend,
And to all elſe I turne the point of it.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Defend your Fathers Enemy?

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Art thou mad?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Are you men rather? ſhall that valour, which
Begot you lawfull honour in the warres,
Prove now the parent of an infamous Baſtard
So foule, yet ſo long liv'd, as murther will
Be to your ſhames? have each of you, alone
With your own dangers onely, purchas'd glory
From multitudes of Enemies, not allowing
Thoſe neereſt to you, to have part in it,
And doe you now joyn, and lend mutuall helpe
Againſt a ſingle oppoſite? hath the mercy
Of the great King, but newly waſh'd away
The blood, that with the forfeit of your life
Cleav'd to your name, and family like an ulcer,
In this againe to ſet a deeper dye
Upon your infamy? you'll ſay he is your foe,
And by his raſhneſſe call'd on his own ruine;
Remember yet, he was firſt wrong'd, and honour
Spur'd him to what he did, and next the place
Where now he is, your houſe, which by the lawes
Of hoſpitable duty ſhould protect him;
Have you been twenty yeeres a ſtranger to it,
To make your entrance now in blood? or thinke you
Your country-man, a true born Spaniard, will be
An offring fit, to pleaſe the genius of it?
No, in this i'le preſume to teach my Father,
And this firſt Act of diſobedience ſhall
Confirme I am moſt dutifull.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: I am pleas'd
With what I dare not give allowance to;
Unnaturall wretch, what wilt thou doe?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Set free
A noble Enemy: come not on, by —
You paſſe to him, through me: the way is open:
Farwell: when next I meet you, doe not look for
A friend, but a vow'd foe; I ſee you worthy,
And therefore now preſerve you, for the honour
Of my ſword onely:

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Were this man a friend,
How would he win me, that being my vow'd foe
Deſerves ſo well? I thanke you for my life;
But how I ſhall deſerve it, give me leave
Hereafter to confider. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Quit thy feare,
All danger is blown over: I have Letters
To the Governour, in the Kings name, to ſecure us,
From ſuch attempts hereafter: yet we need not
That have ſuch ſtrong guards of our own, dread others;
And to encreaſe thy comfort, know, this young man
Whom with ſuch ſervent earneſtneſſe you eye,
Is not what he appeares, but ſuch a one
As thou with joy wilt bleſſe, thy daughter Clara.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: A thouſand bleſſings in that word.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: The reaſon
Why I have bred her up thus, at more leiſure
I will impart unto you: wonder not
At what you have ſeen her doe, it being the leaſt
Of many great and valiant undertakings
She hath made good with honour.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Ile returne
The joy I have in her, with one as great
To you my Alvarez: you, in a man
Have given to me a daughter: in a woman,
I give to you a Sonne: this was the pledge
You left here with me, whom I have brought up
Different from what he was, as you did Clara,
And with the like ſucceſſe; as ſhe appeares
Alter'd by cuſtome, more then woman, he
Transform'd by his ſoft life, is leſſe then man.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Fortune, in this gives ample ſatisfaction
For all our ſorrowes paſt.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My deereſt Siſter.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Kinde brother.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Now our mutuall care muſt be
Imploy'd to help wrong'd nature, to recover
Her right in either of them, loſt by cuſtome:
To you I give my Clara, and receive
My Lucio to my charge: and we'll contend
With loving induſtry, who ſooneſt can
Turne this man woman or this woman, man. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Boy: my Cloake, and Rapier; it fits not a Gentleman of my ranck, to walke the ſtreets in Querpo.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Nay, you are a very ranck Gent. Signior, I am very hungry, they tell me in Civill here, I looke like an Eele, with a mans head: and your neighbour the Smith here hard by, would have borrowed me th'other day, to have fiſh'd with me, becauſe he had loſt his angle-rod.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Oh happy thou Lazarillo (being the cauſe of other mens wits) as in thine own: live leane, and witty ſtill: oppreſſe not thy ſtomach too much: groſſe feeders, great ſleepers: great ſleepers, fat bodies; fat bodies, lean braines: No Lazarillo, I will make thee immortall, change thy humanitie into dietie, for I will teach thee to live upon nothing.

sp.speaker: Laz
sp.p: Faith Signior, I am immortall then already, or very neere it, for I doe live upon little or nothing: belike that's the reaſon the Poets are ſaid to be immortall, for ſome of them live upon their wits, which is indeed as good as little or nothing: But good Maſter, let me be mortall ſtill, and let's goe to ſupper.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Be abſtinent; ſhew not the corruption of thy generation: he that feeds, ſhall die, therefore he that feeds not, ſhall live.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I; but how long ſhall he live? ther's the queſtion.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: As long as he can without feeding: did'ſt thou read of the miraculous maid in Flanders?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: No, nor of any maid elſe; for the miracle of virginitie now adaies ceaſes, ere the virgin can read virginitie?

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: She that liv'd three yeere without any other ſuſtenance then the ſmell of a Roſe.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I heard of her Signior; but they ſay her guts ſhrunck all into Lute-ſtrings, and her neather-parts cling'd together like a Serpents Taile, ſo that though ſhe continued a woman ſtill above the girdle, beneath yet ſhe was monſter.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: So are moſt women, beleeve it.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Nay all women Signior, that can live onely upon the ſmell of a Roſe.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: No part of the Hiſtory is fabulous.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I thinke rather no part of the Fable is Hiſtoricall: but for all this, ſir, my rebellious ſtomach will not let me be immortall: I will be as immortall, as mortall hunger will ſuffer: put me to a certaine ſtint ſir, allow me but a red herring a day.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: O'dedios: would'ſt thou be gluttonous in thy delicacies?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: He that eats nothing but a red herring a day, ſhall neere be broyl'd for the devils raſher: a Pilcher, Signior, a Surdiny, an Olive, that I may be a philoſopher firſt, and immortall after.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Patience Lazarillo; let contemplation be thy food a while: I ſay unto thee, one Peaze was a Souldiers provant a whole day, at the deſtruction of Ieruſalem. Enter Metaldi, & Mendoza.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I; and it were any where, but at the deſtruction of a place i'le be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: Signior Pachieco Alaſto, my moſt ingenious Cobler of Civill, the bonos noxios to your Signiorie.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Signior Metaldi de forgio, my moſt famous Smith, and man of mettle, I returne your curteſie ten fold, and do humble my Bonnet beneath the Shooe-ſoale of your congie: the like to you Signior Mendoza Pediculo de vermim, my moſt exquiſite Hoſe-heeler.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Her's a greeting betwixt a Cobler, a Smith, and a Botcher: they all belong to the foot, which makes them ſtand ſo much upon their Gentrie.

sp.speaker: Mend.
sp.p: Signior Lazarillo.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Ah Signior ſee: nay, we are all Signiors here in Spaine, from the Jakes-farmer to the Grandee, or Adelantado: this botcher looks as if he w're dowgh-bak'd a little butter now, and I could eate him like an oaten-Cake: his fathers diet was new Cheeſe and Onions when he got him: what a ſcallion fac'd-raſcall 'tis?

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: But why Signior Pachieco, do you ſtand ſo much on the prioritie, and antiquitie of your qualitie (as you call it) in compariſon of ours?

sp.speaker: Mend.
sp.p: I; your reaſon for that.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Why thou Iron-pated Smith: and thou wollen-witted Hoſe heeler: heare what I will ſpeak indifferently (and according to Ancient writers) of our three profeſſions: and let the upright Lazarillo be both judge, and moderator.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Still am I the moſt immortally hungrie, that may be.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Suppoſe thou wilt derive thy pedigree, like ſome of the old Heroes, (as Hercules, Aeeas, Achilles) lineally from the Gods, making Saturne thy great Grand-father, and Vulcan thy Father: Vulcan was a God.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: He'll make Vulcan your God-father by and by.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Yet I ſay Saturne was a crabbed block-head, and Vulgan a limping horn-head, for Ʋenus his wife was a ſtrumpet, and Mars begat all her Children; therefore however, thy originall muſt of neceſſitie ſpring from Baſtardie: further, what can be a more deject ſpirit in man, then to lay his hands under every ones horſes feet, to doe him ſervice, as thou do'ſt? For thee, I will be briefe thou do'ſt botch, and not mend, thou art a hider of enormities, viz. ſcabs, chilblaines, and kibed heeles: much proane thou art to Sects, and Hereſies, diſturbing ſtate, and government; for how canſt thou be a ſound member in the Common-wealth, that art ſo ſubject to ſtitches in the anckles? bluſh, and be ſilent then, Oh ye Machanick, compare no more with the politique Cobler: For Coblers (in old time) have propheſied, what may they doe now then, that have every day waxed better, and better? have we not the length of every mans foot? are we not daily menders? yea, and what menders? not horſe-menders.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Nor manners-menders.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.p: But ſoule-menders: Oh divine Coblers; doe we not like the wiſe man ſpin our own threds, (or our wives for us?) doe we not by our ſowing the hide, reape the beefe? are not we of the gentle craft, whil'ſt both you are but crafts-men? You will ſay you feare neither Iron nor ſteele, and what you get is wrought out of the fire, I muſt anſwer you againe, though all this is but forgery, You may likewiſe ſay, a mans a man, that has but a hoſe on his head: I muſt likewiſe anſwer, that man is a botcher, that has a heel'd-hoſe on his head: to conclude there can be no compariſon with the Cobler, who is all in all in the Common-wealth, has his politique eye and ends on every mans ſteps that walkes, and whoſe courſe ſhall be laſting to the worlds end.

sp.speaker: Net.
sp.p: I give place: the wit of man is wonderfull: thou haſt hit the naile on the head, and I will give thee ſix pots for't though I neere clinth ſhooe againe. Enter Vitelli & Alguazier.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p:
Who's this? Oh our Alguazier: as arrant a knave as
E're wore out head under two offices: he is one ſide Alguazier.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: The other ſide Serjeant.

sp.speaker: Mend.
sp.l: That's both ſides carrion I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: This is he apprehends whores in the way of juſtice, and lodges 'em in his own houſe, in the way of profit: he with him, is the Grand-Don Vitelli, 'twixt whom and Fernando Alvarez the mortall hatred is: he is indeed my Dons Bawd, and do's at this preſent lodge a famous Curtizan of his, lately come from Madrill.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Let her want nothing Signior, ſhe can aske:
What loſſe, or injury you may ſuſtaine
I will repaire, and recompence your love:
Onely that fellowes coming I miſlike,
And did fore-warn her of him: beare her this
With my beſt love, at night i'le viſit her.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I reſt your Lordſhips Servant.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Good ev'n, Signiors:
Oh Alvarez, thou haſt brought a Sonne with thee
Both brightnes, and obſcures our Nation,
Whoſe pure ſtrong beames on us, ſhoot like the Suns
On baſer fires: I would to heaven my blood
Had never ſtain'd thy bold unfortunate hand,
That with mine honour I might emulate
Not perſecute ſuch vertue: I will ſee him
Though with the hazard of my life: no reſt
In my contentious ſpirits can I finde
Till I have grateſide him in like kinde. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.p: I know you not: what are ye? hence ye baſe Beſegnios.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Mary Catzo Signior Alguazier, do'ye not know us? why, we are your honeſt neighbours, the Cobler, Smith, and Botcher, that have ſo often ſate ſnoaring cheeke by joll with your ſigniorie in rug at midnight.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Nay, good Signior, be not angry: you muſt underſtand, a Cat and ſuch an Officer ſee beſt in the dark.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: By this hand, I could finde in my heart to ſhooe his head.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Why then know you Signior; thou mongrill begot at midnight, at the Goale gate, by a Beadle, on a Catch-poles wife, are not you he that was whipt out, of Toledo for perjury.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Next, condemn'd to the Gallies for pilfery, to the buls pizell.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: And after call'd to the Inquiſition, for Apoſtacie.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Are not you he that rather then you durſt goe an induſtrious voyage being preſs'd to the Iſlands, skulk'd till the fleet was gone, and then earn'd your royall a day by ſquiring puncks, and puncklings up and down the City?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Are not you a Portuguize borne, deſcended o'the Moores, and came hither into Civill with your Maſter, an errant Taylor, in your red Bonnet, and your Blew Jacket lowſie: though now your block-head be cover'd with the Spaniſh Block, and your laſhed Shoulders with a Velvet Pee?

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Are not you he, that have been of thirty callings, yet ne're a one lawfull? that being a Chandler firſt, profeſs'd ſincerity, and would ſell no man Muſtard to his beefe on the Sabbath, and yet ſold Hypocriſie all your life time?

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: Are not you he, that were ſince a Surgeon to the Stewes, and undertooke to cure what the Church it ſelfe could not, ſtrumpets that riſe to your Office by being a great Dons Baw'd?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: That commit men nightly, offenceleſſe, for the gaine of a groat a Priſoner, which your Beadle ſeemes to put up, when you ſhare three pence?

sp.speaker: Mend.
sp.p: Are not you he, that is a kiſſer of men, in drunkenneſſe, and a berrayer in ſobriety?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.p: Diabolo: they'll raile me into the Gallyes again.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Yes Signior, thou art even he we ſpeake of all this while: thou maiſt by thy place now, lay us by the heeles: 'tis true: but take heed, be wiſer, pluck not ruine on thine own head: for never was there ſuch an Anatomy, as we ſhall make thee then: be wiſe therefore, Oh thou Childe of the night! be friends and ſhake hands, thou art a proper man, if thy beard were redder: remember thy worſhipfull function, a Conſtable though thou turn'ſt day into night, and night into day, what of that? watch leſſe, and pray more: gird thy beares skin (viz. thy Rug-gowne) to thy loyes, take thy ſtaffe in thy hand, and goe forth at midnight: Let not thy mittens abate the talons of thy authority, but gripe theft and whoredom, whereſoever thou meet'ſt 'em: bear'em away like a tempeſt, and lodge 'em ſafely in thine own houſe:

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Would you have whores and theeves lodg'd in ſuch a houſe?

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: They ever doe ſo: I have found a theefe, or a whore there, when the whole Suburbs could not furniſh me.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: But why doe they lodge there?

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: That they may be ſafe, and forth-coming: for in the morning uſually the theefe is ſent to the Goale, and the whore proſtrates her ſelfe to the Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Mend.
sp.p: Admirable Pachieco.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: Thou Cobler of Chriſtendom.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.p: There is no railing with theſe rogues: I will cloſe with'em, till I can cry quittance: why Signiors, and my honeſt neighbours, will you impute that as a neglect of my friends, which is an imperfection in me? I have been Sand-blinde from my infancie: to make you amends, you ſhall ſup with me.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Shall we ſup with'ye ſir? O' my conſcience, they have wrong'd the Gentleman extreamly,

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.p: And after ſupper, I have a project to employ you in ſhall make you drink, & eat merrily this moneth: I am a little knaviſh: why and doe not I know all you to be knaves?

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: I grant you, we are all knaves, and will be your knaves: But, oh, while you live, take heed of being a proud knave.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.p: On then paſſe: I will beare out my ſtaffe, and my ſtaffe ſhall beare out me.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Oh Lazarillo, thou art going to ſupper. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Pray be not angry.

I am angry, and I will be angry diablo': what ſhould you doe in the Kitchin, cannot the Cooks lick their fingers without your overſeeing? nor the maids make pottage, except your dogs-head be in the pot? Don Lucio, Don Quot-queane, Don Spinſter, weare a Petti-coate ſtill, and put on your ſmock a' monday: I will have a badie o' clouts made for it, like a great girl: nay, if you will needs be ſtarching of Ruffs, and ſowing of black-work, I will of a milde, and loving Tutor, become a Tyrant, Your Father has committed you to my charge, and I will make a man, or a mouſe on you.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What would you have me doe? this ſcurvy ſword
So gals my thigh: I would 'twer burnt: piſh, looke
This cloak will ne'r keep on: theſe boots too hide bound,
Make me walk ſtiffe, as if my leggs were frozen,
And my Spurs gingle, like a Morris-dancer:
Lord, how my head akes, with this roguiſh hat;
This maſculine attire, i • moſt uneaſie,
I am bound up in it: I had rather walke
In folio, againe, looſe, like a woman.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: In Foolio, had you not?
Thou mock to heav'n, and nature, and thy Parents,
Thou tender Legge of Lamb; Oh, how he walkes
As if he had be-piſe'd himſelfe, and fleares!
Is this a gate for the young Cavalier,
Don Lucio, Sonne and heire to Alvarez?
Has it a corne? or do's it walke on conſcience,
It treads ſo gingerly? Come on your wayes,
Suppoſe me now your Fathers foe, Vitelli,
And ſpying you i'th' ſtreet, thus I advance,
I twiſt my Beard, and then I draw my ſword.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Alas.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: And thus accoſt thee: traiterous brat,
How dur'ſt thou thus confront me? impious twig
Of that old ſtock, dew'd with my kinſmans gore,
Draw, for i'le quarter thee in peeces foure.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Nay, Prethee Bobadilla, leave thy fooling,
Put up thy ſword, I will not meddle with' ye;
I, juſtle me, I care not: I'le not draw,
Pray be a quiet man.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Do'ye heare: anſwer me, as you would doe Don Vitelli, or i'le be ſo bold as to lay the pomell of my ſword over the hilts of your head, my name's Vitelli, and i'le have the wall.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why then i'le have the kennell: what a coyle you keepe?
Signior, what happen'd 'twixt my Sire and your
Kinſman, was long before I ſaw the world,
No fault of mine, nor will I juſtifie
My Fathers crimes: forget ſir, and forgive,
'Tis Chriſtianity: I pray put up your ſword,
Ile give you any ſatisfaction
That may become a Gentleman; however
I hope you are bred to more humanity
Then to revenge my Fathers wrong on me
That crave your love, and peace: law you now Zancho
Would not this quiet him, were he ten Vitellies.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Oh craven-chicken of a Cock o'th'game: well, what remedy? did thy father ſee this, O' my conſcience, he would cut of thy Maſculine gender, crop thine eares, beat out thine eyes, and ſet thee in one of the Peare-trees for a ſcar-crow: As I am Vitelli, I am ſatisfied but as I am Bobadilla Spindola Zancho, Steward of the houſe, and thy fathers ſervant, I could finde in my heart to lop of the hinder part of thy face, or to beat all thy teeth into thy mouth: Oh thou whay-blooded milk-ſop, Ile waite upon thee no longer, thou ſhaltev'n waite upon me: come your wayes fir, I ſhall take a little paines with ye elſe. Enter Clara.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Where art thou Brother Lucio? ran tan tan ta ran tan ran tan tan, ta ran tan tan tan. Oh, I ſhall no more ſee thoſe golden dayes, theſe clothes will never fadge with me: a—O' this filthie vardingale, this hip hape: brother why are womens hanches onely limited, confin'd, hoop'd in, as it were with theſe ſame ſcurvy vardingales?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Becauſe womens hanches onely are moſt ſubject to diſplay and fly out.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Bobadilla, rogue, ten Duckets, I hit the propoſe of thy Cod-peicu.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Hold, if you love my life, Siſter: I am not Zancho Bobadilla, I am your brother Lucio: what a fright you have put me in?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Brother? and wherefore thus?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Why, Maſter Steward here, Signior Zancho, made me change: he do's nothing but miſuſe me, and call me Cowheard, and ſweares I ſhall waite upon him.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Well: I doe no more then I have authority for: would I were away though: for ſhe's as much too manniſh, as he too womaniſh: I dare not meddle with her, yet I muſt ſet a good face on't (if I had it) I have like charge of you Maddam, I am as well to mollifie you, as to qualifie him: what have you to doe with Armors, and Piſtols, and Javelins, and ſwords, and ſuch tooles? remember Miſtreſſe; nature hath given you a ſheath onely, to ſignifie women are to put up mens weapons, not to draw them: looke you now, it this a fit trot for a Gentlewoman? You ſhall ſee the Court Ladies move like Goddeſſes, as if they trodayre; they will ſwim you their meaſures, like whiting-mops as if their feet were ſinnes, and the hinges of their knees oyld: doe they love to ride great horſes, as you doe? no, they love to ride great aſſes ſooner: faith, I know not what to ſay to'ye both Cuſtome hath turn'd nature topſie-turvy in you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Nay but Maſter Steward.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: You cannot trot ſo faſt, but he ambles as ſlowly.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Signior Spindle, will you heare me,

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: He that ſhall come to beſtride your virginitie, had better be afoot o're the Dragon.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Did ever Spaniſh Lady pace ſo?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Hold theſe a little.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Ile not touch 'em, I.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Firſt doe I breake your Office o're your pate,
You Dog-skin-fac'd-rogue, pilcher, you poore Iohn,
Which I will be at to Stock-fiſh.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Siſter.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Maddam.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You Cittern-head, who have you talk'd to, ha • ?
You naſty, ſtincking, and ill-counten • nc'd Cur.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: By this hand, Ile bang your brother for this, when I get him a lone.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: How? kick him Lucio, he ſhall kick you Bob,
Spight o' the noſe, that's flat: kick him, I ſay,
Or I will cut thy head off.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Softly y'had beſt.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Now, thou leane, dride, and ominous viſag'd kneve,
Thou falſe and peremptory Steward, pray,
For I will hang thee up in thine own Chaine.

sp.speaker: Luc
sp.p: Good Siſter, doe not choake him.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Murder, murder. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Well: I ſhall meet with 'ye: Lucio, who bought this?
'Tis a reaſonable good one; but there hangs one
Spaines Champion ne're uſ'd truer: with this Stuffe
Old Alvarez has led up men ſo cloſe,
They could almoſt ſpit in the Canons mouth,
Whil'ſt I with that, and this, well mounted, ſcurr'd
A Horſe-troope through, and through, like ſwift deſire;
And ſeen poor rogues retire, all gore, and gaſh'd
Like bleeding Shads.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: 'Bleſſe us, Siſter Clara,
How deſperately you talke: what do'ye call
This Gun a dag?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Ile give't thee: a French petronell:
You never ſaw my Barbary, the Infanta
Beſtow'd upon me, as yet Lucio?
Walke down, and ſee it

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What into the Stable?
Not I, the Jades wil kick: the poore Groom there
Was almoſt ſpoyld the other day.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Fie on thee,
Thou wilt ſcarce be a man before thy mother.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: When wil you be a woman?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Would I were none.
But natures privy Seale aſſures me one.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Thou angerſt me: can ſtrong habituall cuſtome
Work with ſuch Magick on the mind, and manners
In ſpight of ſex and nature? finde out ſirha,
Some skilfull fighter.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Yes ſir.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: I wil rectifie,
And redeem eithers proper inclination,
Or bray 'em in a morter, and new mold 'em. Exit.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Believe your eyes ſir; I tell you, we waſh an Ethiop.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ſtrike it for ten Duckets.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: How now Clara,
Your breeches on ſtill? and your petticote
Not yet off Lucio? art thou not guelt?
Or did the cold Muſcovite beget thee,
That lay here Lieger in the laſt great froſt?
Art not thou Clara, turn'd a man indeed
Beneath the girdle? and a woman thou?
Ile have you ſearch'd by—, I ſtrongly doubt;
We muſt have theſe things mended: come go in. Exit.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: With Lucio ſay you? there is for you.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: And there is for thee.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: I thank you: you have now bought a little advice
Of me; if you chance to have conference with that
Lady there, be very civill, or looke to your head: ſhe has
Ten nailes, and you have but two eyes: If any fooliſh
Hot motions ſhould chance to riſe in the horizon
Under your equinoctiall there, qualifie it as well as
You can, for I feare the elevation of your pole will
Not agree with the Horoſcope of her conſtitution:
She is Bell the Dragon I aſſure you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.p: Are you the Lucio, ſir, that ſav'd Vitelli?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Not I indeed ſir, I did never brable;
There walks that Lucio, metamorphoſed. Exit.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Do ye mock me?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: No, he do's not: I am that
Supoſed Lucio, that was but Clara,
That is, and daughter unto Alvarez.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Amazement daunts me; would my life were riddles,
So you were ſtill my faire Expoſitor:
Protected by a Lady from my death.
Oh I ſhall weare an everlaſting bluſh
Upon my cheek from this diſcovery:
On you the faireſt Souldier, I ere ſaw;
Each of whoſe eyes, like a bright beamy ſhield
Conquers, without blowes, the contentious.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Sir, guard your ſelf, you are in your enemies houſe,
And may be injur'd.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Tis impoſſible:
Foe, nor oppreſſing odds dares prove Vitelli,
If Clara ſide him, and wil call him friend;
I would the difference of our bloods were ſuch
As might with any ſhift be wip'd away:
Or would to Heaven your ſelfe were all your name;
That having loſt blood by you, I might hope
To raiſe blood from you. But my black-wing'd fate
Hovers averſely over that fond hope:
And he, whoſe tongue thus gratifies the daughter,
And ſiſter of his enemy, weares a Sword
To rip the father and the brother up.
Thus you, that ſav'd this wretched life of mine,
Have ſavd it to the ruine of your friends.
That my affections ſhould promiſcuouſly
Dart love and hate at once, both worthily?
Pray let me kiſſe your hand.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You are treacherous,
And come to do me miſchiefe.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Speake on ſtill:
Your words are falſer (faire) then my intents,
And each ſweet accent far more treacherous; for
Though you ſpeak ill of me, you ſpeak ſo well,
I doe deſire to heare you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Pray be gone:
Or kill me, if you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: Oh, neither can:
For to be pone, were to deſtroy my life;
And to kill you, were to deſtroy my ſoule:
I am in love, yet muſt not be in love:
Ile get away a pace: yet valiant Lady,
Such gratitude to honour I do owe,
And ſuch obedience to your memory,
That if you will beſtow ſomething, that I
May weare about me, it ſhall bind all wrath,
My moſt inveterate wrath, from all attempts,
Till you and I meet next.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: A favour fir?
Why I wil 'give ye good councell.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: That already
You Have beſtowd. a Ribbon, or a Glove.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay thoſe are tokens for a waiting maid
To trim the Butler with.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Your feather.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Fie; the wenches give them to their Serving-men.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: That little ring.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Twill hold you but by th'finger;
And I would have you faſter.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Any thing
That I may weare, and but remember you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: This ſmile: my good opinion, or my ſelf.
