But that it ſeems you like not.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: Yes, ſo well:
When any ſmiles, I will remember yours;
Your good opinion ſhall in weight poize me
Againſt a thouſand ill: Laſtly, your ſelfe,
My curious eye now figures in my heart,
Where I wil weare you, till the Table breake.
So, whiteſt Angels guard you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Stay ſir, I
Have fitly thought to give, what you as fitly
May not diſdaine to weare.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: This Sword.
I never heard a man ſpeak till this houre.
His words are golden chaines, and now I feare
The Lyoneſſe hath met a tamer here;
Fie, how his tongue chimes: what was I ſaying?
Oh: this favour I bequeath you, which I tie
In a love-knot, faſt, nere to hurt my friends;
Yet be it fortunate 'gainſt all your foes
(For I have neither friend, nor foe, but yours)
As ere it was to me: I have kepit it long,
And value it, next my Virginity:
But good, return it, for I now remember
I vow'd, who purchas'd it, ſhould have me too.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: would that were poſſible: but alas it is not;
Yet this aſſure your ſelfe, moſt honour'd Clara,
Ile not infringe an Article of breath
My vow hath offerd to ye: nor from this part
Whilſt it hath edge, or point, or I a heart. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Oh leave me living: what new exerciſe
Is crept into my breaſt, that blauncheth clean
My former nature? I begin to finde
I am a woman, and muſt learn to fight
A ſofter ſweeter battaile, then with Swords.
I am ſick me thinks, but the diſeaſe I feele
Pleaſeth, and puniſheth: I warrant love
Is very like this, that folks talke of ſo;
I skill not what it is, yet ſure even here,
Even in my heart, I ſenſibly perceive
It glows, and riſeth like a glimmering flame,
But know not yet the eſſence on't nor name. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: He muſt not? nor he ſhall not, who ſhall let him?
You? politique Diego, with your face of wiſdome;
Don-blirt, the —on your aphoriſmes,
Your grave, and ſage Ale phyſiognomy:
Do not I know thee for the Alquazier
Whoſe dunghill all the Pariſh Scavengers
Could never rid? thou Comedy to men,
Whoſe ſerious folly is a but for all
To ſhoot their wits at; whilſt thou haſt not wit,
Nor heart, to anſwer, or be angry.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Lady.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Peace, peace, you rotten rogue, ſupported by
A ſtaffe of rottener office: dare you check
Anys acceſſes, that I wil allow?
Piorato is my friend, and viſits me
In lawfull ſort to eſpouſe me as his wife;
And who wil croſſe, or ſhall our enter-viewes?
You know me ſirha, for no Chambermaid,
That caſt her belly, and her waſtcote lately;
Thou thinkſt thy Conſtableſhip is much: not ſo,
I am ten offices to thee: I, thy houſe,
Thy houſe, and Office is maintain'd by me.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: My houſe of office is maintain'd ith' garden:
Go too, I know you, and I have contriv'd;
Y'are a delinquent, but I have contriv'd
A poyſon, though not in the third degree:
I can ſay, blacks your eye, though it be grey;
I have connivd at this. your friend, and you:
But what is got by this connivency?
I like his feather well: a proper man,
Of good diſcourſe, fine converſation,
Valiant, and a great carrier of the buſineſſe,
Sweet breaſted, as the Nightingale, or Thruſh:
Yet I muſt tell you; you forget your ſelfe,
My Lord Vitellies love, and maintenance
Deſerves no other Jack ith' box, but he:
What though he gather'd firſt the golden fruit,
And blew your pigges-coat up into a bliſter,
When you did wait at Court upon his mother;
Has he not wel provided for the barne?
Beſide, what profit reap I by the other?
If you wil have me ſerve your pleaſure, Lady,
Your pleaſure muſt accommodate my ſervice;
As good be vertuous and poore, as not
Thrive by my knavery: all the world would be
Good, proſper'd goodneſſe like to villany.
I am the Kings vice-gerent by my place;
His right Lieutenant in mine owe precinct.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Thou art a right raſcall in all mens precincts;
Yet now my paire of twins, of foole, and knave,
Looke we are friends; there's Gold for thee, admit
Whom I wil have, and keep it from my Don;
And I will make thee richer then thou art wiſe:
Thou ſhalt be my Bawd, and my Officer:
Thy children ſhall eate ſtill my good night Owle,
And thy old wife ſell Andyrons to the Court,
Be countenanced by the Dons, and weare a hood,
Nay keepe my garden-houſe; Ile call her mother,
Thee father, my good poyſonous red-har'd Dill,
And Gold ſhall daily be thy Sacrifice,
Wrought from a fertill Iſland of mine owne,
Which I wil offer, like an Indian Queen.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: And I wil be thy divel, thou my fleſh,
With which Ile catch the world.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Fill ſome Tobacco,
And bring it in: if Piorato come
Before my Don, admit him; if my Don
Before my Love, conduct him, my deere devill. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I wil my dear fleſh: firſt come, firſt ſerv'd. Wel ſaid.
O equall Heaven, how wiſely thou diſpoſeſt
Thy ſeverall gifts? one's born a great rich foole,
For the ſubordinate knave to worke upon:
Anothers poore, with wits addition,
Which wel or ill uſ'd, builds a living up;
And that too from the Sire oft diſcends:
Onely faire vertue, by traduction
Never ſucceeds, and ſeldome meets ſucceſſe;
What have I then to do with 't? My free will
Left me by Heaven, makes me or good, or ill:
Now ſince vice gets more in this vicious world
Then piety, and my ſtars confluence
Enforce my diſpoſition to affect
Gaine, and the name of rich, let who wil practice
War, and grow that Way great: religious,
And that way good: my chiefe felicity
Is wealth the nurſe of ſenſuality:
And he that mainly labours to be rich,
Muſt ſcratch great ſcabs, and claw a Strumpets itch. Exit.

div.head: Scaena ſecunda.
div.stage: Enter Piorato, and Bobadilla, with Letters.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: To ſay ſir, I wil wait upon your Lord,
Were not to underſtand my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: To ſay ſir
You wil doe any thing but wait upon him,
Were not to underſtand my Lord.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Ile meet him
Some halfe houre hence, and doubt not but to render
His ſonne a man againe: the cure is eaſie,
I have done divers.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Women do ye mean, ſir?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Cures I do mean ſir: be there but one ſparke
Of fire remaining in him unextinct,
With my diſcourſe Ile blow it to a flame;
And with my practice, into action:
I have had one ſo full of childiſh feare,
And womaniſh hearted ſent to my advice,
He durſt not draw a Knife to cut his meat.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: And how ſir, did you help him?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Sir, I kept him
Seaven daies in a darke room by Candle-light,
A plenteous Table ſpread with all good meats,
Before his eyes, a caſe of keen broad Knives,
Upon the board, and he ſo watchd, he might not
Touch the leaſt modicum, unleſſe he cut it:
And thus I brought him firſt to draw a knife.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Good.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Then for ten daies did I diet him
Onely with burnt Porke ſir, and gammons of Bacon;
A pill of Caveary now and then,
Which breeds choler aduſt you know.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Tis true.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: And to purge phlegmatick humor, and cold crudities;
In all that time, he dranke me Aqua fortis,
And nothing elſe but—

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Aqua vite Signior,
For Aqua fortis poyſons.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Aqua fortis
I ſay again: what's one mans poyſon Signior,
Is anothers meat or drinke.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Your patience ſir;
By your good patience, h'ad a huge cold ſtomacke.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: I fir'd it: and gave him then three ſweats
In the Artillery-yard three drilling daies:
And now he'l ſhoot a Gun, and draw a Sword,
And fight with any man in Chriſtendome.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: A receipt for a coward: Ile be bold ſir
To write your good preſcription.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Sir, hereafter
You ſhall, and underneath it put probatum:
Is your chaine right?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Tis both right and juſt ſir;
For though I am a Steward, I did get it
With no mans wrong.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: You are witty.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: So, ſo.
Could you not cure one ſir, of being too raſh
And over-daring? there now's my diſeaſe:
Fool-hardy as they ſay, for that in ſooth
I am.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Moſt eaſily.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: To make you drunke ſir,
With ſmal Beere once a day; and beat you twice,
Till you be bruis'd all over: if that help not,
Knock out your braines.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: This is ſtrong Phyſick Signior,
And never wil agree with my weak body:
I finde the medcine worſe then the malady,
And therefore wil remain fool-hardy ſtil:
You'l come ſir?

sp.speaker: Pio:
sp.l: As I am a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: A man oth' Sword ſhould never break his word.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Ile overtake you: I have onely ſir
A complementall viſitation
To offer to a Miſtris lodgd here by.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: A Gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Yes ſir.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Faire, and comely?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Oh ſir, the Paragon, the Non-parill
Of Civill, the moſt wealthy Mine of Spaine,
For beauty, and perfection.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Say you ſo?
Might not a man entreat a curteſie,
To walke along with you Signior, to peruſe
This dainty Mine, though not to dig in't Sgnior?
Hanh — I hope you'l not deny me, being a ſtranger;
Though I am Steward, I am fleſh and blood,
And fraile as other men.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Sir, blow your noſe:
I dare not for the world: no, ſhe is kept
By a great Don, Vitelli.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Tis true.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: See, things wil veere about: this Don Vitelli
Am I to ſeeke now, to deliver Letters
From my young Miſtris Clara; and I tell you,
Under the Roſe, becauſe you are a ſtranger,
And my ſpeciall friend, I doubt there is
A little fooliſh love betwixt the parties,
Unknown unto my Lord.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Happy diſcovery:
My fruit begins to ripen: hark you ſir,
I would not wiſh you now, to give thoſe Letters:
But home, and ope this to Madona Clara,
Which when I come Ile juſtifie, and relate
More amply, and particularly.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: I approve
Your counſell, and wil practice it: bazilos manos:
Here's two chewres chewrd: when wiſdome is imployd
Tis ever thus: your more acquaintance, Signior:
I ſay not better, leaſt you think, I thought not
Yours good enough. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Your ſervant excellent Steward.
Would all the Dons in Spain had no more brains,
Here comes the Alguazier: dieu vous guard Mounſier.
Is my cuz ſtirring yet?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Your cuz (good coſen?)
A whore is like a foole, akin to all
The gallants in the Town: Your coz, good Signior,
Is gone abroad ſir, with her other coſen,
My Lord Vitelli: ſince when there hath been
Some dozen coſens here to enquire for her.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: 'he's greatly alli'd ſir.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Marry is ſhe ſir,
Come of a luſty kindred: the truth is,
I muſt connive no more: no more admittance
Muſt I conſent to; my good Lord has threatned me,
And you muſt pardon.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Out upon thee man,
Turne honeſt in thine age? one foot ith' grave?
Thou ſhalt not wrong thy ſelfe ſo, for a million:
Looke, thou three-headed Cerberus (for wit
I mean) here is one ſop, and two, and three,
For every chop a hit.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I marry ſir:
Wel, the poore heart loves you but too wel.
We have been talking on you 'faith this houre:
Where, what I ſaid, goe too: ſhe loves your valour;
Oh and your Muſicke moſt abominably:
She is within ſir, and alone: what meane you?

sp.speaker: Pio
sp.l: That is your Sergeants ſide, I take it ſir;
Now I endure your Conſtables much better;
There is leſſe danger in't: for one you know
Is a tame harmleſſe monſter in the light,
The Sergeant ſalvage both by day, and night.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Ile call her to you for that.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: No, I wil charme her. Enter Malroda.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: She's come.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: My Spirit.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Oh my Sweet,
Leape hearts to lips, and in our kiſſes meet.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Turn, turn thy beauteous face away, Song.
How pale and ſickly lookt the day,
In emulation of thy brighter beams?
Oh envious light, flv, fly, he gove,
Come night, and peece two breaſts at one;
When what love does, we will repeat in dreams.
Yet (thy eyes open) who can day hence fright,
Let but their lids fall, and it will be night.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Wel, I wil leave you to your fortitude;
And you to temperance: ah, ye pretty paire,
Twere ſin to ſunder you. Lovers being alone
Make one of two, and day and night all one.
But fall not out, I charge you, keep the peace;
You know my place elſe. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: No, you wil not marry:
You are a Courtier, and can ſing (my Love)
And want no Miſtriſſes: but yet I care not,
Ile love you ſtill; and when I am dead for you,
Then you'l believe my truth.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: You kill me (faire)
It is my leſſon that you ſpeake: have I
In any circumſtance deſerv'd this doubt?
I am not like your falſe and perjur'd Don
That here maintains you, and has vowd his faith,
And yet attempts in way of marriage
A Lady not far off.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: How's that?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Tis ſo:
And therefore Miſtris, now the time is come
You may demand his promiſe; and I ſweare
To marry you with ſpeed.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: And with that Gold
Which Don Vitelli gives, you'l walke ſome voyage
And leave me to my trade; and laugh, and brag,
How you ore-reach'd a whore, and guld a Lord.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: You anger me extreamly: fare you wel.
What ſhould I ſay to be believd? expoſe me
To any hazzard; or like jealous Juno
(Th' incenſed ſtep-mother of Hercules)
Deſigne me labours moſt impoſſible,
Ile doe 'em, or die in 'em; ſo at laſt
You wil believe me.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Come, we are friends: I doe.
I am thine, walk in: my Lord has ſent me outſides,
But thou ſhalt have 'em, the colours are too ſad:

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: 'Faith Miſtris, I want clothes indeed.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: I have
Some Gold too, for my ſervant.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: And I have
A better mettle for my Miſtris. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena tertia.
div.stage: Enter Vitelli and Alguazier, at ſeverall doors.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Undone—wit now or never help me: my Maſter
He wil cut my throat, I am a dead Conſtable;
And he'l not be hangd neither, there's the griefe:
The party ſir is here.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: He was here;
I cry your Lordſhip mercy: but I rattled him;
I told him here was no companions
For ſuch deboſhd, and poor-condition'd fellows;
Ibid him venture not ſo deſperately
The cropping of his eares, ſlitting his noſe,
Or being gelt.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: Twas wel done.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Pleaſe your honour,
I told him there were Stewes, and then at laſt
Swore three or foure great oathes ſhe was remov'd,
Which I did thihke I might in conſcience,
Being for your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: What became of him?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Faith ſir, he went away with a flea in's eare,
Like a poore cur, clapping his trindle taile
Betwixt his legs.—A chi ha, a chi ha, chi ha— now luck.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Tis he, do as I told thee: 'Bleſſe thee Signior.
Oh, my deare Lord.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Malroda, what alone?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: She never is alone, that is accompanied
With noble thoughts, my Lords and mine are ſuch,
Being onely of your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Pretty Laſſe.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Oh my good Lord, my picture's done: but 'faith
It is not like; nay this way ſir, the light
Strikes beſt upon it here.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Excellent wench. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I am glad the danger's over. Exit.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Tis wondrous like,
But that Art cannot counterfeit what Nature
Could make but once.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: All's cleare; another tune
You muſt heare from me now: Vitelli, thou'rt
A moſt perfidious and a perjur'd man,
As ever did uſurpe Nobility.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: What meanſt thou Mal.?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Leave your betraying ſmiles,
And change the tunes of your inticing tongues
To penitentiall prayers; for I am great
In labour even with anger, big with child
Of womans rage, bigger then when my wombe
Was pregnant by thee: goe ſeducer, fly
Out of the world, let me the laſt wretch be
Diſhonoured by thee: touch me not, I loath
My very heart, becauſe thou layſt there long;
A woman's wel helpt up, that's confident
In ere a glittering outſide on you all:
Would I had honeſtly been matchd to ſome
Poore Countrey-ſwaine, ere known the vanity
Of Court: peace then had been my portion,
Nor had been cozend by an houres pompe
To be a whore unto my dying day.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Oh the uncomfortable waies ſuch women have,
Their different ſpeech and meaning, no aſſurance
In what they ſay or do: Diſſemblers
Even in their prayers, as if the weeping Greeke
That flatter'd Troy afire had been their Adam;
Lyers, as if their mother had been made
Onely of all the falſhood of the man,
Diſpoſ'd into that rib: Do I know this,
And more: nay, all that can concern this Sex,
With the true end of my creation?
Can I with rationall diſcourſe ſometimes
Advance my ſpirit into Heaven, before
'T has ſhook hands with my body, and yet blindly
Suffer my filthy fleſh to maſter it,
With ſight of ſuch faire fraile beguiling objects?
When I am abſent, eaſily I reſolve
Nere more to entertaine thoſe ſtrong deſires
That triumph ore me, even to actuall ſin;
Yet when I meet again thoſe ſorſerers eyes,
Their beames my hardeſt reſolutions thaw,
As if that cakes of Ice and July met,
And her ſighes powerfull as the violent North,
Like a light feather twirle me round about
And leave me in mine own low ſtate again.
What aylſt thou? prethee weep not: Oh, thoſe tears
If they were true, and righly ſpent, would raiſe
A flowry ſpring ith' midſt of January:
Celeſtiall Miniſters with Chriſtall cups
Would ſtoop to ſave 'em for immortall drink:
But from this paſſion; why all this?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Do'ye ask?
You are marrying: having made me unfit
For any man, you leave me fit for all:
Porters muſt be my burthens now, to live
And fitting me your ſelfe for Carts, and Beadles
You leave me to 'em: And who of all the world
But the virago, your great Arch-foes daughter?
But on: I care not, this poore ruſh: 'twill breed
An excellent comedy: ha, ha: 't'makes me laugh:
I cannot chooſe: the beſt is, ſome report
It is a match for feare, not love o' your ſide.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Why how the devill knows ſhe, that I ſaw
This Lady? are all whores, peec'd with ſome witch?
I will be merry, 'faith 'tis true, ſweet heart,
I am to marry?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Are you? you baſe Lord.
By — i'le Piſtoll thee.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: A roaring whore?
Take heed, there's a correction houſe hard by:
You ha' learn'd this o' your ſwordman, that I warn'd you of,
Your fencers, and your drunkards: but whereas
You upb aid me with oathes, why I muſt tell you
I nc're promis'd you marriage, nor have vow'd,
But ſaid I lov'd you, long as you remain'd
The woman I expected, or you ſwore,
And how you have fail'd of that (ſweet heart) you know.
You faine would ſhew your power, but fare you well,
Ile keepe no more faith with an infidell.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Nor I my boſome for a Turk: do'ye heare?
Goe, and the devill take me, if ever
I ſee you more: I was too true.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Come, piſh:
That devill take the falſeſt of us two.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Amen.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: You are an ill Clerk; and curſe your ſelfe:
Madneſſe tranſports you: I confeſſe, I drew you
Unto my will: but you muſt know that muſt not
Make me doat on the habit of my ſin.
I will, to ſettle you to your content,
Be maſter of my word: and yet he li'd
That told you I was marrying, but in thought:
But will you ſlave me to your tyranny
So cruelly I ſhall not dare to looke
Or ſpeake to other women? make me not
Your ſmocks Monopolie: come, let's be friends:
Looke, her's a Jewell for thee: I will come
At night, and—

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: What 'yfaith: you ſhall not ſir.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: 'Faith, and troth, and verily, but I will

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Halfe drunck, to make a noiſe, and raile?

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: No, no,
Sober, and dieted for the nonce: I am thine,
I have won the day.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: The night (though) ſhall be mine. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena quarta.
div.stage: Enter Clara, and Bobadilla with Letters.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What ſaid he ſirha?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Little, or nothing: faith I ſaw him not,
Nor will not: he doth love a ſtrumpet, Miſtreſſe,
Nay, keeps her ſpitefully, under the Conſtables noſe,
It ſhall be juſtifi'd by the Gentleman
Your brothers Matter, that is now within
A'practicing: there are your Letters: come
You ſhall not caſt your ſelfe away, while I live,
Nor will I venture my right worſhipfull place Enter
In ſuch a buſineſſe—here's your Mother: downe: Eugenia & Sayavedra.
And he that loves you: another' gates fellow, I wiſh
If you had any grace.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Well rogue.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Ile in, to ſee Don Lucio mannage: he'll make
A pretty peece of fleſh; I promiſe you,
He do's already handle his weapon finely. Exit.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: She knows your love ſir, and the full allowance
Her Father and my ſelfe approve it with,
And I muſt tell you, I much hope it hath
Wrought ſome impreſſion, by her alteration;
She ſighes, and ſaies forſooth, and cries heigh ho,
She'll take ill words oth' Steward, and the Servants,
Yet anſwer affably, and modeſtly:
Things ſir, not uſuall with her: there ſhe is,
Change ſome few words.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Maddam, I am bound to 'ye;
How now, faire Miſtreſſe, working?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Yes forſooth,
Learning to live another day.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: That needs not.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: No forſooth: by my truly but it do's,
We know not what we may come too.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Come, I ha beg'd leave for you to play.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Forſooth
'Tis ill for a faire Lady to be idle.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: She had better be well- buſied, I know that.
Turtle: me thinkes you mourne, ſhall I ſit by you?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: If you be weary ſir, you had beſt be gone
(I work not a true ſtitch) now you'r my mate.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: If I be ſo, I muſt doe more then ſide you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Ev'n what you will, but tread me.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Shall we bill?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Oh no, forſooth.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Being ſo faire, my Clara,
Why do'ye delight in black-worke?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Oh white ſir,
The faireſt Ladies like the blackeſt men:
I ever lov'd the colour: all black things
Are leaſt ſubject to change.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Why, I doe love
A black thing too: and the moſt beauteous faces
Have oftneſt of them: as the blackeſt eyes,
Jet-arched browes, ſuch haire: i'le kiſſe your hand.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Twill hinder me work my ſir: and my Mother
Will chide me, if I doe not doe my taske.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Your Mother, nor your Father ſhall chide: you
Might have a prettier taske, would you be rul'd,
And looke with open eyes.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ſtare upon you:
And broadly ſee you: a wondrous proper man,
Yet 'twere a greater taske for me to love you
Then I ſhall ever work ſir, in ſeven yeer,
— o' this ſtitching, I had rather feele
Two, then ſow one:— this rogue h'as giv'n me a ſtitch
Cleane croſſe my heart: good faith ſir: I ſhall prick you.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: In goodder faith, I would prick you againe.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Now you grow troubleſome: piſh; the man is, fooliſh

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Pray weare theſe trifles.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Neither you, nor trifles,
You are a trifle, weare your ſelfe, ſir, out,
And here no more trifle the time away.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Come; you're deceived in me, I will not wake,
Nor faſt, nor dye for you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Gooſe, be not you deceiv'd,
I can not like, nor love, nor live with you,
Nor faſt, nor watch, nor pray for you.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Her old fit.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Sure, this is not the way: nay, I will breake
Your melancholie.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ſhall breake your pate then,
Away, you ſanguine ſcabbard.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Out upon thee Enter Alvarez, Piorato, Lucio: & Bobadilla.
Thou'lt breake my heart, I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: She's not yet tame.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: On ſir; put home: or I ſhall goad you here
With this old Fox of mine, that will bite better:
Oh, the brave age is gone; in my young daies
A Chevalier would ſtock a needles point
Three times together: ſtrait ith' hams?
Or ſhall I gi'v'ye new Garters?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Faith old Maſter.
There's little hope: the linnen ſure was danck
He was begot in, he's ſo faint, and cold: 2 Torches ready.
Ev'n ſend him to Toledo, there to ſtudy,
For he will never fadge with theſe Toledos;
Beare ye up your point there; pick his teeth: Oh' baſe.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Fie: you are the moſt untoward Scholler: beare
Your body gracefully: what a poſture's there?
You lie too open breaſted.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: You'ld never
Make a good Stateſ-man:

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Pray no more.
I hope to breath in peace, and therefore need not
The practiſe of theſe dangerous qualities,
I doe not meane to live by't; for I truſt
You'l leave me better able.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Not a Button:

sp.speaker: Eugenia,
sp.l: Let's goe get us a new heire.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: I by my troth: your daughter's as untoward.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: I will breake thee bone by bone, and bake thee,
Ere i'le ha' ſuch a woodden Sonne, to inherit:
Take him a good knock; ſee how that will work.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Now, for your life Signior:

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Oh: alas, I am kill'd
My eye is out: looke Father: Zancho: —
Ile play the foole no more thus, that I will not.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Heart: nere a rogue in Spaine ſhall wrong my brother
Whil'ſt I can hold a ſword.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Hold, Maddam, Maddam.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Daughter.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Miſtreſſe:

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Hold, hold I pray.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: The devil's in her, o'the other ſide: ſure,
There's Gold for you: they have chang'd what ye calt's:
Will no cure help? well, I have one experiment,
And if that faile, Ile hang him, then here's an end on't.
Come you along with me: and you ſir: Exit

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Now are you going to drowning. Alv. Eug. Luc. Bob.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Ile ev'n along with ye: ſhe's too great a Lady
For me, and would prove more then my match. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You'r he ſpoke of Vitelli to the Steward?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Yes: and I thank you, you have beat me for't.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But are you ſure you doe not wrong him?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Sure?
So ſure, that if you pleaſe venture your ſelfe
Ile ſhow you him, and his Cockatrice together,
And you ſhall heare 'em talke.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Will you? by — ſir
You ſhall endeere me ever: and I ask
You mercy.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: You were ſomewhat boyſtrous.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: There's Gold to make you amends: and for this paines,
Ile gratifie you further: i'le but maſque me
And walke along with ye: faith let's make a night on't. Exit.

div.head: Scaena quinta.
div.stage: Enter Algnazier, Pachieco, Mendoza. Metaldi, Lazarillo.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.p: Come on my brave water-Spanlels: you that hunt Ducks in the night: and hide more knavery under your gownes then your betters: obſerve my precepts, and edifie by my doctrine: at yond corner will I ſet you; if drunkards moleſt the ſtreet, & fall to brabling, knock you down the malefactors, and take you up their cloaks and hats, and bring them to me: they are lawfull priſoners, and muſt be ranſom'd ere they receive liberty: what elſe you are to execute upon occaſion, you ſufficiently know: and therefore I abbreviat my Lecture.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: We are wiſe enough, and warme enough.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Vice this night ſhall be apprehended.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: The terror of rug-gownes ſhall be known: and our bils
Diſcharge us of after recknings.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I will doe any thing, ſo I may eat.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.p: Lazarillo, We will ſpend no more; now we are growne worſe, we will live better: let us follow our calling faithfully.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Away, then the Common-wealth is our Miſtreſſe: and who
Would ſerve a common Miſtreſſe, but to gaine by her? Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena prima.
div.stage: Enter Ʋitelli, Lamorall, Genevora, Anaſtro, and two Pages with lights.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I pray you ſee the Maſque, my Lord,

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: 'Tis early night yet.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: O if it be ſo late, take me along:
I would not give advantage to ill tongues
To tax my being here, without your preſence
To be my warrant.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: You might ſpare this, Siſter,
Knowing with whom I leave you; one that is
By your allowance, and his choice, your Servant,
And may my councell and perſwaſion work it,
Your husband ſpeedily: For your entertainement
My thankes; I will not rob you of the meanes
To doe your Miſtreſſe ſome acceptable ſervice
In waiting on her to my houſe.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: My Lord,

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: As you reſpect me, without further trouble
Retire, and taſte thoſe pleaſures prepar'd for you,
And leave me to my own wayes.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: When you pleaſe ſir. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena ſecunda.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: You'l leave my Chamber?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Let us but bill once,
My Dove, my Sparrow, and I, with my office
Will be thy ſlaves for ever.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Are you ſo hot?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: But taſte the difference of a man in place,
You'l finde that when authoritie pricks him forward,
Your Don, nor yet your Diego comes not neere him
To doe a Lady right: no men pay deerer
For their ſtolne ſweetes, then we: three minutes trading
Affords to any ſinner a protection
For three yeeres after: thinke on that, I burne;
But one drop of your bounty.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Hence you rogue,
Am I fit for you? is't not grace ſufficient
To have your ſtaffe, a bolt to bar the doore
Where a Don enters, but that you'l preſume
To be his taſter?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Is no more reſpect
Due to this rod of juſtice?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Doe you diſpute?
Good Doctor of the Dungeon, not a word more,
— If you doe, my Lord Vitelli knowes it.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Why I am bigge enough to anſwer him,
Or any man.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: 'Tis well. Ʋitelli within.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: You know the voice, and now crowch like a Cur
Tane worrying ſheepe: I now could have you guelded
For a Bawd rampani: but on this ſubmiſſion
For once I ſpare you

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I Will be reveng'd
My honourable Lord.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: There's for thy care

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I am mad, ſtarck mad: proud Pagan ſcorn her hoſt
I would I were but valiant enough to kick her, Enter Piorato & Clara, above.
Il'd wiſh no manhood elſe.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I am gone. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: You ſee, I have kept my word.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But in this object
Hardly deſerv'd my thanks.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Is there ought elſe
You will command me?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Onely your ſword
Which I muſt have: nay willingly I yet know
To force it, and to uſe it.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: 'Tis yours Lady.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ask no other guard.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: If ſo I leave you:
And now, if that the Conſtable keepe his word,
A poorer man may chance to gull a Lord. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: By this good — you ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: By this—
I mu •• , and will, Malroda; What doe you make
A ſtranger of me?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Ile be ſo to you,
And you ſhall find it.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Theſe are your old arts
T'endeere the game you know I come to hunt for,
Which I have borne too coldly.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Doe ſo ſtill,
For if I h at you, hang me.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: If you doe not
I know who'll ſtarve for't: why, thou ſhame of women,
Whoſe folly, or whoſe impudence is greater
Is doubtfull to det • rmine; this to me
That know thee for a whore.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: And made me one,
Remember that.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Why ſhould I but grow wiſe
And tye that bounty up, which nor diſcretion
Nor honour can give way too; thou wouldſt be
A Bawd e're twenty, and within a moneth
A barefoot, lowzie, and diſeaſed whore,
And ſhift thy lodgings oftner then a rogue
That's whipt from poſt to poſt.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Piſh: all our Colledge
Know you can raile well in this kinde.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: For me
He never ſpake ſo well.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: I have maintain'd thee
The envy of great fortunes, made thee ſhine
As if thy name were glorious: ſtuck thee full
Of jewels, as the firmament of Starrs,
And in it made thee ſo remarkable
That it grew queſtionable, whether vertue poore,
Or vice ſo ſet forth as it is in thee,
Were even by modeſties ſelfe to be prefer'd,
And am I thus repaid?
You are ſtill my debtor;
Can this (though true) be weigh'd with my loſt honour,
Much leſſe my faith? I have liv'd private to you,
And but for you, had ne're known what luſt was,
Nor what the ſorrow for't.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: 'Tis falſe.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: 'Tis true,
But how return'd by you, thy whole life being
But one continued act of luſt, and Shipwrack
Of womens chaſtities.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: But that I know
That ſhe that dares be damn'd dares any thing,
I ſhould admire thy tempting me: but preſume not
On the power you thinke you hold o're my affections,
It will deceive you: yeeld, and preſently
Or by the inflamed blood, which thou muſt quench
Ile make a forcible entrie.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Touch me not:
You know I have a throat, — if you doe
I will cry out a rape, or ſheath this here,
Ere i'le be kept, and us'd for Julip-water
T'allay the heate which luſhious meats and wine
And not deſire hath rais'd.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: A deſperate devill,
My blood commands my reaſon: I muſt take
Some milder way.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: I hope (deere Don) I fit you.
The night is mine, although the day was yours
You are not faſting now: this ſpeeding trick
Which I would as a principle leave to all,
That make their maintenance out of their own Indies
As I doe now; my good old mother taught me,
Daughter, quoth ſhe, conteſt not with your lover
His ſtomach being empty; let wine heat him,
And then you may command him: 'tis a ſure one:
His lookes ſhew he is coming.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: Come this needs not,
Eſpecially to me: you know how deere
I ever have eſteemed you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Loſt again.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: That any ſight of yours, hath power to change
My ſtrongeſt reſolution, and one teare
Sufficient to command a pardon from me,
For any wrong from you, which all mankinde
Should kneel in vaine for.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Pray you pardon thoſe
That need your favour, or deſire it

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Prethee.
Be better temper'd: Ile pay as a forfeit
For my raſh anger, this purſe fil'd with Gold.
Thou ſhalt have ſervants, gownes, attires, what not?
Only continue mine.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: 'Twas this I fiſh'd for

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Look on me, and receive it.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Well, you know
My gentle nature, and take pride t'abuſe it:
You ſee a trifle pleaſes me, we are friends;
This kiſſe, and this confirmes it.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: With my ruine.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: I'le have this dyamond; and this pearle.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: They are yours.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: But wil you not, when you have what you came for,
Take them from me to morrow? tis a faſhion
Your Lords of late have us'd.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: But Ile not follow.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: That any man at ſuch a rate as this
Should pay for his repentance.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Shall we to bed now?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Inſtantly, Sweet: yet now I think on't better
Ther's ſomething firſt that in a word or two
I muſt acquaint you with.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Can I cry ayme,
To this againſt my ſelfe? Ile break this match,
Or make it ſtronger with my bloud. Deſcends.

div.stage: Enter Alguazier, Piorato, Pachieco, Metaldi, Mendoza, Lazarillo, &c.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I am yours,
A Don's not priviledgd here more then yourſelf,
Win her, and weare her.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Have you a Prieſt ready?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I have him for thee, Lad; and when I have
Married this ſcornefull whore to this poor gallant.
She wil make ſuit to me; there is a trick
To bring a high-priz'd wench upon her knees:
For you my fine neat Harpyes ſtretch your tallons
And prove your ſelves true night-Birds.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Take my word
For me and all the reſt.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: If there be meat
Or any banquet ſtirring, you ſhall ſee
How ile beſtow my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: When they are drawn,
Ruſh in upon 'em: al's faire prize you light on:
I muſt away: your officer may give way
To the Knavery of his watch, but muſt not ſee it.
You all know where to finde me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: There look for us.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: My Piorato, welcome, welcome:
Faith had you not come when you did, my Lord
Had done I know not what to me.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: I am gul'd,
Firſt cheated of my Jewels, and then laugh'd at:
Sirha, what make you here?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: A buſineſſe brings me,
More lawfull then your own,

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: How's that, you ſlave?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: He's ſuch, that would continue his a whore
Whom he would make a wife of.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: Ile trea'd upon
The face you doat on, ſtrumpet.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Keep the peace there.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: A plot upon my life too?

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: Down with him.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Show your old valour, and learn from a woman,
One Eagle has a world of odds againſt
A flight of Dawes, as theſe are.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Get you off,
Ile follow inſtantly.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.p: Run for more help there. Exeunt all but Ʋit. and Clara.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: Loſſe of my gold, & jewels, & the wench too
Afflicts me not ſo much, as th'having Clara
The witneſſe of my weakneſſe.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: He turns from me,
And yet I may urge merit, ſince his life
Is made my ſecond gift.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: May I ne'r proſper
If I know how to thank her.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Sir, your pa don
For preſſing thus beyond a Virgins bounds
Upon your privacies: and let my being
Like to a man, as you are, be th'excuſe
Of my ſolliciting that from you, which ſhall not
Be granted on my part, although deſir'd
By any other: ſir, you underſtand me,
And 'twould ſhew nobly in you, to prevent
From me a farther boldneſſe, which I muſt
Proceed in, if you prove not mercifuil,
Though with my loſſe of bluſhes, and good name.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: Madam, I know your wil, and would be thankfull
If it were poſſible I could affect
The Daughter of an enemy.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: That faire falſe one
Whom with fond dotage you have long purſu'd
Had ſuch a father: ſhe to whom you pay
Deerer for your diſhonour, then all titles
Ambitious men hunt for are worth.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: 'Tis truth.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Yet, with her, as a friend you ſtill exchange
Health for diſeaſes, and to your diſgrace
Nouriſh the rivals to your preſent pleaſures,
At your own charge, uſ'd as a property
To give a ſafe protection to her luſt,
Yet ſhare in nothing but the ſhame of it.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: Grant all this ſo, to take you for a wife
Were greater hazard, for ſhould I offend you
(As tis not eaſy ſtill to pleaſe a woman)
You are of ſo great a ſpirit, that I muſt learn
To weare your petticoat, for you wil have
My breeches from me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Rather from this houre
I here abjure all actions of a man,
And wil eſteem it happineſſe from you
To ſuffer like a woman: love, true love
Hath made a ſearch within me, and expel'd
All but my naturall ſoftneſſe, and made perfect
That which my parents care could not begin.
I wil ſhow ſtrength in nothing, but my duty,
And glad deſire to pleaſe you, and in that
Grow every day more able.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: Could this be,
What a brave race might I beget? I finde
A kind of yeelding; and no reaſon why
I ſhould hold longer out: ſhe's yong, and faire,
And chaſt for ſure, but with her leave the Devil
Durſt not attempt her: Madam, though you have
A Souldiers arme, your lips appear as if
They were a Ladies.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: They dare ſir from you
Endure the tryall.

sp.speaker: Ʋit.
sp.l: Ha: once more I pray you:
The beſt I ever taſted; and tis ſaid
I have prov'd many, 'tis not ſafe I feare
To aske the reſt now: wel, I will leave whoring
And luck herein ſend me with her: worthieſt Lady,
Ile wait upon you home, and by the way
(If ere I many, as ile not forſwear it)
Tell you, you are my wife.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Which if you do,
From me all man-kinde women, learne to woe. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Alguazier, Pachieco, Metaldi, Mendoza, Lararillo.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: A cloak? good purchaſe, and rich hangers? well,
Wee'l ſhare ten Piſtolets a man

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Yet ſtill
I am monſtrous hungry: could you not diduct
So much out of the groſſe ſome, as would purchaſe
Eight loynes of Veale, and ſome two dozen of Capons?

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: O ſtrange proportion for five.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: For five? I have
A legion in my ſtomach that have kept
Perpetuall faſt theſe ten years: for the Capons,
They are to me but as ſo many black Birds:
May I but eate once, and be ſatisfied,
Let the fates call me, when my ſhip is fraught,
And I ſhall hang in peace.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Steale well to night,
And thou ſhalt feed to morrow; ſo now you are
Your ſelves againe, ile raiſe another watch
To free you from ſuſpition: ſet on any
You meet with boldly: Ile not be far off,
T'aſſiſt you, and protect you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: O brave officer.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Would every ward had one but ſo well given,
And we would watch for rug, in gownes of velvet.

sp.speaker: Mend.
sp.l: Stand cloſe: a prize.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: Satten, and gold Lace, Lads.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Why do'ſt thou hang upon me?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo darke
I dare not ſee my way: for heaven ſake father
Let us go home.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: No, ev'n here wee'l leave you:
Let's run away from him, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Oh 'las.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Thou haſt made me mad: and I wil beat thee dead
Then bray the in a morter, and now mold thee
But I wil alter thee.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: 'Twill never be:
He has bin three dayes practiſing to drink,
Yet ſtill he ſips, like to a waiting woman,
And looks as he were murdring of a fart
Among wild Iriſh ſwaggerers.

sp.speaker: Luc
sp.l: I have ſtill
Your good word, Zancho, father.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Milk-ſop coward;
No houſe of mine receives thee: I diſclam thee,
Thy mother; on her knees ſhall not entreat me
Hereafter to acknowledge thee.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Pray you ſpeak for me.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: I would; but now I cannot with mine honour.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Ther's only one courſe left, that may redeem thee,
Which is, to ſtrike the next man that you meet,
And if we chance to light upon a woman,
Take her away, and uſe her like a man,
Or I wil cut thy hamſtrings.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: This makes for us

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: What do'ſt thou do now?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Sir, I am ſaying my prayers;
For being to undertake what you would have me,
I know I cannot live.

div.stage: Enter Lamorall, Genevora, Anaſtro, and Pages with lights.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.l: Madam, I fear
You'l wiſh you had uſd your coach: your brothers houſe
Is yet far off.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: The better ſir: this walk
Will help digeſtion after your great ſupper,
Of which I have fed largely.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: To your task,
Or els you know what followes:

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I am dying:
Now Lord have mercy on me: by your favour,
Sir I muſt ſtrike you.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: For what cauſe?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I know not:
And I muſt likewiſe talke with that young Lady,
An houre in private.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: What you muſt, is doubtfull,
But I am certain ſir, I muſt beat you.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Help, help.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Not ſtrik againe?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: How, Alvarez?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: This for my Lord Vitell's love.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Break out,
And like true theeves, make pray on either ſide,
But ſeem to help the ſtranger.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Oh my Lord,
They have beat him on his knees.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Though I want courage:
I yet have a ſons duty in me, and
Compaſſion of a fathers danger; that,
That wholy now poſſeſſes me.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: This is beyond my hope.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: So Lazarillo,
Take up all boy: well done.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: And now ſteale off
Cloſely, and cunningly.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: How? have I found you?
Why Gentlemen, are you madde, to make your ſelves
A prey to Rogues?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Would we were off.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Theeves, theeves.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Defer our own contention: and down with them.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Ile make you ſure.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Now he playes the Devil.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: This place is not for me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Ile follow her
Half of my pennance is paſt ore. Exit.

div.stage: Entes Alguazier, Aſſiſtente and other Watches.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: What noyſe?
What tumult's there? keep the Kings peace I charge you.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: I am glad he's come yet.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: O, you keep good Guard
Upon the City, when men of our ranck
Are ſet upon in the ſtreetes.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: The aſſiſtance
Shall heare oſ't be aſſur'd.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: And if he be
That carefull Governour he is reported,
You will ſmart for it.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Patience, good Signiours:
Let me ſurvey the Raſcals: O, I know them,
And thank you for them: they are pillfring rogues
Of Andaluzia, that have perus'd
All Priſons in Caſtile: I dare not truſt
The dungeon with them: no, ile have them home
To my own houſe.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: We had rather go to priſon.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Had you ſo dog-holts? yes, I know you had:
You there would uſe your cunning fingers on
The ſimple locks; you would: but ile prevent you.

sp.speaker: Lam
sp.l: My Miſtris loſt? good night. Exit.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Your Son's gon to,
What ſhould become of him?

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Come of him, what will:
Now he dares fight, I care not: i'le to bed:
Look to your priſoners Alguazier. Exit with Boba.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Al's cleer'd:
Droop not for one diſaſter: let us hug,
And triumph in our knaveries.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: This confirmes
What was reported of him.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: 'Twas done bravely.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I muſt a little glory in the meanes
We officers have, to play the Knaves, and ſafely:
How we breake through the toyles, pitch'd by the Law,
Yet hang up them that are far leſſe delinquents:
A ſimple ſhopkeeper's carted for a baud
For lodging (though unwittingly) a ſmock-Gamſter:
Where, with rewards, and credit I have kept
Malroda in my houſe, as in a cloyſter,
Without taint, or ſuſpition.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: But ſuppoſe
The Governour ſhould know't?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: He? good Gentleman,
Let him perplex himſelf with prying into
The meaſures in the market, and th'abuſes
The day ſtands guilty of: the pillage of the night
Is only mine, mine own feeſimple;
Which you ſhall hold from me, tennants at will,
And pay no rent for't.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Admirable Landlord.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Now wee'l go ſearch the taverns, commit ſuch
As we finde drinking: and be drunk our ſelves
With what we take from them: theſe ſilly wretches
Whom I for forme ſake only have brought hither
Shall watch without, and guard us.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: And we wil.
See you ſaſe lodg'd, moſt worthy Alguazier,
With all of you his comrads.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: Tis the Governour.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: We are betray'd?

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: My guard there: bind them faſt:
How men in high place, and authority
Are in their lives and eſtimation wrong'd
By their ſubordinate Miniſters? yet ſuch
They cannot but imploy: wrong'd juſtice finding
Scarce one true ſervant in ten officers.
'T'xpoſtulate with you, were but to delay
Your crimes due puniſhment, which ſhall fall upon you
So ſpeedily, and ſeverely, that it ſhall
Fright others by th'example: and confirme
How ever corrupt officers may diſgrace
Themſelves, 'tis not in them to wrong their place.
Bring them away.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Wee'l ſuffer nobly yet,
And like to Spaniſh Gallants.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: And wee'l hang ſo.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: I have no ſtomach to it: but i'le endeavour.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Nay you are rude; pray you forbeare; your offer now
More then the breeding of a Gentleman
Can give you warrant for.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Tis but to kiſſe you,
And think not ile receive that for a favour
Which was enjoyn'd me for a pennance, Lady.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: You have met a gentle confeſſor, and for once
(So men you wil reſt ſatisfied) I vouchſafe it.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Reſt ſatisfide with a kiſſe? why can a man
Deſire more from a woman? is there any
Pleaſure beyond it? may I never live
If I know what it is.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Sweet Innocence.

sp.speaker: Luc
sp.l: VVhat ſtrange new motions do I feele? my veines
Burn with an unknown fire: in every part
I ſuffer alteration: I am poyſond,
Yet languiſh with deſire againe to taſte it,
So ſweetly it works on me.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: I ne'r ſaw
A lovely man, till now.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: How can this be?
She is a wom • n, as my mother is,
And her I have kiſſ'd often, and brought off
My lips unſcortch'd; yours are more lovelie, Lady,
And ſo ſhould be leſſe hurtfull: pray you vouchſafe
Your hand, to quench the heat tane from your Lip,
Perhaps that may reſtore me.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: VVillinglie.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: The flame increaſes: if to touch you, burne thus,
VVhat would more ſtrict embraces do? I know not,
And yet methinks to die ſo; were to aſcend
To Heaven, through Paradiſe.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: I am wounded too,
Though modeſty forbids that I ſhould ſpeake
VVhat ignorance makes him bold in: why do you fix
Your eyes ſo ſtronglie on me?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Pray you ſtand ſtill,
There is nothing els, that is worth the looking on:
I could adore you, Ladie.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Can you love mee?

sp.speaker: Luo.
sp.l: To waite on you, in your chamber, and but touch
VVhat you, by wearing it, have made divine,
Were ſuch a happineſſe. I am reſov'd,
Ile ſell my libertie to you for this glove,
And write my ſelfe your ſlave.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: On eaſier termes,
Receive it as a friend.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: How! giving favour!
I'le have it with his heart.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: VVhat will you doe?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: As you are mercifull, take my life rather.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: VVill you depart with't ſo?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Do's that grieve you?

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: I know not: but even now you appeare valiant.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Twas to preſerve my father: in his cauſe
I could be ſo again.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Not in your own? Kneel to thy rivall and thine enemy?
Away unworthy creature, I begin
To hate my ſelfe, for giving entrance to
A good opinion of thee: For thy torment,
If my poore beauty be of any power,
Mayſt thou doat on it deſperately: but never
Preſume to hope for grace, till thou recover
And weare the favour that was raviſh'd from thee.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: He weares my head to then.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Poore foole, farewell. Exit.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My womaniſh ſoul, which hitherto hath governd
This coward fleſh, I feele departing from me;
And in me by her beauty is inſpir'd
A new, and maſculine one: inſtructing me
What's fit to doe or ſuffer; powerfull love
That haſt with loud, and yet a pleaſing thunder
Rous'd ſleeping manhood in me, thy new creature,
Perfect thy worke ſo that I may make known
Nature (though long kept back) wil have her owne.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Can it be poſſible, that in ſix ſhort houres
The ſubiect ſtill the ſame, ſo many habits
Should be remov'd? or this new Lucio, he
That yeſternight was baffeld and diſgrac'd,
And thankt the man that did it, that then kneeld
And blubberd like a woman, ſhould now dare
One terme of honour ſeeke reparation
For what he then appear'd not capable of?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Such miracles, men that dare doe injuries
Live to their ſhames to ſee, and for puniſhment
And ſcourge to their proud follies.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Prethee leave me:
Had I my Page, or foot-man here to fleſh thee,
I durſt the better heare thee.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: This ſcorn needs not:
And offer ſuch no more.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Why ſay I ſhould,
You'l not be angry?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Indeed I think I ſhal,
Would you vouchſafe to ſhew your ſelfe a Captaine,
And lead a little further, to ſome place
That's leſſe frequented.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: He looks pale.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: If not,
Make uſe of this.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: There's anger in his eyes too:
His geſture, voyce, behaviour, all new faſhion'd;
Wel, if it does endure in act the triall
Of what in ſhow it promiſes to make good,
Ʋlyſſes Cyclops, Io's transformation,
Eurydice fetcht from Hell, with all the reſt
Of Ovids Fables, ile put in your Creed;
And for proofe, all incredible things may be
Writ down that Lucio, the coward Lucio,
The womaniſh Lucio fought.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: and Lamorall,
The ſtil imployd great duelliſt Lamorall.
Took his life from him.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Twill not come to that ſure:
Methinks the onely drawing of my Sword
Should fright that confidence.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: It confirmes it rather.
To make which good, know you ſtand now oppos'd
By one that is your Rivall, one that wiſhes
Your name and title greater, to raiſe his;
The wrong you did, leſſe pardonable then it is,
But your ſtrength to defend it, more then ever
It was when juſtice friended it. The Lady
For whom we now contend, Genevora
Of more deſert, (if ſuch incomparable beauty
Could ſuffer an addition) your love
To Don Vitelli multipli'd, and your hate
Aagainſt my father and his houſe increas'd;
And laſtly, that the Glove which you there wear,
To my diſhonour, (which I muſt force from you)
Were deerer to you then your life.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: You'l finde
It is, and ſo ile guard it:

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: All theſe meet then
With the black infamy, to be foyld by one
That's not allowd a man: to help your valour,
That falling by your hand, I may, or die,
Or win in this one ſingle oppoſition
My Miſtris, and ſuch honour as I may
Inrich my fathers Armes with.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Tis ſaid Nobly;
My life with them are at the ſtake.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: At all then. Fight.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: She's yours: this, and my life, to follow your fortune;
And give not onely back that part the looſer
Scorns to accept of —

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: My poor life,
Which do not leave me as a further torment,
Having diſpoild me of my Sword, mine honour,
Hope of my Ladies grace, fame, and all elſe
That made it worth the keeping.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I take back
No more from you, then what you forc'd from me;
And with a worſer title: yet think not
That Ile diſpute this, as made inſolent
By my ſucceſſe, but as one equall with you,
If ſo you wil accept me; that new courage,
Or call it fortune if you pleaſe, that is
Confer'd upon me by the onely ſight
Of fair Genevora, was not beſtow'd on me
To bloody purpoſes: nor did her command
Deprive me of the happineſſe to ſee her
But till I did redeem her favour from you;
Which onely I rejoyce in, and ſhare with you
In all you ſuffer elſe.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: This curteſie
Wounds deeper then your Sword can, or mine owne;
Pray you make uſe of either, and diſpatch me.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: The barbarous Turke is ſatisfied with ſpoile;
And ſhall I, being poſſeſt of what I came for,
Prove the more Infidell?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: You were better be ſo,
Then publiſh my diſgrace, as tis the cuſtome,
And which I muſt expect.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Judge better on me:
I have no tongue to trumpet mine owne praiſe
To your diſhonour: tis a baſtard courage
That ſeekes a name out that way, no true born one;
Pray you be comforted, for by all goodneſſe
But to her vertuous ſelfe, the beſt part of it,
I never wil diſcover on what termes
I came by theſe: which yet I take not from you,
But leave you in exchange of them, mine own,
With the deſire of being a friend; which if
You wil not grant me, but on further triall
Of manhood in me, ſeeke me when you pleaſe,
(And though I might refuſe it with mine honour)
Win them again, and weare them: ſo good morrow. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I nere knew what true valour was till now;
And have gain'd more by this diſgrace, then all
The honours I have won: they made me proud,
Preſumptuous of my fortune; a meere beaſt,
Faſhion'd by them, onely to dare and doe:
Yeelding no reaſons for my wilfull actions
But what I ſtuck on my Swords point, preſuming
It was the beſt Revenew. How unequall
Wrongs wel maintain'd makes us to others, which
Ending with ſhame teach as to know our ſelves,
I wil think more on't.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: My Lord?

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: I came to ſeeke you.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: And unwillingly;
You nere found me till now: your pleaſure ſir?

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: That which wil pleaſe thee friend: thy vowd love to me
Shall now be put in action: means is offer'd
To uſe thy good Sword for me; that which ſtill
Thou wearſt, as if it were a part of thee.
Where is it?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Tis changd for one more fortunate:
Pray you enquire not how.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Why, I nere thought
That there was muſick int, but aſcribe
The fortune of it to the arme.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Which is grown weaker too. I am not (in a word)
Worthy your friendſhip: I am one new vanquiſh'd,
Yet ſhame to tell by whom.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: But Ile tell thee
Gainſt whom thou art to fight, and there redeeme
Thy honour loſt, if there be any ſuch:
The King, by my long ſuit, at length is pleaſ'd
That Alvarez and my ſelf, with eithers Second,
Shall end the difference between our houſes,
Which he accepts of I make choice of thee;
And where you ſpeak of a diſgrace, the means
To blot it out, by ſuch a publique triall
Of thy approved valour, wil revive
Thy ancient courage. If you imbrace it, doe;
If not, Ile ſeeke ſome other.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: As I am
You may command me.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Spoke like that true friend
That loves not onely for his private end. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena ſecunda.
div.stage: Enter Genevora with a Letter and Bobadilla.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: This from Madona Clara?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Yes, and 't pleaſe you.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Alvarez daughter?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: The ſame, Lady.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: She,
That ſav'd my brothers life?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: You are ſtill in the right,
She wil'd me wait your walking forth: and knowing
How neceſſary a diſcreet wiſe man
Was in a buſineſſe of ſuch weight, ſhe pleaſ'd
To think on me: it may be in my face
Your Ladiſhip not acquainted with my wiſdome
Finds no ſuch matter: what I am, I am;
Thought's free: and think you what you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Tis ſtrange,

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: That I ſhould be wiſe, Madam?

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: No, thou art ſo;
There's for thy paines: and prethee tell thy Lady
I wil not faile to meet her: Ile receive
Thy thanks and duty in thy preſent abſence:
Farewell, farewel, I ſay, now thou art wiſe. Exit Bob.
She writes here, ſhe hath ſomething to impart
That may concerne my brothers life; I know not,
But generall fame does give her out ſo worthy,
That I dare not ſuſpect her: yet wiſh Lucio
Were Maſter of her mind: but fie upon't;
Why do I think on him? ſee, I am puniſh'd for it,
In his unlookd for preſence: Now I muſt
Endure another tedious piece of Courtſhip,
Would make one forſweare curteſie.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Gracious Madam,
The ſorrow paid for your juſt anger towards me
Ariſing from my weakneſſe, I preſume
To preſſe into your preſence, and diſpaire not
An eaſie pardon.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: He ſpeaks ſende: oh ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: And yet believe, that no deſire of mine,
Though all are too ſtrong in me, had the power
For their delight, to force me to iufringe
What you commanded, it being in your part
To leſſen your great rigour when you pleaſe,
And mine to ſuffer wirh an humble patience
What you'l impoſe upon it.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Courtly too.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Yet hath the poore, and contemn'd Lucio, Madam,
(Made able onely by his hope to ſerve you)
Recover'd what with violence, not juſtice,
Was taken from him: and here at your feet
With theſe, he could have laid the conquer'd head
Of Lamorall (tis all I ſay of him)
For rudely touching that, which as a relique
I ever would have worſhip'd, ſince twas yours.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Valiant, and every thing a Lady could
Wiſh in her ſervant.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: All that's good in me,
That heavenly love, the oppoſite to baſe luſt,
Which would have all men worthy, hath created;
Which being by your beames of beauty form'd,
Cheriſh as your own creature.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: I am gone
Too far now to diſſemble: riſe, or ſure
I muſt kneele with you too: let this one kiſſe
Speake the reſt for me: tis too much I doe,
And yet, if chaſtity would, I could wiſh more.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: In overjoying me, you are grown ſad;
What is it Madam? by—
There's nothing that's within my nerves (and yet
Favour'd by you, I ſhould as much as man)
But when you pleaſe, now or on all occaſions
You can think of hereafter, but you may
Diſpoſe of at your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: If you breake
That oath again, you loſt me. Yet ſo wel
I love you, I ſhall never put you to't;
And yet forget it not: reſt ſatisfied
With that you have receiv'd now: there are eyes
May be upon us, till the difference
Between our friends are ended: I would not
Be ſeen ſo private with you.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I obey you.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: But let me heare oft from you, and remember
I am Vitellies ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Luc:
sp.l: What's that Madam?

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Nay nothing, fare you well: who feeles loves fire,
Would ever aske to have means to deſire. Exeunt

div.head: Scena tertia.
div.stage: Enter Aſſiſtente, Sayavedra, Anaſtro, Herald, Attendants.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſ.
sp.l: Are they come in?

sp.speaker: Har.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſ.
sp.l: Read the Proclamation,
That all the people here aſſembled may
Have ſatisfaction, what the Kings deere love,
In care of the Republique, hath ordained;
Attend with ſilence: read aloud.

body.p: FOraſmuch as our high and mighty Maſter, Philip, the potent and moſt Catholique King of Spaine, hath not onely in his own Royall perſon, been long, and often ſollicited, and grieved, with the deadly and uncurable hatred, ſprung up betwixt the two ancient and moſt honourably diſcended Houſes of theſe his two deerely and equally beloved Subjects, Don Ferdinando de Alrarez, and Don Pedro de Vitelli: (all which in vaine his Majeſty hath often endeavoured to reconcile and qualifie:) But that alſo through the debates, quarrels, and outrages daily ariſing, falling, and flowing from theſe great heads, his publique civill Government is ſeditiouſly and barbarouſly moleſted and wounded, and many of his chiefe Gentry (no leſſe tender to his Royall Majeſty then the very branches of his own ſacred blood) ſpoyld, loſt, and ſubmerged, in the impious inundation and torrent of their ſtill-growing malice: It hath therefore pleaſed His ſacred Majeſty, out of His infinite affection to preſerve his Common-wealth, and generall peace, from farther violation, (as a ſweet and heartily loving father of his people) and on the earneſt petitions of theſe Arch-enemies, to Order, and Ordaine, That they be ready, each with his wel-choſen and beloved friend, arm'd at all points like Gentlemen, in the Caſtle of St. Jago, on this preſent Munday morning betwixt eight and nine of the clocke; where (before the combatants be allowed to commence this granted Duell) This to be read aloud for the publique ſatisfaction of his Majeſties welbeloved Subjects.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Hark how their Drums ſpeak their inſatiate thirſt
Of blood, and ſtop their eares 'gainſt pious peace,
Who gently whiſpering, implores their friendſhip?

sp.speaker: Aſſiſ.
sp.l: Kings, nor authority can maſter fate;
Admit 'em then, and blood extinguiſh hate.

div.stage: Enter ſeverally, Alvarez and Lucio, Vitelli and Lamora.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Stay, yet be pleaſd to think, and let not daring
Wherein men nowadaies exceed even beaſts,
And think themſelves not men elſe, ſo tranſport you
Beyond the bounds of Chriſtianity:
Lord Alvarez, Vitelli, Gentlemen,
No Town in Spaine, from our Metropolis
Unto the rudeſt hovell, but is great
With your aſſured valours daily proofes:
Oh wil you then, for a ſuperfluous fame,
A ſound of honour, which in theſe times, all
Like heretiques profeſſe (with obſtinacy)
But moſt erroneouſly, venture your ſoules,
Tis a hard taſque, thorough a Sea of blood
To ſaile, and land at Heaven?

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: I hope not
If juſtice be my Pilot: but my Lord,
You know, if argument, or time, or love,
Could reconcile, long ſince we had ſhook hands;
I dare proteſt, your breath cooles not a veine
In any one of us, but blowes the fire
Which nought but blood reciprocall can quench.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Vitelli, thou ſayſt bravely, and ſayſt right,
And I wil kill thee for't, I love thee ſo.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Ha, ha, old man: upon thy death Ile build
A ſtory (with this arme) for thy old wife
To tell thy daughter Clara ſeven yeeres hence
As ſhe ſits weeping by a wintet fire,
How ſuch a time Vitelli ſlew her husband
With the ſame Sword his daughter favour'd him,
And lives, and weares it yet: Come Lamorall,
Redeeme thy ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Shall on this Sword receive thy bleeding heart,
For my preſented hat, laid at her feet.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Thou talkſt wel Lamorall, but tis thy head
That I wil carry to her to thy hat:
Fie father, I do coole too much.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Oh boy:
Thy fathers true ſonne:
Beat Drums,—and ſo good morrow to your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Brave reſolutions.

sp.speaker: Anaſt.
sp.l: Brave, and Spaniſh right.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: How the devill
Got theſe Cats into th' gutter? my puſſe too?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Heare us.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: We muſt be heard.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: We will be heard
Vitelli; looke, ſee Clara on her knees
Imploring thy compaſſion: Heaven, how ſternly
They dart their emulous eyes, as if each ſcorn'd
To be behind the other in a look!
Mother, death needs no Sword here: oh my ſiſter
(Fate faine would have it ſo) perſwade, entreat,
A Ladies teares are ſilent Orators
(Or ſhould be ſo at leaſt) to move beyond
The honeſt tongu'd-Rethoritian:
Why will you fight? why do's an uncles death
Twentie yeare old, exceed your love to me
But twentie daies? whoſe forc'd cauſe, and faire manner
You could not underſtand, onely have heard.
Cuſtome, that wrought ſo cunningly on nature
In me, that I forgot my ſex, and knew not
Whether my body femall were, or male,
You did unweave, and had the power to charme
A new creation in me, made me feare
To think on thoſe deeds I did perpetrate,
How little power though you allow to me
That cannot with my ſighes, my teares, my prayers
Move you from your own loſſe, if you ſhoule gaine.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: I muſt forget you Clara, 'till I have
Redeem'd my uncles blood, that brands my face
Like a peſtiferous Carbuncle: I am blinde
To what you doe: deafe to your cries: and Marble
To all impulſive exorations.
When on this point, I have pearch'd thy fathers ſoule,
Ile tender thee this bloody reeking hand
Drawne forth the bowels of that murtherer:
If thou canſt love me then, i'le marry thee,
And for thy father loſt, get thee a Sonne;
On no condition elſe.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Moſt barbarous.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Savage.

sp.speaker: Anaſt.
sp.l: Irreligious.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Oh Lucio!
Be thou more mercifull: thou bear'ſt fewer yeers,
Art lately wean'd from ſoft effeminacy,
A maidens manners, and a maidens heart
Are neighbours ſtill to thee: be then more milde,
Proceed not to this combat; bee'ſt thou deſperate
Of thine owne life? yet (deereſt) pitty mine
Thy valour's not thine owne, I gave it thee,
Theſe eyes begot it, this tongue bred it up,
This breaſt would lodge it: doe not uſe my gifts
To mine own ruine: I have made thee rich,
Be not ſo thankleſſe, to undoe me for't.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Miſtreſſe, you know I doe not weare a vaine.
I would not rip for you, to doe you ſervice:
Life's but a word, a ſhadow, a melting dreame,
Compar'd to eſſentiall, and eternall honour.
Why, would you have me value it beyond
Your brother: if I firſt caſt down my ſword
May all my body here, be made one wound,
And yet my ſoule not finde heaven thorough it.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: You would be catter-walling too, but peace,
Goe, get you home, and provide dinner for
Your Sonne, and me: we'l be exceeding merry:
Oh Lucio, I will have thee cock of all
The proud Vitellies that doe live in Sprine:
Fie, we ſhall take cold: hunch:— I am hoarſe
Already.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: How your Siſter whets my ſpleene!
I could eate Lucio now:

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Lamorall: you have often ſworne
You'ld be commanded by me.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Vitelli, Brother,
Ev'n for your Fathers ſoule, your uncles blood,
As you doe love my life: but laſt, and moſt
As you reſpect your own Honour, and Fame,
Throw downe your ſword; he is moſt valiant
That herein yeelds firſt.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Peace, you foole.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Why Lucio,
Doe thou begin; 'tis no diſparagement:
He's elder, and thy better, and thy valour
Is in his infancy.

sp.speaker: Gen
sp.l: Or pay it me,
To whom thou ow'ſt it: Oh, that conſtant time
Would but goe back a week, then Lucio
Thou would'ſt not dare to fight.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Lucio, thy Mother,
Thy Mother beggs it: throw thy ſword down firſt.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Ile throw his head downe after then.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: You have often ſwore you'ld be commanded by me.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Never to this: your ſpight, and ſcorn Genevora,
H'as loſt all power in me:

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Your hearing for ſix words.

sp.speaker: Aſſ.
sp.l: Say. An. Strange obſtinacy!

sp.speaker: Al. Vit. Lu. Lam.
sp.l: We'l ſtay no longer.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Then by thy oath Vitelli,
Thy dreadfull oath, thou wouldſt returne that ſword
When I ſhould aske it, give it to me, now,
This inſtant I require it.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: By thy vow,
As dreadfull, Lucio, to obey my will
In any one thing I would watch to challenge,
I charge thee not to ſtrike a ſtroake: now he
Of our two brothers that loves perjurie
Beſt, and dares firſt be damn'd, infringe his vow.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Excellent Ladies.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Piſh you tyrannize.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: We did equivocate.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: On.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Then Lucio,
So well I love my husband, for he is ſo,
(wanting but ceremony) that I pray
His vengefull ſword may fall upon thy head
ſuccesfully for falſe-hood to his Siſter.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: I likewiſe pray (Vitelli) Lucio's ſword
(who equally is my husband, as thou hers)
May finde thy falſe heart, that durſt gage thy faith,
And durſt not keepe it.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Are you men, or ſtone.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Men, and we'l prove it with our ſwords:

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Your hearing for ſix words, and we have done,
Zancho come forth—we'l fight our challenge too: Enter
Now ſpeake your reſolutions. Bobadilla with two ſwords and a Piſtoll.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Theſe they are,
The firſt blow given betwixt you, ſheathes theſe ſwords
In one anothers boſomes.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: And rogue, looke
You at that inſtant doe diſcharge that Piſtoll
Into my breaſt: if you ſtart back, or quake,
Ile ſtick you like a Pigge.

sp.speaker: A • v.
sp.l: — hold: you are mad.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: This we ſaid: and by our hope of bliffe
This we will doe: ſpeake your intents.

sp.speaker: Cla. Gen.
sp.l: Strike.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Shoot.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Vit. Lu. La. Hold, hold: all friends.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Come downe.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Theſe devilliſh women
Can make men friends and enemies when they liſt.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: A gallant undertaking and a happie;
Why this is noble in you: and will be
A well comer preſent to our Maſter Philip
Then the returne from his Indies. Enter Clara, Genevora Eugenia and Bobadilla.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Father your bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Take her: if he bring not
Betwixt you, boyes that will finde out new worlds,
And win 'em too I'm a falſe Prophet.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Brother.
There is a Siſter: long divided ſtreames
Mix now at length, by fate.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: I am not regarded: I was the carefull Steward that provided theſe Inſtruments of peace, I put the longeſt weapon in your Siſters hand, (my Lord) becauſe ſhe was the ſhorteſt Lady: For likely the ſhorteſt Ladies, love the longeſt—men: And for mine own part, I could have diſcharged it: my Piſtoll is no ordinary Piſtoll, it has two ramming Bullets; but thought I, why ſhould I ſhoot my two bullets into my old Lady? if they had gon, I would not have ſtaid long after: I would ev'n have died too, bravely y'faith, like a Roman-Steward: hung my ſelfe in mine owne Chaine; and there had been a ſtory of Bobadilla, Spindola, Zancho, for after ages to lament: hum: I perceive I am not onely not regarded, but alſo not rewarded.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Prethee peace: 'ſhalt have a new chaine, next
Saint Iaques day, or this new gilt:

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: I am ſatisfied: let vertue have her due: And yet i am melancholy upon this atonement: pray heaven the State rue it not: I would my Lord Vitellies Steward, and I could meet: they ſhould finde it ſhould coſt 'em a little more to make us friends: well, I will forſweare wine, and women for a yeere: and then I will be drunk to morrow, and runne a whoring like a dogge with a broken bottle at's taile; then will I repent next day, and forſweare 'em againe more vehemently: be for-ſworne next day againe, and repent my repentance: for thus a melancholy Gentleman doth, and ought to live.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Nay, you ſhall dine with me: and afterward
Ile with 'ye to the King: But firſt, I will
Diſpatch the Caſtles buſineſſe, that this day
May be compleat. Bring forth the malefactors. Enter Alguazier, Pachieco, Metaldi, Mendoza, Lazaril. Piorato. Malroda, & Guard.
You Alguazier, the Ringleader of theſe
Poore fellowes, are degraded from your office,
You muſt reſtore all ſtolne goods you receiv'd,
And watch a twelve moneth without any pay:
This, if you faile of, (all your goods confiſcate)
You are to be whipt, and ſent into the Gallies.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I like all, but reſtoring that Catholique doctrine
I doe diſlike: Learn all ye officers
By this to live uprightly (if you can) Exit.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: You Cobler, to tranſlate your manners new,
Are doom'd to th' Cloyſter of the Mendicants,
With this your brother; botcher there, for nothing
To cobble, and heel hoſe for the poor Friers,
Till they allow your pennance for ſufficient,
And your amendment; then you ſhall be freed,
And may ſet up againe,

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Mendoza, come.
Our ſoules have trod awry, in all mens ſight,
We'l underlay 'em, till they goe upright. Exit. Pach. & Mend.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Smith, in thoſe ſhackles you for your hard heart
Muſt lye by th'heeles a yeer.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: I have ſhod your horſe, my Lord. Exit.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Away: for you, my hungry white-loaf'd face,
You muſt to th' Gallies, where you ſhall be ſure
To have no more bits, then you ſhall have blowes.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Well, though herrings want, I ſhall have rowes.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Signior, you have prevented us, and puniſh'd
Your ſelfe ſevereller then we would have done.
You have married a whore: may ſhe prove honeſt.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: 'Tis better my Lord, then to marry an honeſt woman
That may prove a whore.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: 'Tis a hanſome wench: and thou canſt keepe her tame:
Ile ſend you what I promis'd.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Ioy to your Lordſhips.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Here may all Ladies learne, to make of foes
The perfect'ſt friends: and not the perfect'ſt foes
Of deereſt friends, as ſome doe now a dayes.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Behold the power of love, to nature loſt
By cuſtome irrecoverably, paſt the hope
Of friends reſtoring, love hath here retriv'd
To her own habit, made her bluſh to ſee
Her ſo long monſtrous metamorphoſes,
May ſtrange affaires never have worſe ſucceſſe. Exeunt.

div.head: EPILOGUE.
div.l: OVr Auhor feares there are ſome Rebell hearts,
Whoſe dulneſſe doth oppoſe loves peircing darts;
Such will be apt to ſay there wanted wit,
The language low, very few ſcaenes are writ
With ſpirit and life; ſuch odde things as theſe
He cares not for, nor ever meanes to pleaſe;
For if your ſelves a Miſtreſſe or loves friends,
Are lik't with this ſmooth Play he hath his ends.

div.head: A PROLOGUE. At the reviving of this Play.
div.l: STatues and Pictures challenge price and fame;
If they can juſtly boaſt, and prove they came
From Phidias or Apelles. None deny,
Poets and Painters hold a ſympathy;
Yet their workes may decay and loſe their grace,
Receiving blemiſh in their limbs or face.
When the minds art has this preheminence,
She ſtill retaineth her firſt excellence.
Then why ſhould not this deere peece be eſteem'd
Child to the richeſt fancies that ere teem'd?
When not their meaneſt off-ſpring, that came forth,
But bore the image of their fathers worth.
Beaumonts, and Fletchers, whoſe deſert outwayes
The beſt applauſe, and their leaſt ſprig of Bayes
Is worthy Phaebus; and who comes to gather
Their fruits of wit, he ſhall not rob the treaſure.
Nor can you ever ſurfeit of the plenty,
Nor can you call them rare, though they be dainty:
The more you take, the more you do them right,
And wee will thanke you for your own delight.

div.head: Scena prima:
div.stage: Enter the Duke of Orleans, and the Earle of Amiens at ſeverall doores.

sp.speaker: Ame.
sp.p: MOrrow my Lord of Orleance.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: You ſalute me like a ſtranger; brother Orleance were to me a Title more belonging, whom you call the husband of your ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: Would the circumſtances of your brotherhood had never offer'd cauſe to make our converſation leſſe familiar: I meet you like a hinderance in your way: your great law ſuit is now upon the tongue, and ready for a judgement.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: Came you from the Hall now?

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: Without ſtay; the Court is full, and ſuch a preſſe of people does attend the iſſue, as if ſome great man were brought to his araignment.

sp.speaker: Orl.
