Much guiltleſſe blood, that uprore ever thirſts,
And for the ſafe-guard of her Son, by me
(As you demand) hath ſent the Lord Euphanes
To plead his owne cauſe, or to ſuffer death
As you ſhall finde him worthy; ſo delivering
The Prince back, I ſhall leave him to your Guard.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: The Queene is good and gracious: kiſſe her hand.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: And ſeale our duties: Sir, depart in peace.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Oh Sir, you now perceive, when in the ſcales
Nature, and fond affection weigh together,
One poyzes like a feather, and you know my Lords
What's to be done.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Your Highneſſe is unarm'd,
Pleaſe you to uſe mine, and to lead the Army
Back to your Mother: Conon, march you with 'em.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I will my Lord: But not ſo farre as not
To bring you help if danger looke upon you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Why doe you looke ſo ſtrangely, fearefully,
Or ſtay your deathfull hande, be not ſo wiſe
To ſtop your rage: looke how unmoov'dly, here
I give my ſelfe my Countries ſacrifice,
An innocent ſacrifice: Truth laughs at death,
And terrifies the killer more then kill'd;
Integrity thus armeleſſe ſeekes her foes,
And never needs the Target, nor the Sword,
Bow, nor invenom'd ſhafts.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: We are amaz'd,
Not at your eloquence, but impudence,
That dare thus front us.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Kill him, who knowes not
The iron forehead that bold miſchiefe weares.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Forbeare a while Agenor, I doe tremble,
And ſomething ſits like vertue in his face,
Which the gods keep.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Agenor, ſtrike Leonidas
You that have purchas'd fame on certaine grounds,
Looſe it on ſuppoſition? ſmeare your hands
In guiltleſſe blood, laugh at my Martyrdome:
But yet remember, when Poſterity
Shall read your Volumes fill'd with vertuous acts,
And ſhall arrive at this black bloody leafe,
Noting yout fooliſh barbariſme, and my wrong,
(As time ſhall make it plaine) what followes this
Diſciphering any noble deed of yours
Shall be quite loſt, for men will read no more.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Why? dare you ſay you are innocent?

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: By all the gods, as they
Of this foule crime, why Gent. pry clean through my life,
Then weigh theſe circumſtances: think you that he
Which made day night, and men to furies turn'd,
Durſt not truſt ſilence, vizors, nor her ſence
That ſuffer'd; but with Charmes and Potions
Caſt her aſleep, (for all this I have enquir'd)
Acted the Fable of Proſerpines Rape,
The place (by all deſcription) like to Hell:
And all to perpetrate unknowne his Luſt,
Would fondly in his Perſon bring a Ring,
And give it a betrothed Wife, ith' ſame houſe
Where the poore injur'd Lady liv'd, and groan'd.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Hell gives us Art to reach the depth of ſin,
But leaves us wretched Fooles, when we are in.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Had it given me that Art, and left me ſo,
I would not thus into the Lyons jawes
Have thruſt my ſelfe (defenceleſſe) for your good,
The Princes ſafety, or the Common-weales:
You know the Queene deny'd me, and ſent us
Commanders to ſurprize you, and to race
This Tower down, we had power enough to doe it,
Or ſtarve you, as you ſaw, and not to tender
My Perſon to your wrath, which I have done,
Knowing my heart as pure as infants ſleep.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What think you Sir?

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: No harme I am ſure: I weepe.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: The gods are juſt, and mighty: but to give you
Further aſſurance, and to make your ſelves
Judges, and witneſſes of my innocency,
Let me demand this queſtion: On what night
Was this foule deed committed?

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: On the Eave
Before our Marriage meant.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: (Your rage being off, that ſtill drownes memory)
Where was your ſelfe and I that very night,
And what our conference?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: By the gods 'tis true:
Both in her Highneſſe Chamber conferring
Even of this Match untill an houre of day,
And then came I to call you: we are ſham'd.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Vtterly loſt, and ſham'd.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Neither, be chear'd,
He that could finde this out can pardon it,
And know this Ring was ſent me from the Queene,
How ſhe came by it, yet is not exquir'd,
Deeper occurrents hang on't: and pray Heaven
That my ſuſpicions prove as falſe as yours,
Which (for the world) till I have greater proofe
I dare not utter what, nor whom they touch;
Only this build upon, with ail my nerves
Ile labour with ye, till time waken truth.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: There are our ſwords Sir, turne the points on us,

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Puniſh Rebellion, and revenge your wrong.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Sir, my revenge ſhall be to make your peace,
Neither was this Rebellion, but raſh love.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: How's this? unarm'd left, now found doubly arm'd?
And thoſe that would have ſlaine him at his feet?
Oh Truth, thou art a mighty Conquereſſe:
The Queene (my Lord) perplex'd in care of you,
That croſſe to her command hazard your ſelfe
In perſon, here is come into the Field,
And like a Leader, marches in the head
Of all her Troopes, vowes that ſhe will demoliſh
Each ſtone of this proud Tower be you not ſafe:
She chafes like ſtormes in Groves, now ſighs, now weepes,
And both ſometimes, like Raine and Wind commixt,
Abjures her Son for ever, leſſe himſelfe
Do fetch you off in perſon, that did give
Your ſelfe to ſave him of your owne free will,
And ſweares he muſt not, nor is ſit to live.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Oh ſhe's a Miſtris for the gods.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: And thou
A godlike ſervant fit for her.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Wide Greece
May boaſt becauſe ſhe cannot boaſt thy like.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Thus Conon tell her Highneſſe.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: My joy flyes.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Let's toward her march: ſterne Drum ſpeake gentle peace.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: We are priſoners, lead us, ne're was knowne
A preſident like this: one unarm'd man
(Suſpected) to captive with golden words
(Truth being his ſheild) ſo many arm'd with ſwords. Ex.

div.stage: Enter (at one Doore) Queen, Theanor, Crates, Conon, Lords, Souldiers, (at another) Euphanes (with two ſwords) Agenor, Leonidas, Souldiers: Euphanes preſents Leonidas on his knees to the Queen: Agenor bare-headed makes ſhew of ſorrow to the Queen, ſhe ſtamps and ſeemes to be angry at firſt, Euphanes perſwades her, layes their ſwords at her feet, ſhe kiſſes him, gives them their ſwords againe, they kiſſe her hand and embrace, the Souldiers lift up Euphanes, and ſhout: Theanor and Crates diſcovered, Conon whiſpers with Crates, Euphanes with Agenor, and Leonidas obſerves it, who ſeeme to promiſe ſomething, Euphanes directs his Page ſomewhat. Exeunt all but Theanor and Crates.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: We are not lucky Crates, this great torrent
Beares all before him.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Such an age as this
Shall ne're be ſeene againe: vertue growes fat,
And villany pines; the Furies are aſleep,
Miſchiefe 'gainſt goodneſſe aym'd is like a ſtone,
Unnaturally forc'd up an imminent hill,
Whoſe weight falls on our heads and buries us,
We ſpringe our ſelves, we ſink in our owne bogs.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: What's to be done?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Repent and grow good.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Piſh,
'Tis not the faſhion (foole) till we grow old:
The peoples love to him now ſcares me more
Then my fond Mothers: both which like two floods
Bearing Euphanes up; will o're-flow me,
And he is worthy, would he were in Heaven,
Be that hereafer: Crates helpe me now,
And henceforth be at eaſe.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Your will my Lord?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Beliza is to marry him forth-with,
I long to have the firſt touch of her too,
That will a little quiet me.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Fie Sir,
You'l be the tyrant to virginity;
To fall but once is manly, to perſevere
Beaſtly, and deſperate.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Croſſe me not but do't:
Are not the meanes, the place, the inſtruments
The very ſame? I muſt expect you ſuddenly. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: I muſt obey you.
Who is in evill once a companion
Can hardly ſhake him off, but muſt run on.
Here I appointed Conon to attend
Him, and his ſword: he promis'd to come ſingle
To avoyd prevention: he is a man on's word.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: You are well met Crates.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: If we part ſo Conon.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Come, we muſt doe theſe mutuall offices,
We muſt be our owne ſeconds, our owne Surgeons,
And fairely fight, like men, not on advantage.

sp.speaker: Caa.
sp.l: You have an honeſt boſome.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Yours ſeemes ſo.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Let's paire our ſwords: you are a juſt Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: You might be ſo: now ſhake hands if you pleaſe,
Though't be the cudgell faſhion, 'tis friendly one.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: So, ſtand off.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: That's my que to beckon 'em. Exit.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Crates, to expoſtulate your wrongs to me
Were to doubt of 'em, or wiſh your excuſe
In words, and ſo returne like maiden Knights:
Yet freely thus much I profeſſe, your ſpleene
And rugged carriage toward your honour'd Brother
Hath much more ſtirr'd me up, then mine owne cauſe,
For I did ne're affect theſe bloody men,
But hold 'em fitter be made publike Hangmen,
Or Butchers call'd, then valiant Gentlemen:
'Tis true ſtamp'd valour do's upon juſt grounds,
Yet for whom juſtlier ſhould I expoſe my life
Than him, unto whoſe vertue I owe all.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Conon, you think by this great deed of yours
To inſinuate your ſelfe a lodging nearer
Unto my Brothers heart: ſuch men as you
Live on their undertakings for their Lords,
And more diſable them by anſwering for 'em
Then if they ſate ſtill, make 'em but their Whores,
For which end Gallants now adayes do fight:
But here we come not to upbraid; what men
Seeme, the raſh world will judge; but what they are
Heaven knowes: and this—Horſes, we are diſcry'd,
One ſtroak for feare of laughter.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Halfe a ſcore.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Hold, hold: on your allegeance hold.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: He that ſtrikks next—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Falls like a Traytor on our ſwords.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Oh Heaven, my Brother bleeds: Conon, thou art
A villaine, an unthankfull man, and ſhalt
Pay me thy blood for his, for his is mine:
Thou wert my friend, but he is ſtill my Brother;
And though a friend ſometimes be nearer ſaid
In ſome gradation, it can never be
Where that ſame Brother can be made a friend,
Which deareſt Crates thus low I implore;
What in my poverty I would not ſeeke,
Becauſe I would not burthen you, now here
In all my height of bliſſe I beg of you,
Your friendſhip; my advancement Sir is yours;
I never held it ſtrange, pray uſe it ſo:
We are but two, which number Nature fram'd
In the moſt uſefull faculties of man,
To ſtrengthen mutually and releeve each other:
Two eyes, two eares, two armes, two leggs and feet,
That where one fail'd the other might ſupply;
And I, your other eye, eare, your arme and legge,
Tender my ſervice, helpe and ſuccour to ye.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Leo, A moſt divine example.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: For deare Brother,
You have been blind, and lame, and deafe to me,
Now be no more ſo: in humility
I give ye the duty of a younger Brother,
Which take you as a Brother, not a Father,
And then you'l pay a duty back to me.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Till now I have not wept theſe thirty yeares.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Diſcording Brothers are like mutuall leggs
Supplanting one another: he that ſeekes
Aid from a ſtranger and forſakes his Brother,
Do's but like him that madly lops his arme,
And to his body joynes a wooden one:
Cuts off his naturall legge, and truſts a Crutch,
Plucks out his eye to ſee with Spectacles.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Moſt deare Euphanes, in this crimſon floud
Waſh my unkindneſſe out: you have ore-come me,
Taught me humanity and brotherhood;
Full well knew Nature thou wert fitter far
To be a Ruler ore me then a Brother,
Which henceforth be: Jove ſurely did deſcend
When thou wert gotten in ſome heavenly ſhape
And greet my Mother, as the Poets tell
Of other women.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Be this Holy-day.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And noted ever with the whiteſt ſtone.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: And pardon me my Lord, looke you, I bleed
Faſter then Crates; what I have done I did
To reconcile your loves, to both a friend,
With my blood ciment, never to part or end.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Moſt worthy Conon.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Happy riſe, this day
Contracts more good then a whole age hath done.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Royall Agenor, brave Leonidas,
You are maine cauſes, and muſt ſhare the fame.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Which in ſome part this hower ſhall requight,
For I have aym'd my black ſhafts at white markes,
And now ile put the clew into your hands
Shall guide ye moſt perſpicuouſly to the depth
Of this dark Laborinth, where ſo long ye were loſt
Touching this old Rape, and a new intent,
Wherein your counſell, and your active wit
My deareſt Brother will be neceſſary.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: My Prophecy is come, prove my hopes true
Agenor ſhall have right, and you no wrong,
Time now will pluck her daughter from her Cave:
Let's hence to prevent rumour; my deare Brother,
Natures divided ſtreames the higheſt ſhelfe
Will over-run at laſt, and flow to it ſelfe. Exeunt

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Crates, Euphanes, Neanthes, Soſicles, Eraton.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: I Have won the Lady to it, and that good
Which is intended to her, your faith onely
And ſecrecie muſt make perfect: Thinke not Sir,
I ſpeake as doubting it, for I dare hazard
My ſoule upon the tryall.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: You may ſafely,
But are Agenor, and Leonidas ready
To ruſh upon him in the Act, and ſeize him
In the height of his ſecurity?

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: At all parts
As you could wiſh them.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Where's the Lady?

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: There
Where you appointed her to ſtay.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: 'Tis wiſely order'd.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Laſt, when you have him ſure compell him this way,
For as by accident here ile bring the Queene
To meet you, 'twill ſtrike greater terrour to him,
To be tane unprovided of excuſe,
And make more for our purpoſes. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Come Neanthes,
Our fames and all are at the ſtake.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: 'Tis fit
That ſince relying on your skill we venture
So much upon one game, you play with cunning
Or we ſhall riſe ſuch loſers: as—

sp.speaker: Soſ.
sp.l: The Prince.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: The plot is laid Sir, howſoe're I ſeem'd
A little ſcrupulous, upon better judgement
I have effected it.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: 'Tis the laſt ſervice
Of this foule kinde I will employ you in.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: We hope ſo Sir.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: And I will ſo reward it—

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: You are bound to that; in every Family
That do's write luſtfull, your fine Bawd gaines more
(For like your Broker, he takes fees on both ſides)
Then all the Officers of the houſe.

sp.speaker: Soſ.
sp.l: For us then
To be a great mans Panders, and live poore,
That were a double fault.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Come, you loſe time Sir,
We will be with you inſtantly: the deed done,
We have a Mask that you expect not.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Thou art ever carefull: for Joves Mercury
I would not change thee. Exit.

sp.speaker: Era.
sp.l: There's an honour for you.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: To be compar'd with the celeſtiall Pimp,
Joves ſmock-ſworne Squire, Dan Hermes.

sp.speaker: Cra,
sp.l: Ile deſerve it,
And Gentlemen be aſſur'd, though what we do now
Will to the Prince Theanor looke like treaſon
And baſe diſloyalty, yet the end ſhall prove,
When he's firſt taught to know himſelfe, then you,
In what he judg'd us falſe we were muſt true. Exeunt

div.head: Scaena Secunda.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Only make haſte (my Lords) in all things elſe
You are inſtructed: you may draw your ſwords
For ſhew if you thinke good, but on my life
You will finde no reſiſtance in his ſervants,
And he's himſelfe unarm'd.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: I would he were not,
My juſt rage ſhould not then be loſt.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Good Sir,
Have you a care no injury be done
Unto the Perſon of the Prince: but Conon,
Have you an eye on both, it is your truſt
That I relye on.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Which I will diſcharge,
Aſſure your ſelfe moſt faithfully.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: For the Lady,
I know your beſt reſpect will nor be wanting:
Then to avoyd ſuſpition and diſcovery,
I hold it requiſite, that as ſoone as ever
The Queene hath ſeene her, ſhe forſake the place,
And fit her ſelfe for that which is projected
For her good, and your honour.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: If this proſper,
Beleeve it you have made a purchaſe of
My ſervice and my life.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Your love I ayme at.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Here I ſhall finde you?

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: With the Qteene.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Enough Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: The Queene enquires for you my Lord, I have met
A dozen Meſſengers in ſearch of you.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: I knew I ſhould be ſought for, as I wiſh'd
She's come her ſelfe in perſon.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Are you found Sir?
I wonder where you ſpend your houres, me thinkes
Since I ſo love your company, and profeſſe
'Tis the beſt comfort this life yeelds me; mine
Should not be tedious to you.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Gracious Madam,
To have the happineſſe to ſee and heare you,
Which by your bounty is conferr'd upon me,
I hold ſo great a bleſſing, that my honours
And wealth compar'd to that are but as Cyphers
To make that number greater: yet your pardon
For borrowing from my duty ſo much time
As the proviſion for my ſudden Marriage
Exacted from me.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: I perceive this Marriage
Will keepe you often from me: but ile beare it.
She's a good Lady, and a faire, Euphanes,
Yet by her leave I will ſhare with her in you:
I am pleas'd that in the night ſhe ſhall enjoy you,
And that's ſufficient for a Wife: the day time
I will divorce you from her.

sp.speaker: Leo. within.
sp.l: We will force you if you reſiſt.

sp.speaker: Queen.
sp.l: What noyce is that?

sp.speaker: The. within.
sp.l: Baſe Traytors.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: It moves this way.

div.stage: Enter Agenor, Leonidas with Theanor, Merione like Beliza, Conon, Crates, Neanthes, Soſicles, Eraton, Guard.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: What ere it be ile meet it,
I was not borne to feare: Who's that Beliza?

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: My worthieſt, nobleſt Miſtris. Exit.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Stay her, ha?
All of you looke as you were rooted here,
And wanted motion: what new Gorgons head
Have you beheld, that you are all turn'd Statues?
This is prodigious: ha's none a tongue
To ſpeake the cauſe?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Could every haire great Queene
Upon my head yeeld an articulate ſound,
And all together ſpeake, they could not yet
Expreſſe the villany we have diſcover'd,
And yet, when with a few unwilling words
I have deliver'd what muſt needs be knowne,
You'l ſay I am too eloquent, and wiſh
I had been borne without a tongue.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Speak boldly,
For I unmov'd with any loſſe will heare.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Then know, we have found out the Raviſher
Of my poore Siſter, and the place, and meanes
By which th' unfortunate though faire Beliza
Hath met a ſecond violence.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: This confirmes
What but before I doubted, to my ruine
My Lady raviſh'd.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Point me out the villaine,
That guilty wretched monſter that hath done this,
That I may looke on him, and in mine eye
He read his Sentence.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: That I truly could
Name any other but the Prince, that heard
You have it all.

sp.speaker: Queen.
sp.l: Wonder not that I ſhake,
The miracle is greater that I live,
Having endur'd the thunder that thy words
Have throwne upon me: dar'ſt thou kneele, with hope
Of any favour, but a ſpeedy death,
And that too in the dreadfull'ſt ſhape that can
Appeare to a diſpairing leaprous ſoule,
If thou haſt any? no, libidinous beaſt,
Thy Luſt hath alter'd ſo thy former being,
By Heaven I know thee not.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Although unworthy
Yet ſtill I am your Son.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Thou lyeſt, lyeſt falſly,
My whole life never knew but one chaſte bed,
Nor e're deſir'd warmth but from lawfull fires,
Can I be then the Mother to a Goat,
Whoſe luſt is more inſatiate then the grave,
And like infectious ayre engenders plagues,
To murder all that's chaſte, or good in woman?
The Gods I from my youth have ſerv'd and fear'd,
Whoſe holy Temples thou haſt made thy Brothells;
Could a Religious Mother then bring forth
So damn'd an Atheiſt? read but o're my life,
My actions, manners, and made perfect in them
But looke into the ſtory of thy ſelfe
As thou art now, not as thou wert Theanor,
And Reaſon will compell thee to confeſſe,
Thou art a ſtranger to me.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Note but how heavie
The weight of guilt is: it ſo low hath ſunke him
That he wants power to riſe up in defence
Of his bad cauſe.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Perſwade me not Euphanes,
This is no Prince, nor can claime part in me:
My Son was borne a Free-man, this a Slave
To beaſtly paſſions, a fugitive,
And run-away from vertue: bring bonds for him.
By all the honour that I owe to Juſtice
He loſes me for ever that ſeekes to ſave him:
Binde him I ſay, and like a wretch that knowes
He ſtands condemn'd before he heares the Sentence,
With his baſe Agents, from my ſight remove him,
And lodge them in the Dungeon: As a Queene
And Patroneſſe to Juſtice I command it:
Thy teares are like unſeaſonable ſhowres,
And in my heart now ſteel'd can make no entrance:
Thou art cruell to thy ſelfe (Foole) 'tis not want
In me of ſoft compaſſion; when thou left'ſt
To be a Son, I ceas'd to be a Mother;
Away with them: The children I will leave
To keepe my name to all poſterities
Shall be the great examples of my Juſtice,
The government of my Country, which ſhall witneſſe
How well I rul'd my ſelfe: bid the wrong'd Ladies
Appeare in Court to morrow, we will heare them;
And by one Act of our ſeverity
For feare of puniſhment, or love to vertue,
Teach others to be honeſt: all will ſhun
To tempt her Lawes, that would not ſpare her Son. Exe.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: Nay Nephew.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Pupill, heare but reaſon.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: No, I have none, and will heare none; oh my honor,
My honour blaſted in the bud, my youth,
My hopefull youth, and all my expectation
Ever to be a man are loſt for ever.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: Why Nephew, we as well as you are dub'd
Knights of the Pantofle.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: And are ſhouted at,
Kick'd, ſcorn'd, and laugh'd at by each Page and Groome,
Yet with erected heads we beare it.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: Alas,
You have yeares, and ſtrength to doe it; but were you
(As I) a tender griſle, apt to bow,
You would like me with Cloakes envelloped,
Walke thus, then ſtamp, then ſtare.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: He will run mad
I hope, and then all's mine.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Why looke you Pupill,
There are for the recovery of your honour
Degrees of Medicines, for a tweak by the Noſe
A man's to travell but fixe moneths, then blow it
And all is well againe: the Baſtinado
Requires a longer time, a yeare or two,
And then 'tis buried: I grant you have been bafful'd,
'Tis but a journey of ſome thirty yeares
And it will be forgotten.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: Thinke you ſo?

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Aſſuredly.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: He may make a ſhorter cut,
But hange, or drowne himſelfe, and on my life
'Twill no more trouble him.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: I could ne're endure
Or Hemp or Water, they are dangerous tooles
For youth to deale with: I will rather follow
My Tutors counſell.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Do ſo.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: And put in
For my ſecurity, that ile not returne
In thirty yeares, my whole ſtate to my Unckle.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: That I like well of.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: Still provided Unckle,
That at my comming home you will allow me
To be of age, that I may call to accompt
This Page, that hath abus'd me.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: 'Tis a march.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: Then Corinth, thus the baſhfull Lamprias
Takes leave of thee: and for this little time
Of thirty yeares will labour all he can,
Though he goes yong forth, to come home a man. Exeu.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Are your Priſoners ready?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: When it ſhall pleaſe the Queene
To call them forth my Lord.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Pray you doe me the favour
To tell me how they have borne themſelves this night
Of their impriſonment?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Gladly Sir; your Brother
With the other Courtiers willingly receiv'd
All courteſies I could offer; eat, and drank,
And were exceeding merry, ſo diſſembling
Their guilt, or confident in their innocence,
That I much wonder'd at it. But the Prince,
That (as borne higheſt) ſhould have grac'd his fall
With greateſt courage, is ſo ſunck with ſorrow,
That to a common judgement ye would ſeeme
To ſuffer like a woman: but to me,
That from the experience I have had of many
Looke further in him, I doe finde the deep
Conſideration of what's paſt, more fright him
Then any other puniſhment.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: That is indeed
True magnanimity: the other but
A deſperate baſtard vallour.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I preſſed to him,
And notwithſtanding the Queenes ſtrict command,
(Having your Lordſhips promiſe to ſecure me)
Offer'd to free him from his bonds, which he
Refus'd, with ſuch a ſorrow mixt with ſcorne
That it amaz'd me; yet I urg'd his Highneſſe
To give one Reaſon for't: he briefly anſwer'd,
That he had ſate in Judgement on himſelfe,
And found that he deſerv'd them: that he was
A Raviſher, and ſo to ſuffer like one,
Which is the reaſon of my teares: he addeth,
For were't not I againe ſhould breake the Lawes,
By ſcorning all their rigour can inflict,
I ſhould dye ſmiling.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: I forbeare to wonder
That you were mov'd that ſaw this: I am ſtrooke
With the relation ſo. 'Tis very well;
See all things ready. I doe wiſh I could
Send comfort to the Prince; be ready with him;
'Tis in the Queenes breaſt only, which for us Bar brought in
To ſearch into were ſawcineſſe, to determine
What ſhe thinkes fit.

div.stage: Enter Leonidas with Merione (in white) Euphanes with Beliza (in black) Queene, Agenor, Conon, Martiall, with Theanor, Crates, Soſicles, Eraton. Lords, Ladies, Guard.

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: Make way there for the Queene.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Read firſt the Law, and what our Anceſtors
Have in this caſe provided, to deter
Such like offenders: To you gentle Ladies
This onely, Would I could as well give comfort,
As bid you be ſecure from feare or doubt
Of our diſpleaſure: be as confident
As if your plea were 'gainſt a common man,
To have all right from us; I will not grieve
For what's not worth my pitty: Read the Law.

body.p: Lycurgus the nineteenth againſt Rapes: It is provided, and publiquely enacted and confirmed, That any man of what degree ſoever, offering violence to the chaſtity of a Virgin, ſhall (Ipſo facto) be lyable to her accuſation, and according to the ſaid Law be cenſur'd; Ever provided, that it ſhall be in the choyce of the ſaid Virgin ſo abuſed, either to compell the Offender to Marry her without a Dowre, if ſo ſhe will be ſatisfied, or demanding his head for the offenoe, to have that accordingly performed.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: You heare this: what doe you demand?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: The benefit
The Law allowes me.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: For the injury
Done to mine Honour, I require his head.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I likewiſe have an eye upon mine Honour,
But knowing that his death cannot reſtore it
I aske him for my Husband.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I was Raviſh'd,
And will have Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I was Raviſh'd too,
I kneele for mercy.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I demand but what
The Law allowes me.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: That which I deſire
Is by the ſame Law warranted.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: The Rape
On me, hath made a forfeit of his life,
Which in revenge of my diſgrace I plead for.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: The Rape on me gives me the priviledge
To be his wife, and that is all I ſue for.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.l: A doubtfull caſe.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Such pretty Lawyers, yet
I never ſaw, nor read of.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: May the Queene
Favour your ſweet plea, Madam.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Is that juſtice?
Shall one that is to ſuffer for a Rape
Be by a Rape defended? Looke upon
The publike enemy of chaſtity,
This luſtfull Satyre, whoſe enrag'd deſires
The ruine of one wretched Virgins honour
Would not ſuffice; and ſhall the wrack of two
Be his protection? May be I was raviſh'd
For his luſt onely, thou for his defence;
O fine evaſion! ſhall with ſuch a ſleight
Your juſtice be deluded? your Lawes cheated?
And he that for one fact deſerv'd to die,
For ſinning often finde impunity?
But that I know thee, I would ſweare thou wert
A falſe impoſtour, and ſubornd to this;
And it may be thou art Merione:
For hadſt thou ſuffer'd truly what I have done,
Thou wouldſt like me complaine, and call for vengeance,
And our wrongs being equall, I alone
Should not deſire revenge: But be it ſo,
If thou prevaile, even he will puniſh it,
And fooliſh mercy ſhew'd to him undoe thee,
Conſider, foole, before it be too late,
What joyes thou canſt expect from ſuch a husband,
To whom thy firſt, and what's more, forc'd embraces,
Which men ſay heighten pleaſure, were diſtaſtefull.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: 'Twas in reſpect, that then they were unlawfull,
Unbleſſ'd by Hymen, and left ſtings behind them,
Which from the marriage bed are ever baniſh'd.
Let this Court be then the image of Joves throne,
Upon which grace and mercy ſtill attend,
To intercede betweene him and his Juſtice;
And ſince the Law allowes as much to me
As ſhe can challenge, let the milder ſentence,
Which beſt becomes a Mother, and a Queene
Now overcome; nor let your wiſdome ſuffer,
In doing right to her, I in my wrong
Indure a ſecond Raviſhment.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You can free him
Onely from that which do's concerne your ſelfe,
Not from the puniſhment that's due to me:
Your injuries you may forgive, not mine;
I plead mine owne juſt wreak, which will right both,
Where that which you deſire robs me of Juſtice;
'Tis that which I appeale to.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Bloody woman,
Doſt thou deſire his puniſhment? Let him live then;
For any man to marry where he likes not
Is ſtill a lingring torment.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: For one Rape
One death's ſufficient, that way cannot catch me.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: To you I fly then, to your mercy Madam,
Exempting not your Juſtice, be but equall;
And ſince in no regard I come behind her,
Let me not ſo be undervalu'd in
Your highneſſe favour, that the world take notice
You ſo prefer'd her, that in her behalf
You kil'd that Son, you would not ſave for me;
Mercy, O mercy Madam.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Great Queen, Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.p: With what a Maſculine conſtancy the grave Lady hath heard them both?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Yet how unmov'd ſhe ſits
In that which moſt concernes her?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Now ſhe riſes,
And having well waigh'd both their arguments,
Reſolves to ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: And yet againe ſhe pauſes;
O Conon, ſuch a reſolution once
A Roman told me he had ſeene in Cato
Before he kill'd himſelf.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: 'Tis now determin'd.
Merione, I could wiſh I were no Queene,
To give you ſatisfaction; no Mother
Beliza, to content you; and would part,
Even with my being, both might have their wiſhes;
But ſince that is impoſſible, in few words
I will deliver what I am reſolved on:
The end for which all profitable Lawes
Were made, looks two waies onely, the reward
Of innocent good men, and the puniſhment
Of bad Delinquents: Ours, concerning Rapes,
Provided that ſame latter clauſe of Marriage
For him that had falne once, not then foreſeeing
Mankinde could prove ſo monſtrous, to tread twice
A path ſo horrid. The great Law-giver
Draco, That for his ſtrange ſeverity
Was ſaid to write his ſterne Decrees in blood,
Made none for Parricides, preſuming that
No man could be ſo wicked: Such might be,
Lycurgus anſwere (did he live) for this.
But ſince I finde that in my Sonne, which was not
Doubted in any elſe, I will adde to it;
He cannot marry both, but for both dying,
Both have their full revenge: You ſee Beliza
You have your wiſh; with you Merione
Ile ſpend a teare or two, ſo Heaven forgive thee.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Upon my knees I do approve your judgement,
And beg that you would put it into act
With all ſpeed poſſible; onely that I may,
Having already made peace with my ſelf,
Part ſo with all the world: Princely Agenor
I aske your pardon; yours my Lord Euphanes;
And Crates, with the reſt too, I forgive you;
Do you the like for me: Yours, gracious Mother,
I dare not ask, and yet if that my death
Be like a Son of yours, though my life was not,
Perhaps you may vouchſafe it: Laſtly that
Both theſe whom I have wrong'd, may wiſh my aſhes
No heavy burden, ere I ſuffer death,
For the reſtoring of Meriones honour,
Let me be married to her, and then dye
For you Beliza.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Thou haſt made in this
Part of amends to me, and to the world,
Thy ſuit is granted, call a Flamyn forth
To do this holy work; with him a Headſman.
Raiſe up thy weeping eyes Merione,
With this hand I confirme thy Marriage,
Wiſhing that now the Gods would ſhew ſome miracle,
That this might not divorſe it.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: To that purpoſe
I am their Miniſter; ſtand not amaz'd,
To all your comforts I will do this wonder,
Your Majeſty (with your pardon I muſt ſpeak it)
Allow'd once heretofore of ſuch a Contract,
Which you repenting afterwards, revok'd it,
Being fully bent to match her with Agenor,
The griev'd Prince knowing this, and yet not daring
To croſſe what you determin'd, by an Oath
Bound me and theſe his followers to doe ſomething
That he might once enjoy her, we ſworne to it,
And eaſily perſwaded, being aſſur'd
She was his Wife before the face of Heaven,
Although ſome Ceremonious formes were wanting,
Committed the firſt Rape, and brought her to him,
Which broke the Marriage; but when we perceiv'd
He purpos'd to abuſe our ready ſervice
In the ſame kinde, upon the chaſte Beliza,
Holding our ſelves leſſe ty'd to him then goodneſſe;
I made diſcovery of it to my Brother,
Who can relate the reſt.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: It is moſt true.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: I would it were.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: In every circumſtance
It is upon my ſoule: For this knowne to me,
I wan Merione in my Ladies habit,
To be againe (but willingly) ſurpriz'd,
But with Agenor, and her noble Brother,
With my approv'd friend Conon, with ſuch ſpeed
She was purſu'd, that the lewd act ſcarce ended,
The Prince (aſſur'd he had enjoy'd Beliza,
For all the time Meriones face was cover'd)
Was apprehended, and b • ought to your preſence,
But not till now diſcover'd, in reſpect
I hop'd the imminent danger of the Prince,
To which his looſe unquenched heats had brought him,
Being purſu'd unto the lateſt tryall
Would worke in him compunction, which it has done;
And theſe two Ladies in their feign'd contentions,
To your delight I hope have ſerv'd as Maskers
To their owne Nuptialls.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: My choyce was worthy
When firſt I look'd on thee, as thou haſt order'd
All ſhall be done, and not the meaneſt that
Plaid in this unexpected Comedy,
But ſhall pertake our bounty: And my Lord,
That with the reſt you may ſeeme ſatisfi'd,
If you dare venture on a Queene, not yet
So farre in debt to yeares▪ but that ſhe may
Bring you a luſty Boy, I offer up
My ſelfe and Kingdome during my life to you.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: It is a bleſſing which I durſt not hope for,
But with all joy receive.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: We all applaud it.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Then on unto the Temple, where the rights
Of Marriage ended, we'l finde new delights. Exeunt.

div.trailer: Here endeth the Queene of Corinth.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: TIs true ſhe is a right good Princes, and a juſt one;
And Florence when ſhe ſets has loſt a Planet.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: My Miſtris? I tell thee gentle Nephew,
There is not ſuch another friend to goodneſſe,
To down-right dealing, to faith and true heart
Within the Chriſtian confines: Before ſhe bleſt us,
Juſtice was a Cheeſe-monger; a meere Cheeſe-monger,
Weigh'd nothing to the World but mytes and maggots,
And a maine ſtinke: Law like a Horſe-courſer,
Her rules, and precepts hung with gawdes and ribbonds,
And pamper'd up to couſen him that bought her,
When ſhe her ſelfe was hackney lame and founder'd.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: But the ſweet Lady,
Belvidere the bright one—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I, there's a face indeed: O my deare Nephew;
Could a young fellow of thy fiery mettle
Freeze, and that Lady in his armes?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I think not.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Thou haſt a parlous judgement; but let that paſſe,
She is as truly vertuous, faire, and noble,
As her great Mother's good; and that's not ordinary.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: But why (ſo many Princes, and ſo great ones
Being Suitors) ſhould the Dutcheſſe deny to match her?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: She is a Jewell man, hangs in her boſome,
Her only Childe: with her eyes ſhe ſees all things,
Diſcourſes with her tongue, and pluck her from her
(So dotingly the old one loves her young one)
You pluck her heart out too: Beſides, of late daies,
The Duke of Millaine, who could never win her
By love, nor treaty, laid a cloſe traine for her
In her owne private walkes: ſome forty Horſe-men,
So to ſurprize her; which we found, and dealt with,
And ſent 'em running home to the Duke their Maſter,
Like Doggs with bottles at their tailes.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Since that, I heard Sir,
She has ſent her to your Cittadell to ſecure her,
My couſen Rodope, your wife attending her.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You heare a truth, and all convenient pleaſures
Are there proportion'd for her.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I would faine Sir,
Like one that owes a dutious ſervice to her
Sometimes, ſo pleaſe you—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Gentle Couſen pardon me,
I muſt not, nor you muſt not dare to offer,
Your friend Sir to command, abroad to love you,
To lend ye any thing I have, to wait upon ye,
But in the Cittadell where I ſtand charg'd,
Not a bit upon a march: no ſervice Sir,
No, good Sir by no meanes: I kiſſe your hands Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: To your keeping only? none elſe to look upon her?
None but Bartello worthy her attendance?
No faith but his to ſerve her? O Belvidere,
Thou Saint to whom my youth is ſacrific'd,
Thou point to which my life turnes, and my fortune,
Art thou lock'd from me now? from all my comforts,
Art thou ſnatch'd violently? thou hear'ſt me not,
Nor canſt thou ſee (faire ſoule) thy Servants mournings,
Yet let thy gentle heart feele what is abſence,
The great divorſe of minds ſo truly loving,
So long, and nurs'd in one affection
Even from our infant eyes, ſuck'd in and nouriſh'd:
O let it feele but that, and there ſtand conſtant
And I am bleſt. My deare Neece Rodope,
That is her Governeſſe, did love me dearely,
There's one hope yet to ſee her: when he is abſent
It may be ventur'd, and ſhe may work it cloſely:
I know the Ladies will goes equall with me,
And ſo the danger of the Edict avoyded;
Let me think more, for I muſt try all hazards.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Will ye go yonder Sir?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Yes marry will I Sir.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: And by this Ladder?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: By that Ladder, coxcomb.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Have ye any more necks at home when this is broken,
For this will crack with the beſt friend he has Sir?
Or can you pitch of all foure, like an Ape now?
Let me ſee you tumble.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You are very pleaſant Sir.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: No truly Sir, I ſhould be loath to ſee ye
Come fluttering down like a yong Rooke, cry ſquab,
And take ye up with your brains beaten into your buttocks

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Hold your peace Aſſe: who's this ſtands muſing here?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Who calls me?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: One moſt glad to ſee you Sir.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: My deareſt Claudio? what make you thus private,
And with a preparation of this nature?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.p: We have leave to play, and are going to climbe Birds neſts.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Prethee what is it friend? why ſtart ye from me?
Is your old Miſtris growne ſo coy and cruell,
She muſt be ſcal'd? it ſeemes you are loath to tell me,
Since twenty yeares continuance of our friendſhip
May not be worth the weight of ſuch a ſecret,
'Twill be but rude to aske againe: 'ſave ye.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay ſtay, deare Silvio, if you love me take it:
For till you know it, never woman labour'd
As I do now.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Ile do my beſt to eaſe it.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You have heard the Lady Belvidere—

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: What heard Sir?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Heard to the Cittadell, upon ſome feares
She is confin'd.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Why dreames he on this beauty?
'Tis true, I have heard it.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And that no acceſſe,
No bleſſing from thoſe eyes but with much hazard,
Even hazard of a life.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: He dares not love her;
I have heard that too: but whither points your purpoſe?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: O Silvio, let me ſpeake that none may heare me,
None but thy truth: I have lov'd this Lady long,
Long given away my life to her devotion,
Long dwelt upon that beauty to my ruine.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Do's ſhe know this?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: No, there begins my miſery,
Ixion-like, I have onely yet claſp'd Clouds,
And fed upon poore empty dreames that ſtarve me.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: And what do you meane to do now?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Though I dye for't,
Though all the tortures in the world hung on me,
Arm'd with imperious Love, I ſtand prepar'd now,
With this to reach her Chamber: there to ſee her,
And tell her boldly with what truth I love her.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: 'Twill not be eaſily done Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: O my Silvio,
The hardeſt things are ſweeteſt in poſſeſſion.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Nor will ſhew much diſcretion.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Love is blinde man,
And he that lookes for reaſon there far blinder.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Have ye conſider'd ripely?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: All that may fall,
And arm'd againſt that all.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Her honour too?
What ſhe may ſuffer in this raſh adventure?
The beauty of her name?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Ile do it cloſely,
And only at her window, with that caution—

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Are there no Guards?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Corruption chokes their ſervice.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Or do you hold her bred ſo light a woman
To hold commerce with ſtrange tongues?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Why this ſervice,
This only hazard of my life muſt tell her,
Though ſhe were Veſtas ſelfe, I muſt deſerve her.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I would not have ye go: pray let it ſinke here,
And think a nobler way to raiſe your ſervice,
A ſafer, and a wiſer.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis too late Sir.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Then I muſt ſay, You ſhall not go.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ſhall not?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: You ſhall not go: that part bred with ye, friendſhip
Bids me ſay boldly ſo, and you obſerve me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You ſtretch that tye too far.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Ile ſtretch it farther:
The honour that I beare that ſpotleſſe vertue
You fouly ſeeke to taint, unnobly covet,
Bids me command ye ſtay: if not, thus force ye.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: This will be worſe then climbing.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Why do ye draw Sir?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: To kill thee, if thy baſe will be thy Maſter.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ever was your friend.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Whilſt thou wert honeſt,
And not a Night-theife of anothers honour;
I never call'd a Foole my friend, a mad-man,
That durſt expoſe his fame to all opinions,
His life to unhoneſt dangers: I never lov'd him,
Durſt know his name, that ſought a Virgins ruine,
Nor ever tooke I pleaſure in acquaintance
With men, that give as looſe raynes to their fancies
As the wilde Ocean to his raging fluxes:
A noble ſoule I twin with, and my love
Followes, his life dares maſter his affections.
Will ye give off, or fight?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I will not fight with ye:
The ſacred name of friend tyes up that anger,
Rather ile ſtudy.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Do, to be a friend ſtill.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: If this way, I ſhall never hold.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Ile watch ye:
And if I catch ye falſe: by Heaven ye dye for't,
All love forgot.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: When I feare that I am fit for't. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Lopez at a Table with jewels and money upon it, an Egge roſting by a Candle.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Whilſt prodigall yong gaudy Fools are banqueting,
And launching out their ſtates to catch the giddy,
Thus do I ſtudy to preſerve my fortune,
And hatch with care at home the wealth that Saints me.
Here's Rubies of Bengala, rich, rich, glorious;
Theſe Diamonds of Ormus bought for little,
Here vented at the price of Princes Ranſomes;
How bright they ſhine like conſtellations,
The South ſeas treaſure here, Pearle, faire and orient
Able to equall Cleapatra's Banket,
Here chaines of leſſer ſtones for Ladies luſtres,
Ingotts of Gold, Rings, Brooches, barrs of Silver,
Theſe are my ſtudies to ſet off in ſale well,
And not in ſenſuall ſurfeits to conſume 'em;
How roſts mine egg? he heats apace, ile turne him:
Penurio, where you knave do you wait? Penurio,
You lazie knave.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Did you call Sir?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Where's your Miſtris?
What vanity holds her from her attendance?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The very ſight of this egge has made him cockiſh,
What would a dozen butter'd do? She is within Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Within Sir, at what thrift ye knave? what getting?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Getting a good ſtomack Sir, & ſhe knew where to get meat to it,
She is praying heartily upon her knees Sir,
That Heaven would ſend her a good bearing dinner.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Nothing but gluttony and ſurfeit thought on,
Health flung behinde: had ſhe not yeſternight firrah
Two Sprats to ſupper, and the oyle allowable?
Was ſhe not ſick with eating? Hadſt not thou,
(Thou moſt vngratefull knave, that nothing ſatisfies)
The water that I boyl'd my other egge in
To make thee hearty broth?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: 'Tis true, I had Sir;
But I might as ſoone make the Philoſophers Stone on't,
You gave it me in water, and but for manners ſake,
I could give it you againe in wind, it was ſo hearty
I ſhall turne piſſing Conduit ſhortly: my Miſtris comes Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Welcome my Dove.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Pray ye keep your welcome to ye,
Unleſſe it carries more then words to pleaſe me,
Is this the joy to be a Wife? to bring with me,
Beſides the nobleneſſe of blood I ſpring from,
A full and able portion to maintaine me?
Is this the happineſſe of youth and beauty,
The great content of being made a Miſtris,
To live a Slave ſubject to wants, and hungers,
To jealouſies for every eye that wanders?
Unmanly jealouſie.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Good Iſabella.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Too good for you: do you think to famiſh me,
Or keep me like an Almes-woman in ſuch rayment,
Such poore unhandſome weeds? am I old, or ugly?
I never was bred thus: and if your miſery
Will ſuffer wilfull blindneſſe to abuſe me,
My patience ſhall be no Bawd to mine owne ruine.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Tickle him Miſtris: to him.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Had ye love in ye,
Or any patt of man—

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Follow that Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Or had humanity but ever knowne ye,
You would ſhame to uſe a woman of my way thus,
So poore, and baſely: you are ſtrangly jealous of me
If I ſhould give ye cauſe.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: How Iſabella?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: As do not venture this way to provoke me.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Excellent well Miſtris,

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: How's this Iſabella?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: 'Twill ſtir a Saint, and I am but a woman,
And by that tenure may.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: By no meanes Chicken,
You know I love ye: fie, take no example
By thoſe young gadding Dames: (you are noted vertuous)
That ſtick their Husbands wealth in trifles on 'em
And point 'em but the way to their owne miſeries:
I am not jealous, kiſſe me, — I am not:
And for your diet, 'tis to keep you healthfull,
Surfits deſtroy more then the ſword: that I am carefull
Your meat ſhould be both neat, and cleanly handled
See, Sweet, I am Cook my ſelfe, and mine owne Cater.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A — of that Cook cannot lick his fingers.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Ile adde another diſh: you ſhall have Milke to it,
'Tis nouriſhing and good.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: With Butter in't Sir?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: This knave would breed a famine in a Kingdom:
And cloths that ſhall content ye: you muſt be wiſe then,
And live ſequeſtred to your ſelfe and me,
Not wandring after every toy comes croſſe ye,
Nor ſtrooke with every ſpleene: what's the knave doing? Penurio.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Hunting Sir, for a ſecond courſe of flyes here,
They are rare new Sallads.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: For certaine Iſabella
This ravening fellow has a Woolf in's belly:
Untemperate knave, will nothing quench thy appetite?
I ſaw him eat two Apples, which is monſtrous.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: If you had given me thoſe 'thad bin more monſtrōs.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Tis a maine miracle to feed this villaine,
Come Iſabella, let us in to Supper,
And think the Romane dainties at our Table,
'Tis all but thought. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Would all my thoughts would do it:
The Devill ſhould think of purchaſing that Egge-ſhell,
To vittle out a Witch for the Burmoothes:
'Tis treaſon to any good ſtomack living now
To heare a tedious Grace ſaid, and no meat to 't,
I have a Radiſh yet, but that's but tranſitory. Exit.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Can any living man unleſſe a Raſcall
That neither knowes himſelfe, nor a faſhion'd Gentleman
Take me for a worſe man then my Maſter now?
I am naturally proud in theſe cloths: but if pride now
Should catch a fall in what I am attempting,
'Tis but a Proverb ſound, and a Neck broken,
That's the worſt can come on't: a Gentleman's gone then,
A Gentleman oth' firſt houſe, there's the end on't:
My Maſter lyes moſt pittifully complaining,
Wringing and kicking up toth' eares in love yonder,
And ſuch a lamentable noyſe he keepes, it kills me:
I have got his cloths, and if I can get to her
By hooke or crooke here, ſuch a ſong ile ſing her—
I think I ſhall be hang'd, but that's no matter,
What's a hanging among friends: I am valiant now as an Elephant;
What's a hanging among friends: I am valiant now as an
I have conſider'd what to ſay too: let me ſee now,
This is the place, 'tis plaguy high: ſtay at that lower window
Let me ayme finely now, like a good Gunner,
It may prove but a whipping.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I ſaw ſome-body
Paſſe by me now, and though it were dark, me thought yet
I knew the clothes: ha, let me not be cozen'd,
The Ladder too, ready to fling it? monſtrous,
'Tis he, 'tis Claudio: moſt voluptuous villaine,
Scandall to womans credit: Love, I forget thee.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: What will he do ith' name of heaven, what's that there?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: And all the friendſhip that I bore thee, bury here.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: What has he in's hand? I hope but a Cudgell.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Thy fault's forgive O Heaven: farewell thou traitor.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I am ſlaine: I am ſlaine.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: He's downe, and dead: dead certaine,
'Twas too raſh, too full of ſpleene, ſtark dead:
This is no place now to repent in, onely
Would I had given this hand that ſhot the Piſtoll
I had miſſ'd thee, and thou wert once more Claudio. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Why ſhould I love thus fooliſhly? thus deſperatly?
And give away my heart where no hope's left me?
Why ſhould not the true counſell of a friend reſtraine me?
The Devills mouth I run into affright me,
The honour of the Lady charme my wildneſſe;
I have no power, no being of my ſelfe,
No reaſon ſtrong enough now left within me
To binde my will: O Love, thou God, or Devill,
Or what thou art that playes the tyrant in me.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Oh.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What's that cry?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: A Surgeon, a Surgeon,
Twenty good Surgeons.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis not far from me,
Some Murther o' my life,

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Will you let me dye here?
No drink come, nor no Surgeon?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis my man ſure,
His voyce, and here he lyes: how is it with thee?

sp.speaker: Sot.
sp.l: I am ſlaine, Sir, I am ſlaine.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Slaine? Who has ſlaine thee?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Kill'd, kill'd, out-right kill'd.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Where's thy hurt?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I know not,
But I am ſure I am kill'd.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Canſt thou ſit up,
That I may finde the hurt out?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I can ſit up,
But ne're the leſſe I am ſlaine.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis not o'this ſide?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: No Sir, I thinke it be not.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nor o' this ſide,
Was it done with a Sword?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: A Gun, a Gun ſweet Maſter.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: The devill a' bullet has been here: thou art well, man.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: No ſure, I am kill'd.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Let me ſee thy thighes, and belly,
As whole as a Fiſh for any thing I ſee yet:
Thou bleed'ſt no where.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I thinke I do not bleed Sir,
But yet I am afraid I am ſlaine.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Stand up Foole,
Thou haſt as much hurt as my naile: who ſhot thee,
A Pottle, or a Pinte?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Signiour Silvio ſhot me
In theſe clothes, taking me for you, and ſeeing
The Ladder in my hand here, which I ſtole from ye,
Thinking to have gone to the Lady my ſelfe, & have ſpoke for ye

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: If he had hit ye home, he had ſerv'd ye right ſirra,
You ſawcy rogue, how poore my intent ſhowes to me,
How naked now, and fooliſh?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Are ye ſure he has not hit me,
It gave a monſtruous bounce?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You riſſe of your right ſide,
And ſaid your prayers too, you had been payed elſe:
But what need'ſt thou a Bullet when thy feare kills thee?
Sirrah, keep your own counſell for all this, you'l be hang'd elſe,
If it be knowne.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: If it be by my meanes let me;
I am glad I am not kill'd, and far more gladder
My gentleman-like humours out: I feele 'tis dangerous,
And to be a gentleman, is to be kill'd twice a week.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Keepe your ſelfe cloſe ith' Country for a while ſirra.
There's Money, walk to your friends.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: They have no Piſtolls,
Nor are no Gentlemen, that's my comfort. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I will retire too, and live private; for this Silvio
Inflam'd with nobleneſſe will be my death elſe;
And if I can forget this love that loades me,
At leaſt the danger: and now I think on't better,
I have ſome concluſions elſe invites me to it. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Rodope, and Silvio at ſeverall doores.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: NEphew.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: My deare Ant.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Would you goe by thus ſlily
And never ſee me, not once ſend in to me
Your loving Neece? ſhe that above all thoſe
I call my Kindred honour'd you, and placed you
Neareſt my heart?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I thanke you worthy Couſen,
But ſuch at this time are my occaſions—

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You ſhall not goe yet, by my faith you ſhall not,
I will not be denyd: why looke ye ſad Nephew?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I am ſeldome other: O, this blood ſits heavy:
As I walk't this way late laſt night,
In meditation of ſome things concern'd me—

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: What Nephew?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Why me thought I heard a Peece, Lady,
A peece ſhot off, much about this place too,
But could not judge the cauſe, nor what it boaded,
Under the Caſtle wall.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: We heard it too,
And the Watch purſu'd it preſently, but found nothing,
Not any tract.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I am right glad to heare it:
The Ruffians ſurely, that command the night
Have found him, ſtript him: and into the River
Convey'd the body.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You looke ſtill ſadder, Nephew,
Is any thing within theſe walls to comfort ye?
Speake, and be maſter of it.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Ye are a right Courtier,
A great Profeſſor, but a poore performer.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Do you doubt my faith: you never found me that way
I dare well ſpeake it boldly, but a true friend.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Continue then.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Try me, and ſee who falters.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I will, and preſently: 'tis in your power
To make me the moſt bound man to your courteſie.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Let me know how, and if I faile—

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: 'Tis thus then,
Get me acceſſe to the Lady Belvidere
But for a minute, but to ſee her: your Husband now
Is ſafe at Court, I left him full employ'd there.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You have ask'd the thing without my power to grant ye,
The Law lyes on the danger: if I lov'd ye not
I would bid ye goe, and there be found, and dye for't.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I knew your love, and where there ſhew'd a danger
How far you durſt ſtep for me: give me a true friend,
That where occaſion is to doe a benefit
Aymes at the end, and not the rubs before it;
I was a foole to aske ye this, a more foole
To thinke a woman had ſo much noble nature
To entertaine a ſecret of this burthen;
Ye had beſt to tell the Dutcheſſe I perſwaded ye,
That's a fine courſe, and one will win ye credit;
Forget the name of Couſen, blot my blood out,
And ſo you raiſe your ſelfe, let me grow ſhorter.
A woman friend? he that beleeves that weakneſſe
Steeres in a ſtormy night without a Compaſſe.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: What is't I durſt not do might not impeach ye?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Why this ye dare not do, ye dare not thinke of.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: 'Tis a maine hazard.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: If it were not ſo
I would not come to you to ſeeke a favour.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You will loſe your ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: The loſſe ends with my ſelfe then.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You will but ſee her?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Onely looke upon her.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Not ſtay?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Preſcribe your time.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Not traffique with her
In any cloſe diſhonourable actions?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Stand you your ſelfe by.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I will venture for ye,
Becauſe ye ſhall be ſure I am a touch'd friend,
Ile bring her to ye: come walke, you know the Garden,
And take this key to open the little Poſterne,
There ſtand no guards.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I ſhall ſoone finde it Couſen. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: 1 Sol.
sp.l: Is the Captaine come home?

sp.speaker: 2 Sol.
sp.l: No, who commands the Guard to night?

sp.speaker: 1 Sol.
sp.l: I thinke Petruchio.

sp.speaker: 2 Sol.
sp.l: What's the Word?

sp.speaker: 1 Sol.
sp.l: None knowes yet.

sp.speaker: 2 Sol.
sp.l: I would this Lady were married out oth' way once,
Or out of our cuſtodies; I wiſh they wold take in more companies,
For I am ſure we feel her in our duties ſhrewdly.

sp.speaker: 1 Sol.
sp.l: 'Tis not her fault I warrant ye, ſhe is ready for't,
And that's the plague, when they grow ripe for marriage
They muſt be ſlipt like Hawkes.

sp.speaker: 2 Sol.
sp.l: Give me a meane wench,
No State doubt lyes on her, ſhe is alwaies ready.

sp.speaker: 1 Sol.
sp.l: Come to the Guard, 'tis late, and ſure the Captaine
Can not be long away.

sp.speaker: 2 Sol.
sp.l: I have watch'd theſe three nights,
To morrow they may keep me tame for nothing. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Silvio, Belvidere, and Rodope with a light.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: This is the place I think; what Light is that there?
The Lady and my Couſen?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Is this the Garden?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Yes Madam.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: O my bleſſed Miſtris,
Saint of my ſoule.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Speake ſoftly: take me to ye,
O Silvio I am thine, thine ever Silvio.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Is this your promiſe Sir? Lady your honour?
I am undone if this be ſeene, diſgrac'd,
Fallen under all diſcredit.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Do you love ſtill?
Deere, do you keepe your old faith?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Ever Lady;
And when that failes me, all that's good forſake me.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Do not you ſhame? Madam, I muſt not ſuffer this,
I will not ſuffer it; men call you vertuous,
What do you meane to loſe your ſelfe thus? Silvio
I charge thee get away, charge you retire ye,
Ile call the watch elſe.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Call all the world to ſee us,
We live in one anothers happineſſe,
And ſo will die.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Here will I hang for ever.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: As ye reſpect me, as hereafter Madam
You would enjoy his love—nothing prevaile with ye?
Il'e try my ſtrength then; get thee gone thou villain,
Thou Promiſe-breaker.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I am tide, I cannot.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Ile ring the Bell then.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Ring it to death, I am fixt here.

div.stage: Enter Bartello, two Souldiers with lights.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: I ſaw a light over the Garden walke,
Hard by the Ladies Chamber, here's ſome knavery
As I live, I ſaw it twice.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: The Guard, the Guard there;
I muſt not ſuffer this, it is too miſchievous.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Light up the torch, I fear'd this, ha? young Silvio?
How got he in?

sp.speaker: 1. Sold.
sp.l: The Divell brought him in ſure
He came not by us.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: My wife between 'em buſling?
Guard, pull him off.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Now, now, ye feele the miſery.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: You, Madam, at an houre ſo far undecent?
Death, O my ſoule! this is a foule fault in ye,
Your mothers care abuſd too, light's to her Chamber,
I am ſorry to ſee this.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Farewell my Sylvio,
And let no danger ſink thee.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Nor death Lady. Exit. Bell. Rod.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Are ye ſo hot? I ſhall prepare ye Phiſick
Will purge ye finely, neatly; you are too fiery,
Think of your prayers, Sir, and you have not forgot 'em;
Can ye fly i'th ayre, or creepe ye in at key-holes?
I have a gyn will catch ye though you conjur'd:
Take him to Guard to night, to ſtrong and ſure Guard;
Ile back to'th Dutcheſſe preſently: no leſſe ſport ſerve ye,
Then the Heire to a Dukedom? play at puſh-pin there Sir?
It was well aim'd, but plague upon't, you ſhot ſhort,
And that will loſe your game.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I know the loſſe then. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Now, in this habit may I ſafely ſee
How my incenſed friend carries my murther,
Who little I imagin'd had been wrought
To ſuch a height of rage; and much I grieve now
Mine owne blinde paſſion had ſo maſter'd me,
I could not ſee his love, for ſure he loves her,
And on a nobler ground then I pretended.
It muſt be ſo, it is ſo; what Penurio,
My ſhotten friend, what winde blew you?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Faith 'tis true,
Any ſtrong winde will blow me like a feather,
I am all Ayre, nothing of earth within me,
Nor have not had this moneth, but that good Dinner
Your Worſhip gave me yeſterday, that ſtaies by me,
And gives me ballaſſe, elſe the Sun would draw me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But do's my Miſtris ſpeake ſtill of me?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Yes Sir,
And in her ſleep, that makes my Maſter mad too,
And turne and fart for anger.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Art ſure ſhe ſaw me?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: She ſaw ye at a window.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt true,
In ſuch a place I ſaw a Gentlewoman,
A young, ſweet hanſome woman.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: That's ſhe, that's ſhe Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And well ſhe view'd me, I view'd her.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Still ſhe Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: At laſt ſhe bluſh'd, and then look't off.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: That bluſh Sir,
If you can read it truly—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But didſt thou tell her,
Or didſt thou foole me, thou knew'ſt ſuch a one?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I told her, and I told her ſuch a ſweet tale—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But did ſhe heare thee?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: With a thouſand eares Sir,
And ſwallow'd what I ſaid as greedily,
As great-bellyed women do Cherries, ſtones and all Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Methinkes ſhe ſhould not love thy Maſter?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Hang him Pilcher,
There's nothing loves him: his owne Cat cannot endure him,
She had better lye with a Beare, for he is ſo hairie,
That a tame warren of flyes frisk round about him.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And wilt thou worke ſtill?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Like a Miner for ye.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And get acceſſe.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Or conjure you together,
'Tis her deſire to meet: ſhe is poyſon'd with him,
And till ſhe take a ſweet freſh ayre, that's you Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: There's money for thee: thou art a precious Varlet,
Be fat, be fat, and blow thy Maſter backward.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Blow you my Miſtris Sir, as flat as a flounder,
Then blow her up againe as Butchers blow their Veales;
If ſhe dye upon the ſame
Bury her, bury her in Gods name.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Thou art a merry knave: by this hand ile feed thee,
Till thou crack'ſt at both ends, if thou dar'ſt do this
Thou ſhalt eat no fantaſticall Porredge,
Nor lick the diſh where oyle was yeſterday,
Duſt, and dead flyes to day; Capons, fat Capons—

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: O hearty ſound.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Cramb'd full of itching Oyſters.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Will ye have the Dutcheſſe?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And Lobſters big as Gauntlets,
Thou ſhalt deſpiſe baſe Beefe.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I do deſpiſe it,
And now me thinkes I feele a Tart come ſliding.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Leaping into thy mouth: but firſt deale faithfully.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: When will ye come?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: To morrow.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Ile attend ye,
For then my Maſter will be out in buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What newes abroad?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: 'Mas as I was comming to you,
I heard that Signiour Silvio, a good Gentleman,
Many a good meale I have eaten with him—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What of him?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Was this day to be Arraigned before the Ducheſſe,
But why I could not heare.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Silvio arraign'd?
Go, get ye gone, and thinke of me.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I fly Sir. Exit Pen.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Arraign'd? for what? for my ſuppoſed death? no,
That cannot be ſure, there's no rumour of it,
Be it what it will, I will be there and ſee it,
And if my help will bring him off he has it. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Quinta.
div.stage: Enter Ducheſſe, Lords, Silvio priſoner, Belvidere, Bartello, Rodope, Clerke, Counſellours, Attendants.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Read the Edict laſt made,
Keepe ſilence there.

body.p: If any man of what condition ſoever, and a ſubject, after the publiſhing of this Edict, ſhall without ſpeciall Licence from the great Ducheſſe, attempt or buy, offer, or make an attempt, to ſolicite the love of the Princeſſe Belvidere, the perſon ſo offending ſhall forfeit his life.

sp.speaker: Counſellour.
sp.l: The reaſon why my Royall Miſtris here
In her laſt Treaty with Siennas Duke,
Promis'd her beauteous Daughter there in marriage,
The Duke of Millaine, rivall in this fortune,
Un-nobly ſought by practiſe to betray her;
Which found, and croſs'd, the Cittadell receiv'd her
There to ſecure her Mothers word; the laſt cauſe
So many Gentlemen of late enamour'd
On this moſt beauteous Princeſſe, and not brooking
One more then other, to deſerve a favour,
Blood has been ſpilt, many brave ſpirits loſt,
And more unleſſe ſhe had been kept cloſe from their violence
Had like to have followed: therefore for due prevention
Of all ſuch hazards and unnoble actions,
This laſt Edict was publiſh'd, which thou Silvio
Like a falſe man, a bad man, and a Traitor
Haſt rent a peeces, and contemn'd; for which cauſe
Thou ſtandeſt a guilty man here now. Ent. Claudio.

sp.speaker: Clark.
sp.l: Speak Silvio,
What canſt thou ſay to avoyd the hand of Juſtice?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Nothing, but I confeſſe, ſubmit, & lay my head to it.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Have ye no eyes my Lords, no underſtandings?
The Gentleman will caſt himſelfe away,
Caſt himſelfe wilfully: are you, or you guilty?
No more is he, no more taint ſticks upon him:
I drew him thether, 'twas my way betray'd him,
I got the entrance kept, I entertain'd him,
I hid the danger from him, forced him to me,
Poore gentle ſoule, he's in no part tranſgreſſing,
I wrot unto him.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Do not wrong that honour,
Caſt not upon that pureneſſe theſe aſperſions,
By Heaven it was my love, my violence,
My life muſt anſwer it: I broke in to her,
Tempted the Law, ſollicited unjuſtly.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: As there is truth in Heaven I was the firſt cauſe,
How could this man have come to me, left naked
Without my counſell and proviſion?
What hower could he finde out to paſſe the Watchs,
But I muſt make it ſure firſt? Reverend Judges,
Be not abus'd, nor let an innocent life lye
Upon your ſhaking Conſcience; I did it,
My love the maine wheele that ſet him a going:
His motion but compell'd.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Can ye beleeve this,
And know with what a modeſty and whiteneſſe
Her life was ever ranck'd? Can you beleeve this
And ſee me here before ye young, and wilfull?
Apt to what danger Love dares thruſt me on,
And where Law ſtops my way, apt to contemne it?
If I were baſhfull, old, or dull, and ſleepy
In Loves allarmes, a woman might awake me,
Direct, and clew me out the way to happineſſe:
But I like fire, kindled with that bright beauty,
Catch hold of all occaſions, and run through 'em.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I charge ye as your honeſt ſoules will anſwer it.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I charge ye, as you are the friends to vertue,
That has no patterne living but this Lady.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Let not his blood—

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Let not her wilfulneſſe—
For then you act a ſcene Hell will rejoyce at.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: He is cleare.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: She is as white in this as infants.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: The god of Love protect your cauſe, and help ye,
Two nobler peeces of affection
Theſe eyes ne're look'd on, if ſuch goodneſſe periſh,
Let never true hearts meet againe, but break. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: A ſtrange example of ſtrong love, a rare one.

sp.speaker: 2 Lord.
sp.l: Madam, we know not what to ſay to think on.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: I muſt confeſſe it ſtrikes me tender too,
Searches my Mothers heart: you found 'em there?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Yes certaine Madam.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: And ſo linked together?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: As they had been one peece of Alablaſter.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Nothing diſhonourable?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: So let my ſoule have happineſſe,
As that thought yet durſt never ſeeke this boſome.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: What ſhall I do? 'has broke my law, abus'd me,
Faine would I know the truth, either confeſſe it,
And let me underſtand the maine offender,
Or both ſhall feele the torture.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Are ye a Mother?
The Mother of ſo ſweet a Roſe as this is?
So pure a Flower? and dare ye loſe that nature?
Dare ye take to your ſelfe ſo great a wickedneſſe,
(O holy Heaven) of thinking what may ruine
This goodly building? this temple where the gods dwell?
Give me a thouſand tortures, I deſerve 'em,
And ſhew me death in all the ſhapes imagin'd.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No death but I will anſwer it, meet it, ſeeke it;
No torture but ile laugh upon't, and kiſſe it.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: This is no way.

sp.speaker: 2 Lord.
sp.l: They ſay no more for certaine
Then their ſtrong hearts will ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: I have bethought me;
No Lords, although I have a Childe offending,
Nature dares not forget ſhe is a Childe ſtill;
Till now I never look'd on love imperious:
I have bethought me of a way to breake ye,
To ſeparate, though not your loves your bodies:
Silvio attend, ile be your Judge my ſelfe now,
The ſentence of your death (becauſe my Daughter
Will beare an equall part in your afflictions)
I take away and pardon: this remaines then
An eaſie, and a gentle puniſhment,
And this ſhall be fulfill'd: becauſe unnobly
You have ſought the love, and marriage of a Princeſſe,
The abſolute and ſole Heire of this Dukedome,
By that meanes as we muſt imagine ſtrongly,
To plant your ſelfe into this Rule hereafter,
We here pronounce ye a man baniſh'd from us.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: For ever baniſh'd Lady?

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Yet more mercy,
But for a yeare: and then againe in this place
To make your full appearance: yet more pitty,
If in that time you can abſolve a queſtion,
Writ down within this ſcrowle, abſolve it rightly,
This Lady is your wife, and ſhall live with ye;
If not, you looſe your head.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I take this honour,
And humbly kiſſe thoſe Royall hands.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Receive it: Bartello, to your old guard take the Princeſſe,
And ſo the Court break up.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Farewell to all,
And to that ſpotleſſe heart my endleſſe ſervice. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1. Lord.
sp.l: What will this prove?

sp.speaker: 2. Lord.
sp.l: Ile tell you a yeare hence, Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Are you pleas'd now? have I not wrought this wonder

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Rarely Penurio.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Cloſe, cloſe then, and work wax.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I am ſtudying for thee
A dinner, that ſhall victuall thee for ten yeare.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Do you heare Miſtris?
You know what a dundier whelp my Maſter is,
I need not preach to ye, how unfit and wanting
To give a woman ſatisfaction:
How he ſtinks, and ſnores, a Bull's a better bed-fellow;
And for his love never let that deceive ye.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Nay ſure he loves me not.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: If he could coyne ye,
Or turne ye into mettle much might be then;
He loves not any thing but what is traffique:
I have heard him ſweare he would ſell ye to the grand Signior.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: The Turk.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The very Turke, and how they would uſe ye.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Ile fit him fort: the Turke?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I know the price too:
Now ye have time to pay him, pay him home Miſtris;
Pay him o'th pate, clout him for all his curteſies;
Here's one that daunces in your eyes, young delicate
To work this vengeance; if ye let it ſlip now,
There is no pittying of ye, od's precious, Miſtris,
Were I his wife, I would ſo mall his Mazard,
'Tis charity, meere charity, pure charity,
Are you the firſt? has it not been from Eves time,
Women would have their ſafe revenges this way?
And good, and gracious women, excellent women;
Is't not a handſome Gentleman? a ſweet Gentleman?
View him from head to foot, a compleat Gentleman;
When can ye hope the like againe? I leave ye,
And my revenge too, with ye; I know my Office,
Ile not be farre off, be not long a fumbling,
When danger ſhall appeare, Ile give the larme. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You are welcome Sir, and would it were my fortune
To afford a Gentleman of your faire ſeeming,
A freer entertainment then this houſe has,
You partly know Sir.—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Know, and pitty Lady,
Such ſweetneſſe in the bud, ſhould be ſo blaſted;
Dare you make me your Servant?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Dare you make Sir,
That ſervice worthy of a womans favour
By conſtancy and goodneſſe?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Here I ſweare to ye,
By the unvalued love I beare this beauty,
(And kiſſe the Book too) never to be recreant,
To honour ye, to truly love, and ſerve ye,
My youth to wait upon ye, what my wealth has.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: O make me not ſo poore, to ſell affection,
Thoſe bought love's Sir, weare faſter then the moneys;
A handſome Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: A moſt delicate ſweet one,
Let my truth Purchaſe then.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I ſhould firſt try it,
But you may happily.—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You ſhall not doubt me,
I hope ſhe loves me; when I prove falſe ſhame take me;
Will ye believe a little?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I feare, too much, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And will ye love a little?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: That ſhould be your part.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Thus I begin then, thus and thus.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: A good beginning,
We have a Proverbe ſaies, makes a good ending.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Say ye ſo? 'tis well infer'd.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Good Sir, your patience:
Me thinks I have ventur'd now, like a weak Bark
Upon a broken billow, that will ſwallow me,
Upon a rough ſea of ſuſpitions,
Stuck round with ieallous rocks.

sp.speaker: Pen. within.
sp.l: A hem, a hem there.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: This is my man; my feares too ſoone have found me,
Now what's the newes?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A pox of yonder old Rigell,
The Captaine, the old Captaine.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: What old Captaine?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Captaine couragious yonder of the Caſtle,
Captaine dondeigo, old Bartello.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Where is he?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: He's comming in:
'Twould vex the Divell, that ſuch an old Potgun as this,
That can make no ſport, ſhould hinder them that can do it.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I would not have him ſee the Gentleman
For all the world, my credit were undone then.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Shall I fling a piſſe-pot on's head as he comes in,
And take him into'th Kitchin, there to dry him.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: That will not do; and he is ſo humerous too
He will come in.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What is he?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: One much troubles me.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: And can do nothing, cannot eat.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Your ſight now,
Out of a driveling dotage he beares to me,
May make him tell my husband, and undo me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What would ye have me do?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: But for a while Sir,
Step here behind this hanging, preſently
I'le anſwer him, and then.—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I will obey ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Where's my rich Jeweller? I have ſtones to ſet.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: He is abroad, and ſure Sir.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Ther's for your ſervice:
Wher's the faire Lady? all alone ſweet beauty?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: She's never much alone Sir, that's acquainted
With ſuch companions as good honeſt thoughts are.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Ile ſit down by thee, and ile kiſſe thy hand too,
And in thine eare ſweare by my life I love thee.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Ye are a merry Captaine.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And a mad one, Lady;
By th'mas thou haſt goodly eyes, excellent eyes, wench,
Ye twinkling rogue, look what thy Captain brings thee,
Thou muſt needs love me, love me heartily,
Hug me, and love me, hug me cloſe.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Fye Captaine.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Nay, I have ſtrength, and I can ſtraine ye ſirrah,
And vault into my ſeat as nimbly, little one.
As any of your ſmooth chinn'd boyes in Florence,
I muſt needs commit a little folly with ye,
Ile not be long, a brideling caſe, and away wench;
The hobnaile thy husband's as fitly out o'th way now.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Do you think he keeps a bawdy houſe?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: That's all one.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Or did you ever ſee that lightneſſe in my carriage,
