That you might promiſe to your ſelf —

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Away foole,
A good turn's a good turne; I am an honeſt fellow.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You have a handſome wife, a vertuous Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: They are not for this time o'th yeer.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: A Lady,
That ever bore that great reſpect to you,
That noble conſtancy.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: That's more then I know.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: O Miſtris, ye are undone, my Maſter's coming.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Coming hard by here.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Plague Conſume the Raſcall,
Shall I make petty-patties of him?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Now what love Sir?
Feare of your comming made him jealous firſt;
Your finding here, will make him mad and deſperate,
And what in that wilde mood he will execute—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I can think of nothing, I have no wit left me,
Certaine my heads a muſtard-pot.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I have thought Sir.
And if you'l pleaſe to put in execution
What I conceive—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'le do it, tell it quickly.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Draw your Sword quickly, and go down inrag'd,
As if you had purſu'd ſome foe up hither,
And grumble to your ſelf extremely, terribly,
But not a word to him, and ſo paſſe by him.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Ile do it perfectly.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Stand you ſtill good Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Raſcall, ſlave, villaine, take a houſe ſo poorely,
After thou haſt wrong'd a Gentleman, a Souldier,
Baſe Poultroon boy, you will forſake your neaſt ſirrah.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: The matter, good ſweet Captain?

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Run-away rogue,
And take a houſe to cover thy baſe cowardize,
Ile whip ye, Ile ſo ſcourge ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Mercy upon me,
What's all this matter wife?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Did you meet the mad man?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I never ſaw the Captain ſo provok't yet.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: O he's a Devill ſure, a moſt bloody devill,
He follow'd a young Gentleman, his ſword drawne,
With ſuch a fury, how I ſhake to think on't,
And foyn'd, and flaſh't at him, and ſwore he'd kill him,
Drove him up hither, follow'd him ſtill bloodily,
And if I had not hid him, ſure had ſlaine him;
A mercileſſe old man.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Moſt vertuous Lady,
Even as the giver of my life, I thank ye.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: This fellow muſt not ſtay here, he is too hanſom;
He is gone Sir, and you may paſſe now with all ſecurity,
Ile be your guide my ſelfe, and ſuch a way
Ile lead ye, none ſhall croſſe, nor none ſhall know ye.
The doore's left open Sirrah, ile ſtarve you for this trick,
Ile make thee faſt o' Sondayes; and for you Lady,
Ile have your lodgings farther off, and cloſer,
Ile have no ſtreet lights to you; will you go Sir?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I thank ye Sir; the Devill take this fortune;
And once more all my ſervice to your goodneſſe. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Now could I eat my very arms for madneſſe,
Croſſ'd in the nick o'th matter? vengeance take it,
And that old Cavalier that ſpoil'd our Cock-fight;
Ile lay the next plot ſurer.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I am glad and ſorry;
Glad, that I got ſo fairely off ſuſpition;
Sorry I loſt my new lov'd friend.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Not loſt Miſtris;
Ile conjure once againe to raiſe that ſpirit;
In, and looke ſoberly upon the matter,
Wee'l ring him one peale more, and if that fall,
The Devill take the clappers, bells, and all. Exeunt

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: NOw, Rhodope, How do you finde my daughter?

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Madam, I finde her now what you would have her,
What the State wiſhes her; I urg'd her fault to her,
Open'd her eyes, and made her ſee the miſchiefe
She was running with a headlong will into,
Made her ſtait at her folly, ſhake and tremble,
At the meere memory of ſuch an ignorance,
She now contemnes his love, hates his remembrance,
Cannot endure to heare the name of Silvio;
His perſon ſpits at.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: I am glad to heare this.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: And humbly now to your will, your care, Madam,
Bends her affections, bowes her beſt obedience;
Syennas Duke, with new eyes now ſhe looks on,
And with a Princely love, ſit for his perſon,
Returnes that happineſſe and joy he look't for;
The generall good of both the neighbour Dukedoms,
Not any private end, or raſh affection
She aims at now: hearing the Duke ariv'd too,
(To whom ſhe owes all honour, and all ſervice,)
She charg'd me kneele thus at your Graces feet,
And not to riſe without a generall pardon.

sp.speaker: Du h.
sp.l: She has it, and my love againe, my old love,
And with more tenderneſſe I meet this penitence,
Then if ſhe ne're had ſtarted from her honour;
I thank ye Rhodopc, am bound to thank ye,
And dayly to remember this great ſervice,
This honeſt faithfull ſervice; go in peace,
And by this Ring, delivered to Bartello,
Let her enjoy our favour, and her liberty,
And preſently to this place, with all honour,
See her conducted.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Your Grace has made me happy. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: Syennas noble Duke, craves his admittance.

div.stage: Enter Duke of Syenna with Attendants.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Go, wait upon his Grace; fair Sir, you are welcome,
Welcome to her ever admir'd your vertues:
And now, me thinks, my Court looks true nobly;
You have taken too much pains, Sir.

sp.speaker: Syen.
sp.l: Royall Lady,
To wait upon your Grace is but my ſervice.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Keep that Sir, for the Saint ye have vow'd it to.

sp.speaker: Syen.
sp.l: I keep a life for her: Since your Grace pleaſes
To jump ſo happily into the matter,
I come indeed to claime your royall promiſe,
The beauteous Belvidere in marriage,
I come to tender her my youth, my fortune,
My everlaſting love.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: You are like to win Sir:
All is forgot, forgiven too; no ſadneſſe
My good Childe, you have the ſame heart ſtill here,
The Duke of Syenna, Childe, pray uſe him nobly.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: An Angell beauty.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Your Grace is fairely welcome,
And what in modeſty a bluſhing maid may
Wiſh to a Gentleman of your great goodneſſe;
But wiſhes are too poore a pay for Princes.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: You have made me richer then all States and Titles,
One kiſſe of this white hand's above all honours,
My faith deare Lady, and my fruitfull ſervice,
My duteous zeale—

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Your Grace is a great Maſter,
And ſpeake too powerfully to be reſiſted:
Once more you are welcome Sir, to me you are welcome,
To her that honoures ye; I could ſay more Sir,
But in anothers tongue 'twere better ſpoken,

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: As wiſe as faire, you have made your Servant happy;
I never ſaw ſo rich a Mine of ſweetneſſe.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Will your Grace pleaſe, after your painfull journy
To take ſome reſt? Are the Dukes Lodgings ready?

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: All Madam.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Then wait upon his Grace, all, and to morrow Sir
We'l ſhew ye in what high eſteeme we hold ye,
Till then a faire repoſe.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: My faireſt ſervice Exit Duke, &c.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: You have ſo honour'd me, my deareſt Daughter,
So truly pleas'd me in this entertainment,
I meane your loving carriage to Syenna,
That both for ever I forget all treſpaſſes,
And to ſecure you next of my full favour,
Aske what you will within my power to grant ye,
Aske freely: and if I forget my promiſe—
Aske confidently.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You are too royall to me,
To me that have ſo fooliſhly tranſgreſs'd you,
So like a Girle, ſo far forgot my vertue,
Which now appeares as baſe and ugly to me,
As did his Dream, that thought he was in Paradice,
Awak'd and ſaw the Devill; how was I wander'd?
With what eyes could I look upon that poore, that courſe thing,
That wretched thing call'd Silvio? that (now) deſpis'd thing?
And loſe an object of that gracefull ſweetneſſe,
That god-like preſence as Syenna is?
Darkneſſe, and cheerfull day had not ſuch difference:
But I muſt ever bleſſe your care, your wiſedome,
That led me from this labirinth of folly,
How had I ſunk elſe? what example given?

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Prethee no more, and as thou art my beſt one,
Aske ſomething that may equall ſuch a goodneſſe.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Why did ye let him go ſo ſlightly from ye,
More like a man in triumph, then condemn'd?
Why did ye make his pennance but a queſtion,
A riddle, every idle wit unlocks.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: 'Tis not ſo,
Nor do not feare it ſo: he will not finde it,
I have given that (unleſſe my ſelfe diſcover it)
Will coſt his head.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Tis ſubject to conſtruction?

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: That it is too.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: It may be then abſolv'd,
And then are we both ſcorn'd and laugh'd at, Madam;
Beſide the promiſe you have ty'd upon it,
Which you muſt never keepe.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: I never meant it.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: For heaven ſake let me know it, 'tis my Suit to ye,
The Boone you would have me aske; let me but ſee it,
That if there be a way to make't ſo ſtrong,
No wit nor powerfull reaſon can run through it,
For my diſgrace, I may beg of heaven to grant it.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Feare not, it has been put to ſharper judgements
Then ere he ſhall arrive at: my deare Father,
That was as fiery in his underſtanding,
And ready in his wit as any living,
Had it two yeares; and ſtudied it, yet loſt it:
This night ye are my Bed-fellow, there Daughter
Into your boſome ile commit this ſecret,
And there we'l both take counſell.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I ſhall finde
Some trick I hope too ſtrong yet for his minde. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Methinks I am batten'd well of late, growne luſty,
Fat, high, and kicking, thankes to the bounteous Rugio;
And now, methinkes I ſcorne theſe poore repaſts,
Cheeſe parings, and the ſtinking tongues of Pilchers;
But why ſhould I remember theſe? they are odious,
They are odious in mine eyes; the full fat diſh now,
The bearing diſh is that I reverence,
The diſh an able Serving-man ſweats under,
And bends ith' hams, as if the houſe hung on him,
That diſh is the diſh: hang your bladder Bankets,
Or halfe a dozen of Turnop, and two Muſhrumps,
Theſe when they breed their beſt, hatch but two Belches;
The ſtate of a fat Turkey, the decorum
He marches in with, all the traine and circumſtance;
'Tis ſuch a matter, ſuch a glorious matter,
And then his ſauce, with Orenges and Onions,
And he diſplay'd in all parts, for ſuch a diſh now,
And at my need I would betray my father,
And for a roaſted Conger, all my Country.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: What my friend Lean-gut, how do's thy beauteous Miſtris?
And where's your Maſter Sirra? where's that horn-pipe?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: My Miſtris Sir, do's as a poore wrong'd Gentlewoman,
Too much heaven knows oppreſt with injuries,
May do and live.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Is the old foole ſtill jealous?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: As old fooles are, and will be ſtill the ſame Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He muſt have cauſe: he muſt have cauſe.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: 'Tis true Sir,
And would he had with all my heart.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He ſhall have.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: For then he had Salt to his Saffron Porredge.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Why do not I ſee thee ſometime? why thou ſtarv'd raſcal?
Why do not ye come to me, you precius bow-caſe?
I keepe good meat at home, good ſtore:

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Yes Sir,
I will not faile ye all next weeke.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Thou art welcome,
I have a ſecret I would faine impart to thee,
But thou art ſo thin the wind will blow it from thee,
Or men will read it through thee.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Wrapt up in beefe Sir,
In good groſſe beefe, let all the world looke on me,
The Engliſh have that trick to keep intelligence.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: A witty knave, firſt there's to tye your tongue up,

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Dumbe as a Dog Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Next, hark in your eare. Sirra.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Well, very well, excellent well: 'tis done Sir,
Say no more to me.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Say and hold.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: 'Tis done Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: As thou lov'ſt butter'd eggs, ſweare.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Let me kiſſe the Booke firſt,
But here's my hand, brave Captaine.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Looke ye hold, ſirra. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: O the moſt precious vanity of this world
When ſuch dry Neatſ-tongues muſt be ſok'd and larded
With young fat ſupple wenches? O the Devill,
What can he do, he cannot ſuck an egge off
But his back's looſe ith' hilts: go thy waies Captaine,
Well may thy Warlike name work Miracles,
But if e're thy founder'd courſer win match more,
Or ſtand right but one traine—

sp.speaker: 1. Gent.
sp.l: Now Signiour Shadow,
What art thou thinking of, how to rob thy Maſter?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Of his good deeds? the Thief that undetakes that
Muſt have a hook will poze all Hell to hammer:
Have ye dined Gentlemen, or do you purpoſe?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Dined, two long houres ago.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Pray ye take me with ye.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: To ſupper do'ſt thou meane?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: To any thing
That has the ſmell of meat in't: tell me true, Gentlemen,
Are not you three now going to be ſinfull,
To jeabard a joynt, or ſo? I have found your faces,
And ſee whore written in your eyes.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: A parlous Raſcall,
Thou art much upon the matter.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Have a care Gentlemen,
'Tis a ſore age, very ſore age, lewd age,
And women now are like old Knights adventures,
Full of inchanted flames, and dangerous.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent,
sp.l: Where the moſt danger is, there's moſt honour.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I grant ye, honour moſt conſiſts in ſufferance,
And by that rule you three ſhould be moſt honourable.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: A ſubtle Rogue: but canſt thou tell Penurio
Where we might light upon—

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A learned Surgeon?

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: Pox take ye foole; I meane good wholſome wenches.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: 'Faith wholſome women will but ſpoyle ye too,
For you are ſo us'd to ſnap-haunces: But take my counſell,
Take fat old women, fat, and five and fifty,
The Dog-dayes are come in.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Take fat old women?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The fatter and the older, ſtill the better,
You do not know the pleaſure of an old Dame,
A fat old Dame, you do not know the knack on't:
They are like our Country grotes, as coole as Chriſtmas,
And ſure ith' keeles.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Hang him ſtarv'd foole, he mocks us.

sp.speaker: 3. Gent.
sp.l: Penurio, thou know'ſt all the hanſome wenches?
What ſhall I give thee for a Merchants wife now?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I take no money Gentlemen, that's baſe,
I trade in meat, a Merchants wife will coſt ye
A glorious Capon, a great ſhoulder of Mutton,
And a Tart as big as a Conjurers circle.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: That's cheap enough.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: And what a Haberdaſhers?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Worſe meat will ſerve for her: a great Gooſe Pye,
But you muſt ſend it out oth' Country to me,
It will not do elſe: with a peece of Bacon,
And if you can a pot of Butter with it.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Now do I ayme at horſe-fleſh: what a Parſons?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A tithe Pig has no fellow, if I fetch her,
If ſhe be Puritane, Plumb-porridge do's it,
And a fat loyne of Veale well ſawc'd and roſted.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Wee'l meet one night, and thou ſhalt have all theſe,
O' that condition we may have the wenches,
A dainty raſcall.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: When your ſtomacks ſerve ye,
(For mine is ever ready) ile ſupply ye.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Farewell, and there's to fill thy paunch.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Brave Gentleman.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Hold ſirrah, there.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Any young wench ith' Towne Sir.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: It ſhall go round. Exit Gent.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Moſt honourable Gentlemen,
All theſe are Courtiers, but they are meere Coxcombs,
And only for a wench, their purſes open,
Nor have they ſo much judgement left to chuſe her;
If e're they call upon me ile ſo fit 'em,
I have a pack of wry-mouth'd mackrell Ladies,
Stinke like a ſtanding ditch, and thoſe deare Damſels;
But I forgot my buſineſſe, I thank ye Mounſieurs,
I have a thouſand whimſies in my braines now. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter (to a Banket) Duches, Syenna, Lords, Attendants.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Your Grace ſhall now perceive how much we honor ye
And in what deare regard we hold your friendſhip
Will you ſit Sir, and grace this homely Banquet?

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Madam, to your poor friend you are too magnificent.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: To the Dukes health, and all the joyes I wiſh him,
Let no man miſſe this cup: have we no Muſick?

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Your noble favours ſtill you heap upon me,
But where's my vertuous Miſtris, ſuch a Feaſt,
And not her ſparkling beauty here to bleſſe it?
Me thinkes it ſhould not be, it ſhewes not fully.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Young Ladies Sir, are long, and curious
In putting on their trims, forget how day goes,
And then 'tis their good morrow when they are ready:
Go ſome and call her, and wait upon her hither,
Tell her the Duke and I deſire her company:
I warrant ye, a hundred dreſſings now
She has ſurvey'd, this, and that faſhion look'd on,
For Ruffs and Gowns; caſt this away, theſe Jewels
Suited to theſe and theſe knots: o' my life Sir,
She feares your curious eye will ſoone diſcover elſe:
Why ſtand ye ſtill, why gape ye on one another?
Did I not bid ye go and tell my Daughter?
Are ye nayled here? nor ſtir? nor ſpeake? who am I,
And who are you?

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: Pardon me, gracious Lady,
The feare to tell you that you would not hear of
Makes us all dumb, the Princeſſe is gone, Madam.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Gone? whither gone? ſome wiſer fellow anſwer me.

sp.speaker: 2 Lord.
sp.l: We ſought the Court all over, and beleeve Lady,
No newes of where ſhe is, nor how convey'd hence.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: It cannot be, it muſt not be.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: 'Tis true Madam,
No roome in all the Court but we ſearch'd through it,
Her women found her want firſt, and they cry'd to us.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Gone? ſtolne away? I am abus'd, diſhonour'd.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: 'Tis I that am abus'd, 'tis I diſhonour'd,
Is this your welcome, this your favour to me?
To foyſt a trick upon me, this trick too,
To cheat me of my love? Am I not worthy?
Or ſince I was your Gueſt, am I growne odious?

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Your Grace miſtakes me, as I have a life, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: And I another, I will never beare this,
Never endure this dor.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: But heare me patiently.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Give me my love.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: As ſoone as care can find her,
And all care ſhall be uſed.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: And all my care too,
To be reveng'd; I ſmell the trick, 'tis too ranke,
Fie, how it ſmells oth' Mother.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: You wrong me, Duke.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: For this diſgrace ten thouſand Florentines
Shall pay their deareſt bloods, and dying curſe ye,
And ſo I turne away, your mortall enemy. Exit.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Since ye are ſo high and hot Sir, ye have half arm'd us,
Be carefull of the Towne, of all the Caſtles,
And ſee ſupplyes of Souldiers every where,
And Muſters for the Field, when he invites us,
For he ſhall know 'tis not high words can fright us.
My Daughter gone? has ſhe ſo finely cozen'd me?
This is for Silvio's ſake ſure, O cunning falſe one;
Publiſh a Proclamation thorough the Dukedome.
That whoſoe're can bring toth' Court young Silvio,
Alive or dead, beſide our thankes and favour,
Shall have two thouſand Duckets for his labour;
See it diſpatch'd, and ſent in haſte: O baſe one. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Iſabella, and Penurio with a Light.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Was't thou with Rugio?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Yes marry was I cloſely.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: And do's he ſtill remember his poore Miſtris?
Do's he deſire to ſee me?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Yes, and preſently:
Puts off all buſineſſe elſe, lives in that memory,
And will be here according to directions.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: But where's thy Maſter?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Where a coxcombe ſhould be,
Waiting at Court with his Jewells,
Safe for this night I warrant ye.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I am bound to thee.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I would ye were; as cloſe as I could tye ye,

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Thou art my beſt, my trueſt friend.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I labour,
I moyle and toyle for ye: I am your hackney.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: If ever I be able—

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Steale the great Cheeſe Miſtris,
Was ſent him out oth' Country.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Any thing.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: That's meat, 'tis lawfull Miſtris: where's the Caſtle Cuſtard
He got at Court?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: He has lock't it in's ſtudy.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Get a warrant to ſearch for counterfeit gold.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Give me thy Candle,
Ile finde a time to be thy carefull Cater.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: And many a time Ile finde to be his Cook,
And dreſſe his Calves head to the ſweeteſt ſauce Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: To bed Penurio, go, the reſt is my charge,
Ile keep the Watch out.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Now if you ſpare him— Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Peace foole,
I hope my Rugio will not faile, 'twould vexe me:
Now to my ſtring; ſo, ſure he cannot miſſe now,
And this end to my finger: ile lye downe,
For on a ſuddaine I am wondrous heavy,
'Tis very late too; if he come, and finde this,
And pull it, though it be with eaſie motion
I ſhall ſoone waken, and as ſoone be with him.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Thou ſecret friend, how am I bound to love thee,
And how to hug thee for thy private ſervice?
Thou art the Star all my ſuſpitions ſaile by,
The fixed point my wronged honour turnes to,
By thee I ſhall know all, finde all the ſubtilties
Of devilliſh women, that torment me daily:
Thou art my Conjurer, my Spell, my Spirit,
All's huſh'd and ſtill, no ſound of any ſtirring,
No tread of living thing: the Light is in ſtill,
And there's my wife, how prettily the foole lyes,
How ſweet, and handſomely, and in her clothes too,
Waiting for me upon my life; her fondneſſe
Would not admit her reſt till I came to her:
O carefull foole, why am I angry with thee?
Why do I think thou hat'ſt thy loving Husband?
I am an Aſſe, an over-doating Coxcombe,
And this ſweet ſoule the mirrour of perfection:
How admirable faire and delicate,
And how it ſtirs me, ile ſing thy ſweets a Requiem,
But will not waken thee.

body.head: Song.
body.l: O Faire ſweet face, O eyes celeſtiall bright,
Twin-ſtars in Heaven that now adorn the night;
O fruitfull lips, where Cherries ever grow,
And Damask cheeks, where all ſweet beauties blow;
O thou from head to foot divinely faire,
Cupids moſt cunning Nets made of that haire,
And as he weaves himſelfe for curious eyes,
O me, O me, I am caught my ſelfe, he cryes:
Sweet reſt ahout this ſweets and golden ſleepe,
Soft peacefull thoughts your how' rely watches keepe,
Whilſt I in wonder ſing this ſacrifice,
To beauty ſacred, and thoſe Angell-eyes.

sp.l: Now will I ſteale a kiſſe, a deare kiſſe from her,
And ſuck the Roſie breath of this bright beauty;
What a Devill is this? ty'd to her finger too?
A ſtring, a damned ſtring to give intelligence
O my lov'd key, how truly has'ſt thou ſerv'd me;
Ile follow this: ſoft, ſoft, toth' doore it goes,
And through toth' other ſide; a damned ſtring 'tis,
I am abus'd, topt, Cuckolded, fooled, jaded,
Ridden to death, to madneſſe; ſtay, this helps not:
Stay, ſtay, and now invention help me,
Ile ſit downe by her, take this from her eaſily,
And thus upon mine owne: Dog, I ſhall catch ye,
With all your cunning Sir: I ſhall light on ye,
I felt it pull ſure: yes, but wondrous ſoftly,
'Tis there againe, and harder now, have at ye:
Now and thou ſcap'ſt, the Devills thy ghoſtly father. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Sure 'twas my Husbands voyce: The ſtring is gone to,
He has found the trick on't: I am undone, betray'd,
And if he meet my friend he periſhes,
What fortune followes me, what ſpightfull fortune?
Hoa, Jaquenet.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Here Miſtris, do you call me?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Didſt thou heare no noiſe?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I heare my Maſter mad yonder,
And ſweares, and chafes—

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Dar'ſt thou do one thing for me?
One thing concernes mine honour, all is loſt elſe?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Name what you will.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: It can bring but a beating,
Which I will recompence ſo largely—

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Name it.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Sit here, as if thou wert aſleep.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Is that all?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: When he comes in, what e're he do unto thee
(The worſt will be but beating) ſpeak not a word,
Not one word as thou loveſt me.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Ile run through it.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Ile carry away the Candle. Exit.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: And I the blowes Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Have you put your light out? I ſhall ſtumble to ye,
You whore, you cunning whore, I ſhal catch your rogue to,
Has light leggs elſe: I had ſo Ferret-claw'd him:
O have I found ye? do ye play at dog-ſleep ſtill whore?
Do you think that can protect ye? yes, I will kill thee,
But firſt ile bring thy friends to view thy villanies,
Thy whoriſh villanies: and firſt ile beat thee,
Beat thee to pin-duſt, thou ſalt whore, thou varlet,
Scratch out thine eyes; ile ſpoile your tempting viſage;
Are ye ſo patient? ile put my nayles in deeper,
Is it good whoring? whoring ye baſe raſcall?
Is it good tempting men with ſtrings to ride ye?
So, ile fetch your kindred, and your friends, whore,
And ſuch a Juſtice I will act upon thee. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: What is he gone?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: The Devill go with him Miſtris,
Has harrowed me, plow'd land was ne're ſo harrowed:
I had the moſt ado to ſave mine eyes.

sp.speaker: Iſah.
sp.l: Has paid thee,
But ile heale all againe with good gold Jaquenet;
Has damned nayles.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: They are ten-penny nayles I think Miſtris:
Ile undertake he ſhall ſtrike 'em through an inch board.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Go up, and waſh thy ſelfe: take my Pomatum,
And now let me alone to end the Tragedy.

sp.speaker: Joq.
sp.l: You had beſt beware.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I ſhall deale ſtoutly with him,
Reach me my book, and ſee the doore made faſt wench,
And ſo good night: now to the matter politick.

sp.speaker: Lop. within
sp.l: You ſhall ſee what ſhe is, what a ſweet jewell.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Who's there, what mad-man knocks? is this an hower
And in mine husbands abſence?

sp.speaker: Lop. within.
sp.l: Will ye open?
You know my voyce ye whore, I am that husband:
Do you mark her ſubtlety? but I have paid her,
I have ſo ferk'd her face: here's the blood Gentlemen,
Ecce ſignum: I have ſpoyl'd her Goatiſh beauty,
Obſerve her how ſhe lookes now, how ſhe is painted,
O 'tis the moſt wicked'ſt whore, and the moſt treacherous-

div.stage: Enter Lopez, Bartello, Gent. and two Gentlewomen.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Here walkes my Couſen full of meditation,
Arm'd with religious thoughts.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Is this the monſter?

sp.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
sp.l: Is this the ſubject of that rage you talk't of,
That naughty woman you had pull'd a peeces?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Here's no ſuch thing.

sp.speaker: 1. Gentlew.
sp.l: How have ye wrong'd this beauty?
Are not you mad my friend? what time o'th Moon is't?
Have not you Maggots in your braines?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe ſure.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Where's the ſcratch'd face ye ſpoke of, the torne garments,
And all the haire pluck'd off her head?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Beleeve me,
'Twere better far you had loſt your paire of pibbles,
Then ſhe the leaſt adornment of that ſweetneſſe.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Is not this blood?

sp.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
sp.l: This is a monſtrous folly,
A baſe abuſe.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Thus he do's ever uſe me,
And ſtickes me up a wonder, not a woman,
Nothing I do but ſubject to ſuſpition;
Nothing I can do able to content him.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Lopez, you muſt not uſe this.

sp.speaker: 2 Gentlew.
sp.l: 'Twere not amiſſe Sir,
To give ye ſauce to your meat, and ſuddainly.

sp.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
sp.l: You that dare wrong a woman of her goodneſſe,
Thou have a wife, thou have a Beare ty'd to thee,
To ſcratch thy jealous itch, were all o' my minde,
I meane all women, we would ſoone disburthen ye
Of that that breeds theſe fits, theſe dog-flawes in ye,
A Sow-guelder ſhould trim ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: A rare cure Lady,
And one as fit for him as a Thief for a halter,
You ſee this youth: will you not cry him quittance,
Body' me, I would pine, but I would pepper him,
Ile come anon, he, hang him, poore pompillion:
How like a wench bepiſt he lookes, ile come Lady:
Lopez, the Law muſt teach ye what a wife is,
A good, a vertuous wife.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Ile ne're live with him,
I crave your loves all to make knowne my cauſe,
That ſo a faire Divorce may paſſe between us,
I am weary of my life: in danger hourely.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You ſee how rude you are, I will not miſſe ye,
Unſufferable rude: ile pay him ſoundly,
You ſhould be whipt in Bedlam: ile reward him.

sp.speaker: 2 Gentlew.
sp.l: Whipping's too good.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I think I am alive ſtill,
And in my wits.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Ile put a trick upon him,
And get his goods Confiſcate: you ſhall have 'em;
I will not faile at nine.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I think I am here too,
And once I would have ſworn I had taken her napping,
I think my name is Lopez.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Fie for ſhame Sir,
You ſee you have abus'd her, foulely wrong'd her,
Hung ſcandalous and courſe opinions on her,
Which now you finde but children of ſuſpition:
Aske her forgiveneſſe, ſhew a penitence,
She is my Kinſ-woman, and what ſhe ſuffers
Under ſo baſe and beaſtly jealouſies,
I will redreſſe elſe, ile ſeeke ſatisfaction.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Why, every Boy ith' Towne will piſſe upon thee.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I am ſorry for't.

sp.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
sp.l: Downe o' your marrow-bones.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Even ſorry from my heart: forgive me ſweet wife,
Here I confeſſe moſt freely I have wrong'd ye,
As freely here I beg a pardon of ye,
From this hower no debate, no croſſe ſuſpition—

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: To ſhew ye Sir I underſtand a wives part,
Thus I aſſure my love, and ſeale your pardon.

sp.speaker: 2 Gentlew.
sp.l: 'Tis well done, now to bed and there confirm it.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: And ſo good night.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Aware relapſes, Lopez. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Now Iſabella tell me truth, and ſuddainly,
And do not juggle with me, nor diſſemble,
For as I have a life ye dye then: I am not mad,
Nor do's the Devill work upon my weakneſſe,
Tell me the trick of this, and tell me freely.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Will then that ſatisfie ye?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: If ye deale ingenuouſly.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Ile tell ye all, and tell ye true and freely,
Bartello was the end of all this jealouſie,
His often viſitations brought by you, firſt
Bred all theſe fits, and theſe ſuſpitions:
I knew your falſe key, and accordingly
I fram'd my plot, to have him take him finely,
Too poore a pennance for the wrong his wife beares,
His worthy vertuous wife: I felt it ſenſibly
When ye tooke off the ſtring, and was much pleas'd in't,
Becauſe I wiſh'd his importunate dotage paid well,
And had you ſtaid two minutes more, ye had had him.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: This ſounds like truth.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Becauſe this ſhall be certaine,
Next time he comes, as long he cannot tarry,
Your ſelf ſhall ſee, and heare, his lew'd temptations.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Till then I am ſatisfied, and if this prove true,
Henceforward Miſtris of your ſelf I give ye,
And I to ſerve ye: For my luſty Captaine,
Ile make him daunce, and make him think the Devill
Clawes at his breech, and yet I will not hurt him:
Come now to bed, and prove but conſtant this way,
Ile prove the man you ever wiſhed.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You have bleſt me. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: WHat labour and what travell have I runne Through?
And through what Cities to abſolve this Riddle?
Diviners, Dreamers, Schoolemen, deep Magitians,
All have I tride, and all give ſeverall meanings,
And from all hope of any future happineſſe,
To this place am I come at length, the country,
The people ſimple, plaine, and harmleſſe witty,
Whoſe honeſt labours Heaven rewards with plenty
Of Corne, Wine, Oyle, which they againe, as thankfull,
To their new Cropps, new paſtimes celebrate,
And crowne their joyfull harveſts with new voyces;
By a rich farmer here I am entertain'd,
And rank't among the number of his Servants,
Not gueſſing what I am, but what he would have me,
Here may be ſo much wit (though much I feare it)
To undo this knotty queſtion; and would to Heaven
My fortunes had been hatch'd with theirs, as innocent,
And never knowne a pitch above their plainneſſe.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: That it is, that it is, what's this word now? this
Is a plaguy word, that it is, r. e. a. that it is, reaſon,
By your leave, Mr. Soto, by your leave, you are too quick, Sir,
Ther's a ſtrange par'lous T. hefore the reaſon,
A very tall T. which makes the word High Treaſon.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: What Treaſon's that? do's this fellow underſtand Himſelfe?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Pitch will infect, ile meddle no more with this geere;
What a Devill ayles this fellow? this fooliſh fellow,
Being admitted to be one of us too,
That are the maſters of the Sports proceeding,
Thus to appeare, before me too, unmorriſſ'd?
Do you know me friend?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: You are my Matters Son, Sir.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: And do you know what ſports are now in ſeaſon?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I heare there are ſome a foot.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Where are your Bells then?
Your Rings, your Ribanes, friend? & your clean Napkins?
Your noſegay in your hat, pinn'd up, am not I here?
My fathers eldeſt Son, and at this time, Sir,
I would have ye know it, though ye be ten times his ſervant,
A better man then my father far, Lord of this Harveſt, Sir,
And ſhall a man of my place want attendance?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: 'Twas want of knowledge, Sir, not duty, bred this,
I would have made ſuit elſe for your Lordſhips ſervice.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: In ſome ſort I am ſatisfied now, mend your maners,
But thou art a melancholly fellow, veng'ance melancholly,
And that may breed a inſurrection amongſt us;
Go too, Ile lay the beſt part of two pots now
Thou art in love, and I can gueſſe with whom too,
I ſaw the wench that twir'd and twinkled at thee,
The other day; the wench that's new come hither,
The young ſmug wench.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: You know more then I feele Sir.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Go too, Ile be thy friend, ile ſpeak a good word for thee,
And thou ſhalt have my Lordſhips countenance to her;
May be I have had a ſnap my ſelf, may be I, may be no,
We Lords are allow'd a little more.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: 'Tis fit Sir;
I humbly thank ye, you are too too tender of me,
But what Sir, I beſeech ye, was that paper,
Your Lordſhip was ſo ſtudiouſly Imployed in,
When ye came out a doores?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Thou meaneſt this paper.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: That Sir, I think.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Why, 'tis a Proclamation,
A notable piece of villany, as ever thou heard'ſt in thy life,
By mine honour it is.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: How Sir? or what concernes it?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: It comes ye from the Ducheſſe, a plaguy wiſe woman,
To apprehend the body of one Silvio,
As arrant a Raſcall as ever piſt againſt poſt,
And this ſame Silvio, or this foreſaid raſcall,
To bring before her, live or dead; for which good ſervice
The man that brings him, has two thouſand Duckets;
Is not this notable matter now?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo indeed,
This Proclamation beares my bane about it;
Can no reſt finde me? no private place ſecure me?
But ſtill my miſeries like blood-hounds haunt me?
Unfortunate young man, which way now guides thee,
Guides thee from death? the Countrey's laid round for thee;
O Claudio, now I feele thy blood upon me,
Now it ſpeaks lowdly here, I am ſure againſt me,
Time now has found it out, and truth proclam'd it,
And Juſtice now cries out, I muſt die for it.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Haſt thou read it?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: And doſt thou know that Silvio.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I never ſaw him, Sir.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I have, and know him too,
I know him as well as I know thee, and better,
And if I light upon him, for a trick he plaid me once,
A certaine kinde of dog-trick, ile ſo fiddle him,
Two thouſand Duckets, ile ſo pepper him,
And with that money ile turne Gentleman,
Worth a browne Bakers dozen of ſuch Silvio's.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: There is no ſtaying here, this rogue will know me,
And for the money ſake betray me too;
I muſt bethink me ſuddenly and ſafely.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Mine owne deare Lady, have at thy honey-comb,
Now, for the honour of our Towne, Boyes, trace ſweetly,
What a vengeance ayles this whobub? pox refuſe 'em,
Cannot they let us dance in our owne defence here?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.l: Arme, honeſt friends, arme ſuddenly & bravely,
And with your antient reſolutions follow me;
Look how the Beacons ſhow like comets, your poor neighbours
Run maddingly affrighted through the Villages;
Syennas Duke is up, burnes all before him,
And with his ſword, makes thouſand mothers childleſſe,

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: What's this to our Morriſdancers?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: This may ſerve my turne.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Theres ne're a Duke in Chriſtendome but loves a May-game.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: At a Horſe you were alwaies ceaz'd, put your Son on him,
And arme him well i'th States name, I command ye;
And they that dare go voluntary, ſhall receive reward.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I dare go no way, Sir, this is ſtrange, Maſter Captaine,
You cannot be content to ſpoile our ſport here,
Which I do not think your Worſhip's able to anſwer,
But you muſt ſet us together by the ears, with I know not who to?
We are for the bodily part o'th dance.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Arme him ſuddenly,
This is no time to foole, I ſhall returne ye elſe,
A rebell to the Generall, State, and Ducheſſe,
And how you'l anſwer then—

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: I have no more Sons, Sir,
This is my onely boy; I beſeech ye Maſter Captain.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I am a rank coward too, to ſay the truth, Sir,
I never had good luck at buffets neither.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: Here's vorty ſhillings, ſpare the childe.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: I cannot.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Are ye a man? will ye caſt away a May-Lord?
Shall all the wenches in the Country curſe ye?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: An't pleaſe you Captaine, ile ſupply his perſon,
'Tis pitty their old cuſtome ſhould be frighted,
Let me have Horſe, and good Armes, ile ſerve willingly,
And if I ſhrink a foot of ground, Hell take me.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: A promiſing aſpect, face full of courage,
Ile take this man, and thank ye too.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: Ther's for thee,
'Tis in a clout, but good old gold.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I thank ye Sir.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: Goe ſaddle my fore-horſe, put his feather on too,
Hee'l praunce it bravely, friend, he feares no Colours,
And take the Armour down, and ſee him dizin'd,

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Farewell, & if thou carrieſt thy ſelf well in this matter,
I ſay no more, but this, there muſt be more May-Lords,
And I know who are ſit.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Dance you, Ile fight, Sir,

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Away, away.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Farewell, I am for the Captaine. Exit.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: Now to this matter againe, my honeſt fellowes,
For if this go not forward, I foreſee friends,
This war will fright our neighbours out o'th villages;
Cheere up your hearts, we ſhall heare better news, boyes.

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: Surely, I will daunce no more, 'tis moſt ridiculous,
I finde my wives inſtructions now meere verities,
My learned wives, ſhe often hath pronounc'd to me
My ſafety Bomby, defie theſe ſports, thou art damn'd elſe,
This Beaſt of Babylon, I will never back againe,
His pace is ſure prophane, and his lewd wihies
The Sons of Hymyn, and Gymyn, in the wilderneſſe.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: Fie neighbour Bomby, in your fits againe,
Your zeale ſwets, this is not carefull, neighbour,
The Hobby-Horſe, is a ſeemely Hobby-Horſe.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: And as pretty a Beaſt on's inches, though I ſay it.

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: The Beaſt is an unſeemely, and a lew'd Beaſt,
And got at Rome by the Popes Coach-Horſes,
His mother was the Mare of ignorance.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Cobler, thou lyeſt, and thou wert a thouſand Coblers,
His mother was an honeſt Mare, & a Mare of good credit,
I know the Mare, and if need be, can bring witneſſe;
And in the way of honeſty I tell thee,
Scorn'd any Coach-Horſe the Pope had, thou art fooliſh,
And thy blind zeale makes thee abuſe the Beaſt.

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: I do defie thee, and thy foot-cloth too,
And tell thee to thy face, this prophaine riding
I feele it in my conſcience, and I dare ſpeake it,
This unedified ambling, hath brought a ſcourge upon us,
This Hobby-horſe ſincerity we liv'd in
War, and the ſword of ſlaughter: I renounce it,
And put the Beaſt off; thus, the Beaſt poluted,
And now no more ſhall hope on high Bomby,
Follow the painted Pipes of worldly pleaſures,
And with the wicked daunce the Devills meaſures;
Away thou pamper'd jade of vanity,
Stand at the Livery of lewd delights now,
And eat the provender of prickear'd folly,
My daunce ſhall be to the pipe of perſecution.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: Will you daunce no more Neighbour?

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: Surely no,
Carry the Beaſt to his Crib: I have renounc'd him,
And all his workes.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Shall the Hobby-horſe be forgot then?
The hopefull Hobby-horſe? ſhall he lye founder'd?
If thou do'ſt this, thou art but a caſt-away Cobler:
My anger's up, think wiſely, and think quickly,
And look upon the quondam beaſt of pleaſure,
If thou doſt this (mark me, thou ſerious Sowter)
Thou Bench-whiſtler of the old tribe of toe-peeces,
If thou do'ſt this there ſhall be no more Shooe-mending,
Every man ſhall have a ſpeciall care of his owne ſoule:
And in his pocket carry his two Confeſſors,
His Yugell, and his Nawle: if thou do'ſt this—

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: He will dance againe for certaine.

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: I cry out on't,
'Twas the fore-running ſin brought in thoſe Tilt-ſtaves,
They brandiſh 'gainſt the Church, the Devill calls May-poles,
Take up your Horſe againe, and girth him to ye,
And girth him handſomely good neighbour Bomby.

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: I ſpit at him.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Spit in the Horſe face, Cobler?
Thou out of tune-Pſalm-ſinging Slave; ſpit in his viſnomy?

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: I ſpit againe, and thus I riſe againſt him:
Againſt this Beaſt: that ſignifi'd deſtruction,
Fore-ſhew'd ith' falls of Monarchies.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Ith' face of him?
Spit ſuch another ſpit, by this hand Cobler
Ile make ye ſet a new peece o' your noſe there,
'Tak't up I ſay, and dance without more bidding,
And dance as you were wont: you have been excellent
And art ſtill, but for this new nicity,
And your wives learned Lectures: take up the Hobby-horſe
Come, 'tis a thing thou haſt lov'd with all thy heart Bomby
And would'ſt do ſtill but for the round-breecht Brothers:
You were not thus in the morning, tak't up I ſay,
Do not delay but do it: you know I am officer,
And I know 'tis unfit all theſe good fellowes
Should wait the cooling of your zealous porridge;
Chuſe whether you will dance, or have me execute:
Ile clap your neek ith' Stocks, and there ile make ye
Dance a whole day, and dance with theſe at night too,
You mend old Shooes well, mend your old manners better,
And ſuddenly ſee you leave off this ſincereneſſe.
This new hot batch borrowed from ſome brown Baker,
Some learned Brother, or ile ſo bait ye for't,
Take it quickly up.

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: I take my perſecution,
And thus I am forced a by-word to my Brethren.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Strike up, ſtrike up: ſtrike merrily.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: To it roundly,
Now to the harveſt feaſt: then ſport againe Boyes. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: What ſhall I do? live thus unknown, and baſe ſtill?
Or thruſt my ſelf into the head oth' Battell?
And there, like that I am, a Gentleman,
And one that never fear'd the face of danger,
(So in her angry eyes ſhe carried honour)
Fight nobly, and (to end my cares) dye nobly?
SIlvio go on, and raiſe thy noble minde
To noble ends; fling courſe baſe thoughts behinde:
Silvio, thou Sonne of everliving fame,
Now aime at vertue, and a Noble Name.
Silvio conſider, Honour is not wonne,
Nor vertue reach't, till ſome brave thing be done:
Thy Country calls thee now; ſhe burnes, and bleeds,
Now raiſe thy ſelf, young man, to noble deeds.
Into the Battell Silvio, there ſeeke forth
Danger, and blood, by them ſtands ſacred worth.
What heavenly voice is this that followes me?
This is the ſecond time 't has waited on me,
Since I was arm'd, and ready for the Battell;
It names me often, ſteeles my heart with courage,
And in a thouſand ſweet noates comforts me;
What Beldom's this? how old ſhe is, and ugly,
Why do's ſhe follow me?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Be not diſmaid, Son,
I wait upon thee, for thy good, and honour,
'Twas I that now ſung to thee, ſtir'd thy minde up,
And raiſ'd thy ſpirits to the pitch of nobleneſſe.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Though ſhe be old, and of a crooked carkaſſe,
Her voice is like the harmony of Angels.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Thou art my darling, all my love dwells on thee
The Son of vertue, therefore I attend thee;
Enquire not what I am, I come to ſerve thee,
For if thou beeſt inquiſitive, thou haſt loſt me:
A thouſand long miles hence my dwelling is,
Deep in a Cave, where but mine owne, no foot treads,
There by mine Art, I found what danger (Silvio)
And deep diſtreſſe of heart, thou wert growne into,
A thouſand leagues I have cut through empty aire,
Far ſwifter then the ſayling tack that gallops
Upon the wings of angry winds, to ſeeke thee.
Sometimes 'ore a ſwelling tide, on a Dolphins back I ride,
Sometimes paſſe the earth below, and through the unmoved Center go;
Sometimes in a flame of fire, like a Meteor I aſpire,
Sometimes in mine own ſhape, thus, when I helpe the vertuous,
Men of honourable minds, command my Art in all his kinds;
Purſue the noble thought of war, from thy Guard ile not be far,
Get thee worſhip on thy foe, laſting fame is gotten ſo.
Single Syennas Duke alone, heare thy friends, thy Country grone,
And with thy manly arme ſtrike ſure, then thou haſt wrought thine owne free cure.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Some Sybell ſure, ſome ſoule heaven loves, and favours.
And lends her their free powers, to worke their wonders?
How ſhe incites my courage?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I knew thee many daies a go,
Foreſaw thy love to Belvidere, the Ducheſſe Daughter, and her Heire;
Knew ſhe lov'd thee, and know what paſt, when you were found i'th Caſtle faſt
In one anothers armes; foreſaw the taking of ye, and the Law;
And ſo thy innocence I loved, the deepeſt of my skill I proved;
Be rul'd by me, for to this houre I have dwelt about thee with my powre.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I will, and in the courſe of all obſerve thee,
For thou art ſure an Angell good ſent to me.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Get thee gone then to the fight, longer ſtay but robs thy right;
When thou grow'ſt weary ile be neere, then think on beauteous Belvidere,
For every precious thought of her, ile lend thine honour a new ſpurre;
When all is done, meet here at night; Go and be happy in the fight. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I certainly believe I ſhall do nobly,
And that Ile bravely reach at too, or die. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Is ſhe ſo loving ſtill?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: She is mad with love,
As mad as ever unworm'd dogge was, Signior,
And do's ſo weep, and curſe, for your prevention,
Your croſſes in your love; it frets me too,
I am falne away to nothing, to a ſpindle,
Growne a meere man of mat, no ſoule within me,
Pox o' my Maſter, Sir, will that content ye?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: This rogue but cozens me, and ſhe neglects me,
Upon my life there are ſome other gamſters,
Neerer the winde then I, and that prevents me,
Is there no other holds acquaintance with her?
Prethee be true, be honeſt, do not mock me,
Thou knoweſt her heart, no former intereſt
She has vow'd a favour to? and cannot handſomly
Go off, but by regaining ſuch a friendſhip?
There are a thouſand handſom men, young, wealthy,
That will not ſtick at any rate, nor danger,
To gaine ſo ſweet a prize; nor can I blame her,
If where ſhe finds a comfort ſhe deale cunningly,
I am a ſtranger yet.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Ye are all ſhe looks for,
And if there be any other, ſhe neglects all,
And all for you: I would you ſaw how grievouſly
And with what hourely lamentations.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I know thou flatter'ſt me; tell me but truth,
Looke here, look well, the beſt meat in the Dukedom,
The rareſt, and the choiceſt of all diets,
This will I give thee, but to ſatisfie me;
That is, not to diſſemble; this rare Lobſter,
This Pheaſant of the ſea, this diſh for Princes,
And all this thou ſhalt enjoy, eat all thy ſelfe,
Have good Greeke wine, or any thing belongs to it,
A wench if it deſire one.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: All this, Signior?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: All, and a greater far then this.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A greater?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: If thou deſerve by telling truth.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A wench too?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Or any thing, but if you play the knave now,
The Cozening knave beſides the loſſe of this,
In which thou haſt parted with a paradiſe,
I neare will give thee meat more, not a morſell,
No ſmell of meat by my meanes ſhall come neere thee,
Nor name of any thing that's nouriſhing,
But to thy old part Tantalus againe,
Thou ſhalt returne, and there ſnap at a ſhadow.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Upon this point, had I intended Treaſon,
Or any thing might call my life in queſtion,
Follow'd with all the tortures time could think on,
Give me but time to eat this lovely Lobſter,
This Alderman o'th Sea, and give me wine to him,
I would reveale all, and if that all were too little,
More then I knew; Bartello holds in with her,
The Captain of the Cittadell, but you need not fear him,
His tongue's the ſtiffeſt weapon that he carries.
He is old, and out of uſe; there are ſome other,
Men young enough, handſome, and bold enough,
Could they come to make their game once; but they want Sir,
They want the unde quare, they are laid by then,
You onely are the man ſhall knock the nayle in—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: How now Penurio?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Your Worſhip's fairely met, Sir.
You ſhall heare further from me, ſteale aſide Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Remember your Maſter for thoſe Chaines.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: They are ready, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: What young thing's this? by his habit hee's a Merchant;
I feare he trades my way too, you dryed dog-fiſh,
What bait was that?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Who Sir, the thing went hence now?
A notable young whelp.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: To what end Sirrah?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Came to buy Chaines and Rings, is to be married,
An Aſſe, a Coxcomb, has nothing in his houſe, Sir;
I warrant you think he came to ſee my Miſtris?

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: I doubt it ſhrewdly.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Away, away, 'tis fooliſh;
He has not the face to look upon a Gentlewoman,
A poore skym'd thing, his Mothers maids are faine, Sir,
To teach him how to kiſſe, and againſt he is married,
To ſhew him on which ſide the ſtirrop ſtands.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: That's a fine youth.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Thou wouldſt hang thy ſelf, that thou hadſt half his power,
Thou empty Potgun.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Am I come fit Penurio?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: As fit as a fiddle,
My Matter's now abroad about his buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: When thou cam'ſt to me home to day, I half ſuſpected
My wife was jealous, that ſhe whiſpered to thee.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: You deſerve well the whil'ſt, ther's no ſuch matter,
She talk'd about ſome toyes my Maſter muſt bring to her,
You muſt not know of.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Ile take noat, Penurio.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: No, Nor you ſhall not, till you have it ſoundly.
This is the braveſt Capitano Pompo,
But I ſhall pump ye anon Sir.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: O my Bartello?

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Ye pretty Rogue, you little Rogue, you ſweet Rogue,
Away Penurio, go and walk i'th Horſe-Fayre.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You do not love me?

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Thou lyeſt thou little Raſcall;
There Sirrah, to your Centry.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: How the Colt itches?
Ile help ye to a Curry-comb ſhall claw ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: And how much doſt thou love me?

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Let's go in quickly,
Ile tell thee preſently, ile meaſure it to thee.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: No buſſes firſt? ſit 'o my knee, my brave boy,
My valiant boy; do not look ſo fiercely on me,
Thou wilt fright me with thy face; come buſſe againe Chick,
Smile in my face you mad thing.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: I am mad indeed wench,
Precious I am all o' fire.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Ile warrant thee better.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Ile warme thee too, or ile blow out my bellowes;
Ha, ye ſweet rogue, you loving rogue, a Boy now,
A Souldier I will get ſhall prove a fellow.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Miſtris, looke to your ſelfe, my Maſter's comming.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: The Devill come, and go with him.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The Devill's come indeed, he brings your wife, Sir.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: We are undone, undone then.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: My wife with him?
Why this is a diſmall day.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: They are hard by too, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I muſt not, dare not ſee her.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Nor my Husband,
For twenty thouſand pound.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: That I were a Cat now,
Or any thing could run into a Bench-hole,
Saint Anthonies Fire upon the Rogue has brought her;
Where ſhall I be? juſt in the nick oth' matter?
When I had her at my mercy: think for heaven ſake,
My wife, all the wilde furies hell has.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Up the Chimney.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: They'l ſmoke me out there preſently.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: There, there, it muſt be there,
We are all undone elſe: it muſt be up the Chimney.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Give me a Ladder.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You muſt uſe your Art Sir,
Alas, we have no Ladders.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Pox o' thy husband,
Do's he never mend his houſe?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: No, nor himſelfe neither:
Up nimbly Sir, up nimbly.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Thou know'ſt I am fat,
Thou mercileſſe leane Rogue.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Will ye be kill'd?
For if he take ye—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Lend me thy ſhoulder.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Soft Sir,
You'l tread my ſhoulder-bones into my ſides elſe,
Have ye faſt hold oth' barrs?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: A vengeance bar 'em.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Patience good Captain, patience: quickly, quickly.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Do you think I am made of ſmoke?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Now he talkes of ſmoke,
What if my Maſter ſhould call for fire?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Will ye Martyr me?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: He muſt needs have it.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Will ye make me Bacon?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: We'l do the beſt we can, are all things ready?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: All, all, I have 'em all.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Go, let 'em in then,
Not a word now on your life.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I hang like a Meteor.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: You are welcome Lady.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: You are too too curteous,
But I ſhall make amends, faire Iſabella.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Welcome my worthy friend, moſt kindely welcome.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: I heare on't, and ile fit him for his foolery.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Some ſweet meats wife: ſome ſweet meats preſently.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: O my ſowre ſauce.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Away quick Iſabella. Exit Iſab.
Did you heare him?

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Yes, yes, perfectly, proceed Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Speake loud enough: Dare ye at length but pitty me?

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: 'Faith Sir, you have us'd ſo many reaſons to me,
And thoſe ſo powerfully—

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Keep this kiſſe for me.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And do I ſtand and heare this?

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: This for me Sir,
This is ſome comfort now: Alas my Husband—
But why Do I think of ſo poore a fellow,
So wretched, ſo deboſh'd?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: That's I, I am bound to heare it.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: I dare not lye with him, he is ſo ranke a Whore-maſter.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And that's a dangerous point.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Upon my conſcience Sir,
He would ſtick a thouſand baſe diſeaſes on me.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And now muſt I ſay nothing.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I am ſound Lady.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: That's it that makes me love ye.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Let's kiſſe againe then.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Do, do.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Do, the Devill.
And the grand Pox do with ye.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Do ye heare him? well—
Now, what's the newes with you?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The ſound of War Sir,
Comes ſtill along: The Duke will charge the City,
We have loſt they ſay.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: What ſhall become of me then,
And my poore wealth?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Even hang'd, I hope.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Remove your Jewells preſently,
And what you have of wealth into the Cittadell,
I here all's ſecure.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I humbly thank ye Lady:
Penurio, get me ſome can climbe the Chimney,
For there my Jewells are, my beſt, my richeſt,
I hid 'em, fearing ſuch a blow.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Moſt happily:
I have two Boyes, that uſe to ſweep fould Chimnies,
Truly I brought 'em Sir, to mock your worſhip,
For the great Fires ye keep, and the full diet.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I forgive thee knave, where are they?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Here Sir, here:
Mounſieur Black will your ſmall worſhip mount?

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: Madam è be com to creep up into your Chimney, and make you. Boy ſings.
Cleane, as any Lady in de world: Ma litla, litla frera, and è,
Chanta, frere, chanta.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Come Mounſieur, mounte, mountè, mount Mounſieur Muſterd-pot. Boy ſings.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: Mounſieur è have dis for votra barba, ple ta von Mounſieur.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.p: Mòunte Mounſieur, mountè dere be ſome fine tings.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: Me will creep like de Ferret Mounſieur.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Dere in the Chimney. The Boy above ſinging.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: He be de ſheilde due ſhauſon, Madam.

div.stage: Boy goes in behinde the Arras.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: There's a Birds-neaſt, I wound have ye climbe it Mounſieur,
Up my fine ſinging Mounſieur: that's a fine Mounſieur.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Watch him, he do not ſteale.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I warrant ye Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Theſe Boyes are knaviſh. Boy within, Madam here be de Rat, de Rat Madam.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Ile looke to him tithly

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Lord, what comes here, Boy ſings upon Bartellas ſhoulder.
A walking apparition?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Saint Chriſtopher.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Mercy o' me, what is it?
How like my Husband it lookes?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Get ye downe Devill,
Ile breake your neck elſe: was ever man thus chimnied?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Go pay the Boyes well: ſee them ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Come Mounſieur Devills, come my Black-berries
Ile butter ye o' both ſides.

div.stage: Boye Exit ſaying, Adieu Madam, adieu Madam.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Nay, ev'n look Sir, are you cooled now, Captaine?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I am Cuckolled, and fool'd to boot too:
Fool'd fearefully, fool'd ſhamefully.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: You are welcome Sir,
I am glad I have any thing within theſe doores Sir
To make ye merry; you love my wife, I thank ye,
You have ſhew'd your love.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Wife, am I this? this odde matter,
This monſtrous thing?

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: You ought, but yet you are not:
I have been bold with you Sir, but yet not baſely,
As I have faith I have not.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Sir, beleeve it;
'Twas all meant but to make you feele your treſpaſſe;
We new your howre, and all this faſhion'd for it.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Were you oth' plot too?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Yes by my troth, ſweet Captaine.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You will forgive me wife?

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: You will deſerve it?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Put that toth' venture.

sp.speaker: Rho:
sp.l: Thus am I friends againe then,
And as you ne're had gone aſtray, thus kiſſe ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And ile kiſſe you, and you too ask forgiveneſſe;
Kiſſe my wife Lopez, 'tis but in jeſt remember;
And now all friends together to my Caſtle,
Where we'l all dine, and there diſcourſe theſe ſtories,
And let him be Chimney-ſwept in's luſt that glories. Exe.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Haile reverent Dame, heaven wait upon thy ſtudies.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You are well met Son: what is the Battell ended?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Mother, 'tis done.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: How has thy honour proſper'd?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: The Dutcheſſe has the day, Syenna's Priſoner:
Arm'd with thy powrefull Art, this arme diſmounted him,
Receiv'd him then on foot, and in faire valour
Forc'd him mine owne, this Jewell I tooke from him,
It hung upon his cask, the Victors triumph:
And to the Dutcheſſe now a Priſoner
I have renderd him: Come off againe unknown, Mother.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Tis well done, let me ſee he jewell Son;
'Tis a rich one, curious ſet, fit a Princeſſe Burgonet:
This rich token late was ſent, by the Dutcheſſe with intent
The Marriage next day to begin: Do'ſt thou know what's hid within?
Wipe thine eyes, and then come neere, ſee the beautious Belvidere:
Now behold it.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: O my Saint.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: We are it nobly, do not faint.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: How bleſt am I in this rich ſpoile, this picture,
For ever will I keep it here, here Mother,
For ever honour it: how oft, how chaſtly
Have I embrac'd the life of this, and kiſt it?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: The day drawes on that thou muſt home returne,
And make thy anſwer to the Dutcheſſe queſt on
I know it troubles thee, for if thou faile in't—

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: O, I muſt dye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Feare not, feare not, ile be nigh,
Caſt thy trouble on my back, art nor cunning ſhal not lack
To preſerve thee, ſtill to keepe, what thy envious foemen ſeeke;
Go boldly home, and let thy minde, no diſtruſtfull croſſes finde:
All ſhall happen for the beſt; ſouls walk through ſorrowes that are bleſt.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Then I go confident.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: But firſt my Son, a thankfull ſervice muſt be done,
The good old woman for her paine, when every thing ſtands faire againe,
Muſt ask a poore Boon, and that granting, there's nothing to thy journey wanting.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Except the triall of my ſoul to miſchief,
And as I am a Knight, and love mine honour,
I grant it whatſoever.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Thy pure ſoule
Shall never ſinke for me, nor howle.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Then any thing.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: When I ſhall aske remember.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: If I forget, heavens goodneſſe forget me.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: On thy journey then a while, to the next croſſe way and ſtile
Ile conduct thee, keepe thee true, to thy Miſtris and thy vow,
And let all their envies fall, ile be with thee and quench all.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: LAdy, the ſtubborn war's more milde then you are,
That allowes Ranſome, and the Priſoner taken—

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: We muſt not be too haſty: Remember Sir,
The wrong and violence you have offer'd us,
Burnt up our Frontire Townes, made prey before ye
Both of our Beaſts, and Corne; ſlaine our deare Subjects,
Open'd the fountaine eyes of thouſand widowes,
That daily fling their curſes on your fury;
What ordinary ſatisfaction can ſalve this?
What haſty thought-on Ranſome give a remedy?
You muſt excuſe us yet, we'l take more counſell:
In the meane time, not as a Priſoner,
But as a noble Prince we entertaine ye.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: I am at your mercy Lady, 'tis my fortune,
My ſtubborne fate; the day is yours, you have me,
The valour of one ſingle man has croſs'd me,
Croſt me and all my hope; for when the Battells
Were at the hotteſt game of all their furies,
And conqueſt ready then to crowne me Victor,
One ſingle man broke in, one ſword, one vertue,
And by his great example thouſands followed,
O how I ſhame to think on't, how it ſhakes me!
Nor could our ſtrongeſt head then ſtop his fury,
But like a tempeſt 'bore the field before him,
Till he arriv'd at me, with me he buckell'd,
A while I held him play; at length his violence
Beat me from my Saddle, then on foot purſu'd me,
There triumph'd once againe, then tooke me Priſoner:
When I was gone a feare poſſeſt my people.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: One ſingle arme, in a juſt dauſe, heaven proſpers.
Is not this ſtranger Knight as yet diſcover'd,
That we may give his vertue a doe honour?

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: Not yet that we hear Madam, but to that purpoſe,
Two dayes ago we publiſh'd Proclamations

div.stage: Enter Soto with a Trumpet, and Silvio.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: O dainty Ducheſſe, here I bring that Knight
Before thy fragrant face, that warlike wight,
He that Syenna's Duke, and all his Louts
Beat (as the Proverb ſeemly ſayes) to clouts:
He that unhorſs'd the man of fame to boot,
And bootleſſe taught his Grace to walk afoot:
He that your writings (pack'd to every pillar)
Promis'd promotion to, and ſtore of filler,
That very man I ſet before thy Grace,
And once againe pronounce this man it was.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: A pretty fooliſh Squire, what muſt the Knight be?

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Some Jugler, or ſome Mad-man.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I was not ſo,
When thy faint Troopes in flockes I beat before me,
When through the thickeſt of thy warlike horſe
I ſhot my ſelfe, even to thy Standard Duke,
And there found thee, there fingled thee, there ſhew'd thee
The temper of my Sword. 'Tis true, thou ſtood'ſt me,
And like a noble Souldier bid'ſt me welcome;
And this ile ſay, More honour in that arme
I found and tryed, then all thy Army carried:
What followes thy Imprisonment can tell thee.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: His faire relation carries truth and vertue,
And by thoſe Armes I ſee (for ſuch were his,
So old, ſo ruſty) this may be he that forc'd me.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Do you know this Jewell, from your Cask I rent it,
Even as I clos'd, and forced ye from your ſaddle;
Do you now remember me?

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: This is the valour
Madam, for certaine he, it muſt be he,
That day I wore this Jewell, you remember it.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Yes, very well; not long before I ſent it.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: That day I loſt this Jewell, in fight I loſt it,
I felt his ſtroakes, and felt him take it from me,
I wore it in my Cask; take it againe Sir,
You won it nobly, 'tis the prize of honour.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: My Father, and my ſelfe are made for ever.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Kneele down brave Sir, thus my Knight firſt I raiſe ye,
Gird on a Sword; next Generall of my Army,
Give him a Staffe; laſt, one in Counſell neare me.
Now, make us happy with your ſight: how? Silvio?
Have I on thee beſtow'd this love, this honour?
The Treaſons thou haſt wrought ſet off with favours?
Unarme him preſently: O thou foule Traitor,
Traitor to me, mine honour, and my Country,
Thou kindler of theſe Warres.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Miſtake not Madam.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Away with him to priſon,
See him ſafe kept, the Law ſhall ſhortly Sirra,
Finde fitter titles for ye, then I gave ye.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: This is the youth that kild me, ile be quit with him,
What a blinde rogue was I, I could never know him?
And't pleaſe your Grace, I claime the benefit
Of the Proclamation that proclam'd him Traitor,
I brought him in.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt have thy reward for't.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Let him be hang'd, or drown'd then.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Away with him.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Madam, I crave your promiſe firſt; you are tyed to it,
You have paſt your Princely word.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Prove it, and take it.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: This is the day appointed,
Appointed by your Grace for my appearance,
To anſwer to the Queſtion.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: I remember it.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I claime it then,

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: If you performe it not,
The penalty you claime too.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I not repent it;
If I abſolve the words?

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Your life is free then,
You have drawne a ſpeedy courſe above my wiſhes,
To my rezenge, be ſure ye hit it right,
Or ile be ſure you ſhall not ſcape the danger.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: My reſt is up now Madam.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Then play it cunningly.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Now, where's the Hag? where now are all her promiſes,
She would be with me, ſtrengthen me, informe me?
My death will now be double death, ridiculous:
She was wont ſtill to be neare, to feele my miſeries,
And with her Art, I ſee her no where now;
What have I undertaken? now ſhe failes me,
No comfort now I finde, how my ſoule ſtaggers?
Till this houre never fear, nor doubt poſſeſt me,
She cannot come, ſhe will not come, ſhe has fool'd me;
Sure, ſhe is the Devill, has drawne me on to ruine,
And now to death bequeaths me in my danger.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: He ſtands diſtracted, and his colour changes.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: I have given him that will make his blood forſake him;
Shortly his life.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: His hands and contemplation
Have motion ſtill, the reſt is earth already.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Come, will ye ſpeak or pray? your time growes out Sir;
How every where he looks? he's at laſt caſt.

div.stage: Enter Belvidere, and ſecretly gives him a paper, and Exit.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: His colour comes againe freſh.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: 'Tis a flaſh, Sir,
Before the flame burnes out; can ye yet anſwer?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Yes Madam, now I can.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: I feare you'l faile in't.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: And do not think my ſilence a preſage,
Or Omen to my end, you ſhall not finde it;
I am bred a Souldier, not an Orator,
Madam, peruſe this ſcrowle, let that ſpeake for me,
And as you are Royall, wrong not the conſtruction.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: By Heaven you ſhall have faire play.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I ſhall looke for't.
Tell me what it that onely thing,
For which all women long;
Yet having what they moſt deſire,
To have it do's them wrong.
Tis not to be chaſte, nor faire,
Such gifts malice may impaire;
Richly trim'd, to walke or ride,
Or to wanton uneſpi'd;
To preſerve an honeſt name,
And ſo to give it up to fame;
Theſe are toyes. In good or ill
They deſire, to have their will;
Yet when they have it, they abuſe it,
For they know not how to uſe it.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: You have anſwer'd right, and gain'd your life,
I give it.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: O happy Hag! But my moſt gracious Madam,
Your promiſe tide a nobler favour to me.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: 'Tis true, my daughter too.

sp.speaker: Sil
sp.l: I hope you will keep it.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: 'Tis not in my powre now, ſhe is long ſince wanderd,
Stolne from the Court, and me; and what I have not
I cannot give: no man can tell me of her,
Nor no ſearch finde her out: and if not Silvio,
Which ſtrongly I beleeve—

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Mock me not Lady,
For as I am a ſervant to her vertue,
Since my firſt howre of exile, I ne're ſaw her

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: That ſhe is gone 'tis too too true, and lamentable,
Our laſt hope was in you.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: What do I heare then,
And wherefore have I life beſtow'd and honour?
To what end do I walk? for men to wonder at,
And fight, and foole? pray ye take your honours from me,
(My ſorrowes are not fit companions for 'em)
And when ye pleaſe my life: Art thou gone Miſtris,
And wander'ſt heaven knowes where? this vow I make thee,
That till I finde thee out, and ſee thoſe faire eyes,
Thoſe eyes that ſhed their lights, and life into me,
Never to know a friend, to ſeeke a kindred,
To reſt where pleaſure dwells, and painted glory,
But through the world, the wide world thus to wander,
The wretched world alone, no comfort with me,
But the meere meditations of thy goodneſſe:
Honour and greatneſſe, thus adieu.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Stay Silvio,
And Lady ſit againe, I come for Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: What would ſhe now?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: To claime thy promiſe Silvio,
The Boone thou ſwor'ſt to give me.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: What may this be,
A woman, or a Devill?

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: 'Tis a Witch ſure,
And by her meanes he came to untwiſt this Riddle,

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: That I am bound to her for my liffe, mine honour,
And many other thouſand waies for comfort
I here confeſſe: Confeſſe a promiſe too,
That what ſhe would aske me to requite theſe favours,
Within the endeavour of my life to grant,
I would; and here I ſtand my words full maſter.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I wiſh no more: great Lady, witneſſe with me,
The Boone I crave for all my ſervice to thee,
Is now to be thy wife, to grant me marriage.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: How? for to marry thee? aske againe woman,
Thou wilfull woman, aske againe.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No more Sir.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Aske land, and life.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I aske thee for a Husband.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Marry her, and beat her into Gun-powder,
She would make rare Crackers.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Aske a better fortune,
Thou art too old to marry: I a Souldier,
And alwaies married to my ſword.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Thy word Foole,
Breake that, and ile breake all thy fortunes yet.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: He ſhall not,
I am witneſſe to his faith: and ile compell it.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: 'Tis fit ye hold your word, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: O moſt wretched.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: This was a fortune now beyond my wiſhes,
For now my Daughter's free, if e're I finde her.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: But not from me.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: You are ſharer in this happineſſe,
My ſelfe will wait upon this marriage,
And do the old woman all the honour poſſible.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Ile lead the Knight, and what there wants in dalliance,
Wee'l take it out in drinke.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: O wretched Silvio. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Haſt thou ſent for him?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Yes,

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A young man, ſaiſt thou?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Yes, very young, and very amarous.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And handſom?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: As the Town affords.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And dar'ſt thou
Be ſo farre good, and Miſtris of thine honour,
To ſleight theſe?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: For my husbands ſake to curſe 'em,
And ſince you have made me Miſtris of my fortune,
Never to point at any ioy, but husband,
I could have cozen'd ye, but ſo much I love ye,
And now ſo much I weigh the eſtimation
Of an unſpotted wife—

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I dare believe thee,
And never more ſhall doubt torment my ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: How now Penurio?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The thing is comming, Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Ile take my ſtanding.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Do, and ile take mine. Exit Lopes.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Where didſt thou leave him?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I left him in a Cellar,
Where he has paid me titely, paid me home Miſtris,
We had an hundred & fifty healths to you, ſweet Miſtris,
And three ſcore and ten damnations to my Maſter;
Miſtris, ſhall I ſpeak a fooliſh word to ye?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: What's that Penurio?
The fellow's drunke.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I would faine know your body.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: How's that? how's that prethee?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I would know it carnally,
I would conglutinate.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: The reaſon ſirrah?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Lobſter, ſweet Miſtris, Lobſter.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Thy Maſter heares.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Lobſter, ſweet Maſter, Lobſter.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Thou art the moſt precious rogue.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Moſt pretious Lobſter.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Do you ſee who's here? go ſleep ye drunken raſcall.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.p: Remember you refuſe me arm'd in Lobſter. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: O my loſt Rugio, welcome, welcome, welcome,
A thouſand welcomes here Ile ſeale.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Pray ye ſtay, Lady,
Do you love me ever at this rate? or is the fit now,
By reaſon of ſome wrong done by your husband,
More fervent on ye?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Can I chuſe but love thee?
Thou art my Martyr, thou haſt ſuffered for me,
My ſweet, ſweet Rugio.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Do you do this ſeriouſly?
'Tis true, I would be entertained thus.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Theſe are nothing,
No kiſſes, no embraces, no endeerements,
To thoſe—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Do what you will.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Thoſe that ſhall follow,
Thoſe I will crowne our love withall; why ſigh ye?
Why look ye ſad my deere one?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay faith nothing,
But me thinks ſo ſweet a beauty, as yours ſhowes to me,
And ſuch an innocence as you may make it,
Should hold a longer Siege.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Ha, you ſpeake truth, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I would not have it ſo.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: And now methinkes,
Now I conſider truly what becomes me,
I have been cozen'd, fearefully abus'd,
My reaſon blinded.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay, I did but jeſt with ye.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Ile take ye at your word, and thank ye for't Sir;
And now I ſee no ſweetneſſe in that perſon,
Nothing to ſtir me to abuſe a Husband,
To ruine my faire fame.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Good Iſabella.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: No hanſome man, no any thing to doat on,
No face, no tongue to catch me, poore at all points,
And I an aſſe.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Why do ye wrong me Lady?
If I were thus, and had no youth upon me,
My ſervice of ſo meane a way to win ye,
(Which you your ſelfe are conſcious muſt deſerve ye,
If you had thrice the beauty you poſſeſſe, muſt reacht ye)
If in my tongue your fame lay wrack't, and ruin'd
With every cup I drink: if in opinion
I were a loſt, defam'd man: but this is common
Where we love moſt, where moſt we ſtake our fortunes,
There leaſt and baſeſt we are rewarded: fare ye well,
Know now I hate you too as much, contemne ye,
And weigh my credit at as high a value.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: May be I did but jeſt.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Ye are a woman,
And now I ſee your wants, and mine owne follies,
And task my ſelfe with indiſcretion,
For doating on a face ſo poore.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Say ye ſo Sir,
(I muſt not loſe my end) I did but jeſt with you,
Only fool'd thus to try your faith: my Rugio,
Do you think I could forget?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay, 'tis no matter.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Is't poſſible I ſhould forſake a conſtancy,
So ſtrong, ſo good, ſo ſweet?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: A ſubtle woman.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You ſhall forgive me, 'twas a trick to try ye,
And were I ſure ye lov'd me—

sp.speaker: Cla.
