How now? hah? what prodigious bravery's this?
A moſt prepoſterous Gallant, the Doublet ſits
As if it mockt the breeches.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Save you, Sir,

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Has put his tongue in the fine ſuit of words too.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: How doe's the party?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Takes me for a Scrivener. Which of the parties?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Hum, ſimplicity betide thee—
I would faine heare of the party; I would be loath to go
Further with her; honour is not a thing to be dallied withall,
No more is reputation, no nor fame, I take it, I muſt not
Have her wrong'd when I'me abroad, my party is not
To be compell'd with any party in an oblique way;
'Tis very dangerous to deale with women;
May prove a Lady too, but ſhall be nameleſſe,
Ile bite my tongue out, e're it prove a Traitor.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Upon my life I know her.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Not by me,
Know what you can, talke a whole day with me,
Y'are ne're the wiſer, ſhe comes not from theſe lips.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: The old Knights Neece.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: 'Slid he has got her, pox of his heart that told him,
Can nothing be kept ſecret? let me entreat you
To uſe her name as little as you can, though.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: 'Twill be ſmall pleaſure, Sir, to uſe her name.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I had intelligence in my ſolemne walks,
'Twixt Paddington and Pancridge, of a Scarfe,
Sent for a token, and a Jewell follow'd,
But I acknowledge not the receipt of any,
How e're 'tis carried, believe me Sir,
Upon my reputation I received none.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: What, neither Scarfe nor Jewell?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: 'Twould be ſeene
Some where about me, you may well think that,
I have an arme for a Scarfe, as others have,
And dare to hang a Jewell too, and that's more
Then ſome men have, my betters a great deale,
I muſt have reſtitution, where e're it lights.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And reaſon good.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: For all theſe tokens, Sir,
Paſſe i' my name.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: It cannot otherwiſe be.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Sent to a worthy friend.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I, that's to thee.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I'me wrong'd under that title.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I dare ſweare thou art,
'Tis nothing but Sir Gregories circumvention,
His envious ſpite, when thou'rt at Paddington,
He meets the gifts at Pancridge.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Ah falſe Knight?
Falſe both to honour, and the Law of Arms?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: What wilt thou ſay if I be reveng'd for thee?
Thou ſit as witneſſe?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I ſhould laugh in ſtate then.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Ile fobb him, here's my hand.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I ſhould be as glad as any man alive, to ſee him well fob'd, Sir; but now you talk of fobbing, I wonder the Lady ſends not forme according to promiſe? I ha' kept out a Towne theſe two daies, a purpoſe to be ſent for; I am almoſt ſtarv'd with walking.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Walking gets men a ſtomack.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: 'Tis moſt true, Sir, I may ſpeake it by experience, for I ha' got a ſtomack ſix times, and loſt it agen, as often as a traveller from Chelſy ſhall loſe the ſight of Pauls, and get it agen.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Go to her, man.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Not for a Million, enfringe my oath? there's a toy call'd a vowe, has paſt betweene us, a poore trifle, Sir; Pray do me the part and office of a Gentleman, if you chance to meet a Footman by the way, in orange tawny ribbands, running before an empty Coach, with a Buzzard i'th Poope on't, direct him and his horſes toward the new River by Iſlington, there they ſhall have me looking upon the Pipes, and whiſtling. Exit Clow.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: A very good note; this love makes us all Monkeyes,
But to my work: Scarfe firſt? and now a Diamond? theſe
Should be ſure ſignes of her affections truth;
Yet Ile go forward with my ſurer proofe. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Is't poſſible?
Nay here's his Letter too, there's a fine Jewell in't,
Therefore I brought it to you.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: You tedious Mongrill! Is't not enough
To grace thee, to receive this from thy hand,
A thing which makes me almoſt ſick to do,
But you muſt talke too?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I ha' done

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Fall back,
Yet backer, backer yet, you unmannerly puppy,
Do you not ſee I'me going about to reade it?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Nay theſe are golden daies, now I ſtay by't,
She was wont not to endure me in her ſight at all,
The world mends, I ſee that.

sp.speaker: N • ece.
sp.l: What an ambiguous Superſcription's here?
To the beſt of Neeces. Why that title may be mine,
And more then her's:
Sure I much wrong the neatneſſed of his art;
'Tis certaine ſent to me, and to requite
My cunning in the carriage of my Tokens,
Us'd the ſame Fop for his.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: She nodded now to me, 'twill come in time.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: What's here? an entire Rubye, cut into a heart.
And this the word, Iſtud Amoris opus?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Yes, yes, I have heard him ſay that love is the beſt ſtone-cutter.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Why thou ſawcy iſſue of ſome travelling Sow-gelder,
What makes love? thy mouth? is it a thing
That ever will concerne thee? I do wonder
How thou dar'ſt think ont? haſt thou ever hope
To come i' the ſame roome where lovers are;
And ſcape unbrain'd with one of their velvet ſlippers?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Love tricks breake out I ſee, and you talk of ſlippers once,
'Tis not farre off to bed time.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Is it poſſible thou canſt laugh yet?
I would ha' undertooke to ha' kill'd a ſpider
With leſſe venome far, then I have ſpit at thee.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: You muſt conceive,
A Knight's another manner a peece of fleſh.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Back, Owles face.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Do, do.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: 'Tis my Uncles voyce, that:
Why keep you ſo farre off, Sir Gregory?
Are you afraid, Sir, to come neare your Miſtris?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Is the proud heart come downe? I lookt for this ſtill.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: He comes not this way yet: Away, you dog-whelp;
Would you offer to come neare me, though I ſaid ſo?
Ile make you underſtand my minde in time;
Your running greedily like a hound to his breakfaſt,
That chops in head and all to beguile his fellowes;
I'me to be eaten, Sir, with Grace and leiſure,
Behaviour and diſcourſe, things that ne're trouble you;
After I have pelted you ſufficiently,
I tro you will learne more manners.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I'me wondring ſtill when we two ſhall come together?
Tueſday's at hand, but I'me as farre off, as I was at firſt,
I ſweare.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: Now Cuningame, Ile be reveng'd at large:
Lady, what was but all this while ſuſpition,
Is truth, full blowne now, my Neece weares your Scarfe.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Hah?

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: Do but follow me, Ile place you instantly
Where you ſhall ſee her courted by Cuningame.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: I go with greedineſſe; we long for things
That break our hearts ſometimes, there's pleaſures miſery,

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Where are thoſe gad-flies going? to ſome Junket now;
That ſome old humble-bee toles the yoūg one forth
To ſweet meats after kinde, let 'em looke to't,
The thing you wot on, be not miſt or gone,
I bring a Maiden-head, and I looke for one. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Cunningame (in diſcourſe with a Mask't Gentlewoman in a broad hat and ſcarf'd,) Neece at another doore.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Too manifeſt now, the Scarfe and all.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: It cannot be, you're ſuch a fearefull ſoule.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Ile give her cauſe of feare e're I part from her.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Will you ſay ſo? Is't not your Aunts deſire too?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.p: What a diſſembling groane's that? ſhee'l forſwear't now.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I ſee my project takes, yonder's the grace on't.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Who would put confidence in wit againe,
I'me plagu'd for my ambition, to deſire
A wiſe man for a husband, and I ſee
Fate will not have us go beyond our ſtint,
We are allow'd but one diſh, and that's Woodcock,
It keeps up wit to make us friends and fervants of,
And thinks any thing's good enough to make us husbands
Oh that whores hat a' thine, a' the riding block,
A ſhade for lecherous kiſſes.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Make you doubt on't?
Is not my love of force?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Yes, me it forces
To teare that ſorcerous ſtrumpet from th'imbraces.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Lady?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Oh thou haſt wrong'd the exquiſit'ſt love—

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: What meane you Lady?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Mine, you'l anſwer for't.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Alas, what ſeek you?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Sir, mine owne with loſſe.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: You ſhall.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: I never made ſo hard a bargaine.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Sweet Lady?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Unjuſt man, let my wrath reach her,
As you owe vertue duty; your cauſe trips you,
Now Minion, you ſhall feele what loves rage is,
Before you taſte the pleaſure; ſmile you falſe, Sir?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: How can I chuſe? to ſee what paines you take,
Upon a thing will never thank you for't?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: See what things you women be, Lady,
When cloathes are taken for the beſt part of you?
This was to ſhow you, when you think I love you not,
How y'are deceiv'd ſtill, there the Morall lyes,
'Twas a trap ſet to catch you, and the only bait
To take a Lady nibling, is fine clothes;
Now I dare boldly thank you for your love,
I'me pretty well reſolv'd in't by this fit,
For a jealous ague alwaies uſhers it.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Now bleſſings ſtill maintaine this wit of thine,
And I'me an excellent fortune comming in thee,
Bring nothing elſe I charge thee.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Not a groat I warrant ye.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt be worthily welcome, take my faith for't,
Next opportunity ſhall make us.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: The old Gentlewoman has fool'd her revenge ſweetly.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Laſſe 'tis her part, ſhe knowes her place ſo well yonder;
Alwaies when women jumpe upon three ſcore,
Love ſhoves 'em from the chamber to the doore.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Thou art a precious ſhe-wit. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Cunningame (at one doore) Winy Pate, Ruinous, L. Ruinous, and Priſcian (at the other.)

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: FRiend, met in the harveſt of our deſignes,
Not a thought but's buſle.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: I knew it man,
that made me provide theſe needfull Reapers,
Hooks, Rakers, Gleaners; wee'l ſing it home
With a melodious Horne-pipe; this is the Bond,
That as we further in your great affaire,
You'l ſuffer us to gleane, pick up for crums,
And if we ſnatch a handfull from the ſheafe,
You will not looke a churle on's.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Friend, wee'l ſhare
The ſheaves of gold, only the Love Aker
Shall be peculiar.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Much good do you, Sir,
Away, you know your way, and your ſtay; get you
The Muſick ready, while we prepare the dancers.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: We are a conſort of our ſelves.

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: And can ſtrike up luſtily.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: You muſt bring Sir Fop.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: That's perfect enough.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: Bring all the Fops you can, the more the better fare,
So the proverbe runs backwards. Exeunt Ruin. & Priſ.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: Ile bring the Ladies. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Do ſo firſt, and then the Fops will follow;
I muſt to my father, he muſt make one. Exit.

div.stage: Enter two Servants with a Banquet.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: While I diſpatch a buſineſſe with the Knight,
And I go with you. Well ſed, I thank you,
This ſmall Banquet will fusniſh our few Gueſts
With taſte and ſtate enough; one reach my Gowne,
The action craves it rather then the weather.

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: There's one ſtaies to ſpeake with you Sir.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: What is he?

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: Faith I know not what, Sir, a foole I thinke,
That ſome Brokers ſhop has made half a Gentleman;
Has the name of a Worthy too..

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Pompey? is't not?

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: That's he, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Alas poore fellow, prethee enter him, he will need too,
sp.stage: Enter ſecond Servant with a Gowne.
sp.l: He ſhall ſerve for a Witneſſe. Oh Gramercy:
If my friend Sir Gregory comes, you know him,
Entertaine him kindly. Oh Maſter Pompey, how is't man?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: 'Snailes, I'me almoſt ſstarv'd with love, and cold, and one thing or other;
Has not my Lady ſent for me yet?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: Not that I heare, ſure ſome unfriendly Meſſenger Is imployed betwixt you,

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I was ne're ſo cold in my life, in my conſcience I have been ſeven mile in length, along the new River; I have ſeene a hundred ſtickle bags; I do not thinke but there's gudgeons too; 'twill ne're be a true water.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Why thinke you ſo?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I warrant you, I told a thouſand Millers thumbs in it,
Ile make a little bold with your Sweet-meats.
And welcome Pompey.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: 'Tis is a ſtrange thing, I have no taſte in any thing.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Oh, that's Love, that diſtaſts any thing but it ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: 'Tis worſe then Cheeſe in that point, may not a man breake his word with a Lady? I could finde in my heart and my hoſe too.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: By no meanes Sir, that breakes all the Lawes of Love.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Well, ile ne're paſſe my word without my deed to Lady, while I live agen, I would faine recover my taſte.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Well, I have newes to tell you.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Good newes, Sir?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: Happy newes, I help you away with a Rivall your Maſter beſtow'd

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Where for this plumbs ſake—

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Nay liſten me.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I warrant you, Sir, I have two eares to one mouth,
I heare more then I eat, i'de ne're row by Queen Hive
While lived elſe.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: I have a wife for him, and that ſhall witneſſe the Contract.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: The old one I hope, 'tis not the Lady?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Choak him firſt, 'tis one which thou ſhalt ſee,
See him, ſee him deceiv'd, ſee the deceit, only
The injunction is, you ſhall ſmile with modeſty.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Ile ſimper ifaith, as cold as I am yet, the old one I hope.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Sir, here's Sir Gregory.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Ud' ſo ſhelter, ſhelter, if you be ſeene
All's ravell'd out agen; ſtand there private,
And you'le finde the very opportunity
To call you forth, and place you at the Table.
You are welcome Sir, this Banquet will ſerve,
When it is crown'd with ſuch a dainty as you
Expect, and muſt have.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Tuſh, theſe ſweet-meats are but ſauce to that,
Well, if there be any honeſty or true word in a dreame,
She's mine owne, nay, and chang'd extreamely,
Not the ſame woman.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Who? not the Lady?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg,
sp.l: No, not to me, the edge of her tongue is taken off,
Gives me very good words, turn'd upſide downe to me,
And we live as quietly as two Tortuſſes, if ſhe hold on
As ſhe began in my dreame. Soft Muſick.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Nay, if Love ſend forth ſuch Predictions,
You are bound to beleeve 'em, there's the watch-word
Of her coming, to your practis'd part now,
If you hit it, Aequus Cupido nobis.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I will warrant you Sir, I will give armes to
Your Gentry, looke you forward to your buſineſſe,
I am an eye behind you, place her in that Chaire,
And let me alone to grope her out.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Silence, Lady, your ſweet preſence illuſtrates
This homely roofe, and as courſe entertainment;
But where affections are both Hoſt and Gueſt,
They cannot meet unkindly, pleaſe you fit,
Your ſomething long ſtay made me unmannerly,
To place before you, you know this friend here,
He's my Gueſt, and more eſpecially,
That this our meeting might not be too ſingle,
Without a witneſſe to't.

sp.speaker: Mirab.
sp.l: I came not unreſolv'd, Sir,
And when our hands are claſp'd in that firme faith
Which I expect from you; fame ſhall be bold
To ſpeake the lowdeſt on't: oh, you graſpe me.
Somewhat too hard friend.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: That's Loves eager will,
Ile touch it gentlier. Kiſſe her hand.

sp.speaker: Mirab.
sp.l: That's too low in you,
Leſſe it be doubly recompenc'd in me. She kiſſes his hand.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Puh, I muſt ſtop my mouth, I ſhall be choakt elſe.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Come, wee'le not play and trifle with delayes,
We met to joyne theſe hands, and willingly
I cannot leave it till confirmation.

sp.speaker: Mirab.
sp.p: One word firſt, how does your friend, kinde Sir Gregory?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Why do you mention him? you love him not?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I ſhall love you the leſſe if you ſay ſo, Sir,
In troth I love him, but 'tis you deceive him,
This flattering hand of yours does rob him now,
Now you ſteale his right from him, and I know
I ſhall have hate for't, his hate extreamly.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Why I thought you had not come ſo weakly arm'd,
Upon my life the Knight will love you for't,
Exceedingly love you, for ever love you.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I, you'le perſwade me ſo.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Why he's my friend,
And wiſhes me a fortune equall with him,
I know, and dare ſpeake it for him.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Oh, this hand betrayes him, you might remember him in ſome courteſie yet at leaſt.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I thank your help in't, here's to his health
Where e're he be.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ile pledge it were it againſt my health.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Oh. oh, my heart hops after twelve mile a day, upon a good returne, now could I walke three hundred mile a foot, and laugh forwards and backwards.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You'le take the Knights health Sir,

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Yes, yes forſooth, oh my ſides! ſuch a Banquet once a weeke, would make me grow fat in a fortnight.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Well, now to cloſe our meeting, with the cloſe
Of mutuall hands and hearts, thus I begin,
Here in Heavens eye, and all loves ſacred powers,
(Which in my prayers ſtand propitious)
I knit this holy hand faſt, and with this hand
The heart that owes this hand, ever binding
By force of this initiating Contract
Both heart and hand in love, faith, loyalty,
Eſtate, or what to them belongs, in all the dues;
Rights and honours of a faithfull husband,
And this firme vow henceforth till death to ſtand
Irrevocable, ſeal'd both with heart and hand.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Which thus I ſecond, but oh, Sir Gregory.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Agen? this interpoſition's ill, beleeve me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Here in Heavens eye, and all Loves ſacred powers
I knit this holy hand faſt, and with this hand
The heart that owes this hand, ever binding
Both heart and hand in love, honour, loyalty,
Eſtate, or what to them belongs in all the dues,
Rights, and duties of a true faithfull wife;
And this firme Vow henceforth till death to ſtand,
Irrevocable ſeal'd both with heart and hand.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: A full agreement on both parts.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I, here's witneſſe of that.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Nay, I have over-reacht you Lady, and that's much,
For any Knight in England to over-reach a Lady.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I rejoyce in my deceit, I am a Lady
Now, I thanke you Sir.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Good morrow Lady Fop.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: 'Snailes, i'me gull'd, made a worſhipfull aſſe, this is not my Lady.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: But it is Sir, and true as your dreame told you,
That your Lady was become another woman.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Ile have another Lady Sir, if there were no more Ladies in London, blinde-man buffe is an unlawfull Game.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Come, downe on your knees firſt, and thanke your ſtars.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: A fire of my ſtars, I may thanke you I think.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: So you may pray for me, and honour me,
That have preſerv'd you from a laſting torment,
For a perpetuall comfort; did you call me friend?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: I pray pardon me for that, l did miſcall you, I confeſſe.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And ſhould I receiving ſuch a thankfull name
Abuſe it in the act? ſhould I ſee my friend
Bafful'd, diſgrac'd, without any reverence
To your title to be call'd ſlave, raſcall?
Naay curſt to your face, fool'd, ſcorn'd, beaten downe
With a womans peeviſh hate, yet I ſhould ſtand
And ſuffer you to be loſt, caſt away?
I would have ſeene you buried quick firſt,
Your ſpurrs of Knight-hood to have wanted rowels,
And to be kickt from your heeles; ſlave, raſcall?
Heare this tongue?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: My deareſt Love, ſweet Knight, my Lord, my Husband.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: So, this is not ſlave and raſcall then.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What ſhall your eye command, but ſhall be done,
In all the duties of a loyall wife?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Good, good, are not curſes fitter for you? wer't not better
Your head were broke with the handle of a fanne,
Or your noſe bor'd with a ſilver bodkin?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why, I will be a ſervant in your Lady.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Pox, but you ſhall not, ſhe's too good for you,
This contract ſhall be a nullity, ile breake't off,
And ſee you better beſtow'd.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: 'Slid, but you ſhall not Sir, ſhe's mine owne, And I am hers, and we are one anothers lawfully, and let me ſee him that will take her away by the Civill Law, if you be my friend keepe you ſo, if you have done me a good turne, do not hit me ith' teeth with't, that's not the part of a friend.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: If you be content —

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Content? I was never in better contention in my life,
Ile not change her for both the Exchanges, New or the Old;
Come, kiſſe me boldly.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Give you joy, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Oh Sir, I thanke you as much as though I did, you are beloved of Ladies, you ſee we are glad of under women.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Ladies? let not Ladies be diſgrac'd, you are as it were a married man, and have a Family, and for the parties ſake that was unnam'd before, being Peſe-cod time, I am appeas'd, yet I would wiſh you make a ruler of your tongue.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Nay, no diſſention here, I muſt bar that,
And this (friend) I entreat you, and be advis'd,
Let this private contract be yet conceal'd,
And ſtill ſupport a ſeeming face of love
Unto the Lady; marke how it availes you,
And quits all her ſcornes, her Unckle is now hot
In purſuit of the match, and will enforce her
Bend her proud ſtomack, that ſhe ſhall proffer
Her ſelfe to you, which when you have flouted,
And laught your fill at, you ſhall ſcorne her off
With all your diſgraces trebled upon her,
For there the pride of all her heart will bow,
When you ſhall foot her from you, not ſhe you.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Good ifaith; ile continue it, i'de faine laugh at the old fellow too, for he has abus'd me as ſcurvily as his Neece, my Knight-hood's upon the ſpur, wee'le go to Bed, and then to Church as faſt as we can.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I do wonder I do not heare of the Lady yet.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: The good minute may come ſooner then you are aware of,
I do not thinke but 'twill e're night yet as neare as 'tis.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Well, I will go walke by the new River in that meditation, I am o're ſhooes I'me ſure upon the dry bank, this gullery of my Maſter will keepe me company this two houres too, if love were not an enemy to laughter I ſhould drive away the time well enough; you know my walke Sir, if ſhe ſends, I ſhall be found angling, for I will try what I can catch for luck ſake, I will fiſh faire for't.
sp.l: Oh Knight that thou ſhould'ſt be gull'd ſo; ha, ha, it does me good at heart,
But oh Lady, thou tak'ſt downe my merry part. Exit

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Friend.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Here friend.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: All's afoot, and will go ſmooth away,
The woman has conquer'd the women, they are gone,
Which I have already complain'd to my Father,
Suggeſting that Sir Gregory is falne off
From his charge, for neglects and ill uſage,
And that he is moſt violently bent
On Gentries wife (whom I have call'd a widow)
And that without moſt ſudden prevention
He will be married to her.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Foot, all this is wrong,
This wings his purſuit, and will be before me; I am loſt for ever.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: No, ſtay, you ſhall not go
But with my Father, on my wit let it lye,
You ſhall appeare a friendly aſſiſtant,
To helpe in all affaires, and in execution
Helpe your ſelfe only.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Would my beleefe
Were ſtronge in this aſſurance.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: You ſhall credit it,
And my wit ſhall be your ſlave if it deceive you.
My Father —

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Oh Sir, you are well met, where's the Knight your friend?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Sir, I thinke your Sonne has told you.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Shall I ſtand to tell't agen? I tell you he loves,
But not my Kinſ-woman, her baſe uſage,
And your ſlack performance which he accuſes moſt
Indeed, has turn'd the Knights heart upſide downe.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Ile curbe her for't, can he be but recover'd,
He ſhall have her, and ſhe ſhall be dutifull,
And loue him as a wife too.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: With that condition Sir,
I dare recall him were he enter'd the Church,
So much intereſt of love I aſſure in him.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Sir, it ſhall be no loſſe to you if you do.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: I, but theſe are words ſtill, will not the deeds Be wanting at the recovery, if it ſhould be agen?

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Why here foole, I am provided, five hunder'd in earneſt,
Of the thouſands in her Dower, but were they married once,
I'de cut him ſhort enough, that's my agreement.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: I, now I perceive ſome purpoſe in you, Father.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: But wherefore is ſhe then ſtolne out of doores to him?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: To him? oh fye upon your errour, ſhe has another objett, beleeve it Sir.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: I never could perceive it.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: I did Sir, and to her ſhame I ſhould ſpeake it,
To my owne ſorrow I ſaw it, dalliance,
Nay dotage with a very Clowne, a Foole.

sp.speaker: O.K.
sp.l: Wit and wantons? nothing elſe? nothing elſe?
She love a Foole? ſhe'le ſooner mate a foole
Of a wiſe man.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I, my friend complaines ſo,
Sir Gregory ſayes flatly ſhe makes a foole of him,
And theſe bold circumſtances are approv'd;
Favours have been ſent by him, yet he ignorant
Whither to carry 'em; they have been underſtood,
And taken from him, certaine Sir, there is
An unſuſpected fellow lyes conceal'd,
What, or where e're he is, theſe ſlight neglects
Could not be of a Knight elſe.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.p: Well Sir, you have promis'd (if we recover him Unmarried) to ſalve all theſe old bruiſes?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Ile do my beſt Sir.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: I ſhall thanke you, coſtly Sir, and kindly too.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Will you talke away the time here Sir, and come behirtde all your purpoſes?

sp.speaker: O.K.
sp.l: Away good Sir.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Then ſtay a little good Sir, for my adviſe,
Why Father are you broke? your wit begger'd,
Or are you at your wits end? or out of
Love with wit? no trick of Wit to ſurprize
Thoſe deſignes, but with open Hue and Cry,
For all the world to talke on? this is ſtrange,
You were not wont to slubber a project ſo.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Can you helpe at a pinch now? ſhew your ſelfe
My ſonne, go too, I leave this to your wit,
Becauſe ile make a proofe on't.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: 'Tis thus then,
I have had late intelligence, they are now
Buxſome as Bachus Froes, revelling, dancing,
Telling the Muſicks numbers with their feet,
Awaiting the meeting of premoniſht friends,
That's queſtionleſſe, little dreading you,
Now Sir, with a dexterous trick indeed, ſuddaine
And ſufficient were well, to enter on um
As ſomething like the abſtract of a Maſque;
What though few perſons? if beſt for our purpoſe
That commends the project.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: This takes up time.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Not at all, I can preſently furniſh
With looſe diſguiſes that ſhall fit that Scene.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Why what wants then?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Nothing but charge of Muſick,
That muſt be paid you know.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: That ſhall be my charges, ile pay the Muſick,
What e're it coſt.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: And that ſhall be all your charge,
Now on, I like it, there will be wit in't Father.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I will neither diſtruſt his wit nor friendſhip,
Yet if his maſter braine ſhould be o're-throwne
My reſolution now ſhall ſeize mine owne. Exit

div.stage: Enter Neece, Lady Ruinous, Gardianeſſe, Ruinous, Priſcian (with inſtrumenes maſqu't.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: Nay, let's have Muſick, let that ſweet breath at leaſt
Give us her ayrie welcome, 'twill be the beſt
I feare this ruin'd receptacle will yeeld,
But that moſt freely.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: My welcome followes me,
Elſe I am ill come hither, you aſſure me
Still Mr. Cuningame will be here, and that it was
His kinde entreaty that wiſht me meet him.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: Elſe let me be that ſhame unto my Sex,
That all beleefe may fly um.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Continue ſtill
The Knights name unto my Gardianeſſe,
She expects no other.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: He will, he will aſſure you
Lady, Sir Gregory will be here, and ſuddainely
This Muſick fore-ran him, is't not ſo conſorts?

sp.speaker: Ruin,
sp.l: Yes Lady, he ſtaies on ſome device to bring along
Such a labour he was buſie in, ſome witty device.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: 'Twill be long e're he comes then, for wit's a great Labour to him.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: Well, well, you'le agree better one day.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Scarce two I think.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: Such a mock-begger ſuit of clothes as led me
Into the fooles paire of Dice, with dewze ace,
He that would make me Miſtris Cun, Cun, Cunnie,
He's quite out of my minde, but I ſhall ne're
Forget him while I have a hole in my head,
Such a one I think would pleaſe you better,
Though he did not abuſe you.

sp.speaker: Ruin,
sp.l: Fye, ſpeake well of him now,
Your Neece has quitted him.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: I hope ſhe has,
Elſe ſhe looſes me for ever; but for Sir Gregory,
Would he were come. I ſhall ill anſwer this
Unto your Unckle elſe.

sp.speaker: Nei.
sp.l: You know 'tis his pleaſure
I ſhould keepe him company.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: I, and ſhould be your owne
If you did well too, Lord, I do wonder
At the niceneſſe of you Ladies now a dayes,
They muſt have Husbands with ſo much wit forſooth.
Worſhip and wealth were both wont to be
In better requeſt I'me ſure, I cannot tell,
But they get ne're the wiſer children that I ſee.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: La, la, la, la, Sol, this Muſick breathes in vaine,
Me thinks 'tis dull to let it move alone,
Let's have a female motion, 'tis in private,
And wee'le grace't our ſelves how ever it deſerves.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: What ſay you Gardianeſſe?

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: 'Laſſe i'me weary with the walke,
My jaunting dayes are done.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: Come, come, we'le fetch her in by courſe, or elſe,
She ſhall pay the Muſick.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: Nay, ile have a little for my money then.

div.stage: The Dance, a Cornet is winded.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: Hark? upon my life the Knight; 'tis your friend,
This was the warning-peece of his approach.

div.stage: Enter Old Knight, Witty-pate, Cuningame, Maſqu'd, and take them to dance.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: Ha? no words but mum? well then,
We ſhall need no counſell-keeping

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Yes, feare nothing.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Feare? why do you tell me of it?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Your Unckles here.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Aye me.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Peace.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: We have caught 'em.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Thanke my wit Father.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: Which is the Knight thinke you?

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: I know not, he will be found when be ſpeakes,
No Maske can diſguiſe his tongue.

sp.speaker: Wity.
sp.l: Are you charg'd?

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Are you awake?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: I'me anſwer'd in a queſtion.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Next change we meet, we looſe our hands no more.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Are you prepar'd to tye 'em?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Yes,
You muſt go with me.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: Whether Sir? not from my charge beleeve me.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: She goes a long.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Will you ventur and my Unckle here?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: His ſtay's prepar'd for. Exeunt they two.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: 'Tis the Knight ſure, ile follow.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: How now, the Muſick tyr'd before us?

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: Yes Sir, we muſt be paid now.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Oh, that's my charge Father.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: But ſtay, where are our wanton Ladies gone?
Sonne, where are they?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Onely chang'd the roome in a change, that's all ſure.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Ile make 'em all ſure elſe, and then returne to you.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: You muſt pay for your Muſick firſt, Sir.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Muſt? are there muſty Fidlers? are Beggers chooſers now?
Ha? why Witty-pate, Sonne, where am I?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: You were dancing e'ne now, in good meaſure Sir,
Is your health miſcarried ſince? what ayle you, Sir?

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Death, I may be gull'd to my face, where's my Neece?
What are you?

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: None of your Neece, Sir.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: How now? have you loud Inſtruments too? ile heare
No more I thanke you, what have I done tro
To bring theſe feares about me? Sonne, where am I?

sp.speaker: VVitty.
sp.l: Not where you ſhould be, Sir, you ſhould be paying
For your Muſick, and you are in a maze.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Oh, is't ſo, put up, put up, I pray you,
Here's a crowne for you.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: Piſh, a crowne?

sp.speaker: Ru. Priſ.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, a crowne?

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Which way do you laugh? I have ſeene a crowne
Has made a Conſort laugh heartily.

sp.speaker: VVitty.
sp.l: Father,
To tell you truth, theſe are no ordinary
Muſitians, they expect a bounty
Above their punctuall deſert.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: A — on your Puncks, and their deſerts too.
Am I not cheated all this while thinke you?
Is not your pate in this?

sp.speaker: VVitty.
sp.l: If you be cheated,
You are not to be Indicted for your owne goods,
Here you trifle time to market your bounty
And make it baſe, when it muſt needs be free
For ought I can perceive.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Will you know the loweſt price, Sir?

sp.speaker: VVitty.
sp.l: That I will Sir, with all my heart.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Unleſſe I was diſcover'd, and they now fled
Home agen for feare, I am abſolutely beguil'd,
That's the beſt can be hop'd for.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Faith 'tis ſomewhat too deare yet, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: There's not a Denier to be bated, Sir.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Now Sir, how deare is it?

sp.speaker: VVitty.
sp.l: Bate but the tother ten pound?

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: Not a Bawbee, Sir.

sp.speaker: O. R.
sp.l: How? bate ten pound? what's the whole ſumme then?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Faith Sir, a hundred pound, with much a doe,
I got fifty bated, and faith Father, to ſay truth,
'Tis reaſonable for men of their faſhion.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: La, la, la, downe, a hunder'd pound? la, la, la,
You are a Conſort of Theeves, are you not?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: No Muſitians Sir, I told you before.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Fiddle faddle, is it not a robbery? a plaine robbery?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: No, no, no, by no meanes Father, you have receiv'd
For your money, nay, and that you cannot give back,
'Tis ſomewhat deare I confeſſe, but who can helpe it?
If they had been agreed with before hand,
'Twas ill forgotten.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: And how many ſhares have you in this? I ſee my force,
Caſe up your Inſtruments, I yield, here, as rob'd and
Taken from me, I deliver it.

sp.speaker: VVitty.
sp.p: No Sir, you have perform'd your promiſe now, which was, to pay the charge of Muſick, that's all.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.p: I have heard no Muſick, I have receiv'd none, Sir, There's none to be found in me, nor about me.

sp.speaker: VVitty.
sp.l: Why Sir, here's witneſſe againſt you, you have danc'd,
And he that dances acknowledges a receit
Of Muſick.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.p: I deny that Sir, looke you, I can dance without Muſick, do you ſee Sir? and I can ſing without it too; you are a conſort of Theeves, do you heare what I do?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Pray you take heed Sir, if you do move the Muſick agen, it may coſt you as much more.

sp.speaker: O.K.
sp.p: Hold, hold, ile depart quietly, I need not bid you farewell, I think now, ſo long as that hundred pound laſts with you.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: Ha, ha, am I ſnapt ifaith?
Oh, Sir, Perfidious.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.p: I, I, ſome howling anotherwhile, Muſick's too damnable deare.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.p: Oh Sir, my heart-ſtrings are broke, if I can but live to tell you the tale I care not, your Neece my charge is —

sp.speaker: O.K.
sp.p: What, is ſhe ſick?

sp.speaker: Gard,
sp.p: No, no Sir, ſhe's luſtity well married.

sp.speaker: O.K.
sp.p: To whom?

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.p: Oh, to that cunning diſſembler, Cuningame.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.p: Ile hang the Prieſt, firſt, what was he?

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.p: Your Kinſman Sir, that has the Welch Benefice.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.p: I ſav'd him from the Gallowes to that end, good, is there any more?

sp.speaker: Garde
sp.p: And Sir Gregory is married too.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.p: To my Neece too, I hope, and then I may hang her.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.p: No Sir, to my Neece, thank Cupid; and that's all that's likely to recover me, ſhe's Lady Fop now, and I am One of her Aunts I thanke my promotion.

div.stage: Enter Credulous, Cuningame, Neece, Sir Gregory, and Mirabell.

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.p: I hate perform'd your beheſt Sir.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.p: What have you perform'd Sir?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Faith Sir, I muſt excuſe my Couſen in this act,
If you can excuſe your ſelfe for making him
A Prieſt, there's the moſt difficult anſwer
I put this practiſe on him as from your deſire,
A truth, a truth Father.

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.p: I proteſt Sir, he tells you truth, he mov'd me to't in your name.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.p: I protest Sir, he told you a lye in my name, and were you ſo eaſie Mr. Credulous to beleeve him?

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.p: If a man ſhould not beleeve his Couſen Sir, whom ſhould he beleeve?

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Godden to you good Mr. Couſen Cuningame,
And your faire Bride, my Couſen Cuningame too,
And how do you, Sir Gregory, with your faire Lady?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: A little better then you would have had me, I thanke you Sir, the dayes of Puppy, and Slave, and Raſcall are pretty well blowne over now, I know Crabs from Verjuyce, I have tryed both, and thoud'ſt give me thy Neece for nothing i'de not have her.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: I thinke ſo Sir Gregory, for my ſake you would not.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: I wo'd thou had'ſt ſcap'd her too, and then ſhe had dyed of the greene ſickneſſe, know this, that I did marry in ſpight, and I will kiſſe my Lady in ſpight, and love her in ſpight, and beget children of her in ſpight, and when I dye they ſhall have my Lands in ſpight; this was my reſolution, and now 'tis out.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: How ſpightfull are you now, Sir Gregory?
Why looke you, I can love my deareſt Husband,
With all the honours, duties, ſweet embraces,
That can be throwne upon a loving man.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: — This is afore your Unckles face, but behinde his back in private you'le ſhew him another tale.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: You ſee Sir, now the irrecoverable ſtate of all theſe things before you, come out of your muſe, they have been but wit weapons, they were wont to love the play.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.p: Let me alone in my muſe a little Sir, I will wake to you anon.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: U'd ſo, your friend Pompey, how will you anſwer him?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.p: Very well, if you'le but ſecond it, and help me.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I do heare ſtrange ſtories, are Ladies things obnoxious?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.p: Oh, the diſſembling falſeſt wretch is come.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: How now Lady?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Let me come to him, and in ſtead of love
Let me have revenge.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Pray you now, will you firſt examine, whither he be guilty or no.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: He cannot be excus'd,
How many Meſſengers (thou perjur'd man)
Haſt thou return'd with Vowes and Oathes? that thou
Wouldſt follow, and never till this unhappy houre
Could I ſet eye of thee, ſince thy falſe dye
Drew my heart to it? oh I could teare thee now,
In ſtead of ſoft embraces, pray give me leave—

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Faith this was ill done of you Sir, if you promis'd otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: By this hand, never any Meſſenger came at me ſince the firſt time I came into her company; that a man ſhould be wrong'd thus?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Did not I ſend thee Scarfes and Diamonds?
And thou returnd'ſt me letters, one with a faife heart in't.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: On fye to receive favours, returne falſe-hoods, and hold a Lady in hand —

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Will you believe me Sir? if ever I receiv'd Diamonds, or Scarfe, or ſent any Letter to her, would this Sword might ne're go through me.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Some bad Meſſengers have gone betweene you then.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.p: Take him from my fight, if I ſhall ſee to morrow.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Pray you forbeare the place, this diſcontent may impaire her health much.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Foot, if a man had been in any fault 'twould ne're have griev'd him, Sir, if you'le beleeve.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Nay, nay, proteſt no more, I do believe you,
But you ſee how the Lady is wrong'd by't;
She has caſt away her ſelfe it is to be fear'd,
Againſt her Unckles will, nay, any conſent,
But out of a meere neglect, and ſpight to her ſelfe,
Married ſuddenly without any advice.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Why who can helpe it? if ſhe be caſt away ſhe may thanke her ſelfe, ſhe might have gone further and far'd worſe; I could do no more then I could do, 'twas her owne pleaſure to command me that I ſhould not come till I was ſent for, I had been with her every minute of an houre elſe.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Truly I believe you.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Night and day ſhe might have commanded me, and that ſhe knew well enough; I ſaid as much to her between her and I, yet I proteſt ſhe's as honeſt a Lady for my part, that i'de ſay if ſhe would ſee me hang'd, if ſhe be cast away I cannot helpe it, ſhe might have ſtay'd to have ſpoke with a man.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Well, 'twas a hard miſſe on both parts.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: So 'twas, I was within one of her, for all this croſſe luck, I was ſure I was between the Knight and home.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.p: Not gone yet? oh my heart! none regard my health?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Good Sir, forbeare her ſight a while, you heare how ill ſhe brookes it.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Fooliſh woman, to over-throw her fortunes ſo; I ſhall thinke the worſe of a Ladies wit while I live for't— I could almoſt cry for anger, if ſhe ſhould miſcarry now, 'twould touch my conſcience a little, and who knowes what love and conceit may do? what would people ſay as I go along? there goes he that the Lady dyed for love on, lam ſure to heare on't ith' streets. I ſhall weepe before hand; fooliſh woman, I do grieve more for thee now then I did love thee before; well, go thy waies, would'ſt thou ſpare thy Husbands head and breake thine owne heart? if thou hadſt any wit, I would ſome other had been the cauſe of thy undoing, I ſhall be twitted i'th teeth with't, i'me ſure of that, fooliſh Lady. Exit.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.p: So, ſo, this trouble's well ſhooke off, Unckle, how dee? there's a Dowrie due, ſir.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: We have agreed it, ſweeteſt,
And finde your Unckle fully recover'd, kinde to both of us.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: To all the rest I hope;

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Never to thee, nor thee, eaſie couſen Credulous,
Was your wit ſo raw?

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: Faith yours Sir, ſo long ſeaſon'd
Has been faulty too, and very much to blame,
Speaking it with reverence, Unckle.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Yes faith, Sir, you have paid as deare for your time as any man here.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p:
I Sir, and ile reckon it to him. Imprimis, The firſt preface cheat of a paire of peeces to the Beggers, you
remember that I was the example to your bounty there, I ſpake Greeke, and Syriacke, Sir, you underſtand me now. Next, the Robbery put upon your indulgent Couſen, which indeed was no Robbery, no Conſtable, no Juſtice, no Thiefe, but all Cheaters; there was a hunder'd Mark, mark you that. Laſtly, this memorable 100. pounds worth of Muſick, this was but cheats and wit too, and for the aſſiſtance, this Gentleman to my Couſen (for which I am to have a Fee) that was a little practice of my wit too, Father; will you come to compoſition yet, Father?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: Yes faith Sir, do, two hunder'd a yeare will be eaſier then ſo much weekly, I do not think he's barren if he ſhould be put to't agen.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Why this was the day I look'd for, thou ſhalt have't,
And the next cheat makes it up three hunder'd;
Live thou upou thy ten pound Vicarage,
Thou get'ſt not a penny more, here's thy full
Hire now.

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: I thanke you Sir.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Why there was the ſumme of all my wit Father,
To ſhove him out of your favour, which I fear'd
Would have diſ-inherited me.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Moſt certaine it had,
Had not thy wit recover'd it; is there any here
That had a hand with thee?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Yes, all theſe Sir.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Nephew, part a hunder'd pound amongſt 'em,
Ile repay it; wealth, love me as I love wit;
When I dye,
Ile build an Almeſ-houſe for decay'd wits.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Ile entertaine one in my life time; Schollar, you ſhall be my Chaplaine, I have the gift of twenty Benefices, ſimple as I am here.

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: Thankes my great Patron.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: Sir, your Gentry and your name ſhall both be rais'd as high as my fortunes can reach 'em, for your friends ſake.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Something will be in my preſent power, the future more,
You ſhall ſhare with me.

sp.speaker: Ruin. and VVife.
sp.l: Thankes worthy Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Sir, I would beg one thing of you?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: You can beg nothing of me.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Oh Sir, if ſhe begs, there's your power over her.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: She has begg'd me for a foole already, but 'tis no matter,
I have begg'd her for a Lady that ſhe might have been,
That's one for another.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Nay, but if ſhe beg—

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Let her beg agen then.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: That your man Pompeyes Coat may come over his eares backe agen, I would not he ſhould be loſt for my ſake.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Well, 'tis granted, for mine owne ſake.

sp.speaker: Mirab.
sp.l: Ile entreat it Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Why then 'tis granted for your ſake.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Come, come, downe with all weapons now, 'tis
Muſicke time,
So it be purchas'd at an eaſie rate;
Some have receiv'd the knocks, ſome given the hits,
And all concludes in love, there's happy wits. Exeunt

div.head: The Epilogue at the reviving of this Play.
div.l: WE need not tell you Gallants, that this night
The VVits have jumpt, or that the Scenes hit right,
'Twould be but labour loſt for to excuſe
VVhat Fletcher had to do in, his brisk Muſe
VVas ſo Mercuriall, that if he but writ
An Act, or two, the whole Play riſe up wit.
Wee'le not appeale unto thoſe Gentlemen
Judge by their Clothes, if they ſit right, nor when
The Ladies ſmile, and with their Fannes delight
To whiske a climb aſide, then all goes right:
'Twas well receiv'd before, and we dare ſay,
You now are welcome to no vulgar Play.

back.trailer: Here endeth Wit at ſeverall Weapons.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: I Never ſaw the like, ſhee's no more ſtirr'd,
No more another woman, no more alter'd,
With any hopes or promiſes layd to her
(Let 'em be nev'r ſo waighty, nev'r ſo winning,
Then I am with the motion of my owne legs.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: You are a ſtranger yet in theſe deſignes,
At leaſt in Rome; tell me, and tell me truth,
Did you ere know in all your courſe of practiſe,
In all the wayes of woman you have runne through
(For I preſume you have been brought up Chilax,
As we to fetch and carry.)

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: True I have ſo:

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Did you I ſay againe in all this progreſſe,
Ever diſcover ſuch a peece of beauty,
Ever ſo rare a Creature, and no doubt
One that muſt know her worth too, and affect it,
I and be flatter'd, elſe tis none: and honeſt?
Honeſt againſt the tide of all temptations,
Honeſt to one man, to her husband only,
And yet not eighteene, not of age to know
Why ſhe is honeſt?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I confeſſe it freely,
I never ſaw her fellow, nor er'e ſhall,
For all our Graecian Dames, all I have tri'd,
(And ſure I have tri'd a hunderd, if I ſay two
I ſpeake within my compaſſe) all theſe beauties,
And all the conſtancy of all theſe faces,
Mayds, Widdows, Wives, of what degree or calling,
So they be Greekes, and fat, for there's my cunning,
I would undertake and not ſweat ſor't, Proculus,
Were they to try againe, ſay twice as many,
Vnder a thouſand pound, to lay 'em bedrid;
But this Wench ſtaggers me.

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: Doe you ſee theſe Iewells?
You would thinke theſe pretty baytes; now Ile aſſure ye
Here's halfe the wealth of Aſia.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: Theſe are nothing
To the full honours I propounded to her;
I bid her think, and be, and preſently
What ever her ambition, what the Councell
Of others would adde to her, what her dreames
Could more enlarge, what any Preſident
Of any woman riſing up to glory,
And ſtanding certaine there, and in the higheſt,
Could give her more, nay to be Empreſſe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: And cold at all theſe offers?

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: Cold as Chriſtall,
Never to be thaw'd again,

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I trid her further,
And ſo farre, that I think ſhe is no woman,
At leaſt as women goe now.

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: Why what did you?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I offerd that, that had ſhe been but Miſtris
Of as much ſpleene as Doves have, I had reach'd her▪
A ſafe revenge of all that ever hates her,
The crying down for ever all beauties
That may be thought come neare her.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: That was pretty.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I never knew that way faile, yet Ile tell ye
I offerd her a gift beyond all yours,
That, that had made a Sainct ſtart, well conſiderd,
The Law to be her creature, ſhe to make it,
Her mouth to give it, every creature living
From her aſpect, to draw their good or evill
Fixd in'em ſpight of Fortune; a new Nature
She ſhould be called, and mother of all ages,
Time ſhould be hers, and what ſhe did lame vertue
Should bleſſe to all poſterities: her aire
Should give us life, her earth and water feed us.
And laſt, to none but to the Emperour,
(And then but when ſhe pleaſ'd to have it ſo,)
She ſhould be held for mortall.

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: And ſhe heard you?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Yes, as a Sick man heares a noiſe, or he
That ſtands condemn'd his Iudgment, let me periſh,
But if there can be vertue, if that name
Be any thing but name and emptie title,
If it be ſo as fooles have been pleaſ'd to ſaigne it,
A power that can preſerve us after aſhes,
And make the names of men out-reckon ages,
This Woman has a God of vertue in her.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: I would the Emperor were that God.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: She has in her
All the contempt of glory and vaine ſeeming
Of all the Stoicks, all the truth of Chriſtians,
And all their Conſtancy: Modeſty was made
When ſhe was firſt intended: When ſhe bluſhes
It is the holyeſt thing to looke upon;
The pureſt temple of her ſect, that ever
Made nature a bleſt Founder.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Is there no way
To take this Phenix?

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: None but in her aſhes.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: If ſhe were fat, or any way inclining
To eaſe or pleaſure, or effected glory,
Proud to be ſeene and worſhip'd, t'were a venture;
But on my ſoule ſhe is chaſter then cold Camphire.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: I thinke ſo too; for all the wayes of woman,
Like a full ſaile ſhe bears againſt: I aske her
After my many offers, walking with her,
And her as many down-denyals, how
If the Emperor grown mad with love ſhould force her;
She pointed to a Lucrece, that hung by,
And with an angry looke, that from her eyes
Shot Veſtall fire againſt me, ſhe departed.

sp.speaker: Bro.
sp.l: This is the firſt wench I was ever poſ'd in,
Yet I have brought young loving things together
This two and thirty yeare.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I find by this wench
The calling of a Bawd to be a ſtrange,
A wiſe, and ſubtile calling; and for none
But ſtaid, diſcreet, and underſtanding people:
And as the Tutor to great Alexander,
Would ſay a young man ſhould not dare to read
His morall books, till after five and twenty;
So muſt that he or ſhe, that will be bawdy,
(I meane diſcreetly bawdy, and be truſted)
If they will riſe, and gaine experience,
Wel ſteept in yeares, and diſcipline, begin it,
I take it tis no boys play.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: Well, what's thought off?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: The Emperour muſt know it.

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: If the women ſhould chance to faile too,

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: As tis ten to one,

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Why what remaines, but new nets for the purchaſe?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Let's goe conſider then: and if all faile,
This is the firſt quick Eele, that ſav'd her taile. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ardelia.
sp.l: You ſtill inſiſt upon that Idoll, Honour,
Can it renue your youth, can it adde wealth,
That takes off wrinkles: can it draw mens eyes,
To gaze upon you in your age? can honour,
That truly is a Saint to none but Souldiers,
And lookd into, beare no reward but danger,
Leave you the moſt reſpected perſon living?
Or can the common kiſſes of a husband,
(Which to a ſprightly Lady is a labour)
Make ye almoſt Immortall? ye are cozend,
The honour of a woman is her praiſes;
The way to get theſe, to be ſeene, and ſought too,
And not to bury ſuch a happy ſweetneſſe
Vnder a ſmoaky roofe.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Ile heare no more:

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: That white, and red, and all that bleſſed beauty,
Kept from the eyes, that make it ſo, is nothing;
Then you are rarely faire, when men proclaime it;
The Phenix, were ſhe never ſeene, were doubted,
That moſt unvalued Horne the Vnicorne
Beares to oppoſe the Huntſman, were it nothing
But tale, and meere tradition, would help no man,
But when the vertue's knowne, the honor's dobled:
Vertue, is either lame, or not at all,
And Love a ſacriledge, and not a Saint,
When it bars up the way to mens Petitions.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: Nay ye ſhal love your husband too; we come not
To make a Monſter of yee;

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Are ye women?

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: You'l find us ſo, and women you ſhall think too,
If you have grace to make your uſe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Eye on yee,

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Alas poore baſhfull Lady, by my ſoule,
Had ye no other vertue, but your bluſhes,
And I a man, I ſhould run mad for thoſe;
How daintlily they ſet her off, how ſweetly?

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: Come Goddeſſe, come, you move too neer the earth,
It muſt not be, a better orbe ſtaies for you:
Here: be a mayd, and take'en,

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Pray leave me.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: That were a ſin ſweet Lady, and a way
To make us guilty of your melancholly;
You muſt not be alone; In converſation
Doubts are reſolvd, and what ſticks neer the conſcience
Made eaſie, and allowable.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Ye are Devills,

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: That you may one day bleſſe for your damnation.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I charge ye in the name of Chaſtity,
Tempt me no more; how ugly ye ſeem to me?
There is no wonder men defame our Sex,
And lay the vices of all ages on us,
When ſuch as you ſhall beare the names of women;
If ye had eyes to ſee your ſelves, or ſence
Above the baſe rewards ye play the bawds for:
If ever in your lives ye heard of goodneſſe,
(Though many Regions off, as men heare thunder)
If ever ye had Mothers, and they ſoules:
If ever Fathers, and not ſuch as you are;
If ever any thing were conſtant in you,
Beſide your ſins, or comming but your curſes,
If ever any of your Anceſtors
Dyde worth a noble deed, that would be cheriſhd,
Soule-frighted with this black infection,
You would run from one another, to repentance,
And from your guilty eyes drop out thoſe ſins,
That made ye blind, and beaſts.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Ye ſpeak well Lady;
A ſigne of fruitfull education,
If your religious Zeale had wiſdome with it.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: This Lady was ordain'd to bleſſe the Empire,
And we may all give thanks for't.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: I beleive ye,

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: If any thing redeem the Emperour,
From his wild flying courſes, this is ſhe;
She can inſtruct him if ye mark; ſhe is wiſe too.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Exceeding wiſe, which is a wonder in her,
And ſo religious, that I well believe,
Though ſhe would ſinne ſhe cannot.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: And, beſides
She has the Empires cauſe in hand, not loves;
There lies the maine conſideration,
For which ſhe is chiefly borne.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: She finds that point
Stronger then we can tell her, and believe it
I look by her meanes for a reformation,
And ſuch a one, and ſuch a rare way carried
That all the world ſhall wonder at.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: Tis true;
I never thought the Emperor had wiſdom,
Pittie, or faire affection to his Country,
Till he profeſt this love: gods give'em Children,
Such as her vertues merit, and his zeale.
I looke to ſee a Numa from this Lady,
Or greater then Octavius.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Do you mark too,
Which is a Noble vertue, how ſhe bluſhes,
And what a flowing modeſty runs through her,
When we but name the Emperour?

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: But mark it,
Yes, and admire it too, for ſhe conſiders,
Though ſhe be faire as heaven, and vertuous
As holy truth, yet to the Emperour
She is a kind of nothing but her ſervice,
Which ſhe is bound to offer, and ſhe'l do it,
And when her Countries cauſe commands affection;
She knows obedience is the key of vertues,
Then flye the bluſhes out like Cupids arrowes,
And though the tye of marriage to her Lord,
Would faine cry ſtay Lucina, yet the cauſe
And generall wiſdom of the Princes love,
Makes her find ſurer ends and happier,
And if the firſt were chaſte, this is twice dobled.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Her tartnes unto us too.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: That's a wiſe one.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: I rarely like, it ſhewes a riſing wiſdom,
That chides all common fooles as dare enquire
What Princes would have private.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: What a Lady
Shall we be bleſt to ſerve?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Goe get ye from me.
Ye are your purſes Agents, not the Princes:
Is this the vertuous Lore yee traind me out too?
Am I a woman fit to imp your vices?
But that I had a Mother, and a woman
Whoſe ever living fame turnes all it touches,
Into the good it ſelfe is, I ſhould now
Even doubt my ſelfe, I have been ſearch't ſo neere
The very ſoule of honour: why ſhould you two,
That happily have been as chaſt as I am,
Fairer, I think, by much, for yet your faces,
Like ancient well built piles, ſhew worthy ruines,
After that Angell age, turne mortall Devills?
For ſhame, for woman-hood, for what ye have been,
For rotten Cedars have borne goodly branches,
If ye have hope of any Heaven, but Court,
Which like a Dreame, you'l find hereafter vaniſh,
Or at the beſt but ſubject to repentance,
Study no more to be ill ſpoken of;
Let women live themſelves, if they muſt fall,
Their owne deſtruction find 'em, not your ſevours.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: Madam, yee are ſo excellent in all,
And I muſt tell it you with admiration,
So true a joy ye have, ſo ſweet a feare,
And when ye come to anger, tis ſo noble,
That for mine own part, I could ſtill offend,
To heare you angry; women that want that,
And your way guided (elſe I count it nothing)
Are either Fooles, or Cowards.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: She were a Miſtris for no private greatneſſe,
Could ſhe not frowne a raviſhd kiſſe from anger,
And ſuch an anger as this Lady learnes us,
Stuck with ſuch pleaſing dangers. Gods (I aske ye)
Which of ye all could hold from?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I perceive ye,
Your owne dark ſins dwell with yee, and that price
You ſell the chaſtitie of modeſt wives at
Runs to diſeaſes with your bones: I ſcorne ye,
And all the nets ye have pitcht to catch my vertues
Like Spiders Webs, I ſweep away before me.
Goe tell the Emperour, yee have met a woman,
That neither his owne perſon, which is God-like,
The world he rules, nor what that world can purchaſe,
Nor all the glories, ſubject to a Ceſar,
The honours that he offers for my body,
The hopes, gifts, everlaſting flatteries,
Nor any thing that's his, and apt to tempt me,
No not to be the Mother of the Empire,
And Queene of all the holy fires he worſhips,
Can make a Whore of.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: You miſtake us Lady.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Yet tell him this ha's thus much weakend me,
That I have here his knaves, and you his Matrons,
Fit Nurſes for his ſins, which gods forgive me,
But ever to be leaning to his folly,
Or to be brought to love his luſt, aſſure him,
And from her mouth, whoſe life ſhal make it certain
I never can: I have a Noble husband,
Pray tell him that too, yet a noble name,
A Noble Family, and laſt a Conſcience:
Thus much for your anſwer: For your ſelves,
Ye have liv'd the ſhame of women, dye the better, Exit

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: What's now to doe? Lucina.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: Ev'n as ſhe ſaid, to dye,
For ther's no living here, and women thus,
I am ſure for us two.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Nothing ſtick upon her?

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: We have loſt a maſſe of mony; wel Dame vertue,
Yet ye may halt if good luck ſerve.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Wormes take her,
She has almoſt ſpoil'd our trade.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: So godly;
This is ill breeding Phorba.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: If the women
Should have a longing now to ſee this Monſter,
And ſhe convert 'em all,

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: That may be Phorba,
But if it be, Ile have the young men gelded:
Come, let's goe think, ſhe muſt not ſcape us thus;
There is a certain ſeaſon, if we hit,
That women may be rid without a bit. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I cannot blame the Nations noble friend,
That they fall off fo faſt from this wild man,
When (under our Allegeance be it ſpoken,
And the moſt happy tye of our affections)
The worlds weight groanes beneath him; where lives vertue,
Honour, diſcretion, wiſdom? who are cald
And choſen to the ſtleering of the Empire
But Baudes, and ſinging Girles? ô my Aecius,
The glory or a Souldier, and the truth
Of men made up for goodneſſe ſake, like ſhells
Grow to the ragged walls for want of action:
Only your happy ſelfe, and I that love ye,
Which is a larger meanes to me then favour.

sp.speaker: Aecius
sp.l: No more my worthy friend, though theſe be truths,
And though theſe truthes would aske a Reformation,
At leaſt a little ſquaring; yet remember,
We are but ſubjects Maximus; obedience
To what is done, and griefe for what is ill done,
Is all we can call ours: the hearts of Princes
Are like the Temples of the gods; pure incenſe,
Vntill unhallowed hands defile thoſe off • ings,
Burnes ever there; we muſt not put 'em out,
Becauſe the Prieſts that touch thoſe ſweetes are wicked;
We dare not deereſt friend, nay more we cannot,
While we conſider why we are, and how,
To what lawes bound, much more to what Law-giver;
Whileſt majeſtie is made to be obeyed,
And not inquired into, whileſt Gods and Angels
Make but a rule as we do, though a ſtricter;
Like deſperate and unſeaſon'd fooles let fly
Our killing angers, and forſake our honors.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: My noble Freind, from whoſe Inſtructions
I never yet tooke ſurfet, weigh but thus much,
Nor thinke I ſpeake it with ambition,
For by the Gods I do not, why Aecius,
Why are we thus, or how become thus wretched?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: You'l fall againe into your fit.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I will not.
Or are we now no more the ſons of Romanes,
No more the followers of their happy fortunes,
But conquer'd Gaules, or Quivers for the Parthians?
Why is this Emperor, this man we honor,
This God that ought to be?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: You are too curious.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Good, give me leave, why is this Author of us?

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: I dare not heare ye ſpeake thus.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Ile be modeſt,
Thus led away, thus vainly led away,
And we beholders, miſconceive me not,
I ſow no danger in my words; but wherefore
And to what end, are we the ſonnes of Fathers
Famous, and faſt to Rome? Why are their vertues
Stampt in the dangers of a thouſand Battailes,
For goodneſſe ſake, their honors, time out daring,
I thinke for our example.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Ye ſpeake nobly.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Why are we ſeeds of theſe then, to ſhake hands
With Bawdes and baſe Informers, kiſſe diſcredit,
And court her like a Miſtris? pray, your leave yet;
You'l ſay the Emperor is young, and apt
To take impreſſion rather from his pleaſures
Then any conſtant worthynſſe, it may be.
But why do theſe, the people call his pleaſures,
Exceed the moderation of a man?
Nay to ſay juſtly freind, why are they vices
And ſuch as ſhake our worthes with forraigne Nations?

sp.speaker: Aec.
sp.l: You ſearch the ſoare too deep, and I muſt tel ye,
In any other man this had been boldneſſe,
And ſo rewarded; pray depreſſe you ſpirit,
For though I conſtantly beleeve ye honeſt,
Ye were no freind for me elſe, and what now
Ye freely ſpake, but good ye owe toth Empire,
Yet take heed worthy Maximus, all eares
Heare not with that diſtinction mine doe, few
You'l find admoniſhers, but urgers of your actions,
And to the heavieſt (freind;) and pray conſider
We are but ſhadowes, motions others give us,
And though our pitties may become the times,
Iuſtly our powers cannot; make me worthy
To be your ever freind in faire allegiance,
But not in force: For durſt mine own ſoule urge me
(And by that ſoule, I ſpeake my juſt affections)
To turn my hand from truth, which is obedience,
And give the helme my vertue holds, to Anger,
Though I had both the bleſſings of the Brutij,
And both their Inſtigations, though my cauſe
Carried a face of Iuſtice beyond theirs,
And as I am a ſervant to my fortunes,
That daring ſoule, that firſt taught diſobedience,
Should feele the firſt example: Say the Prince,
As I may well beleeve, ſeemes vitious,
Who juſtly knowes tis not to try our honors?
Or ſay he be an ill Prince, are we therefore
Fit fires to purge him? No, my deareſt freind
The Elephant is never won with anger,
Nor muſt that man that would reclaime a Lyon,
Take him by'th teeth.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I pray miſtake me not.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Our honeſt actions, and the light that breakes
Like morning from our ſervice, chaſte and bluſhing
Is that, that pulls a Prince backe; then he ſees,
And not till then truly repents his errors,
When ſubjects Chryſtall ſoules are glaſſes to him.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: My ever honored freind, Ile take your councel:
The Emperor appeares, Ile leave ye to him,
And as we both affect him, may he flouriſh. Exit Max.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.p: Is that the beſt newes? Enter the Emperor and Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Yet the beſt we know Sir.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: Bid Maximus come to me, and be gone then:
Mine own head be my helper, theſe are fooles;
How now Aecius, are the Souldiers quiet?

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Better I hope Sir, then they were.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: They are pleas'd I heare,
To cenſure me extremely for my pleaſures,
Shortly the'l fight againſt me.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Gods defend Sir.
And for their cenſures they are ſuch ſhrew'd Iudgers;
A donative of ten Seſterties
Ile undertake ſhall make 'em ring your praiſes,
More then they ſang your pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: I beleeve thee.
Art thou in love Aecius yet?

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: O no Sir.
I am too courſe for Ladies; my embraces
That only am acquainted with Alarums,
Would break their tender bodies.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: Never feare it,
They are ſtronger then ye think, they'le hold the hammer
My Empreſſe ſweares thou art a luſty Souldier,
A good one I beleeve thee.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: All that goodneſſe
Is but your Graces creature.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: Tell me truly,
For thou darſt tell me.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Any thing concernes ye,
That's fit for me to ſpeake and you to pardon.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: What ſay the ſoldiers of me, and the ſame words,
Mince 'em not good Aecius, but deliver
The very forms and tongues they talke withall,

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Ile tell your Grace, but with this caution
You be not ſtirr'd, for ſhould the Gods live with us,
Even thoſe we certainly beleeve are righteous.
Give 'em but drinke, they would cenſure them too.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: Forward.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Then to begin, they ſay you ſleep too much
By which they judge your Majeſty too ſenſuall,
Apt to decline your ſtrength to eaſe and pleaſures,
And when you do not ſleepe, you drink too much,
From which they feare ſuſpitions firſt, then ruines;
And when ye neither drinke nor ſleepe, ye wench much,
Which they affirm firſt breakes your underſtanding,
Then takes the edge of honor, make us ſeeme,
That are the ribbes, and rampires of the Empire,
Fencers, and beaten Fooles, and ſo regarded;
But I beleive 'em not; for were theſe truths,
Your vertue can correct them.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: They ſpeake plainly.

sp.speaker: Aec.
sp.l: They ſay moreover (ſince your grace wil have it,
For they will talke their freedoms, though the ſword
Were in their throat) that of late time, like Nero,
And with the ſame forgetfullnes of glory,
You have got a vaine of filing, ſo they terme it.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: Some drunken dreames Aecius.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: So I hope Sir.
And that you rather ſtudy cruelty,
And to be feared for blood, then lov'd for bounty.
Which makes the Nations, as they ſay, deſpiſe ye,
Telling your yeares and actions by their deathes,
Whoſe truth, and ſtrength of duty made you Caeſar.
They ſay beſides you nouriſh ſtrange devourers,
Fed with the fat o'th Empires, they call Bawdes,
Lazie and luſtfull creatures that abuſe ye,
A people as they terme 'em, made of paper,
In which the ſecret ſins of each mans monyes
Are ſealed and ſent a working.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: What ſin's next?
For I perceive they have no mind to ſpare me.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Nor hurt ye ô my ſoule Sir; but ſuch people
(Nor can the power of man reſtraine it)
When they are full of meat and eaſe, muſt prattle.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: Forward.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: I have ſpoken too much Sir.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: Ile have all.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: It fits not
Your eares ſhould heare their vanities; no profit
Can juſtly riſe to you from their behaviour,
Vnleſſe ye were guilty of thoſe crimes.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: It may be
I am ſo, therefore forward.

sp.speaker: Aeci
sp.l: I have ever
Learn'd to obey, nor ſhall my life reſiſt it.

sp.speaker: Empe.
sp.l: No more Apologies.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: They greive beſides Sir,
To ſee the nations, whom our ancient vertue
With many a weary march and hunger conquer'd,
With loſſe of many a daring life ſubdude,
Fall from their faire obedience, and even murmure
To ſee the warlike Eagles mew their honors
In obſcure Townes, that wont to prey on Princes,
They cry for enemies, and tel the Captaines
The fruits of Italy are luſcious, give us Aegypt,
Or ſandy Affrick to diſplay our valours,
There where our Swords may make us meat, and danger
Digeſt our well got Vyands: here our weapons
And bodyes that were made for ſhining braſſe,
Are both unedg'd and old with eaſe, and women;
And then they cry agen, where are the Germaines,
Linde with hot Spaine, or Gallia, bring 'em on,
And let the ſon of war, ſteel'd Mithridates,
Lead up his winged Parthians like a ſtorme,
Hiding the face of Heaven with ſhowres of arrowes;
Yet we dare fight like Romanes; then as Souldiers
Tyr'd with a weary march, they tell their wounds
Even weeeping ripe they were no more nor deeper,
And glory in thoſe ſcarrs that make 'em lovely,
And ſitting where a Campe was, like ſad Pilgrims
They reckon up the times, and living labours
Of Julius or Germanicus, and wonder
That Rome, whoſe turrets once were topt with honours,
Can now forget the Cuſtome of her conqueſts:
And then they blame your Grace, and ſay who leads us,
Shall we ſtand here like Statues? were our Fathers
The Sonnes of lazie Moores, our Princes Perſians,
Nothing but ſilkes, and ſoftneſſe? curſes on 'em
That firſt taught Nero wantonneſſe, and bloud,
Tiberius doubts, Caligula all vices;
For from the ſpring of theſe ſucceeding Princes
Thus they talke Sir;

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Well,
Why doe you heare theſe things?

sp.speaker: Aec.
sp.l: Why do you do 'em?
I take the gods to witneſſe, with more ſorrow,
And more vexation, doe I heare theſe taintures,
Then were my life dropt from me through an hour-glaſſe

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Belike then you beleeve 'em, or at leaſt
Are glad they ſhould be ſo; take heed, you were better
Build your own Tomb, and runne into it living,
Then dare a Princes anger.

sp.speaker: Aec.
sp.l: I am old Sir,
And ten yeares more addition, is but nothing:
Now if my life be pleaſing to ye, take it,
Vpon my knees, if ever any ſervice,
As let me brag, ſome have bin worthy notice,
If ever any worth, or truſt ye gave me,
Deſerv'd a faire reſpect, if all my actions,
The hazards of my youth, colds, burnings, wants,
For you and for the Empire, be not vices,
By that ſtile ye have ſtampt upon me, Souldier,
Let me not fall into the hands of wretches.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: I underſtand ye not.

sp.speaker: Aec.
sp.l: Let not this body,
That has lookd bravely in his bloud for Ceſar,
And covetous of wounds, and for your ſafety,
After the ſcape of Swords, Speares, Slings, and Arrows,
Gainſt which my beaten body was mine Armour,
The Seas, and thirſtie deſerts, now be purchaſe
For Slaves, and baſe Informers: I ſee anger,
And death look through your eyes: I am markt for ſlaughter
And know the telling of this truth has made me
A man cleane loſt to this world; I embrace it;
Only my laſt Petition ſacred Ceſar,
Is, I may dye a Roman.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Riſe my friend ſtill,
And worthy of my love; Reclaime the Souldier,
Ile ſtudy to doe ſo upon my ſelfe too,
Goe keep your command, and proſper.

sp.speaker: Aec.
sp.p: Life to Ceſar —Exit Aecius—Enter Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Lord Maximus attends your Grace.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Goe tell him,
Ile meete him in the gallery.
The honeſty of this Aecius
Who is indeed the Bull-wark of the Empire,
Has div'd ſo deep into me, that of all
The ſins I covet, but this womans beautie,
With much repentance, now I could be quit of:
But ſhe is ſuch a pleaſure, being good,
That though I were a god, ſhe would fire my bloud. Exit

div.head: Scaena prima.
div.stage: Enter the Emperour, Maximus, Lycinius, Proculus, Chilax, as at Dice.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: NAY ye ſhall ſet my hand out, tis not juſt
I ſhould neglect my fortune, now tis proſperous.

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: If I have any thing to ſet your Grace,
But Clothes or good conditions, let me periſh,
You have all my mony Sir;

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: And mine,

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: And mine too.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Vnleſſe your Grace will credit us,

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: No bare boord,

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: Then at my Garden-Houſe;

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: The Orchard too.

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: And't pleaſe your Grace,

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Have at 'em,

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: They are loſt;

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: Why farewell Fig-trees,

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Who ſets more?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: At my Horſe Sir,

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: The dapl'd Spaniard?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: He.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: He's mine,

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: He is ſo;

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Your ſhorthorſe is ſoone curried:

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: So it ſeemes Sir,
So may your Mare be too, if luck ſerve.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Ch.
sp.l: Nothing my Lord but grieving at my fortune,

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Come Maximus, you were not wont to flinch thus

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: By Heaven Sir, I have loſt all.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Ther's a ring yet,

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: This was not made to looſe Sir,

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Some love token;
Set it I ſay;

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I doe beſeech your Grace,
Rather name any houſe I have.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: How ſtrange,
And curious you are growne of toyes? redeem't
If ſo I win it, when you pleaſe, to morrow,
Or next day as ye will, I care not,
But only for my luck ſake: Tis not Rings
Can make me richer.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Will you throw Sir? there 'tis:

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Why then have at it fairely: myne.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Your Grace
Is only ever fortunate: to morrow,
An't be your pleaſure Sir, Ile pay the price on't;

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: To morrow you ſhall have it without price Sir,
But this day 'tis my victory: good Maximus,
Now I bethink my ſelfe, goe to Aecius,
And bid him muſter all the Cohorts preſently;
They mutiny for pay I heare, and be you
Aſſiſtant to him; when you know their numbers,
Ye ſhall have monyes for 'em, and above
Something to ſtop their tongues withall.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I will Sir,
And gods preſerve you in this mind ſtill.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Shortly Ile ſee 'em march my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Gods ever keep ye. —Exit Max.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: To what end doe you think this ring ſhall ſerve now?
For you are fellowes only know by roate,
As birds record their leſſons.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: For the Lady,

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: But how for her?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: That I confeſſe I know not,

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Then pray for him that do's: fetch me an Eunuch
That never ſaw her yet: and you two ſee. Exit. Chil.
The Court made like a Paradiſe.

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: We will Sir.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Full of faire ſhewes and Muſiques; all your arts
(As I ſhall give inſtructions) ſcrew to'th higheſt,
For my maine peece is now a doing: and for feare
You ſhould not take, Ile have an other engine,
Such as if vertue be not only in her,
She ſhall not chooſe but leane to, let the women
Put on a graver ſhew of welcome.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Well Sir.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.p: They are a thought too eager.— Enter Chilax and Lycias the Eunuch.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Here's the Eunuch,

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: Long life to Ceſar.
