sp.l: The place is unlucky,

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No certaine, tis ſcarcity of mony; doe not you here the Lawyers complain of it? men have as much malice as ever they had to wrangle, but they have no mony: whether ſhould this mony be tralaunct?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: To the Devill I think.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Tis with his cofferer I am certaine, that's the Vſurer.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Our cheating does not proſper ſo well as it was wont to doe.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No ſure, why in England we coo'd cozen 'em as familiarly, as if we had travaild with a Briefe, or a Lotterie.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: I'th Low-countries we did prety well.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: So ſo, as long as we kept the Mop-headed butter-boxes ſober; marry when they were drunke, then they grew buzards: You ſhould have them reel their heads together, and deliberate; your Dutchman indeed when he is foxt, is like a Fox; for when hee's ſunke in drink, quite earth to a mans thinking, tis full Exchange time with him, then hee's ſubtleſt; but your Switzert, was nothing to cheate him.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Nothing?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No nor conſcience to bee made of it; for ſince nature afore-hand cozend him of his wit, 'twas the leſſe ſinne for us to cozen him of his mony.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: But theſe Italians are more nimble-pated, wee muſt have ſome new trick for them, I proteſt but that our Hoſtiſſe daughter is a ſweet laſſe, and drawes great reſort to'th houſe, we were as good draw teeth a horſeback.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I told 'em in the Market place you could conjure, and no body would beleeve me: but ere long I will make'em beleeve you can conjure with ſuch a figuary.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: What language ſhal's conjure in? high Dutch
I thinke, that's full i'th mouth.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No, no, Spaniſh, that roares beſt; and will appeare more dreadfull.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Prethee tell me thy conceit thou haſt to gull them.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No, no, I will not ſteale it; but my dear Iews-trump, for thou art but my inſtrument, I am the plotter, and when we have cozen'd 'em moſt titely, thou ſhalt ſteale away the Inn-keepers daughter, I'le provide my ſelfe of another moveable: and wee will moſt purely retire our ſelues to Geneva.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Thou art the compaſſe I ſaile by.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Was ever expectation of ſo Noble
A requitall anſwered with ſuch contumely!
A wild Numidian that had ſuck't a Tigreſſe,
Would not have bin ſo barbarous; did he threat
To cut thy hand off?

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Yes Sir, and his ſlaves were ready to perform't.

sp.speaker: Bapt.
sp.l: What hindred it?

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Onely his ſonnes intreaty.

sp.speaker: Bapt.
sp.l: Noble youth,
I wiſh thou wert not of his blood; thy pitty
Gives me a hope thou art not.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: You miſtake Sir,
The injury that followed from the ſonne,
sp.p: Was worſe then the fathers; he did firſt diſarme and tooke from me a Iewell which I prize above my hand or life.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Take thy ſword from thee?
He ſtole it like a thiefe rather, he could not
I'th field deprive thee of it.

sp.speaker: Ment
sp.l: He tooke it from me,
And ſent me forth ſo thinne, and ſo unmade up,
As if I had bin a Foote-boy.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: O my fury!
I muſt now aske thee forgiveneſſe, that my raſhneſſe
Bred out of too much friendſhip, did expoſe thee
To ſo eminent a danger; which I vowe
I will revenge on the whole Family:
All the calamities of my whole life,
My baniſhment from Genoa, my wifes loſſe
Compar'd to this indignity is nothing;
Their Family ſhall repair't; it ſhall be to them
Like a plague, when the Dog-ſtar reignes moſt hot:
An Italians revenge may pauſe, but's ne're forgot. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: I would I had conceal'd this from my father,
For my intereſt in Clariſſa; my care now
Muſt be to untangle this diviſion,
That our moſt equall flames may be united;
And from theſe various and perturbed ſtreames
Riſe like a ſweet morne after terrible dreames.— Exit

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: I am happy in your recovery,
And I Siſter, am ever beſt pleaſed in your happineſſe:
But I wiſh a toy ſhould be on your finger.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: My Ring this morning when I waſh't
I put it off, ti's in my windowe.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: Wher's your Looking-glaſſe?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Here Sir.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: T'is a faire one.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: T'is pure Chryſtall.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: Can a Diamond cut in Cryſtall? let me ſee,
I'le grave my name in't.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Oh, you'l ſpoyl my glaſſe.
Would you not have your brother in your eye?

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: I had thougt he had bin Planted in your heart,
Looke you, the Diamond cuts quaintly, you are cozen'd,
Your Cryſtall is too britle.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: T'is the Ring
I gave unto Mentivole, ſure the ſame.
You put me to amazement Sir, and horror;
How came you by that ring?

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: Does the blood riſe?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Pray Sir reſolve me, ô for pitty doe;
And take from me a trembling at the heart,
That elſe will kill me: for I too much feare
Nothing but Death could raviſh ir from his hand
That wore it.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Was it given to Mentivola on that condition?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Tell me of his health firſt.
And then I'le tell you any thing.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: By my life he's well,
In better health then I am.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Then it was Sir.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Then ſhall I ever hate thee, oh thou falſe one;
Haſt thou a Faith to give unto a friend,
And breake it to a brother? did I not
By all the tyes of blood importune thee
Never to part with it without my knowledge?
Thou might'ſt have given it to a Muliter,
And made a contract with him in a ſtable
At as cheap a price of my vengeance: never more
Shall a Womans truſt beguile me; You are all
Like Reliques: you may well be look't upon,
But come a man to'th handling of you once,
You fall in peeces.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Dear Sir, I have no way
Look't either beneath reaſon or my ſelfe
In my election; there's parity in our blood,
And in our fortunes, ancient amity
Betwixt our parents: to which wants nothing,
But the fruit of bleſt marriage between us,
To add to their poſterities: nor does now
Any impeachment riſe, except the ſad
And unexpected quarrell which divided
So noble and ſo excellent a friendſhip,
Which as I ner'e had Magick to foreſee
So I could not prevent.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Well you muſt give me leave
To have a hand in your diſpoſing, I ſhall
In the abſence of my father be your Guardian;
His Suit muſt paſſe through my office. Mentivole,
He has too much of my blood already; he has,
And he gets no more of't—
Wherefore weep you mother?

sp.speaker: Marian.
sp.l: T'is occaſion'd by a ſorrow,
Wherein you have a childs part, and the maineſt,
Your Father's dead.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Dead?

sp.speaker: Marian.
sp.l: There's one can relate the reſt.

sp.speaker: Sailor.
sp.l: I can Sir, your Father's drown'd,
Moſt unfortunately drownd.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: How? in a tempeſt?

sp.speaker: Sailor.
sp.l: No Sir, in a calme,
calme as this evening; the Gunner being drunk,
Forgot to faſten the Ordnance to their ports,
When came a ſuddain guſt which tumbled them
All to the ſtarboord ſide, o'returnd the ſhip,
And ſunck her in moment, ſome ſix men
That were upon the deck were ſaved: the reſt
Periſh't with your Father.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: O my deareſt Father—

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I pray thee leave us.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: I have a ſorrow of another nature, equall to the former.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: And moſt commonly they come together.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: The Family of the Baptiſti
Are growne to faction, and upon diſtaſt
Of the injury late offerd in my houſe,
Have vowd a moſt ſevere, and fell revenge
'Gainſt all our family, but eſpecially
'Gainſt you my deere Caeſario.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Let them threat, I am prepard to oppoſe them.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: And is your loſſe then
Of ſo eaſie an eſtimation, what comfort
Have I but in your life, and your late danger
Preſents afore me what I am to ſuffer,
Should you miſcarry; therefore ile adviſe you
When the Funerall is over, you would travaile,
Both to prevent their fury, and weare out the injury.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: No Mother, I will not travaile,
So in my abſence he may marry my Siſter,
I will not travaile certaine.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: O my Caeſario,
Whom I reſpect and love 'bove my owne life,
Indeed with a kind of dotage, he ſhall never
Goe forth a doores, but the contrary faction
Will indanger's life, and then am I moſt wretched.
I am thinking of a ſtrange prevention,
Which I ſhall witneſſe with a bleeding eye,
Fondneſſe ſometimes is worſe then cruelty. —Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena prima.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: HAunted, my houſe is hanted with goblins. I ſhal be frighted out of my wits, and ſet up a ſigne only to invite carriers and Foot-poſts; ſcar-crows to keep off the Cavelrie, and Gentry of the beſt rank. I will naile up my doors, and wall up my girle (wife) like an Anchoreſſe; or ſhe will be raviſht before our faces, by raſcalls and cacafugo's (wife) cacafugo's.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſſe.
sp.p: Theſe are your In-comes, remember your own proverb, the ſavour of every gaine ſmelt ſweet; thank nobody but your ſelfe for this trouble.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: No gaulling (deere Spouſe) no gaulling, every dayes new vexation abates mee two inches in the waſt, terrible pennance for an Hoſt, Girle, girle, girle, which of all this gally-maufry of mans fleſh appears tolerable to thy choice; ſpeak ſhortly, and ſpeak truly: I muſt and will know, muſt and will; here ye that?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Sir, be not jealous of my care and duty;
I am ſo far from entertaining thoughts
Of liberty, that much more excellent objects
Then any of ſuch courſe contents as theſe are,
Could not betray mine eye to force my heart;
Conceive a wiſh of any deerer happineſſe
Then your direction warrants. I am yours ſir.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſſe
sp.p: What thinks the man now? is not this ſtrange at 13.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Very good words, ther's a tang in 'em, and a ſweet one, tis muſicke (wife) and now I come t'ee. Let us a little examine the ſeverall conditions of our Paragraphiſticall ſuitors. The firſt, a travailing Tailor, who by the miſtery of his needle and thimble, hath ſurveyd the faſhions of the French, and Engliſh; this Signior Ginger-bread ſtitcht up in the ſhreds of a gaudy outſide, ſowes lineings with his croſſe legd complement, like an Ape doing tricks over a ſtaffe, cringes, and crouches, and kiſſes his fore-finger.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſſe.
sp.p: Out upon him.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: A ſecond, a lavolteteere, a ſaltatory, a dancer with a Kit at his bum, one that by teaching great Madonuas to foot it, has miraculouſly purchaſt a ribanded waſtcote, and foure cleane paire of ſocks; a fellow that skips as hee walkes, and inſtead of ſenſible diſcourſe vents the curious conceit of ſome new tune ſtolne from a Maske, or a bawdie dittie elevated for the Pole Artick of a Ladies chamber, in that fyle ſtands another of your inamoratoes

sp.speaker: Hoſteſſe.
sp.p: Hang him and his fiddle together, hee never fidles any child of ours.

sp.speaker: Host.
sp.p: The third, a Mongrell, got by a Switzer on an Italian, this puppy, being left well eſtated, comes ſo Florence, that the world may take notice, how impoſſible it is for experience to alter the courſe of nature, a foole (wife) and indeed a Clown turnd gallant, ſeldom or never proves other then a gallant foole, this toy prates to little purpoſe other then what's a clock, ſhall's go drink, de'e forſooth, and thank ye heartily; I feare no art in him to catch thee, and yet wee muſt bee tormented with this buzzard amongſt the reſt.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſſe.
sp.p: Tis your owne folly, forbid him the houſe.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: The 4th, a Mule-driver, a ſtubborn & a harſh knave: the fifth a School-Maſter, a very amorous Pedant, run almoſt mad with ſtudy df Sonnets and Complements out of old play-ends, the laſt an Advocates clerk, that ſpeaks pure Fuſtion in Law termes, excellent Courtiers all, and all as neate as a Magnifico's poſt new painted at his entrance to an office; thou ſhalt have none of 'em. Laugh at 'em doe. I ſay thou ſhalt have none of 'em.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Still your command to me ſhall ſtand a Law.

sp.speaker: Host.
sp.p: Now they throng like ſo many horſe-courſers at a faire, in cluſters about the man of art, for love powders, ingredients, potions, counſailes, poſtures, complements, philters: the devill and the—how now? tumults? batteries, noiſe? ha, get from my ſight. Clown cries within

div.stage: Enter Foroboſco and Clowne, his head bloody.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Murther me, do, pound me to Mummye, doe; ſee what will come on't.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Dog, leave thy ſnarling, or i'le cut thy tongue out,
Thou unlikt beare, darſt thou yet ſtand my fury,
My generous rage? yet! by the ſulpherous damps
That feed the hungry and inceſſant darkneſſe,
Which curles round the grim Alaſtors back,
Mutter againe, and with one powerfull word,
Ile call an Hoſt up from the Stygian lakes,
Shall waft thee to the Acherontick fennes;
Where choak't with miſts as black as thy impoſtors,
Thou ſhalt live ſtill a dying.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Conjure mee to the devill and you can. I live in hell upon earth 'em already, and you had any mercy, you would not practiſe upon a kind heart thus.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: You have drawne blood from him Signior, Is his offence unpardonable?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A lump of ignorance, pray ſpeak not for him,
A drowſie groſſeneſſe, in all chriſtian kingdomes,
The mention of my art, my name, my practiſe
Merit and glory hath begot at once
Delight and wonder; ile not be entreated;
Spare interceſſion for him,—ô thou ſcorne
Of learning, ſhame of duty; muſt thy ſloth
Draw my juſt fame in queſtion? I diſcharge thee
From my ſervice; ſee me no more henceforth.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Diſcharge me, is that my yeares wages!
Ile not be ſo anſwerd.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Not Camell, ſirra I am liberall to thee;
Thou haſt thy life, begon.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Vengeance, ſweet vengeance.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Do'e mumble?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Ile be revengd, monſtrouſly, ſudainly, and inſatiably; my bulke begins to ſwell.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Call up your ſpirits, I defie 'em; well have law for my broken pate, twelve ounces of pure bloud; Troy-weight. In deſpight of thee my Maſter, and thy Maſter the grand devill himſelfe, vindicta, vindicta. —Exit.

sp.speaker: Host.
sp.l: Signior you are exceeding mov'd.

sp.speaker: Hoſtes.
sp.l: Mercy upon us, what terrible words thou talk't?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A ſlave, a curre—but be not you affrighted
Young Virgin, 'twere an injury to ſweetneſſe:
Should any rough ſound draw from your cheekes,
The pretious tincture which makes nature proud
Of her own workmanſhip.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Wife, Marke, mark that wife.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Shake then your anger off Sir;

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: You command it
Faire one, mine Hoſt and Hoſteſſe, with your leaves
I have a motion joyntly to you all.

sp.speaker: Hosteſſe.
sp.l: An honeſt one I hope.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Well put in wife.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A very neceſſary one, the Meſſe
Stooles out. And halfe of ſuiters, that attend touſher
Their loves ſit reverence to your daughter, waite
With one conſent, which can beſt pleaſe her eye;
In offering at a dance, I have provided
Muſick. And 'twill be ſomething I dare promiſe
Worthy your laughter, ſhal they have admittance?

sp.speaker: H.
sp.l: By any means, for I am perſwaded the manner will be ſo
Ridiculous, that it will confirm the aſſurance of their
Miſerable fooleries, but no longer trouble with 'em here,
Then they are in theſe May-games.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: So I am reſolvd.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſſe.
sp.l: Nor any wiſe word of ſenceleſſe love.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Not any; I have charm'd them, did you ſee
How they prepared themſelves, how they ſtroak up
Their foretops, how they juſtle for the Looking-glaſſe,
To ſet their Faces by it;
You would look for ſome moſt impoſſible antick. See they muſter.

div.stage: Enter Tailor, Dancer, Mute Driver, Schoole-Maſter, Clarke: (all with ſeverall papers, and preſent 'em to Foroboſco.)

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: So, ſo, ſo, ſo, here flutter the neſt of hornets, the hotch-potch of raſcallity, now, now, now, now, the dung-hill of corruption hath yawnd forth the burthen of abhomination. I am vext, vext to the ſoule, will rid my houſe of this unchriſtend fry, and never open my doores again.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Some other time, ile give no anſwer now,
But have preferred your ſuits, here ſhew your cunning.
Firſt every one in order do his honour
To the faire mark you ſhoot at; courtly, courtly,
Convay your ſeverall loves in lively meaſure:
Come, let us take our ſeates, ſome ſprightly muſick.

sp.speaker: Host.
sp.l: Dance all and part, tis a very neceſſary farewell.

div.stage: Enter Caeſario, They all make ridiculous tonges, to Bianca: ranck themſelves, and dance in ſeverall postures: during the dance. Enter Caeſario, and ſtands off.

sp.speaker: Host.
sp.l: Well done my luſty blouds, preciouſly well done,
One luſty rouſe of wine, and take leave on all ſides.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Thanks for your revells Gentlemen; accept
This Gold, and drink as freely as you danc'd.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: My noble Lord Ceſario, cleer the rooms ſirs.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Away. Attend your anſwers.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.p: With your favour Rolando, I would change a word or two with your faire daughter.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: At your Lordſhips pleaſure, come wife, no muttering, have a care girle, my love, ſervice, and duty to your good Lordſhip. —Exeunt and Wife.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: My often viſits (ſweet Bianca) cannot
But conſtantly inform thy judgment, wherein
Thy happineſſe conſiſts, for to ſteale minutes
From great imployments, to converſe with beauty,
Lodg'd in ſo meane a fortune, to lay by
Conſideration of the unequall diſtance
Between my blood and thine, to ſhun occaſions
Of courtſhip with the Ladies of the time:
Noble, and faire, only for love to thee,
Muſt of neceſſity invite a tenderneſſe;
As low as nature could have ſtampt a bond womans.
To entertaine quick motions of rare gratitude
For my uncommon favours.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Deed my Lord, as far as my ſimplicity can leade mee,
I freely thank your curteſies.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: To thank them, is to reward them pretty one.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Then teach me
How I may give them back again; in truth
I never yet receiv'd a paire of Gloves:
A trifling ring from any that expected
An equall ſatisfaction, but as willingly
I parted with the gift unto the owner, as he beſtowd it.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: But I pow're before thee
Such plenties, as it lyes not in the ability
Of thy whole kindred to returne proportionable
One for a thouſand.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: You my Lord conclude
For my inſtruction, to ingage a debt
Beyond a poſſibilitie of paiment,
I ever thought a ſinne; and therefore juſtly
Without conceit of ſcorne or curious rudeneſſe,
I muſt refuſe your bounty.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Canſt thou love?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Love! is there ſuch a word in any language
That carries honeſt ſence?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Never dwelt ignorance
In ſo ſweet-ſhap't a building, love Bianca,
Is that firme knot which tyes two hearts in one,
Shall ours be tyed ſo?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Vſe a plainer word,
My Lord. Inſteed of tyes, ſay marries hearts,
Then I may underſtand.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Their hearts are married
Whoſe enterchange of pleaſures and embraces,
Soft kiſſes, and the privacies of ſweetes,
Keeps conſtant league together, when temptation
Of great mens oathes and gifts ſhall urge contempt,
Rather then batter reſolution, novelty
Of ſights, or taſte of new delights in wantonneſſe,
Breeds ſurfeit more then appetite in any
Reſerv'd to noble vowes; my excellent maide
Live thou but true to me, and my contents,
Mine only, that no partner may pertake
The treaſure of thoſe ſweets thy youth yet glories in
And I will raiſe thy lowneſſe to abundance
Of all varieties, and more triumph
In ſuch a miſtris, then great Princes doating
On truth-betraying wives.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Thus to yeeld up then
The cottage of my vertue to be ſwallow'd
By ſome hard-neighboring landlord ſuch as you are
Is in effect to love, a Lord ſo vicious!
O where ſhall innocence find ſome poore dwelling
Free from temptations tirrany.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Nay prethee;

sp.speaker: Byan.
sp.l: Gay clothes, high feeding, eaſie beds of luſt,
Change of unſeemly ſights; with baſe diſcourſe,
Draw curſes on your Pallaces; for my part
This I will be confirmd in, I will eate
The bread of labour, know no other reſt
Then what is earnd from honeſt paines, ere once more
Lend eare to your vild toyles; Sir, would you were
As noble in deſires, as I could be in knowing vertue.
Pray doe not afflict a poore ſoule thus.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.p: I ſweare.—to me? —Bianca steales off.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: The Duke my Lord commands your ſpeedy preſence
For anſwering agreivances late urg'd
Againſt you by your Mother.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: By my Mother.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: The Court is neere on ſitting.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I waite on it Sir, —Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Duke, Magiſtrate, Secretary, Baptista, Attendants, Mentivole: (they ſit) Mentivole ſtands by.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What waſt of bloud, what tumults, what diviſions,
What outrages, what uprores in a ſtate,
Factions though iſſuing from meane ſprings at firſt
Have (not reſtraind) flowed to, the ſad example
At Rome betweene the Ʋrſins and Columnies,
Nay here at home in Florence, twixt the Neers
And the Bianchi can too mainly witneſſe.
I ſit not at the helme (my Lords) of ſoveraignty
Deputed Pilot for the Common-wealth,
To ſleep whiles others ſteere (as their wild fancies
Shall councell) by the compaſſe of diſorders.
Baptiſta, This ſhort Preface is directed
Chiefly to you, the petty brawles and quarrels
Late urg'd betwixt th' Alberti and your family
Muſt, yes and ſhall like tender unknit joynts
Faſten againe together of themſelves:
Or like an angry Chyrurgion, we will uſe
The roughneſſe of our juſtice, to cut off
The ſtubborne rancour of the limbes offending.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Moſt gracious Florence.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Our command was ſignified,
That neither of the followers of each party
Should appeare here with weapons.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Tis obeyd Sir, on my ſide.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: We muſt leave the generall cauſe
Of State employments to give eare to brawles
Of ſome particular grudges, pollitick government
For tutord Princes, but no more henceforth.
sp.stage: Ent. Mariana, and Clariſſa, at one door Ceſario at the other.
sp.l: Our frowne ſhall check preſumption, not our clemency,

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: All bleſſings due to unpartiall Princes,
Crowne Florence with eternity of happineſſe.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: If double praiers can double bleſſings (great Sir)
Mine joyne for your proſperity with my mothers.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Riſe both; now briefly (Lady) without circumſtance
Deliver thoſe agrievances which lately
Your importunity poſſeſt our counſaile
Were fit for audience, wherein you petitiond,
You might be heard without an Advocate
Which boone you find is granted.

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: Though divided.
I ſtand between the laws of truth and modeſty,
Yet let my griefes have vent: Yet the cleerneſſe
Of ſtrange neceſſity requires obedience
To nature and your mercy, in my weeds
Of mourning, emblems of too deer misfortunes,
Badges of griefes, and Widdowhood, the burthen
Of my charg'd ſoule muſt be layd downe before you;
Wherein if ſtrict opinion cancell ſhame,
My frailty is my plea;
Stand forth young man,
And heare a ſtory that will ſtrike all reaſon
Into amaſement.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I attend.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Alberto (peace dwell upon his aſhes) ſtill the huſband
Of my remembrance and unchanging vowes,
Has by his death left to his heire poſſeſſion
Of faire revenew, which this young man claymes
As his inheritance. I urgd him gently,
Friendly, and privately to grant a partage
Of this eſtate to her who ownes it all
This his ſuppoſed Siſter.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: How ſuppoſed?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Pray Madam recollect your ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: The reliſh
Of a ſtrange truth begins to work like Phyſick
Already: I have bitterneſſe to mingle
With theſe preparatives, ſo deadly loathſome;
It will quite choake digeſtion; ſhortly heare it
Ceſario, for I dare not rob unjuſtly
The poore ſoule of his name; this, this Ceſario
Neither for Father had Alberto, me
For Mother, nor Clariſſa for his Siſter.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: Mother, ô Mother.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: I am in a Dream ſure.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No interruptions. Lady on,

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: How ever

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: A Faulkners ſonne:

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: Miſtake not
Great Duke of Tuſcany or the beginning
Or proceſſe of this novelty; my husband
The now deceaſd Alberto, from his youth
In-urd to an impatiency, and roughneſſe
Of diſpoſition, when not many monthes
After our marriage were worne out, repin'd
At the unfruitfull barrenneſſe of youth,
Which as he pleaſd to terme it, cut our hops off
From bleſſing of ſome iſſue, to prevent it;
I grew ambitious of no fairer honor
Then to preſerve her love, and as occaſions
Still call'd him from me, ſtudied in his abſence
How I might frame his welcome home with comfort.
At laſt I faynd my ſelfe with child; the Meſſage
Of freedome or reliefe to one halfe ſtervd
In priſon is not utter'd with ſuch greedineſſe;
Of expectation and delight as this was
To my much affected Lord, his care, his goodneſſe;
(Pardon me that I uſe the word) exceeded
All former feares, the houre of my deliverance
As I pretended drawing nee'r, I faſhiond
My birth-rights at a Country Garden houſe,
Where then my Faulkners wife was brought a bed
Of this Ceſario; him I ownd for mine;
Preſented him unto a joyfull Father.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Can you prove this true?

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: Proofes I have moſt evident;
But O the curſe of my impatiency; ſhortly
Ere three new Moones had ſpent their borrowed lights,
I grew with child indeed, ſo juſt is Heaven,
The iſſue of which burthen was this daughter;
Iudge now moſt gracious Prince my Lords and you,
What combats then and ſince I have indur'd
Between a mothers piety and weakeneſſe
Of a Soul trembling wife; to have reveal'd
This ſecret to Alberto, had bin danger
Of ruine to my fame, beſides the conflict
Of his diſtractions; now to have ſuppreſt it,
Were to defeate my child, my only child,
Of her moſt lawfull honors, and inheritance.
Caeſario, th'art a man ſtill, Education
Hath moulded thee a Gentleman, continue ſo;
Let not this fall from greatneſſe, ſinke thee lower
Then worthy thoughts may warrant, yet diſclaime
All intereſt in Albertos blood, thou haſt not
One drop of his or mine.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Produce your witneſſe.

sp.speaker: Marian.
sp.l: The Faulconers wife his mother,
And ſuch women as waited then upon me,
Sworne to the privacy of this great ſecret.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Give them all their oathes.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: O let me crave forberance, gracious Sir,
Vouchſafe me hearing.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Speake Caeſario.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Thus long
I have ſtood ſilent, and with no unwillingneſſe,
Attended the relation of my fall,
From a fair expectation; what I fear'd
(Sinc the firſt ſillable this Lady utter'd
Of my not being hers) benevolent Fates
Have eaſ'd me off; for to be baſely born,
If not baſe-born, detracts not from the bounty
Of natures freedom or an honeſt birth.
Nobilitie claym'd by the right of blood,
Sh • wes chiefly that our Anceſtors deſir'd
What we inherit; but that man whoſe actions
Purchaſe a reall merit to himſelfe,
And rancks him in the file of of prayſe and honour,
Creates his own advancement; let me want
The fuell which beſt feedes the fires of greatneſſe,
Lordly poſſeſſions, yet ſhall ſtill my gratitude
By ſome attempts of mention not unworthy
Indeavour to returne a fit acquittance
To that large debt I owe your favours (Madam)
And great Alberto's memory and goodneſſe;
O that I could as gently ſhake off paſſion
For the loſſe of what great brave man as I can ſhake off
Remembrance of that once I was reputed;
I have not much to ſay, this Princely preſence
Needs not too ſtrictly to examine farther
The truth of this acknowlegment; a mother
Dares never diſavowe her only ſonne,
And any woman muſt come ſhort of Piety,
That can or diſ-inherit her own iſſue,
Or feares the voice of rumor for a ſtranger.
Madam, you have confeſt, my Father was
A ſervant to your Lord and you: by intereſt
Of being his ſonne, I cannot but claime juſtly
The honour of continuing ſtill my ſervice
To you and yours; which granted, I beg leave
I may for this time be diſmiſt.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Bold ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: I love thee now with pitty;

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Goe not yet—
A ſuddain tempeſt that might ſhake a rock,
Yet he ſtands firm againſt it; much it moves me,
He not Alberto's ſonne, and ſhe a widdow,
And ſhe a widdow,— Lords your eare.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: Your pleaſure.— Whiſpers.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: So, Lady, what you heard avouch't is truth.

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: Truth onely, gracious Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Heare then our Sentence.
Since from his cradle you have fed and foſtered
Caeſario as your ſonne, and train'd him up
To hopes of greatneſſe; which now in a moment
You utterly againe have ruin'd, this way
We with our Councell are reſolv'd, you being
A widdow ſhall accept him for a husband.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Husband to me Sir?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: T'is in us to raiſe him
To honours, and his vertues will deſerve 'em.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: But Sir, 'tis in no Prince nor his preogative,
To force a womans choice againſt her heart.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: True, if then you appeale to higher juſtice,
Our doome includes this clauſe upon refuſall
Out of your Lords revenues ſhall Caeſario
Aſſure to any whom he takes for wife
The inheritance of three parts; the leſſe remainer
Is dowry large enough to marry a daughter;
And we by our prerogative which you queſtion
Will publiquely adopt him into'th name
Of your deceaſ'd Alberto, that the memory
Of ſo approv'd a Peer may live in him
That can preſerve his memory leſſe you find out
Some other meanes which may as amply ſatisfie
His wrong, our Sentence ſtands irrevocable:
What think you Lords?

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: The Duke is juſt and honorable.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Let me embrace Caeſario, henceforth ever
I vow a conſtant friendſhip.

sp.speaker: Mentivole.
sp.l: I remit all former difference.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I am too poore
In words to thanke this Iuſtice. Madam alwayes
My ſtudies ſhall be love to you, and duty.
Duke Replyes we admit none. Caeſario waite on us.

div.stage: Exeunt. Manent Mentivole, Bap. Mari. Clariſ.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Looke on Clariſſa, ſhee's noble, rich, young, faire.

sp.speaker: Mentivole.
sp.l: My Lord, and vertuous.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Mentivole and vertuous.—Madam.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Tyranny of juſtice, I ſhall live reports deriſion,
That am compeld to exchange a gracefull widdow-hood
For a continuall Martyrdome in marriage,
With one ſo much beneath me.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: I'le plead for ye
Boldly and conſtantly, let you • daughter only
Admit my ſonne her ſervant, at next viſit
Madam ile be a meſſenger of comfort.
Mentivole, be confident and earneſt. Exit.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Married again, to him too! better t'had been
The young man ſhould have ſtill retain'd the honors
Of old Albertos ſon, then I the ſhame
Of making him ſucceſſor of his bed; I was too blam,

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Indeed without offence,
Madame I thinke you were,

sp.speaker: Claris.
sp.l: You urge it fairely, and like a worthy freind.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: can you ſay any thing
In commendation of a Muſhroome withered
Aſſoone as ſtarted up?

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: You ſcorne an Innocent
Of noble growth, for whiles your husband liv'd
I have heard you boaſt Ceſario in all actions
Gave matter of report of Imitation,
Wonder and envy; let not diſcontinuance
Of ſome few dayes eſtrange a ſweet opinion
Of vertue, cheifely when in ſuch extremity,
Your pitty not contempt will argue goodneſſe.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: O Sir,

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: If you would uſe a thriving courtſhip,
You cannot utter a more powerfull language
That I ſhall liſten to with greater greedineſſe
Then th'argument you proſecute; this ſpeakes you
A man compleat and excellent;

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: I ſpeake not, they are his owne deſerts.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Good Sir forbeare,
I am now fully ſenſible of running
Into a violent Lethargy, whoſe deadlineſſe
Locks up all reaſon, I ſhall never henceforth
Remember my paſt happineſſe.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Theſe clouds may be diſperſt,

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: I feare continuall night
Will over-ſhroud me, yet poore youth his treſpaſſe
Lies in his fortune, not the cruelty
Of the Dukes ſentence.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I dare thinke it does,

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: If all faile I will learne thee to conquer
Adverſity with ſufferance.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: You reſolve Nobly. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena prima.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Let any freind have entrance,

sp.speaker: Servant.
sp.l: Sir a'ſhall.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Any, I except none,

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Wee know, your minde Sir —Exit.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Pleaſures admit no bounds.
I am pitcht ſo high
To ſuch a growth of full proſperities
That to conceale my fortunes were an injury?
To gratfulneſſe and thoſe more liberall favours
By whom my glories proſper. He that flowes
In gracious and ſwolne tydes of beſt abundance,
Yet will be Ignorant of his owne fortunes,
Deſerves to live contemn'd, and dye forgotten;
The harveſt of my hopes is now already
Ripen'd and gather'd, I can fatten youth
With choice of plenty, and ſupplies of comforts,
My fate ſprings in my owne hand, and Ile uſe it.
Tis my place,
Yours- here faire one, Ile aquaint my Lord,
He's here, go to him boldly.
Pleaſe you to let him underſtand how readily
I waited on your errand?
Saucy fellow, you muſt excuſe his breeding,

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Whats the matter
Biancha, my Biancha, to your offices. Exit Ser.
This viſit (Sweet) from thee (my pretty deere)
By how much more twas unexpected, comes
So much the more timely: witnes this free welcome,
What ere occaſion led thee?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: You may guſſe Sir,
Yet indeed tis a rare one,

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Prethee ſpeake it, my honeſt vertuous maide,

sp.speaker: Bian,
sp.l: Sir I have heard
Of your misfortune, and I cannot tell you
Whether I have more cauſe of joy or ſadneſſe,
To know they are a truth.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: What truth Bianca! misfortunes, how, wherein?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: You are diſclaym'd
For being the Lord Albertos ſonne, and publickly
Acknowledg'd of as meane a birth as mine is,
It cannot chuſe but greive thee

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Greive me, ha ha ha ha? is this all?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: This all.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Thou art ſorry for't
I warrant thee, alas good ſoule, Biancha,
That which thou call'ſt misfortune is my happines,
my happines Biancha.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: If you love me, it may prove mine too,
May it, I will love thee.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: My good good maid,
If that can make thee happy,
Better and better love thee,

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Without breach then
Of modeſty I come to claime the Intereſt
Your proteſtations both by vowes and letters
Have made me owner of, from the firſt houre
I ſaw you, I confeſſe I wiſht J had beene
Or not ſo much below your ranke and greatneſſe,
Or not ſo much above thoſe humble flames
That ſhould have warm'd my boſome with a temperate
Equality of deſires in equall fortunes.
Still as you utter'd Language of affection,
I courted time to paſſe more ſlowly on
That I might turne more food to lend attention
To what I durſt not credit nor yet hope for:
Yet ſtill as more I heard, I wiſht to heare more,

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Didſt thou introth wench

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Willingly betraid
My ſelfe to hopeleſſe bondage.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: A good girle,
I thought I ſhould not miſſe
What eare thy anſwer was.

sp.speaker: Biancha.
sp.l: But as I am a maid Sir, and I'faith
You may beleeve me, for I am a maid,
So deerely I reſpected both your fame
And quality, that I would firſt have periſht
In my ſicke thoughts then ere have given conſent
To have undone your fortunes by inviting
A marriage with ſo meane a one as I am,
I ſhould have dyed ſure, and no creature knowne
The ſickneſſe that had kill'd me.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Pretty heart, good ſoule, alas. alas.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Now ſince I know
There is no difference twixt your birth and mine.
Not much twixt our eſtates, if any bee,
The advantage is on my ſide, I come willingly
To tender you the firſt fruits of my heart,
And am content t'accept you for my husband,
Now when you are at loweſt.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: For a husband?
Speake ſadly, doſt thou meane ſo?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: In good deed Sir,
Tis pure love makes this proffer.

sp.speaker: Ceſ
sp.l: I beleeve thee,
What counſaile urg'd thee on, tell me, thy Father
My worſhipfull ſmug Hoſt? waſt not he wench?
Or mother Hoſteſſe? ha?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: D'ee mock my parentage?
I doe not ſcorne yours.
Meane folkes are as worthy
To be well ſpoken of if they deſerve well,
As ſome whoſe only fame lies in their bloud.
O y'are a proud poore man: all your oathes falſhood,
your vowe deceite, your letters forg'd, and wicked.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Thou'dſt be my wife. J dare ſware,

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Had your heart,
Your hand and tongue been twins, you had reputed
This courteſy a benefit,

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Simplicity,
How prettily thou mov'ſt me? why Biancha
Report has cozned thee, I am not fallen
From my expected honors, or poſſeſſions.
Though from the hope of birthright.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Are you not?
Then I am loſt againe, I have a ſuit too;
Youle grant it if you be a good man.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Any thing,

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Pray doe not talke of ought what I have ſaid tee.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: As I wiſh health I will not.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Pitty me, but never love me more.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Nay now y'are cruell,
Why all theſe teares?—Thou ſhalt not goe.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Ile pray for yee
That you may have a vertuous wife, a faire one,
And when I am dead—

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Fy, fy,

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Thinke on me ſometimes,
With mercy ſo this treſpaſſe.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Let us kiſſe
At parting as at comming.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: This I have
As a free dower to a virgins grave,
All goodneſſe dwell with yee. —Exit.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Harmeleſſe Biancha? unskild,
What hanſome toyes are maids to play with?
How innocent. but I have other thoughts
Of nobler meditation.—my felicity,
Thou commeſt as I could wiſh, lend me a lip
Soft, as melting as when old Alberto
After his firſt nights triall taking farewell
Of thy youthes conqueſt taſted.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: You are uncivill.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: I will be Lord of my owne pleaſures, Madame
Y'are mine, mine freely,
Come, no whimpering henceforth
New con the leſſons of loves beſt experiencd,
That our delights may meet in equal meaſure
Of reſolutions and deſires; this ſullenes
Is ſcurvy, I like it not,

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Be modeſt.
And doe not learne Ceſario how to proſtitute
The riot of thy hopes to common folly;
Take a ſad womans word, how ere thou doateſt
Vpon the preſent graces of thy greatnes,
Yet I am not falne ſo belowe my conſtancy
To vertue, nor the care which I once tendred
For thy behoof that I prefer a ſentence
Of cruelty before my honor.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Honor!

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Hear me, thou ſeeſt this girle! now the comfort
Of my laſt dayes. She is the onely pledge
Of a bed truly noble, ſhee had a father
(I need not ſpeake him more then thou remembreſt)
Whom to diſhonor by a meaner choice,
Were injury and infamy,

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: to goodnes,
To time and vertuous mention.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I have vow'd,
Obſerve me now Cſeario, that how ere
I may be forc't to marry, yet no tyranny,
Perſwaſions, flattery, guifts, intreats, or tortures,
Shall draw me to a ſecond bed.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Tis Iuſt too

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Yes and tis Iuſt Clariſſa. I allow
The Dukes late ſentence, am reſolv'd young man
To be thy wife, but when the ceremony
Of marriage is perform'd, in life I wil bee
Though not in name a widdow.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Pray a word Tee,
Shall I in earneſt never be your bedfellow?

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Never, ô never; and tis for your good too.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Prove that.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Alas too many yeares are numbred
In my account to entertaine the benefit
Which youth in thee Ceſario and ability
Might hope for and require, it were Injuſtice
To rob a gentleman deſerving memory
Of Iſſue to preſerve it.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: No more herein,
You are an excellent patterne of true piety,
Let me now turne your advocate. Pray looke into
The order of the Duke, Jnjoynd, admit
J ſatisfie the ſentence without mariage
with you, how then?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Ceſario.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: If I know
How to acquit your feares, yet keepe th'injunction
In every clauſe whole and entire, your charity
Will call me ſtill your ſervant.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Still my ſon.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Right Madam, now you have it, ſtill your ſon.
The Genius of your bleſſings hath inſtructed
Your tongue oraculouſly, wee wil forget
How once I and Clariſſa enterchangd
The tyes of brother and of ſiſter, henceforth
New ſtile us man and wife.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: By what authority

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Heavens great appointment, yet in all my dotage
On thy perfections, when I thought Clariſſa
Wee had beene pledges of one wombe, no looſe
No wanton heat of youth, deſir'd to claime
Priority in thy affections, other
Then nature might commend. Chaſtly I tendred
Thy farewell as a brother ought; but ſince
Our bloods are ſtrangers, let our hearts contract
A long life-laſting unity, for this way
The ſentence is to be obſervd or no way.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Then no way.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: I expected other anſwer Madam from you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No, every age ſhall curſe me,
The monſter, and the prodigie of nature,
Horrors beyond extremity,

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Pray mother confine the violence of greife

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Yes mother, pray do.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Thus ſome catch at a matrons honor
By flying luſt to plot Inceſtuous witchcrafts,
More terrible then whoredomes; cruell mercy
When to preſerve the body from a death
The ſoule is ſtrangled.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: This is more then paſſion.
It comes neere to diſtraction.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am quieted.
Ceſario, thou maieſt tell the Duke ſecurely
Albertos titles, honors and revenues,
The Duke may give away, Injoy them thou.
Clariſſas birthright, Marianas dower
Thou ſhalt be Lord of; turne us to the world
Vnpittyed and unfreinded, yet my bed
Thou never ſleep'ſt in; as for her; ſhe heares me,
If ſhe as much as in a thoughts conſent;
That thou may'ſt call her wife, a Mothers curſe
Shall never leave her.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: As a brother once
I lov'd you, as a noble freind yet honor ye,
But for a husband ſir, I dare not owne you,
My faith is given already.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: To a Villaine, Ile cut his throat.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why this is more then paſſion?
It comes neere a diſtraction.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Call to minde Sir.
How much you have abated of that goodneſſe
Which once raign'd in ye, they appear'd ſo lovely
That ſuch as freindſhip led to obſervation
Courted the great example.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Left and flatterd into abroad deriſion

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why dee thinke ſo?
My Lord Baptiſta, is your ſonne growne cold
In haſting on the marriage, which his vowes
Have ſeald to my wrongd daughter?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Wee come Lady, to conſummate the contract.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: With Mentivole? is he the man?

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Clariſſas, troth and mine,
Ceſario are recorded in a character
So plaine and certaine, that except the hand
Of heaven, which writ it firſt, would blot it out againe,
No human power can raze it.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: But ſay you ſo too? young Lady,

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ſhould els betray
My heart to falſhood, and my tongue to perjury.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Madam, you know the ſentence.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: From the Duke,
I have particular comforts which require
A private eare.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I ſhall approve it gladly,
Wee are reſolvd Ceſario.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Be not inſolent upon a Princes favour.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Looſe no glory,
Your younger yeares have purchaſt.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: And deſervd too y'have many worthy freinds.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Preſerve and uſe them. Exeunt: Manet Ceſar.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Good, very good, why heres a complement
Of mirth in deſperation, I could curſe
My fate. ô with what ſpeed men tumble downe
From hopes that ſoare to high. Biancha now
May ſcorne me juſtly too, Clariſſa married,
Albertos widdow reſolute, Biancha
Refuſd, and I forſaken, let me ſtudy,
I can but dye a Batchelor thats the worſt on't. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Hoſt, Taylor, Muliter, Dancer, Pedant, Coxcombe.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Come Gentlemen,
This is the day that our great artiſt hath
Promiſt to give all your ſeverall ſuites ſatisfaction.

sp.speaker: Dancer.
sp.l: Is he ſtirring?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: He hath beene at his booke theſe two houres.

sp.speaker: Pedant.
sp.l: Hees a rare Phyſitian.

sp.speaker: Host.
sp.l: Why Ile tell you,
Were Paracelſus the German now
Living, heed take up his ſingle rapier againſt his
Terrible long ſword, he makes it a matter of nothing
To cure the goute, ſore eyes he takes out as familiarly,
Waſhes them, and puts them in againe,
As you'd blanch almonds.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: They ſay he can make gold.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I, I, he learnt it of Kelly in Germany.
Theres not a Chimiſt
In chriſtendome can goe beyond him for multiplying.

sp.speaker: Pedant.
sp.l: Take heed then,
He get not up your daughters belly my Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: You are a merry Gentleman
And the man of art will love you the better.

sp.speaker: Dancer.
sp.l: Does he love mirth and crotchets?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: O hees the moſt courteous Phyſitian,
You may drink or drab in's company freely,
The better he knowes how your diſeaſe growes,
The better he knowes how to cure it.

sp.speaker: Danc.
sp.l: But I wonder my Hoſt
He has no more reſort of Ladyes to him.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Why Sir?

sp.speaker: Dan.
sp.l: O divers of them have great beleife in conjurers
Lechery is a great helpe to the quality.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Hee's ſcarce knowne to be in towne yet,
Ere long we ſhall have em come
hurring hither in Fetherbeds.

sp.speaker: Dan.
sp.l: How? bedridden.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: No ſir, in fetherbeds that move upon 4 wheeles in Spaniſh caroches.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Pray acquaint him we give attendance.

sp.speaker: Host,
sp.l: I ſhall gentlemen. I would faine be rid
Of theſe raſcalls, but that they raiſe profit
To my wine-ſeller;
When I have made uſe of them ſufficiently,
I will intreat the conjurer to tye crackers to their tailes,
And ſend them packing.

div.stage: Enter Foroboſco as in his Study. (A paper)

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Come hither mine Hoſt looke here.

sp.speaker: Host.
sp.l: Whats that?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A challenge from my man.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: For breakings pate?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: He writes here if I meet him not
Ith Feild within this halfe houre,
I ſhall heare more from him.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: O ſir, minde your profit,
Nere thinke of the raſcall, here are the gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Morrow my worthy clients,
What are you all prepard of your queſtions?
That I may give my reſolution upon them,

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: We are ſir.

sp.speaker: Pedant,
sp.l: And have brought our mony.

sp.speaker: Foro
sp.l: Each then in order,
And differ not for precedency.

sp.speaker: Dan.
sp.l: I am buying of an office ſir,
And to that purpoſe I would faine learne
to diſſemble cunningly.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Doe you come to me for that? you ſhould rather
Have gone to a cunning woman.

sp.speaker: Danc.
sp.l: I ſir but their Inſtructions are but like women,
Pretty well but not to the depth, as I'do have it,
You are a conjurer, the devils maſter,
And I would learn it from you ſo exactly,

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: That the divill himſelfe
Might not go beyond you,

sp.speaker: Danc.
sp.l: You are ith right ſir.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: And ſo your mony for your purchaſe
Might come in againe within a 12 month.

sp.speaker: Danc.
sp.l: I would be a Graduate ſir, no freſhman.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Heres my hand ſir,
I will make you diſſemble ſo methodically,
As if the divell ſhould be ſent from the great Turke,
In the ſhape of an Embaſſador
To ſet all the chriſtian princes at variance.

sp.speaker: Danc.
sp.l: I cannot with any modeſty deſire any more,
Theres your mony ſir,

sp.speaker: Foco.
sp.l: For the art of diſſembling.

sp.speaker: Cox.
sp.l: My ſuite ſir will be newes to you when I tell it,

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Pray on.

sp.speaker: Cox.
sp.l: I would ſet up a preſſe here in Italy,
To write all the Caranta for Chriſtendome.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Thats newes indeed,
And how would you imploy me in't?

sp.speaker: Cox.
sp.l: Marry ſir, from you
I would gaine my intelligence.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: I conceave you, you would have me furniſh you
With a ſpirit to informe you.

sp.speaker: Cox.
sp.l: But as quiet a Divell as the woman,
The firſt day and a halfe after ſhe's married,
I can by no meanes indure a terrible one.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: No, no, Ile qualifie him,
He ſhall not fright you,
It ſhall be the ghoſt of ſome lying Stationer,
sp.p: A Spirit ſhall looke as if butter would not melt in his mouth, A new Mercurius Gallobelgicus.

sp.speaker: Coxc.
sp.l: O there was a captaine was rare at it,

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Nere thinke of him,
Though that captaine writ a full hand gallop,
And waſted indeed more harmeleſſe paper then
Ever did laxative Phyſick,
Yet wil I make you to out-ſcribble him,
And ſet downe what you pleaſe,
The world ſhall better beleeve you.

sp.speaker: Cox.
sp.l: Worthy ſir I thanke you, there's mony.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A new office
For writing pragmaticall Curranto's

sp.speaker: Pedant.
sp.l: I am a ſchoole-maſter ſir,
And would faine conferre with you
About erecting 4 new ſects of religion at Amſterdam.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: What the Divell ſhould
New ſects of religion doe there?

sp.speaker: Pedaot.
sp.l: I aſſure you I would get
A great deale of mony by it.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: And what are the 4 new ſects
Of religion you would plant there?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Why thats it I come about ſir,
Tis a Divel of your raiſing muſt invent 'em,
I confeſſe I am too weake to compaſſe it.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: So ſir, then you make it a matter of no difficulty
To have them tolerated.

sp.speaker: Pedant.
sp.l: Trouble not your ſelfe for that,
Let but your Divel ſet them a foot once,
I have Weavers, and Ginger-bread makers,
And mighty Aquavitae-men, ſhall ſet them a going.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: This is ſomewhat difficult,
And will aske ſome conference with the divell.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Take your owne leaſure ſir,
I have another buſines too, becauſe I meane
To leave Jtaly, and bury my ſelfe in thoſe neather parts
Of the low countries.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Whats that ſir.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Marry I would faine make 9 dayes to the weeke, for the more ample benefit of the captaine.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: You have a ſhrewd pate ſir.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: But how this might be compaſd?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Compaſd eaſily; tis but making
A new Almanacke, and dividing the compaſſe
Of the yeare into larger penny-worths,
As a Chandler with his compaſſe makes
A Geometrick proportion of the Holland cheeſe
He retailes by ſtivers.
But for getting of it licenc'd.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Trouble not your ſelfe with that ſir,
Theres your mony,

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: For foure new ſects of religions,
And 9 dayes to the weeke.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: To be brought in at generall pay-dayes,
Write I beſeech you.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: At generall pay-dayes.

sp.speaker: Taylor.
sp.l: I am by profeſſion a taylor,
You have heard of me.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Yes ſir, and will not ſteale from you
The leaſt part of that commendation I have heard utterd.

sp.speaker: Taylor.
sp.l: I take meaſure of your worth ſir,
And becauſe I will not afflict you with any large bill
Of circumſtances, I will ſnip off particulars.
I would faine invent ſome ſtrange
And exquiſite new faſhions.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Are you not travel'd ſir.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Yes ſir, but have obſerv'd all we can ſee
Or invent are but old ones with new names to'em,
Now I would ſome way or other grow more curious.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Let me ſee to deviſe new faſhions.
Were you never in the Moone?

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: In the Moone taverne! yes ſir: often.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: No, I do meane in the new world,
In the world thats in the Moone yonder.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: How? a new world ith moone?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Yes I aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: And peopled?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: O moſt fantaſtically peopled.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Nay certaine then ther's worke for taylors?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: That there is I aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Yet I have talked with a Scotch taylor
That never diſcover'd ſo much to me,
Though he has travail'd far, and was a pedlar in Poland.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: That was out of his way,
This lies beyond China,
You would ſtudy new faſhions you ſay?
Take my councell, make a voyage,
And diſcover that new world.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Shall I be a moon-man?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: I am of opinion, the people of that world
(Jf they be like the nature of that climate they live in)
Do vary the faſhion of their cloathes oftner then any
Quick-ſilver'd nation in Europe.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Not unlikely, but what ſhould that be we call
The man in the moone then?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Why tis nothing but an Engliſhman
That ſtands there ſtarke naked,
With a paire of ſheires in one hand,
And a great bundle of broad cloath in the other
(Which reſembles the buſh of thornes)
Cutting out of new faſhions.

sp.speaker: Taylor
sp.l: I have heard ſomewhat like this,
But how ſhall I get thither?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Ile make a new compaſſe ſhall direct you.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Certaine?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Count me elſe for no man of direction.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Theres 20 duckats in hand, at my returne
Ile give you a 100.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A new voyage to diſcover new faſhions.

sp.speaker: Mul.
sp.l: I have been a travailer too ſir,
That have ſhewed ſtrange beaſts in Chriſtendome,
And got mony by them, but I finde the trade to decay.
Your Camelion, or Eaſt-Indian hedg-hog
Gets very little mony, and your Elephant devoures
So much bread, brings in ſo little profit,
His keeper were better every morning
Cram 15 Taylors with white manchet,
I would have ſome new ſpectacle,
And one that might be more attractive.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Let me ſee, were you ever in Spaine?

sp.speaker: Mule.
sp.p: Not yet Sir.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: I would have you go to Madrill, and againſt ſome great feſtivall, when the court lies there, provide a great and ſpacious Engilſh Oxe, and rode him whole, with a pudding in's belly; that would be the eight wonder of the world in thoſe parts I aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Mule.
sp.p: A rare project without queſtion.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Goe beyond all their garlike olla Podrithoes, though you ſod one in Garquentuas cauldron, bring in more mony, then all the monſters of Affrick.

sp.speaker: Host.
sp.p: Good Sir do your beſt for him; he's of my acquaintance, and one if ye knew him—

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: What is he?

sp.speaker: Host.
sp.p: He was once a man of infinite letters.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: A Scholler?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: No ſir, a packet carrier, which is alwaies a man of many letters, yon know: then he was Mule-driver, now hee's a gentleman, and feedes monſters.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: A moſt ungratefull calling.

sp.speaker: Mule.
sp.p: Ther's mony for your direction; the price of the Oxe Sir.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A hundred French crownes, for it muſt be a Lincolne ſhire Oxe, and a prime one:
For a rare and monſtrous ſpectacle, to be ſeen at Madrill.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſ.
sp.p: Pray forbeare ſir, we ſhall have a new quarrell.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: You durſt not meet me ith' field, I am therefore come to ſpoyle your market.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Whats the newes with you ſir.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Gentlemen, you that come hither to be moſt abominably cheated, liſten, and be as wiſe as your plannet will ſuffer you, keep your mony, be not guld, be not laught at.

sp.speaker: Pedant.
sp.p: What meanes this? would I had my mony againe in my pocket.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: The fellow is full of malice, do not mind him.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: This profeſt cheating rogue was my maſter, and I confeſſe my ſelfe a more preternotorious rogue then himſelfe, in ſo long keeping his villainous counſell.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Come, come, I will not heare you.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No couzner, thou wouldeſt not heare me, I do but dare thee to ſuffer me to ſpeake, and then thou and all thy divells ſpit fire, and ſpoute Aqua fortis.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Speake on, I freely permit thee.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Why then know all you ſimple animals, you whoſe purſes are ready to caſt the calfe, if they have not caſt it already, if you give any credit this jugling raſcal, you are worſe then ſimple widgins, and will be drawne into the net by this decoy ducke, this tame cheater.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha, pray marke him.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: He does profeſſe Phyſicke, and counjuring; for his Phyſicke; he has but two medicins for all manner of diſeaſes; when he was i'th low countryes, he us'd nothing but butterd beere, colourd with Allegant, for all kind of maladies, and that he called his catholick medcine; ſure the ducth ſmelt out it was butterd beere, elſe they would never have endur'd it for the names ſake: then does he miniſter a grated dogs turd inſtead of Rubarbe, many times of Vnicornes horne, which working ſtrongly with the conceit of the Patient, would make them beſcummer to the height of a mighty purgation.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: The rogue has ſtudied this invective.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Now for his conjuring, the witches of Lapland are the divells chaire-women to him, for they will ſell a man a winde to ſome purpoſe; he ſells winde, and tells you fortye lyes over and over.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſſ.
sp.p: I thought what we ſhould find of him.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Hold your prating, be not you an hereticke.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Conjure! Ile tell you, all the divells names he calls upon, are but fuſtian names, gatherd out of welch heraldry; in breife, he is a rogue of ſix reprieves, foure pardones of courſe, thrice pilloried, twince ſung Lacrymae to the Virginalls of a carts taile, h'as five times been in the Gallies, and will never truly run himſelfe out of breath, till he comes to the gallowes.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: You have heard worthy gentlemen, what this lying detracting raſcall has vomited.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.p: Yes certaine, but we have a better truſt in you, for you have taine our mony.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: I have ſo, truth is he was my ſervant, and for ſome chaſtiſement I gave him, he does practiſe thus upon me; ſpeake truly ſirra, are you certaine I cannot conjure?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Conjure! ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Nay, nay, but be very ſure of it.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Sure of it? why Ile make a bargaine with thee, before all theſe gentlemen, uſe all thy art, all thy roguery, and make me do any thing before al this company I have not a mind to, Ile firſt give thee leave to claime me for thy bond ſlave, and when thou haſt done hang me.

sp.speaker: Foro,
sp.p: Tis a match, ſirra, Ile make you caper ith' aire preſently.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I have too ſolid a body, and my beleife is like a Puritans on Good-Friday, too high fed with capon.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: I will firſt ſend thee to Greeke land for a haunch of veniſon, juſt of the thickneſſe of thine own tallow.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha, Ile not ſtir an inch for thee.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Thence to Amboyna ith' Eaſt-Jndies, for pepper to bake it.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: To Amboyna? ſo I might be pepperd.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Then will I conveigh thee ſtrark naked to Develing to beg a paire of brogs, to hide thy mountainous buttocks.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: And no doublet to 'em?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: No ſir, I intend to ſend you of a ſleeveleſſe errand; but before you vaniſh, in regard you ſay I cannot conjure, and ar ſo ſtupid, and opinionated a ſlave, that neither I, nor my art can compell you to do any thing thats beyond your own pleaſure, the gentlemen ſhall have ſome ſport; you cannot endure a cat ſirra?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Whats that to thee Iugler?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Nor you'l do nothing at my entreaty?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Ile be hang'd firſt.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Sit Gentlemen, and whatſoever you ſee, be not frighted;

sp.speaker: Hosteſſ:
sp.p: Alas I can endure no coniuring.

sp.speaker: Hoſt:
sp.p: Stir not wife.

sp.speaker: Bian:
sp.p: Pray let me go ſir, I am not fit for theſe fooleryes.

sp.speaker: Hoſt:
sp.p: Move not daughter.

sp.speaker: For:
sp.p: I wil make you dance a new dance calld leap-frog.

sp.speaker: Clow:
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Fro:
sp.p: And as naked as a frog.

sp.speaker: Clow:
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha, I defye thee.

div.stage: Foro. lookes in a booke, ſtrikes with his wand, Muſick playes. Enter 4. Boyes ſhap't like Frogs, and dance.

sp.speaker: Pedant:
sp.l: Spirits of the water in the likenes of frogs.
Tay: he has fiſht faire beleeve me.

sp.speaker: Mule:
sp.p: See, ſee, he ſweats and trembles.

sp.speaker: Foro:
sp.p: Are you come to your quavers?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Oh, oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Ile make you run diviſion on that o's ere I leave you; looke you, here are the playfellowes that are ſo indeerd to you; come ſir, firſt uneaſe, and then dance, nay Ile make him daunce ſtark naked.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Oh let him have his ſhirt on, and his Mogols breeches, here are women ith' houſe.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Well for their ſakes he ſhall.

div.stage: Clown teares off his doublet, making ſtrange faces as if compeld to it, falls into the Daunce.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.p: He daunces, what a lying rogue was this to ſay the gentleman could not conjure?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: He does prettily well, but tis voluntary, I aſſure you, I have no hand in't.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: As you are a Counjurer, and a rare Artiſt, free me from theſe couplets; of all creatures I cannot endure a Frog.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: But your dauncing is voluntary, I can compell you to nothing.

sp.speaker: Hosteſ.
sp.p: O me, danghter, lets take heed of this fellow, he'le make us dance naked, an' we vex him.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Now cut capers ſirra, Ile plague that chin of yours.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Oh, oh, oh, my kidneys are roſted, I drop away like a pound of butter roſted.

sp.speaker: Tayl.
sp.p: He will daunce himſelfe to death.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: No matter Ile ſell his fat to the Pothecaries, and repaire my injury that way.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Enough in conſcience.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Well, at your entreaty vaniſh. And now I wil only make him breake his neck in doing a ſommerſet, and thats all the revenge I meane to take of him.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: O gentlemen, what a rogue was I to belye ſo an approved Maſter in the noble datk ſcience? you can witneſſe, this I did only to ſpoyle his practiſe and deprive you of the happyneſſe of injoying his worthy labours; rogue that I was to do it, pray ſir forgive me.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: With what face canſt thou ask it?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: With ſuch a face as I deſerve, with a hanging looke, as all here can teſtifie.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Well gentlemen, that you may perceive the goodnes of my temper, I will entertain this rogue again in hope of amendment, for ſhould I turn him off, he would be hanged.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: You may read that in this foule coppy.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Only with this promiſe, you ſhall never cozen any of my patients.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Never.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: And remember hence forward, that though I cannot counjure, I can make you daunce ſirra, go get your ſelfe into the cottage againe. —Enter Caeſario.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I will never more daunce leape Frog: now I have got you into credit, hold it up, and cozen them in abundance.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Oh rare raſcall —Exit Clown.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.p: How now, a Frankford mart here, a Mountebanke, and his worſhipfull auditory.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: They are my ghueſts Sir.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.p: A—upon them, ſhew your jugling tricks in ſome other roome.

sp.speaker: Hoſt,
sp.p: And why not here Sir?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.p: Hence, or ſirra I ſhall ſpoile your figure flinging, and all their radicall queſtions.

sp.speaker: Omnes
sp.p: Sir we vaniſh. —Exeunt. Manet Hoſt. & Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Host.
sp.l: Signior Caeſario, you make bold with me,
And ſomewhat I muſt tell you to a degree
of ill manners, they are my ghueſts, and men I live by,
And I would know by what authority
You command thus far.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.p: By my intereſt in your daughter.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Intereſt do you call't? as J remember I never put her out to Vſury on that condition.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.p: Pray thee be not angry.

sp.speaker: Hosteſ.
sp.l: I am come to make thee happy, and her happy:
Shee's here; alas my pretty ſoule, I am come
To give aſſurance thats beyond thy hope,
Or thy beleife, I bring repentance 'bout me,
And ſatisfaction, I will marry thee.

sp.speaker: Bianca.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: As I live I will, but do not entertain't
With too quick an apprehenſion of joy,
For that may hurt thee, I have heard ſome dye of't,

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Do not feare me.

sp.speaker: Caeſar
sp.l: Then thou think'ſt I faigne
This proteſtation, I will inſtantly
Before this teſtimony, my new alliance,
Contract my ſelfe unto thee, then I hope
We may be more private.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: But thou ſhalt not ſir,
For ſo has many a maiden-head been loſt, and many a baſtard gotten,

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Then to give you the beſt of any aſſurance in the world,
Entreat thy father to goe fetch a Preiſt
Wee will inſtantly to bed, and there be married.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Pride hath not yet foſaken you I ſee,
Though proſperity has.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Sir you are too confident
To faſhion to your ſelfe a dreame of purchaſe
When you are a begger,

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: you are bold with me.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſ.
sp.l: Doe we not know your value is cried downe
Foureſcore i'th hundred.

sp.speaker: Bian
sp.l: Oh ſir I did love you
With ſuch a fixed heart, that in that minute
Wherein you ſlighted, or contemn'd me rather,
I tooke a vow to obey your laſt decree,
And never more looke up at any hope
Should bring me comfort that way, and though ſince
Your Foſter-mother, and the faire Clariſſa
Have in the way of marriage deſpis'd you,
That hath not any way bred my revenge,
But compaſſion rather. I have found
So much ſorrow in the way to a chaſte wedlock
That here I will ſet downe, and never wiſh
To come to'th journies end. Your ſuite to mee
Henceforth be ever ſilenc't.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: My Bianca.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſ.
sp.l: Henceforward pray forbeare her and my houſe:
She's a poore vertuous wench, yet her eſtate
May weigh with yours in a gold balance.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Yes, and her birth in any Heralds office in Chriſtendome.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſ.
sp.l: It may prove ſo:
When you'l ſay, you have leapt a Whiteing. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ceſ,
sp.l: How far am I growne behind hand with fortune?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Here's Ceſario▪
My ſon ſir is to morrow to be married
Vnto the faire Clariſſa,

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: So.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Wee hope youle be a gueſte there?

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: No I will not grace your triumph ſo much.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: I will not tax your breeding.
But it alters not your birth ſir, fare you well.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Oh ſir doe not greive him,
He has to much affliction already. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Every way ſcorn'd and loſt,
Shame follow you
For I am growne moſt miſerable.

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: Sir doe you know a Ladies ſon in towne here
They cal Ceſario?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Ther's none ſuch I aſſure thee;

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: I was told you were the man.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Whats that to thee?

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: A—on't. You are melancholy, will you drink Sir?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: With whom?

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.p: With mee Sir; deſpiſe not this pitcht Canvas; the time was wee have knowne them lined with Spaniſh Duckets: I have news for you:

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: For me!

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: Not unleſſe you'l drink;
We are like our Sea proviſion, once out of pickle,
We require abundance of drink; I have news to tell you
That were you Prince,
Would make you ſend your mandate
To have a thouſand bonfires made 'ith City,
And piſt out agen with nothing but Greek wine.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Come, I wil drink with thee howſoever,

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.p: And upon theſe terms I wil utter my mind to you. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena prima.
div.stage: Enter Alberoto, Proſpero, Juliana, and Saylors.

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: SHall we bring your neceſſaries aſhore my Lord?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Do what you pleaſe, I am land-ſicke, worſe by far
Then ere I was at ſea.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: Collect your ſelfe

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: O my moſt worthy Proſpero, my beſt friend,
The noble favor I receivd from thee
In freeing me from the Turks I now accompt
Worſe than my death; for I ſhall never live
To make requitall; what doe you attend for?

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: To underſtand your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: They doe mock me;
I doe proteſt I have no kind of pleaſure
In any thing i'th world, butin thy friendſhip,
I muſt ever except that.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.p: Pray leave him, leave him. —Exeunt Sailors.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: The newes I heard related ſince my landing
Of the diviſion of my Family,
How is it poſſible for any man
To bear't with a ſet patience?

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: You have ſuffer'd
Since your impriſonment more waighty ſorrowes.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: I, then I was a man of fleſh and bloud,
Now I am made up of fire, to the full height
Of a deadly Calenture; ô theſe vild women
That are ſo ill preſervers of mens honors,
They cannot governe their own honeſties.
That I ſhould thirty and odde winters feed
My expectation of a noble heire,
And by a womans falſhood finde him now
A fiction, a meare dreame of what he was;
And yet I love him ſtill.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: In my opinion
The ſentence (on this tryall) from the Duke
Was noble, to repaire Ceſarios loſſe
With the marriage of your wife, had you been dead.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: By your favor but it was not, I conceive
T'was diſparagment to my name, to have my widdow
Match with a Faulkners ſon, and yet beleev't
I love the youth ſtill, and much pitty him.
I doe remember at my going to Sea,
Vpon a quarrell, and a hurt receiv'd
From young Mentivole, my rage ſo farre
Oretopt my nobler temper, I gave charge
To have his hand cut off, which ſince I heard,
And to my comfort, brave Caeſario,
Worthyly prevented.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: And 'twas nobly done.

sp.speaker: Albert.
sp.l: Yet the revenge, for this intent of min •
Hath bred much ſlaughter in our families,
And yet my wife (which infinitly moanes me)
Intends to marry my ſole heire Clariſſa
To the head branch of the other faction.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: Tis the meane to work reconcilement.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Betweene whom?

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: Your ſelfe, and the worthy Baptiſta.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Never.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: O you have been of a noble and remarkable freindſhip,
And by this match tis generally in Florence
Hop'd, twill fully be reconcild; to me
'Twould be abſolute content.

sp.speaker: Iulia.
sp.l: And to my ſelfe, I have maine intereſt in it.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Noble Sir, you may command my heart to breake for you
But never to bend that way; poore Caeſario
When thou puft'ſt on thy mournfull willow garland,
Thy enemy ſhall be ſuted (I do vow)
In the ſame livery, my Caeſario
Loved as my foſter child, though not my ſonne,
Which in ſome countryes formerly were barbarous,
Was a name held moſt affectionate; thou art loſt,
Vnfortunate young man, not only ſlighted
Where thou received'ſt thy breeding, but ſince ſcorn'd
Ith' way of marriage, by the poore Bianca
The In-keepers daughter.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: I have heard of that too;
But let not that afflict you; for this Lady
May happily deliver at more leaſure
A circumſtance may draw a faire event,
Better then you can hope for.
For this preſent we muſt leave you,
And ſhall viſit you againe within theſe two houres.

sp.speaker: Albert.
sp.l: Ever to me moſt welcome,—O my Caeſario.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: I am none of yours Sir, ſo tis proteſted;
And I humbly beg,
Since tis not in your power to preſerve me
Any longer in a noble courſe of life,
Give me a worthy death.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: The youth is mad.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Nay Sir, I will inſtruct you in a way
To kill me honorably.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: That were moſt ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: I am turning Pirate, You may be imployed
By the Duke to fetch me in; and in a ſea-fight
Give me a noble grave.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Queſtionleſſe he's mad; I would give any Doctor
A thouſand crownes to free him from this ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.p: Here's the Phyſitian. —Shewes a Poniard

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Hold Sir, I did ſay
To free you from the ſorrow, not from life.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Why life and ſorrow are unſeparable.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Be comforted Caeſario, Mentivole
Shall not marry Clariſſa.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: No Sir, ere he ſhall, Ile kill him.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: But you forfeit your own life then.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Thats worth nothing.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Caeſario, be thy ſelfe, be mine Caeſario,
Make not thy ſelfe uncapable of that portion
I have full purpoſe to confer upon thee;
By falling into madneſſe, beare thy wrongs
With noble patience, the afflicted freind
Which ever in all actions crownes the end.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: You well awake me▪ nay recover'd me
Both to ſence and full life, ô moſt noble ſir,
Though I have loſt my fortune, and loſt you
For a worthy Father: yet I will not looſe
My former vertue, my integrity
Shall not yet forſake me; but as the wilde Ivy,
Spredds and thrives better in ſome pittious ruin
Of tower, or defac'd Temple, then it does
Planted by a new building- ſo ſhall I
Make my adverſity my inſtrument
To winde me up into a full content.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Tis worthily reſolv'd; our firſt adventure
Is to ſtop the marriage; for thy other loſſes,
Practis'd by a womans malice, but account them
Like conjurers windes rais'd to a fearefull blaſt,
And doe ſome miſcheife, but do never laſt. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Now ſir, will you not acknowledge that I have mightily advancte your practice?

sp.speaker: Foroboſ.
sp.p: Tis confeſt, and I will make thee a great man for't.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I take a courſe to do that my ſelfe, for I drinke ſack in abundance.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: O my rare raſcall. We muſt remove.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Whither?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Any whither: Europe is to little to be cozned by us, I am ambitious to goe to the Eaſt-Indies, thou and I to ride on our brace of Elephants.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: And for my part I long to be in England agen; you wil never get ſo much as in England, we have ſhifted many countryes, and many names: but traunce the world over you ſhall never purſe up ſo much gold as when you were in England, and call'd your ſelfe Doctor Lambeſtones.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Twas an atractive name I confeſſe, women were then my only admirers.

sp.speaker: Clow,
sp.p: And all their viſits was either to further their luſt, or reveng injuries.

sp.speaker: Foro
sp.p: You ſhould have forty in a morning beleager my cloſett, and ſtrive who ſhould be cozend firſt, amongſt foureſcore love-ſick waighting women that has come to me in a morning to learne what fortune ſhould betide them in their firſt marriage, I have found above 94 to have loſt their maidenheads.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: By their owne confeſſion, but I was faine to be your male midwife, and worke it out of them by circumſtance.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Thou waſt, and yet for all this frequent reſort of women and thy handling of their urinalls and their caſes, thou art not given to lechery, what ſhould be the reaſon of it? thou haſt wholſome fleſh enough about thee; me thinkes the divell ſhould tempt thee too't.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: What need he do that, when he makes me his inſtrument to tempt others.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Thou canſt not chuſe but utter thy rare good parts; thou waſt an excellent baude I acknowledge.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Well, and what I have done that way I will ſpare to ſpeake of all you and I have done ſir, and though we ſhould—

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: We will for England, thats for certaine.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: We ſhall never want there.

sp.speaker: Foro,
sp.p: Want? the Court of Wards ſhall want mony firſt, for I profeſſe my ſelfe Lord Paramount over fooles and madfolkes.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Do but ſtore your ſelfe with lyes enough againſt you come thither,

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: VVhy thats all the familarity I ever had with the Divell, my guift of lying, they ſay hees the Father of lyes, and though I cannot conjure, yet I profeſſe my ſelfe to be one of his poore goſſips. I will now reveale to thee a rare peece of ſervice.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: VVhat is it my moſt worſhipful Doctor Lambſtones.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: There is a Captaine come lately from Sea,
They call Proſper I ſaw him this morning
Through a chincke of wainſcote that divides my lodging
