Beleeve me, I am proud—

sp.speaker: La Ca.
sp.l: Fair Sir, I thank ye:
Moùnſieur de Gard, you are welcom from your journey,
Good men, have ſtil good welcom: give me your hand, Sir.
Once more, you are welcom home: you look ſtill younger.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: Time has no leaſure to look after us,
We wander, every where: Age cannot find us.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: And how does all?

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: All well, Sir; and all luſty.

sp.speaker: La Ca.
sp.l: I hope my Son be ſo, I doubt not Sir,
But you have often ſeen him in your journeis,
And bring me ſome fair Newes.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: Your Son is well, Sir,
And grown a proper Gentleman: he is well, and luſtie,
Within this eight houres, I took leave of him,
And over-eyd him, having ſome ſlight buſines
That forc'd me out o'th' way: I can aſſure you
He will be here to night.

sp.speaker: La Ca.
sp.l: Ye make me glad Sir,
For o' my faith, I almoſt long to ſee him,
Me thinks he has been away —

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: 'Tis but your tenderneſs;
What are three yeares? a love-ſick wench will allow it?
His friends that went out with him are come back too;
Beleure, and young Pinac: he bid me ſay little,
Becauſe he meanes to be his own glad Meſſenger.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: I thank ye for this newes, Sir, he ſhalbe welcom,
And his friends too: Indeed I thank you heartily:
And how (for I dare ſay, you will not flatter him)
Has Italy wrought on him? ha's he mew'd yet
His wild fantaſtick Toyes? they ſay that Climate
Is a great purger of thoſe humorous Fluxes.
How is he improved, I pray ye?

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: No doubt Sir, well.
H'as born himſelf a full, and noble Gentleman,
To ſpeak him farther, is beyond my Charter,

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: I am glad to hear ſo much good: Come, I ſee
You long to enjoy your Siſter: yet I muſt intreat ye
Before I go, to ſup with me to night
And muſt not be deni'd.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: I am your ſervant.

sp.speaker: La. C.
sp.l: Where you ſhall meet fair, merry, and noble Company.
My neighbour Natolet, and his two fair daughters.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.p: Your ſupper's ſeaſon'd well, Sir. I ſhall wait upon ye.

sp.speaker: La Ca.
sp.l: Till then I'll leave ye: and y' are once more welcom.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: I thank ye, noble Sir. Now Oriana, Exit.
How have ye done ſince I went? Have ye had your health well?
And your mind free?

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: You ſee I am not bated;
Merry, and eat my meat.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: A good preſervative.
And how have you been us'd? You know Oriana,
Upon my going out, at your requeſt,
I left your Portion in La-Caſtres hands,
(The main Means you muſt ſtick to) for that reaſon
(And 'tis no little one) I aſk ye, Siſter,
With what humanitie he entertains ye,
And how ye find his curteſie?

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Moſt ready.
I can aſſure you, Sir, I am us'd moſt nobly.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: I am glad to hear it: But I pre'thee tell me,
(And tell me true) what end had you Oriana,
In truſting your money here? He is no Kinſman,
Nor any tie upon him of a Guardian;
Nor dare I think ye doubt my prodigality.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: No, certain, Sir, none of all this provoked me;
Another private reaſon.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: 'Tis not private,
Nor carryed ſo: 'tis common (my fair Siſter)
Your love to Mirabell; your bluſhes tell it:
'Tis too much known, and ſpoken of too largely;
And with no little ſhame I wonder at it.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Is it a ſhame to love?

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: To Love undiſcreetly:
A Virgin ſhould be tender of her honour,
Cloſe, and ſecure.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I am as cloſe as can be,
And ſtand upon as ſtrong and honeſt guards too,
Unleſs this Warlike Age need a Port-cullis:
Yet I confeſs, I love him.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: Hear the people.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Now I ſay hang the people: He that dares
Believe what they ſay, dares be mad, and give
His Mother, nay his own Wife up to Rumor;
All grounds of truth they build on, is a Tavern,
And their beſt cenſure's Sack, Sack in abundance:
For as they drink, they think: they ne'r ſpeak modeſtly
Unleſs the wine be poor, or they want money.
Beleeve them? beleeve Amadis de Gaul,
The Knight o'th' Sun, or Palmerin of England;
For theſe, to them, are modeſt, and true ſtories.
Pray underſtand me; if their tongues be truth,
And if in Vino veritas be an Oracle,
What woman is, or has been ever honeſt?
Give 'em but ten round cups, they'll ſwear Lucretia
Dy'd not for want of power to reſiſt Tarquine,
But want of Pleaſure, that he ſtayd no longer:
And Portia, that was famous for her Pietie
To her lov'd Lord, they'll face ye out, dy'd o'th' pox.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: Well, there is ſomething, Siſter.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: If there be, Brother,
'Tis none of their things, 'tis not yet ſo monſtrous;
My thing is Mariage: And at his return
I hope to put their ſquint-eyes right again.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: Mariage? 'tis true: his father is a rich man;
Rich both in land and money: he his heir,
A young and handſom man, I muſt confeſs too;
But of ſuch qualities, and ſuch wild flings,
Such admirable imperfections, Siſter,
(For all his travaile, and bought experience)
I ſhould be loth to own him for my brother:
Me thinks a rich mind in a ſtate indifferent
Would prove the better fortune.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: If he be wild,
The reclaming him to good, and honeſt (brother)
Will make much for my honor; which, if I proſper,
Shall be the ſtudy of my love, and life too.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: Ye ſay well; would he thought as well, and loved too.
He mary? he'll be hang'd firſt: he knows no more
What the conditions and the ties of Love are,
The honeſt purpoſes and grounds of Mariage,
Nor will know, nor be ever brought t' endeavour,
Than I do how to build a Church; he was ever
A looſe and ſtrong defier of all order,
His Loves are wanderers, they knock at each door,
And taſt each diſh, but are no reſidents:
Or ſay he may be brought to think of Mariage
(As 't will be no ſmall labour) thy hopes are ſtrangers.
I know there is a labour'd match, now follow'd,
(Now at this time, for which he was ſent for home too)
Be not abus'd, Natolet has two fair daughters,
And he muſt take his choice.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Let him take freely;
For all this I deſpair not: my mind tells me
That I, and onely I, muſt make him perfect;
And in that hope I reſt.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: Since y' are ſo confident
Proſper your hope: I'll be no adverſary:
Keep your ſelf fair and right, he ſhall not wrong ye.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.p: When I forget my vertue, no man know me. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA SECUNDA.
div.stage: Enter Mirabell, Pinac, Belleure, and Servants.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Welcom to Paris once more, Gentlemen:
We have had a merry, and a luſty Ord'nary,
And wine, and good meat, and a bounſing Reckning;
And let it go for once; 'Tis a good phyſick:
Only the wenches are not for my dyet,
They are too lean and thin; their embraces brawn-fall'n.
Give me the plump Venetian, fat, and luſty,
That meets me ſoft and ſupple; ſmiles upon me,
As if a cup of full wine leap'd to kiſs me;
Theſe ſlight things I affect not.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: They are ill built;
Pin-buttockt, like your dainty Barbaries,
And weak i'th paſterns; they'l endure no hardneſs.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: There's nothing good, or handſom, bred amongſt us;
Till we are travail'd, and live abroad, we are coxcombs:
Ye talk of France, a ſlight, unſeaſon'd Country;
Abundance of groſs food, which makes us block-heads:
We are fair ſet-out indeed, and ſo are fore-horſes.
Men ſay we are great Courtiers, men abuſe us:
We are wiſe, and valiant too, non credo Signior:
Our women the beſt Linguiſts, they are Parrats;
O' this ſide the Alpes they are nothing but meer Drollaries:
Ha Roma la Santa, Italie for my money:
Their policies, their cuſtoms, their frugalities,
Their curteſies ſo open, yet ſo reſerved too,
As when ye think y' are known beſt, ye are a ſtranger;
Their very pick-teeth ſpeak more man than we do,
And ſeaſon of more ſalt.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: 'Tis a brave Country;
Not peſter'd with your ſtubborn preciſe puppies,
That turn all uſefull, and allow'd contentments
To ſcabs and ſcruples; hang 'em Capon-worſhippers.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I like that freedom well, and like their women too,
And would fain do as others do; but I am ſo baſhfull,
So naturally an Aſs: Look ye, I can look upon 'em,
And very willingly I go to ſee 'em,
(There's no man willinger) and I can kiſs 'em,
And make a ſhift—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: But if they chance to flout ye,
Or ſay ye are too bold; fie Sir remember;
I pray ſit farther off;—

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Tis true, I am humbled,
I am gone, I confeſs ingenuouſly I am ſilenced,
The ſpirit of Amber cannot force me anſwer.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Then would I ſing and dance.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You have wherewithall, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: And charge her up again.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I can be hang'd firſt:
Yet where I faſten well, I am a tyrant.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why, thou darſt fight?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Yes, certainly, I dare fight;
And fight with any man, at any weapon,
Would th' other were no more; but, a pox on't,
When I am ſometimes in my height of hope,
And reaſonable valiant that way, my heart harden'd,
Some ſcornfull jeſt or other, chops between me
And my deſire: What would ye have me to do then, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Belvere, ye muſt be bolder: Travell three years,
And bring home ſuch a baby to betray ye
As baſhfulneſs? a great fellow, and a ſouldier?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You have the gift of impudence, be thankful;
Every man has not the like talent: I will ſtudy
And if it may be reveal'd to me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Learn of me,
And of Pinac: no doubt you'll find imployment;
Ladies will look for Courtſhip.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: 'Tis but fleſhing,
But ſtanding one good brunt or two: ha'ſt thou any mind to mariage?
Wee'll provide thee ſome ſoft-natur'd wench, that's dumb too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Or an old woman that cannot refuſe thee in charity.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: A dumb woman, or an old woman, that were eager,
And car'd not for diſcourſe, I were excellent at.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You muſt now put on boldneſs, there's no avoyding it;
And ſtand all hazards; fly at all games bravely;
They'll ſay you went out like an Ox, and return'd like an Aſs elſe.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I ſhall make danger ſure.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I am ſent for home now,
I know it is to mary, but my father ſhall pardon me,
Although it be a witty ceremony,
And may concern me hereafter in my gravitie;
I will not loſe the freedom of a Traveller;
A new ſtrong luſty Bark cannot ride at one anchor;
Shall I make divers ſuits to ſhew to the ſame eyes?
'Tis dull, and home-ſpun: Study ſeverall pleaſures,
And want employments for 'em? I'll be hang'd firſt;
Tie me to one ſmock? make my travels fruitleſs?
I'll none of that: For every freſh behaviour,
By your leave, father, I muſt have a freſh Miſtris,
And a freſh favour too.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I like that paſſingly;
As many as you will, ſo they be willing;
Willing, and gentle, gentle.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: There's no reaſon
A Gentleman, and a Traveller, ſhould be clapt up,
For 'tis a kind of Baeboes to be maryed
Before he manifeſt to the world his good parts:
Tug ever like at a raſcall at one oar?
Give me the Italian liberty.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That I ſtudy;
And that I will enjoy: Come, go in Gentlemen,
There mark how I behave my ſelf, and follow. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA TERTIA.
div.stage: Enter La-Caſtre, Natolet, Lugien, Roſa Lieura, Lylia-Biancha.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: You and your beauteous daughters are moſt welcom,
Beſhrew my blood they are fair ones; welcom Beauties,
Welcom ſweet birds.

sp.speaker: Na.
sp.l: They are bound much to your curteſies.

sp.speaker: La Ca.
sp.l: I hope we ſhall be nearer acquainted.

sp.speaker: Na.
sp.l: That's my hope too.

sp.speaker: Na.
sp.l: For certain, Sir, I much deſire your Alliance.
You ſee 'em, they are no Gipſcies; for their breeding,
It has not been ſo coarſe, but they are able
To rank themſelves with women of fair faſhion;
Indeed they have been trained well.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Thank me.

sp.speaker: Na.
sp.l: Fit for the heirs of that ſtate I ſhall leave 'em;
To ſay more, is to ſell 'em. They ſay your ſon
Now he has travail'd muſt be wondrous curious,
And choice in what he takes: Theſe are no coarſe ones;
Sir, here's a merry wench, let him look to himſelf,
(All heart, y'faith) may chance to ſtartle him;
For all his care, and travail'd caution,
May creep into his eye; if he love Gravitie,
Affect a ſolemn face, there's one will fit him.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: So young, and ſo demure?

sp.speaker: Na.
sp.l: She is my daughter,
Elſe I would tell you, Sir, ſhe is a Miſtris
Both of thoſe manners, and that modeſty,
You would wonder at: She is no often ſpeaker,
But when ſhe does, ſhe ſpeaks well; Nor no Reveller,
Yet ſhe can dance, and has ſtudied the Court Elements,
And ſings, as ſome ſay, handſomly; if a woman,
With the decencie of her ſex, may be a Scholar,
I can aſſure ye, Sir, ſhe underſtands too.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Theſe are fit Garments, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Thank them that cut 'em:
Yes, they are handſom women; they have handſom parts too;
Prettie becoming parts.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: 'Tis like they have, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Yes, yes, and handſom Education they have had too:
Had it abundantly; they need not bluſh at it;
I taught it, I'll avouch it.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Ye ſay well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: I know what I ſay, Sir, and I ſay but right, Sir.
I am no trumpet of their commendations
Before their father; elſe I ſhould ſay farther.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Pray ye, what's this Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Na.
sp.l: One that lives with me, Sir;
A man well bred and learn'd, but blunt and bitter,
Yet it offends no wiſe man; I take pleaſure in't:
Many fair gifts he has, in ſome of which
That lie moſt eaſie to their underſtandings,
Has handſomly bred up my girls, I thank him.
I have put it to 'em, that's my part, I have urg'd it,
It ſeems they are of years now to take hold on't.

sp.speaker: Na.
sp.l: He's wondrous blunt.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: By my faith I was afraid of him:
Does he not fall out with the Gentlewomen ſometimes?

sp.speaker: Na.
sp.l: No, no; he's that way moderate, and diſcreet, Sir.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: If he did, we ſhould be too hard for him.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Well ſaid Sulphur:
Too hard for thy huſbands head, if he wear not armour.

sp.speaker: Na.
sp.p: Many of theſe bickrings, Sir. Enter Mirabell, Pinac, de Gard, and Oriana.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: I am glad they are no Oracles:
Sure, as I live, he beats them, he's ſo puiſant.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Well, if ye do forget—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Pre'thee hold thy peace;
I know thou art a prettie wench; I know thou lov'ſt me,
Preſerve it till we have a fit time to diſcourſe on't,
And a fit place: I'll eaſe thy heart, I warrant thee:
Thou ſeeſt I have much to do now.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I am anſwer'd, Sir:
With me ye ſhall have nothing on theſe conditions.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: Your father, and your friends.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: You are welcom home, Sir;
'Bleſs ye, ye are very welcom.
'Pray know this Gentleman,
And theſe fair Ladies.

sp.speaker: Na.
sp.l: I am much affected with your fair return, Sir:
You bring a generall joy.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I bring you ſervice,
And theſe bright beauties, Sir.

sp.speaker: Na.
sp.l: Welcom home, Gentlemen,
VVelcom, with all my heart.

sp.speaker: Bel. Pi.
sp.l: VVe thank ye, Sir.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Your friends will have their ſhare too.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Sir, we hope
They'll look upon us, though we ſhew like ſtrangers.

sp.speaker: Na.
sp.l: Monſieur de-Gard, I muſt ſalute you alſo,
And this fair Gentlewoman: you are welcom from your Travell too.
All welcom, all.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: VVe render ye our loves, Sir;
The beſt wealth we bring home: By your favours, Beauties,
One of theſe two: you know my meaning.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: VVell Sir;
They are fair and handſom, I muſt needs confeſs it;
And let it prove the worſt, I ſhall live after it,
Whilſt I have meat & drink, Love can not ſtarve me;
For if I dye o'th' firſt fit, I am unhappy,
And worthy to be buried with my heels upward.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: To mary, Sir?

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: You know I am an old man,
And every hour declining to my grave,
One foot already in, more ſons I have not,
Nor more I dare not ſeek whilſt you are worthy,
In you lies all my hope, and all my name,
The making good or wretched of my memory,
The ſafety of my ſtate.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And you have provided
Out of this tenderneſs this handſom Gentlewoman,
Daughters to this rich man, to take my choice of?

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: I have, dear ſon.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis true, ye are old, and feebled;
Would ye were young again, and in full vigor;
I love a bounteous fathers life, a long one,
I am none of thoſe that when they ſhoot to ripeneſs,
Do what they can to break the boughs they grew on:
I wiſh ye many years, and many riches,
And pleaſures to enjoy 'em: But for Mariage,
I neither yet beleeve in't, nor affect it,
Nor think it fit.

sp.speaker: La. C.
sp.l: You will render me your reaſons?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, Sir, both ſhort and pithy; and theſe they are:
You would have me mary a Mayd?

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: A Mayd? what elſe?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, there be things called Widdows, dead-mens Wills,
I never lov'd to prove thoſe; nor never long'd yet
To be buried alive in anothers mans cold Monument.
And there be Maids appearing, and Maid … ing:
The appearing, are fantaſtick things, meer ſhadows;
And if you mark 'em well, they want their heads too;
Onely the world, to coſen myſtie eyes,
Has clapt 'em on new faces. The Mayds being,
A man may venture on, if he be ſo mad to mary;
If he have neither fear before his eyes, nor fortune;
And let him take heed how he gather theſe too;
For look ye, father, they are juſt like Melons,
Muſk-Melons are the Emblems of theſe Mayds;
Now they are ripe, now cut 'em, they taſte pleaſantly,
And are a dainty fruit, digeſted eaſily:
Neglect this preſent time, and come to morrow,
They are ſo ripe they are rotten gon, their ſweetneſs
Run into humour, and their taſte to ſurfeit.

sp.speaker: La. C.
sp.l: Why theſe are now ripe ſon.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I'll try them preſently,
And if I like their taſte—

sp.speaker: La. C.
sp.l: 'Pray ye pleaſe your ſelf, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That liberty is my due, and I'll maintain it.
Lady, what think you of a handſom man now?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: A wholſom too, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That's as you make your bargain.
A handſom, wholſom man then, and a kind man,
To chear your heart up, to rejoyce ye, Lady?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes, Sir, I love rejoycing.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: To ly cloſe to ye?
Cloſe as a cockle? keep the cold nights from ye?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: That will be lookt for too, our bodies aſk it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And get two Boyes at every birth?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: That's nothing,
I have known a Cobler do it, a poor thin Cobler;
A Cobler out of mouldy cheeſe perform it,
Cabbage, and coarſe black bread: me thinks a Gentleman
Should take foul ſcorn to have a Nawl out-name him.
Two at a birth? why every Houſe-dove has it:
That man that feeds well, promiſes as well too,
I ſhould expect indeed ſomething of worth from
Ye talk of two?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: She would have me get two dozen,
Like Buttons, at a birth.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: You love to brag, Sir.
If you proclame theſe offers at your Mariage,
Ye are a pretty timber'd man, take heed,
They may be taken hold of, and expected,
Yes, if not hoped for at a higher rate too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I will take heed, and thank ye for your counſell:
Father, what think ye?

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: 'Tis a merry Gentlewoman;
Will make, no doubt, a good wife.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Not for me:
I mary her, and happily get nothing;
In what a ſtate am I then? Father, I ſhall ſuffer

For any thing I hear t •
• he contrary, more majorum,
I were as ſure to be a Cuckold, Father,
A Gentleman of Antler.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Away, away fool.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: As I am ſure to fail her expectation,
I had rather get the pox than get her babies.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Ye are much too blame; if this do not affect ye,
Pray try the other; ſhe is of a more demure way.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: That I had but the audacitie to talk thus!
I love that plain-ſpoken Gentlewoman admirably,
And certain I could go as near to pleaſe her,
If down-right doing— ſhe has a per'lous countenance,
If I could meet one that would beleeve me,
And take my honeſt meaning without circumſtance.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You ſhall have your will, Sir, I will try the other,
But 'twill be to ſmall uſe. I hope, fair Lady
(For methinks in your eyes I ſee more mercy)
You will enjoyn your Lover a leſs penance;
And though I'll promiſe much, as men are liberall,
And vow an ample ſacrifice of ſervice,
Yet your diſcretion, and your tenderneſs,
And thriftineſs in Love, good houſwives carefulnes
To keep the ſtock entire—

sp.speaker: Lyl.
sp.l: Good Sir, ſpeak louder,
That theſe may witneſs too ye talk of nothing,
I ſhould be loth alone to bear the burthen
Of ſo much indiſcretion.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Heark ye, heark ye;
Od's-bobs, you are angry, Lady.

sp.speaker: Lyl.
sp.l: Angry? no, Sir;
I never own'd an anger to loſe poorly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: But you can love, for all this, and delight too,
For all your ſet-auſteritie, to hear
Of a good huſband, Lady?

sp.speaker: Lyl.
sp.l: You ſay true, Sir:
For by my troth, I have heard of none theſe ten year,
They are ſo rare, and there are ſo many, Sir,
So many longing-women on their knees too,
That pray the droping down of theſe good huſbands,
The droping down from heaven: for they are not bred here,
That you may gheſs at all my hope, but hearing—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why may not I be one?

sp.speaker: Lyl.
sp.l: You were near 'em once, Sir,
When ye came ore the Alpes; thoſe are near heaven:
But ſince ye miſt that happineſs, there's no hope of ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Can ye love a man?

sp.speaker: Lyl.
sp.l: Yes, if the man be lovely;
That is, be honeſt, modeſt: I would have him valiant,
His anger ſlow, but certain for his honor;
Travail'd he ſhould be, but through himſelf exactly;
For 'tis fairer to know manners well, than Countries;
He muſt be no vain talker, nor no Lover
To hear himſelf talk, they are brags of a wanderer,
Of one finds no retreict for fair behaviour;
Would ye learn more?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lyl.
sp.l: Learn to hold your peace then,
Fond girls are got with tongues, women with tempers.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Women, with I know what; but let that vaniſh:
Go thy way good wife Bias; ſure thy husband
Muſt have a ſtrong Philoſophers ſtone, he will ne'r pleaſe thee elſe.
Heer's a ſtarcht peece of Auſteritie: do you hear, father?
Do you hear this morall Lecture?

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Yes, and like it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why there's your judgment now; there's an old bolt ſhot:
This Thing muſt have the ſtrangeſt obſervation,
Do you mark me (father?) when ſhe is maryed once,
The ſtrangeſt cuſtom too of admiration
On all ſhe do's and ſpeaks, 'twill be paſt ſufferance;
I muſt not lie with her in common language,
Nor cry, have at thee Kate, I ſhall be hiſt then;
Nor eat my meat without the ſawce of Sentences,
Your powder'd beef, and problemes, a rare dyet;
My firſt ſon, Monſieur Ariſtotle, I know it,
Great Maſter of the Metaphyſicks, or ſo;
The ſecond Solon, and the beſt Law-ſetter;
And I muſt look Egyptian God-fathers,
Which will be no ſmall trouble: My eldeſt daughter
Sapho, or ſuch a fidling kind of Poeteſs,
And brought up, invita Minerva, at her needle.
My dogs muſt look their names too, and all Spartan,

Lelaps, Mel …
: no more Fox and Baudiface.

I maryed to •
•• llen ſet of Sentences?
To one that weighs her words and her behaviours
In the Gold-weights of diſcretion? I'll be hang'd firſt.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: 'Pre'thee reclame thy ſelf.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Pray ye give me time then;
If they can ſet me any thing to play at,
That ſeems fit for a Gameſter, have at the faireſt
Till I ſee more, and try more.

sp.speaker: L. C.
sp.l: Take your time then,
I'll bar ye no fair liberty: Come Gentlemen,
And Ladies, come; to all once more a welcom,
And now let's in to ſupper.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How do'ſt like 'em?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: They are fair enough, but of ſo ſtrange behaviors.

sp.speaker: Mir
sp.l: Too ſtrange for me; I muſt have thoſe have mettle,
And mettle to my mind: Come lets be merry.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Bleſs me from this woman: I would ſtand the Cannon
Before ten words of hers.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: Do you find him now?
Do you think he will be ever firm?

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I fear not. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: NE'r tel me of this happineſs, 'tis nothing;
The ſtate they bring with being ſought to ſcurvey,
I had rather make mine own play, and I will do.
My happineſs is in mine own content,
And the deſpiſing of ſuch glorious trifles,
As I have done a thouſand more. For my humour
Give me a good free fellow, that ſticks to me,
A joviall fair companion; there's a Beauty:
For women, I can have too many of them;
Good women too, as the Age reckons 'em,
More than I have employment for.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: You are happy.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: My only fear is, that I muſt be forced
Againſt my nature, to conceal my ſelf.
Health, and an able body are two jewels.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: If either of theſe two women were offer'd to me now,
I would think otherwiſe, and do accordingly:
Yes, and recant my hereſies, I would Sir;
And be more tender of opinion,
And put a little off my travail'd Libertie
Out of the way, and look upon 'em ſeriouſly.
Me-thinks this grave-carried wench.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Me-thinks the other,
The home-ſpoken Gentle-woman, that deſires to be fruitfull,
That treats of the full mannage of the matter,
For there lies all my aim; that wench, me-thinks
If I were but well ſet-on; for ſhe is a fable,
If I were but hounded right, and one to teach me;
She ſpeaks to th' matter, and comes home to th' point:
Now do I know I have ſuch a body to pleaſe her,
As all the kingdom cannot fit her with, I am ſure on't,
If I could but talk my ſelf into her favour.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That's eaſily done.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: That's eaſily ſaid, would 'twere done;
You ſhould ſee then how I would lay about me;
If I were vertuous, it would never grieve me,
Or any thing that might juſtifie my modeſty,
But when my nature is prone to do a charitie,
And my calfs-tongue will not help me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Will ye go to 'em?
They cannot but take it curteouſly.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I'll do my part,
Though I am ſure 'twil be the hardeſt I e'r plaid yet,
A way I never try'd too, which will ſtagger me,
And if it do not ſhame me, I am happy.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Win 'em, and wear 'em, I give up my intereſt.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: What ſay ye, Monſieur Bellure?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Would I could ſay,
Or ſing, or any thing that were but handſom,
I would be with her preſently.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Yours is no venture;
A merry ready wench.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: A vengeance ſquibber;
She'll fleer me out of faith too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I'll be near thee;
Pluck up thy heart, I'll ſecond thee at all brunts;
Be angry if ſhe abuſe thee, and beat her a little,
Some women are won that way.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Pray be quiet,
And let me think: I am reſolv'd to go on;
But how I ſhall get off again—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I am perſwaded
Thou wilt ſo pleaſe her, ſhe will go neer to raviſh thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I would 'twere come to that once: Let me pray a little.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Now for thine honor Pinac; board me this modeſty,
Warm but this frozen ſnow-ball, 'twill be a conqueſt
(Although I know thou art a fortunate Wencher,
And haſt done rarely in thy daies) above all thy ventures.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You will be ever neer?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: At all neceſſities,
And take thee off, and ſet thee on again, Boy;
And cheriſh thee, and ſtroak thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Help me out too?
For I know I ſhall ſtick 'ith' mire: if ye ſee us cloſe once,
Be gone, and leave me to my fortune, ſuddainly,
For I am then determin'd to do wonders.
Farewell, and fling an old ſhooe: how my heart throbs?
Would I were drunk: Farewell Pinac; heaven ſend us
A joyfull and a merry meeting, man.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Farewell,
And chear thy heart up; and remember Bellure
They are but women.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I had rather they were Lyons.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: About it; Ill be with you inſtantly. Exeunt.
Shall I ne'r be at reſt? no peace of conſcience? Enter Oriana.
No quiet for theſe creatures? Am I ordain'd
To be devour'd quick by theſe ſhe-Canibals?
Here's another they call handſom, I care not for her,
I ne'r look after her: When I am half tipled
It may be I ſhould turn her, and peruſe her,
Or in my want of women, I might call for her;
But to be haunted when I have no fancie,
No maw to th' matter—Now, why do you follow me?

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I hope, Sir, 'tis no blemiſh to my vertue,
Nor need you (out of ſcruple) aſk that queſtion,
If you remember ye, before your Travell
The contract you ty'd to me: 'tis my love, Sir,
That makes me ſeek ye, to confirm your memory,
And that being fair and good, I cannot ſuffer:
I come to give ye thanks too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: For what 'prethee?

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: For that fair peece of honeſty ye ſhew'd, Sir,
That conſtant nobleneſs.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How? for I am ſhort headed.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I'll tell ye then; for refuſing that free offer
Of Monſieur Nantolets; thoſe handſom Beauties,
Thoſe two prime Ladies, that might well have preſt ye,
If not to have broken, yet to have bow'd your promiſe.
I know it was for my ſake, for your faith ſake,
You ſlipt 'em off: your honeſty compell'd ye.
And let me tell ye, Sir, it ſhew'd moſt handſomly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And let me tell thee, there was no ſuch matter:
Nothing intended that way of that nature;
I have more to do with my honeſty than to fool it,
Or venture it in ſuch leak-barks as women;
I put 'em off; becauſe I lov'd 'em not,
Becauſe they are too queazie for my temper,
And not for thy ſake, nor the Contract ſake,
Nor vows, nor oathes; I have made a thouſand of 'em,
They are things indifferent, whether kept or broken;
Meer veniall ſlips, that grow not near the Conſcience;
Nothing concerns thoſe tender parts; they are trifles;
For, as I think, there was never man yet hop'd for
Either conſtancie, or ſecrecie, from a woman,
Unleſs it were an Aſs ordain'd for ſufferance;
Nor to contract with ſuch can be a Tiall;
So let them know again; for 'tis a Juſtice,
And a main point of civill policie,
Whate're we ſay or ſwear, they being Reprobates,
Out of the ſtate of faith, we are clear of all ſides,
And 'tis a curious blindneſs to beleeve us.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: You do not mean this ſure?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes ſure, and certain,
And hold it poſitively, as a Principle,
As ye are ſtrange things, and made of ſtrange fires and fluxes,
So we are allow'd as ſtrange wayes to obtain ye,
But not to hold; we are all created Errant.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: You told me other tales.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I not deny it;
I have tales of all ſorts for all ſorts of women,
And proteſtations likewiſe of all ſizes,
As they have vanities to make us coxcombs;
If I obtain a good turn, ſo it is,
I am thankfull for it: if I be made an Aſs,
The mends are in mine own hands, or the Surgeons,
And there's an end on't.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Do not you love me then?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: As I love others, heartily I love thee,
When I am high and luſty, I love thee cruelly
After I have made a plenteous meal, and ſatisfi'd
My ſenſes with all delicates, come to me,
And thou ſhalt ſee how I love thee.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Will not you mary me?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, certain, no, for any thing I know yet;
I muſt not loſe my liberty, dear Lady,
And like a wanton ſlave cry for more ſhackles.
What ſhould I mary for? Do I want any thing?
Am I an inch the farther from my pleaſure?
Why ſhould I be at charge to keep a wife of mine own,
When other honeſt maryed men will eaſe me?
And thank me too, and be beholding to me:
Thou thinkſt I am mad for a Maiden-head, thou art cozen'd;
Or if I were addicted to that diet
Can you tell me where I ſhould have one? thou art eighteen now,
And if thou haſt thy Maiden-head yet extant,
Sure 'tis as big as Gods-head: and thoſe grave diſhes
I never love to deal withall: Do'ſt thou ſee this book here?
Look over all theſe ranks; all theſe are Women,
Mayds, and pretenders to Maiden-heads; theſe are my conqueſts,
All theſe I ſwore to mary, as I ſwore to thee,
With the ſame reſervation, and moſt righteouſly,
Which I need not have don neither; for alas they made no ſcruple,
And I enjoy'd 'em at my will, and left 'em:
Some of 'em are maried ſince, and were as pure mayds again,
Nay o' my conſcience better than they were bred for;
The reſt fine ſober women.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Are ye not aſham'd, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No by my troth, Sir; there's no ſhame belongs to it;
〈◊〉 hold it as commendable to be wealthy in pleaſure,
As others do in rotten ſheep, and paſture. Enter de Gard.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Are all my hopes come to this? is their no faith?
No troth? nor modeſty in men?

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: How now Siſter,
Why weeping thus? did I not propheſie?
Come tell me why—

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I am not well; 'pray ye pardon me. Exit.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: Now Monſieur Mirabell, what ails my Siſter?
You have been playing the wag with her.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: As I take it,
She is crying for a cod-peece; is ſhe gone?
Lord, what an Age is this? I was calling for ye,
For as I live I thought ſhe would have raviſh'd me.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: Ye are merry Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou know'ſt this book, de Gard, this Inventory.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: The Debt-book of your Miſtriſſes, I remember it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why this was it that anger'd her; ſhe was ſtark mad
She found not her name here, and cry'd down-right,
Becauſe I would not pitty her immediately,
And put her in my liſt.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: Sure ſhe had more modeſty.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Their modeſty is anger to be over-done;
They'll quarrell ſooner for precedence here,
And take it in more dudgen to be ſlighted,
Than they will in publique meetings; 'tis their natures:
And alaſs I have ſo many to diſpatch yet,
And to provide my ſelf for my affairs too,
That in good faith—

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: Be not too glorious fooliſh;
Summe not your Travails up with vanities,
It ill becomes your expectation:
Temper your ſpeech, Sir; whether your looſe ſtory
Be true, or falſe (for you are ſo free, I fear it)
Name not my Siſter in't; I muſt not hear it;
Upon your da •• er name her not: I hold her
A Gentlewom • n of thoſe happy parts and carriage,
A good mans tongue may be right proud to ſpeak her.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Your Siſter, Sir? d'ye blench at that? d'ye cavill?
Do you hold her ſuch a peece, ſhe may not be play'd withall?
I have had an hundred handſomer and nobler,
Has ſu'd to me too for ſuch a curteſie:
Your Siſter comes i'th' rear: ſince ye are ſo angry,
And hold your Siſter ſuch a ſtrong Recuſant,
I tell ye I may do it, and it may be will too,
It may be have too; there's my free confeſſion;
Work upon that now.

sp.speaker: de G.
sp.l: If I thought ye had, I would work,
And work ſuch ſtubborn work, ſhould make your heart ake;
But I beleeve ye, as I ever knew ye,
A glorious talker, and a Legend maker
Of idle tales, and trifles; a depraver
Of your own truth; their honours fly about ye;
And ſo I take my leave, but with this caution,
Your ſword be ſurer than your tongue, you'll ſmart elſe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I laugh at thee, ſo little I reſpect thee;
And I'll talk louder, and deſpiſe thy Siſter;
Set up a Chamber-maid that ſhall out-ſhine her,
And carry her in my Coach too, and that will kill her.
Go get thy Rents up, go.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: Ye are a fine Gentleman. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Now have at my two youths, I'll ſee how they do,
How they behave themſelves, and then I'll ſtudy
What wench ſhall love me next, and when I'll looſe her. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Art thou her ſervant, ſaiſt thou?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Her poor creature,
But ſervant to her horſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Canſt thou ſhew me
The way to her chamber? or where I may conveniently
See her, or come to talk to her?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: That I can, Sir;
But the queſtion is whether I will or no.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Why I'll content thee.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Why I'll content thee then; now ye come to me.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: There's for your diligence.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: There's her chamber, Sir;
And this way ſhe comes out; ſtand ye but here, Sir,
You have her at your proſpect, or your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Is ſhe not very angry?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You'll find that quickly:
'May be ſhe'll call ye ſawcy ſcurvey fellow,
Or ſome ſuch familiar name: 'may be ſhe knows ye,
And will fling a Piſs-pot at ye, or a Pantofle,
According as ye are in acquaintance: if ſhe like ye,
'May be ſhe'll look upon ye, 'may be no,
And two moneths hence call for ye.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: This is fine.
She is monſtrous proud then?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: She is a little haughtie;
Of a ſmall body, ſhe has a mind well mounted.
Can ye ſpeak Greek?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: No certain.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Get ye gon then;
And talk of ſtars, and firmaments, and fire-drakes,
Do you remember who was Adams School-maſter,
And who taught Eve to ſpin? ſhe knowes all theſe,
And will run ye over the beginning o'th' world
As familiar as a Fidler.
Can ye ſit ſeven hours together, and ſay nothing?
Which ſhe will do, and when ſhe ſpeaks ſpeak Oracles;
Speak things that no man underſtands, nor her ſelf neither.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Thou mak'ſt me wonder.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Can ye ſmile?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Yes willingly:
For naturally I bear a mirth about me.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: She'll ne'r endure ye then; ſhe is never merry;
If ſhe ſee one laugh, ſhe'll ſwound paſt Aquavitae;
Never come near her, Sir; if ye chance to venture,
And talk not like a Doctor, you are damn'd too;
I have told ye enough for your Crown, and ſo good ſpeed ye. Ex.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I have a pretty taſk, if ſhe be thus curious,
As ſure it ſeems ſhe is; if I fall off now,
I ſhall be laugh'd at fearfully; if I go forward,
I can but be abus'd, and that I look for,
And yet I may hit right, but 'tis unlikely.
Stay, in what mood and figure ſhall I attempt her?
A careleſs way? no, no, that will not waken her;
Beſides, her gravity will give me line ſtill,
And let me loſe my ſelf; yet this way often
Has hit, and handſomly. A wanton method?
I, if ſhe give it leave to ſink into her conſideration;
But there's the doubt: if it but ſtir her blood once,
And creep into the crannies of her phanſie,
Set her a gog: but if ſhe chance to ſlight it,
And by the pow'r of her modeſty fling it back,
I ſhall appear the arrantſt Raſcal to her,
The moſt licentious knave, for I ſhall talk lewdly.
To bear my ſelf auſterely? rate my words,
And fling a generall gravitie about me,
As if I meant to give Laws? but this I cannot do,
This is a way above my underſtanding;
Or if I could, 'tis ods ſhe'll think I mock her;
For ſerious and ſad things are ever ſtill ſuſpicious.
Well, I'll ſay ſomething.
But learning I have none, and leſs good manners,
Eſpecially for Ladies; well, I'll ſet my beſt face; Enter Lilia, Petella.
I hear ſome coming; this is the firſt woman
I ever fear'd yet, the firſt face that ſhakes me.

sp.speaker: Li.
sp.l: Give me my hat Petella, take this veil off,
This ſullen cloud, it darkens my delights;
Come wench be free, and let the Muſick warble,
Play me ſome luſty meaſure.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: This is ſhe ſure,
The very ſame I ſaw, the very woman,
The Gravitie I wonder'd at: Stay, ſtay,
Let me be ſure; ne'r truſt me, but ſhe danceth,
Summer is in her face now, and ſhe ſkippeth:
I'll go a little nearer.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Quicker time fellows, Enter Mirabell
I cannot find my legs yet, now Petella.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I am amaz'd, I am founder'd in my fancie.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Hah, ſay ye ſo; is this your gravitie?
This the auſteritie ye put upon ye?
I'll ſee more o'this ſport.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: A Song now;
Call in for a merry, and a light Song,
And ſing it with a liberall ſpirit. Enter a man.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Yes, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: And be not amaz'd ſirha, but take us for your own company.
Let's walk our ſelves; come wench, would we had a man or two.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Sure ſhe has ſpi'd me, and will abuſe me dreadfully,
She has put on this for the purpoſe; yet I will try her.
Madam, I would be loth my rude intruſion,
Which I muſt crave a pardon for—

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: O ye are welcom,
Ye are very welcom, Sir, we want ſuch a one;
Strike up again: I dare preſume ye dance well:
Quick, quick, Sir, quick, the time ſteals on.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I would talk with ye.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Talk as ye dance.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: She'll beat him off his legs firſt.
This is the fineſt Maſque.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Now how do ye, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: You have given me a ſhrew'd heat.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: I'll give ye a hundred.
Come ſing now, ſing; for I know ye ſing well.
I ſee ye have a ſinging face.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: A fine Modeſty!
If I could ſhe'd never give me breath,
Madam would I might ſit and recover.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Sit here, and ſing now,
Let's do things quickly, Sir, and handſomly,
Sit cloſe wench, cloſe, begin, begin. Song.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I am leſſon'd.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: 'Tis very pretty y'faith, give me ſome wine now.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I would fain ſpeak to ye.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: You ſhall drink firſt, believe me:
Here's to ye a luſty health.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I thank ye Lady.
Would I were off again; I ſmell my miſery;
I was never put to this rack; I ſhall be drunk too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: If thou be'ſt not a right one, I have loſt mine aim much:
I thank heaven that I have ſcap'd thee: To her Pinac;
For thou art as ſure to have her, and to groan for her—
I'll ſee how my other youth does; this ſpeeds trimly:
A fine grave Gentlewoman, and worth much honour. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Now? how do ye like me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I like ye rarely.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Ye ſee, Sir, though ſometimes we are grave and ſilent,
And put on ſadder diſpoſitions,
Yet we are compounded of free parts, and ſometimes too
Our lighter, airie, and our fierie mettles
Break out, and ſhew themſelves; and what think you of that Sir?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Good Lady ſit, for I am very weary;
And then I'll tell ye.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Fie, a young man idle:
Up, and walk; be ſtill in action.
The motions of the body are fair beauties,
Beſides 'tis cold; ods-me Sir, let's walk faſter.
What think ye now of the Lady Felicia?
And Bella-fronte the Dukes fair daughter? ha?
Are they not handſom things? thereis Duarta,
And brown Olivia.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I know none of 'em.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: But brown muſt not be caſt away, Sir; if young Lelia
Had kept her ſelf till this day from a huſband,
Why what a Beauty, Sir? you know Iſmena
The fair Jem of Saint Germins?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: By my troth I do not.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: And then I know you muſt hear of Briſac,
How unlike a Gentleman—

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: As I live I have heard nothing.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Strike me another Galliard.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: By this light I cannot;
In troth I have ſprain'd my leg, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Now ſit ye down, Sir,
And tell me why ye came hither, why ye choſe me out?
What is your buſineſs? your errant? diſpatch, diſpatch;
'May be ye are ſome Gentlemans man, and I miſtook ye,
That have brought me a Letter, or a haunch of Veniſon,
Sent me from ſome friend of mine.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Do I look like a Carrier?
You might allow me what I am, a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Cry 'ye mercie, Sir, I ſaw ye yeſterday,
You are new come out of Travail, I miſtook ye;
And how do's all our impudent friends in Italie?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Madam, I came with duty, and fair curteſie,
Service, and honour to ye.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Ye came to jeer me:
Yee ſee I am merry, Sir, I have chang'd my coppy:
None of the Sages now, and 'pray ye proclame it,
Fling on me what aſperſion you ſhall pleaſe, Sir,
Of wantonneſs, or wildneſs, I look for it;
And tell the world I am an hypocrite
Maſk in a forc'd and borrow'd ſhape, I expect it;
But not to have you beleev'd; for mark ye, Sir,
I have won a nobler eſtimation,
A ſtronger tie by my diſcretion
Upon opinion (how ere you think I forced it)
Than either tongue or art of yours can ſlubbber,
And when I pleaſe I will be what I pleaſe, Sir,
So I exceed not Mean; and none ſhall brand it
Either with ſcorn or ſhame, but ſhall be ſlighted.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Lady, I come to love ye.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Love your ſelf, Sir.
And when I want obſervers, 'll ſend for ye:
Heigh, ho; my fit's almoſt off, for we do all by fits, Sir:
If ye be weary, ſit till I come again to ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: This is a wench of a dainty ſpirit; but hang me if I know yet
Either what to think, or make of her; She had her will of me,
And baited me abundantly, I thank her.
And I confeſs I never was ſo blurted,
Nor never ſo abus'd; I muſt bear mine own ſins;
Ye talk of Travails, here's a curious Country,
Yet I will find her out, or forſwear my facultie. Exit.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ne'r vex your ſelf, nor grieve; ye are a fool then.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I am ſure I am made ſo: yet before I ſuffer
Thus like a girl, and give him leave to triumph—

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: You ſay right; for as long as he perceives ye
Sink under his proud ſcornings, he'll laugh at ye:
For me, ſecure your ſelf; and for my Siſter,
I partly know her mind too: howſoever
To obey my Father we have made a tender
Of our poor beauties to the travail'd Monſieur;
Yet two words to a bargain; he ſlights us
As ſkittiſh things, and we ſhun him as curious.
May be my free behaviour turns his ſtomach,
And makes him ſeem to doubt a looſe opinion.
I muſt be ſo ſometimes, though all the world ſaw it.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Why ſhould not ye? Are our minds only meaſur'd?
As long as here ye ſtand ſecure.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ye ſay true;
As long as mine own conſcience makes no queſtion,
What care I for Report: That woman's miſerable
That's good or bad for their tongues ſake: Come let's retire.
And get my veil wench: By my troth your ſorrow,
And the conſideration of mens humorous maddings,
Have put me into a ſerious contemplation. Enter Mirabell and Bellure.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Come 'faith, let's ſit and think.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: That's all my buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Why ſtandſt thou peeping here? thou great ſlug, forward.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: She is there, peace.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why ſtandſt thou here then,
Sneaking, and peaking, as thou would'ſt ſteal linnen?
Haſt thou not place and time?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I had a rare ſpeech
Studied, and almoſt ready, and your violence
Has beat it out of my brains.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Hang your rare ſpeeches,
Go me on like a man.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Let me ſet my Beard up.
How has Pinac performed?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: He has won already:
He ſtands not thrumming of caps thus.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Lord, what ſhould I ail?
What a cold I have over my ſtomack; would I had ſome Hum.
Certain I have a great mind to be at her:
A mighty mind.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: On fool.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Good words, I beſeech ye;
For I will not be abuſed by both.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Adieu, then,
I will not trouble you, I ſee you are valiant,
And work your own way.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Hiſt, hiſt, I will be rul'd
I will y'faith, I will go preſently:
Will ye forſake me now and leave me i'th' ſuds:
You know I am falſe-hearted this way; I beſeech ye,
Good ſweet Mirabell; I'll cut your throat if ye leave me,
Indeed I will ſweet heart.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I will be ready,
Still at thine elbow; take a mans heart to thee,
And ſpeak thy mind: the plainer ſtill the better.
She is a woman of that free behaviour,
Indeed that common curteſie, ſhe cannot deny thee;
Go bravely on.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Madam—keep cloſe about me,
Still at my back. Madam, ſweet Madam.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ha;
What noiſe is that, what ſaucy ſound to trouble me?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What ſayd ſhe?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I am ſaucy.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis the better.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: She comes; muſt I be ſaucie ſtill?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: More ſaucie.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Still troubled with theſe vanities? heaven bleſs us;
What are we born to? would ye ſpeak with any of my people?
Go in, Sir, I am buſie.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: This is not ſhe ſure:
Is this two children at a Birth? I'll be hang'd then:
Mine was a merry Gentlewoman, talkt daintily,
Talkt of thoſe matters that befitted women;
This is a parcell-pray'r-book; I'm ſerv'd ſweetly;
And now I am to look too; I was prepar'd for th' other way.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Do you know that man?

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Sure I have ſeen him, Lady.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Me-thinks 'tis pitty ſuch a luſty fellow
Should wander up and down and want employment.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: She takes me for a Rogue: you may do well Madam,
To ſtay this wanderer, and ſet him a work, forſooth,
He can do ſomething that may pleaſe your Ladiſhip.
I have heard of women that deſire good breedings,
Two at a birth, or ſo.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: The fellow's impudent.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Sure he is crazed.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I have heard of men too that have had good manners;
Sure this is want of grace; indeed 'tis great pitty
The young man has been bred ſo ill; but this lewd Age
Is full of ſuch examples.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I am founder'd,
And ſome ſhall rue the ſetting of me on.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ha? ſo bookiſh, Lady, is it poſſible?
Turn'd holy at the heart too? I'll be hang'd then:
Why this is ſuch a feat, ſuch an activitie,
Such faſt and looſe: a veyl too for your knavery?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: What do you take me for, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: An hypocrite, a wanton, a diſſembler,
How e're ye ſeem, and thus ye are to be handled.
Mark me Bellure, and this you love, I know it.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Stand off, bold Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You wear good clothes to this end,
Jewels, love Feaſts, and Maſques.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ye are monſtrous ſaucie.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: All this to draw on fools? and thus, thus Lady,
Ye are to be lull'd.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Let her alone, I'll ſwinge ye elſe,
I will y'faith; for though I cannot ſkill o'this matter
My ſelf, I will not ſee another do it before me,
And do it worſe.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Away, ye are a vain thing;
You have travail'd far Sir, to return again
A windy and poor Bladder: you talk of women,
That are not worth the favour of a common one;
The grace of her grew in an Hoſpitall:
Againſt a thouſand ſuch blown fooleries
I am able to maintain good womens honours,
Their freedoms, and their fames, and I will do it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: She has almoſt ſtruck me dumb too.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: And declame
Againſt your baſe malicious tongues; your noyſes;
For they are nothing elſe: You teach behaviours?
Or touch us for our freedoms? teach your ſelves manners,
Truth and ſobriety, and live ſo clearly
That our lives may ſhine in ye; and then taſk us:
It ſeems ye are hot, the ſuburbs will ſupply ye,
Good women ſcorn ſuch Gameſters; ſo I'll leave ye.
I am ſorry to ſee this; 'faith Sir live fairly. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This woman, if ſhe hold on, may be vertuous,
'Tis almoſt poſſible: we'll have a new day.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Ye brought me on, ye forced me to this foolery;
I am ſham'd, I am ſcorn'd, I am flurted; yes, I am ſo:
Though I cannot talk to a woman like your worſhip,
And uſe my phraſes, and my learned figures,
Yet I can fight with any man.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Fie.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I can, Sir,
And I will fight.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: With whom?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: With you, with any man;
For all men now will laugh at me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Pre'thee be moderate.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: And I'll beat all men. Come.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I love thee dearly.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I beat all that love, Love has undone me;
Never tell me, I will not be a Hiſtory.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou art not.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Sfoot I will not; give me room,
And let me ſee the proudeſt of ye jeer me,
And I'll begin with you firſt.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Pre'thee Bellure;
If I do not ſatisfie thee —

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Well, look ye do:
But now I think on't better, 'tis impoſſible;
I muſt beat ſome body, I am maul'd my ſelf,
And I ought in Juſtice—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, no, no, ye are couzen'd;
But walk, and let me talk to thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Talk wiſely,
And ſee that no man laugh upon no occaſion;
For I ſhall think then 'tis at me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Nor no more talk of this.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Do'ſt think I am maddiſh?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I muſt needs fight yet; for I find it concerns me,
A pox on't, I muſt fight.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Y'faith thou ſhalt not. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter De Gard, and Leverdure, alias, Lugier.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: I Know ye are a Scholar, and can do wonders.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: There's no great Scholarſhip belongs to this, Sir;
What I am, I am; I pitty your poor Siſter,
And heartily I hate theſe Travellers,
Theſe Gim-cracks, made of Mops, and Motions:
There's nothing in their houſes here but humings;
A Bee has more brains. I grieve, and vex too
The inſolent licentious carriage
Of this out-facing fellow, Mirabell,
And I am mad to ſee him prick his plumes up.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: His wrongs you partly know.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Do not you ſtir, Sir,
Since he has begun with wit, let wit revenge it;
Keep your ſword cloſe, wee'll cut his throat a new way.
I am aſham'd the Gentlewoman ſhould ſuffer
Such baſe lewd wrongs.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: I will be rul'd, he ſhall live,
And left to your revenge.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: I, I, I'll fit him:
He makes a common ſcorn of handſom women;
Modeſty, and good manners are his May-games:
He takes up Maidenheads with a new Commiſſion;
The Church, warrant's out of date: follow my Counſell
For I am zealous in the Cauſe.

sp.speaker: de Gr.
sp.l: I will, Sir;
And will be ſtill directed: for the truth is
My Sword will make my ſiſter ſeem more monſtrous:
Beſides there is no honor won on Reprobates.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: You are ith' right: The ſlight he has ſhew'd my Pupills
Setts me a fire too: goe Ile prepare your Siſter,
And as I told ye.

sp.speaker: de Gr.
sp.l: Yes all ſhalbe fit, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: And ſeriouſly, and handſomely.

sp.speaker: de Gr.
sp.l: I warrant ye.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: A little councell more.

sp.speaker: de Gr.
sp.l: 'Tis well.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: Moſt ſtately.
See that obſerv'd; and then.

sp.speaker: de Gr.
sp.l: I have ye every way.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: Away then and be ready.

sp.speaker: de Gr.
sp.l: With all ſpeed Sir. —Exit.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: Wee'll learne to travell too, may be beyond him
Good day, Faire beauties.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: You have beautified us.
We thank ye Sir, ye have ſet us off moſt gallantly
With your grave precepts.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We expected Husbands
Out of your Documents, and taught behaviours;
Excellent Husbands, thought men would run ſtarck mad on us
Men of all Ages, and all States: we expected
An Inundation of deſires, and Offers,
A Torrent of trym Suitors: all we did,
Or ſaid, or purpos'd to be Spels about us,
Spells to provoake.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Ye have provoak'd us finely,
We follow'd your directions, we did rarely,
We were Stately, Coy, Demure, Careleſs, Light, Giddy,
And plai'd at all points: This you ſwore would Carry.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We made Love, and Contemn'd Love. Now ſeemd holy
With ſuch a reverent put-on Reſervation
Which could not miſſe according to your Principles,
Now gave more hope again. Now cloſe, Now publick,
Still up and down, we beate it like a Billowe;
And ever thoſe Behaviours you read to us,
Subtile, and new. But all this will not help us.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: They help to hinder us of all Acquaintance,
They have frighted off all Friends: what am I better
For all my Learning, if I love a Dunce,
A handſome dunce? to what uſe ſerves my Reading,
You ſhould have taught me what belongs to Horſes,
Doggs, dice, Hawkes, Banketts, masks, free and faire Meetings
To have ſtudied Gownes and Dreſſings.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: Ye are not mad ſure,

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We ſhalbe if we follow your encouragements;
I'le take mine own way now:

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: And I my Fortune.
We may live Maids elſe till the Moon drop Milſtones;
I ſee your modeſt Women are tak'en for Monſters,
A Dowry of good breeding is worth nothing.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: Since ye take it ſo toth' heart, pray'ye give me leave yet
And ye ſhall ſee how I'le convert this Heretique;
Mark how this Mirabell.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Name him no more:
For, though I long for a husband, I hate him,
And would be marryed ſooner to a Monkey,
Or to a Jack of Straw, then ſuch a Juggler.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I am of that minde too; he is too nimble,
And plays at faſt and looſe too learnedly
For a plain-meaning Woman; thats the truth on't.
Here's one too, that we love well, would be angry;
And reaſon why: No, no, we will not trouble ye
Nor him, at this time: may he make you happy.
We'll turn our ſelves looſe now, to our faire Fortunes,
And the down-right way.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: The winning-way wee'll follow,
Wee'll bait, that men may bite fair, and not be frighted;
Yet wee'll not be carryed ſo cheap neither: wee'll have ſom ſport,
Some mad-Morryſſe or other for our money (Tutor.)

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: 'Tis like enough: proſper your own Devices;
Ye are old enough to Chooſe: But for this Gentlewoman
So pleaſe her, give me leave.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I ſhall be glad Sir,
To finde a Friend, whoſe pity may direct me.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: Ile doe my beſt, and faithfully deale for ye;
But then ye muſt be ruled.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: In all, I vo • to ye.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Doe, doe: he has a lucky hand ſomtimes, Ile aſſure ye:
And hunts the recovery of a loſt Lover deadly.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: You muſt away ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: And Ile inſtruct ye:
Here ye can know no more.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: By your leave, ſweet Ladies,
And all our Fortunes, arive at our own wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Amen, Amen.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: I muſt borrow your man.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: 'Pray take him;
He is within: to doe her good, take any thing,
Take us, and all.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: No doubt ye may finde Takers;
And ſo wee'll leave ye to your own diſpoſes. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Now which way, Wench.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Wee'll goe a brave way; fear not:
A ſafe, and ſure way too: and yet a by-way,
I muſt confeſs I have a great minde to be marryed.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: So have I too, a grudging of good-will that way;
And would as fain be diſpatch'd. But this Monſieur Quickſilver.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: No, no: we'll bar him, by, and Mayne: Let him trample;
There is no ſafety in his Surquedrie:
An Army-Roiall of Women, are too few for him,
He keeps a Journall of his Gentleneſs,
And will go near to print his fair Diſpatches,
And call it his Triumph over Time and Women:
Let him paſs out of memory: what think ye
Of his two Companions?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Pinac methinks is reaſonable;
A little Modeſtie he has brought home with him,
And might be taught in time ſome handſome duty.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: They ſay he is a Wencher too.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I like him better:
A free light Touch or two becomes a Gentleman,
And ſets him ſeemly off: ſo he exceed not,
But keep his Compaſs, clear he may be lookt at;
I would not marry a man that muſt be taught,
And conjur'd up with Kiſſes; the beſt Game
Is plaid ſtill by the beſt Gameſters.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Fie upon thee!
What talk haſt thou?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Are not we alone, and merry?
Why ſhould we be aſham'd to ſpeak what we think? thy Gentleman
The tall fat: Follow; he that came to ſee thee.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Is't not a goodly man?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: A wondrous goodly!
'Has weight enough I warrant thee: Mercy upon me;
What a Serpent wilt thou ſeem under ſuch a St George.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Thou art a Fool; give me a man brings Mettle.
Brings ſubſtance with him; needs no Brothes to Lare him:
Theſe little Fellows ſhew like Fleas in boxes,
Hop up and down, and keep a ſtir to vex us;
Give me the puiſſant Pike, take you the ſmall Shot.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Of a great thing I have not ſeen a Duller,
Therefore methinks, ſweet Siſter.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Peace: he's modeſt:
A baſhfulneſs, which is a point of grace, Wench:
But when theſe Fellows come to moulding, Siſter,
To heat, and handling: as I live, I like him; Enter Mirabell.
And methinks I could form him.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Peace: the Fire-drake.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Bleſs ye ſweet Beauties: ſweet incomparable Ladies:
Sweet wits: ſweet humours: 'Bleſs you, Learned Lady,
And you, moſt holy Nun; 'Bleſs your Devotions,

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: And 'bleſs your brains, Sir, your moſt pregnant brains, Sir,
They are in Travail, may they be delivered
Of a moſt hopefull Wild-Gooſe.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: 'Bleſs your manhood:
They ſay ye are a Gentleman of Action,
A fare accompliſh'd man; and a rare Engineer,
You have a trick to blow-up Maidenheads,
A ſubtle trick, they ſay abroad.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I have Lady.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: And often glory in their Ruines.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes forſooth;
I have a ſpeedy trick: pleaſe you to try it:
My Engine will diſpatch ye inſtantly.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I would I were a Woman, Sir, fit for ye,
As there be ſuch, no doubt, may Engine you too;
May with a Counter-mine blow up your valour:
But in good faith, Sir, we are both too honeſt;
And the plague is, we cannot be perſwaded:
For, look ye: if we thought it were a glory
To be the laſt of all your lovely Ladies.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Come, come; leave prating: this has ſpoil'd your Market;
This pride, and pufft-up heart, will make ye faſt (Ladies)
Faſt, when ye are hungry too.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: The more our pain, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: The more our health, I hope too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Your behaviours
Have made men ſtand amaz'd; thoſe men that lov'd ye;
Men of fair States and parts; your ſtrange conventions
Into I know not what, nor how, nor wherefore;
Your ſcorns of thoſe that came to viſit ye;
Your ſtudied Whim-whams; and your fine ſet Faces:
What have theſe got ye? proud, and harſh opinions:
A Travail'd-Monſieur, was the ſtrangeſt Creature,
The wildeſt Monſter to be wondred at:
His Perſon made a publique Scoff, his Knowledge,
(As if he had been bred 'mongſt Bears or Bandoggs)
Shunn'd and avoided: his converſation ſnuft at.
What Harveſt brings all this?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I pray ye proceed, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Now ye ſhall ſee in what eſteem a Travailer,
An under ſtanding Gentleman, and a Monſieur
Is to be held, and to your greifes confes it,
Both to your greifes, and gaules.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: In what I pray ye, Sir?
We would be glad to underſtand your Excellence

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Goe on, (ſweet Ladies) it becomes ye rarely
For me, I have bleſt me from ye, ſcoff on, ſeriouſly,
And note the Man ye mock'd: you, (Lady Learning)
Note the poore Traveller, that came to viſit ye,
That flat unfurniſh'd Fellow: note him throughly,
You may chance to ſee him anon.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: 'Tis very likely

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And ſee him Courted, by a Travell'd Lady,
Held deer, and honour'd by a vertuous virgin,
May be a Beautie, not far ſhort of yours, neither
It may be, cleerer.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Not unlikely

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Younger:
As killing eyes as yours: a wit as poynant
May be, a State to that may top your Fortune;
Enquire how ſhe thinks of him, how ſhe holds him;
His good parts; in what precious price already;
Being a ſtranger to him, how ſhe courts him;
A ſtranger to his Nation too, how ſhe dotes on him:
Enquire of this; be ſick to know: Curſe, Lady,
And keep your Chamber: cry, and curſe, a ſweet one,
A thouſand in yearly land; well bred; well friended:
Travell'd, and highly followed for her faſhions.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: 'Bleſs his good Fortune, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This ſcurvy fellow;
I think they call his name Pinac; this ſerving-man
That brought ye Veniſon, as I take it, Madam;
Note but this Scab; 'tis ſtrange that this courſe creature,
That has no more ſet off, but his jugglings,
His travell'd tricks.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Good, ſir, I grieve not at him,
Nor envy not his Fortune: yet I wonder,
He's handſom; yet I ſee no ſuch perfection.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Would I had his Fortune: for 'tis a woman
Of that ſweet temper'd nature, and that judgment,
Beſides her ſtate, that care, clear underſtanding,
And ſuch a wife to bleſs him.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Pray ye whence is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Of England and a moſt accompliſh'd Lady,
So modeſt that mens eies are frighted at her, Enter a Boy.
And ſuch a noble carriage. How now Sirrah?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Sir, the great Engliſh Lady.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What of her, ſir?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Has newly left her Coach, and coming this way,
Where you may ſee her plain: Monſieur Pinac,
The onely man that leades her.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: He is much honored;
Would I had ſuch a favour: now vex Ladies,
Envy, and vex, and raile.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ye are ſhort of us, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Bleſs your fair Fortune, ſir.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I Nobly thank ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Is ſhe married, friend?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: No, no.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A goodly Lady;
A ſweet and delicate Aſpect: mark, mark, and wonder!
Haſt thou any hope of her?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: A little.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Follow cloſe then:
Looſe not that hope.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: To you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Gentle Lady.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: She is fair indeed.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I have ſeen a fairer, yet
She is well.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Her clothes ſit handſome too.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: She dreſſes prettily.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: And by my faith ſhe is rich; ſhe looks ſtil ſweeter.
A well-bred woman, I warrant her.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Do you hear, Sir;
May I crave this Gentlewomans name?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Mariana, Lady.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I will not ſay I ow ye a quarel Monſieur
For making me your Stale: a noble Gentleman
Would have had more curteſie; at leaſt, more faith,
Then to turn of his miſtris at firſt trial:
You know not what reſpect I might have ſhew'd ye;
I finde ye have worth.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I cannot ſtay to anſwer ye;
Ye ſee my charge: I am beholding to ye
For all your merry tricks ye put upon me,
Your bobs, and baſe accounts: I came to love ye,
To woo ye, and to ſerve ye; I am much endebted to ye
For dancing me off my legs; and then for walking me;
For telling me ſtrange tales I never heard of,
More to abuſe me; for miſtaking me,
When ye both knew I was a Gentleman,
And one deſerv'd as rich a match as you are.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Be not ſo bitter, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: You ſee this Lady:
She is young enough, and fair enough to pleaſe me,
A woman of a loving minde, a quiet,
And one that weighs the worth of him that loves her,
I am content with this, and bleſs my Fortune,
Your curious Wits, and Beauties.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Faith ſee me once more.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I dare not trouble ye.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: May I ſpeak to your Lady?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I pray ye content your ſelf: I know ye are bitter,
And in your bitterneſs, ye may abuſe her;
Which if ſhe comes to know, (for ſhe underſtands ye not)
It may breed ſuch a quarrel to your kindred,
And ſuch an indiſcretion fling on you too;
For ſhe is Nobly friended.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I could eat her.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Reſt as ye are, a modeſt noble Gentlewoman,
And afford your honeſt neighbours ſom of your prayers. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What think you now?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Faith ſhe's a pretty Whiting;
She has got a pretty catch too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You are angry;
Monſtrous angry now; grievouſly angry;
And the pretty heart does ſwell now.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: No in troth, ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And it will cry anon; a pox upon it:
And it will curſe it ſelf: and eat no meat, Lady;
And it will fight.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Indeed you are miſtaken;
It will be very merry.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Why, ſir, do you think
There are no more men living, nor no handſomer
Then he, or you; By this light there be ten thouſand
Ten thouſand thouſand: comfort your ſelf, dear Monſieur,
Faces, and Bodies, Wits, and all Abilliments
There are ſo many we regard 'em not.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That ſuch a noble Lady, I could burſt now.
So far above ſuch triffles?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You did laugh at me,
And I know why ye laughed.

sp.speaker: 1. Gen.
sp.l: I pray ye be ſatisfied;
If we did laugh, we had ſome private reaſon,
And not at you.

sp.speaker: 2. Gen.
sp.l: Alas, we know you not, ſir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'll make you know me; ſet your faces ſoberly;
Stand this way, and look ſad; I'll be no May-game;
Sadder; demurer yet.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: What's the matter?
What ailes this Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: go off now backward, that I may behold ye;
And not a ſimper on you lives.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: He's mad ſure.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Do you obſerve me too?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I may look on ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Why do you grin? I know your minde.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You do not.
You are ſtrangely humorous: Is there no mirth, nor pleaſure,
But you muſt be the object?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Mark, and obſerve me;
Where ever I am nam'd;
The very word ſhall raiſe a general ſadneſs,
For the diſgrace this ſcurvy woman did me;
This proud pert thing; take heed ye laugh not at me;
Provoke me not, take heed.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I would fain pleaſe ye;
Do any thing to keep ye quiet.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Hear me,
Till I receive a ſatisfaction
Equal to the diſgrace, and ſcorn ye gave me:
Ye are a wreatched woman; till thou woo'ſt me,
And I ſcorn thee aſmuch, as, ſeriouſly,
Gear, and abuſe thee; ask what Gill thou art;
Or any baſer name; I will proclaim thee;
I will ſo ſing thy vertue; ſo be-paint thee,

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Nay, good ſir, be more modeſt.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Do you laugh again?
Becauſe ye are a woman ye are lawleſs,
And out of compaſs of an honeſt anger.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Good ſir, have a better belief of me.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Away deare ſiſter. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Is not this better now, this ſeeming madneſs,
Then falling out with your friends.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Have I not frighted her?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Into her right wits, I warrant thee: follow this humor,
And thou ſhalt ſee how proſperouſly 'twil guide thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I am glad I have found a way to woo yet, I was afraid once
I never ſhould have made a civill Suiter.
Well, I'le about it ſtill. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Doe, doe, and proſper.
What ſport do I make with theſe fools? What pleaſure
Feeds me, and fats my ſides at their poor innocence? Enter Leverduce, des Lugier, Mr. Illiard.
Wooing and wiving, hang it: give me mirth,
Witty and dainty mirth: I ſhall grow in love ſure
With mine own happy head. Who's this? To me, Sir?
What youth is this?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Yes, Sir, I would ſpeak with you,
If your name be Monſieur Mirabel.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ye have hit it.
Your buſineſſe, I beſeech yee.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: This it is, Sir.
There is a Gentlewoman hath long time affected yee,
And lov'd ye dearly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Turn over, and end that ſtory,
'Tis long enough: I have no faith in women, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo, Sir: I do not come to woo for her,
Or ſing her praiſes, though ſhe well deſerve 'em.
I come to tell ye, ye have been cruel to her,
Unkind and cruell, falſer of faith, and careleſſe,
Taking more pleaſure in abuſing her,
Wreſting her honour to your wild diſpoſes,
Then noble in requiting her affection:
Which, as ye are a man, I muſt deſire ye
(A Gentleman of rank) not to perſiſt in;
No more to load her fair name with your injuries.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why, I beſeech ye, Sir?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Good Sir, I'le tell ye.
And I'le be ſhort: I'le tell yee, becauſe I love ye,
Becauſe I would have you ſhun the ſhame may follow:
There is a noble man, new come to Town, Sir,
A noble and a great man that affects her,
A Countreyman of mine, a brave Savoyan,
Nephew to th'Duke, and ſo much honours her,
That 'twill be dangerous to purſue your old way,
To touch at any thing concerns her honour,
Believe, moſt dangerous; her name is Oriana,
And this great man will marry her: take heed, Sir;
For howſoev'r her brother, a ſtaid Gentleman,
Lets things paſſe upon better hopes, this Lord, Sir,
Is of that fiery, and that poynant metall,
(Eſpecially provok'd on by affection)
That 'twill be hard: but you are wiſe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A Lord, ſir?

sp.speaker: Lev.
sp.l: Yes, and a noble Lord.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Send her good fortune.
This will not ſtir her Lord; a Barronneſs,
Say ye ſo; ſay ye ſo: by'r Lady, a brave title;
Top, and top gallant now; 'ſave her great Ladiſhip.
I was a poor ſervant of hers, I muſt confeſs, Sir,
And in thoſe daies, I thought I might be jovy,
And make a little bold to call into her:
But Baſto, now; I know my rules and diſtance;
Yet, if ſhe want an Uſher; ſuch an implement;
One that is throughly pac'd; a clean made gentleman;
Can hold a hanging up; with approbation
Plant his Hat formally, and wait with patience
I do beſeech you, ſir.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Sir, leave your ſcoffing;
And as ye are a Gentleman, deal fairly:
I have given ye a friends councel, ſo I'll leave ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: But hark ye, hark ye, ſir; is't poſſible
I may beleeve what you ſay?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: You may chuſe, ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No Baites? No Fiſh-hooks, ſir? No Gins? No Nooſes?
No Pitfals to catch Puppies?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: I tell ye certain;
You may beleeve; if not, ſtand to the danger. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A Lord of Savoy ſaies he? The Dukes Nephew?
A man ſo mighty? By 'Lady a fair marriage;
By my faith, a handſom Fortune: I muſt leave prating;
For to confeſs the truth, I have abuſed her,
For which I ſhould be ſorry; but that will ſeem ſcurvy;
I muſt confeſs, ſhe was ever ſince I knew her
As modeſt, as ſhe was fair: I am ſure ſhe lov'd me;
Her means good; and her breeding excellent;
And for my ſake ſhe has refus'd fair matches:
I may play the fool finely. Stay who are theſe? Enter De-Gard, Oriana, and Attendants.
'Tis ſhe, I am ſure; and that the lord it ſhould ſeem,
He carries a fair Port; is a handſom man too:
I do begin to feel, I am a Coxcomb.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Good my Lord, chuſe a nobler: for I know
I am ſo far below your rank and Honor,
That what ye can ſay this way, I muſt credit,
But ſpoken to beget your ſelf ſport: Alas, Sir,
I am ſo far off, from deſerving you,
My Beauty ſo unfit for your Affection,
That I am grown the ſcorn of common Railers,
Of ſuch injurious Things, that when they cannot
Reach at my perſon, lie with my reputation:
I am poor beſides.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: Ye are all wealth and goodneſs;
And none but ſuch as are the ſcum of men,
The Ulcers of an honeſt State; Spight-weavers,
That live on poyſon onely, like ſwoln Spiders,
Dare once profane ſuch excellence, ſuch ſweetneſs.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This man ſpeaks loud indeed.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: Name but the men, Lady;
Let me but know theſe poor, and baſe depravers;
Lay but to my revenge their perſons open,
And you ſhall ſee how ſuddenly, how fully
For your moſt Beautious ſake, how direfully
I'll handle their deſpights. Is this thing one?
Be what he will.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: Dare your malicious tongue, ſir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I know you not; nor what ye mean.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Good my Lord.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: If he, or any he.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I beſeech your Honor.
This Gentleman's a ſtranger to my knowledge,
And no doubt, ſir, a worthy man.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: Your mercy;
But had ye been attaint of your Honor;
A blaſter of thoſe beauties raign within ye;
But we ſhall finde a fitter time: dear Lady,
As ſoon as I have freed ye from your Guardian,
And done ſome honour'd offices unto ye,
I'll take ye with thoſe faults the world flings on ye;
And dearer then the whole world I'll eſteem ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This is a thundring Lord; I am glad I ſcap'd him:
How lovingly the wench diſclaim'd my villany?
I am vext now heartily that he ſhall have her;
Not that I care to marry, or to loſe her;
But that this Bilbo-Lord ſhall reap that Maiden-head
That was my due; that he ſhall rig and top her;
Ide give a thouſand Crowns now, he might miſs her.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Nay, if I bear your blowes, and keep your councel,
You have good luck, Sir; I'll teach ye to ſtrike lighter.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Come hether, honeſt Fellow; canſt thou tell me
Where this great Lord lies? This Savoy Lord? Thou met'ſt him;
He now went by thee certain.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Yes, he did, Sir;
I know him; and I know you are fool'd.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Come hether.
Here's all this, give me truth.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Not for your money;
(And yet that may do much) but I have been beaten:
And by the worſhipful Contrivers beaten, and I'll tel ye;
This is no Lord, no Savoy Lord.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Go forward.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: This is a Trick, and put upon ye groſly
By one Lugier; the Lord is Monſieur De-Gard, Sir;
An honeſt Gentleman, and a neighbour here;
Their ends you underſtand better then I, ſure.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Now I know him.
Know him now plain.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: I have diſcharg'd my Colours; ſo God by ye, ſir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What a purblinde Puppy was I; now I remember him.
All the whole caſt on's face, though 'twere umber'd,
And mask'd with patches: what a dunder-whelp
To let him domineer thus: how he ſtrutted,
And what a load of Lord he clapt upon him?
Would I had him here again, I would ſo bounce him,
I would ſo thank his Lordſhip for his lewd plot:
Do they think to carry it away, with a great band made of bird-pots.
And a pair of pin-buttockt breeches? Ha! 'Tis he again
He comes, he comes, he comes; have at him. Enter De-Gard, Oriana, &c.

sp.speaker: Sings.
sp.l: My Savoy Lord, why doſt thou frown on me?
And will that favour never ſweeter be?
