Wilt thou I ſay, for ever play the fool?
De-Gard, be wiſe, and Savoy go to School.
My Lord De-Gard, I thank ye for your Antick,
My Lady bright, that will be ſometime Frantick;
You worthy Train, that wait upon this Pair,
'Send you more wit, and they a bouncing Baire;
And ſo I take my humble leave of your honors. Exit.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: We are diſcover'd, there's no remedy;
Lelia, Biancha's man upon my life,
In ſtubbornneſs, becauſe Lugier corrected him.
(A ſhameleſs Slaves-plague on him for a Raſcal.)

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I was in a perfect hope; the bane on't is now;
He will make mirth on mirth, to perſecute us.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: We muſt be patient; I am vext to the proof too.
I'll try once more; then if I fail: Hear's one ſpeaks.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Let me be loſt, and ſcorn'd firſt.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: Well, we'll conſider.
Away, and let me ſhift; I ſhall be hooted elſe. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaen. 1.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: FAint not; but do as I direct ye, truſt me;
Beleeve me too, for what I have told ye, (Lady)
As true as you are Lelia, is Authentick;
I know it; I have found it; 'tis a poor courage
Flies off for one repulſe; theſe Travellers
Shall finde before we have done, a home-ſpun wit,
A plain French underſtanding may cope with 'em;
They have had the better yet, thank your ſweet Squire, here;
And let 'em brag: You would be reveng'd?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Yes ſurely.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: And married too?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I think ſo.

sp.speaker: Leug.
sp.l: Then be Counſel'd;
You know how to proceed: I have other Irons
Heating as well as yours: and I will ſtrike
Three blowes with one Stone home, be rul'd, and hapie;
And ſo I leave yee. Now is the time.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I am ready.
If he doe come to do me.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Will ye ſtand here,
And let the people think, ye are God knows what, Miſtris;
Let Boyes, and Prentizes preſume upon ye.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Pre'thee hold thy peace.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Stand at his dore, that hates ye?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Pre'thee leave prating.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Pray ye goe to th' Tavern. Ile give ye a Pint of wine there;
If any of the Mad-cap Gentlemen ſhould come by
That take up women upon ſpeciall warrant,
You were in a wiſe caſe now.

div.stage: Enter, Mirabell, Pinac, Mariana, Prieſt, Attendants.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Give me the Garland,
And wait you here.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: She is here to ſeeke thee, Sirrah.
I told thee what would follow; ſhe is mad, for thee;
Shew, and advance. So early ſtirring Lady,
It ſhewes a buſie mind, a fancie troubled:
A willowgh Garland too. Is't poſſible,
'Tis pitty ſo much Beautie ſhould lie muſtie,
But 'tis not to be help'd now.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: The more's my Miſerie
Good fortune to ye (Ladie) you deſerve it:
To me: too late Repentance; I have ſought it:
I doe not envy, though I greive a little,
You are Miſtris of that happines, thoſe Joyes
That might have bin, had I bin wiſe: but fortune.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: She underſtands ye not, 'pray ye doe not trouble her;
And do not croſſe me like a Hare thus, 'tis as ominous.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I come not to upbraid, your Levitie
Though ye made ſhew of Love, and though I lik'd ye
To claime an Intereſt; we are yet both Strangers,
But what we might have bin, had you perſever'd, Sir,
To be an eye-ſore to your loving Lady;
This garland ſhewes, I give my ſelf forſaken;
(Yet She muſt pardon me, 'tis moſt unwillingly:)
And all the power and intereſt I had in ye?
As I perſwade my ſelf, ſomewhat ye Lov'd me;
Thus patiently I render up, I offer
To her that muſt enjoy ye: and ſo bleſſe ye;
Onely, I heartily deſire this Courteſie,
And would not be denide: to wait upon ye
This day, to ſee ye tide, then no more trouble ye.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: It need not, Ladie.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Good, Sir, grant me ſo much.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: 'Tis privat, and we make no Invitation.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: My preſence, ſir, ſhall not proclaim it publick.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: May be 'tis not in Town.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I have a Coach, ſir.
And a moſt ready will to do you ſervice.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Strike now or never; make it ſure: I tell thee,
She will hang her ſelf; if ſhe have thee not.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: 'Pray ye, ſir,
Entertain my noble miſtris: onely a word or two
With this importunate woman, and I'll relieve ye.
Now ye ſee what your flings are, and your fancies,
Your States, and your wild ſtubbornes, now ye finde
What 'tis to gird and kick at mens fair ſervices,
To raiſe your pride to ſuch a pitch, and glory
That goodneſs ſhews like Gnats, ſcorn'd under ye,
'Tis ugly, naught, a ſelf-will in a woman,
Chain'd to an over-weening thought, is Peſtilent,
Murthers fair Fortune firſt; Then fair opinion?
There ſtands a Patern, a true patient Patern,
Humble, and ſweet.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I can but grieve my ignorance.
Repentance ſome ſay too, is the beſt Sacrifice;
For ſure, Sir, if my chance had been ſo happy,
(As I confeſs I was mine own deſtroyer)
As to have arrived at you; I will not propheſie,
But certain, as I think, I ſhould have pleas'd ye;
Have made ye as much wonder at my curteſie,
My love, and duty, as I have diſhearten'd ye,
Some hours we have of youth, and ſome of folly;
And being free-born Maides, we take a liberty,
And to maintain that, ſometimes we ſtrain highly.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Now ye talk reaſon.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: But being yoak'd, and govern'd,
Married, and thoſe light vanities purg'd from us;
How fair we grow, how gentle, and how tender
We twine about thoſe loves that ſhoot-up with us?
A ſullen woman fear, that talks not to ye;
She has a ſad and darkn'd ſoul, loves dully:
A merry and a free wench, give her liberty;
Beleeve her in the lighteſt form ſhe appears to ye;
Beleeve her excellent, though ſhe deſpiſe ye;
Let but theſe fits and flaſhes paſs, ſhe will ſhew to ye;
As Jewels rub'd from duſt, or Gold new burniſh'd:
Such had I been, had you beleev'd.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Is't poſſible.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: And to your happineſs, I dare aſſure ye
If True love be accounted ſo; your pleaſure,
Your will, and your command had tyed my Motions:
But that hopes gone; I know you are young, and giddy,
And till you have a Wife can govern with ye,
You ſaile upon this world-Sea, light and empty;
Your Bark in danger daily; 'tis not the name neither
Of Wife can ſteer ye; but the noble nature,
The dilligence, the Care, the Love, the Patience,
She makes the Pilat, and preſerves the Husband,
That knowes, and reckons every Ribb, he is built on;
But this I tell ye, to my ſhame.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I admire ye,
And now am ſorry, that I ayme beyond ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: So, ſo, ſo: faire and ſoftly. She is thine own (Boy)
She comes now, without Lure.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: But that it muſt needes
Be reckon'd to me as a wantonneſſe,
Or worſſe, a Madneſſe, to forſake a Bleſſing,
A Bleſſing of that hope.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I dare not urge ye;
And yet deare, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt certain, I had rather,
If 'twere in mine owne Choice, for you are my Country-woman,
A Neighbour here borne by me, She a Stranger;
And who knowes how her Friends?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Doe as you pleaſe, Sir,
If ye be faſt: not all the world: I love ye,
'Tis moſt true: and cleer, I would perſwade ye;
And I ſhall love ye ſtill.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Goe, • et before me:
So much ye have won upon me: doe it preſently:
Here's a Preiſt ready: Ile have you.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: not now, Sir,
No, you ſhall pardon me: advance your Lady,
I dare not hinder your moſt high preferment,
'Tis honor enough for me, I have unmask'd ye.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: How's that.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I have caught ye, Sir; alas, I am no States-woman,
Nor no great Traveller, yet I have found ye,
I have found your Lady too: your beauteous Lady;
I have found her Birth, and Breeding too: her diſciplin:
Who brought her over, and who kept your Lady:
And when he laid her by, what vertuous Nunnery
Received her in: I have found all theſe: are ye blanck now,
Methinks ſuch travel'd wiſdomes ſhould not foole thus:
Such excellent Indiſcretions.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How could ſhe know this?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: 'Tis true ſhe is Engliſh borne: but moſt part French now,
And ſo I hope you will find her, to your comfort,
Alas, I am ignorant of what, She coſt ye:
The price of theſe hired Clothes I doe not know Gentlemen;
Thoſe Jewells are the Broakers, how ye ſtand bound for 'em.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Will you make this good?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Yes, yes, and to her face, Sir,
That ſhe is an Engliſh whore, a kind of fling duſt
One of your London Light o'Loves: a right one,
Came over in thin Pumps; and half a Petcicote,
One faith, and one Smock, with a broken Haberdaſher;
I know all this, without a Conjurer:
Her name is Jumping-Jone, an ancient Sin-Weaver;
She was firſt a Ladies Chamber-maid, there ſlip'd
And broke her leg above the knee: departed
And ſet up ſhop her ſelf. Stood the fierce Conflicts
Of many a furious Tearme; there loſt her Colours,
And laſt ſhipt over hither.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: We are betray'd.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Doe you come to fright me with this Miſterie?
To ſtirre me with a ſtink none can endure, Sir?
I pray ye proceed, the Wedding will becom ye,
Who gives the Lady? you? an excellent Father:
A carefull man, and one that knows a Beautie,
'Send ye faire ſhipping, Sir, and ſo Ile leave ye;
Be wiſe and manly, then I may chance to love ye. —Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: As I live I am aſham'd, this wench has reach'd me,
Monſtrous aſham'd, but there's no remedie,
This skew'd-eyde Carren.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: This I ſuſpected ever,
Come, Come, uncaſe, we have no more uſe of ye;
Your Clothes, muſt back againe.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Sir, ye ſhall pardon me:
'Tis not our Engliſh uſe to be degraded:
If you will viſit me and take your venture,
You ſhall have pleaſure for your properties;
And ſo ſweet heart.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Let her goe, and the Devill goe with her:
We have never better luck with theſe preludiums:
Come, be not daunted: think ſhe is but a woman,
And let her have the devills witt, wee'll reach her. —Exit.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ye have now redeem'd my good opinion (Tutor)
And ye ſtand faire again.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: I can but labour,
And ſweat in your Affaires: I am ſure Bellure:
Wilbe here inſtantly, and uſe his Anger
His wonted harſhneſs.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I hope he will not beate me.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: No ſure; he has more manners: be you ready.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes, yes, I am: and am reſolv'd to fit him,
With patience to out-doe all he can offer;
But how do's Oriana?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Worſe, and worſe ſtill:
There is a ſad houſe for her: ſhe is now
Poore Ladie, utterly diſtracted.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Pittie:
Infinite pittie: 'tis a handſom Ladie,
That Mirabel's a Beaſt, worſe then a Monſter.
If this affliction work not.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Are ye readie?
Bellure is comming on, here, hard behind me,
I have no leyſure to relate my Fortune.
Onely I wiſh you may come off as handſomely,
Upon the ſign you know what. Exit.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Well, well, leave me, Enter Bellure.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: How now?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ye are welcome, ſir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Tis well ye have manners:
That Curt'ſy again, and hold your Countenance ſtaidly;
That looks too light; take heed: ſo, ſit ye down now,
And to confirm me that your gall is gone,
Your bitterneſs diſpers'd, for ſo I'll have it;
Look on me ſtedfaſtly; and whatſoe'er I ſay to ye,
Move not, nor alter in your face, ye are gon then;
For if you do expreſs the leaſt diſtaſte,
Or ſhew an angry wrinkle; mark me, woman,
We are now alone, I will ſo conjure thee:
The third part of my Execution
Cannot be ſpoke.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I am at your diſpoſe, ſir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Now riſe, and woo me a little, let me hear that faculty;
But touch me not; nor do not lie, I charge ye.
Begin now.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: If ſo mean and poor a Beauty
May ever hope the grace.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Ye Cog, ye flatter
Like a lew'd thing, ye lie: may hope that grace?
Why, what grace canſt thou hope for? Anſwer not,
For if thou doſt, and lyeſt again, I'll ſwindge thee;
Do not I know thee, for a peſtilent woman?
A proud at both ends? Be not angry;
Nor ſtir not o' your life?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I am counſeld, ſir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Art thou not now, (confeſs, for I'll have the truth out)
As much unworthy of a man of merit,
Or any of ye all? Nay of meer man?
Though he were crooked, cold, all wants upon him;
Nay of any diſhoneſt thing, that bears that figure;
As Devils are of mercy?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We are unworthy.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Stick to that truth, and it may chance to ſave thee;
And is it not our bounty that we take ye?
That we are troubled, vex'd, or tortur'd with ye?
Our meer, and ſpecial bounty?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Our pitty,
That for your wickedneſs we ſwindge ye ſoundly;
Your ſtubbornneſs and ſtout hearts, we be-labour ye?
Anſwer, to that?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I do confeſs your pitty.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: And doſt not thou deſerve in thine own perſon?
(Thou Impudent, thou Pert; do not change countenanance?)

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I dare not, ſir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: For if ye do.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I am ſetled.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Thou Wag-tail, Peacock, Puppy; look on me:
I am a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: It ſeems no leſs, ſir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: And dareſt thou in thy Surquedry?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I beſeech ye.
It was my weakneſs, ſir; I did not view ye;
I took not notice of your noble parts;
Nor call'd your perſon, nor your proper faſhion.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: This is ſome amendes yet.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I ſhall mend, ſir, daily.
And ſtudy to deſerve.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Come a little neerer:
Canſt thou repent thy Villany?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Moſt ſeriouſly.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: And be aſham'd?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I am aſham'd.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Cry.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: It will be hard to do, ſir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Cry now inſtantly;
Cry monſtrouſly, that all the Town may hear thee;
Cry ſeriouſly; as if thou hadſt loſt thy Monkey;
And as I like thy Tears. Enter Lilia and four women laughing.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Now.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: How? How? do ye jear me?
Have ye broke your bounds again Dame?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes, and laugh at ye;
And laugh moſt heartily.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: What are theſe, Whirl-winds?
Is Hell broke looſe, and all the Furies flutter'd?
Am I greas'd once again?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes indeed are ye;
And once again ye ſhall be, if ye quarrel:
Do you come to vent your fury on a Virgin?
Is this your manhood, ſir?

sp.speaker: 1. VVo.
sp.l: Let him do his beſt:
Let's ſee the utmoſt of his indignation:
I long to ſee him angry: come, proceed, ſir.
Hang him, he dares not ſtir; a man of Timber.

sp.speaker: 2. Wo.
sp.l: Come hither to fright Maids, with thy Bul-faces?
To threaten Gentlewomen? Thou a man? A May-pole.
A great dry Pudding.

sp.speaker: 3. Wo.
sp.l: Come, come, do your worſt, ſir;
Be angry if thou dar'ſt.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: The Lord deliver me.

sp.speaker: 4. Wo.
sp.l: Do but look ſcurvily upon this Lady,
Or give us one foul word. We are all miſtaken;
This is ſome mighty Dairy-Maid in mans clothes.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: I am of that minde too.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: What will they do to me?

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: And hired to come and abuſe us; a man has manners;
A Gentleman, Civility, and Breeding:
Some Tinkers Trull with a beard glew'd on.

sp.speaker: 1. VVo.
sp.l: Let's ſearch him;
And as we finde him.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Let me but depart from ye,
Sweet Chriſtian women.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Hear the Thing ſpeak, Neighbours.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Tis but a ſmall requeſt: if ere I trouble ye,
If ere I talk again of beating Women,
Or beating any thing that can but turn to me;
Of ever thinking of a handſom Lady
But vertuouſly and well: of ever ſpeaking
But to her honor: This I'le promiſe ye,
I will take Rhubarb; and purge Choler mainly,
Abundantly Ile purge.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Ile ſend ye Brothes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I will be laugh'd at, and endure it patiently,
I will doe any thing.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ile be your Bayle then:
When ye com next to woo, 'pray ye com not boiſtrouſly
And furniſh'd like a Bear-ward.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No in truth, forſooth.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I ſented ye long ſince.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I was to blame, ſure;
I will appear a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: 'Tis the beſt for ye,
For a true noble Gentleman's a brave thing;
Upon that hope we quit ye: You fear ſeriouſly?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Yes truly do I; I confeſs I fear ye,
And honor ye, and any thing.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Farewel then.

sp.speaker: Wo.
sp.p: And when ye come to woo next bring more mercy. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: A Dary-Maid? A Tinkers-Trull: Heaven bleſs me:
Sure if I had provok'd 'em, they had quarter'd me. Enter two Gentlemen.
I am a moſt ridiculous Aſs, now I perceive it:
A Coward, and a Knave too.

sp.speaker: 1. Gen.
sp.l: 'Tis the mad Gentleman.
Let's ſet our Faces right.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No, no, laugh at me;
And laugh aloud.

sp.speaker: 2. Gen.
sp.l: We are better manner'd, ſir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I do deſerve it; call me Patch, and Puppy,
And beat me if you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: 1. Gen.
sp.l: No indeed: We know ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Death, do as I would have ye.

sp.speaker: 2. Gen.
sp.l: Ye are an Aſs then;
A Coxcomb, and a Calf.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I am a great Calf:
Kick me a little now: Why, when? Sufficient:
Now laugh aloud, and ſcorn me; ſo good buy'ye;
And ever when ye meet me laugh.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: We will, ſir. Exeunt.

div.head: SCAEN. 3.
div.stage: Enter Nantolet, la-Caſtre, de-Gard, Lugier, Mirabell.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Your Patience, Gentlemen; why do ye bait me?

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.l: Is't not a ſhame you are ſo ſtubborn-hearted,
So ſtony and ſo dull to ſuch a Lady,
Of her Perfections, and her Miſery?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Does ſhe not love ye? does not her diſtraction
For your ſake only, her moſt pityed Lunacie
Of all but you, ſhew ye? does it not compell ye?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Soft and fair, Gentlemen, pray ye proceed temperately.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: If ye have any feeling, any ſenſe in ye,
The leaſt touch of a noble heart.

sp.speaker: le-Caſt.
sp.l: Let him alone;
It is his glory that he can kill Beauty,
Ye bear my Stamp, but not my Tenderneſs;
Your wild unſavoury Courſes ſet that in ye!
For ſhame be ſorry, though ye cannot Cure her,
Shew ſomething of a Man, of a fair Nature.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ye make me Mad.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: Let me pronounce this to ye,
You take a ſtrange felicity in ſlighting
And wronging Women; which my poor ſiſter feels now,
Heavens hand be gentle on her: Mark me, Sir,
That very hour ſhe dyes; there's ſmall hope otherwiſe,
That minute you and I muſt grapple for it;
Either your life or mine.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Be not ſo hot, Sir,
I am not to be wrought on by theſe Policies;
In truth I am not; Nor do I fear the Tricks,
Or the high ſounding Threats of a Savoyen:
I glory not in Cruelty; ye wrong me;
Nor grow up water'd with the Tears of Women;
This let me tell ye, howſoe're I ſhew to ye
Wilde, as you pleaſe to call it; or ſelf-will'd;
When I ſee cauſe, I can both doe, and ſuffer, Enter Roſaluce & Lelia.
Freely, and feelingly, as a true Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: O pity, pity; thouſand thouſand pities!

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Alas, poor ſoul! ſhe will die; ſhe is grown ſenſleſs;
She will not know, nor ſpeak now.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Die for Love,
And Love of ſuch a Youth? I would die for a Dog, firſt.
He that kils me, Ile give him leave to eat me;
Ile know men better ere I ſigh for any of 'em.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Ye have don a worthy act, Sir; a moſt famous;
Ye have kild a Maid the wrong way; ye are a conqueror.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: A Conqueror? a Cobler; hang him Sowter;
Goe hid thy ſelf for ſhame; go loſe thy Memory;
Live not 'mongſt Men; thou art a Beaſt, a Monſter;
A Blatant Beaſt.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: If ye have yet any honeſtie,
Or ever heard of any; take my Counſell;
Off with your Garters; and ſeek out a Bough,
A handſom Bough; (for I would have ye hang like a Gentleman;)
And write ſome dolefull matter to the world,
A warning to hard-hearted men.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Out Kitlings:
What Catterwalling's here? what gibbing?
Do you think my heart is ſoftned with a black Santis;
Shew me ſome Reaſon. Enter Oriana on a bed.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Here then, here is a reaſon.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: Now, if ye be a man, let this ſight ſhake ye.

sp.speaker: la-C.
sp.l: Alas poor Gentlewoman! do ye know me Lady?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: How ſhe looks up and ſtares.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I know ye very well:
You are my Godfather; and that's the Monſieur.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: And who am I?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: You are Amadis de Gaule, Sir.
Oh, oh, my heart! were you never in love, ſweet Lady?
And do you never dream of Flowres and Gardens;
I dream of walking Fires: take heed, It comes now,
Who's that? pray ſtand away; I have ſeen that face ſure;
How light my head is.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Take ſome reſt.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I cannot.
For I muſt be up to morrow, to go to Church:
And I muſt dreſs me, put my new Gown on,
And be as fine to meet my Love: Heig ho!
Will not you tell me where my Love lies buried?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: He is not dead: beſhrew my heart ſhe ſtirs me.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: He is dead to me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Is't poſſible my Nature
Should be ſo dampnable, to let her ſuffer;
Give me your hand.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: How ſoft you feel; how gentle?
Ile tell ye your fortune, Friend.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How ſhe ſtares on me?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: You have a flattring face; but 'tis a fine one;
I warrant you may have a hundred Sweet-hearts:
Will ye pray for me? I ſhall die to morrow;
And will ye ring the Bells?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I am moſt unworthy;
I doe confeſs unhappy; doe you know me?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I would I did.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Oh fair tears; how ye take me.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Do you weep too? you have not loſt your Lover?
You mock me: Ile go home and pray.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Pray ye pardon me:
Or if it pleaſe ye to conſider juſtly,
Scorn me; for I deſerve it: Scorn, and ſhame me:
Sweet Oriana.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Let her alone; ſhe trembles.
Her fits will grow more ſtrong, if ye provoke her;

sp.speaker: Ca-Laſt.
sp.l: Certain ſhe knowes ye not, yet loves to ſee ye
How ſhe ſmiles now:

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Where are ye? oh, why doe not ye laugh: come laugh at me;
Why a devill, art thou ſad, and ſuch a ſubject,
Such a ridiculous ſubject, as I am
Before thy face?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Pre'thee put off this Lightnes,
This is no time for mirth, nor place: I have us'd too much on't:
I have undon my ſelf and a ſweet Ladie,
By being too Indulgent to my Foolery
Which truly I repent: looke here.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: What ayles ſhe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Alas ſhe is mad.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Mad.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, too ſure for me too.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Doſt thou wonder at that? by this good light, they are all ſo;
They are coz'ning mad, they are brawling mad, they are proud mad.
They are all, all mad: I came from a world of mad women,
Mad as march Haires: get 'em in Chaines, then deale with 'em.
There's one that's mad: ſhe ſeemes well, but ſhe is dog mad:
Is ſhe dead, do'ſt think?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Dead? heaven forbid.

sp.speaker: Bel
sp.l: Heaven further it.
For till they be key-cold dead, there's no truſting of 'em
What ere they ſeeme, or howſoere they carry it,
Till they be chap-falne, and their Tongues at peace,
Nayl'd in their Coffins ſure, Ile ne're beleeve 'em,
Shall I talk with her.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, deer friend, be quiet;
And be at peace a while.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Ile walk a ſide,
And come again anon: But take heed to her
You ſay ſhe is a woman?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Take great heed:
For if ſhe doe not Cozen thee, then hang me:
Let her be mad, or what ſhe will, ſhee'll cheate thee —Exit

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Away wild Foole: how vild this ſhewes in him now?
Now take my faith, before ye all I ſpeake it,
And with it, my repentant Love.

sp.speaker: La-Caſt.
sp.l: This ſeemes well.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Were but this Lady cleere again, whoſe ſorrowes
My very hart melts for; were ſhe but perfect
(For thus to marry her, would be two Miſeries,)
Before the riſheſt, and the nobleſt Beautie,
France, or the world could ſhew me; I would take her
As ſhe is now, my Teares, and praires ſhall wed her.

sp.speaker: de-Ga.
sp.l: This makes ſome ſmall amends.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: She beckens to ye.
To us too, to goe off.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: Let's draw aſide all.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh my beſt friend: I would faine.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What? ſhe ſpeakes well,
And with another voice.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: But I am fearfull,
And ſhame a little, ſtops my tongue.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Speake boldly.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Tell ye, I am well, I am perfect well. 'pray ye mock not;
And that I did this to provoke your Nature,
Out of my infinite, and reſtles Love,
To win your pitty: pardon me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Goe forward;
Who ſet ye on?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: None, as I live, no Creature.
Not any knew, or ever dreamt, what I meant:
Will ye be mine?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis true, I pittie ye;
But when I marry ye, ye muſt be wiſer;
Nothing but Tricks? deviſes?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Will ye ſhame me?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, marry will I: Come neer, Come neer, a Miracle,
The Womans well: ſhe was only mad for Mariage,
Stark mad to be ſton'd to death; give her good Councel,
Will this world never mend? are ye caught, Damſell?

div.stage: Enter Bellure, la. Caſtre, Lugier, Nantolet, de-Gard, Roſaluce, Bianth.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: How goes it now?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou art a kind of Prophet,
The woman's well again; and would have gull'd me,
Well, excellent well: and not a Taynt upon her.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Did not I tell ye? Let'em be what can be;
Saints, Devills, any thing, they will abuſe us;
Thou wert an Aſſe to beleeve her ſo long: a Coxcomb;
Give 'em a minute, they'll abuſe whole Millions.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And am not I a rare Phiſitian, Gentlemen?
That can cure deſperate mad Mindes?

sp.speaker: de-Ga.
sp.l: Be not inſolent.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Well, goe thy waies: from this howre, I diſclame thee,
Unles thou haſt a Trick above this: then Ile love thee.
Ye owe me for your Cure; pray have a Care of her,
For fear ſhe fall into Relaps; Come Bellure
We'll ſet up Bills, to Cure diſeaſed virgins.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Shall we be merry?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: But Ile no more projects;
If we could make 'em mad, it were ſome Maſtery. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: I am glad ſhe is well again.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: So am I, certain
Be not aſhamed.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I ſhall never ſee a man more.

sp.speaker: de-G.
sp.l: Come ye are afoole: had ye but told me this Trick,
He ſhould not have gloried thus.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: He ſhall not long neither.

sp.speaker: la-Caſt.
sp.l: Be rul'd, and be at peace: ye have my Conſent,
And what powre I can work with.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: Come, leave bluſhing;
We are your Friends; an honeſt way compell'd ye;
Heaven will not ſee ſo true a love unrecompenc'd;
Come in, and ſlight him too.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: The next ſhall hit him. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: 'TWill be diſcover'd.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: That's the worſt can happen:
If there be any way, to reach, and work upon him;
Upon his nature ſuddenly, and catch him: That he loves,
Though he diſſemble it, and would ſhew contrary,
And will at length relent: I'll lay my Fortune,
Nay more, my life.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: Is ſhe won?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Yes, and ready,
And my deſignments ſet.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: They are now for Travel,
All for that Game again: they have forgot wooing.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Let 'em; we'll travel with 'em.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: Where's his Father?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Within; he knows my minde too, and allows it;
Pitties your Siſters Fortune moſt ſincerely;
And has appointed, for our more aſſiſtance,
Some of his ſecret Friends.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: 'Speed the plowgh.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Well ſaid;
And be you ſerious too.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: I ſhall be diligent.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Let's break the Ice for one, the reſt will drink too
(Beleeve me, ſir) of the ſame Cup; my young Gentlewomen
Wait but who ſets the Game a foot; though they ſeem 'ſtubborn,
Reſerv'd, and proud now, yet I know their hearts,
Their pulſes, how they heat, and for what cauſe, Sir;
And how they long to venture their Abilities
In a true Quarrel; Husbands they muſt, and will have,
Or Nunneries, and thin Collations
To cool their bloods; Let's all about our buſineſs,
And if this faile, let Nature work.

sp.speaker: De-G.
sp.l: Ye have arm'd me. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: La Caſt.
sp.l: Will ye be wilful then?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Pray, ſir, your pardon,
For I muſt Travel: lie lazy here;
Bound to a Wife; Chain'd to her ſubtleties,
Her humors, and her wills, which are meer Fetters;
To have her today pleas'd, to morrow peeviſh,
The third day mad, the fourth rebellious;
You ſee, before they are married, what Moriſcoes,
What Maſques, and Mummeries they put upon us,
To be ty'd here, and ſuffer their Lavalto's?

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.l: 'Tis your own ſeeking.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, to get my freedom;
Were they as I could wiſh 'em.

sp.speaker: la-Caſt.
sp.l: Fools, and Meacocks,
To endure what you think fit to put upon 'em:
Come, change your minde.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Not before I have chang'd air (Father)
When I know women worthy of my company,
I will return again and wait upon 'em;
Till then (dear Sir) I'll amble all the world over,
And run all hazards, miſery, and poverty, Enter Pinac & Bellure.
So I eſcape the dangerous Bay of Matrimony.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Are ye reſolv'd?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes certain; I will out again.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: We are for ye, ſir; we are your ſervants once more;
Once more we'll ſeek our fortune in ſtrange Countries;
Ours is too ſcornful for us.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Is there ne'er a Land
That ye have read, or head of, (for I care not how far it be,
Nor under what Peſtiferous Star it lies)
A happy Kingdom, where there are no Women?
Nor have been ever? Nor no mention
Of any ſuch lewd Things, with lewder qualities?
For thether would I Travel; where 'tis Fellony
To confeſs he had a Mother: a Miſtris, Treaſon?

sp.speaker: la-Caſt.
sp.l: Are you for Travel too?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: For any thing;
For living in the Moon, and ſtopping hedges,
E'er I ſtay here to be abus'd, and baffell'd.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: Why did ye not break your minds to me? They are my daughters;
And ſure I think I ſhould have that command over 'em?
To ſee 'em well beſtow'd: I know ye are Gentlemen,
Men of fair Parts and States; I know your Parents;
And had ye told me of your fair Affections:
Make but one Tryal more; and let me ſecond ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No I'll make Hob-nailes firſt, and mend old Kettles:
Can ye lend me an Armor of high proof, to appear in,
And two or three field pieces to defend me?
The Kings Guard are meer Pigmeys.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: They will not eat ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Yes, and you too, and twenty fatter Monſieurs,
If their high ſtomacks hold: They came with Chopping-knives,
To cut me into Rands, and Surloyns, and ſo powder me.
Come, ſhall we go?

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: You cannot be ſo diſcurteous
(If ye intend to go) as not to viſit 'em,
And take your leaves.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That we dare do, and civilly,
And thank 'em too.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Yes, ſir, we know that honeſty.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'll come i'th Rear, forty foot off, I'll aſſure ye,
With a good Gun in my hand; I'll no more Amazous,
I mean, no more of their frights; I'll make my three legs,
Kiſs my hand twice; and if I ſmell no danger;
If the enterview be clear, may be I'll ſpeak to her;
I'll ware a privy coat too; and behind me,
To make thoſe parts ſecure, a Bandog.

sp.speaker: la-Caſt.
sp.l: You are a merry Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: A wary Gentleman; I do aſſure ye,
I Have been warn'd, and muſt be arm'd.

sp.speaker: la-Caſt.
sp.l: Well, Son,
Theſe are your haſty thoughts, when I ſee you are bent to it,
Then I'll beleeve, and joyn with ye; So we'll leave ye:
There's a Trick will make ye ſtay.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: I hope ſo. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: We have won immortal Fame now, if we leave 'em.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: You have, but we have loſt.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Pinac, Thou art cozen'd;
I know they Love ye; and to gain ye handſomly,
Not to be thought to yeeld, they would give millions;
Their Fathers willingneſs, that muſt needs ſhew ye.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: If I thought ſo.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ye ſhall be hang'd, ye Recreant,
Would ye turn Renegado no?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No lets away, Boyes,
Out of the Air, and tumult of their Villanies;
Though I were married to that Graſhopper,
And had her faſt by th' legs I ſhould think ſhe would cozen me.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.p: Monſieur Mirabel, I take it? Enter a young Factor.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Y'are ith' right, ſir.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: I am come to ſeek ye, ſir; I have been at your Fathers,
And underſtanding you were here.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ye are welcome:
May I crave your name?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Foſſe, Sir, and your ſervant;
That you may know me better; I am Factor
To your old Merchant, Levordare.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How do's he?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Well, ſir, I hope: he is now at Orleance,
About ſome buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You are once more welcom.
Your Maſter's a right honeſt man; and one
I am much beholding too, and muſt very ſhortly
Trouble his love again.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: You may be bold, ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Your buſineſs if you pleaſe now?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: This it is, ſir.
I know ye well remember in your Travel
A Genea Merchant.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I remember many.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: But this man, ſir, particularly; your own benefit
Muſt needs imprint him in ye: one Alberto;
A Gentleman you ſav'd from being Murther'd
A little from Bollonia,
I was then myſelf in Italie, and ſupplide ye,
Though happely, you have forgot me now.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, I remember ye,
And that Alberto too: a noble Gentleman:
More to remember, were to thanck myſelf, Sir.
What of that Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: He is dead:

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I am ſorry.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: But on his death bed, leaving to his Siſter.
All that he had beſide ſome Certaine Jewells,
Which with a Ceremony, he bequeathd to you,
In gratefull memory: he commanded ſtrictly
His Siſter, as ſhe lov'd him and his peace,
To ſee thoſe Jewells ſafe, and true deliverd;
And with them, his laſt Love. She, as tender
To obſerve this wil, not truſting friend, nor Servant,
With ſuch a weight, is come her ſelf to Paris
And at my Maſters Houſe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You tell me a wonder.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: I tell ye a truth, Sir: She is young, and handſom,
And well attended: of much State, and Riches;
So loving, and obedient to her Brother;
That on my Conſcience, if he had given her alſo,
She would moſt willingly have made her tender.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: May not I ſee her?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: She deſires it hartily.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And preſently?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: She is now about ſome Buſineſs,
Paſſing Accompts of ſome few debts here owing,
And buying Jewells of a Merchant,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Is ſhe wealthie.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: I would ye had her, Sir, at all adventure.
Her Brother had, a main State.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And faire too?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: The prime of all thoſe parts of Italie,
For Beautie, and for Curteſie.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I muſt needs ſee her.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: 'Tis all her Buſineſs, Sir. Ye may now ſee her,
But to morrow will be fitter for your viſitation;
For ſhe is not yet prepared.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Onely, her ſight, Sir.
And when you ſhall think fit for further viſit.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Sir, ye may ſee her; and Ile wayt your Coming.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And Ile be with ye inſtantly. I know the houſe,
Mean time, my love, and thanks, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Your poore Servant —Exit.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.p: Thou haſt the ſtrangeſt Luck: What was that Alberto?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: An honeſt noble Marchant, 'twas my chance
To reſcue from ſome Rogues had almoſt ſlain him;
And he in kindneſs to remember this.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Now we ſhall have you:
For all your proteſtations, and your forwardneſs,
Finde out ſtrange Fortunes in this Ladies eyes,
And new entirements to put off your journey;
And who ſhall have honor then?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, no, never fear it:
I muſt needs ſee her, to receive my Legacy.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: If it be tide up in her ſmock, Heaven help thee:
May not we ſee too?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, afore we go:
I muſt be known my ſelf e'er I be able
To make thou welcom: wouldſt thou ſee more women?
I thought you had been out of love with all:

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I may be,
I finde that with the leaſt encouragement,
Yet I deſire to ſee whether all Countries
Are naturally poſſeſs'd with the ſame ſpirits;
For if they be, I'll take a Monaſtery,
And never Travel; for I had rather be a Frier,
And live mewed up, then be a fool and flouted.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Well, well, I'll meet ye anon; then tell you more, Boys;
How e'er, ſtand prepar'd, preſt for our journey;
For certain, we ſhall go, I think, when I have ſeen her.
And view'd her well.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Go, go, and we'll wait for ye;
Your fortune directs ours.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You ſhall finde us ith' Tavern,
Lamenting in Sack and Suger for our loſſes;
If ſhe be right Italian, and want ſervants,
You may prefer the propereſt man,
How I could worry a woman now?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Come, come, leave prating;
Ye may have enough to do, without this boaſting Exeunt.

div.head: Scaen. 3.
div.stage: Enter Lugier, de-Gard, Roſalu. and Lillia.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: This is the laſt adventure.

sp.speaker: de-G.
sp.l: And the happieſt,
As we hope too.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We ſhould be glad to finde it.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Who ſhall conduct us thither?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Your man is ready.
For I muſt not be ſeen; no, nor this Gentleman;
That may beget ſuſpition: all the reſt
Are people of no doubt; I would have ye, Ladies,
Keep your old liberties, and as we inſtruct ye:
Come, look not pale; you ſhall not loſe your wiſhes;
Nor beg 'em neither: but be your ſelves, and happy.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I tell ye true, I cannot hold off longer,
Nor give no more hard language.

sp.speaker: de-G.
sp.l: You ſhall not need.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I love the Gentleman, and muſt now ſhow it;
Shall I beat a propper man out of heart?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: There's none adviſes ye.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: 'Faith I repent me too.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Repent, and ſpoil all.
Tell what ye know, ye had beſt.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: I'll tell what I think;
For if he ask me now, if I can love him,
I'll tell him yes, I can: The man's a kinde man;
And out of his true honeſty affect me;
Although he plaid the fool, which I required;
Muſt I ſtill hold him at the ſtaves end?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: You are two ſtrange woman.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We may be, if we fool ſtill.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Dare ye beleeve me?
Follow but this advice I have ſet you in now,
And if ye loſe: would ye yeeld now ſo baſely?
Give up without your honors ſaved?

sp.speaker: de-G.
sp.l: Fie, Ladies.
Preſerve your freedom ſtill.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Well, well, for this time.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: And carry that full ſtate.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: That's as the winde ſtands:
If it begin to chop about, and ſcant us;
Hang me, but I know what Ile do: come direct us,
I make no doubt, we ſhall do handſomly.

sp.speaker: de-G.
sp.l: Some part o' th' way, we'll wait upon ye, Ladies;
The reſt your man ſupplies:

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Do well, I'll honor ye. Exeunt.

div.head: SCAEN. 4.
div.stage: Enter Factor and Mirabel, Oriana and two Merchants.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Look ye, Sir, there ſhe is, you ſee how buſie;
Methinks you are infinitely bound to her, for her journey.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How gloriouſly ſhe ſhews? She is a tall woman.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Of a fair Size, ſir. My Maſter not being at home,
I have been ſo out of my wits, to get her company:
I mean, ſir, of her own fair Sex, and faſhion.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A far off, ſhe is moſt fair too.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Neer, moſt Excellent.
At length, I have entreated two fair Ladies,
And happily you know 'em: the young daughters
Of Monſieur Nantolet.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I know 'em well, ſir.
What are thoſe? Jewels?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: All.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: They make a rich ſhew?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: There is a matter of ten thouſand pounds too
Was owing here: you ſee thoſe Merchants with her;
They have brought it in now.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How handſomly her ſhape ſhews?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Thoſe are ſtill neate: your Italians are moſt curious.
Now ſhe looks this way.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: She has a gooly preſence.
How full of curteſie? Well, ſir, I'll leave ye.
And if I may be bold to bring a friend or two;
Good noble Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: No doubt, ye may, ſir.
For you have moſt command.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I have ſeen a wonder. Exit.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Is he gon?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Taken to the utmoſt.
A wonder dwels about him.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: He did not gueſs at me?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: No, be ſecure; ye ſhew another woman.
He is gone to fetch his friends.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Where are the Gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Here, here, now they are come, Enter Roſaluce, Lillia, Servant.
Sit ſtill, and let them ſee ye.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Pray ye, where's my friend, Sir?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: She is within, Ladies, but here's another Gentlewoman;
A ſtranger to this Towne: ſo pleaſe you viſit her,
'Twill be well taken.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Where is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: There, Above; Ladies.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Bleſs me: what Thing is this? two Pinacles,
Upon her pate! Is't not a glode to catch Wood-cocks?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Peace, ye rude, knave.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: What a bouncing Bum ſhe has too?
There's Saile enough for a Carreck.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: What is this Lady?
For as I live, ſhe's a goodly woman.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Gheſs, gheſs.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: I have not ſeen a nobler Preſence.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Tis a luſtie wench: now could I ſpend my forty-pence,
With all my heart, to have but one fling at her;
To give her but a waſhing blow.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Ye Raſcall.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I that's all a man has, for's goodwill: 'twil be long enough,
Before ye cry come Anthonie, and kiſs me.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Ile have ye whipt.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Has my friend ſeen this Lady?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Yes, yes, and is well known to her.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I much admire her Preſence.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Soe do I too:
For I proteſt, ſhe is the handſomeſt,
The rareſt, and the neweſt to mine eie
That ever, I ſaw yet.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I long to know her;
My friend ſhall doe that kindneſs.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: So ſhe ſhall Ladies.
Come, pray ye come up.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: O, me,

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Hang me if I knew her:
Were I a man my ſelf, I ſhould now love ye;
Nay, I ſhould doate.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I dare not, truſt mine eies;
For as I live ye are the ſtrangeſt alter'd
I muſt come up to know the truth.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: So muſt I, Lady;
For I am a kind of unbeleever too.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Get ye gon, Sirrah;
And what ye have ſeen, be ſecret in: you are paid elſe;
No more of your long tongue.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Will ye goe in Ladies,
And talke with her. Theſe venturers will come ſtrait:
Away with this fellow.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: There, Sirrah, goe, diſport ye.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: I would the Trunck-hos'd-woman, would goe with me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Is ſhe ſo glorious handſome?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You would wonder:
Our Women look like Gipſies, like Gills to her:
Their Clothes and faſhions beggerly, and Bankrupt:
Baſe, old, and ſcurvy.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: How lookes her face?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Moſt heavenly:
And the becoming-motion of her Bodie
So ſetts her off.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Why then we ſhall ſtay.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Pardon me:
That's more then I know: if ſhe be that Woman,
She appeares to be.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: As 'tis impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I ſhall then tell ye more.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Did ye ſpeake to her?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, no, I onely ſaw her: She was buſie
Now I goe for that end: And mark her (Gentlemen)
If ſhe appear, not to ye, one of the ſweeteſt,
The handſomeſt: the fayreſt, in behaviour,
We ſhall meet the two wenches there too, they come to viſit her,
To wonder, as we doe.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Then we ſhall meet 'em.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I had rather meet two Beares.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: There you may take your leaves, diſpatch that buſineſs,
And as ye find their humours.

sp.speaker: Pi
sp.l: Is your Love there too?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No certain, ſhe has no great heart to ſet out againe.
This is the houſe, Ile uſher ye?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Ile bleſs me,
And take a good heart if I can:

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Come, nobly Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: They are come in: Sit you two off, as Strangers,
There Ladie: where's the Boy? be readie, Sirrha
And cleere your Pipes, the Muſick now: they enter. Muſick. then Enter Mirabell, Pinac and Bellure.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: What a State ſhe keepes? how far off they ſit, from her?
How rich ſhe is, I marry, this ſhewes bravely.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: She is a luſty wench: and may allure a good man,
But if ſhe have a Tongue, Ile not give two pence for her:
There fits my Fury: how I ſhake to ſee her.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Madam this is the Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Mir,
sp.l: How ſweet ſhe kiſſes?
She has a Spring dwells on her lipps: a paradize
This is the Legacie.
From the honor'd dead I bring
Thus his love and laſt offring.
From a faith &c.
Take it nobly, 'tis your due,
From a friendſhip ever true.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Moſt noble, Sir.
This from my now dead Brother, as his love,
And gratefull memory of your great benefit:
From me my thanks, my wiſhes, and my Service,
Till I am more acquainted I am ſilent,
Onely I dare ſay this, you are truly noble.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What ſhould I think?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Think ye have a handſome fortune,
Would I had ſuch another.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ye are well mett Gentlemen,
We heare ye are for Travell?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Ye heare true, Ladie,
And come to take our Leaves.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Wee'll along with ye,
We ſee you are growne ſo witty by your Journey,
We cannot chooſe but ſtep out too: This Lady,
We mean to wait upon as far as Italy.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'll travel into Wales, amongſt the Mountains;
I hope they cannot finde me.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: If you go further;
So good, and free ſociety we hold ye,
We'll jog along too.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Are ye ſo valiant Lady?

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: And we'll be merry, Sir, and laugh.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: It may be
We'll go by Sea.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Why 'tis the the onely voyage;
I love a Sea-voyage, and a bluſtring Tempeſt;
And let all ſplit.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: This is a dainty Damoſel:
I think 'twill tame ye: can ye ride poſt?

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: 'O excellently: I am never weary that way:
A hundred mile a day is nothing with me.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'll travel under ground: do you hear (ſweet Lady?)
I finde it will be dangerous for a woman.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: No danger, ſir, I warrant; I love to be under.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I ſee ſhe will abuſe me all the world over:
But ſay we paſs through Germany, and drink hard?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We'll learn to drink and ſwagger too.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: She'll beat me.
Lady, I'll live at home.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: And I'll live with thee;
And We'll keep houſe together.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'll keep hounds firſt;
And thoſe I hate right hartily.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I go for Turky,
And ſo it may be up into Perſia.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: We cannot know to much, I'll travel with ye.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: And you'll abuſe me?

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Like enough.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: 'Tis dainty.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I will live in a bawdy-houſe.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I dare come to ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Say, I am diſpos'd to hang my ſelf?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: There I'll leave ye:

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I am glad I know how to avoid ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: May I ſpeak yet?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: She beckons to ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Lady, I could wiſh, I know to recompence,
Even with the ſervice of my life, thoſe paines,
And thoſe high favours you have thrown upon me;
Till I be more deſertful in your eye;
And till my duty ſhall make known I honor ye:
Nobleſt of Women, do me but this favour,
To accept this back again, as a poor teſtimony.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I muſt have you too with 'em; elſe the Will,
That ſays they muſt reſt with ye, is infring'd, ſir,
Which pardon me, I dare not do.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Take me then;
And take me with the trueſt love.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: 'Tis certain,
My Brother lov'd ye dearly, and I ought
As dearly to preſerve that love. But, Sir;
Though I were willing; theſe are but your Ceremonies.

sp.speaker: Mir,
sp.l: As I have life, I ſpeak my ſoul.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I like ye.
But how you can like me, without I have Teſtimony,
A Stranger to ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I'll marry ye immediately.
A fair State, I dare promiſe ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Yet ſhe'll cozen thee.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Would ſome fair Gentlemen durſt promiſe for ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: By all that's good Enter la-Caſtre Nantolet, Lugier, & de-Gard.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: And we'll make up the reſt, Lady.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Then Oriana takes ye; nay, ſhe has caught ye;
If ye ſtart now let all the World cry ſhame on ye:
I have out Travell'd ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: did not I ſay ſhe would cheat thee?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I thank ye, I am pleas'd, ye have deceived me;
And willingly I ſwallow it, and joy in't;
And yet perhaps I know ye: whoſe plot was this?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: He is not aſham'd that caſt it: he that executed
Followed your Fathers will.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What a world's this, nothing but craft, and cozenage?

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Who begun, ſir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Well; I do take thee upon meer Compaſſion;
And I do think, I ſhall love thee. As a Teſtimony,
I'll burn my book, and turn a new leafe over.
But theſe fine clothes you ſhall wear ſtill.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I • obey you, ſir, in all.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: And how! How, daughters! What ſay you to theſe Gentlemen?
What ſay ye, Gentlemen, to the Girles?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: By my troth—if ſhe can love me.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: —How long?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Nay, if once ye love.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Then take me,
And take your chance.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Moſt willingly, ye are mine, Lady:
And if I uſe ye not, that ye may love me.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: A Match y' faith.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Why now ye travel with me.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: How that thing ſtands?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: It will, if ye urge it.
'Bleſs your five wits.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Nay, 'prethe ſtay, I'll have thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You muſt ask me leave firſt.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Wilt thou uſe me kindly;
And beat me but once a week?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: If ye deſerve no more.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: And wilt thou get me with child?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Doſt thou ask me ſeriouſly?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes indeed do I.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Yes, I will get thee with child: Come preſently,
And 't be but in revenge, I'll do thee that curteſie.
Well, if thou wilt fear God, and me; have at thee.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I'll love ye, and I'll honor ye:

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I am pleas'd then.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This Wild-Gooſe-Chaſe is done, we have won o' both ſides.
Brother, your love: and now to Church of all hands;
Let's loſe no time.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Our Travelling, lay by.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No more for Italy; for the Low-Countries,
